To see polynomials in unknown *x*, we have just to replace α by *x*. Since α can generate all nonzero elements of  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 cubed" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 cubed](images/c03_697.png),  <math alttext="StartSet 1 comma alpha comma alpha squared EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#945;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>}</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![StartSet 1 comma alpha comma alpha squared EndSet](images/c03_698.png) is a polynomial basis.

### 3.2.4 Extension Fields

First of all, it is worth noticing that in cryptography,  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c03_699.png) fields are often used. In computers, data is represented as bit strings spanning one or multiple words. For example, a positive integer may be represented as a 64-bits word. Hence, it is of interest to consider fields built over binary set  <math alttext="StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet](images/c03_700.png).

In Example [3.25](#c03.xhtml#c03-mthst-0025), it is shown that  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript 2 cubed" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>&#8484;</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript 2 cubed](images/c03_701.png) is not a finite field under the usual addition and multiplication operations  <math alttext="m o d 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ![m o d 8](images/c03_702.png). In general,  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>&#8484;</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c03_703.png) is not a field under the usual addition and multiplication operations, because even numbers have no multiplicative inverses  <math alttext="m o d 2 Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![m o d 2 Superscript m](images/c03_704.png). Thus, there exist two alternatives: i) use only ℤ[p], with prime *p* or ii) redefine the addition and multiplication operations to make  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c03_705.png) a finite field for any positive integer *m*. It is worth noticing that computations are faster in  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c03_706.png) than in ℤ[p]. For example,  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c03_707.png) uses the XOR bitwise operation, while ℤ[p] makes use of addition  <math alttext="m o d m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![m o d m](images/c03_708.png).

#### *3.2.4.1 Special Case:  <math alttext="upper F 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F 2](images/c03_709.png)*

 <math alttext="upper F 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F 2](images/c03_710.png) field is the smallest field. The set of elements of field  <math alttext="upper F 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F 2](images/c03_711.png) is  <math alttext="StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet](images/c03_712.png).

Addition operation:  <math alttext="0 plus 0 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![0 plus 0 equals 0](images/c03_713.png),  <math alttext="1 plus 0 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![1 plus 0 equals 1](images/c03_714.png),  <math alttext="0 plus 1 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![0 plus 1 equals 1](images/c03_715.png),  <math alttext="1 plus 1 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![1 plus 1 equals 0](images/c03_716.png). Therefore, the addition operation in  <math alttext="upper F 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F 2](images/c03_717.png) is the binary  <math alttext="upper X upper O upper R" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> ![upper X upper O upper R](images/c03_718.png) operation (denoted ⊕).

Multiplication operation:  <math alttext="0 asterisk 0 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![0 asterisk 0 equals 0](images/c03_719.png),  <math alttext="1 asterisk 0 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![1 asterisk 0 equals 0](images/c03_720.png),  <math alttext="0 asterisk 1 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![0 asterisk 1 equals 0](images/c03_721.png),  <math alttext="1 asterisk 1 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![1 asterisk 1 equals 1](images/c03_722.png). Therefore, the multiplication operation in  <math alttext="upper F 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F 2](images/c03_723.png) is the binary  <math alttext="upper A upper N upper D" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>N</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> ![upper A upper N upper D](images/c03_724.png) operation (denoted ∧).

Additive inverse:  <math alttext="1 plus 1 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![1 plus 1 equals 0](images/c03_725.png). Thus, 1 is the additive inverse of 1; and  <math alttext="0 plus 0 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![0 plus 0 equals 0](images/c03_726.png); so, 0 is the additive inverse of 0.

Multiplicative inverse:  <math alttext="1 asterisk 1 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![1 asterisk 1 equals 1](images/c03_727.png). Thus, 1 is the multiplicative inverse of 1. 0 has no multiplicative inverse.

#### *3.2.4.2 Representation and Construction of  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c03_728.png) **Fields***

***Definition 3.40 Binary polynomial***: *a binary polynomial is a polynomial over*  <math alttext="upper F 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F 2](images/c03_729.png)*, i.e. with coefficients in*  <math alttext="StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet](images/c03_730.png).

***Definition 3.41 Binary field****: a field of the form*  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c03_731.png) *is called binary field and it has exactly*  <math alttext="2 Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript m](images/c03_732.png) *elements, which are usually represented as* *m-bit strings*  <math alttext="left-parenthesis a Subscript m minus 1 Baseline a Subscript m minus 2 Baseline ellipsis a 1 a 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8230;</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis a Subscript m minus 1 Baseline a Subscript m minus 2 Baseline ellipsis a 1 a 0 right-parenthesis](images/c03_733.png)*ranging from*  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 000 ellipsis 000 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>000</mn><mo>&#8230;</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 000 ellipsis 000 right-parenthesis](images/c03_734.png) *to*  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 111 ellipsis 111 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>111</mn><mo>&#8230;</mo><mn>111</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 111 ellipsis 111 right-parenthesis](images/c03_735.png).

***Definition 3.42 Polynomial basis of***  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c03_743.png)**:** *the set of polynomials*  <math alttext="StartSet x Superscript m minus 1 Baseline comma x Superscript m minus 2 Baseline comma ellipsis comma x Superscript 1 Baseline comma 1 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet x Superscript m minus 1 Baseline comma x Superscript m minus 2 Baseline comma ellipsis comma x Superscript 1 Baseline comma 1 EndSet](images/c03_744.png) *forms a basis to the field*  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c03_745.png).

***Corollary* 3.3** Existence of binary reduction polynomial: for every field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c03_746.png), there exists at least one polynomial of degree *m* irreducible over  <math alttext="upper F 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F 2](images/c03_747.png).

Corollary 3.3 is a consequence of Theorem 3.18.

#### *3.2.4.3 Generator of Field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c03_770.png)*

By definition 3.38, a primitive polynomial of an extension field  <math alttext="normal upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript normal m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![normal upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript normal m](images/c03_771.png) is of degree *m*, with coefficients in  <math alttext="normal upper F 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![normal upper F 2](images/c03_772.png), and irreducible in  <math alttext="normal upper F 2 left-bracket x right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![normal upper F 2 left-bracket x right-bracket](images/c03_773.png).

***Definition 3.43 Field generator*** *or* ***primitive element****: given a field*  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c03_774.png) *and a primitive polynomial*  <math alttext="f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c03_775.png) *of degree* *m, an element*  <math alttext="g element-of upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m Subscript Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![g element-of upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m Subscript Baseline](images/c03_776.png)*is called generator (or primitive element) of*  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c03_777.png) *if and only if* *g* *is a root of*  <math alttext="f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c03_778.png) *in*  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c03_779.png) *and every nonzero element of*  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c03_780.png) *can be uniquely written as a power of* *g*.

The two theorems above are very useful to quickly calculate multiplicative inverses and exponentiation with large exponents.

***Corollary* 3.4** By Theorems 3.22 and 3.24, if  <math alttext="2 Superscript m Baseline minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript m Baseline minus 1](images/c03_803.png) is prime, then the square root of any element  <math alttext="x element-of upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![x element-of upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c03_804.png) is  <math alttext="StartRoot x EndRoot equals x Superscript 2 Super Superscript m minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msqrt><mi>x</mi></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![StartRoot x EndRoot equals x Superscript 2 Super Superscript m minus 1](images/c03_805.png).

Therefore, by Theorem 3.23,  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 cubed" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 cubed](images/c03_815.png) has six generators, which are  <math alttext="2 comma 3 comma 4 comma 5 comma 6 comma 7" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> ![2 comma 3 comma 4 comma 5 comma 6 comma 7](images/c03_816.png).

Let  <math alttext="f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x cubed plus x plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x cubed plus x plus 1](images/c03_817.png), which is an irreducible polynomial, be the reduction polynomial for field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 cubed" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 cubed](images/c03_818.png).

By Theorem 3.1,  <math alttext="phi left-parenthesis 16 minus 1 right-parenthesis equals phi left-parenthesis 5 right-parenthesis asterisk phi left-parenthesis 3 right-parenthesis equals 4 asterisk 2 equals 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ![phi left-parenthesis 16 minus 1 right-parenthesis equals phi left-parenthesis 5 right-parenthesis asterisk phi left-parenthesis 3 right-parenthesis equals 4 asterisk 2 equals 8](images/c03_850.png). By theorem 3.23,  <math alttext="normal upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![normal upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 4](images/c03_851.png) has  <math alttext="phi left-parenthesis 16 minus 1 right-parenthesis equals 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ![phi left-parenthesis 16 minus 1 right-parenthesis equals 8](images/c03_852.png) generators.

Let  <math alttext="f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 4 Baseline plus x plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 4 Baseline plus x plus 1](images/c03_853.png), which is an irreducible polynomial over  <math alttext="upper F 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F 2](images/c03_854.png), be the reduction polynomial for field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 4](images/c03_855.png).

*   Example of addition:  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 1101 right-parenthesis plus left-parenthesis 1000 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 0101 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1101</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1000</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>0101</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 1101 right-parenthesis plus left-parenthesis 1000 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 0101 right-parenthesis](images/c03_856.png)
    
    In polynomial form over  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 4 Subscript Baseline colon left-parenthesis x cubed plus x squared plus 1 right-parenthesis plus left-parenthesis x cubed right-parenthesis equals 2 x cubed plus x squared plus 1 equals x squared plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow></msub><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 4 Subscript Baseline colon left-parenthesis x cubed plus x squared plus 1 right-parenthesis plus left-parenthesis x cubed right-parenthesis equals 2 x cubed plus x squared plus 1 equals x squared plus 1](images/c03_857.png).
    
*   Example of multiplication over  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 4 Subscript Baseline colon left-parenthesis 1110 right-parenthesis asterisk left-parenthesis 1000 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 1001 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow></msub><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1110</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1000</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1001</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 4 Subscript Baseline colon left-parenthesis 1110 right-parenthesis asterisk left-parenthesis 1000 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 1001 right-parenthesis](images/c03_858.png) explained as follows:
    
     <math alttext="left-parenthesis x cubed plus x squared plus x right-parenthesis asterisk left-parenthesis x cubed right-parenthesis m o d f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis x Superscript 6 Baseline plus x Superscript 5 Baseline plus x Superscript 4 Baseline right-parenthesis m o d left-parenthesis x Superscript 4 Baseline plus x plus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext>\*</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>6</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>5</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis x cubed plus x squared plus x right-parenthesis asterisk left-parenthesis x cubed right-parenthesis m o d f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis x Superscript 6 Baseline plus x Superscript 5 Baseline plus x Superscript 4 Baseline right-parenthesis m o d left-parenthesis x Superscript 4 Baseline plus x plus 1 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis x cubed plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c03_859.png)

xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper Q left-parenthesis x Thus, the inverse of 3 in  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 4](images/c03_898.png) is 14.
    
    Calculation using Theorem 3.21 with generator  <math alttext="g equals 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![g equals 2](images/c03_899.png):
    
    Element 3 is generated by *g* power 4. Thus, by Theorem 3.21,  <math alttext="3 Superscript negative 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![3 Superscript negative 1](images/c03_900.png) is equal to
    
     <math alttext="x Superscript 16 minus 4 minus 1 Baseline m o d left-parenthesis x Superscript 4 Baseline plus x plus 1 right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 11 Baseline m o d left-parenthesis x Superscript 4 Baseline plus x plus 1 right-parenthesis equals x cubed plus x squared plus x period" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> ![x Superscript 16 minus 4 minus 1 Baseline m o d left-parenthesis x Superscript 4 Baseline plus x plus 1 right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 11 Baseline m o d left-parenthesis x Superscript 4 Baseline plus x plus 1 right-parenthesis equals x cubed plus x squared plus x period](images/c03_901.png)
    
    Since  <math alttext="x cubed plus x squared plus x" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> ![x cubed plus x squared plus x](images/c03_902.png) is the polynomial associated with element 14, the inverse of 3 in  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 4](images/c03_903.png) is 14.
    

#### *3.2.4.4 Selection of Reduction Polynomial for Field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c03_904.png)*

By Theorem 3.18, given a prime power  <math alttext="q equals 2 Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![q equals 2 Superscript m](images/c03_905.png), there always exists at least one reduction polynomial  <math alttext="f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c03_906.png) of degree *m* over  <math alttext="upper F 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F 2](images/c03_907.png) to construct the field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c03_908.png). Notice that the set of elements of a finite field is the same, whatever is the selected reduction polynomial. However, the calculations (i.e. addition, subtraction, multiplication, and multiplicative inverse) on elements yield different results under different reduction polynomials.

To simplify the Euclidian division, the polynomial  <math alttext="f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c03_909.png) usually selected is a trinomial of the form  <math alttext="x Superscript m Baseline plus x plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![x Superscript m Baseline plus x plus 1](images/c03_910.png) or, if all trinomials are reducible, select pentanomials of the form  <math alttext="x Superscript m Baseline plus x Superscript k Baseline 3 Baseline plus x Superscript k Baseline 2 Baseline plus x Superscript k Baseline 1 Baseline plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![x Superscript m Baseline plus x Superscript k Baseline 3 Baseline plus x Superscript k Baseline 2 Baseline plus x Superscript k Baseline 1 Baseline plus 1](images/c03_911.png), with  <math alttext="k Baseline 1 comma k Baseline 2 comma k Baseline 3 element-of left-parenthesis 1 comma m minus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mn>3</mn><mo>&#8712;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![k Baseline 1 comma k Baseline 2 comma k Baseline 3 element-of left-parenthesis 1 comma m minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c03_912.png) \[[7](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0007)\].

For real cryptosystem implementation, the standard X9.142 \[[8](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0008)\] recommends the following reduction polynomials depending on *q*:

*   If  <math alttext="q equals 2 Superscript 233" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>233</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![q equals 2 Superscript 233](images/c03_913.png), then use  <math alttext="f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 233 Baseline plus x Superscript 74 Baseline plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>233</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>74</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 233 Baseline plus x Superscript 74 Baseline plus 1](images/c03_914.png).
*   If  <math alttext="q equals 2 Superscript 283" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>283</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![q equals 2 Superscript 283](images/c03_915.png), then use  <math alttext="f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 283 Baseline plus x Superscript 12 Baseline plus x Superscript 7 Baseline plus x Superscript 5 Baseline plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>283</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>7</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>5</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 283 Baseline plus x Superscript 12 Baseline plus x Superscript 7 Baseline plus x Superscript 5 Baseline plus 1](images/c03_916.png).
*   If  <math alttext="q equals 2 Superscript 409" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>409</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![q equals 2 Superscript 409](images/c03_917.png), then use  <math alttext="f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 409 Baseline plus x Superscript 87 Baseline plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>409</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>87</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 409 Baseline plus x Superscript 87 Baseline plus 1](images/c03_918.png).
*   If  <math alttext="q equals 2 Superscript 571" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>571</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![q equals 2 Superscript 571](images/c03_919.png), then use  <math alttext="f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 571 Baseline plus x Superscript 10 Baseline plus x Superscript 5 Baseline plus x squared plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>571</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>5</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 571 Baseline plus x Superscript 10 Baseline plus x Superscript 5 Baseline plus x squared plus 1](images/c03_920.png).

Assuming that 2 is a generator, do the following operations over  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 4](images/c03_968.png):

## 3.3 Computation Algorithms

The previous sections presented theorems and lemmas, which are of paramount importance to cryptographic algorithms. Often, computations are needed to find elements (e.g. multiplicative inverses, square roots, etc.). Such computations are time consuming in particular when large numbers are of concern. Many algorithms exist in literature aiming to optimize computations in general and in cryptosystems in particular. This section presents the most commonly used algorithms to speed up computations in cryptographic algorithms. They include Extended Euclidean algorithm to find the greatest common divider and multiplicative inverse, Square-and-multiply method to perform modular exponentiation, Montgomery multiplication to compute modular multiplication, Gauss’s algorithm to solve congruence systems, Tonelli-Shanks algorithm to find modular square roots, and Rabin’s algorithm to test irreducibility of polynomials.

### 3.3.1 Euclidean and Extended Euclidean Algorithms

#### 3.3.1.1 Euclidean Algorithm

The Euclidean algorithm is the most known and used method for computing the greatest common divider (*GCD*) of two integers. There exist different ways to describe the Euclidean algorithm. Below is a pseudocode for the description of the Euclidean algorithm:

In addition to the  <math alttext="upper G upper C upper D" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> ![upper G upper C upper D](images/c03_1000.png) computation, the Extended Euclidean algorithm computes two coefficients (called Bezout’s identity coefficients) *x* and *y*, such that  <math alttext="a x plus b y equals upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis a comma b right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>G</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![a x plus b y equals upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis a comma b right-parenthesis](images/c03_1001.png). #### 3.3.1.3 Finding Multiplicative Inverse

Finding multiplicative inverse in  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c03_1002.png), with *p* a prime, is a very frequent operation in cryptography. Below, two methods, often used to find multiplicative inverses, are introduced. They differ in terms of time computation.

##### *3.3.1.3.1 Finding Multiplicative Inverse Using Euler’s Theorem*

Euler’s theorem states that if *a* and *p* are two coprime positive integers, then  <math alttext="a Superscript phi left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis Baseline identical-to 1 m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![a Superscript phi left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis Baseline identical-to 1 m o d p](images/c03_1003.png), where  <math alttext="phi left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![phi left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c03_1004.png) *is* the Euler’s totient.

Multiply both sides of the congruence by  <math alttext="a Superscript negative 1 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![a Superscript negative 1 Baseline](images/c03_1005.png) yields  <math alttext="a Superscript phi left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis Baseline asterisk a Superscript negative 1 Baseline identical-to a Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![a Superscript phi left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis Baseline asterisk a Superscript negative 1 Baseline identical-to a Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d p](images/c03_1006.png).

Hence, *a*^(*φ*(*p*)-1) ≡ *a*^(\-1) *mod p*, which means that the multiplicative inverse is obtained by exponentiation.

We know, by Theorem 3.1, that if *p* is a prime, then  <math alttext="phi left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis equals p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#981;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![phi left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis equals p minus 1](images/c03_1007.png). Hence,  <math alttext="a Superscript phi left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis minus 1 Baseline equals a Superscript p minus 2 Baseline identical-to a Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![a Superscript phi left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis minus 1 Baseline equals a Superscript p minus 2 Baseline identical-to a Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d p](images/c03_1008.png), if *p* is prime.

##### *3.3.1.3.2 Finding Multiplicative Inverse Using Extended Euclidean Algorithm*

The Extended Euclidean algorithm finds *x* and *y* such that  <math alttext="a x plus b y equals upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis a comma b right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>G</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![a x plus b y equals upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis a comma b right-parenthesis](images/c03_1016.png). Let us see why the Extended Euclidean algorithm is appropriate to compute the multiplicative inverse. By definition of a multiplicative group  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript n Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript n Superscript asterisk](images/c03_1017.png), any element  <math alttext="alpha element-of double-struck upper Z Subscript n Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![alpha element-of double-struck upper Z Subscript n Superscript asterisk](images/c03_1018.png) is less than *n* and has an inverse  <math alttext="alpha Superscript negative 1 Baseline element-of double-struck upper Z Subscript n Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![alpha Superscript negative 1 Baseline element-of double-struck upper Z Subscript n Superscript asterisk](images/c03_1019.png). Since α is invertible in  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript n Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript n Superscript asterisk](images/c03_1020.png),  <math alttext="normal upper G normal upper C normal upper D left-parenthesis p comma alpha right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![normal upper G normal upper C normal upper D left-parenthesis p comma alpha right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c03_1021.png).

By definition of multiplicative inverse:

 <math alttext="alpha asterisk alpha Superscript negative 1 Baseline identical-to 1 m o d n right double arrow there-exists k element-of double-struck upper Z Subscript n Baseline vertical-bar alpha asterisk alpha Superscript negative 1 Baseline equals 1 plus k asterisk n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8658;</mo><mo>&#8707;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></math> ![alpha asterisk alpha Superscript negative 1 Baseline identical-to 1 m o d n right double arrow there-exists k element-of double-struck upper Z Subscript n Baseline vertical-bar alpha asterisk alpha Superscript negative 1 Baseline equals 1 plus k asterisk n](images/c03_1022.png).

Thus,  <math alttext="alpha asterisk alpha Superscript negative 1 Baseline minus k asterisk n equals n asterisk left-parenthesis negative k right-parenthesis plus alpha asterisk left-parenthesis alpha Superscript negative 1 Baseline right-parenthesis equals 1 equals GCD left-parenthesis n comma alpha right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>\*</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>\*</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mtext>GCD</mtext><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![alpha asterisk alpha Superscript negative 1 Baseline minus k asterisk n equals n asterisk left-parenthesis negative k right-parenthesis plus alpha asterisk left-parenthesis alpha Superscript negative 1 Baseline right-parenthesis equals 1 equals GCD left-parenthesis n comma alpha right-parenthesis](images/c03_1023.png).

Hence, given α and *n*, applying the Extended Euclidean algorithm to  <math alttext="n asterisk left-parenthesis negative k right-parenthesis plus alpha asterisk left-parenthesis alpha Superscript negative 1 Baseline right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>\*</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>\*</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![n asterisk left-parenthesis negative k right-parenthesis plus alpha asterisk left-parenthesis alpha Superscript negative 1 Baseline right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c03_1024.png) returns  <math alttext="negative k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> ![negative k](images/c03_1025.png) and  <math alttext="alpha Superscript negative 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![alpha Superscript negative 1](images/c03_1026.png). In other words, we substitute *n* to *a*, α to *b*,  <math alttext="negative k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> ![negative k](images/c03_1027.png) to *x*, and  <math alttext="alpha Superscript negative 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![alpha Superscript negative 1](images/c03_1028.png) to *y* in the equality  <math alttext="a x plus b y equals GCD left-parenthesis a comma b right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>GCD</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![a x plus b y equals GCD left-parenthesis a comma b right-parenthesis](images/c03_1029.png) and keep the returned value for *y*.

### 3.3.2 Modular Exponentiation: Square-and-Multiply

Some cryptographic algorithms, such as RSA, make use of modular exponentiation to encrypt or decrypt messages. Since cryptographic algorithms use very large numbers (in magnitude of thousands of bits), it is of paramount importance to use efficient modular exponentiation algorithms to get messages encrypted or decrypted in reasonable time to not jeopardize the performance of cryptosystems.

Square-and-Multiply algorithms are useful to compute large integer powers of a number, for example  <math alttext="7 Superscript 3110190717 Baseline m o d 1001" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>7</mn><mrow><mn>3110190717</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1001</mn></mrow></math> ![7 Superscript 3110190717 Baseline m o d 1001](images/c03_1030.png)**.** The most known and used algorithm in the Square-and-Multiply algorithm family is called *right-to-left*[^(12)](#c03.xhtml#c03-note-0012) *binary exponentiation algorithm*, or simply *binary exponentiation algorithm*. To better understand the Square-and-Multiply method, recall the following rules of modular arithmetic:

In the congruence  <math alttext="a Superscript m Baseline m o d n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![a Superscript m Baseline m o d n](images/c03_1034.png), *a* is called the base, *m* the exponent, and *n* the modulus. To compute  <math alttext="a Superscript m Baseline m o d n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![a Superscript m Baseline m o d n](images/c03_1035.png), the *right-to-left binary exponentiation method* is based on the reuse of powers of 2 of *a*. Let us see an example to show computation principle of the method:

 <math alttext="5 Superscript 11 Baseline m o d 14 identical-to question-mark" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mo>?</mo></mrow></math> ![5 Superscript 11 Baseline m o d 14 identical-to question-mark](images/c03_1036.png)

 <math alttext="5 Superscript 11 Baseline equals 5 Superscript 4 asterisk 2 plus 2 plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![5 Superscript 11 Baseline equals 5 Superscript 4 asterisk 2 plus 2 plus 1](images/c03_1037.png) (11, the power of 5, is expressed as a sum of powers of 2.)

 <math alttext="5 Superscript 11 Baseline m o d 14 identical-to left-parenthesis left-parenthesis left-parenthesis 5 squared right-parenthesis Superscript 4 Baseline right-parenthesis asterisk left-parenthesis 5 squared right-parenthesis asterisk 5 right-parenthesis m o d 14" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mn>5</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>\*</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mn>5</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![5 Superscript 11 Baseline m o d 14 identical-to left-parenthesis left-parenthesis left-parenthesis 5 squared right-parenthesis Superscript 4 Baseline right-parenthesis asterisk left-parenthesis 5 squared right-parenthesis asterisk 5 right-parenthesis m o d 14](images/c03_1038.png).

By the modular arithmetic rules recalled above:

 <math alttext="5 Superscript 11 Baseline m o d 14 identical-to left-parenthesis left-parenthesis 5 squared m o d 14 right-parenthesis Superscript 4 Baseline asterisk left-parenthesis 5 squared m o d 14 right-parenthesis asterisk left-parenthesis 5 m o d 14 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis m o d 14" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mn>5</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>\*</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mn>5</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![5 Superscript 11 Baseline m o d 14 identical-to left-parenthesis left-parenthesis 5 squared m o d 14 right-parenthesis Superscript 4 Baseline asterisk left-parenthesis 5 squared m o d 14 right-parenthesis asterisk left-parenthesis 5 m o d 14 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis m o d 14](images/c03_1039.png).

Replace  <math alttext="5 squared m o d 14 identical-to 11" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>5</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow></math> ![5 squared m o d 14 identical-to 11](images/c03_1040.png) and  <math alttext="5 m o d 14 identical-to 5" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>5</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> ![5 m o d 14 identical-to 5](images/c03_1041.png) in the previous equation:

 <math alttext="5 Superscript 11 Baseline m o d 14 identical-to left-parenthesis 11 right-parenthesis Superscript 4 Baseline asterisk left-parenthesis 11 right-parenthesis asterisk left-parenthesis 5 right-parenthesis m o d 14 identical-to left-parenthesis 11 Superscript 5 Baseline asterisk 5 right-parenthesis m o d 14" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>\*</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mo>(</mo><msup><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow><mn>5</mn></msup><mo>\*</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![5 Superscript 11 Baseline m o d 14 identical-to left-parenthesis 11 right-parenthesis Superscript 4 Baseline asterisk left-parenthesis 11 right-parenthesis asterisk left-parenthesis 5 right-parenthesis m o d 14 identical-to left-parenthesis 11 Superscript 5 Baseline asterisk 5 right-parenthesis m o d 14](images/c03_1042.png)

 <math alttext="11 Superscript 5 Baseline m o d 14 identical-to left-parenthesis left-parenthesis 11 squared m o d 14 right-parenthesis squared asterisk 11 right-parenthesis m o d 14 identical-to left-parenthesis 9 right-parenthesis squared asterisk 11 m o d 14 identical-to 9" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow><mn>5</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>\*</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>\*</mo><mn>11</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>9</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![11 Superscript 5 Baseline m o d 14 identical-to left-parenthesis left-parenthesis 11 squared m o d 14 right-parenthesis squared asterisk 11 right-parenthesis m o d 14 identical-to left-parenthesis 9 right-parenthesis squared asterisk 11 m o d 14 identical-to 9](images/c03_1043.png).

Thus,  <math alttext="5 Superscript 11 Baseline m o d 14 identical-to 9 asterisk 5 m o d 14 identical-to 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>5</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>3</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![5 Superscript 11 Baseline m o d 14 identical-to 9 asterisk 5 m o d 14 identical-to 3](images/c03_1044.png).

The right-to-left binary exponentiation method computes  <math alttext="a Superscript k Baseline m o d n identical-to b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![a Superscript k Baseline m o d n identical-to b](images/c03_1045.png) as follows:

1.  Convert *k* in binary notation  <math alttext="k equals k Subscript upper L minus 1 Baseline k Subscript upper L minus 2 Baseline dot dot dot k 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![k equals k Subscript upper L minus 1 Baseline k Subscript upper L minus 2 Baseline dot dot dot k 0](images/c03_1046.png),  <math alttext="k Subscript i Baseline element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet comma left-parenthesis 0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to upper L minus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![k Subscript i Baseline element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet comma left-parenthesis 0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to upper L minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c03_1047.png).
2.  Thus,  <math alttext="k equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 0 Overscript i equals upper L minus 1 Endscripts 2 Superscript i Baseline asterisk k Subscript i Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></msup><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mstyle><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![k equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 0 Overscript i equals upper L minus 1 Endscripts 2 Superscript i Baseline asterisk k Subscript i Baseline](images/c03_1048.png).
3.   <math alttext="a Superscript k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![a Superscript k](images/c03_1049.png) is considered as a product of powers of  <math alttext="2 colon a Superscript k Baseline equals a Superscript left-parenthesis sigma-summation Underscript i equals 0 Overscript i equals upper L minus 1 displaystyle="true"><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></msup><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mstyle></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><msubsup><mo>&#8719;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow></msup></mrow></mstyle></mrow></math> Super Subscript i Superscript Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript 2 Super Superscript i](images/c03_1050.png).
4.  For *i* from 0 to  <math alttext="upper L minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper L minus 1](images/c03_1051.png):  <math alttext="b Subscript i Baseline identical-to left-parenthesis a Superscript k Super Subscript i Superscript Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript 2 Super Superscript i Superscript Baseline m o d n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![b Subscript i Baseline identical-to left-parenthesis a Superscript k Super Subscript i Superscript Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript 2 Super Superscript i Superscript Baseline m o d n](images/c03_1052.png).

### 3.3.3 Fast Modular Multiplication and Montgomery’s Multiplication

Given three positive integers *a*, *b*, and *n*, the modular multiplication  <math alttext="a asterisk b m o d upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>b</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![a asterisk b m o d upper N](images/c03_1055.png) finds an integer *r* such that:  <math alttext="there-exists q element-of double-struck upper N vertical-bar a asterisk b equals q asterisk upper N plus r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8707;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>q</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>&#8469;</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> ![there-exists q element-of double-struck upper N vertical-bar a asterisk b equals q asterisk upper N plus r](images/c03_1056.png). If *a* and *b* are less than *N*, then the product  <math alttext="a asterisk b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![a asterisk b](images/c03_1057.png) is less than or equal to  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper N minus 1 right-parenthesis squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper N minus 1 right-parenthesis squared](images/c03_1058.png).

In regular modular multiplication, the bit-length of arguments *a*, *b*, and *N* are assumed to be less than or equal to *w*, the word bit-length of the underlying hardware. Often, *w* is 32 or 64. If arguments *a* and *b* have a bit-length less than or equal to *w*, then the naïve modular multiplication is performed with four basic operations: a multiplication  <math alttext="upper P 1 equals a asterisk b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P 1 equals a asterisk b](images/c03_1059.png), a division  <math alttext="q equals left ceiling StartFraction upper P 1 Over upper N EndFraction right ceiling" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>&#8968;</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>&#8969;</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![q equals left ceiling StartFraction upper P 1 Over upper N EndFraction right ceiling](images/c03_1060.png), a multiplication  <math alttext="upper P 2 equals q asterisk upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P 2 equals q asterisk upper N](images/c03_1061.png), and a subtraction  <math alttext="r equals upper P 1 minus upper P 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![r equals upper P 1 minus upper P 2](images/c03_1062.png).

It is commonly admitted that division is an expensive operation (in time computation) and numbers used in cryptography are (very) large integers, which have bit-length in hundreds or in thousands (128, 512, 1024, 2048, etc.). Consequently, cryptographic numbers may be composed of several machine words and the naïve modular multiplication results in excessive computation time. That would jeopardize the performance of cryptosystems. Therefore, to implement cryptographic algorithms, specific computation techniques are required. This chapter presents the Montgomery multiplication \[[9](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0009)\], which is the most known and fast used modular multiplication method in cryptographic algorithm implementation. The efficiency of Montgomery multiplication comes from the avoidance of expensive division operations.

#### 3.3.3.1 Single-precision Montgomery Multiplication Algorithm

Basic Montgomery multiplication is applicable if single-precision arguments, i.e. *a*, *b*, and *n* take values less than  <math alttext="2 Superscript w" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>w</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript w](images/c03_1063.png), where *w* denotes the word bit-length of the underlying hardware. When properly implemented, the Montgomery multiplication reduces the computation time due to division and consequently it accelerates modular multiplication. The main principle behind Montgomery multiplication is to change the representation of arguments *a* and *b* and change the modular multiplication accordingly. The Montgomery multiplication does not directly compute  <math alttext="a asterisk b m o d upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>b</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![a asterisk b m o d upper N](images/c03_1064.png). Instead, it computes  <math alttext="k equals k Subscript upper L minus 1 Baseline k Subscript upper L minus 2 Baseline dot dot dot k 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![k equals k Subscript upper L minus 1 Baseline k Subscript upper L minus 2 Baseline dot dot dot k 0](images/c03_1065.png) for a carefully chosen integer *R*, which is called *Montgomery radix*. When Montgomery multiplication is used in cryptosystems, *R* is chosen to be equal to a power of 2, greater than *n*, and coprime to *N*. For example, if  <math alttext="upper N equals 103" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>103</mn></mrow></math> ![upper N equals 103](images/c03_1066.png), *R* may be 128, 256, etc.

***Definition 3.44 Montgomery reduction****: let* *n* *and* *R* *be two integers such that*  <math alttext="upper R ampersand gt semicolon upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>&#38;gt;</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R ampersand gt semicolon upper N](images/c03_1067.png) *and*  <math alttext="normal upper G normal upper C normal upper D left-parenthesis upper N comma upper R right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![normal upper G normal upper C normal upper D left-parenthesis upper N comma upper R right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c03_1068.png)*. For any integer* *T, such that*  <math alttext="0 less-than-or-equal-to upper T less-than upper N asterisk upper R" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> ![0 less-than-or-equal-to upper T less-than upper N asterisk upper R](images/c03_1069.png)*, the Montgomery reduction of* *T, denoted*  <math alttext="upper R upper E upper D upper C left-parenthesis upper T right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper R upper E upper D upper C left-parenthesis upper T right-parenthesis](images/c03_1070.png) *modulo* *n* *w.r.t*. *R* *is defined by*:  <math alttext="upper R upper E upper D upper C left-parenthesis upper T right-parenthesis equals upper T asterisk upper R Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R upper E upper D upper C left-parenthesis upper T right-parenthesis equals upper T asterisk upper R Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d upper N](images/c03_1071.png).

Montgomery reduction function described below enables to quickly compute  <math alttext="k equals k Subscript upper L minus 1 Baseline k Subscript upper L minus 2 Baseline dot dot dot k 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![k equals k Subscript upper L minus 1 Baseline k Subscript upper L minus 2 Baseline dot dot dot k 0](images/c03_1072.png):
