*   ***Why does Montgomery’s method speed up the modulation multiplication?***

1.  First, in cryptosystems that use Montgomery multiplication, *R*,  <math alttext="upper R Superscript negative 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper R Superscript negative 1](images/c03_1108.png),  <math alttext="upper N Superscript negative 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper N Superscript negative 1](images/c03_1109.png), and  <math alttext="upper N prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> ![upper N prime](images/c03_1110.png) are computed once and used in several modular multiplications. Therefore, their computation time has a negligible impact on the cryptosystem performance. For example, in RSA the modulus *n* is computed from two large primes, then the public and private keys are computed and the same pair (public and private keys) is used to encrypt and decrypt messages for a long time (maybe in months).
2.  Second, when *R* is a power of 2, multiplication and division by *R* are efficiently performed with left and right bit-shifting, which are very fast operations in hardware. Therefore, *t* in line 2 of DECR is computed with a *w*\-right-shift.
3.  Third, in line 1 of DECR function,  <math alttext="m o d upper R" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> ![m o d upper R](images/c03_1111.png) is used instead of  <math alttext="m o d upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![m o d upper N](images/c03_1112.png). Since *R* is a power of 2,  <math alttext="k equals k Subscript upper L minus 1 Baseline k Subscript upper L minus 2 Baseline dot dot dot k 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![k equals k Subscript upper L minus 1 Baseline k Subscript upper L minus 2 Baseline dot dot dot k 0](images/c03_1113.png) can be efficiently computed with shifting operations as follows: for any integer *x*,  <math alttext="x identical-to z m o d upper R identical-to z m o d 2 Superscript w" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#160;z&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>R</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mi>z</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>w</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![x identical-to z m o d upper R identical-to z m o d 2 Superscript w](images/c03_1114.png). By definition of modulo  <math alttext="z equals x minus left floor StartFraction x Over 2 Superscript w Baseline EndFraction right floor asterisk 2 Superscript w" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mrow><mo>&#8970;</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>x</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>w</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>&#8971;</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>w</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![z equals x minus left floor StartFraction x Over 2 Superscript w Baseline EndFraction right floor asterisk 2 Superscript w](images/c03_1115.png). Therefore,  <math alttext="k equals k Subscript upper L minus 1 Baseline k Subscript upper L minus 2 Baseline dot dot dot k 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![z](images/c03_1116.png) is computed by a *w*\-right-shift (i.e.  <math alttext="q equals left floor StartFraction x Over 2 Superscript w Baseline EndFraction right floor" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>&#8970;</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>x</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>w</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>&#8971;</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![q equals left floor StartFraction x Over 2 Superscript w Baseline EndFraction right floor](images/c03_1117.png)), a *w*\-left-shift (i.e.  <math alttext="p equals q asterisk 2 Superscript w" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>w</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![p equals q asterisk 2 Superscript w](images/c03_1118.png)), and a subtraction (i.e.  <math alttext="z equals x minus p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![z equals x minus p](images/c03_1119.png)).

#### 3.3.3.2 Multi-precision Montgomery Multiplication Algorithm

A large integer *X* is represented as an array of *l* *w*\-bit-words  <math alttext="left-parenthesis x 0 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript l minus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis x 0 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript l minus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c03_1120.png) such that:

 <math alttext="upper X equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 0 Overscript l minus 1 Endscripts x Subscript i Baseline asterisk left-parenthesis 2 Superscript w Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript i Baseline equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 0 Overscript l minus 1 Endscripts x Subscript i Baseline asterisk upper B Superscript i Baseline comma left-parenthesis 0 less-than-or-equal-to x Subscript i Baseline less-than upper B comma i equals 0 comma ellipsis comma l minus 1 right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true" mathsize="140%"><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover></mstyle><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>w</mi></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>i</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true" mathsize="140%"><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover></mstyle><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper X equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 0 Overscript l minus 1 Endscripts x Subscript i Baseline asterisk left-parenthesis 2 Superscript w Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript i Baseline equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 0 Overscript l minus 1 Endscripts x Subscript i Baseline asterisk upper B Superscript i Baseline comma left-parenthesis 0 less-than-or-equal-to x Subscript i Baseline less-than upper B comma i equals 0 comma ellipsis comma l minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c03_1121.png)

where  <math alttext="upper B equals 2 Superscript w" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>w</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper B equals 2 Superscript w](images/c03_1122.png) is called *representation basis*. For example, in hexadecimal format,

 <math alttext="upper X equals 112233445566778899 upper A upper A upper B upper B upper C upper C upper D upper D upper E upper E upper F upper F Baseline 00" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>112233445566778899</mn><mi>A</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>F</mi><mn>00</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X equals 112233445566778899 upper A upper A upper B upper B upper C upper C upper D upper D upper E upper E upper F upper F Baseline 00](images/c03_1123.png) is represented as:

two 64-bit words:  <math alttext="x 1 equals 99 upper A upper A upper B upper B upper C upper C upper D upper D upper E upper E upper F upper F Baseline 00" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>99</mn><mi>A</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>F</mi><mn>00</mn></mrow></math> ![x 1 equals 99 upper A upper A upper B upper B upper C upper C upper D upper D upper E upper E upper F upper F Baseline 00](images/c03_1124.png)

or alternatively, as four 32-bit words:  <math alttext="x 0 equals 11223344" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>11223344</mn></mrow></math> ![x 0 equals 11223344](images/c03_1125.png),  <math alttext="x 1 equals 55667788" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>55667788</mn></mrow></math> ![x 1 equals 55667788](images/c03_1126.png),  <math alttext="x 2 equals 99 upper A upper A upper B upper B upper C upper C" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>99</mn><mi>A</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> ![x 2 equals 99 upper A upper A upper B upper B upper C upper C](images/c03_1127.png),  <math alttext="x 4 equals upper D upper D upper E upper E upper F upper F Baseline 00" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>F</mi><mn>00</mn></mrow></math> ![x 4 equals upper D upper D upper E upper E upper F upper F Baseline 00](images/c03_1128.png).

Large integers are called multi-precision integers and arithmetic operations on large integers are said to be multi-precision operations. One multi-precision operation requires multiple simple-precision operations to be performed. Multi-precision addition, subtraction, and multiplication are introduced.[^(13)](#c03.xhtml#c03-note-0013)

When computing modular multiplication  <math alttext="upper X asterisk upper Y m o d upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>Y</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![upper X asterisk upper Y m o d upper N](images/c03_1165.png) over large integers, the Montgomery multiplication is valuable to speed up computations. The modulus *n* and arguments and *X* and *Y* are represented as *l* words in base *B*:

 <math alttext="upper N equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 0 Overscript l minus 1 Endscripts n Subscript i Baseline asterisk left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis Superscript i Baseline comma" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow></mstyle><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> ![upper N equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 0 Overscript l minus 1 Endscripts n Subscript i Baseline asterisk left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis Superscript i Baseline comma upper X equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 0 Overscript l minus 1 Endscripts x Subscript i Baseline asterisk left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis Superscript i upper Y equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 0 Overscript l minus 1 Endscripts y Subscript i Baseline asterisk left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis Superscript i](images/c03_1166.png)

Arguments are padded on the left with zero-words if needed.

The Montgomery radix *R* is chosen such that *n* is coprime to *R* and  <math alttext="upper N less-than upper R equals upper B Superscript l" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>B</mi><mi>l</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper N less-than upper R equals upper B Superscript l](images/c03_1169.png) (in cryptography  <math alttext="upper R equals 2 Superscript l asterisk w" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper R equals 2 Superscript l asterisk w](images/c03_1170.png) where *w* denotes the word bit-length). Before performing modular multiplication,  <math alttext="upper N prime equals minus upper N Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ![upper N prime equals minus upper N Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d upper B](images/c03_1171.png) is computed. Notice that  <math alttext="m o d upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ![m o d upper B](images/c03_1172.png) is used and not  <math alttext="m o d upper R" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> ![m o d upper R](images/c03_1173.png) (as in single-precision Montgomery reduction). *R* and  <math alttext="upper N prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> ![upper N prime](images/c03_1174.png) are computed once and used in several modular multiplications with the same modulus *n*. Pseudocode of the multi-precision Montgomery multiplication is as follows:

The multi-precision Montgomery multiplication computes  <math alttext="upper X asterisk upper Y asterisk upper R Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![upper X asterisk upper Y asterisk upper R Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d upper N](images/c03_1190.png). Therefore, to find the modular multiplication, the returned result is multiplied by *R*.

**Note**. The multi-precision Montgomery multiplication makes use of multi-precision addition, subtraction, and multiplication. In addition, division by  <math alttext="upper N prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![upper N prime](images/c03_1191.png) and  <math alttext="m o d upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ![m o d upper B](images/c03_1192.png) operations are performed using shift operations.

**Example 3.40**  <math alttext="upper N equals 50021" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50021</mn></mrow></math> ![upper N equals 50021](images/c03_1193.png) (*n* is a prime),  <math alttext="upper X equals 15063" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15063</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X equals 15063](images/c03_1194.png),  <math alttext="upper Y equals 37551" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>37551</mn></mrow></math> ![upper Y equals 37551](images/c03_1195.png), Base  <math alttext="upper B equals 100" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow></math> ![upper B equals 100](images/c03_1196.png)

*X* is three 2-decimal-digit-words:  <math alttext="upper X equals left-parenthesis 01 comma 50 comma 63 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>01</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>50</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>63</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper X equals left-parenthesis 01 comma 50 comma 63 right-parenthesis](images/c03_1197.png).

We choose  <math alttext="upper R equals 100 Superscript 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>100</mn></mrow><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![upper R equals 100 Superscript 4](images/c03_1198.png), which meets the conditions  <math alttext="upper R ampersand gt semicolon upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>&#38;gt;</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R ampersand gt semicolon upper N](images/c03_1199.png) and  <math alttext="normal upper G normal upper C normal upper D left-parenthesis upper R comma upper N right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![normal upper G normal upper C normal upper D left-parenthesis upper R comma upper N right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c03_1200.png).

 <math alttext="upper R equals 100 Superscript 4 Baseline equals 100 Superscript l Baseline right double arrow l equals 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>100</mn></mrow><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mrow><mn>100</mn></mrow><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>&#8658;</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![upper R equals 100 Superscript 4 Baseline equals 100 Superscript l Baseline right double arrow l equals 4](images/c03_1201.png)

Compute  <math alttext="upper N prime equals minus upper N Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ![upper N prime equals minus upper N Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d upper B](images/c03_1202.png)

 <math alttext="upper N prime equals minus 50021 Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d 100 equals negative 81 m o d 100 equals 19" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mrow><mn>50021</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>100</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>81</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>100</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>19</mn></mrow></math> ![upper N prime equals minus 50021 Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d 100 equals negative 81 m o d 100 equals 19](images/c03_1203.png)

Below are the computations in multi-precision Montgomery multiplication:

![](images/c03_1205.png)

The multi-precision Montgomery multiplication returns 2793, which represents  <math alttext="upper X asterisk asterisk upper R Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>\*</mo><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![upper X asterisk asterisk upper R Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d upper N](images/c03_1209.png). Multiplying by *R* yields  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper X asterisk upper Y asterisk upper R Superscript negative 1 Baseline right-parenthesis asterisk upper R m o d upper N identical-to upper X asterisk upper Y m o d upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>\*</mo><mi>R</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>Y</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper X asterisk upper Y asterisk upper R Superscript negative 1 Baseline right-parenthesis asterisk upper R m o d upper N identical-to upper X asterisk upper Y m o d upper N](images/c03_1210.png)

Thus,  <math alttext="upper N prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![upper N prime](images/c03_1211.png).

### 3.3.4 Chinese Remainder Theorem and Gauss’s Algorithm

The Chinese remainder theorem (CRT) was introduced in the 3rd century. It provides a powerful tool for solving problems involving congruences. In particular, the CRT helps solving congruences including large numbers (see Exercise 3.26).

**Example 3.41**

 <math alttext="StartLayout Enlarged left-brace 1st Row StartLayout 1st Row x identical-to 1 m o d 5 2nd Row x identical-to 2 m o d 7 EndLayout 2nd Row StartLayout 1st Row x identical-to 3 m o d 9 2nd Row x identical-to 4 m o d 11 EndLayout EndLayout" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>2</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>3</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>9</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>4</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow></math> ![StartLayout Enlarged left-brace 1st Row StartLayout 1st Row x identical-to 1 m o d 5 2nd Row x identical-to 2 m o d 7 EndLayout 2nd Row StartLayout 1st Row x identical-to 3 m o d 9 2nd Row x identical-to 4 m o d 11 EndLayout EndLayout](images/c03_1216.png)

In the equation system above,  <math alttext="n 1 equals 5 comma n 2 equals 7 comma n 3 equals 9 comma n 4 equals 11" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow></math> ![n 1 equals 5 comma n 2 equals 7 comma n 3 equals 9 comma n 4 equals 11](images/c03_1217.png),  <math alttext="a 1 equals 1 comma a 2 equals 2 comma a 3 equals 3 comma" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![a 1 equals 1 comma a 2 equals 2 comma a 3 equals 3 comma](images/c03_1218.png) and  <math alttext="a 4 equals 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![a 4 equals 4](images/c03_1219.png). All  <math alttext="n Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![n Subscript i](images/c03_1220.png)’s are pairwise coprime and  <math alttext="0 less-than-or-equal-to a Subscript i Baseline less-than n Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![0 less-than-or-equal-to a Subscript i Baseline less-than n Subscript i](images/c03_1221.png) for every *i*.  <math alttext="x equals 1731" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1731</mn></mrow></math> ![x equals 1731](images/c03_1222.png) is a solution, since:

1.   <math alttext="1731 less-than 5 asterisk 7 asterisk 9 asterisk 11 equals 3465" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1731</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3465</mn></mrow></math> ![1731 less-than 5 asterisk 7 asterisk 9 asterisk 11 equals 3465](images/c03_1223.png)
2.   <math alttext="1731 identical-to 1 m o d 5" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1731</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> ![1731 identical-to 1 m o d 5](images/c03_1224.png)   <math alttext="1731 identical-to 3 m o d 9" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1731</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>9</mn></mrow></math> ![1731 identical-to 3 m o d 9](images/c03_1225.png)   <math alttext="1731 identical-to 4 m o d 11" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1731</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn></mrow></math> ![1731 identical-to 4 m o d 11](images/c03_1226.png)

*   **Gauss’s algorithm**

The Chinese remainder theorem says that there is a unique solution when some conditions are met, but it does not say how to find it. This is usually done using Gauss’s algorithm.

Given a system of *k* congruence equations that fulfill the conditions of application of Chinese remainder theorem, Gauss’s algorithm finds the solution to the congruence equation system as follows:

**Example 3.42** Find *x* for the following congruence equation system using Gauss’s algorithm.

 <math alttext="StartLayout Enlarged left-brace 1st Row StartLayout 1st Row x identical-to 1 m o d 5 2nd Row x identical-to 2 m o d 7 EndLayout 2nd Row StartLayout 1st Row x identical-to 3 m o d 9 2nd Row x identical-to 4 m o d 11 EndLayout EndLayout" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>2</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>3</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>9</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>4</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow></mrow></math> ![StartLayout Enlarged left-brace 1st Row StartLayout 1st Row x identical-to 1 m o d 5 2nd Row x identical-to 2 m o d 7 EndLayout 2nd Row StartLayout 1st Row x identical-to 3 m o d 9 2nd Row x identical-to 4 m o d 11 EndLayout EndLayout](images/c03_1236.png)

The constants of the congruence equation system are:

 <math alttext="a 1 equals 1 comma a 2 equals 2 comma a 3 equals 3 comma a 4 equals 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![a 1 equals 1 comma n a 2 equals 2 comma a 3 equals 3 comma a 4 equals 4](images/c03_1237a.png)   <math alttext="a 1 equals 1 comma a 2 equals 2 comma a 3 equals 3 comma a 4 equals 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![a 1 equals 1 comma a 2 equals 2 comma a 3 equals 3 comma a 4 equals 4](images/c03_1237.png)

All  <math alttext="n Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![n Subscript i](images/c03_1238.png)’s are pairwise coprime and  <math alttext="a Subscript i Baseline less-than n Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![a Subscript i Baseline less-than n Subscript i](images/c03_1239.png), for every *i*. Therefore, the conditions to use the Chinese remainder theorem are met.

Steps of calculation of *x* using Gauss’s algorithm:

*   Common modulus *N* = 5 \* 7 \* 9 \* 11 = 3465
*    <math alttext="upper N 1 equals StartFraction 3465 Over 5 EndFraction equals 693 comma upper N 2 equals StartFraction 3465 Over 7 EndFraction equals 495 comma upper N 3 equals StartFraction 3465 Over 9 EndFraction equals 385 comma upper N 4 equals StartFraction 3465 Over 11 EndFraction equals 315" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3465</mn></mrow><mn>5</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>693</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3465</mn></mrow><mn>7</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>495</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3465</mn></mrow><mn>9</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>385</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3465</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>315</mn></mrow></math> ![upper N 1 equals StartFraction 3465 Over 5 EndFraction equals 693 comma upper N 2 equals StartFraction 3465 Over 7 EndFraction equals 495 comma upper N 3 equals StartFraction 3465 Over 9 EndFraction equals 385 comma upper N 4 equals StartFraction 3465 Over 11 EndFraction equals 315](images/c03_1240.png)

### 3.3.5 Finding Modular Square Roots

#### 3.3.5.1 Tonelli-Shanks Algorithm for Finding Modular Square Roots of Primes

The most commonly used algorithm to find modular square roots, i.e. to solve congruence of the form  <math alttext="r squared identical-to a m o d p comma when p identical-to 1 m o d 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mi>a</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;when&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![r squared identical-to a m o d p comma when p identical-to 1 m o d 4](images/c03_1251.png) is Tonelli-Shanks algorithm \[[10](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0010)\]. Pseudocode of the latter is as follows:

**Example 3.43** Find the square roots of  <math alttext="111 m o d 113" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>111</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>113</mn></mrow></math> ![111 m o d 113](images/c03_1270.png).

*   – Check, by Euler’s criterion (Theorem 3.7), that a square root exists:
    
     <math alttext="111 Superscript StartFraction 113 minus 1 Over 2 EndFraction Baseline m o d 113 equals 111 Superscript 56 Baseline m o d 113 equals left-parenthesis left-parenthesis negative 2 right-parenthesis Superscript 56 Baseline right-parenthesis m o d 113 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mrow><mn>111</mn></mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>113</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>111</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>56</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>56</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![111 Superscript StartFraction 113 minus 1 Over 2 EndFraction Baseline m o d 113 equals 111 Superscript 56 Baseline m o d 113 equals left-parenthesis left-parenthesis negative 2 right-parenthesis Superscript 56 Baseline right-parenthesis m o d 113 equals 1](images/c03_1271.png). Thus, there exists a solution.
    
*   –  <math alttext="113 equals 2 Superscript 4 Baseline asterisk 7 plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>\*</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![113 equals 2 Superscript 4 Baseline asterisk 7 plus 1](images/c03_1272.png). Thus,  <math alttext="s equals 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![s equals 4](images/c03_1273.png) and  <math alttext="q equals 7" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> ![q equals 7](images/c03_1274.png).
*   – Selection of a quadratic nonresidue *u* using an iterative search:
    
    Check element 1:  <math alttext="1 Superscript StartFraction 113 minus 1 Over 2 EndFraction Baseline m o d 113 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>1</mn><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>113</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![1 Superscript StartFraction 113 minus 1 Over 2 EndFraction Baseline m o d 113 equals 1](images/c03_1275.png). Thus, 1 is a quadratic residue.
    
    Check element 2:  <math alttext="2 Superscript StartFraction 113 minus 1 Over 2 EndFraction Baseline m o d 113 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>113</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript StartFraction 113 minus 1 Over 2 EndFraction Baseline m o d 113 equals 1](images/c03_1276.png). Thus, 2 is a quadratic residue.
    
    Check element  <math alttext="r squared identical-to a m o d p comma when p identical-to 1 m o d 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mi>a</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;when&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![r squared identical-to a m o d p comma when p identical-to 1 m o d 4](images/c03_1277.png). Thus, 3 is a quadratic nonresidue. We keep  <math alttext="u equals 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![u equals 3](images/c03_1279.png).

         <math alttext="b equals 40 Superscript 2 Super Superscript left-parenthesis 4 minus 2 minus 1 right-parenthesis Superscript Baseline m o d 113 equals 40 squared m o d 113 equals 18" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>40</mn></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>40</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>18</mn></mrow></math> ![b equals 40 Superscript 2 Super Superscript left-parenthesis 4 minus 2 minus 1 right-parenthesis Superscript Baseline m o d 113 equals 40 squared m o d 113 equals 18](images/c03_1287.png)
        
         <math alttext="m equals 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![m equals 2](images/c03_1288.png)
        
         <math alttext="c equals 18 squared m o d 113 equals 98" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>18</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>98</mn></mrow></math> ![c equals 18 squared m o d 113 equals 98](images/c03_1289.png)
        
         <math alttext="t equals 98 asterisk 18 squared m o d 113 equals 112" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>98</mn><mo>\*</mo><msup><mrow><mn>18</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>112</mn></mrow></math> ![t equals 98 asterisk 18 squared m o d 113 equals 112](images/c03_1290.png)
        
         <math alttext="upper R equals 16 asterisk 18 m o d 113 equals 62" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>18</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>62</mn></mrow></math> ![upper R equals 16 asterisk 18 m o d 113 equals 62](images/c03_1291.png)
        
    2.  Iteration 2: *t* is not equal to 1. Hence, computations continue

Thus,  <math alttext="k equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![k equals 1](images/c03_1293.png).
        
         <math alttext="b equals 98 Superscript 2 Super Superscript left-parenthesis 2 minus 1 minus 1 right-parenthesis Superscript Baseline m o d 113 equals 98 Superscript 2 Super Superscript 0 Superscript Baseline m o d 113 equals 98" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>98</mn></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>98</mn></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>0</mn></msup></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>98</mn></mrow></math> ![b equals 98 Superscript 2 Super Superscript left-parenthesis 2 minus 1 minus 1 right-parenthesis Superscript Baseline m o d 113 equals 98 Superscript 2 Super Superscript 0 Superscript Baseline m o d 113 equals 98](images/c03_1294.png)
        
         <math alttext="m equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![m equals 1](images/c03_1295.png)
        
         <math alttext="c equals 98 squared m o d 113 equals 112" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>98</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>112</mn></mrow></math> ![c equals 98 squared m o d 113 equals 112](images/c03_1296.png)
        
         <math alttext="t equals 112 asterisk 98 squared m o d 113 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>112</mn><mo>\*</mo><msup><mrow><mn>98</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![t equals 112 asterisk 98 squared m o d 113 equals 1](images/c03_1297.png)
