***Problem* ***4.2*****

Euler’s theorem states that if  <math alttext="a element-of double-struck upper Z Subscript n Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![a element-of double-struck upper Z Subscript n Superscript asterisk](images/c04_281.png), then  <math alttext="a Superscript left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis Baseline identical-to 1 m o d n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![a Superscript left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis Baseline identical-to 1 m o d n](images/c04_282.png), which can be written as  <math alttext="a asterisk a Superscript left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis minus 1 Baseline 1 m o d n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![a asterisk a Superscript left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis minus 1 Baseline 1 m o d n](images/c04_283.png). Using the definition of multiplicative inverse, we can derive that  <math alttext="a Superscript left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![a Superscript left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis minus 1](images/c04_284.png) is the inverse of *a*.

By definition of Euler’s totient (Theorem 3.1),  <math alttext="phi left-parenthesis 26 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 13 minus 1 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis 2 minus 1 right-parenthesis equals 12" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#981;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>26</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>13</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow></math> ![phi left-parenthesis 26 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 13 minus 1 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis 2 minus 1 right-parenthesis equals 12](images/c04_285.png).

Therefore, using Euler’s theorem (Theorem 3.4),  <math alttext="a Superscript negative 1 Baseline identical-to a Superscript 12 minus 1 Baseline m o d 26 identical-to a Superscript 11 Baseline m o d 26" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>26</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>26</mn></mrow></math> ![a Superscript negative 1 Baseline identical-to a Superscript 12 minus 1 Baseline m o d 26 identical-to a Superscript 11 Baseline m o d 26](images/c04_286.png).

***Problem*** ***4.3***

Recall that in affine ciphers, letters are mapped to integers, which represent letter indices in the alphabet. In order to decrypt, affine ciphers do calculations over multiplicative group  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript m Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript m Superscript asterisk](images/c04_287.png), where  <math alttext="m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![m](images/c04_288.png) denotes the number of letters in alphabet. An affine function is defined by:  <math alttext="y equals a x plus b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![y equals a x plus b](images/c04_289.png); the slope  <math alttext="a element-of StartAbsoluteValue double-struck upper Z Subscript m Superscript asterisk Baseline EndAbsoluteValue" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![a element-of StartAbsoluteValue double-struck upper Z Subscript m Superscript asterisk Baseline EndAbsoluteValue](images/c04_290.png) and the intercept  <math alttext="b element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 comma ellipsis comma m minus 1 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![b element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 comma ellipsis comma m minus 1 EndSet](images/c04_291.png). A key is a pair  <math alttext="left-parenthesis a comma b right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis a comma b right-parenthesis](images/c04_292.png). Therefore, the number of distinct keys is  <math alttext="StartAbsoluteValue double-struck upper Z Subscript m Superscript asterisk Baseline EndAbsoluteValue asterisk m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>\*</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![StartAbsoluteValue double-struck upper Z Subscript m Superscript asterisk Baseline EndAbsoluteValue asterisk m](images/c04_293.png).

Assume that we start with an alphabet of 13 letters. Hence,  <math alttext="m equals 13" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow></math> ![m equals 13](images/c04_294.png). Since 13 is prime, the cardinality of  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z 13 Superscript asterisk Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mrow><mn>13</mn></mrow><mo>\*</mo></msubsup><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z 13 Superscript asterisk Baseline](images/c04_295.png) is of 12. Therefore, the slope *a* can take any of the 12 values of  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z 13 Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mrow><mn>13</mn></mrow><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z 13 Superscript asterisk](images/c04_296.png), i.e.  <math alttext="a element-of StartSet 1 comma 2 comma 3 comma ellipsis comma 12 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![a element-of StartSet 1 comma 2 comma 3 comma ellipsis comma 12 EndSet](images/c04_297.png). The intercept *b* is any value in  <math alttext="StartSet 0 comma 1 comma 2 comma 3 comma ellipsis comma 12 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 0 comma 1 comma 2 comma 3 comma ellipsis comma 12 EndSet](images/c04_298.png). Therefore, the number of combinations of the key is  <math alttext="12 asterisk 13 equals 156" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>156</mn></mrow></math> ![12 asterisk 13 equals 156](images/c04_299.png).

Now, assume that we widen the alphabet to 18 letters. First, compute  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z 18 Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mrow><mn>18</mn></mrow><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z 18 Superscript asterisk](images/c04_300.png). (See how to find the elements of a multiplicative finite field in Section 3.2.2):  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z 18 Superscript asterisk Baseline equals StartSet 1 comma 5 comma 7 comma 11 comma 13 comma 17 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mrow><mn>18</mn></mrow><mo>\*</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z 18 Superscript asterisk Baseline equals StartSet 1 comma 5 comma 7 comma 11 comma 13 comma 17 EndSet](images/c04_301.png).

With the second alphabet, the slope *a* can take any of the six values of  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z 18 Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mrow><mn>18</mn></mrow><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z 18 Superscript asterisk](images/c04_302.png), while the intercept *b* can take any value in  <math alttext="StartSet 0 comma 1 comma 2 comma 3 comma ellipsis comma 17 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>17</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 0 comma 1 comma 2 comma 3 comma ellipsis comma 17 EndSet](images/c04_303.png). Hence, the number of combinations of the key is  <math alttext="6 asterisk 18 equals 108" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>18</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>108</mn></mrow></math> ![6 asterisk 18 equals 108](images/c04_304.png).

Therefore, the number of attempts, in a brute-force attack, is larger with a smaller alphabet.

***Problem*** ***4.4***

Let  <math alttext="upper M Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript j](images/c04_305.png) and  <math alttext="upper K Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript j](images/c04_306.png) denote the *j*^(th) letter of the plaintext and the <math alttext="j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>j</mi></mrow></math> ![j](images/c04_307.png)^(th) letter of expanded key, respectively.

If the plaintext is used as a key in Vigenere’s ciphering, then  <math alttext="upper K Subscript j Baseline equals upper M Subscript j Baseline comma for 0 less-than-or-equal-to j less-than-or-equal-to l e n g t h left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;for&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>j</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript j Baseline equals upper M Subscript j Baseline comma for 0 less-than-or-equal-to j less-than-or-equal-to l e n g t h left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis](images/c04_308.png). Vigenere’s encryption for letter  <math alttext="upper M Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript j](images/c04_309.png) is

 <math alttext="upper M prime Subscript j Baseline equals left-parenthesis upper M Subscript j Baseline plus upper K Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis m o d 26 equals left-parenthesis 2 upper M Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis m o d 26" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>'</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>26</mn><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>26</mn></mrow></math> ![upper M prime Subscript j Baseline equals left-parenthesis upper M Subscript j Baseline plus upper K Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis m o d 26 equals left-parenthesis 2 upper M Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis m o d 26](images/c04_310.png)

Therefore,  <math alttext="upper M Subscript j Baseline equals 2 Superscript negative 1 Baseline upper M prime Subscript j m o d 26" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msubsup><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>'</mo></msubsup><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>26</mn></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript j Baseline equals 2 Superscript negative 1 Baseline upper M prime Subscript j m o d 26](images/c04_311.png) is used as decryption function by the adversary to recover the plaintext.

In general, it is recommended not to use English texts as keys when encrypting with Vigenere’s cipher.

***Problem*** ***4.5***

Let the ciphertext be

KAR KRPYREFKNER DH ADXA. KAR FMFHJF IRFE MRUK KAR IMNR PVNSKFDS F TRRJ FXV FSO PVQRO KV KAR EDQRE. DK UDHARH HFMPVS.

Frequencies of letters in ciphertext are:

| Letters || Frequency || Letters || Frequency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R || 15/92 || M, P, S || 4/92 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| F, K || 10/92 || N || 3/92 |
| A || 7/92 || I, J, O, Q, U, X || 2/92 |
| D || 6/92 || T, Y || 1/92 |
| E, H, V || 5/92 || B, C, G, L, W, Z || 0/92 |

Using the frequency of letters in English texts, the search should start with the highest-frequency letters, that is:

| Letter || Frequency || Letter || Frequency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| e || 12.02 || i || 7.31 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| t || 9.10 || n || 6.95 |
| a || 8.12 || s || 6.28 |
| o || 7.68 || r || 6.02 |

In the ciphertext, the guessed letters are in lower cases. Since there is lot of attempts before disclosing the plaintext, we only show the guesses that lead to recover the plaintext:

*   e, t, or a could be R, F, or K.
    
    Associations R↔e and K↔t lead to
    
    “tAe tePYeEFtNEe DH ADXA. tAe FMFHJF IeFE MeUt tAe IMNe PVNStFDS F TeeJ FXV FSO PVQeO tV tAe EDQeE. Dt UDHAeH HFMPVS”.
    
*   Since two sentences start with tAe, there is a high probability that A is associated with h. F is alone; it is likely to be associated with article a. Associations A↔h and F↔a lead to
    
    “the tePYeEatNEe DH hDXh. the aMaHJa IeaE MeUt the IMNe PVNStaDS a TeeJ aXV aSO PVQeO tV the EDQeE. Dt UDHheH HaMPVS”.
    
*   Next high-frequency letter is o. It may be associated with D, E, H, or V. Association V↔o leads to
    
    “the tePYeEatNEe DH ADXh. the aMaHJa IeaE MeUt the IMNe PoNStaDS a TeeJ aXo aSO PoQeO to the EDQeE. Dt UDHheH HaMPoS”.
    
*   Next high-frequency letter is i. It may be associated with D, because Dt at the beginning of a sentence is likely to be it. Association D↔i leads to
    
    “the tePYeEatNEe iH hiXh. the aMaHJa IeaE MeUt the IMNe PoNStaiS a TeeJ aXo aSO PoQeO to the EiQeE. it UiHheH HaMPoS”.
    
*   The next high frequency letters are n, s, and r; they may be associated with E, H, M, P, and S. Associations E↔r, H↔s, and S↔n lead to
    
    “the tePYeratNre is hiXh. the aMasJa Iear MeUt the IMNe PoNntain a TeeJ aXo anO PoQeO to the riQer. it Uishes saMPon”.
    
*   It is likely that aXo is ago and anO is and. Associations X↔g and O↔d lead to
    
    “the tePYeratNre is high. the aMasJa Iear MeUt the IMNe PoNntain a TeeJ ago and PoQed to the riQer. it Uishes saMPon”.
    
*   From “the tePYeratNre is high” it is likely that P is m, Y is p, and N is u. Associations P↔m, Y↔p, and N↔u lead to
    
    “the temperature is high. the aMasJa Iear MeUt the IMue mountain a TeeJ ago and moQed to the riQer. it Uishes saMmon”.
    
*   The remaining letters have low frequency; hence, many attempts are to do before recovering the plaintext.
    
    If “Uishes” is “fishes”, then “saMmon” is “salmon.” Associations U↔f and M↔l lead to
    
    “the temperature is high. the alasJa Iear left the Ilue mountain a TeeJ ago and moQed to the riQer. it fishes salmon”. “moQed to the riQer” is likely to be “moved to the river”,
    
    Associations Q↔v leads to
    
    “the temperature is high. the alasJa Iear left the Ilue mountain a TeeJ ago and moved to the river. it fishes salmon”.
    
    From the words river, fishes, and salmon, we can guess Alaska and week by associations J↔k and T↔w. The last words to guess are bear and blue.
    
    Therefore, the plaintext was: ”the temperature is high. the alaska bear left the blue mountain a weeJ ago and moved to the river. it fishes salmon”., which has been encrypted with an affine cipher  <math alttext="y equals 3 x plus 5" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> ![y equals 3 x plus 5](images/c04_312.png).
    

***Problem*** ***4.6***

1.  In Caesar’s cipher, any letter *x* is replaced by a letter *y* using formula  <math alttext="y equals x plus k m o d 26" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>26</mn></mrow></math> ![y equals x plus k m o d 26](images/c04_313.png). Therefore, a single letter *x*[1] and its encrypted letter  <math alttext="y 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![y 1](images/c04_314.png) are enough to recover Caesar’s cipher key *k*. That is,  <math alttext="k equals y 1 minus x 1 m o d 26" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>26</mn></mrow></math> ![k equals y 1 minus x 1 m o d 26](images/c04_315.png).
2.  In affine cipher, any letter *x* is replaced by a letter *y* using formula  <math alttext="y equals x plus k m o d 26" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>26</mn></mrow></math> ![y equals x plus k m o d 26](images/c04_316.png), where  <math alttext="a double-struck upper Z 26 Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mrow><mn>26</mn></mrow><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![a double-struck upper Z 26 Superscript asterisk](images/c04_317.png) and  <math alttext="b double-struck upper Z 26" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><msub><mi>&#8484;</mi><mrow><mn>26</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![b double-struck upper Z 26](images/c04_318.png). Therefore, two distinct letters *x*[1] and *x*[2] and their encrypted letters  <math alttext="y 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![y 1](images/c04_319.png) and  <math alttext="y 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![y 2](images/c04_320.png) are enough to recover an affine cipher key  <math alttext="left-parenthesis a comma b right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis a comma b right-parenthesis](images/c04_321.png). That is, given two equations  <math alttext="y 1 equals a x 1 plus b m o d 26" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>26</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![y 1 equals a x 1 plus b m o d 26](images/c04_322.png) and <math alttext="y 2 equals a x 2 plus b m o d 26" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>26</mn></mrow></math> ![y 2 equals a x 2 plus b m o d 26](images/c04_323.png), *a* and *b* are unique.
3.  In Vigenere’s cipher, any letter  <math alttext="upper M Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript j](images/c04_324.png) of message *M* is encrypted using letter  <math alttext="upper K Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript j](images/c04_325.png) of the expanded key, as  <math alttext="upper M prime Subscript j Baseline equals left-parenthesis upper M Subscript j Baseline plus upper K Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis m o d 26 comma 0 j l e n left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>'</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>26</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mi>j</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper M prime Subscript j Baseline equals left-parenthesis upper M Subscript j Baseline plus upper K Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis m o d 26 comma 0 j l e n left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis](images/c04_326.png). Thus,  <math alttext="upper M prime Subscript j Baseline minus upper M Subscript j Baseline equals upper K Subscript j Baseline m o d 26" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>'</mo></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>26</mn></mrow></math> ![upper M prime Subscript j Baseline minus upper M Subscript j Baseline equals upper K Subscript j Baseline m o d 26](images/c04_327.png). Therefore, *L* distinct pairs of letters and their encryptions are enough to recover a Vigenere’s cipher key of length *L*.

***Problem*** ***4.7***

Let *n* be the number of rotors installed in an Enigma machine, where  <math alttext="n equals StartSet 3 comma 4 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![n equals StartSet 3 comma 4 EndSet](images/c04_328.png). Let  <math alttext="r Subscript n Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![r Subscript n Baseline](images/c04_329.png) and  <math alttext="r 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![r 1](images/c04_330.png) denote the leftmost and rightmost rotors, respectively.

If all rotors have a single notch, then each rotor *r[i+1]* makes a step when rotor *r[i]* finishes a full revolution. Therefore, Enigma returns to its start position after pressing  <math alttext="26 Superscript n Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>26</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![26 Superscript n Baseline](images/c04_332.png) keys.

As mentioned previously, some rotors may have two (or even more) notches. If a rotor  <math alttext="r Subscript i Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![r Subscript i Baseline](images/c04_333.png) has two notches, then in a full revolution, it triggers two steps of rotor  <math alttext="r Subscript i plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![r Subscript i plus 1](images/c04_334.png). Thus, rotor  <math alttext="r Subscript i plus 1 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![r Subscript i plus 1 Baseline](images/c04_335.png) makes a full revolution after 13 full revolutions of rotor  <math alttext="r Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![r Subscript i](images/c04_336.png). Therefore, the period of ciphering alphabet of Enigma with *n* rotors is  <math alttext="StartFraction 26 Superscript n Baseline Over product Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n minus 1 Endscripts c Subscript i Baseline EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>26</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mstyle displaystyle="true" mathsize="140%"><mo>&#8719;</mo></mstyle><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![StartFraction 26 Superscript n Baseline Over product Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n minus 1 Endscripts c Subscript i Baseline EndFraction](images/c04_337.png), where  <math alttext="c Subscript i Baseline element-of StartSet 1 comma 2 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![c Subscript i Baseline element-of StartSet 1 comma 2 EndSet](images/c04_338.png) denotes the number of notches of rotor  <math alttext="r Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![r Subscript i](images/c04_339.png). Therefore, doubling the notches on rotors reduces the security strength of ciphering.

***Problem* ***4.8*****

Let  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper M 1 comma upper C 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper M 1 comma upper C 1 right-parenthesis](images/c04_340.png) and  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper M 2 comma upper C 2 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper M 2 comma upper C 2 right-parenthesis](images/c04_341.png) be two pairs of plaintext–ciphertext. The same OTP key *k* is used to encrypt both plaintexts. Hence,  <math alttext="upper C 1 equals upper M 1 circled-plus k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>k</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper C 1 equals upper M 1 circled-plus k](images/c04_342.png) and  <math alttext="upper C 2 equals upper M Subscript 2 Baseline circled-plus k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C 2 equals upper M Subscript 2 Baseline circled-plus k](images/c04_343.png) and  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper M 2 comma upper C 2 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper M 2 comma upper C 2 right-parenthesis](images/c04_345.png) are known to the adversary. Thus, the latter can compute:

 <math alttext="StartLayout 1st Row upper C 1 circled-plus upper C 2 equals left-parenthesis upper M 1 circled-plus k right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper M 2 circled-plus k right-parenthesis 2nd Row equals left-parenthesis upper M 1 circled-plus upper M 2 right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis k circled-plus k right-parenthesis equals upper M 1 circled-plus upper M 2 EndLayout" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mtable columnalign="left"><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> ![StartLayout 1st Row upper C 1 circled-plus upper C 2 equals left-parenthesis upper M 1 circled-plus k right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper M 2 circled-plus k right-parenthesis 2nd Row equals left-parenthesis upper M 1 circled-plus upper M 2 right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis k circled-plus k right-parenthesis equals upper M 1 circled-plus upper M 2 EndLayout](images/c04_346.png)

Notice that to recover both plaintexts, the latter must be of the same bit-length.

Let  <math alttext="upper M Subscript 1 comma i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript 1 comma i](images/c04_347.png) and  <math alttext="upper M Subscript 2 comma i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript 2 comma i](images/c04_348.png) denote letter *i* in plaintexts  <math alttext="upper M 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 1](images/c04_349.png) and  <math alttext="upper M 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 2](images/c04_350.png), respectively. Also, let  <math alttext="l e f t Baseline 3 left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>t</mi><mn>3</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![l e f t Baseline 3 left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis](images/c04_351.png) denote the three leftmost bits of a 7-bit ASCII letter  <math alttext="l" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> ![l](images/c04_352.png).

Without loss of generality, we only focus on uppercase letters and space. Recall the ASCII codes (in Hexadecimal): space  <math alttext="right-arrow 20 Subscript 16 Baseline comma upper A right-arrow 41 Subscript 16 Baseline comma upper B right-arrow 42 Subscript 16 Baseline comma upper O right-arrow 4 upper F 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8594;</mo><msub><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>A</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8594;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mrow><mn>41</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>B</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8594;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mrow><mn>42</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>O</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8594;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![right-arrow 20 Subscript 16 Baseline comma upper A right-arrow 41 Subscript 16 Baseline comma upper B right-arrow 42 Subscript 16 Baseline comma upper O right-arrow 4 upper F 16](images/c04_353.png),  <math alttext="right-arrow 50 Subscript 16 Baseline comma ellipsis comma" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8594;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mrow><mn>50</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![right-arrow 50 Subscript 16 Baseline comma ellipsis comma](images/c04_354.png)  <math alttext="right-arrow upper Y 59 Subscript 16 Baseline comma upper Z right-arrow 5 upper A 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8594;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>Y</mi><msub><mrow><mn>59</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>Z</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8594;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![right-arrow upper Y 59 Subscript 16 Baseline comma upper Z right-arrow 5 upper A 16](images/c04_355.png). The ASCII code has some characteristics that can serve the adversary to speed up the attack (i.e. recover plaintexts):

*   If  <math alttext="upper M Subscript 1 comma i Baseline circled-plus upper M Subscript 2 comma i Baseline equals 00" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>00</mn></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript 1 comma i Baseline circled-plus upper M Subscript 2 comma i Baseline equals 00](images/c04_356.png), then  <math alttext="upper M Subscript 1 comma i Baseline equals upper M Subscript 2 comma i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript 1 comma i Baseline equals upper M Subscript 2 comma i](images/c04_357.png). Therefore, recovering a letter in one ciphertext results in recovering the same letter in the other ciphertext.
*   Space code is  <math alttext="20 Subscript 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![20 Subscript 16](images/c04_358.png), having a single 1-bit, and the codes of uppercase letters are greater than  <math alttext="41 Subscript 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mrow><mn>41</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![41 Subscript 16](images/c04_359.png). If  <math alttext="upper M Subscript 1 comma i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript 1 comma i](images/c04_360.png) and  <math alttext="upper M Subscript 2 comma i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript 2 comma i](images/c04_361.png) are two letters, then  <math alttext="upper M Subscript 1 comma i Baseline circled-plus upper M Subscript 2 comma i Baseline less-than 1 upper A 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript 1 comma i Baseline circled-plus upper M Subscript 2 comma i Baseline less-than 1 upper A 16](images/c04_362.png). If  <math alttext="upper M Subscript 1 comma i Baseline circled-plus upper M Subscript 2 comma i Baseline ampersand gt semicolon 20 Subscript 16 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#38;gt;</mo><msub><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript 1 comma i Baseline circled-plus upper M Subscript 2 comma i Baseline ampersand gt semicolon 20 Subscript 16 Baseline](images/c04_363.png), then either  <math alttext="upper M Subscript 1 comma i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript 1 comma i](images/c04_364.png) or  <math alttext="upper M Subscript 2 comma i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript 2 comma i](images/c04_365.png) is a space. Hence,  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper M Subscript 1 comma i Baseline circled-plus upper M Subscript 2 comma i Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus 20 Subscript 16 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper M Subscript 1 comma i Baseline circled-plus upper M Subscript 2 comma i Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus 20 Subscript 16 Baseline](images/c04_366.png) is a letter included in one plaintext; and the other plaintext has a space at the same position. Example,  <math alttext="5 upper A 16 circled-plus 20 Subscript 16 Baseline equals 3 upper A 16 ampersand gt semicolon 20 Subscript 16 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#38;gt;</mo><msub><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![5 upper A 16 circled-plus 20 Subscript 16 Baseline equals 3 upper A 16 ampersand gt semicolon 20 Subscript 16 Baseline](images/c04_367.png). Therefore, one plaintext has a letter *Z* and the other has a space. Such a property is very useful to speed up the attack, since spaces are very frequent in English text (nearly 19% of characters are spaces). In addition, spaces are unlikely to occur at the same positions in distinct plaintexts, which results in more letters recovered in both ciphertexts.
*   Codes of letters *A* to *O* start with 100, while codes of letters *P* to *Z* start with 101. If  <math alttext="l e f t Baseline 3 left-parenthesis upper M Subscript 1 comma i Baseline circled-plus upper M Subscript 2 comma i Baseline right-parenthesis equals 000" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>t</mi><mn>3</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow></math> ![l e f t Baseline 3 left-parenthesis upper M Subscript 1 comma i Baseline circled-plus upper M Subscript 2 comma i Baseline right-parenthesis equals 000](images/c04_368.png), then both letters  <math alttext="upper M Subscript 1 comma i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript 1 comma i](images/c04_369.png) and  <math alttext="upper M Subscript 2 comma i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript 2 comma i](images/c04_370.png) are in the same half of alphabet, i.e. either in  <math alttext="left-bracket upper A comma upper O right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow><mo>\]</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![left-bracket upper A comma upper O right-bracket](images/c04_371.png) or in  <math alttext="left-bracket upper P comma upper Z right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket upper P comma upper Z right-bracket](images/c04_372.png). If  <math alttext="l e f t Baseline 3 left-parenthesis upper M Subscript 1 comma i Baseline circled-plus upper M Subscript 2 comma i Baseline right-parenthesis equals 001" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>t</mi><mn>3</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>001</mn></mrow></math> ![l e f t Baseline 3 left-parenthesis upper M Subscript 1 comma i Baseline circled-plus upper M Subscript 2 comma i Baseline right-parenthesis equals 001](images/c04_373.png), then letters  <math alttext="upper M Subscript 1 comma i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript 1 comma i](images/c04_374.png) and  <math alttext="upper M Subscript 2 comma i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript 2 comma i](images/c04_375.png) are not in the same half of alphabet. Such property is useful while testing different letters.

The adversary takes advantage of the ASCII characteristics to automatically recover some letters. Then, he/she applies a crib dragging technique, i.e. guess some words likely to be in the original plaintexts, XOR them with the ciphertexts and derive a part of the key, which, in turn, serves to recover a word in the other ciphertext. Repeat the guess until both plaintexts are recovered.

***Problem*** ***4.9***

1.  Indeed, OTP suffers malleability vulnerability under the man-in-the-middle attack, which can be shown as follows:

Bob sends a ciphertext  <math alttext="upper C 1 equals upper M 1 circled-plus k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C 1 equals upper M 1 circled-plus k](images/c04_376.png) to Alice.

Eve, the adversary, intercepts ciphertext  <math alttext="upper C 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 1](images/c04_377.png) and computes  <math alttext="upper C prime equals upper C 1 circled-plus upper M prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>M</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![upper C prime equals upper C 1 circled-plus upper M prime](images/c04_378.png), where  <math alttext="upper M prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![upper M prime](images/c04_379.png) is either a random or a specific plaintext chosen by Eve.

When Alice receives the ciphertext  <math alttext="upper C prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>C</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> ![upper C prime](images/c04_380.png), she obtains, after decryption, a plaintext  <math alttext="upper M 2 colon upper M 2 equals upper C Superscript prime Baseline circled-plus k equals upper C 1 circled-plus upper M prime circled-plus k equals upper M 1 circled-plus k circled-plus upper M prime circled-plus k equals upper M 1 circled-plus upper M prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>k</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> ![upper M 2 colon upper M 2 equals upper C Superscript prime Baseline circled-plus k equals upper C 1 circled-plus upper M prime circled-plus k equals upper M 1 circled-plus k circled-plus upper M prime circled-plus k equals upper M 1 circled-plus upper M prime](images/c04_381.png)

 <math alttext="upper M 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 2](images/c04_382.png) is distinct from  <math alttext="upper M 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 1](images/c04_383.png). Therefore, integrity is no more assured to Alice.

1.  2\. In the ciphertext *C* intercepted by Eve, a value of  <math alttext="1000 Subscript 10 Baseline equals 0011 1110 1000 Subscript 2 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mrow><mn>1000</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0011</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1110</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mrow><mn>1000</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![1000 Subscript 10 Baseline equals 0011 1110 1000 Subscript 2 Baseline](images/c04_384.png) is included starting from bit-position *p*. 3.  [**3**](#c04.xhtml#rc04-note-0003) Rotors numbered VI, VII, and VIII have two, or even more, turnover notches; thus, they trigger two (or more) steps for the rotor on their left after a full revolution. It has been shown that it was not a good idea from security point of view, because double stepping of the rotor on the left reduces the substitution alphabet period.
4.  [**4**](#c04.xhtml#rc04-note-0004) “Six” is the number of rotors arrangements in the earliest versions of Enigma machine.
5.  [**5**](#c04.xhtml#rc04-note-0005) “Randomly selected” means that any key *K* has a probability of  <math alttext="StartFraction 1 Over StartAbsoluteValue script upper K EndAbsoluteValue EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![StartFraction 1 Over StartAbsoluteValue script upper K EndAbsoluteValue EndFraction](images/c04_403.png) to be selected.
6.  [**6**](#c04.xhtml#rc04-note-0006) In the information theory, the *entropy* of a random variable *X*, denoted  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis](images/c04_404.png), is the average level of *uncertainty* inherent in the variable possible outcomes (see [Chapter 16](#c16.xhtml)).
7.  [**7**](#c04.xhtml#rc04-note-0007) In the information theory, the *conditional entropy*, denoted  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper M vertical-bar upper C right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper M vertical-bar upper C right-parenthesis](images/c04_405.png), quantifies the amount of information needed to describe the outcome of a random variable *M* given that the value of another random variable *C* is known.
