# 5   
Hash Functions, Message Authentication Codes, and Digital Signature

This chapter introduces three aspects of cryptography, namely hash functions, Message Authentication Codes, and Digital signature. All of them are of paramount importance for providing integrity and authentication guarantees. Hash functions produce digital fingerprints, also called Message Authentication Codes (MAC), which are used to meet multiple needs:

*   Verifying integrity of messages and files: a hash works like a fingerprint, which uniquely represents data. Thus, any change in an email, a file, a software, an image, and so on, results in a hash, which does not match the hash generated by the sender.
*   Generating and verifying digital signatures,[¹](#c05.xhtml#c05-note-0001) which enable to verify the authenticity of a message. If the encrypted hash is altered, the verification fails and if the message is altered, the hash computed by the recipient does not match the message. In both cases, the message is rejected.
*   Facilitating secure password storage and verification: instead of storing and exchanging passwords, hashes of passwords are stored and used to control local and remote logins.
*   Since hashes look like random values, hash functions may be used as pseudorandom bit generators.

It is worth noticing that MAC algorithms provide stronger assurance of data integrity than a checksum or an error detecting code. The verification of a checksum or an error detecting code is designed to detect only accidental modifications of data, while MAC is designed to detect intentional, unauthorized modifications of data, as well as accidental modifications.

MACs can be generated either by hash functions alone or by block ciphers. The first category of MACs is addressed in this chapter, while block cipher modes of operation that generate MACs are addressed in [Chapter 9](#c09.xhtml).

## 5.1 Hash Functions

***Definition 5.1 Hash function****: it is a mathematical function that takes an arbitrary data input and produces a fixed-size output called a hash value*, *digest*, *hash code, or just hash. A* *hashing algorithm*[²](#c05.xhtml#c05-note-0002) *is an algorithm founded on a hash function and implements hashing operations.*

Formally, a hash function  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>(</mo><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c05_1.png) is defined by:  <math alttext="upper H colon StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript upper N Baseline right-arrow StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>N</mi></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper H colon StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript upper N Baseline right-arrow StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n](images/c05_2.png), where  <math alttext="StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>N</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript upper N](images/c05_3.png) is the set of input space and  <math alttext="StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n](images/c05_4.png) the set of output space. *N* and *n* are the bit-lengths of spaces.  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05_5.png) is the hash or digest of input *x*. In practice *n* is between 160 and 512, while *N* may be very large.[³](#c05.xhtml#c05-note-0003)

Since the input space is much larger than the output space, two distinct inputs  <math alttext="x and x prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mtext>&#160;and&#160;</mtext><mi>x</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![x and x prime](images/c05_6.png) may result in the same output, which is a circumstance called *collision*. The larger the number of possible hashes, the smaller the chance that two values will create the same hash. In existing hash functions, collisions are unavoidable, but the probability of collision occurrence should be minimized.

### 5.1.1 Properties of Hash Functions

In order not to compromise either the security or the performance of the underlying systems, hash functions should possess the following properties:

*   *Determinism*: the same input always results in the same output.
*   *Efficiency*: the computation of hash value should be low.
*   *Security*: hash functions should be practically irreversible (i.e. one-way) in order to be attack resistant.

*   ***Preimage resistance***

This property means given a hash value *z*, it should be computationally infeasible to find an input value *x* that hashes to *z*. Formally:

 <math alttext="for-all z element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n Baseline comma upper P r left-parenthesis upper F i n d i n g x vertical-bar x element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript upper N Baseline comma upper H left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals z right-parenthesis approximately-equals 0" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>z</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>F</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>x</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>N</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8195;</mtext><mtext>&#8195;</mtext><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8773;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![for-all z element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n Baseline comma upper P r left-parenthesis upper F i n d i n g x vertical-bar x element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript upper N Baseline comma upper H left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals z right-parenthesis approximately-equals 0](images/c05_7.png)

 <math alttext="probability left-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>Pr</mtext><mo>(</mo><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![probability left-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c05_8.png) denotes probability. Preimage resistance property of hash function protects against an attacker who has a hash and wants to find the associated data. For example, the attack would be the recovery of a password from the hash of the password.

*   ***Second preimage resistance*** (also referred to as *weak collision resistance*)

This property means given an input *x*[1], it is computationally infeasible to find an input *x*[2] distinct from *x*[1] with the same hash. Formally:

 <math alttext="for-all x 1 element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript upper N Baseline comma upper P r left-parenthesis upper F i n d i n g x 2 vertical-bar x 2 element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript upper N Baseline comma x 1 not-equals x 2 comma upper H left-parenthesis x 1 right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis x 2 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis approximately-equals 0" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8704;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>N</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>F</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>N</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8195;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8195;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8773;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![for-all x 1 element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript upper N Baseline comma upper P r left-parenthesis upper F i n d i n g x 2 vertical-bar x 2 element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript upper N Baseline comma x 1 not-equals x 2 comma upper H left-parenthesis x 1 right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis x 2 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis approximately-equals 0](images/c05_9.png)

Second preimage resistance property of hash function protects against an attacker who has an input value and its hash and wants to substitute a forged value to the original input value. In other words, pre-image resistance preserves data integrity.

*   ***Collision resistance***

This property means it should be computationally infeasible to find any two inputs that result in the same hash. Formally:

 <math alttext="upper P r left-parenthesis upper F i n d i n g x 1 comma x 2 vertical-bar x 1 comma x 2 element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript upper N Baseline comma upper H left-parenthesis x 1 right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis x 2 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis approximately-equals 0" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>F</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>N</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8773;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper P r left-parenthesis upper F i n d i n g x 1 comma x 2 vertical-bar x 1 comma x 2 element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript upper N Baseline comma upper H left-parenthesis x 1 right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis x 2 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis approximately-equals 0](images/c05_10.png)

Notice that if a hash function is collision-resistant, then it is second preimage resistant (see Problem 5.7). Collision resistance prevents from creating two distinct data or messages with the same hash. For example, in password management systems, hashes are associated with passwords. Passwords are supplied to users when they register and hashes are stored in the password file in the authentication system. When a user tries to log in the system, he/she provides his/her password, then the verification system computes the hash of the password entered by the user and compares it to the one stored in the password hash file. Consequently, distinct hashes should be associated to distinct passwords; otherwise, a user may be admitted to access a service granted to another user.

Even the hash functions, which have been considered secure for a long time, may have collisions. For example, [Figure 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0001) shows a collision attack against MD5, a hash function widely used in the past. Two documents, File1.ps and File2.ps, with distinct contents have the same MD5 hash.

![Figure 5.1 Example of collision attack against MD5. MD5(File1.ps) = a25f7f0b29ee0b3968c860738533a4b9. MD5(File2.ps) = a25f7f0b29ee0b3968c860738533a4b9. From: http://web.archive.org/web/20071226014140 /http://www.cits.rub.de/MD5Collisions.](images/c05f001.png)

[**Figure 5.1**](#c05.xhtml#rc05-fig-0001) Example of collision attack against MD5. MD5(File1.ps) = a25f7f0b29ee0b3968c860738533a4b9. MD5(File2.ps) = a25f7f0b29ee0b3968c860738533a4b9. *From*: [http://web.archive.org/web/20071226014140](http://web.archive.org/web/20071226014140) /[http://www.cits.rub.de/MD5Collisions](http://www.cits.rub.de/MD5Collisions).

The output of hash functions used in operational cryptosystems looks like[⁴](#c05.xhtml#c05-note-0004) a random string and any small change (of one bit or one byte) results in entirely different hash. Below are three examples of hashes produced by SHA256 algorithm associated with two strings “Hello” and “hello” which have major differences:

SHA256(“Hello”) = 185f8db32271fe25f561a6fc938b2e264306ec304eda518007d1764826381969  
SHA256(“hello”) = 2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824

### 5.1.2 Generic Attacks Against Hash Functions

A generic attack is an attack that tries to break hash functions without any knowledge of their internal structure. In other words, generic attacks apply to all hash functions, while specific attacks take advantage of the internal structure of hash functions. By internal structure, we mean for example the number of rounds and the forms of block transformation operations.

Attacks against hash functions are directly linked to resistance properties. Thus, attacks against hash functions are categorized into three classes:

1.  Collision attacks aiming to find a hash collision.
2.  Preimage attacks aiming to recover a data given its hash (for example, recovering a password once its hash has been intercepted).
3.  Second preimage attacks aiming to alter the content of message while keeping its hash.

The number of steps[⁵](#c05.xhtml#c05-note-0005) of a generic attack is the number of hash function tries before breaking the hash function. The best known generic (second) preimage attack is brute-force attack, which requires 2^n steps and the best known collision attack is birthday attack, which requires  <math alttext="2 Superscript left-parenthesis n plus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript left-parenthesis n plus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2](images/c05_11.png) steps, where 2^n denotes the cardinality of the hash space. Proof of attack complexity is addressed in Problems 5.13 and 5.14.

It is worth noticing that in literature,  <math alttext="2 Superscript left-parenthesis n plus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2 Baseline equals 2 Superscript 1 slash 2 Baseline asterisk 2 Superscript n slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript left-parenthesis n plus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2 Baseline equals 2 Superscript 1 slash 2 Baseline asterisk 2 Superscript n slash 2](images/c05_12.png) is often approximated by  <math alttext="2 Superscript n slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript n slash 2](images/c05_13.png), when *n* is large. Therefore, the security strength of hash functions to resist to all three forms of generic attacks is  <math alttext="min left-parenthesis 2 Superscript n slash 2 Baseline comma 2 Superscript n Baseline right-parenthesis equals 2 Superscript n slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>min</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![min left-parenthesis 2 Superscript n slash 2 Baseline comma 2 Superscript n Baseline right-parenthesis equals 2 Superscript n slash 2](images/c05_14.png).

### 5.1.3 Overall Operation Principle of Hashing Algorithms

There are many hashing algorithms used by services and applications with different security and performance requirements. The most popular hashing algorithms include:

*   SHA family (SHA-0, SHA-1, SHA-2, SHA-3)
*   MD family (MD2, MD3, MD4, MD5, MD6)
*   Blake family (Blake1, Blake2, Blake3)
*   RIPEMD, Tiger, Whirlpool, etc.

MD5 (Message Digest 5) was the most popular and widely used hash function for many years. It was adopted as an internet standard. In 2004, collisions were found in MD5. Published collision-attacks showed that MD5 is not entirely secure and hence it is no longer recommended. [Figure 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0001) shows an example of MD5 collision.

#### 5.1.3.1 Merkle-Damgård Construction

Most hashing algorithms, including MD5, SHA-1, and SHA-2, are designed according to model known as Merkle-Damgård construction \[[1](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0001), [2](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0002)\], which operates as follows (see [Figure 5.2](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0002)):

![Figure 5.2 Overall operation of hashing algorithm.](images/c05f002.png)

[**Figure 5.2**](#c05.xhtml#rc05-fig-0002) Overall operation of hashing algorithm.

*   Padding bytes are appended to the data so that the length of padded data is multiple of a chosen block bit-length *L*. Padding bits are appended to the end of the initial data in a format known to both parties; so that the verifier of the hash uses the same padding bits. There exist different ways to encode the data length in the padding field depending on hash functions. Then, padded data to hash is divided into *m* blocks *B*¹,  <math alttext="upper B squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![upper B squared](images/c05_15.png), …,  <math alttext="upper B Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper B Superscript m](images/c05_16.png) of equal length *L*.
*   Each block is hashed separately with additional input as follows:

Block *B*¹: the hash function takes a combination of *B*¹ and an initialization value, also known as initialization vector ( <math alttext="upper I upper V" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> ![upper I upper V](images/c05_17.png)), and returns a hash value *H*¹. Block *i* ( <math alttext="i equals 2 comma ellipsis comma m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![i equals 2 comma ellipsis comma m](images/c05_18.png)): the hash function takes a combination of  <math alttext="upper B Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper B Superscript i](images/c05_19.png) and the hash value  <math alttext="upper H Superscript i minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper H Superscript i minus 1](images/c05_20.png) and returns hash value *H*^i.

*   The hash function is a series of rounds and each round is made of a series of transformations (bit string additions, permutations, etc.).
*   The output of the final round of the last block of message is the hash to the entire message. Hash bit-length is denoted *n*.

If any block or the final hash is altered, the final hash computed by the data integrity verifier does not match the data. Hash bit-length *n* is a parameter of hashing algorithms. In existing hashing functions, parameter *n* takes its value form the set  <math alttext="StartSet 128 comma 160 comma 192 comma 224 comma 256 comma 384 comma 512 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>128</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>160</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>192</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>224</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>256</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>384</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>512</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 128 comma 160 comma 192 comma 224 comma 256 comma 384 comma 512 EndSet](images/c05_21.png). The security and performance of the hashing algorithm are dependent on the hash length. The larger the hash length is, the lower the collision probability is. The larger the hash length is, the higher the hash computation time is.

#### 5.1.3.2 Vulnerability to Length Extension Attack

Some cryptographic algorithms using hash functions based on Merkle-Damgård construction are vulnerable to a specific attack called *length extension attack*. In the latter, the adversary knows a message *M*, a hash  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis k e y StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis k e y StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M right-parenthesis](images/c05_22.png), and the length of  <math alttext="k e y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ![k e y](images/c05_23.png),  <math alttext="l e n left-parenthesis k e y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![l e n left-parenthesis k e y right-parenthesis](images/c05_24.png), but the value of the  <math alttext="k e y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ![k e y](images/c05_25.png) is unknown. Problem 5.15 discusses why the key length is required. For example, after signing a message, the sender transmits the message and the signature, but the private key used to sign is not sent. In a similar way, when MAC (message authentication code) is used, the sender transmits the message and its MAC, but not the key used to generate the MAC. If the three items (*M*,  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis k e y StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis k e y StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M right-parenthesis](images/c05_26.png), and  <math alttext="l e n left-parenthesis k e y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![l e n left-parenthesis k e y right-parenthesis](images/c05_27.png)) are available to an adversary, he/she can extend the original message and generate a hash without using the key. Upon reception, the verifier validates the (forged) message as if it were generated by a legitimate party using the appropriate key.

Below is how the length extension attack can be realized:

When the legitimate party generates  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis k e y StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis k e y StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M right-parenthesis](images/c05_28.png) using the  <math alttext="k e y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ![k e y](images/c05_29.png) known to him/her, a padding string *P* is appended at the end of the string  <math alttext="k e y StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> ![k e y StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M](images/c05_30.png). The length of padding string *P* is such that  <math alttext="l e n left-parenthesis k e y StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper M EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![l e n left-parenthesis k e y StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper M EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P right-parenthesis](images/c05_31.png) is a multiple of the block length *L* of the hash function *H* (e.g.  <math alttext="upper L equals 1024" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1024</mn></mrow></math> ![upper L equals 1024](images/c05_32.png) in case of SHA-2). Then, before hashing, the string  <math alttext="k e y StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper M EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![k e y StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper M EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P](images/c05_33.png) is represented as a sequence of *m* blocks  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper B Superscript 1 Baseline comma upper B squared comma ellipsis comma upper B Superscript m Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>B</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>B</mi><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper B Superscript 1 Baseline comma upper B squared comma ellipsis comma upper B Superscript m Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c05_34.png) with equal length *L*.

Recall that in hash functions based on Merkle-Damgård construction (see [Figure 5.2](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0002)), block *B*¹ and initialization vector  <math alttext="upper I upper V" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> ![upper I upper V](images/c05_35.png), which also is referred to as  <math alttext="upper H Superscript 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![upper H Superscript 0](images/c05_36.png), are used by the hash function to produce *H*¹, then *H*¹ and  <math alttext="upper B squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![upper B squared](images/c05_37.png) are used to produce  <math alttext="upper H squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![upper H squared](images/c05_38.png), …, and finally,  <math alttext="upper H Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>H</mi><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper H Superscript m](images/c05_39.png) represents the hash of the entire message.

Length extension attack assumes that the length of the key is known to the adversary. Thus, the latter can easily compute the padding string *P* and forges a string Ӻ starting with *P* and continuing with a fake data string Ӻ of interest to him/her. The forged message is  <math alttext="upper M prime equals upper M parallel-to upper P parallel-to German Ƒ" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8741;</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>&#8741;</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#401;</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M prime equals upper M parallel-to upper P parallel-to German Ƒ](images/c05_40.png).

Length extension attack takes advantage of the design of Merkle-Damgård construction to adapt[⁶](#c05.xhtml#c05-note-0006) the hash function *H*, such that  <math alttext="upper H 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper H 0](images/c05_41.png) is not the constant initialization vector, rather it takes the value of  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis k e y parallel-to upper M parallel-to upper P right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8741;</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8741;</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis k e y parallel-to upper M parallel-to upper P right-parenthesis](images/c05_42.png), which is known to the adversary Thus, hashing block(s) of Ӻ looks like a continuation of blocks of string  <math alttext="k e y StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper M EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![k e y StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper M EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P](images/c05_43.png) and the resulting hash  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis German Ƒ right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#401;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis German Ƒ right-parenthesis](images/c05_44.png) matches the hash  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis k e y parallel-to upper M parallel-to upper P StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue German Ƒ" display="inline" produced by a normal hash function.

*Proof of correctness*

Let  <math alttext="upper P prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![upper P prime](images/c05_46.png) be the padding string to append to fake data Ӻ, such that  <math alttext="l e n left-parenthesis German Ƒ StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P prime right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#401;</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>P</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![l e n left-parenthesis German Ƒ StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P prime right-parenthesis](images/c05_47.png) is a multiple of the block size *L* and *K*, the number of blocks of the string  <math alttext="German Ƒ StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#401;</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![German Ƒ StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P prime](images/c05_48.png).

The adversary knows the hash *v* computed by the legitimate sender,  <math alttext="v equals upper H left-parenthesis k e y StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper M EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P comma upper I upper V right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![v equals upper H left-parenthesis k e y StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper M EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P comma upper I upper V right-parenthesis](images/c05_65.png). He/she modifies the hash function to use a chosen initialization vector and computes  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis German Ƒ StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P prime comma v right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#401;</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis German Ƒ StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P prime comma v right-parenthesis](images/c05_66.png). Thus, the hash computed by the adversary is the same as the one computed by the verifier; and the received message  <math alttext="upper M prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![upper M prime](images/c05_67.png) is validated.□

## 5.2 Secure Hash Algorithms (SHA)

SHA algorithm family is the most used hashing algorithms in current cryptosystems and it is very likely to dominate in the next decade(s). SHA family is a set of NIST standards named SHA-0, SHA-1, SHA-2, and SHA-3. The most popular algorithm is SHA-1. SHA-0 was published in 1993, SHA-1 in 1995, SHA-2 in 2002, and SHA-3 in 2015. SHA-0 was replaced by SHA-1, which in turn was attacked with success, but still used. Current and future cryptosystems are either using or moving to SHA-2 or SHA-3.

Each subfamily may have more than one variant. SHA variants differ in terms of maximum message size, hash size, block size, and number of rounds (see [Table 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0001)). SHA-1 and SHA-2 are similar in design, while SHA-3 relies on different design principles. SHA-1 and SHA-2 make use of Merkle-Damgård hash construction model \[[1](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0001), [2](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0002)\], while SHA-3 makes use of sponge construction model \[[3](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0003), [4](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0004)\].

![Table 5.1 Main characteristics of SHA algorithms.](images/c05_68.png)

[**Table 5.1**](#c05.xhtml#rc05-tbl-0001) Main characteristics of SHA algorithms.

SHA-2 and SHA-3 offer the same set of hash lengths and the same security strengths levels. Main characteristics of SHA variants are summarized in [Table 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0001). It is worth noticing that the most important characteristic, when security is of concern, is the message digest size.

### 5.2.1 SHA-1 and SHA-2 Algorithms

The first version of SHA-1 was published in 1995 \[[5](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0005)\]. The last revisions of SHA-1 and SHA-2 algorithms were published in 2012 under the name of SHS (Secure Hash Standard) \[[6](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0006)\]. SHS includes seven variants: SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA-512/224, and SHA-512/256. Notice that SHA-2 is not used alone in certificates, instead its variants are used. In the sequel, SHA-x denotes one of the seven SHS variants.

The following principles are common to all SHA-1 and SHA-2 variants:

· *Input and output*

Input of SHA-x is a bit string of an arbitrary size. However, the maximum message size is fixed (see [Table 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0001)).

SHA-x produces hashes with fixed length (see [Table 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0001)).

· *Data representation*

–Hashing algorithms manipulate words of either 32 or 64 bits. An integer between 0 and  <math alttext="2 Superscript 32 Baseline minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 32 Baseline minus 1](images/c05_75.png) (or  <math alttext="2 Superscript 64 Baseline minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 64 Baseline minus 1](images/c05_76.png)) is represented by a word of 32 or 64 bits, respectively. The least significant bits of an integer are rightmost bits of the word.

–Message to hash is split into blocks with a fixed size of either  <math alttext="512 or 1024" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>512</mn><mtext>&#160;or&#160;</mtext><mn>1024</mn></mrow></math> ![512 or 1024](images/c05_77.png) bits.

–Blocks of the message to hash are labeled  <math alttext="upper B Superscript 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma upper B Superscript m Baseline comma where m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>B</mi><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;where&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![upper B Superscript 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma upper B Superscript m Baseline comma where m](images/c05_78.png) is the number of blocks of the message including padding bits.

–To be processed, each block  <math alttext="upper B Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper B Superscript i](images/c05_79.png) is stored in 16 words labeled  <math alttext="upper B 0 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mn>0</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper B 0 Superscript i](images/c05_80.png),  <math alttext="upper B 1 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper B 1 Superscript i](images/c05_81.png), …,  <math alttext="upper B 15 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper B 15 Superscript i](images/c05_82.png).

*   *Message padding*

The purpose of padding is to ensure that the bit-length of the padded message is a multiple of block size. Padding bits are appended to the end of the initial message in a format known to both parties. Let *l* denote the bit-length of the message *M* to hash. Two distinct padding methods are used:

Padding in SHA-1, SHA-224, and SHA-256 is done as follows: append a bit “1” at the end of message *M*, followed by *k* zero bits, where *k* is the smallest positive integer such that  <math alttext="l plus 1 plus k Baseline 448 m o d 512" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mn>448</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>512</mn></mrow></math> ![l plus 1 plus k Baseline 448 m o d 512](images/c05_83.png), then append the binary value of *l* represented on 64 bits.

Padding in SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA-512/224, and SHA-512/256 is done as follows: append a bit “1” at the end of message *M*, followed by *k* zero bits, where *k* is the smallest positive integer such that  <math alttext="l plus 1 plus k Baseline 896 m o d 1024" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mn>896</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1024</mn></mrow></math> ![l plus 1 plus k Baseline 896 m o d 1024](images/c05_84.png), then append the binary value of *l* represented on 128 bits.

*   *Bit operations used by SHA-x*

Bitwise operations used by SHA-x are: ∧ (and), ∨ (or), ⊕ exclusive or, and ¬ (complement).

The sum of integers *x* and *y* is  <math alttext="z equals left-parenthesis x plus y right-parenthesis m o d 2 Superscript 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![z equals left-parenthesis x plus y right-parenthesis m o d 2 Superscript 32](images/c05_85.png) (or  <math alttext="m o d 2 Superscript 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![m o d 2 Superscript 64](images/c05_86.png)).

 <math alttext="upper R upper O upper T upper L Superscript n Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>T</mi><msup><mi>L</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper R upper O upper T upper L Superscript n Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05_87.png) denotes the circular shift (i.e. rotation) of a word *x* by *n* bit-positions to the left.

 <math alttext="upper R upper O upper T upper R Superscript n Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>T</mi><msup><mi>R</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper R upper O upper T upper R Superscript n Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05_88.png) denotes the circular shift (i.e. rotation) of a word *x* by *n* bit-positions to the right.

 <math alttext="upper S upper H upper R Superscript n Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mi>H</mi><msup><mi>R</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S upper H upper R Superscript n Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05_89.png) denotes the right shift of a word *x* by *n* bit-positions.

*   *Logical functions and constants*

SHA variants make use of logical functions and constants to brew the blocks. Constants appear as random values and are in hexadecimal representation.

#### 5.2.1.1 SHA-1 Algorithm

*   *SHA-1 sizes, constants, and logical functions*

SHA-1 processes 512-bit blocks. It uses a schedule of 80 rounds and five 32-bit working variables *a*, *b*, *c*, *d*, and *e*. 32-bit round words are labeled  <math alttext="upper W 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper W 0](images/c05_90.png), …,  <math alttext="upper W 79" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mn>79</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper W 79](images/c05_91.png). 32-bit words of hash value of block  <math alttext="upper B Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper B Superscript i](images/c05_92.png) are labeled  <math alttext="upper H 0 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H 0 Superscript i](images/c05_93.png),  <math alttext="upper H 1 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H 1 Superscript i](images/c05_94.png),  <math alttext="upper H 2 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H 2 Superscript i](images/c05_95.png),  <math alttext="upper H 3 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>3</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H 3 Superscript i](images/c05_96.png),  <math alttext="upper H 4 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>4</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H 4 Superscript i](images/c05_97.png) (i.e. 5\*32 bits = 160 bits). SHA-1 uses a sequence of eighty constant 32-bit words, *K*[0], *K*[1], …, *K*[79] defined by:

#### 5.2.1.2 SHA-256 Algorithm

*   *SHA-256 sizes, constants, and logical functions*

SHA-256 processes 512-bit blocks. It uses a schedule of 64 rounds and eight 32-bit working variables *a*, *b*, *c*, *d*, *e*, *f*, *g*, and *h*. 32-bit round words are labeled  <math alttext="upper W 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper W 0](images/c05_112.png), …,  <math alttext="upper W 63" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mn>63</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper W 63](images/c05_113.png). Words of hash value of block  <math alttext="upper B Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper B Superscript i](images/c05_114.png) are labeled  <math alttext="upper H 0 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H 0 Superscript i](images/c05_115.png),  <math alttext="upper H 1 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H 1 Superscript i](images/c05_116.png),  <math alttext="upper H 2 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H 2 Superscript i](images/c05_117.png),  <math alttext="upper H 3 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>3</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H 3 Superscript i](images/c05_118.png),  <math alttext="upper H 4 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>4</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H 4 Superscript i](images/c05_119.png),  <math alttext="upper H 5 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>5</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H 5 Superscript i](images/c05_120.png),  <math alttext="upper H 6 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>6</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H 6 Superscript i](images/c05_121.png),  <math alttext="upper H 7 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>7</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H 7 Superscript i](images/c05_122.png) (i.e. 8\*32 bits = 256 bits).

A sequence of six logical functions are used in SHA-224 and SHA-256. Each function operates on one or three 32-bit words and produces a 32-bit word as output. Those functions are defined by:

#### 5.2.1.3 SHA-224 Algorithm

SHA-224 is defined exactly as SHA-256, with two exceptions:

*   The constants used in the initialization step are as follows:

*   The message hash is obtained by keeping only 7 words of the final block hash, i.e.  <math alttext="upper H 0 Superscript m Baseline StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper H 1 Superscript m Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper H 2 Superscript m Baseline EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper H 3 Superscript m Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper H 4 Superscript m Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper H 6 Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn><mi>m</mi></msubsup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi></msubsup><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msubsup><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>3</mn><mi>m</mi></msubsup><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>4</mn><mi>m</mi></msubsup><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>6</mn><mi>m</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H 0 Superscript m Baseline StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper H 1 Superscript m Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper H 2 Superscript m Baseline EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper H 3 Superscript m Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper H 4 Superscript m Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper H 6 Superscript m](images/c05_137.png).

#### 5.2.1.4 SHA-512 Algorithm

*   *SHA-512 sizes, constants, and logical functions*

SHA-512 processes 1024-bit blocks. Blocks of padded message are labeled *B*¹,  <math alttext="upper B squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![upper B squared](images/c05_138.png), …,  <math alttext="upper B Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper B Superscript m](images/c05_139.png), where *m* is the number of blocks of padded message. Each block  <math alttext="upper B Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper B Superscript i](images/c05_140.png) is represented as sixteen 64-bit words labeled  <math alttext="upper B Subscript t Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript t Superscript i](images/c05_141.png) ( <math alttext="0 less-than-or-equal-to t less-than-or-equal-to 15" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow></math> ![0 less-than-or-equal-to t less-than-or-equal-to 15](images/c05_142.png)).

SHA-512 uses a schedule of 80 rounds and eight 64-bit working variables *a*, *b*, *c*, *d*, *e*, *f*, *g*, and *h*. 64-bit round words are labeled  <math alttext="upper W 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper W 0](images/c05_143.png), …,  <math alttext="upper W 79" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mn>79</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper W 79](images/c05_144.png). Words of hash value of block  <math alttext="upper B Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper B Superscript i](images/c05_145.png) are labeled  <math alttext="upper H 0 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H 0 Superscript i](images/c05_146.png),  <math alttext="upper H 1 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H 1 Superscript i](images/c05_147.png),  <math alttext="upper H 2 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H 2 Superscript i](images/c05_148.png),  <math alttext="upper H 3 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>3</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H 3 Superscript i](images/c05_149.png),  <math alttext="upper H 4 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>4</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H 4 Superscript i](images/c05_150.png),  <math alttext="upper H 5 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>5</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H 5 Superscript i](images/c05_151.png),  <math i](images/c05_152.png),  <math alttext="upper H 7 Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>7</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H 7 Superscript i](images/c05_153.png) (i.e. 8 \* 64 bits = 512 bits).

#### 5.2.1.5 SHA-384, SHA-512/224, and SHA-512/256 Algorithms

SHA-384, SHA-512/224 algorithms are defined exactly as SHA-512 algorithm with the following exceptions:

*   Initialization values are as follows:

*   – SHA-384 initialization

#### 5.2.1.6 SHA-1 Security

In 2005, a method was proposed for finding SHA-1 collisions under restrictive conditions; the number of rounds was 53 instead of 80 in the standard SHA-1. From that time, SHA-1 security became doubtful, but no formal proof of its insecurity was provided. As of 2020, attacks against SHA-1 have become practical. As such, it is recommended to withdraw SHA-1 from existing products as soon as possible and use SHA-2 or SHA-3 instead. As far as we know, the most efficient attack against SHA-1 has been published in 2020 \[[7](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0007)\]. It belongs to chosen-prefix collision attacks. In the designed attack, the adversary starts with two prefixes  <math alttext="upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P](images/c05_194.png) and  <math alttext="upper P prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![upper P prime](images/c05_195.png), then computes two parts *M* and  <math alttext="upper M prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![upper M prime](images/c05_196.png), such that  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper P StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis upper P prime StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M prime right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper P StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis upper P prime StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M prime right-parenthesis](images/c05_197.png). Chosen-prefix collision attack has a complexity of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 63.4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>63.4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 63.4](images/c05_198.png) and is far from the brute-force attack that has a complexity of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 160 slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>160</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 160 slash 2](images/c05_199.png).

### 5.2.2 SHA-3 Functions

SHA-3 is based on an instance of Keccak[⁹](#c05.xhtml#c05-note-0009) algorithm, which was selected as the winner of SHA-3 public cryptographic hash algorithm competition, initiated by NIST in 2007, after serious attacks were published against SHA-1. SHA-3 was published in 2015 \[[8](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0008)\]. The security strength levels provided by SHA-3 are the same as the ones of SHA-2.

Four hash functions, namely SHA3-224, SHA3-256, SHA3-384, and SHA3-512 along with two extendable-output functions, Shake128 and Shake256, form the SHA-3 family. Shake128 and Shake256 are not hash functions, but can be specialized to hash functions. They are not described in the sequel. The four SHA-3 functions are based on the sponge construction model \[[3](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0003), [4](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0004)\] in which the main component is the Keccak permutation.

*Notation*:

SHA-3 function specification makes use of polymorphic functions. To be used in a specific context, a polymorphic function ϕ must first be instantiated to produce a concrete function, which in turn is called at multiple times to return a result. In  <math alttext="phi left-bracket upper I 1 comma upper I 2 comma ellipsis right-bracket left-parenthesis c 1 comma c 2 comma ellipsis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#981;</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>I</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![phi left-bracket upper I 1 comma upper I 2 comma ellipsis right-bracket left-parenthesis c 1 comma c 2 comma ellipsis right-parenthesis](images/c05_200.png),  <math alttext="upper I 1 comma upper I 2 comma ellipsis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>I</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></mrow></math> ![upper I 1 comma upper I 2 comma ellipsis](images/c05_201.png) denote the instantiation parameters and  <math alttext="c 1 comma c 2 comma ellipsis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></mrow></math> ![c 1 comma c 2 comma ellipsis](images/c05_202.png) denote the call (or input) parameters. For example,  <math alttext="upper S p o n g e" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></math> ![upper S p o n g e](images/c05_203.png) function is instantiated to produce a hash function of a cryptosystems, then the produced hash function is used to return hash digests (see [Section 5.2.2.2](#c05.xhtml#c05-sec-03010)).

#### 5.2.2.1 Keccak-p Permutation

A Keccak-p[^(10)](#c05.xhtml#c05-note-0010) permutation is denoted  <math alttext="upper K e c c a k bar p left-bracket b comma upper N Subscript r Baseline right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper K e c c a k bar p left-bracket b comma upper N Subscript r Baseline right-bracket](images/c05_204.png), where *b* is the input bit-string size and  <math alttext="upper N Subscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper N Subscript r](images/c05_205.png) the number of rounds. Input string size *b* is any value in  <math alttext="StartSet 25 comma 50 comma 100 comma 200 comma 400 comma 800 comma 1600 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>25</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>50</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>100</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>200</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>400</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>800</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1600</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 25 comma 50 comma 100 comma 200 comma 400 comma 800 comma 1600 EndSet](images/c05_206.png) and  <math alttext="upper N Subscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper N Subscript r](images/c05_207.png) is any positive integer.  <math alttext="upper K e c c a k bar p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K e c c a k bar p](images/c05_208.png) provides foundations to design a large variety of hash functions to fulfill specific application requirements. However, the current SHA-3 standard chose a single pair of value parameters <math alttext="b equals 1600" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1600</mn></mrow></math> ![b equals 1600](images/c05_209.png) and  <math alttext="upper N Subscript r Baseline equals 24" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>24</mn></mrow></math> ![upper N Subscript r Baseline equals 24](images/c05_210.png).

A round consists of a sequence of five transformations, which are called step mappings labeled θ, ρ, π, χ, and τ.

##### *5.2.2.1.1 State Array*

Bit strings manipulated by Keccak-p transformations are represented as 3-dimensional arrays of bits, called *state arrays*. Any string used in a permutation is represented as a 3D array,  <math alttext="55 w" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>55</mn><mi>w</mi></mrow></math> ![55 w](images/c05_211.png) array of bits, where  <math alttext="w equals b slash 25" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow></math> ![w equals b slash 25](images/c05_212.png). The 2D sub-arrays are called *sheets*, *planes*, and *slices*; and 1D sub-arrays are called *rows*, *columns*, and *lanes* (see [Figure 5.3](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0003)). Thus, the state array associated with a bit string of a bit-length of *b* is composed as follows: five planes, five sheets, and *w* slices. Two quantities, labeled *w* and *l*, are associated with each bit string length *b* (see [Table 5.2](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0002)). They are used in transformation specification.

![Figure 5.3 Parts of the state 3D-array (100-bit string).](images/c05f003.png)

[**Figure 5.3**](#c05.xhtml#rc05-fig-0003) Parts of the state 3D-array (100-bit string).

[**Table 5.2**](#c05.xhtml#rc05-tbl-0002) Keccak-p permutation (width *b* and related quantities, *w* and *l*).

| *b* || 25 || 50 || 100 || 200 || 400 || 800 || 1600 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *w* || 1 || 2 || 4 || 8 || 16 || 32 || 64 |
| *l* || 0 || 1 || 2 || 3 || 4 || 5 || 6 |

*Rules for conversion*

1.  A string *S* of size *b*, whose bits are labeled  <math alttext="upper S left-bracket 0 right-bracket comma upper S left-bracket 1 right-bracket comma ellipsis comma upper S left-bracket b minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S left-bracket 0 right-bracket comma upper S left-bracket 1 right-bracket comma ellipsis comma upper S left-bracket b minus 1 right-bracket](images/c05_213.png) is converted into a state array <math alttext="upper A" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> ![upper A](images/c05_214.png) as follows:

For all triples  <math alttext="left-parenthesis x comma y comma z right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis x comma y comma z right-parenthesis](images/c05_215.png) such that  <math alttext="0 less-than-or-equal-to x less-than 5" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> ![0 less-than-or-equal-to x less-than 5](images/c05_216.png),  <math alttext="0 less-than-or-equal-to y less-than 5" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> ![0 less-than-or-equal-to y less-than 5](images/c05_217.png),  <math alttext="0 less-than-or-equal-to z less-than w" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></math> ![0 less-than-or-equal-to z less-than w](images/c05_218.png) do:

 <math alttext="upper A left-bracket comma y comma z right-bracket equals upper S left-bracket w left-parenthesis 5 y plus x right-parenthesis plus z right-bracket" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mi>w</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper A left-bracket comma y comma z right-bracket equals upper S left-bracket w left-parenthesis 5 y plus x right-parenthesis plus z right-bracket](images/c05_219.png)

*   2\. A state array *A* is converted into a bit string *S* of size *b*, whose bits are as follows:

 <math alttext="upper S equals upper P l a n e left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper P l a n e left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P l a n e left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper P l a n e left-parenthesis 3 right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P l a n e left-parenthesis 4 right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S equals upper P l a n e left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper P l a n e left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P l a n e left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper P l a n e left-parenthesis 3 right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P l a n e left-parenthesis 4 right-parenthesis](images/c05_220.png)
