*Security of HMAC*

The security of HMAC depends on the security strength of the underlying hash function *H*, which in turn depends on the size of hash function output. HMAC is resistant to common attacks against MAC, including recovering the private key or altering the message content. In HMAC, the inner hash (i.e.  <math alttext="h Subscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![h Subscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c05_384.png)) would be vulnerable to length-extension attack, while the outer hash (i.e.  <math alttext="upper H upper M upper A upper C left-parenthesis upper M comma k right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H upper M upper A upper C left-parenthesis upper M comma k right-parenthesis](images/c05_385.png)) is not (see Problem 5.19).

#### 5.3.2.2 KMAC

KMAC is the acronym for *Keccak Message Authentication Code*. It is based on Keccak function of SHA-3 \[[11](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0011)\]. Two variants exist, KMAC-128 and KMAC-256. Notice that  <math alttext="128 and 256" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>128</mn><mtext>&#160;and&#160;</mtext><mn>256</mn></mrow></math> ![128 and 256](images/c05_386.png) in KMAC variants refer to the capacity of the sponge function (see [Section 5.2.2.3](#c05.xhtml#c05-sec-03011)). KMAC functions take the following parameters:

*   *K*, a key of a variable bit-length, which depends on the required security strength, but  <math alttext="l e n left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![l e n left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis](images/c05_387.png) is at most  <math alttext="2 Superscript 2040" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>2040</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 2040](images/c05_388.png).
*   *M*, a message of a variable bit-length.
*   *L*, the requested bit-length of the output (i.e. the tag length), with  <math alttext="upper L less-than 2 Superscript 2040" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>2040</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper L less-than 2 Superscript 2040](images/c05_389.png).
*   *S*, an optional customization bit-string, which may be empty, of length  <math alttext="l e n left-parenthesis upper S right-parenthesis less-than 2 Superscript 2040" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#60;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>2040</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![l e n left-parenthesis upper S right-parenthesis less-than 2 Superscript 2040](images/c05_390.png).

Let  <math alttext="upper K upper M upper A upper C left pointing angle m right pointing angle" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>&#9001;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#9002;</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper K upper M upper A upper C left pointing angle m right pointing angle](images/c05_391.png) denote either  <math alttext="upper K upper M upper A upper C Baseline 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mn>128</mn></mrow></math> ![upper K upper M upper A upper C Baseline 128](images/c05_392.png) or  <math alttext="upper K upper M upper A upper C Baseline 256" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mn>256</mn></mrow></math> ![upper K upper M upper A upper C Baseline 256](images/c05_393.png).  <math alttext="upper K upper M upper A upper C left pointing angle m right pointing angle" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>&#9001;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#9002;</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper K upper M upper A upper C left pointing angle m right pointing angle](images/c05_394.png) is defined by:

*KMAC internal functions*

#### 5.3.2.3 Generic Attacks Against Hash Function-based MAC Algorithms

MAC systems may be a target for attacks either to recover the secret key or to forge messages. More specifically, the common generic attacks against MACs include:

*   A1: Recover the secret key.
*   A2: Append fake information to the end of the original message.
*   A3: Substitute a fake message for the original one.
*   A4: Existential forgery: it is the ability of the adversary to create a message and its MAC that have not been generated in the past by the legitimate sender.

In A1, given a message *M* and the keyed hash  <math alttext="upper M upper A upper C left-parenthesis upper M comma k right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper M upper A upper C left-parenthesis upper M comma k right-parenthesis](images/c05_427.png), the attack (without knowledge of the internal structure of the hash function) is a brute-force attack, which requires to test all potential keys concatenated to *M*, either on the left (in case of secret prefix MAC) or on the right (in case of secret suffix MAC) of *k*. Thus, the resistance to attack A1 depends on the length of the secret key.

In A2, given a message *M* and the keyed hash  <math alttext="upper M upper A upper C left-parenthesis upper M comma k right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper M upper A upper C left-parenthesis upper M comma k right-parenthesis](images/c05_428.png), adversary can append fake data to *M* and generate a keyed hash without knowledge of the secret key if the secret prefix MAC approach is used, i.e.  <math alttext="upper M upper A upper C left-parenthesis upper M comma k right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis k StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper M upper A upper C left-parenthesis upper M comma k right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis k StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M right-parenthesis](images/c05_429.png). (see [Section 5.1.3.2](#c05.xhtml#c05-sec-03002) and Problem 5.18).

In A3, given a message *M* and the keyed hash  <math alttext="upper M upper A upper C left-parenthesis upper M comma k right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper M upper A upper C left-parenthesis upper M comma k right-parenthesis](images/c05_430.png), to substitute  <math alttext="upper M prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> ![upper M prime](images/c05_431.png) to  <math alttext="k StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> ![k StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M](images/c05_432.png) or to  <math alttext="upper M StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue k](images/c05_433.png), without controlling the content of  <math alttext="upper M prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![upper M prime](images/c05_434.png), the adversary must find a second preimage collision, which is known to be computationally infeasible.

In A4, the adversary has to find a collision, which is known to be computationally infeasible. In addition, MAC algorithms**,** such as HMAC, make use of two hash function calls (producing inner and outer hashes), which makes them very secure regarding collision attacks (see Problem 5.19).

### 5.3.3 Block Cipher-based MACs

Modes of operation of block ciphers have been standardized by the NIST to provide methods for authenticated encryption and MAC generation. They include CMAC (Cipher MAC), CCM (Counter with Cipher block chaining-MAC), GCM (Galois/Counter MAC), GMAC (Galois MAC), and AES-GCM-SIV. All those MAC generation methods will be addressed in [Chapter 9](#c09.xhtml).

## 5.4 Digital Signature

Digital signature algorithms are the most important application of hash functions in the cyberspace.

### 5.4.1 Digital Signature in Public Key World

In paper documents, the issuer manually signs his/her documents to provide proof of authenticity that can be checked by document recipients. In the digital space (or cyberspace), data included in messages are used for Internet shopping, banking, stock exchange, voting, company transactions, etc. Public key cryptosystems evolve in a world where messages and unencrypted data (including public keys) are not hidden to observers. The big question is: how can the recipient trust the sender? Message signature is the answer to this question.

A digital signature (or simply signature) is a cryptographic transformation, which is similar to handwritten signature to provide assurance of authenticity of the sender. Digital signature also is used for *non-repudiation*: the signing individual cannot deny he/she has not been the signer. For example, one may electronically sign a car rental contract, which states he/she must pay monthly $500. Then, he/she cannot claim either the amount to pay is $400 or worse, he/she has never signed the contact. Non-repudiation is of paramount importance in the cyberspace. Digital signature also is a means of guaranteeing integrity. If a message is altered during transport, the signature will no more match the received message and the received message is rejected. Two digital signature methods exist:

*   *Signature with appendix*[^(14)](#c05.xhtml#c05-note-0014): given a message *M*, the signer generates a signature *S* from the hash of message and sends a pair  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper S comma upper M right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper S comma upper M right-parenthesis](images/c05_435.png). The verifier decrypts the signature *S* to yield a hash  <math alttext="upper H prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![upper H prime](images/c05_436.png), computes *H*, the hash of the received message, then compares both hashes (see [Figure 5.8](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0008)).
    
    ![Figure 5.8 Overall scheme of digital signature with appendix.](images/c05f008.png)
    
    [**Figure 5.8**](#c05.xhtml#rc05-fig-0008) Overall scheme of digital signature with appendix.
    
*   *Signature with message recovery*: given a message *M*, all or some of message *M* is embedded in the signature *S*. When the message is entirely embedded, the verification procedure requires only the signature *S* and recovers *M* from the signature.

In symmetric cryptosystems, the same key, which is shared by both parties, is used for generating and verifying signature. In asymmetric cryptosystems, the signer makes use of his/her private key to generate the signature, while the verifier makes use of the public key of the signer to verify the signature.

Digital signature algorithms include:

*   RSASSA (RSA Signature Scheme with Appendix), presented in Section 12.2.6.
*   DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm), presented in Section 12.4.
*   ElGamal signature algorithm, presented in Section 12.3.4.2.
*   ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) and EdDSA (Edwards Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm), presented in Sections 13.5.5–13.5.6.

All those algorithms make use of hash functions. They are addressed in detail in [Chapters 12](#c12.xhtml)–[14](#c14.xhtml) when the foundations of the underlying public key are introduced. Then, attacks against digital signatures produced by public key algorithms are discussed.

### 5.4.2 Attacks Against Digital Signature Schemes

Hand signature is approximately the same in all documents signed by a given person. The difficulty in forging a hand signature is directly linked to the graphic pattern elaborated, thanks to the ingenuity of the signer. Some hand signatures are easy to reproduce, while others are too complex requiring a high level of imitation to reproduce them. Hand signatures may be imitated even carefully designed by their owners. To enforce signature, public notaries play a third party role. It is commonly considered that a document, double-checked and signed by a notary, includes an authentic signature.

In the cyberspace, digital signature is a cryptographic transformation. Consequently, the difficulty in forging signatures is linked to the mathematical foundations used to design digital signature schemes. Thus, digital signatures are by far more difficult to forge than hand signatures.

Attacks against digital signature may be categorized into three groups:

*   Universal forgery: adversary is able to recover the private key of the signer and then signs any message on behalf of the legitimate key owner.
*   Selective forgery: adversary is able to create valid signatures for messages of his/her choice.
*   Existential forgery: adversary can generate a pair composed of a signature and a message without controlling the message content.

## 5.5 Concluding Remarks

Digital signature and MACs are used for guaranteeing message integrity and authentication. MAC algorithms do not provide non-repudiation service because the secret used to produce MACs may be shared by more than two users; and even with two users**,** both can produce MACs. Whereas with digital signatures, each key is private to each user; hence, there is non-repudiation as only the private keyholder can sign with his/her key.

It is worth noticing that message authentication and user authentication are distinct services. Message authentication, also called message origin authentication, enables the receiver to check that the MAC accompanying a message has been generated by a user sharing a key with him/her. Whereas user authentication (also called entity authentication) enables the recipient to check if the message sender engaged in the current session is really the person who is pretending to be. Let us take the following two scenarios to show the difference between both authentications.

Alice, Bob, and Eve share a secret. Bob computes the MAC of a message, then sends the message and its MAC to Alice. Alice forwards the message and the MAC to Eve, who can verify that the message was originated by a holder of the shared secret. However, Eve is not communicating with Bob; thus, she cannot authenticate him.

Alice and Eve know the public key of Bob. Bob signs a message and sends the message and its signature to Alice. Alice forwards the message and signature to Eve, who can verify that the message was signed by Bob. However, Eve is not communicating with Bob; thus, she cannot authenticate him. Thus, used alone, neither MACs nor signatures provide entity authentication. Other mechanisms are required to provide user authentication (see [Chapter 15](#c15.xhtml)).

***Problem*** ***5.10***

One of the applications of hash functions is the protection of passwords in authentication systems. Instead of storing the passwords in clear, only password hashes are stored. To authenticate a user, his/her password is hashed and the resulting hash is compared to that stored on the authentication system. Therefore, even if the password file is stolen, the passwords are very hard to recover. Assume that the hash function used by an attacked authentication system is known to the adversary.

1.  Is it secure to use a hash bit-length of 10 to protect 500 passwords?
2.  Assume that an adversary has access to 1000 hashes of 8-byte passwords. Is it difficult, from the computational feasibility point of view, for the adversary to gain access to the system as a legitimate user with a brute-force attack?
3.  Assume that each of 1000 passwords is concatenated to a random input called *salt* so that the appended password has a bit-length of 512. The authentication system stores the 128-bit hashes of passwords in a file and the salts in another file. Consider an adversary who has access to the hash file but not the salt file. Can the adversary gain access to the system?

***Problem*** ***5.11***

Assume that the hash function used by Alice manipulates blocks with a length of 512 bits and the maximum size of data to hash is 1 G bytes. Alice has an album of 1000 pictures each of 1 M bytes. She has two alternatives to send her album to Bob: either hash and send each picture separately or zip the album, then hash and send the hashed zipped file.

1.  What is the most attack-resistant alternative?
2.  Assume that the second preimage is feasible but at a high cost for the adversary. Which alternative is preferred if integrity is of interest?

***Problem*** ***5.12***

Deterministic generic attacks are attacks that break hash resistance whatever is the hash function. What is the maximum number of steps required for a generic deterministic attack to succeed in finding a preimage, a second preimage or a collision? Assume that no dictionary is built in advance.

## 5.6.2 Solutions to Problems

***Problem*** ***5.1***

Fundamental security properties include confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, and non-repudiation.

1.  Digital signature provides guarantees regarding integrity, authenticity, and non-repudiation. However, if the plaintext is not encrypted, the digital signature cannot provide confidentiality.
2.  MACs provide integrity and message authenticity guarantees. They do not guarantee confidentiality, if the message is not encrypted. They do not provide non-repudiation guarantees, as well.

***Problem*** ***5.2***

Hashing and encryption are two distinct cryptographic functions. Encryption is something used to convert plaintext (readable) into ciphertext (indecipherable). Decryption is done either with the same ciphering key, which is a secret, in symmetric systems or with a key mathematically related to the encryption key in asymmetric systems. In asymmetric systems, messages are encrypted with public keys and then decrypted with private keys. Hashing is a technique used to produce a fingerprint to characterize uniquely a data, while it does not hide data. In hashing, nothing is secret. Encryption is for ensuring confidentiality, while hashing is for ensuring integrity.

***Problem*** ***5.3***

1.   <math alttext="upper H 1 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H 1 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05_467.png) is a function that returns the parity bit of  <math alttext="x" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> ![x](images/c05_468.png).
    
    Given a value of parity bit (i.e. 0 or 1), the half of the input space matches the chosen value. Thus,  <math alttext="upper H 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper H 1](images/c05_469.png) is not preimage resistant.
    
    The probability of collision is 50%. Thus,  <math alttext="upper H 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper H 1](images/c05_470.png) is not collision-resistant.
    
2.   <math alttext="upper H 2 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H 2 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05_471.png) is defined by  <math alttext="upper H 2 left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis equals upper P left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis m o d g left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H 2 left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis equals upper P left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis m o d g left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05_472.png).
    
    Let *k* denote the degree of polynomial  <math alttext="g left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![g left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05_473.png), *L* denote the degree of polynomial  <math alttext="upper P left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis](images/c05_474.png), and  <math alttext="upper Q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper Q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05_475.png) a polynomial of degree  <math alttext="upper L minus k period" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> ![upper L minus k period](images/c05_476.png)
    
    Given a hash *z*, any message *M* such that  <math alttext="upper P left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis equals g left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis asterisk upper Q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis plus upper P left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis equals g left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis asterisk upper Q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis plus upper P left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis](images/c05_477.png) matches the chosen hash *z*.  <math alttext="upper P left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis](images/c05_478.png) denotes the polynomial associated with the bit string representing *z*. Thus,  <math alttext="upper H 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper H 2](images/c05_479.png) is not preimage-resistant.
    
    All message  <math alttext="upper M prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![upper M prime](images/c05_480.png) such that  <math alttext="upper P left-parenthesis upper M prime right-parenthesis equals g left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis asterisk upper Q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis plus r left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P left-parenthesis upper M prime right-parenthesis equals g left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis asterisk upper Q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis plus r left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05_481.png), where  <math alttext="r left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05_482.png) is a polynomial of degree less than *k*, have the same hash, which is  <math alttext="r left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05_483.png). Thus,  <math alttext="upper H 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper H 2](images/c05_484.png) is not collision-resistant.
    

***Problem*** ***5.4***

With the given function, the MAC is computed as:  <math alttext="upper M upper A upper C left-parenthesis upper X comma upper K right-parenthesis equals upper C Subscript m Baseline plus upper K m o d 2 Superscript 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>K</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper M upper A upper C left-parenthesis upper X comma upper K right-parenthesis equals upper C Subscript m Baseline plus upper K m o d 2 Superscript 128](images/c05_485.png)

No collision resistance: it is easy to find collisions. For example, all permutations of three blocks have the same MAC. That is:

***Problem*** ***5.5***

Recall that CRC-based technique to detect transmission operates as follows:

Let *S* denote a bit string to transmit. A polynomial  <math alttext="upper S left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05_497.png) is associated with the string *S*, where the polynomial coefficients are the bits of *S*. A generator polynomial  <math alttext="upper G left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper G left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05_498.png) of degree *n* (*n* is the number of bits of CRC) is used to compute the CRC as:

 <math alttext="upper C upper R upper C left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis identical-to left-parenthesis upper S left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis asterisk x Superscript n Baseline right-parenthesis m o d upper G left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis period" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>G</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> ![upper C upper R upper C left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis identical-to left-parenthesis upper S left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis asterisk x Superscript n Baseline right-parenthesis m o d upper G left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis period](images/c05_499.png)

For example, compute a 3-bit CRC for string 10111 with  <math alttext="upper G left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x cubed plus x plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper G left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x cubed plus x plus 1](images/c05_500.png).

 <math alttext="upper C upper R upper C left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis identical-to left-parenthesis left-parenthesis x Superscript 4 Baseline plus x squared plus x plus 1 right-parenthesis asterisk x cubed right-parenthesis m o d left-parenthesis x cubed plus x plus 1 right-parenthesis equals x plus 1 period" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8801;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> ![upper C upper R upper C left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis identical-to left-parenthesis left-parenthesis x Superscript 4 Baseline plus x squared plus x plus 1 right-parenthesis asterisk x cubed right-parenthesis m o d left-parenthesis x cubed plus x plus 1 right-parenthesis equals x plus 1 period](images/c05_501.png)

Thus, the CRC is 011.

CRC-based functions cannot be securely used as hash functions, because of the following:

No collision resistance: it is easy to find collisions, because any pair of bit strings  <math alttext="upper S 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S 1](images/c05_502.png) and  <math alttext="upper S 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S 2](images/c05_503.png) such that  <math alttext="upper S 1 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals upper S 2 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis plus q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis asterisk upper G left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo><mi>G</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S 1 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals upper S 2 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis plus q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis asterisk upper G left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05_504.png) or  <math alttext="upper S 2 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals upper S 1 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis plus q prime left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis asterisk upper G left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>'</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo><mi>G</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S 2 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals upper S 1 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis plus q prime left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis asterisk upper G left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05_505.png), where  <math alttext="q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05_506.png) and  <math alttext="q prime left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>'</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![q prime left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05_507.png) are two polynomials with binary coefficients, have the same CRC.

No preimage resistance: it is easy to find the preimage given a CRC *C*, because any bit string *S* such that  <math alttext="upper S left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals upper C left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis plus q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis asterisk upper G left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo><mi>G</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals upper C left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis plus q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis asterisk upper G left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05_508.png) is a preimage to *C*, where  <math alttext="q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05_509.png) is a polynomial.

No second preimage resistance: it is easy to change a bit string  <math alttext="upper S 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S 1](images/c05_510.png) to another bit string  <math alttext="upper S 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S 2](images/c05_511.png) while keeping the original hash *C*, if  <math alttext="upper S 2 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals upper S 1 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis plus q prime left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis asterisk upper G left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>'</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo><mi>G</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S 2 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals upper S 1 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis plus q prime left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis asterisk upper G left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05_512.png).

***Problem*** ***5.6***

Collisions are intrinsic to all existing hash functions. Collison-free hash functions do not exist for, at least, the following reasons:

In practice, the input space is much larger than the input space. Thus, the same output value is an image for multiple input values. In mathematics, the *pigeonhole principle* states that if *N* items are put into *m* containers, with  <math alttext="upper N ampersand gt semicolon m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#38;gt;</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![upper N ampersand gt semicolon m](images/c05_513.png) then at least one container must contain more than one item.

Even if the output space size is equal or greater than the input space size, the probability of collision in all existing hash functions is not zero. In addition, increasing the size of the hash function output results in more consumption or storage and communication resources.

***Problem*** ***5.7***

Recall that attack-resistance of hash functions qualifies the difficulty, from the computational point of view, of finding collisions or preimage and not the property that collisions do not exist or that preimage can never be found. The statement to prove is: a collision-resistant hash function also is second-preimage resistant. The suggested proof is by contradiction. Assume that a hash function *H* is collision-resistant but not second-preimage resistant. If *H* is not second-preimage resistant, then, given an input *x*, one can find an input  <math alttext="x prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![x prime](images/c05_514.png) such that  <math alttext="x not-equals x prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![x not-equals x prime](images/c05_515.png) and  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis x prime right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis x prime right-parenthesis](images/c05_516.png). However, if one can find two distinct inputs with the same hash, he/she can prove that *H* is not collision-resistant, which is a contradiction with the hypothesis that *H* is collision-resistant.

***Problem*** ***5.8***

Thus, a collision is found and consequently  <math alttext="upper H 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper H 3](images/c05_552.png) is not collision-resistant.

*    <math alttext="upper H 4 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals upper H 1 left-parenthesis x circled-plus c right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper H 4 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals upper H 1 left-parenthesis x circled-plus c right-parenthesis](images/c05_553.png), *c* is a constant integer less than *x*.

Let  <math alttext="c 0 comma c 1 comma ellipsis comma c Subscript k minus 1 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![c 0 comma c 1 comma ellipsis comma c Subscript k minus 1 Baseline](images/c05_554.png) be the bits of constant *c*.

Let *x*[1] and *x*[2] be two bit strings that differ at least by one bit at position *i* such that  <math alttext="0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to k minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to k minus 1](images/c05_555.png):  <math alttext="x 1 equals z StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue 0 EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ![x 1 equals z StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue 0 EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue y](images/c05_556.png) and  <math alttext="x 2 equals z StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ![x 2 equals z StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue y](images/c05_557.png)

If  <math alttext="c Subscript i Baseline equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![c Subscript i Baseline equals 1](images/c05_558.png), then  <math alttext="x 1 circled-plus c equals x 2 circled-plus c equals z StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue 0 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ![x 1 circled-plus c equals x 2 circled-plus c equals z StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue 0 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue y](images/c05_559.png).

By construction of  <math alttext="upper H 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper H 4](images/c05_560.png):

 <math alttext="upper H 4 left-parenthesis x 1 right-parenthesis equals upper H 1 left-parenthesis x 1 circled-plus c right-parenthesis equals upper H 1 left-parenthesis z StartAbsoluteValue Thus, a collision is found and consequently  <math alttext="upper H 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper H 4](images/c05_563.png) is not collision-resistant.

***Problem*** ***5.10***

1.  With a hash bit-length of 10, the hash space is of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 10" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 10](images/c05_564.png). If the number of hashed passwords is 500, any randomly chosen password, whatever is its length, has a chance of  <math alttext="StartFraction 500 Over 2 Superscript 10 Baseline EndFraction almost-equals one-half" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>500</mn></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#8776;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></math> ![StartFraction 500 Over 2 Superscript 10 Baseline EndFraction almost-equals one-half](images/c05_565.png) to have a hash, which is present in the authentication system list. Therefore, using small hash length is not secure to protect passwords.
2.  The password space is of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 8 asterisk 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 8 asterisk 8](images/c05_566.png). Computing the hashes of all potential passwords is computationally feasible. The number of hash computations is  <math alttext="2 Superscript 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 64](images/c05_567.png), which is low compared to the bound of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 90" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>90</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 90](images/c05_568.png) (i.e. the limit of computationally feasibility with current technologies). Then, the adversary builds an attack dictionary of 1000 entries each containing a valid hash (i.e. a hash that is included in the list stolen by the adversary) and the corresponding passwords. Then, the adversary selects a password to log in the system.
3.  The space of passwords with salt is of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 512" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>512</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 512](images/c05_569.png) and that of hashes is of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 128](images/c05_570.png) but only 1000 passwords were hashed. The probability to pick a random password and a random salt such that the resulting hash is in the system list is  <math alttext="StartFraction 1000 Over 2 Superscript 128 Baseline EndFraction almost-equals StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript 118 Baseline EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1000</mn></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#8776;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>118</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![StartFraction 1000 Over 2 Superscript 128 Baseline EndFraction almost-equals StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript 118 Baseline EndFraction](images/c05_571.png). Computing the hashes of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 512" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>512</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 512](images/c05_572.png) distinct passwords is computationally infeasible. Therefore, adding salt and using large hash bit-length make the authentication system resistant to hash file theft.

***Problem*** ***5.11***

1.  Attack-resistance means resistance to preimage, second preimage, and collision attacks. The security strength of a hash function depends on the hash size and not on the size of the hashed data size. Thus, from the hash attack perspective, both alternatives are equivalent.
2.  *Integrity* means integrity of pictures received by Bob. In the first alternative, if a picture is second-preimage attacked, Bob receives a fake picture (but he does know it is a fake picture!). In the second alternative, if the entire album is second-preimage attacked, Bob receives a fake album (but he does know it is a fake album!). Finding a fake image for each of the 1000 pictures takes more time than finding one fake image for the entire album. Therefore, the first alternative provides more chance to Bob to receive authentic pictures.

***Problem*** ***5.12***

A deterministic attack provides absolute guarantees that the searched information is found when the attack ends. Let 2^n be the hash space size and *S* the size of the input space. In generic deterministic attack, the adversary tests one by on each element in the input space and stops when the searched element is found.

Let  <math alttext="upper C left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis comma" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper C left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis comma](images/c05_573.png)  <math alttext="0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript n](images/c05_574.png), be the number of elements, which hash to *i*.

Let  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis comma" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis comma](images/c05_575.png)  <math alttext="0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript n](images/c05_576.png), be the set of input elements, which hash to *i*.

Deterministic preimage attack:

The worst case to the deterministic preimage attack is when the given hash *z* has the lowest value of  <math alttext="upper C left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c05_577.png), i.e.  <math alttext="upper C left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals min Underscript 0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript n Baseline Endscripts upper C left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mrow><mi>min</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></munder><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals min Underscript 0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript n Baseline Endscripts upper C left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c05_578.png), and the elements of the subset  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis](images/c05_579.png) are last to be tested. The attack ends when the first element of  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis](images/c05_580.png) is tested. Thus, the worst case of test number for a deterministic preimage attack is:  <math alttext="upper S minus left-parenthesis min Underscript 0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript n Baseline Endscripts upper C left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis minus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><munder><mrow><mi>min</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></munder><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S minus left-parenthesis min Underscript 0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript n Baseline Endscripts upper C left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c05_581.png).

Deterministic second-preimage attack:

The worst case to the deterministic second-preimage attack is when the given element *x* hashes to z, which has the lowest value of  <math alttext="upper C left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c05_582.png), i.e.  <math alttext="upper C left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals min Underscript 0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript n Baseline Endscripts upper C left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mrow><mi>min</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></munder><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals min Underscript 0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript n Baseline Endscripts upper C left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c05_583.png), and the elements of subset  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis minus StartSet x EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis minus StartSet x EndSet](images/c05_584.png) are last to be tested. The attack ends when the first element of  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis minus StartSet x EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis minus StartSet x EndSet](images/c05_585.png) is tested. Thus, the worst case of test number for a deterministic second-preimage attack is:  <math alttext="upper S minus left-parenthesis min upper C left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis Underscript 0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript n Baseline Endscripts minus 1 minus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><munder><mrow><mi>min</mi><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></munder><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S minus left-parenthesis min upper C left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis Underscript 0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript n Baseline Endscripts minus 1 minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c05_586.png).

Deterministic collision attack:

The attack may be history-aware (i.e. the adversary caches the hashes already computed) or memoryless (i.e. adversary does not cache the hashes already computed). In memoryless attack, the adversary selects randomly an input element and tries to find another input element with the same hash. The worst-case test number is the same as for the second-preimage attack. In case of history-aware, the worst case for testing occurs when all the first 2^n input elements have distinct hashes. Thus, the worst-case test number is  <math alttext="2 Superscript n Baseline plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript n Baseline plus 1](images/c05_587.png) for history-aware collision-attack.

***Problem*** ***5.13***

Preimage brute-force attack takes as input a hash *h* and tries to find a message *x* that hashes to *h*. The adversary takes a random message and compares its hash to *h*. If hashes are distinct, he/she tries another message until the calculated hash matches the given hash *h*. Let  <math alttext="upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis](images/c05_588.png) denote the probability that the hash of the  <math alttext="upper N Superscript t h Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper N Superscript t h Baseline](images/c05_589.png) message matches the given hash *h*.

 <math alttext="ModifyingAbove upper P With bar left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis equals 1 minus upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![ModifyingAbove upper P With bar left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis equals 1 minus upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis](images/c05_590.png) denotes that the probability that no matching hash is found with the *N* tested (distinct) messages. Since there exist 2^n hash values, given a random message *M*, the probability[^(15)](#c05.xhtml#c05-note-0015) that  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis not-equals h" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis not-equals h](images/c05_591.png) is  <math alttext="1 minus StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript n Baseline EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![1 minus StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript n Baseline EndFraction](images/c05_592.png). Thus,  <math alttext="ModifyingAbove upper P With bar left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 1 minus StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript n Baseline EndFraction right-parenthesis Superscript upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>N</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![ModifyingAbove upper P With bar left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 1 minus StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript n Baseline EndFraction right-parenthesis Superscript upper N](images/c05_593.png).

 <math alttext="StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript n Baseline EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript n Baseline EndFraction](images/c05_594.png) is a very small value. Therefore, we can use Taylor’s formula for exponentiation approximation:  <math alttext="e Superscript minus StartFraction 1 Over 2 Super Superscript n Superscript EndFraction Baseline almost-equals 1 minus StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript n Baseline EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo>&#8776;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![e Superscript minus StartFraction 1 Over 2 Super Superscript n Superscript EndFraction Baseline almost-equals 1 minus StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript n Baseline EndFraction](images/c05_595.png)

By substitution and simplification:
