In the previous formula,  <math alttext="upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c05_601.png) cannot be used. Thus, the probability of success is  <math alttext="1 minus epsilon" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> ![1 minus epsilon](images/c05_602.png).  <math alttext="upper N almost-equals 2 Superscript n Baseline asterisk ln left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over epsilon EndFraction right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8776;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>\*</mo><mi>ln</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>&#949;</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper N almost-equals 2 Superscript n Baseline asterisk ln left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over epsilon EndFraction right-parenthesis](images/c05_603.png). At  <math alttext="epsilon equals 0.01" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow></math> ![epsilon equals 0.01](images/c05_604.png),  <math alttext="ln left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over epsilon EndFraction right-parenthesis equals 3.0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>&#949;</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>3.0</mn></mrow></math> ![ln left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over epsilon EndFraction right-parenthesis equals 3.0](images/c05_605.png) and at  <math alttext="epsilon equals 10 Superscript negative 20" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![epsilon equals 10 Superscript negative 20](images/c05_606.png),  <math alttext="ln left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over epsilon EndFraction right-parenthesis equals 6.79" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>&#949;</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>6.79</mn></mrow></math> ![ln left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over epsilon EndFraction right-parenthesis equals 6.79](images/c05_607.png). Thus, when *n* is large, 2^n is a good approximation of *N*.

***Problem*** ***5.14***

1.  In the basic birthday paradox, the problem is to find the minimum number of people such that at least a pair among them share the same birthday. When collision attack is of concern, the birthday problem may be reformulated as: find the number of input elements so that two elements have the same hash. In case of collision birthday attack, input elements are selected randomly and hashes are associated with them. The hash is the equivalent of the birthday in the basic paradox. Hence, the input space is the hash space. The attack terminates when two hashes are equal. In Section 3.4, three approximations of the number of elements to use for finding two elements with the same value are presented. In the general case, two formulas may be used to approximate the required number of elements:  <math alttext="upper N almost-equals StartRoot 2 upper S asterisk upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis EndRoot" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8776;</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>S</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> ![upper N almost-equals StartRoot 2 upper S asterisk upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis EndRoot](images/c05_608.png) or  <math alttext="upper N almost-equals StartRoot 2 upper S asterisk l n left-parenthesis 1 slash left-parenthesis 1 minus upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis right-parenthesis EndRoot" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8776;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>S</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> ![upper N almost-equals StartRoot 2 upper S asterisk l n left-parenthesis 1 slash left-parenthesis 1 minus upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis right-parenthesis EndRoot](images/c05_609.png) where *S* denotes the cardinality of the input space and  <math alttext="upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis](images/c05_610.png) the probability of finding two equal elements among *N* randomly selected elements. In case of collision birthday attack, *S* is the cardinality of the input hash space function of 2^n, where *n* is the hash bit-length. By substitution with  <math alttext="upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis equals 0.5" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow></math> ![upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis equals 0.5](images/c05_611.png):

First approximation yields:  <math alttext="upper N almost-equals StartRoot 2 asterisk 2 Superscript n Baseline asterisk 0.5 EndRoot equals" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8776;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>\*</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> ![upper N almost-equals StartRoot 2 asterisk 2 Superscript n Baseline asterisk 0.5 EndRoot equals](images/c05_612.png)  <math alttext="StartRoot 2 Superscript n Baseline EndRoot equals 2 Superscript n slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![StartRoot 2 Superscript n Baseline EndRoot equals 2 Superscript n slash 2](images/c05_613.png)

Second approximation yields:  <math alttext="upper N almost-equals StartRoot upper S asterisk 2 asterisk ln left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis EndRoot equals 2 Superscript n slash 2 Baseline asterisk 1.77 less-than 2 Superscript left-parenthesis n plus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8776;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msqrt><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>\*</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>\*</mo><mn>1.77</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper N almost-equals StartRoot upper S asterisk 2 asterisk ln left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis EndRoot equals 2 Superscript n slash 2 Baseline asterisk 1.77 less-than 2 Superscript left-parenthesis n plus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2](images/c05_614.png).

*   2\. “always succeed” means finding a collision with a probability of 1. Approximation  <math alttext="upper N almost-equals StartRoot 2 upper S asterisk upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis EndRoot" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8776;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>S</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> ![upper N almost-equals StartRoot 2 upper S asterisk upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis EndRoot](images/c05_615.png) may be used with  <math alttext="upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis equals 100 percent-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> ![upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis equals 100 percent-sign](images/c05_616.png) and results in  <math alttext="upper N almost-equals 2 Superscript 1 slash 2 Baseline asterisk 2 Superscript n slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8776;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper N almost-equals 2 Superscript 1 slash 2 Baseline asterisk 2 Superscript n slash 2](images/c05_617.png), which may be approximated by  <math alttext="2 Superscript n slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript n slash 2](images/c05_618.png) when *n* is large.

Approximation  <math alttext="StartRoot 2 upper S asterisk ln left-parenthesis 1 slash left-parenthesis 1 minus upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis right-parenthesis EndRoot" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>S</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> ![StartRoot 2 upper S asterisk ln left-parenthesis 1 slash left-parenthesis 1 minus upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis right-parenthesis EndRoot](images/c05_619.png) cannot be used with  <math alttext="upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis equals 100 percent-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> ![upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis equals 100 percent-sign](images/c05_620.png), but with  <math alttext="upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis equals 1 minus epsilon" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis equals 1 minus epsilon](images/c05_621.png), where ε is a positive integer very close to 0. Thus, the approximation becomes:  <math alttext="upper N almost-equals StartRoot upper S asterisk 2 asterisk ln left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over epsilon EndFraction right-parenthesis EndRoot equals 2 Superscript n slash 2 Baseline asterisk StartRoot 2 asterisk ln left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over epsilon EndFraction right-parenthesis EndRoot" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8776;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msqrt><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>\*</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><mi>ln</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>&#949;</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>\*</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><mi>ln</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>&#949;</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> ![upper N almost-equals StartRoot upper S asterisk 2 asterisk ln left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over epsilon EndFraction right-parenthesis EndRoot equals 2 Superscript n slash 2 Baseline asterisk StartRoot 2 asterisk ln left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over epsilon EndFraction right-parenthesis EndRoot](images/c05_622.png).

At  <math alttext="epsilon equals 0.01" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow></math> ![epsilon equals 0.01](images/c05_623.png),  <math alttext="StartRoot 2 asterisk ln left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over epsilon EndFraction right-parenthesis EndRoot equals 3.0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><mi>ln</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>&#949;</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>3.0</mn></mrow></math> ![StartRoot 2 asterisk ln left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over epsilon EndFraction right-parenthesis EndRoot equals 3.0](images/c05_624.png) and at  <math alttext="epsilon equals 10 Superscript negative 10" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![epsilon equals 10 Superscript negative 10](images/c05_625.png),  <math alttext="StartRoot 2 asterisk ln left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over epsilon EndFraction right-parenthesis EndRoot equals 6.7" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><mi>ln</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>&#949;</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>6.7</mn></mrow></math> ![StartRoot 2 asterisk ln left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over epsilon EndFraction right-parenthesis EndRoot equals 6.7](images/c05_626.png). Thus, when *n* is large,  <math alttext="2 Superscript n slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript n slash 2](images/c05_627.png) is a good approximation of *N*.

***Problem*** ***5.15***

Given a message *M*, the adversary easily computes the length of padding string for *M*. However, the sender computes the padding string for string  <math alttext="k e y StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> ![k e y StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M](images/c05_628.png) to generate  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis k e y StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis k e y StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M right-parenthesis](images/c05_629.png). Without knowing the length of  <math alttext="k e y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ![k e y](images/c05_630.png), the adversary is unable to compute the length for padding string  <math alttext="k e y StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> ![k e y StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M](images/c05_631.png). Therefore, he/she cannot run the length extension attack.

***Problem*** ***5.16***

1.  In SHA-384, SHA-512/224, and SHA-512/256, the initialization hash  <math alttext="upper H Superscript 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![upper H Superscript 0](images/c05_632.png) and the block hashes  <math alttext="upper H Superscript i Baseline comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![upper H Superscript i Baseline comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper N](images/c05_633.png), are represented as eight words of 64 bits. But, the message hash is produced by truncation of  <math alttext="upper H Superscript upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mi>N</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper H Superscript upper N](images/c05_634.png), the hash of the last block. From the later, SHA-384 keeps six 64-bit words, SHA-512/224 keeps three 64-bit words and the left half of the fourth 64-bit word, and SHA-512/256 keeps four 64-bit words. Message hash and initialization hash  <math alttext="upper H Superscript 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![upper H Superscript 0](images/c05_635.png) have different lengths. Consequently, the message hash cannot be used as  <math alttext="upper H Superscript 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![upper H Superscript 0](images/c05_636.png) to enable the adversary extend the original message. In other words, hash obtained by truncation prevents the hash function from length extension attack.
2.  In SHA-3, the hash function output length *d* is the half of Keccak-p permutation capacity *c*. Inside the sponge function, Keccak-p permutation takes an input of *b* bits, called state array, with  <math alttext="b ampersand gt semicolon c" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>&#38;gt;</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> ![b ampersand gt semicolon c](images/c05_637.png). In squeezing step, the message hash is produced by truncation. Consequently, the message hash intercepted by the adversary cannot be substituted to the initial state array to realize a length extension attack.

***Problem*** ***5.17***

Recall that non-repudiation is the assurance that a message originator cannot deny having sent the message (e.g. denying having sent a newspaper article). First, since MACs do not address confidentiality, messages with MACs can be checked by more than one receiver and any user who share the secret with the sender(s) can produce valid MACs. For example, a pool of journalists shares the same secret with their editor. Second, in case the sender is malicious (e.g. a malicious editor), he/she can generate a MAC and then claims he/she received it from a journalist. Consequently, if the sender and receiver get involved in a dispute over message origination, MACs cannot provide a proof that a message was indeed sent by the designated sender.

***Problem*** ***5.18***

Length extension means appending a bit string *F* to the end of the original message. Without loss of generality, assume that the length of string *F* is a multiple of the block length of the targeted hash function.

1.  In secret prefix MAC,  <math alttext="upper M upper A upper C left-parenthesis upper M comma k e y right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis k e y StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper M upper A upper C left-parenthesis upper M comma k e y right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis k e y StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M right-parenthesis](images/c05_638.png).

The input bit string  <math alttext="k e y StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper M EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![k e y StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper M EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P](images/c05_639.png) are structured into a sequence  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper B Superscript 1 Baseline comma upper B squared comma ellipsis comma upper B Superscript n Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>B</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>B</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper B Superscript 1 Baseline comma upper B squared comma ellipsis comma upper B Superscript n Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c05_640.png) of blocks of fixed size *L*, which is a parameter of the hash function. *P* denotes the padding bits added so that the length of  <math alttext="k e y StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper M EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![k e y StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper M EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P](images/c05_641.png) is a multiple of the block length of the hash function.

The sequences *B* and *A* start with the same blocks, which represent the  <math alttext="k e y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ![k e y](images/c05_662.png). ***Problem*** ***5.19***

Inner hash of HMAC is  <math alttext="h Subscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis Baseline equals upper H left-parenthesis k prime circled-plus i upper P a d StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![h Subscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis Baseline equals upper H left-parenthesis k prime circled-plus i upper P a d StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper M right-parenthesis](images/c05_679.png) and its outer hash is  <math alttext="h Subscript left-parenthesis o right-parenthesis Baseline equals upper H left-parenthesis k Superscript prime Baseline circled-plus o upper P a d StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue h Subscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>o</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>o</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![h Subscript left-parenthesis o right-parenthesis Baseline equals upper H left-parenthesis k Superscript prime Baseline circled-plus o upper P a d StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue h Subscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c05_680.png). The outer hash is the output of HMAC algorithm.

The inner hash is designed according to the secret prefix MAC; hence, it is vulnerable to length extension attack (see Problem 5.18).

Assume that the adversary appends a fake string *F* to the original message *M*. Let  <math alttext="upper M prime equals upper M StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper F" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M prime equals upper M StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper F](images/c05_681.png). The length extension attack works like if the first part of  <math alttext="upper M prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> ![upper M prime](images/c05_682.png), i.e. *M*, is hashed at sender and the second part, i.e. *F*, is hashed at adversary as a continuation using the hash produced by the sender. However, the inner hash is not available to the adversary and the output of HMAC is a hash of a hash combined with the key. Hence, the adversary has no means to use a hash output to substitute to initialization vector to continue hashing. Thus, HMAC algorithm is not vulnerable to length extension attack.

# 6   
Stream Ciphers

Stream ciphers are symmetric ciphers that encrypt and decrypt bits individually. They are used to secure communications in wireless and cellular networks. Stream ciphers are well-suited to hardware implementation and they are generally faster than block ciphers. They also are well-suited to encrypt and decrypt continuous data (e.g. phone communication) at high rate and when devices have limited memory to store long messages. That is why, stream ciphers are often used in telecommunication networks, such as 3G, 4G, and 5G.

ChaCha20 stream cipher is an Internet standard; it is recommended as a cipher in TLS protocol to secure communications between clients and web servers \[[1](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0001)\]. Most common stream ciphers are built around linear feedback shift registers, which makes them easy to implement in hardware.

This chapter aims at presenting the principles and standard algorithms related to stream ciphers.

## 6.1 Stream Ciphers

### 6.1.1 Principles of Stream Ciphers

***Definition 6.1 Stream cipher****: it is a symmetric cipher where plaintext bits are pairwise combined with bits of a key stream. Each bit of ciphertext is yielded by a bitwise XOR operation.*

***Definition 6.2 Initialization vector (IV)****: it is a bit string computed for each plaintext (or for a set of plaintexts) and used jointly with the secret key to generate the keystream.*

There are two main reasons to use and frequently change initialization vectors: 1) long sequences of keystream require periodic synchronization of encryption and decryption processes (because of transmission errors) and 2) encrypting distinct plaintexts with the same key is insecure. Therefore, initialization vectors is a solution to generate different pseudorandom sequences without necessarily changing the secret key.

***Definition 6.3 Key-Scheduling Algorithm (KSA)****: it is the operation of mixing the secret key and the Initialization vector to yield a key, which is then used to encrypt/decrypt a single plaintext.*

As shown in [Figure 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0001), the main building block of cipher stream is the keystream generator. The latter is a PRNG (pseudo random number generator), which generates a stream of bits given a secret key and an initialization vector.

![Figure 6.1 General structure of stream cipher (synchronous model).](images/c06f001.png)

[**Figure 6.1**](#c06.xhtml#rc06-fig-0001) General structure of stream cipher (synchronous model).

Stream ciphers were inspired by One-time pad cipher (see Section 4.6). Unlike OTP cipher, in which the key stream is at least as long as the data to encrypt, stream ciphers make use of periodic PRNGs.

The secret key is shared by both parties. Therefore, the keystream generators on both sides generate the same sequence of keystream bits. Encryption and decryption operations are very simple. Let  <math alttext="a Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![a Subscript i](images/c06_1.png) and  <math alttext="s Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![s Subscript j](images/c06_2.png) be the current plaintext and keystream bits, respectively. Formally,

*   Encryption is:  <math alttext="c Subscript i Baseline equals a Subscript i Baseline circled-plus s Subscript j Baseline m o d Baseline 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![c Subscript i Baseline equals a Subscript i Baseline circled-plus s Subscript j Baseline m o d Baseline 2](images/c06_3.png)
*   Decryption is:  <math alttext="a Subscript i Baseline equals c Subscript i Baseline circled-plus s Subscript j Baseline m o d Baseline 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![a Subscript i Baseline equals c Subscript i Baseline circled-plus s Subscript j Baseline m o d Baseline 2](images/c06_4.png)

where ⊕ denoted the XOR bitwise[¹](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0001) operation.

Since the keystream generator produces a keystream, which is periodic, the same keystream may be used to encrypt (or decrypt) more than one plaintext (or ciphertext). That is why two distinct indices  <math alttext="i and j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mtext>&#160;and&#160;</mtext><mi>j</mi></mrow></math> ![i and j](images/c06_5.png) are used.

It is very easy to check that the decryption process is correct:

### 6.1.2 Synchronous vs Self-synchronized Keystream Generators

To decrypt correctly, both parties must use the same keystream to encrypt and recover the same plaintext bit. Therefore, both parties need to be synchronized when using keystream bits. There exist two types of keystream generators: synchronous and self-synchronized.

***Definition 6.4 Synchronous stream cipher****: it is a cipher in which the keystream is generated independently of the plaintext and of the ciphertext.*

***Definition 6.5 Self-clocking stream cipher****: it is a cipher in which the keystream is generated from a key function and a fixed number of previous ciphertext bits.*

#### 6.1.2.1 Synchronous Stream Ciphers

In a synchronous stream cipher, both parties initialize one time (per session or message) their keystream with the same values (i.e. secret key and initialization vector) and then encrypt and decrypt bits until the end of session or message. Formally, encryption and decryption may be described as follows:

Let  <math alttext="upper I n i t left-parenthesis upper K comma upper I upper V right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper I n i t left-parenthesis upper K comma upper I upper V right-parenthesis](images/c06_13.png) be a function that initializes the keystream cipher using a secret key *K* and an initialization vector  <math alttext="upper I upper V" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> ![upper I upper V](images/c06_14.png) and  <math alttext="upper N e x t left-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>(</mo><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper N e x t left-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c06_15.png) a function, which yields the next state of the keystream generator. In [section 6.1.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-sec-02004a),  <math alttext="upper N e x t left-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>(</mo><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper N e x t left-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c06_16.png) function will be addressed in detail. Let  <math alttext="sigma Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![sigma Subscript i](images/c06_17.png) denote the state and  <math alttext="g left-parenthesis sigma Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![g left-parenthesis sigma Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06_18.png), the output of the keystream generator at cycle *i*,  <math alttext="i equals 0 comma 1 comma ellipsis period" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> ![i equals 0 comma 1 comma ellipsis period](images/c06_19.png) Then, encryption and decryption can be described as:

![](images/c06_20.png)

Synchronous stream ciphers have at least two advantages and one drawback.

Advantages: i) If a bit is modified but not deleted, the process of decryption continues to correctly decrypt the remaining bits. Therefore, synchronous stream ciphers are not error-propagation sensitive. ii) If some bits are inserted, by an adversary, the receiver will lose synchronization and the forged bits as well as the remaining bits are very likely to be discarded. Therefore, synchronous stream ciphers are more prone to support the detection of some attacks.

Drawback: if a bit is lost (because of transmission error), the receiver is desynchronized and the decryption may fail starting from the missing bits if no re-synchronization mechanism is used.

Therefore, synchronous stream ciphers are very useful to encrypt streaming media (voice, audio, and video) where the speed of data-traffic is more important than the integrity of the data (e.g. loss of a few pixels or images in video streaming is not damaging).

It is worth noticing that synchronous stream ciphers are the most common in practice. To alleviate the drawback above, the common approach, is to reinitialize the keystream generator each limited-length message.

#### 6.1.2.2 Self-synchronized Stream Ciphers

As mentioned previously, stream ciphers are well-suited to secure continuous-flow communication such as voice in which a continuous message is encrypted bit per bit. Transmission errors may occur while bits are transmitted through the channel. Can you imagine phone subscribers accepting phone call breaks because of loss of one bit? Self-synchronizing stream ciphers are a solution to prevent desynchronization due to bit loss or fraudulent insertion. They are suited to flows (such as voice of video) that tolerate bit loss. One simplest way to describe self-synchronizing stream ciphers is given below.

Self-synchronizing stream ciphers rely on a synchronization window of length *l* bits. At the beginning of cycle *i* (i.e. cycle of processing the plaintext bit  <math alttext="a Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![a Subscript i](images/c06_28.png)), the synchronization window denoted  <math alttext="script upper C Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![script upper C Subscript i](images/c06_29.png) is the set of the *l* most recent ciphertext bits, i.e.  <math alttext="script upper C Subscript i Baseline equals left-parenthesis c Subscript i minus l Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![script upper C Subscript i Baseline equals left-parenthesis c Subscript i minus l Baseline](images/c06_30.png). A function  <math alttext="omega left-parenthesis script upper C Subscript i Baseline comma upper K right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![omega left-parenthesis script upper C Subscript i Baseline comma upper K right-parenthesis](images/c06_32.png) computes the output  <math alttext="s Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![s Subscript i](images/c06_33.png) of the keystream generator at cycle *i* using the synchronization window bits and the secret key *K* (see [Figure 6.2](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0002)). If neither bit loss nor bit insertion occur, the set  <math alttext="script upper C Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![script upper C Subscript i](images/c06_34.png) is the same on both sides. Therefore, both sides compute the same keystream bit  <math alttext="s Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![s Subscript i](images/c06_35.png). Now, let us consider two scenarios: bit loss and bit insertion.

*   *Bit loss*. In the event of transmission error,[²](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0002) no ciphertext bit is correctly received during cycle *i*. Thus, the receiver has no valid ciphertext bit to append to the synchronization window set. Rather, it appends the undefined binary value denoted  <math alttext="script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></math> ![script upper O](images/c06_36.png). Therefore, it cannot correctly compute the keystream bits for bits from  <math alttext="i plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![i plus 1](images/c06_37.png) to  <math alttext="i plus l" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> ![i plus l](images/c06_38.png). The synchronization resumes at bit  <math alttext="i plus l plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![i plus l plus 1](images/c06_39.png). One strategy, under the assumption that the application is loss-tolerant, is to discard *l* bits starting from bit *i*. Thus, self-synchronizing stream ciphers have the advantage of limiting the propagation of transmission errors to a few bits of a continuous flow. Example [6.2](#c06.xhtml#c06-mthst-0002) illustrates how the self-synchronization is reestablished.
*   *Bit insertion*.[³](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0003) By adversary: assume that bit  <math alttext="c Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![c Subscript i](images/c06_40.png) is replaced by bit  <math alttext="c prime Subscript i Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>c</mi><msub><mo>'</mo><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![c prime Subscript i Baseline](images/c06_41.png). In such a case, the set  <math alttext="script upper C Subscript i plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![script upper C Subscript i plus 1](images/c06_42.png) at sender differs from the set  <math alttext="script upper C Subscript i plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![script upper C Subscript i plus 1](images/c06_43.png) at receiver, which results in distinct keystream bits for bits  <math alttext="i plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![i plus 1](images/c06_44.png) to  <math alttext="i plus l" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> ![i plus l](images/c06_45.png), which results in a decryption error. The synchronization resumes at bit  <math alttext="i plus l" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> ![i plus l](images/c06_46.png). Example [6.2](#c06.xhtml#c06-mthst-0002) illustrates how the self-synchronization is reestablished.

![Figure 6.2 General structure of self-synchronizing stream cipher.](images/c06f002.png)

[**Figure 6.2**](#c06.xhtml#rc06-fig-0002) General structure of self-synchronizing stream cipher.

Self-synchronizing stream ciphers have the advantage of limiting the propagation of transmission errors and malicious bit alterations to a few bits of a continuous flow. Below is the pseudocode of self-synchronizing stream cipher operations.

![](images/c06_47.png)

 <math alttext="upper T x bar e r r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> ![upper T x bar e r r](images/c06_57.png) is a function, which returns *True*, in the event of a bit-transmission error.

 <math alttext="upper U p d a t e left-parenthesis script upper C Subscript i Baseline comma e right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>U</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper U p d a t e left-parenthesis script upper C Subscript i Baseline comma e right-parenthesis](images/c06_58.png) is a function that removes the oldest element of set  <math alttext="script upper C Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![script upper C Subscript i](images/c06_59.png) and adds element *e*.

**Example 6.2**

*   – Bit loss

Assume that *l*, the length of synchronization window, is 5 and a transmission error occurs on bit *i*. The table below shows the synchronization window bits at each cycle on both sides. At, cycle *i*, both parties have the same bit set, but the receiver cannot decrypt the errored bit. Therefore, it includes the undefined value  <math alttext="script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></math> ![script upper O](images/c06_60.png) in its set. Next, from cycle  <math alttext="i plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![i plus 1](images/c06_61.png) to cycle  <math alttext="i plus 5" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> ![i plus 5](images/c06_62.png), the receiver has a distinct synchronization window set and consequently, it cannot not decrypt correctly. Next, staring from cycle  <math alttext="i plus 6" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> ![i plus 6](images/c06_63.png), both parties have the same set and the decryption resumes correctly.

![](images/c06_64.png)

*   – Bit insertion

Assume that *l*, the length of synchronization window, is 4 and a bit *i* has been altered by an adversary. Let  <math alttext="c prime Subscript i Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>c</mi><msub><mo>'</mo><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![c prime Subscript i Baseline](images/c06_84.png) denote the received ciphertext bit. The table below shows the synchronization window bits at each cycle on both sides. At cycle *i*, both parties have the same bit set, but the receiver decrypts an altered bit and updates its synchronization set with  <math alttext="c prime Subscript i Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>c</mi><msub><mo>'</mo><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![c prime Subscript i Baseline](images/c06_85.png). Next, from cycle  <math alttext="i plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![i plus 1](images/c06_86.png) to cycle  <math alttext="i plus 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![i plus 4](images/c06_87.png), the parties have two distinct synchronization sets. Therefore, their keystream bits are distinct resulting in bits of plaintext that are different from the decrypted bits. Starting from cycle  <math alttext="i plus 5" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> ![i plus 5](images/c06_88.png), both parties have the same set and the decryption resumes correctly. Notice that the receiver has no means, at this stage, to know that a bit had been altered.

![](images/c06_89.png)

### 6.1.3 How to Generate Random Keystream Bits?

Keystream generators are the core of stream ciphers. They are Pseudo Random Bit Generators. There exist two main approaches to design the keystream generators: linear congruential generators (LCG) and Linear-feed-back-shift-register-based generators. Most common stream ciphers belong to the second category, which is addressed in detail in the next section. This subsection just surveys the linear congruential generators.

In general, a linear congruential generator is defined as a process that produces random values as follows:

Let *A*, *B*, *m*, and  <math alttext="z 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![z 0](images/c06_106.png) be parameters of the generator. The number generated at cycle *i*, denoted  <math alttext="z Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![z Subscript i](images/c06_107.png), is defined by:  <math alttext="z Subscript i Baseline equals upper A asterisk z Subscript i minus 1 Baseline plus upper B m o d m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![z Subscript i Baseline equals upper A asterisk z Subscript i minus 1 Baseline plus upper B m o d m](images/c06_108.png). It is easy to find *A* and *B* with plaintext attack (see Problem 6.2).

If the LCG is used in a stream cipher, its output  <math alttext="z Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![z Subscript i](images/c06_109.png) is a string of  <math alttext="l o g 2 m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![l o g 2 m](images/c06_110.png) bits used for encryption and decryption. At least *A* and *B* must be secret. Like affine cipher presented in Section 4.3, stream ciphers relying on LCG are vulnerable to plaintext attacks.  <math alttext="3 asterisk left ceiling l o g 2 m right ceiling" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>\*</mo><mrow><mo>&#8968;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo>&#8969;</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![3 asterisk left ceiling l o g 2 m right ceiling](images/c06_111.png) bits of plaintext and their corresponding ciphertext bits are enough to recover the secret key formed by *A* and *B* (see Problem 6.3).

### 6.1.4 Linear-Feedback Shift Registers (LFSRs)

#### 6.1.4.1 LFSR Principle and Properties

Linear-feedback shift registers (LFSRs) are building blocks for a wide variety of applications including cryptography, cyclic redundancy check (CRC), and pseudorandom number generators. When cryptography is of concern, LFSRs provide key streams to encryption and decryption operations of stream ciphers.

An LFSR is a register composed of *m* flip-flop[⁴](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0004) elements (also called cells or simply bits) driven by a clock; i.e. at each clock impulse the state of register changes. The output of each element *i*, denoted  <math alttext="upper F upper F Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>F</mi><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F upper F Subscript i](images/c06_112.png), is the current output value in the element. The rightmost element of the LFSR is the register output.

[Figure 6.3](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0003) shows a simplified structure of shift register without feedback, where ρ denotes the register output. The *m* flip-flop (FF) elements of the register are initialized to a selected value, called *seed*, say  <math alttext="10 ellipsis 10" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>&#8230;</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math> ![10 ellipsis 10](images/c06_113.png). That is, the first register output is  <math alttext="s Subscript t Baseline equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![s Subscript t Baseline equals 0](images/c06_114.png). Then, at next clock impulse, the register elements are one-position right-shifted and the second register output  <math alttext="s Subscript t plus 1 Baseline equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![s Subscript t plus 1 Baseline equals 1](images/c06_115.png). At the  <math alttext="m minus 1 Superscript t h" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![m minus 1 Superscript t h](images/c06_116.png) clock impulse, the register output is  <math alttext="s Subscript t plus m minus 1 Baseline equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![s Subscript t plus m minus 1 Baseline equals 1](images/c06_117.png). Then, the register output does not change (i.e. all register elements are zeros).

![Figure 6.3 General structure of no-feedback shift register.](images/c06f003.png)

[**Figure 6.3**](#c06.xhtml#rc06-fig-0003) General structure of no-feedback shift register.

If a non-feedback register has enough bits, it can be used to deliver the key in one-time pad cipher. Unfortunately, since the secret key is at least as long as the message and messages may have a long length, non-feedback shift registers are not appropriate to implement OTP ciphers in hardware.

Shift registers, used in hardware implementation of stream ciphers, are characterized by feedback; that is why they are called Feedback Shift Registers. That is, the output of some or all flip-flop elements are used to generate an input to the first element. Not all the elements are required to generate feedback. Thus, binary coefficients, denoted *c[m]*,  <math alttext="c Subscript m minus 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![c Subscript m minus 2](images/c06_118.png), …, and  <math alttext="c 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![c 1](images/c06_119.png), indicate if the output of flip-flop elements are used or not. In [Figure 6.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0004), the operation ⊗ denotes binary multiplication (i.e. the output of  <math alttext="upper F upper F Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>F</mi><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F upper F Subscript i](images/c06_120.png) participates in the feedback only if  <math alttext="c Subscript i Baseline equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![c Subscript i Baseline equals 1](images/c06_121.png)). The flip-flops that impact the feedback are called *taps* or *feedback coefficients*. The feedback is yielded by a linear function; that is why LFSRs are called linear. There exist other LFSRs that are not linear. The operation of an LFSR can be described as follows:

![Figure 6.4 General structure of Linear-Feedback Shift Register.](images/c06f004.png)

[**Figure 6.4**](#c06.xhtml#rc06-fig-0004) General structure of Linear-Feedback Shift Register.

The state of an LFSR at time *t*, denoted  <math alttext="sigma left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![sigma left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c06_131.png), is the product of the states of its flip-flop elements. That is,  <math alttext="sigma left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis upper F upper F Subscript m Baseline left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis comma upper F upper F Subscript m minus 1 Baseline left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis comma ellipsis comma upper F upper F 1 left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>F</mi><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>F</mi><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![sigma left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis upper F upper F Subscript m Baseline left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis comma upper F upper F Subscript m minus 1 Baseline left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis comma ellipsis comma upper F upper F 1 left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c06_132.png), where  <math alttext="upper F upper F Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>F</mi><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper F upper F Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c06_133.png) denotes the state of flip-flop *i* at time *t*. In bit representation, the state of LFSR is a bit string ranging from  <math alttext="000 ellipsis 001" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>000</mn><mo>&#8230;</mo><mn>001</mn></mrow></math> ![000 ellipsis 001](images/c06_134.png) to  <math alttext="111 ellipsis 111" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>111</mn><mo>&#8230;</mo><mn>111</mn></mrow></math> ![111 ellipsis 111](images/c06_135.png).

At each clock impulse, the LFSR delivers a bit and register elements are right-shifted. Therefore, the register output is a bit stream that starts with string  <math alttext="s Subscript t plus m minus 1 Baseline comma s Subscript t plus m minus 2 Baseline comma ellipsis period comma s Subscript t plus 1 Baseline comma s Subscript t Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![s Subscript t plus m minus 1 Baseline comma s Subscript t plus m minus 2 Baseline comma ellipsis period comma s Subscript t plus 1 Baseline comma s Subscript t Baseline](images/c06_136.png). The first bit produced by the LFSR is  <math alttext="s Subscript t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![s Subscript t](images/c06_137.png). The next bits of the keystream are computed as follows:

***Properties of LFSRs***

1.  The output of LFSR, which has *N* distinct states, is a bit string, which repeats every *N* bits. Therefore, the state of flip-flop *i* at time  <math alttext="t plus k upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![t plus k upper N](images/c06_143.png), with  <math alttext="k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> ![k](images/c06_144.png) a positive integer, is the same as at time *t*.
2.  An LFSR with *n* flip-flops is said to be maximal-length LFSR, if it has exactly  <math alttext="2 Superscript n Baseline minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript n Baseline minus 1](images/c06_145.png) distinct states.
3.  An LFSR, which reaches a state where all flip-flop states are  <math alttext="0 s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>0</mn><mtext>s</mtext></math> ![0 s](images/c06_146.png), has a constant[⁶](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0006) output equal to 0.

**Example 6.3**

[Figure 6.5](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0005) shows an example of LFSR with four FF elements. To simplify the LFSR structure, an equivalent representation is used; if  <math alttext="c Subscript i Baseline equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![c Subscript i Baseline equals 1](images/c06_147.png), then the output of element  <math alttext="upper F upper F Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>F</mi><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F upper F Subscript i](images/c06_148.png) is connected to the XOR feedback line; and there is no connection otherwise.

![Figure 6.5 Examples of Linear-Feedback Shift Registers.](images/c06f005a.png)

[**Figure 6.5**](#c06.xhtml#rc06-fig-0005) Examples of Linear-Feedback Shift Registers.

The initial state of the LFSR is  <math alttext="1100 period t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1100.</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> ![1100 period t](images/c06_149.png) denotes clock impulses. It is worth noticing that the first LFSR has only 6 distinct states, while the second has 15 distinct states. The second LFSR is maximal-length. #### 6.1.4.2 Feedback Polynomial of LFSRs

To build stream ciphers, LFSRs with *m* cells are commonly used under computations over either extension fields (i.e. fields of the form  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c06_150.png)) or prime fields (i.e. fields of the form  <math alttext="upper F Subscript p Baseline comma" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript p Baseline comma](images/c06_151.png) with *p* prime). Most common stream ciphers based on LFSRs rely on extension fields. In such a case, an LFSR with feedback coefficients  <math alttext="c Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![c Subscript i](images/c06_152.png),  <math alttext="i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>&#8230;</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma m](images/c06_153.png), where  <math alttext="m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![m](images/c06_154.png) is the number of register bits and  <math alttext="c Subscript i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma m Baseline element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>&#8230;</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo>{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![c Subscript i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma m Baseline element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet](images/c06_155.png), can be represented as a polynomial, called *feedback polynomial*,  <math alttext="script upper F left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![script upper F left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c06_156.png), defined by:

 <math alttext="script upper F left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals 1 plus left-parenthesis sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript m Endscripts c Subscript i Baseline x Superscript i Baseline right-parenthesis mod 2" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#8497;</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow></mstyle></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>mod</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![script upper F left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals 1 plus left-parenthesis sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript m Endscripts c Subscript i Baseline x Superscript i Baseline right-parenthesis mod 2](images/c06_157.png)(6.2) 

In Example [6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-mthst-0001),  <math alttext="script upper F left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 4 Baseline plus x cubed plus x plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![script upper F left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 4 Baseline plus x cubed plus x plus 1](images/c06_158.png); in [Figure 6.5a](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0005) and  <math alttext="script upper F left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 4 Baseline plus x plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![script upper F left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 4 Baseline plus x plus 1](images/c06_159.png) in [Figure 6.5b](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0005). Polynomial and diagram representations are equivalent. That is, from a feedback polynomial, the structure of LFSR can be drawn; and from a structure of an LFSR, the feedback polynomial can be derived. Polynomial representation is used when mathematical analysis is of concern.

A proof of Lemma [6.2](#c06.xhtml#c06-mthst-0005) is given in \[[2](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0002)\]. Recall that a primitive polynomial  <math alttext="p left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![p left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c06_163.png), of degree *m*, is a polynomial irreducible in  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>&#8484;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z 2](images/c06_164.png) that can generate all elements of a field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c06_165.png) (see Section 3.2.4). For any integer  <math alttext="m greater-than-or-equal-to 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![m greater-than-or-equal-to 2](images/c06_166.png), there exists at least one primitive polynomial of degree *m* to generate a field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c06_167.png). The number of distinct primitive polynomials of degree *m* grows quasi-exponentially with *m*. Therefore, there exist multiple combinations of tags to build LFSRs with a cycle of  <math alttext="2 Superscript m Baseline minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript m Baseline minus 1](images/c06_168.png). To reduce the hardware implementation of LFSRs (i.e. reduce the number of connections and XOR circuits due to tags), sparse primitive polynomials of degree *m*, i.e. with the least number of monomials, are preferred.

[Table 6.2](#c06.xhtml#c06-tbl-0002) \[[3](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0003)\] provides a list of examples of feedback polynomials with minimal cost (i.e. with minimum electronic circuits) to build LFSRs with 2 to 32 bits.

![Table 6.2 Feedback polynomials of LFSR with 2 to 20 and 32 bits.](images/c06_169.png)

[**Table 6.2**](#c06.xhtml#rc06-tbl-0002) Feedback polynomials of LFSR with 2 to 20 and 32 bits.

### 6.1.5 LFSRs for Building Stream Ciphers

LFSRs are common building blocks to design and implement stream ciphers. In such a case, the seed of initialization of LFSR is the secret key shared between parties. Unfortunately, a single LFSR is vulnerable to plaintext attacks (see Problem 6.7). Therefore, it is not recommended to use a single LFSR.

There exist two basic approaches to use LFSRs to build stream cipher. The first is to use several LFSRs in parallel and combine their outputs in a secure way (i.e. hard to attack) to generate the key stream. Such generators are called combination generators. The second approach is to use a single LFSR, then apply a nonlinear function to its output to generate the key stream. The registers in the second category are called *filter generators*. Both approaches can be mixed to yield highly secure stream ciphers. Therefore, the recommended approach to build LFSR-based stream ciphers is to mix several LFSRs that run in parallel and combine their outputs.

A huge number of solutions have been proposed to design LFSR-based stream ciphers. They differ regarding how the LFSRs are clocked and how their outputs are combined. As shown in [Figure 6.6](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0006), the LFSR-based stream ciphers are characterized by two components: Logic of clocking and logic of output combination. Thus, LFSR-based stream cipher design approaches can be classified according to their components.

![Figure 6.6 General architecture for building LFSR-based stream ciphers.](images/c06f006.png)

[**Figure 6.6**](#c06.xhtml#rc06-fig-0006) General architecture for building LFSR-based stream ciphers.

1.  Clocking technique
    
    *   – *Regular clocking*: all the LFSRs are clocked at the same rate to produce their output.
    *   – *Irregular clocking*: only LFSRs that match a given condition are clocked. In general, the output or some specific bits of certain LFSRs are used to clock other LFSRs. [Figure 6.7](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0007) shows an example of irregular clocking.  <math alttext="upper L upper F upper S upper R 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper L upper F upper S upper R 3](images/c06_207.png) is clocked only if both outputs of  <math alttext="upper L upper F upper S upper R 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper L upper F upper S upper R 1](images/c06_208.png) and  <math alttext="upper L upper F upper S upper R 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper L upper F upper S upper R 2](images/c06_209.png) are 1, and  <math alttext="upper L upper F upper S upper R 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper L upper F upper S upper R 4](images/c06_210.png) is clocked only if the output of  <math alttext="upper L upper F upper S upper R 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper L upper F upper S upper R 2](images/c06_211.png) is 0. The standard E0, which is presented in 6.2.1, is based on irregular clocking.
        
        ![Figure 6.7 Example of irregular clocking of LFSRs.](images/c06f007.png)
        
        [**Figure 6.7**](#c06.xhtml#rc06-fig-0007) Example of irregular clocking of LFSRs.
        
2.  Combination of LFSR outputs
    
    There exist two main approaches:
    
    *   – Use of a nonlinear function *F* to combine the outputs of the LFSRs. Since a function is used to filter outputs, the generators are called *filtering generators*. In [Figure 6.8](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0008), the output of the keystream generator is a nonlinear combination of four LFSRs. Let  <math alttext="s Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![s Subscript i](images/c06_212.png) denote the output of  <math alttext="upper L upper F upper S upper R Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper L upper F upper S upper R Subscript i](images/c06_213.png). Therefore, the output of the entire keystream generator is  <math alttext="upper F left-parenthesis 1 comma 2 comma 3 comma 4 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis not-sign s 1 logical-and s 2 right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis not-sign left-parenthesis s 3 circled-plus s 4 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>&#172;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8743;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>&#172;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper F left-parenthesis 1 comma 2 comma 3 comma 4 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis not-sign s 1 logical-and s 2 right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis not-sign left-parenthesis s 3 circled-plus s 4 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c06_214.png).
        
        ![Figure 6.8 Example of nonlinear combination generator.](images/c06f008.png)
        
        [**Figure 6.8**](#c06.xhtml#rc06-fig-0008) Example of nonlinear combination generator.
        
    *   – Use of Finite state machine (FSM): to increase nonlinearity, function *F* may be designed as an FSM. With FSM, the keystream generator makes use of past computations to produce keystream bits, thus reinforcing the security level. Most standard stream ciphers, including SNOW 3G and ZUC presented in 6.2, rely on FSM.

**Note**. Since mathematical proofs of security of LFSR-based keystream generators are not yet known, such generators can only be deemed as computationally secure.

## 6.2 Examples of Standard Keystream Generators

Several stream ciphers have been proposed and some of them have been standardized and widely used in operational networks. Recall that standardization organizations involved in networks and telecommunications are mainly IEEE,[⁷](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0007) 3GPP,[⁸](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0008) ETSI,[⁹](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0009) IETF,[^(10)](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0010) and ISO,[^(11)](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0011)

Standard stream ciphers include A5/1, E0, SNOW 3G, ZUC, Chacha20, and RC4, which are presented in the sequel.

**Note**. In the sequel, the presentation of keystream generators preserves the notations of standards. Therefore, different notations for numbering cells and states will be used depending on the standard.

### 6.2.1 A5/1 Keystream Generator

A5/1 is a cipher stream used to secure communications between mobile phones and base stations in GSM networks (i.e. 2G cellular networks). Billions of phones used A5/1 to protect communications while propagating over the air.

A5/1 relies on a key stream generator composed of three LFSRs with irregular clocking and defined by feedback polynomials:

right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 23 Baseline plus x Superscript 22 Baseline plus x Superscript 21 Baseline plus x Superscript 8 Baseline plus 1 EndLayout](images/c06_215.png)

Therefore, in total,  <math alttext="19 plus 22 plus 23" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>19</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>22</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>23</mn></mrow></math> ![19 plus 22 plus 23](images/c06_216.png) bits are used to deliver a key stream. The registers are initialized using a key of 64 bits stored on the mobile phone.

A5/1 output is an XOR of the output of the three registers. In each register, a specific bit, called clocking bit, is used to know when the shift operation is to perform. In [Figure 6.9](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0009), bit 8 is the bit clocking of the first and second registers and bit 10 is the bit clocking of the third register. At each cycle, the clocking bits of the three registers are examined. A register is clocked (i.e. a clock signal is delivered to the register; thus, it shifts its cells to the right) if the current state of its clocking bit agrees with the majority of clocking bits. Therefore, at each cycle, two or three register shifts are performed. The state of register of which the clocking bit differs from the clocking bits of the other registers does not change.

![Figure 6.9 General structure of random generator of A5/1 cipher.](images/c06f009.png)

[**Figure 6.9**](#c06.xhtml#rc06-fig-0009) General structure of random generator of A5/1 cipher.

The irregularity of register clocking was a countermeasure against plaintext attacks against LFSR (see attack against LFSR, Problem 6.7). Unfortunately, even with irregular clocking of registers, several attacks succeeded and showed that A5/1 was not secure. From then on, A5/1 was no longer a solution for cellular networks.

Another countermeasure was proposed in A5/2 cipher, with four registers, but it is no more recommended, because of reported attacks.

In addition to the four registers, E0 cipher makes use of two internal 2-bit-words denoted  <math alttext="c Subscript t minus 1 Baseline and c Subscript t Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mtext>&#160;and&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![c Subscript t minus 1 Baseline and c Subscript t Baseline](images/c06_219.png) initialized to 00. The main steps of E0 cipher are Generation of key stream and Initialization.

*Generation of key stream bits*
