*Initialization of LFSRs (Key Scheduling Algorithm)*

Before starting the generation of key stream bits, the four LFSRs and the two 2-bit words,  <math alttext="c Subscript negative 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![c Subscript negative 1](images/c06_241.png) and  <math alttext="c 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![c 0](images/c06_242.png), are initialized using four inputs: an encryption key  <math alttext="upper K Subscript e n c" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript e n c](images/c06_243.png), 128 publicly known random bits, a 48-bit Bluetooth device address, and 26 central’s clock bits. All the initialization inputs (i.e.  <math alttext="l e n left-parenthesis upper K Subscript e n c Baseline right-parenthesis plus 128 plus 48 plus 26" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>128</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>48</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>26</mn></mrow></math> ![l e n left-parenthesis upper K Subscript e n c Baseline right-parenthesis plus 128 plus 48 plus 26](images/c06_244.png) bits) enter the four registers, in a specific order, and keystream generator is clocked without producing key stream bits. Then, after some cycles of registers, the entire key stream generator becomes ready to deliver the first bit of the key stream. The encryption key  <math alttext="upper K Subscript e n c" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript e n c](images/c06_245.png) is derived by a function called E3 using the link key exchanged during the authentication step performed by Bluetooth devices.

### 6.2.3 SNOW 3G Keystream Generator

SNOW 3G is keystream generator chosen by 3GPP for confidentiality and integrity guarantees in 3G cellular networks \[[5](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0005)\]. SNOW 3G also is included in the ISO/IEC 18033-4 standard \[[6](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0006)\]. Unlike A5/1 and E0 keystream generators, in which LFSR elements are bits, SNOW 3G is a word-keystream generator. That is, the elements (also called stages) of SNOW 3G LFSR are 32-bit words. At every clock tick, SNOW 3G produces a 32-bit word of output, which is then used to encrypt/decrypt 32 bits of data. SNOW 3G is composed of two components: an LFSR of sixteen 32-bit stages and an FSM of three 32-bit registers (see [Figure 6.11](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0011)). FSM registers are not LFSRs; they are updated using substitutions.

![Figure 6.11 SNOW 3G keystream generator.](images/c06f011.png)

[**Figure 6.11**](#c06.xhtml#rc06-fig-0011) SNOW 3G keystream generator.

#### 6.2.3.1 Formal Description of SNOW 3G

LFSR of SNOW 3G is defined over field[^(12)](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0012)  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 32](images/c06_246.png). The 32-bit elements of LFSR are denoted  <math alttext="s 15" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![s 15](images/c06_247.png),  <math alttext="s 14 comma ellipsis comma s 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>14</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![s 14 comma ellipsis comma s 0](images/c06_248.png) (see [Figure 6.11](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0011)). Notice that stage  <math alttext="s 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![s 0](images/c06_249.png) is the rightmost element of the LFSR. Hence, the feedback polynomial of SNOW 3G is defined by:

 <math alttext="script upper F left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals alpha x Superscript 16 Baseline circled-plus x Superscript 14 Baseline circled-plus alpha Superscript negative 1 Baseline x Superscript 5 Baseline plus 1 element-of upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 32 Subscript Baseline left-bracket x right-bracket" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8853;</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>14</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msup><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msup><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![script upper F left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals alpha x Superscript 16 Baseline circled-plus x Superscript 14 Baseline circled-plus alpha Superscript negative 1 Baseline x Superscript 5 Baseline plus 1 element-of upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 32 Subscript Baseline left-bracket x right-bracket](images/c06_250.png)

The feedback word, at cycle  <math alttext="t plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![t plus 1](images/c06_251.png), is recursively computed as:

 <math alttext="s 15 Superscript t plus 1 Baseline equals alpha Superscript negative 1 Baseline asterisk s 11 Superscript t Baseline circled-plus s 2 Superscript t Baseline circled-plus alpha asterisk s 0 Superscript t" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>\*</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>\*</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![s 15 Superscript t plus 1 Baseline equals alpha Superscript negative 1 Baseline asterisk s 11 Superscript t Baseline circled-plus s 2 Superscript t Baseline circled-plus alpha asterisk s 0 Superscript t](images/c06_252.png)

where:

 <math alttext="s Subscript i Superscript t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![s Subscript i Superscript t](images/c06_253.png) denotes the state, at cycle *t*, of stage *i* ( <math alttext="i equals 0 comma 1 comma ellipsis comma 15" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>15</mn></mrow></math> ![i equals 0 comma 1 comma ellipsis comma 15](images/c06_254.png)),

 <math alttext="alpha Superscript negative 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![alpha Superscript negative 1](images/c06_261.png) is the multiplicative inverse of α over  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 32](images/c06_262.png).

where  <math alttext="upper S 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S 1](images/c06_267.png) and  <math alttext="upper S 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S 2](images/c06_268.png) are two 32-bit to 32-bit substitution boxes.  <math alttext="upper S 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S 1](images/c06_269.png) and  <math alttext="upper S 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S 2](images/c06_270.png) s-boxes make use of two small 8-bit s-boxes  <math alttext="upper S Subscript upper R" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>R</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript upper R](images/c06_271.png) and  <math alttext="upper S Subscript upper Q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript upper Q](images/c06_272.png).  <math alttext="upper S Subscript upper R" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>R</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript upper R](images/c06_273.png) is the well-known s-box used in AES cipher (see Section 7.3).

#### 6.2.3.2 Algorithmic Description of SNOW 3G

SNOW 3G relies on a series of functions, substitution boxes, and clocking modes, which are presented below.

##### *6.2.3.2.1 Notations and Functions of SNOW 3G*

*Notations*

*   0[X]: hexadecimal notation of an 8-bit value (i.e. a byte).
*   0[X] ≪*[n]* *t*: *t*\-bit left shift of an *n*\-bit register; *t* is the number of shifting positions.
*   *V*, *c*: 8-bit values.   *W*: 32-bit word
*    <math alttext="upper W equals upper W 0 parallel-to upper W 1 parallel-to upper W 2 parallel-to upper W 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8741;</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8741;</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8741;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper W equals upper W 0 parallel-to upper W 1 parallel-to upper W 2 parallel-to upper W 3](images/c06_278.png): 32-bit word, with *W*[0] the most and  <math alttext="upper W 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper W 3](images/c06_279.png) the least significant byte.
*    <math alttext="s Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![s Subscript i](images/c06_280.png): element *i* of LFSR,  <math alttext="i equals 0 comma ellipsis comma 15" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow></math> ![i equals 0 comma ellipsis comma 15](images/c06_281.png)     <math alttext="s Subscript i comma k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![s Subscript i comma k](images/c06_282.png): byte *k* ( <math alttext="k equals 0 comma 1 comma 2 comma 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![k equals 0 comma 1 comma 2 comma 3](images/c06_283.png)) of element <math alttext="s Subscript i Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![s Subscript i Baseline](images/c06_284.png)
*    <math alttext="upper R Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper R Subscript j](images/c06_285.png): register  <math alttext="upper R Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper R Subscript j](images/c06_286.png) ( <math alttext="j equals 1 comma 2 comma 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![j equals 1 comma 2 comma 3](images/c06_287.png)) of the FSM
*   ⊕: addition  <math alttext="m o d u l o Baseline 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![m o d u l o Baseline 2](images/c06_288.png)⊞:    addition  <math alttext="m o d u l o 2 Superscript 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![m o d u l o 2 Superscript 32](images/c06_289.png)

SNOW 3G makes uses of four functions:

1.   <math alttext="upper M upper U upper L normal x" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>U</mi><mi>L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M upper U upper L normal x](images/c06_290.png) function: maps eight bits to eight bits as follows:

##### *6.2.3.2.3 SNOW 3G Clocking*

*Clocking the LFSR*

Two modes of LFSR clocking are distinguished:

1.  LFSR clocking in initialization mode

LFSR receives a 32-bit word *F* from the FSM, then performs the following:

##### *6.2.3.2.4 Operation of SNOW 3G*

*Initialization (Key Scheduling Algorithm)*

SNOW 3G is initialized with a key *K* composed of four 32-bit words, denoted *K*[1],  <math alttext="upper K 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K 2](images/c06_334.png), <math alttext="upper K 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K 3](images/c06_335.png), and <math alttext="upper K 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K 4](images/c06_336.png) and an initialization variable  <math alttext="upper I upper V" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> ![upper I upper V](images/c06_337.png) composed of four 32-bit words, denoted  <math alttext="upper I upper V 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper I upper V 1](images/c06_338.png),  <math alttext="upper I upper V 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper I upper V 2](images/c06_339.png),  <math alttext="upper I upper V 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper I upper V 3](images/c06_340.png), and  <math alttext="upper I upper V 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper I upper V 4](images/c06_341.png). LFSR element initialization is as follows (where  <math alttext="upper Omega equals 0 normal x upper F upper F upper F upper F upper F upper F upper F upper F" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#937;</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> ![upper Omega equals 0 normal x upper F upper F upper F upper F upper F upper F upper F upper F](images/c06_342.png)):

![](images/c06_343.png)

The FSM registers  <math alttext="upper R 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper R 1](images/c06_359.png),  <math alttext="upper R 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper R 2](images/c06_360.png), and  <math alttext="upper R 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper R 3](images/c06_361.png) are all set to 0. Then, the following two steps are repeated 32 times:

1.  FSM is clocked to produce a 32-bit word *F*.
2.  LFSR is clocked according to initialization mode using word *F*.

*Generation of keystream*

First, the FSM is clocked once and its output is discarded. Then, the LFSR is clocked according to the keystream mode. After that, keystream 32-bit words are produced by repeating the following steps as long as keystream bits are needed to encrypt/decrypt messages:

1.  FSM is clocked to produce a 32-bit word *F*.
2.  The next keystream word is produced as  <math alttext="z Subscript t Baseline equals upper F circled-plus s 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>F</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![z Subscript t Baseline equals upper F circled-plus s 0](images/c06_362.png).
3.  LFSR is clocked according to the keystream mode.

**Note**. For interested readers, some issues regarding the resynchronization mechanism of SNOW 3G are discussed in \[[7](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0007)\].

### 6.2.4 ZUC Keystream Generator

#### 6.2.4.1 Principle of ZUC Keystream Generator

ZUC[^(13)](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0013) is stream cipher proposed in China for support of security in cellular networks \[[8](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0008)\]. ZUC also is an ETSI standard \[[9](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0009)\]. There exist two ZUC versions: ZUC-128 for 4G/LTE and ZUC-256 for 5G networks. The structure and operations of both versions are the same; they differ in the length of the key and the initialization vector and in the register initialization phase. ZUC-128 is 128-bit key-based, while ZUC-256 is 256-bit key-based. Therefore, ZUC-256 provides a higher security strength. In the sequel, ZUC description refers to ZUC-128.

ZUC is organized into three logical layers: LFSR, bit reorganization, and an FSM (see [Figure 6.12](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0012)). It is worth noticing that the bit reorganization layer extracts halves of eight LFSR stages, which are then used in a nonlinear function *F*. Such a design makes (till now) the standard cryptanalysis against common stream ciphers not directly applicable to break ZUC cipher.

![Figure 6.12 SNOW 3G keystream generator.](images/c06f012.png)

[**Figure 6.12**](#c06.xhtml#rc06-fig-0012) SNOW 3G keystream generator.

Like SNOW 3G, ZUC is a word-keystream cipher. It takes a key of 128 bits and an initialization vector of 128 bits to deliver a 32-bit word of keystream bits used to encrypt/decrypt data.

ZUC has an LFSR of sixteen 31-bit stages denoted  <math alttext="s 0 comma s 1 comma ellipsis comma s 14 comma s 15" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>14</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![s 0 comma s 1 comma ellipsis comma s 14 comma s 15](images/c06_363.png).

The design of ZUC differs from common stream ciphers, such as SNOW 3G, which are defined only over extension fields, i.e.  <math alttext="upper F 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F 2](images/c06_364.png),  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>8</mn></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 8](images/c06_365.png), and  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c06_366.png). Rather, the LFSR of ZUC is defined over a prime field *F[p]*, with  <math alttext="p equals upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 31 Subscript minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>31</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![p equals upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 31 Subscript minus 1](images/c06_367.png), while the FSM registers[^(14)](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0014) are defined over extension field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 32](images/c06_368.png).

The feedback word, at cycle  <math alttext="t plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![t plus 1](images/c06_369.png), is recursively computed as:

#### 6.2.4.2 ZUC Algorithm

**Notes**

*   – In ZUC, addition and multiplication of LFSR stages are over prime field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 31 Subscript minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>31</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 31 Subscript minus 1](images/c06_372.png).
*   – If  <math alttext="s 15 Superscript t plus 1 Baseline equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![s 15 Superscript t plus 1 Baseline equals 0](images/c06_373.png), then  <math alttext="s 15 Superscript t plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> ![s 15 Superscript t plus 1](images/c06_374.png) is replaced by  <math alttext="2 Superscript 31 Baseline minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>31</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 31 Baseline minus 1](images/c06_375.png) (because in  <math alttext="upper F Subscript p Baseline comma p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript p Baseline comma p](images/c06_376.png) and 0 are equivalent).
*   – Any element  <math alttext="a element-of upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 31 Subscript minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>31</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![a element-of upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 31 Subscript minus 1](images/c06_377.png) can be written as  <math alttext="a equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 0 Overscript 30 Endscripts a Subscript i Baseline 2 Superscript i Baseline comma a Subscript i equals 0 comma ellipsis comma 30 Baseline element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>30</mn></mrow></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></mstyle></mrow></math> ![a equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 0 Overscript 30 Endscripts a Subscript i Baseline 2 Superscript i Baseline comma a Subscript i equals 0 comma ellipsis comma 30 Baseline element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet](images/c06_378.png). Then,  <math alttext="for-all x element-of upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 31 Subscript minus 1 Baseline comma k less-than 31 comma 2 Superscript k Baseline asterisk x colon equals x very-much-less-than Subscript 31 Baseline k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8704;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>x</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>31</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>31</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>\*</mo><mi>x</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>x</mi><msub><mo>&#8920;</mo><mrow><mn>31</mn></mrow></msub><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> ![for-all x element-of upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 31 Subscript minus 1 Baseline comma k less-than 31 comma 2 Superscript k Baseline asterisk x colon equals x very-much-less-than Subscript 31 Baseline k](images/c06_379.png). This makes implementation of ZUC quite efficient.  <math alttext="x very-much-less-than Subscript 31 Baseline k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>x</mi><msub><mo>&#8920;</mo><mrow><mn>31</mn></mrow></msub><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> ![x very-much-less-than Subscript 31 Baseline k](images/c06_380.png) denotes a left circular shift of 31-bit element by *k* positions.

##### *6.2.4.2.1 ZUC LFSR Modes*

Stages of LFSR are 31-bits. Like in SNOW 3G, the LFSR of ZUC operates in two modes: Initialization and keystream generation.

1.  LFSR Initialization mode (Key Scheduling Algorithm)

In LFSR initialization mode, ZUC performs the following:

Receive a 32-bit word *W* from the nonlinear function.

 <math alttext="u equals upper W much-greater-than 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>W</mi><mo>&#8811;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![u equals upper W much-greater-than 1](images/c06_381.png) (i.e. remove the rightmost bit of *W* to match LFSR stage length)

##### *6.2.4.2.2 ZUC Bit Reorganization*

From the stages of the LFSR, four 32-bit words are formed as follows:

 <math alttext="upper X 0 equals s Subscript 15 upper H Baseline parallel-to s Subscript 14 upper L Baseline upper X 1 equals s Subscript 11 upper L Baseline parallel-to s Subscript 9 upper H Baseline upper X 2 equals s Subscript 7 upper L Baseline parallel-to s Subscript 5 upper H Baseline upper X 3 equals s Subscript 2 upper L Baseline parallel-to s Subscript 0 upper H Baseline" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>15</mn><mi>H</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8741;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>14</mn><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>11</mn><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8741;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>9</mn><mi>H</mi></mrow></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8741;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn><mi>H</mi></mrow></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8741;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mi>H</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper X 0 equals s Subscript 15 upper H Baseline parallel-to s Subscript 14 upper L Baseline upper X 1 equals s Subscript 11 upper L Baseline parallel-to s Subscript 9 upper H Baseline upper X 2 equals s Subscript 7 upper L Baseline parallel-to s Subscript 5 upper H Baseline upper X 3 equals s Subscript 2 upper L Baseline parallel-to s Subscript 0 upper H Baseline](images/c06_391.png)

where  <math alttext="s Subscript i upper L" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![s Subscript i upper L](images/c06_392.png) and  <math alttext="s Subscript i upper H" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>H</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![s Subscript i upper H](images/c06_393.png) denote the leftmost and rightmost 16 bits of stage *i*, respectively.

##### *6.2.4.2.4 ZUC Initialization*

Let  <math alttext="upper K equals upper K 0 parallel-to upper K 1 parallel-to ellipsis parallel-to upper K Subscript 14 Baseline parallel-to upper K 15" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8741;</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8741;</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>&#8741;</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>14</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msub><mo>&#8741;</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K equals upper K 0 parallel-to upper K 1 parallel-to ellipsis parallel-to upper K Subscript 14 Baseline parallel-to upper K 15](images/c06_404.png) be the secret key and  <math alttext="upper I upper V equals upper I upper V 0 parallel-to upper I upper V 1 parallel-to ellipsis parallel-to upper I upper V Subscript 14 Baseline parallel-to upper I upper V 15" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8741;</mo><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8741;</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>&#8741;</mo><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mrow><mn>14</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msub><mo>&#8741;</mo><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper I upper V equals upper I upper V 0 parallel-to upper I upper V 1 parallel-to ellipsis parallel-to upper I upper V Subscript 14 Baseline parallel-to upper I upper V 15](images/c06_405.png) the initialization vector. Each  <math alttext="upper K Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript i](images/c06_406.png) or  <math alttext="upper I upper V Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper I upper V Subscript i](images/c06_407.png),  <math alttext="i equals 0 comma ellipsis comma 15" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>15</mn></mrow></math> ![i equals 0 comma ellipsis comma 15](images/c06_408.png), is an 8-bit value. Perform the following steps:

*   – *R[1]* = *R[2]* = 0
*   – Run *Bit reorganization*
*   – *W* = *F* (*X[0], X[1], X[2]*)
*   – Run *LFSR initialization mode* with  <math alttext="w much-greater-than 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>&#8811;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![w much-greater-than 1](images/c06_413.png). ( <math alttext="w much-greater-than 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>&#8811;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![w much-greater-than 1](images/c06_414.png) denotes 1-bit right shift of *w*).

##### *6.2.4.2.5 Keystream Generation*

After the initialization phase, execute once the following steps and discard the output of function *F*:

*   Run *Bit reorganization*

*    <math alttext="w equals upper F left-parenthesis upper X 0 comma upper X 1 comma upper X 2 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![w equals upper F left-parenthesis upper X 0 comma upper X 1 comma upper X 2 right-parenthesis](images/c06_415.png)
*   Run *LFSR work* *mode*.

Then, ZUC enters in phase of generation of keystream bits. At each cycle, a 32-bit word *Z* is produced as an output of the ZUC keystream generator as follows:

*   Run *Bit reorganization*

### 6.2.5 ChaCha20 Stream Cipher

ChaCha20[^(15)](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0015) is a stream cipher designed by D. Bernstein \[[10](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0010)\]. It is an IETF standard \[[11](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0011)\] recommended in particular as a cipher in TLS protocol \[[1](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0001)\].

Some performance analyses showed that ChaCha20 is around three times fast as AES (the standard block cipher, presented in the next chapter), when both are software-only implemented. Another interesting property of ChaCha20 is that it is not sensitive to timing attacks. ChaCha20 takes a 256-bit key, a 32-bit counter, and a 96-bit nonce; and generates a 64-byte keystream block.

#### 6.2.5.1 ChaCha20 State

The state of Chacha20 is composed of sixteen 32-bit words, denoted  <math alttext="upper S 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S 0](images/c06_417.png),  <math alttext="upper S 15" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S 15](images/c06_418.png), generally organized in a matrix, as illustrated by [Figure 6.13](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0013).

![Figure 6.13 ChaCha20 state structure.](images/c06f013.png)

[**Figure 6.13**](#c06.xhtml#rc06-fig-0013) ChaCha20 state structure.

The initial state of Chacha20 is set as shown in [Figure 6.14](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0014):

![Figure 6.14 ChaCha20 initial state.](images/c06f014.png)

[**Figure 6.14**](#c06.xhtml#rc06-fig-0014) ChaCha20 initial state.

*   The first matrix row is initialized using four constants:

#### 6.2.5.2 ChaCha20 Quarter Round

The basic function of the ChaCha20 algorithm is the quarter-round, denoted  <math alttext="upper Q upper R o u n d" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> ![upper Q upper R o u n d](images/c06_427.png); it takes four 32-bits integers *a*, *b*, *c*, and *d*; and it performs the following operations:

#### 6.2.5.3 ChaCha20 Keystream Block Generation

To generate a 512-bit keystream block, ChaCha20 takes an initial state. Then, ten series of quarter-rounds are performed. Each series is composed of eight quarter-rounds; therefore, in total 80 quarter-rounds (i.e. 20 full rounds) are run to yield one keystream block. As shown in [Figure 6.15](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0015), quarter-round operating on words of the same column are called *column quarter-rounds*; and those operation on words in four distinct columns are called *diagonal quarter-rounds*. [Figure 6.15](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0015) also shows the order in which the state words are used to form inputs of quarter-rounds. Using such a scanning of state words, ChaCha20 realizes a very fast diffusion.

![Figure 6.15 Order in which state words are used to form one 8-quarter-round series.](images/c06f015.png)

[**Figure 6.15**](#c06.xhtml#rc06-fig-0015) Order in which state words are used to form one 8-quarter-round series.

The full pseudocode of the Keystream block generation function is given below.

#### 6.2.5.4 Plaintext Encryption and Decryption Using ChaCha20

A nonce is associated with each plaintext. Then, the plaintext is split into 64-byte blocks. An initial counter *C* is associated with the first plaintext block; the counter is incremented for each plaintext block. A 512-bit keystream is XORed with each plaintext block to yield a ciphertext block. If the plaintext byte-length is not a multiple of 64 bytes, the last plaintext block is a non-complete block; only a portion of the last generated keystream block is used to yield the last ciphertext block.

Below is the pseudocode of ChaCha20 plaintext encryption. The decryption is identical to the encryption (only the input and output differ).  <math alttext="upper B l e n left-parenthesis upper P right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper B l e n left-parenthesis upper P right-parenthesis](images/c06_460.png) means the byte-length of byte-string *P*.

### 6.2.6 RC4 Stream Cipher

RC4 (also known as Rivest Cipher 4) is a stream cipher, initially protected by US patent. After the discovery of its internal operation, it became public and widely used as building block in many services including SSL (secure socket layer), TLS ((transport layer security), SSH (Secure Shell), Wired Equivalent Privacy (WEP), and Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA). However, because of flaws discovered, the IETF has banned the use of RC4 since 2015 in almost all security services. Some vulnerabilities of RC4 are discussed in \[[12](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0012)\].

RC4 is presented in this chapter for pedagogical purpose as it is a well-known cipher not based on LFSRs and which is easy to implement in software \[[13](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0013)\].

RC4 does not rely on LFSRs. It makes use of a permutation vector *S* of 256 elements denoted  <math alttext="upper S left-bracket 0 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S left-bracket 0 right-bracket](images/c06_472.png),  <math alttext="upper S left-bracket 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S left-bracket 1 right-bracket](images/c06_473.png),  <math alttext="upper S left-bracket 2 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S left-bracket 2 right-bracket](images/c06_474.png), …,  <math alttext="upper S left-bracket 255 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>255</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S left-bracket 255 right-bracket](images/c06_475.png). Each element  <math alttext="upper S left-bracket i right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S left-bracket i right-bracket](images/c06_476.png) is a byte. Vector *S* contains all the values from 0 to 255, stored in a random way. Therefore, taking one element of vector *S* looks like a generation of a random number between 0 and 255.

#### 6.2.6.1 RC4 Key-scheduling Algorithm

RC4 takes a key *K* of a variable-length ranging from 1 to 256 bytes. In initialization phase, called key scheduling algorithm, RC4 produces the first permutation *S* as follows:

 <math alttext="upper K left-bracket i right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper K left-bracket i right-bracket](images/c06_477.png) denotes byte *i* of key *K*, with  <math alttext="i equals 0 comma 1 comma ellipsis comma l e n left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![i equals 0 comma 1 comma ellipsis comma l e n left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis](images/c06_478.png) and  <math alttext="l e n left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![l e n left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis](images/c06_479.png) denotes the byte-length of key *K*. Swap(*S\[i\]*, *S\[j\]*) is a function to swap the contents of elements *S\[i\]* and *S\[j\]*.

If the length of key *K* is 256, key *K* is used once. Otherwise, it is used many times.

#### 6.2.6.2 Keystream Generation Phase

Keystream generation of RC4 is depicted on [Figure 6.16](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0016). From two current variables *i* and *j*, do the following: swap elements  <math alttext="upper S left-bracket i right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S left-bracket i right-bracket](images/c06_480.png) and  <math alttext="upper S left-bracket j right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S left-bracket j right-bracket](images/c06_481.png), then deliver  <math alttext="upper S left-bracket upper S left-bracket i right-bracket plus upper S left-bracket j right-bracket m o d Baseline 256 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>256</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S left-bracket upper S left-bracket i right-bracket plus upper S left-bracket j right-bracket m o d Baseline 256 right-bracket](images/c06_482.png) as keystream output.

![Figure 6.16 General structure of RC4 stream ciphering.](images/c06f016.png)

[**Figure 6.16**](#c06.xhtml#rc06-fig-0016) General structure of RC4 stream ciphering.

### 6.2.7 Lightweight Cryptography Stream Ciphers

Lightweight cryptography (LWC) is a vital and fast growing field in today’s world where billions of IoT (Internet of Things) devices (including RFIDs, sensors, and actuators) need to communicate wirelessly. Such devices have limited resources (memory, CPU, and battery) and require light techniques to secure their communications. LWC is a collection of solutions of encryption techniques that features low computational complexity devices. It is aimed at expanding the applications of cryptography to limited-resource devices, while providing a high level of security.

Many companies and laboratories proposed various solutions to secure limited-resource-devices. Almost all the LWC ciphers make use of nonlinear feedback shift registers (NLFSR).

From the standardization perspective, the ISO/IEC 29192-3 standard \[[14](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0014)\] specified two LWC stream ciphers, *Trivium* and *Enocoro v2*, which are presented in this subsection.

#### 6.2.7.1 Trivium Stream Cipher

Trivium is a synchronous stream cipher inspired by the design of block ciphers \[[15](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0015), [16](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0016)\]. It takes an 80-bit key and an 80-bit IV and generates a keystream of length up to  <math alttext="2 Superscript 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 64](images/c06_483.png) bits.  <math alttext="2 Superscript 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 64](images/c06_484.png) bits represent the number of bits transmitted at  <math alttext="1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![1](images/c06_485.png) Gbps over 2^(34) seconds. The period of the keystream generator output is  <math alttext="2 Superscript 93 Baseline minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>93</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 93 Baseline minus 1](images/c06_486.png), which makes Trivium secure against cryptanalysis. As shown on [Figure 6.17](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0017), Trivium architecture makes use of three NLFSR registers of variable length, providing a total of 288 bits. The three registers are connected with nonlinear functions.

![Figure 6.17 Internal structure of Trivium keystream generator.](images/c06f017.png)

[**Figure 6.17**](#c06.xhtml#rc06-fig-0017) Internal structure of Trivium keystream generator.

1.  *Keystream generation*

Trivium interval state is composed of 288 register bits, denoted  <math alttext="s 1 comma s 2 comma ellipsis comma s 288" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>288</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![s 1 comma s 2 comma ellipsis comma s 288](images/c06_487.png), among which 15 bits are iteratively used to generate *N* keystream bits,  <math alttext="upper N less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper N less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript 64](images/c06_488.png), as follows:

#### 6.2.7.2 Enocoro Stream Cipher

Enocoro stream cipher family consists of two algorithms, Enocoro-80, which has a key length of 80 bits and Enocoro-128v2, which has a key length of 128 bits \[[17](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0017)\]. Enocoro-80 is obsoleted because of its weak security level. In the sequel, Enocoro implicitly refers to Enocoro-128v2.

Enocoro has a reduced hardware circuit size. Compared to AES, the current de facto standard for data encryption, Enocoro achieves the encryption process with about 1/10 of the amount of power consumption.

Enocoro keystream generator (KSG) consists of an initialization function, an output function, and a finite state machine. The latter consists of an internal state  <math alttext="upper S Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper S Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c06_502.png), which is updated by a function  <math alttext="upper N e x t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> ![upper N e x t](images/c06_503.png) at each clock step.  <math alttext="upper I n i t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> ![upper I n i t](images/c06_504.png) function generates the first state  <math alttext="upper S Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper S Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis](images/c06_505.png).  <math alttext="upper O u t p u t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> ![upper O u t p u t](images/c06_506.png) function generates the keystream bit  <math alttext="upper Z Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>Z</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper Z Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c06_507.png).

The internal state of Enocoro KSG has two parts: a state *a* and a buffer (NLFSR) *b* (see [Figure 6.18](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0018)). The state *a* is composed of two bytes denoted  <math alttext="a 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![a 0](images/c06_508.png) and  <math alttext="a 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![a 1](images/c06_509.png). Buffer *b* is composed of *n[b]* bytes denoted  <math alttext="b 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![b 0](images/c06_510.png), …,  <math alttext="b Subscript n Sub Subscript b Subscript minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![b Subscript n Sub Subscript b Subscript minus 1](images/c06_511.png).

![Figure 6.18 Internal structure of Enocoro keystream generator \[17\].](images/c06f018.png)

[**Figure 6.18**](#c06.xhtml#rc06-fig-0018) Internal structure of Enocoro keystream generator \[[17](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0017)\].

Enocoro is a byte-keystream cipher. Thus, the operations are byte-oriented. Addition is the XOR bitwise operation and the multiplication is performed over the extension field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>8</mn></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 8](images/c06_512.png), under the primitive polynomial  <math alttext="phi 8 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 8 Baseline plus x Superscript 4 Baseline plus x cubed plus x squared plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>&#966;</mi><mn>8</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>8</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![phi 8 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 8 Baseline plus x Superscript 4 Baseline plus x cubed plus x squared plus 1](images/c06_513.png).

At time *t*, the content of state *a* is denoted  <math alttext="a Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![a Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c06_514.png) and that of the buffer,  <math alttext="b Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![b Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c06_515.png). The update function  <math alttext="upper N e x t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> ![upper N e x t](images/c06_516.png) is composed of two functions denoted ρ and λ. Thus, Enocoro may be specified as follows:

Enocoro family has 11 parameters denoted:

*    <math alttext="n Subscript b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![n Subscript b](images/c06_520.png): byte-length of the buffer.
*    <math alttext="q 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![q 1](images/c06_521.png),  <math alttext="p 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![p 1](images/c06_522.png),  <math alttext="q 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![q 2](images/c06_523.png),  <math alttext="p 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![p 2](images/c06_524.png),  <math alttext="q 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![q 3](images/c06_525.png), and  <math alttext="p 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![p 3](images/c06_526.png): numbers of buffer elements (boxes) used in  <math alttext="lamda" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mtext>&#955;</mtext></math> ![lamda](images/c06_527.png) function.
*    <math alttext="k 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![k 1](images/c06_528.png),  <math alttext="k 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![k 2](images/c06_529.png),  <math alttext="k 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![k 3](images/c06_530.png), and  <math alttext="k 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![k 4](images/c06_531.png): numbers of buffer elements used in ρ function.

Different choices of the parameters result in different internal structures. In the standard Enocoro 128-v2, the parameters are fixed as follows:

After initialization of the state (i.e. *a* and *b*) using the key, the initialization vector, and constants, the state is updated with 96 iterations of two functions (namely, XORing the iteration counter and register element  <math alttext="b 31" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>31</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![b 31](images/c06_543.png) followed by  <math alttext="upper N e x t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> ![upper N e x t](images/c06_544.png) function). The iteration counter is initialized by  <math alttext="0 normal x Baseline 01" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>01</mn></mrow></math> ![0 normal x Baseline 01](images/c06_545.png) and incremented by the multiplication by  <math alttext="0 normal x Baseline 02" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>02</mn></mrow></math> ![0 normal x Baseline 02](images/c06_546.png) over the extension field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>8</mn></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 8](images/c06_547.png), under the primitive polynomial  <math alttext="phi 8 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>&#966;</mi><mn>8</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![phi 8 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c06_548.png). Then, the KSG delivers the first byte of the keystream, which is used to encrypt or decrypt one byte.

### 6.3.1 List of Exercises and Problem

***Exercise*** ***6.1***

Let  <math alttext="upper R" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R](images/c06_549.png) be an LFSR defined with the following parameters:

Seed:  <math alttext="upper F upper F 1 equals 0 comma upper F upper F 2 equals 0 comma upper F upper F 3 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>F</mi><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>F</mi><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>F</mi><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper F upper F 1 equals 0 comma upper F upper F 2 equals 0 comma upper F upper F 3 equals 1](images/c06_550.png)

    Second LFSR: feedback polynomial  <math alttext="script upper F 2 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x cubed plus x squared plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![script upper F 2 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x cubed plus x squared plus 1](images/c06_554.png) and seed  <math alttext="equals left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 comma 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![equals left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 comma 0 right-parenthesis](images/c06_555.png)
    
2.  Why the second LFSR has more states?

***Exercise*** ***6.3***

1.  What is the maximum byte-length of plaintexts that can be encrypted with ChaCha20?
2.  What is the maximum amount of data that can be encrypted with the same ChaCha20 key?

***Problem*** ***6.1***

1.  Consider a self-synchronizing stream cipher (S3C) with a large synchronization window. Discuss why synchronous stream ciphers (S2Cs) are less impacted by transmission errors than S3Cs.
2.  Consider a self-synchronizing stream cipher (S3C) with a short synchronization window. Discuss why it is more difficult to detect bit deletion or insertion with S3Cs than with S2C.

***Problem*** ***6.2***

1.  Show that it is easy to recover the parameters *A* and *B* of a linear congruential generator if three outputs and the modulus *m*, which is a prime, are known.
2.  Assume that three LCG values are known:  <math alttext="z 1 equals 13" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow></math> ![z 1 equals 13](images/c06_556.png),  <math alttext="z 2 equals 6" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> ![z 2 equals 6](images/c06_557.png), and  <math alttext="z 3 equals 5" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> ![z 3 equals 5](images/c06_558.png) and the modulus *m* is 20. Find parameters of LCG.
3.  Assume that three LCG values are known:  <math alttext="z 1 equals 6" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> ![z 1 equals 6](images/c06_559.png),  <math alttext="z 2 equals 5" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> ![z 2 equals 5](images/c06_560.png), and  <math alttext="z 3 equals 5" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> ![z 3 equals 5](images/c06_561.png) and the modulus *m* is 20. Find parameters of LCG.
4.  What do you conclude?

1.  Show that it is easy to recover the secret key  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper A comma upper B right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper A comma upper B right-parenthesis](images/c06_562.png) of a stream cipher based on a linear congruential generator if  <math alttext="3 n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![3 n](images/c06_563.png) bits of plaintext and their cipher bits and the modulus *m* of the LCG are known. ***Problem*** ***6.6***

***Problem*** ***6.7***

Assume that the adversary knows  <math alttext="2 m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![2 m](images/c06_583.png) bits of plaintext (for example, he/she knows the header of a message) and their ciphertext. He/she also knows that the sender is using a stream cipher based on an LFSR with *m* bits. Assume that known bits of plaintext are located at the beginning of a message. Show that LFSR-based ciphers are vulnerable to plaintext attack.

***Problem*** ***6.8***

A plaintext  <math alttext="upper M equals 1001 0010 0110 1101 1001 0010 0110" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1001</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0010</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0110</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1101</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1001</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0010</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0110</mn></mrow></math> ![upper M equals 1001 0010 0110 1101 1001 0010 0110](images/c06_584.png) is encrypted with an LFSR-based stream cipher and the ciphertext is  <math alttext="upper C equals 1011 1100 0011 0001 0010 1011 0001" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1011</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1100</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0011</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0001</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0010</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1011</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0001</mn></mrow></math> ![upper C equals 1011 1100 0011 0001 0010 1011 0001](images/c06_585.png). Assume that the pair  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper M comma upper M prime right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper M comma upper M prime right-parenthesis](images/c06_586.png) is given and the period of the keystream generator is less than 15.

1.  What is the period of the keystream generator used to encrypt *M*?
2.  What is its degree, initialization value, and feedback polynomial?

***Problem*** ***6.9***

Consider a keystream generator with a period of *L* bits. The adversary can intercept all the traffic. All the encrypted messages start with a content (e.g. an application protocol header) of *k* bits known to adversary. No other characteristics of the code are known.

What is the potential vulnerability of the considered encryption system (i.e. under which conditions the code can be broken)?

***Problem*** ***6.10***

Consider a user who has a series of documents to encrypt with a stream cipher and then store them. All documents are English texts including only uppercase letters and space in 7-bit ASCII code. Given the large size of the documents, the user decides to restart (with the same initial value) the keystream generator to encrypt each document. Show that if the number of documents is enough large, an adversary, who has copies of the encrypted documents, can recover partially or entirely all the documents.

***Problem*** ***6.11***

Imagine a text-source sending a text in natural language. In such a case, some portions of plaintext are likely to be the same. The adversary can take advantage of plaintext redundancy to derive relations between keystream bits, which contribute to recover the key. Consider a simple stream cipher composed of an LFSR with feedback polynomial  <math alttext="x cubed plus x plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![x cubed plus x plus 1](images/c06_587.png) and a key  <math alttext="upper K equals left-parenthesis upper K 0 comma upper K 1 comma upper K 2 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 0 comma 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper K equals left-parenthesis upper K 0 comma upper K 1 comma upper K 2 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 0 comma 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c06_588.png), as illustrated by [Figure 6.19](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0019). Show how an adversary who knows the positions, denoted *i* and *j*, of two portions of plaintext of *L*\-bit length,  <math alttext="upper L greater-than-or-equal-to 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![upper L greater-than-or-equal-to 3](images/c06_589.png), can recover the key.

![Figure 6.19 Simple LFSR.](images/c06f019.png)

Feedback coefficients:  <math alttext="c 1 equals 1 comma c 2 equals 0 comma c 3 equals 1 period" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1.</mn></mrow></math> ![c 1 equals 1 comma c 2 equals 0 comma c 3 equals 1 period](images/c06_591.png)

![](images/c06_592.png)

From the table above, we see that the register has a cycle of 7. Another way to find the register cycle is to inspect the feedback polynomial, which is equal to  <math alttext="x cubed plus x plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![x cubed plus x plus 1](images/c06_595.png). The same ChaCha20 key can be used with up to  <math alttext="2 Superscript 96" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>96</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 96](images/c06_615.png) nonces; and each nonce can be used with up to  <math alttext="2 Superscript 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 32](images/c06_616.png) counter values to generate a maximum of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 96 Baseline asterisk 2 Superscript 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>96</mn></mrow></msup><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 96 Baseline asterisk 2 Superscript 32](images/c06_617.png) keystream blocks. Each keystream block is used to encrypt a 64-byte plaintext block. Therefore, the maximum amount of data that can be encrypted with the same ChaCha20 key is of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 134" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>134</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 134](images/c06_618.png) bytes.

***Problem*** ***6.1***

Let *n* be the number of bits in the synchronization window of a self-synchronized (S3C).

1.  Assume that *n* is large and a transmission error occurs when transmitting bit *i*. With a synchronous stream cipher (S2C), the receiver just discards the bit *i*. With an S3C, the receiver cannot correctly decrypt *n* bits, starting with bit *i*. For example, if the continuous flow being transmitted is composed of pixels represented with eight bits, with an S2C, a single pixel is discarded, while  <math alttext="left ceiling n slash 8 right ceiling" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8968;</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo>&#8969;</mo></mrow></math> ![left ceiling n slash 8 right ceiling](images/c06_619.png) pixels are discarded with an S3C.
2.  Assume that *n* is low and a few bits have been inserted or deleted by an adversary. In the S2C, the receiver loses synchronization and the forged bits as well as the remaining bits are very likely to be discarded. This helps in detecting attacks because of inconsistency between the message content before and after the alteration. In S3C, only bits altered in synchronization window may be discarded, which reduces the chance to detect attacks. For example, imagine that the adversary changes an amount 10 to 1000 in a text. On the receiver side, in S2C, it is very likely that the part of the message starting from the altered amount will be entirely different from the original one and the receiver has chance to detect the attack. In the S3C, only the amount and may be a few other characters in encrypted message will be different from the characters in decrypted message. Therefore, the receiver has less chance to detect the attack.

Assume that three successive outputs, denoted  <math alttext="z 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![z 1](images/c06_620.png),  <math alttext="z 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![z 2](images/c06_621.png), and  <math alttext="z 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![z 3](images/c06_622.png), of a linear congruential generator are known as well as the modulus *m*.

In the following, computations are over  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript m Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript m Superscript asterisk](images/c06_623.png) (i.e. the set of invertible elements of  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript m](images/c06_624.png)). By definition of LCG, the following equalities hold:

 <math alttext="z 2 equals upper A asterisk z 1 plus upper B m o d m" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![z 2 equals upper A asterisk z 1 plus upper B m o d m](images/c06_625.png) <math alttext="z 3 equals upper A asterisk z 2 plus upper B m o d m" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![z 3 equals upper A asterisk z 2 plus upper B m o d m](images/c06_626.png)

Thus,
