*   3\. Make substitutions in the last equation:

 <math alttext="upper A equals left-parenthesis 5 minus 2 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis 6 minus 2 right-parenthesis Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d Baseline 20" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>20</mn></mrow></math> ![upper A equals left-parenthesis 5 minus 2 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis 6 minus 2 right-parenthesis Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d Baseline 20](images/c06_638.png) <math alttext="equals 3 asterisk left-parenthesis 4 right-parenthesis Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d Baseline 20" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>\*</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>20</mn></mrow></math> ![equals 3 asterisk left-parenthesis 4 right-parenthesis Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d Baseline 20](images/c06_639.png)

Since 4 and 20 are not coprime, <math alttext="4 Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d Baseline 20" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>4</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>20</mn></mrow></math> ![4 Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d Baseline 20](images/c06_640.png) does not exist. Thus, *A* and *B* cannot be recovered.

*   4\. From the previous example, we conclude that if the modulus *m* is not a prime, some elements of  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript m](images/c06_641.png) do not belong to  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript m Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript m Superscript asterisk](images/c06_642.png). In particular,  <math alttext="left-parenthesis z 1 minus z 2 right-parenthesis Superscript negative 1 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis z 1 minus z 2 right-parenthesis Superscript negative 1 Baseline](images/c06_643.png) may not exist in  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript m Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript m Superscript asterisk](images/c06_644.png) and consequently, the 3-known-value attack may fail to recover *A* and *B*. Therefore, a non-prime modulus is preferred when security is of concern.

***Problem*** ***6.3***

1.  Let the known bits be  <math alttext="a Subscript 3 n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![a Subscript 3 n](images/c06_645.png),  <math alttext="a Subscript 3 n minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![a Subscript 3 n minus 1](images/c06_646.png), ...,  <math alttext="a 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![a 2](images/c06_647.png),  <math alttext="a 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![a 1](images/c06_648.png) and their corresponding cipher bits <math alttext="be c Subscript 3 n Baseline comma c Subscript 3 n minus 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma c 2 comma c 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>be&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![be c Subscript 3 n Baseline comma c Subscript 3 n minus 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma c 2 comma c 1](images/c06_649.png). The modulus  <math alttext="2 Superscript n Baseline minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript n Baseline minus 1](images/c06_650.png) of the linear congruential generator (LCG) also is known. Each LCG output is of a length of *n* bits. Thus, LCG output *k* ( <math alttext="k equals 1 comma 2 comma 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![k equals 1 comma 2 comma 3](images/c06_651.png)) can be written as  <math alttext="z Subscript k Baseline equals left-parenthesis z Subscript k comma n Baseline comma z Subscript k comma n minus 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma z Subscript k comma 1 Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![z Subscript k Baseline equals left-parenthesis z Subscript k comma n Baseline comma z Subscript k comma n minus 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma z Subscript k comma 1 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06_652.png).

Assume that the known bits are the first bits of a message. Therefore, the keystream bits used to encrypt them form the first three outputs of LCG, i.e.  <math alttext="z 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![z 1](images/c06_653.png),  <math alttext="z 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![z 2](images/c06_654.png), and  <math alttext="z 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![z 3](images/c06_655.png). From the plaintext and ciphertext, keystream bits can be derived as follows:

 <math alttext="z Subscript 1 comma i Baseline equals a Subscript i Baseline circled-plus" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo></mrow></math> ![z Subscript 1 comma i Baseline equals a Subscript i Baseline circled-plus](images/c06_656.png) <math alttext="c Subscript i Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![c Subscript i Baseline](images/c06_657.png)., for  <math alttext="i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c06_658.png).

 <math alttext="z Subscript 2 comma i Baseline equals a Subscript i plus n Baseline circled-plus" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo></mrow></math> ![z Subscript 2 comma i Baseline equals a Subscript i plus n Baseline circled-plus](images/c06_659.png) <math alttext="c Subscript i plus n Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![c Subscript i plus n Baseline](images/c06_660.png), for  <math alttext="i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c06_661.png).

 <math alttext="z Subscript 3 comma i Baseline equals a Subscript i plus 2 n Baseline circled-plus" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo></mrow></math> ![z Subscript 3 comma i Baseline equals a Subscript i plus 2 n Baseline circled-plus](images/c06_662.png) <math alttext="c Subscript i plus 2 n Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![c Subscript i plus 2 n Baseline](images/c06_663.png), for  <math alttext="i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c06_664.png).

Then, once the three values  <math alttext="z 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![z 1](images/c06_665.png),  <math alttext="z 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![z 2](images/c06_666.png), and  <math alttext="z 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![z 3](images/c06_667.png) are computed, it easy to recover the key  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper A comma upper B right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper A comma upper B right-parenthesis](images/c06_668.png) as in Problem 6.2.

1.  2\. Find the secret key  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper A comma upper B right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper A comma upper B right-parenthesis](images/c06_669.png), if the modulus is  <math alttext="m equals 7" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> ![m equals 7](images/c06_670.png) and the known plaintext is  <math alttext="a equals 101010101" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>101010101</mn></mrow></math> ![a equals 101010101](images/c06_671.png) and the ciphertext  <math alttext="c equals 000100111" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>000100111</mn></mrow></math> ![c equals 000100111](images/c06_672.png). From the known elements, keystream bits are derived as:

 <math alttext="z Subscript 1 comma 1 Baseline equals 1 circled-plus 1 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![z Subscript 1 comma 1 Baseline equals 1 circled-plus 1 equals 0](images/c06_673.png)    <math alttext="z Subscript 1 comma 2 Baseline equals 0 circled-plus 1 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![z Subscript 1 comma 2 Baseline equals 0 circled-plus 1 equals 1](images/c06_674.png)    <math alttext="z Subscript 1 comma 3 Baseline equals 1 circled-plus 1 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![z Subscript 1 comma 3 Baseline equals 1 circled-plus 1 equals 0](images/c06_675.png)

 <math alttext="z Subscript 2 comma 1 Baseline equals 0 circled-plus 0 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![z Subscript 2 comma 1 Baseline equals 0 circled-plus 0 equals 0](images/c06_676.png)    <math alttext="z Subscript 2 comma 2 Baseline equals 1 circled-plus 0 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![z Subscript 2 comma 2 Baseline equals 1 circled-plus 0 equals 1](images/c06_677.png)    <math alttext="z Subscript 2 comma 3 Baseline equals 0 circled-plus 1 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![z Subscript 2 comma 3 Baseline equals 0 circled-plus 1 equals 1](images/c06_678.png)

 <math alttext="z Subscript 3 comma 1 Baseline equals 1 circled-plus 0 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![z Subscript 3 comma 1 Baseline equals 1 circled-plus 0 equals 1](images/c06_679.png)    <math alttext="z Subscript 3 comma 2 Baseline equals 0 circled-plus 0 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![z Subscript 3 comma 2 Baseline equals 0 circled-plus 0 equals 0](images/c06_680.png)    <math alttext="z Subscript 3 comma 3 Baseline equals 1 circled-plus 0 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![z Subscript 3 comma 3 Baseline equals 1 circled-plus 0 equals 1](images/c06_681.png)

Thus,  <math alttext="z 1 equals 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![z 1 equals 2](images/c06_682.png),  <math alttext="z 2 equals 6" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> ![z 2 equals 6](images/c06_683.png), and  <math alttext="z 3 equals 5" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> ![z 3 equals 5](images/c06_684.png)

By design of LCG:

 <math alttext="6 equals upper A asterisk 2 plus upper B m o d Baseline 7" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>\*</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> ![6 equals upper A asterisk 2 plus upper B m o d Baseline 7](images/c06_685.png) <math alttext="5 equals upper A asterisk 6 plus upper B m o d Baseline 7" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>\*</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> ![5 equals upper A asterisk 6 plus upper B m o d Baseline 7](images/c06_686.png)

Hence,

 <math alttext="1 equals negative upper A asterisk 4 m o d Baseline 7" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>\*</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> ![1 equals negative upper A asterisk 4 m o d Baseline 7](images/c06_687.png) <math alttext="upper A equals left-parenthesis negative 1 right-parenthesis asterisk 4 Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d Baseline 7 equals minus 2 m o d Baseline 7 equals 5" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>4</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> ![upper A equals left-parenthesis negative 1 right-parenthesis asterisk 4 Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d Baseline 7 equals minus 2 m o d Baseline 7 equals 5](images/c06_688.png) <math alttext="upper B equals 6 minus 2 asterisk upper A m o d Baseline 7 equals minus 4 m o d Baseline 7 equals 3" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![upper B equals 6 minus 2 asterisk upper A m o d Baseline 7 equals minus 4 m o d Baseline 7 equals 3](images/c06_689.png)

***Problem*** ***6.4***

*R* is an LFSR defined by feedback polynomial  <math alttext="script upper F left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 4 Baseline plus x plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![script upper F left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 4 Baseline plus x plus 1](images/c06_690.png). Hence, its feedback coefficients are  <math alttext="c 1 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![c 1 equals 1](images/c06_691.png),  <math alttext="c 2 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![c 2 equals 0](images/c06_692.png),  <math alttext="c 3 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![c 3 equals 0](images/c06_693.png),  <math alttext="c 4 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![c 4 equals 1](images/c06_694.png). The property of the output sequence of *R* is proven by induction.

***Problem*** ***6.6***

LFSR state is the content of a register of *m* bits. The maximum number of distinct values of an *m*\-bit register is  <math alttext="2 Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript m](images/c06_741.png). If an LFSR reaches a state with all flip-flops at 0, it will no more change its state. Therefore, the maximum of non-zero states is  <math alttext="2 Superscript m Baseline minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript m Baseline minus 1](images/c06_742.png).

Let  <math alttext="sigma Subscript t Baseline equals left-parenthesis s Subscript t Superscript 1 Baseline comma s Subscript t Superscript 2 Baseline comma ellipsis comma s Subscript t Superscript m Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>m</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![sigma Subscript t Baseline equals left-parenthesis s Subscript t Superscript 1 Baseline comma s Subscript t Superscript 2 Baseline comma ellipsis comma s Subscript t Superscript m Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06_743.png) denote the initial state of the register and  <math alttext="s Subscript t Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![s Subscript t Superscript i](images/c06_744.png) the state of each element *i*, respectively. The same repeats after *kN* iterations (*k* is a positive integer). Thus, the output of LFSR follows a cyclic pattern of bits with a period of *N*.□

***Problem*** ***6.7***

Assume that the adversary knows  <math alttext="2 m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![2 m](images/c06_749.png) bits of plaintext (for example, he/she knows the header of a message) and their ciphertext. He/she also knows that the sender is using a stream cipher based on an LFSR with *m* bits.

Without loss of generality, assume that known bits of plaintext are located at the beginning of a message and denoted  <math alttext="a Subscript 2 m minus 1 Baseline comma a Subscript 2 m minus 2 Baseline comma ellipsis comma a 1 comma a 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![a Subscript 2 m minus 1 Baseline comma a Subscript 2 m minus 2 Baseline comma ellipsis comma a 1 comma a 0](images/c06_750.png). The ciphertext bits are denoted  <math alttext="a prime Subscript 2 m minus 1 Baseline comma a prime Subscript 2 m minus 2 comma ellipsis comma a prime 1 comma a prime 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>'</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>'</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn><mo>'</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn><mo>'</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![a prime Subscript 2 m minus 1 Baseline comma a prime Subscript 2 m minus 2 comma ellipsis comma a prime 1 comma a prime 0](images/c06_751.png). By definition of a stream cipher, given a plaintext and its ciphertext, it is easy to compute the key bit string  <math alttext="left-parenthesis s Subscript 2 m minus 1 Baseline comma s Subscript 2 m minus 2 Baseline comma ellipsis comma s 1 comma s 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis s Subscript 2 m minus 1 Baseline comma s Subscript 2 m minus 2 Baseline comma ellipsis comma s 1 comma s 0 right-parenthesis](images/c06_752.png). That is,

Feedback coefficients  <math alttext="c Subscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![c Subscript m](images/c06_760.png),  <math alttext="c Subscript m minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![c Subscript m minus 1](images/c06_761.png), …, *c[1]* are given by solving the linear equation system above.

*Example*:

The LFSR output is given by the rightmost bit. As shown on [Figure 6.5b](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0005), the first eight outputs of LFSR *R* defined by polynomial  <math alttext="x Superscript 4 Baseline plus x plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![x Superscript 4 Baseline plus x plus 1](images/c06_762.png) are  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 1 comma 0 comma 1 comma 1 comma 1 comma 1 comma 0 comma 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 1 comma 0 comma 1 comma 1 comma 1 comma 1 comma 0 comma 0 right-parenthesis](images/c06_763.png); they represent the key bit string of the stream cipher. Hence,  <math alttext="s 7 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>7</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![s 7 equals 1](images/c06_764.png),  <math alttext="s 6 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![s 6 equals 0](images/c06_765.png),  <math alttext="s 5 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![s 5 equals 1](images/c06_766.png),  <math alttext="s 4 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![s 4 equals 1](images/c06_767.png),  <math alttext="s 3 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![s 3 equals 1](images/c06_768.png),  <math alttext="s 2 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![s 2 equals 1](images/c06_769.png),  <math alttext="s 2 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![s 2 equals 1](images/c06_770.png), and  <math alttext="s 0 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![s 0 equals 0](images/c06_771.png).

Let  <math alttext="a equals left-parenthesis 1 comma 1 comma 0 comma 1 comma 1 comma 1 comma 0 comma 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![a equals left-parenthesis 1 comma 1 comma 0 comma 1 comma 1 comma 1 comma 0 comma 0 right-parenthesis](images/c06_772.png) be the plaintext. The ciphertext yielded by a stream cipher relying on LFSR *R* is  <math alttext="a prime equals left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 comma 1 comma 0 comma 0 comma 0 comma 0 comma 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![a prime equals left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 comma 1 comma 0 comma 0 comma 0 comma 0 comma 0 right-parenthesis](images/c06_773.png).

Given the plaintext and ciphertext, the adversary derives the keystream bits as follows:

By definition of LFSR with  <math alttext="m equals 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![m equals 4](images/c06_775.png),  <math alttext="s Subscript i plus 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![s Subscript i plus 4](images/c06_776.png) is yielded by feedback polynomial using  <math alttext="s Subscript i plus 3 Baseline comma s Subscript i plus 2 Baseline comma s Subscript i plus 1 Baseline comma s Subscript i Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![s Subscript i plus 3 Baseline comma s Subscript i plus 2 Baseline comma s Subscript i plus 1 Baseline comma s Subscript i Baseline](images/c06_777.png). ><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>7</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext></mrow></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math> The previous linear equation system can be easily solved with Gaussian elimination, which yields the solution:  <math alttext="c 1 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![c 1 equals 1](images/c06_779.png),  <math alttext="c 2 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![c 2 equals 0](images/c06_780.png),  <math alttext="c 3 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![c 3 equals 0](images/c06_781.png),  <math alttext="c 4 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![c 4 equals 1](images/c06_782.png).

***Problem*** ***6.8***

                           <math alttext="upper M equals 1001 0010 0110 1101 1001 0010 0110" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1001</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0010</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0110</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1101</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1001</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0010</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0110</mn></mrow></math> ![upper M equals 1001 0010 0110 1101 1001 0010 0110](images/c06_783.png) and

 <math alttext="upper C equals 1011 1100 0011 0001 0010 1011 0001 period" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1011</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1100</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0011</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0001</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0010</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1011</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0001</mn></mrow><mo>.</mo></math> ![upper C equals 1011 1100 0011 0001 0010 1011 0001 period](images/c06_784.png)

1\. Period and degree of the keystream generator

The keystream used to encrypt *M* is:

 <math alttext="1001 0010 0110 1101 1001 0010 0110 circled-plus" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1001</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0010</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0110</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1101</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1001</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0010</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0110</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo></mrow></math> ![1001 0010 0110 1101 1001 0010 0110 circled-plus](images/c06_785.png) <math alttext="1011 1100 0011 0001 0010 1011 0001 equals" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1011</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1100</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0011</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0001</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0010</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1011</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0001</mn><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> ![1011 1100 0011 0001 0010 1011 0001 equals](images/c06_786.png) <math alttext="0010 1110 0101 1100 1011 1001 0111" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0010</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1110</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0101</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1100</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1011</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1001</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0111</mn></mrow></math> ![0010 1110 0101 1100 1011 1001 0111](images/c06_787.png)

We observe that the repeated keystream pattern is either 0010111 or 00101110010111.

Therefore, the period of the keystream generator is either 7 or 14.

2\. Degree of the keystream generator

By Lemma [6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-mthst-0003), an LFSR with *m* bits can have a maximum period of  <math alttext="2 Superscript m Baseline minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript m Baseline minus 1](images/c06_788.png). Therefore, the LFSR under consideration cannot have less than *m* = 3 bits. Therefore, the degree is  <math alttext="m greater-than-or-equal-to 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![m greater-than-or-equal-to 3](images/c06_789.png). Notice that at this point, we are not yet sure that the degree is *m* = 3 or  <math alttext="m equals 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![m equals 4](images/c06_790.png).

3\. Initialization vector and feedback polynomial

If the degree is 3, then the keystream bits generated in the first period are:

 <math alttext="left-parenthesis s 0 equals 0 comma s 1 equals 0 comma s 2 equals 1 comma s 3 equals 0 cedilla s 4 equals 1 comma s 5 equals 1 comma s 6 equals 1 right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>&#184;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis s 0 equals 0 comma s 1 equals 0 comma s 2 equals 1 comma s 3 equals 0 cedilla s 4 equals 1 comma s 5 equals 1 comma s 6 equals 1 right-parenthesis](images/c06_791.png)

Under the assumption that the degree is *m* = 3. The initialization vector is 100, because the *m* first bits (i.e. <math alttext="s 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![s 0](images/c06_792.png),  <math alttext="s 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![s 1](images/c06_793.png), and  <math alttext="s 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![s 2](images/c06_794.png)) delivered by a keystream generator are equal to the initialization vector. Then, the coefficients of the LFSR result from the following equations:

Therefore, the feedback polynomial is  <math alttext="script upper F left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x cubed plus x squared plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#8497;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![script upper F left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x cubed plus x squared plus 1](images/c06_799.png), which is a primitive polynomial; that is why the period of the LFSR is  <math alttext="2 cubed minus 1 equals 7" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> ![2 cubed minus 1 equals 7](images/c06_800.png) (by Lemma [6.2](#c06.xhtml#c06-mthst-0005)). The internal structure is shown in [Figure 6.20](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0020) . Now, we are able to confirm that degree is  <math alttext="m equals 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![m equals 3](images/c06_801.png).

![Figure 6.20 LFSR structure.](images/c06f020.png)

***Problem*** ***6.9***

Assuming that all the encrypted messages start with a known header of *k* bits, an adversary can break a code based on a keystream generator with a period of *L* bits if the adversary can collect a set of ciphertexts such that he/she can rebuilt an entire period of the keystream generator as follows:

Let *m*[1],  <math alttext="m 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![m 2](images/c06_802.png), …, *m*[t] be the intercepted messages and  <math alttext="upper I left-parenthesis m Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper I left-parenthesis m Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06_803.png) denote the index of the first bit used in the keystream period to encrypt message *m[i]*. For example,  <math alttext="upper L equals 127" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>127</mn></mrow></math> ![upper L equals 127](images/c06_804.png) and five intercepted messages of the following lengths:

Thus,  <math alttext="upper I left-parenthesis m 1 right-parenthesis equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper I left-parenthesis m 1 right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c06_806.png),  <math alttext="upper I left-parenthesis m 2 right-parenthesis equals 72" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>72</mn></mrow></math> ![upper I left-parenthesis m 2 right-parenthesis equals 72](images/c06_807.png),  <math alttext="upper I left-parenthesis m 3 right-parenthesis equals 55" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>55</mn></mrow></math> ![upper I left-parenthesis m 3 right-parenthesis equals 55](images/c06_808.png),  <math alttext="upper I left-parenthesis m 4 right-parenthesis equals 95" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>95</mn></mrow></math> ![upper I left-parenthesis m 4 right-parenthesis equals 95](images/c06_809.png),  <math alttext="upper I left-parenthesis m 5 right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper I left-parenthesis m 5 right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c06_810.png)

***Problem*** ***6.10***

Let  <math alttext="upper C 1 comma upper C 2 comma ellipsis comma upper C Subscript n Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 1 comma upper C 2 comma ellipsis comma upper C Subscript n Baseline](images/c06_819.png) be the *n* known encrypted documents. Each document is composed of uppercase letters and space in 7-bit ASCII code. Recall ASCII codes (in Hexa): space  <math alttext="right-arrow 20 Subscript 16" display="inline" 16](images/c06_827.png).

The attacker exploits two advantages: i) space character is frequent in English texts (nearly 19% characters are spaces in English texts) and ii) XORing any letter with space character returns a value greater than  <math alttext="20 Subscript 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![20 Subscript 16](images/c06_828.png) and XORing two letters returns a value less than  <math alttext="20 Subscript 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![20 Subscript 16](images/c06_829.png). Attacker exploits all pairs of ciphertexts, and for each pair  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i Baseline comma upper C Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i Baseline comma upper C Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06_830.png),  <math alttext="1 less-than-or-equal-to i comma j less-than-or-equal-to n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![1 less-than-or-equal-to i comma j less-than-or-equal-to n](images/c06_831.png),  <math alttext="i not-equals j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></math> ![i not-equals j](images/c06_832.png), performs the following:

*K* is the keystream generator output, which is the same for all ciphertexts.

Let  <math alttext="s equals min left-parenthesis l e n left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis comma l e n left-parenthesis upper C Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>min</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![s equals min left-parenthesis l e n left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis comma l e n left-parenthesis upper C Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c06_833.png).

Reduce both bit string  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i](images/c06_834.png) and  <math alttext="upper C Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript j](images/c06_835.png) to the same bit-length *s*, i.e. the longer document is truncated.

XOR the ciphertexts:

Exploit the property of XORing a letter and space.

For each *k*,  <math alttext="1 less-than-or-equal-to k less-than-or-equal-to s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> ![1 less-than-or-equal-to k less-than-or-equal-to s](images/c06_839.png):

If  <math alttext="upper D Subscript i comma k Baseline circled-plus upper D Subscript j comma k Baseline circled-plus 20 Subscript 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper D Subscript i comma k Baseline circled-plus upper D Subscript j comma k Baseline circled-plus 20 Subscript 16](images/c06_840.png), then  <math alttext="upper D Subscript i comma k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper D Subscript i comma k](images/c06_841.png) is a space and  <math alttext="upper D Subscript j comma k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper D Subscript j comma k](images/c06_842.png) is a letter or vice versa. Check which alternative is more likely to appear in the documents under consideration and act accordingly (i.e. either confirm a letter and a space in documents or mark pending alternatives).

The more spaces are discovered, the more letters are confirmed in documents. If the number of encrypted documents is enough, and given that the spaces do not appear at the same positions in distinct English text documents, it is very likely that the attacker recovers all the documents entirely. Nevertheless, it takes time to succeed!

***Problem*** ***6.11***

Since the LFSR has a primitive feedback polynomial of degree 3, it generates a periodic 7-bit sequence equal to 0111001. Assume that two portions of a plaintext *P*, located at positions *i* and *j*, of bit-length *L*, are identical, i.e.  <math alttext="upper P Subscript i plus b Baseline equals upper P Subscript j plus b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P Subscript i plus b Baseline equals upper P Subscript j plus b](images/c06_843.png), for  <math alttext="b equals 0 comma ellipsis comma upper L minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![b equals 0 comma ellipsis comma upper L minus 1](images/c06_844.png). Let *C* be the ciphertext associated with *P*. Thus,  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i plus b Baseline circled-plus upper C Subscript j plus b Baseline equals left-parenthesis upper P Subscript i plus b Baseline circled-plus s Subscript i plus b Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper P Subscript j plus b Baseline circled-plus s Subscript j plus b Baseline right-parenthesis equals s Subscript i plus b Baseline circled-plus s Subscript j plus b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i plus b Baseline circled-plus upper C Subscript j plus b Baseline equals left-parenthesis upper P Subscript i plus b Baseline circled-plus s Subscript i plus b Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper P Subscript j plus b Baseline circled-plus s Subscript j plus b Baseline right-parenthesis equals s Subscript i plus b Baseline circled-plus s Subscript j plus b](images/c06_845.png), for  <math alttext="b equals 0 comma ellipsis comma upper L minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![b equals 0 comma ellipsis comma upper L minus 1](images/c06_846.png).

*Encryption step*

Consider a plaintext  <math alttext="upper P equals 11011001 11011001" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>11011001</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>11011001</mn></mrow></math> ![upper P equals 11011001 11011001](images/c06_847.png) composed of two identical bytes. The keystream, denoted *S*, used to encrypt *P* is composed of bits of two LFSR periods plus two bits, i.e.  <math alttext="upper S equals 01 0111001 0111001" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>01</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0111001</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0111001</mn></mrow></math> ![upper S equals 01 0111001 0111001](images/c06_848.png).

Thus,  <math alttext="upper S equals 01 0111001 0111001" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>01</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0111001</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0111001</mn></mrow></math> ![upper S equals 01 0111001 0111001](images/c06_849.png). Let  <math alttext="upper P Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P Subscript i](images/c06_850.png),  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i](images/c06_851.png), and  <math alttext="upper S Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript i](images/c06_852.png),  <math alttext="i equals 0 comma ellipsis comma 15" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>15</mn></mrow></math> ![i equals 0 comma ellipsis comma 15](images/c06_853.png), denote bits of plaintext, ciphertext, and keystream, respectively. # 7   
Block Ciphers: Basics, TDEA, and AES

This chapter focuses on block ciphers, which are the most commonly used algorithms to encrypt confidential data. In addition to ciphering, block ciphers can be used as stream ciphers and pseudorandom number generators or used to build hash functions and MACs (Message Authentication Codes). Therefore, block ciphers are of prime importance to build cryptosystems.

A huge number of block ciphers are published in literature; but a very small number of them are standards used in operational cryptosystems. This chapter aims at introducing the basics of construction of block ciphers and present in detail the standard block ciphers, currently in use, namely TDEA (Triple Data Encryption Algorithm) and AES (Advanced Encryption Standard). Both ciphers are NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology, US) standards. It is worth noticing that, because of some reported attacks (even if they are theoretical) against TDEA, AES would be the dominating block cipher in the near future and for a long time.

## 7.1 Construction Principles for Block Cipher Design

***Definition 7.1 Block cipher****: it is an encryption–decryption scheme where a block of plaintext is treated as a single block and is used to obtain a block of ciphertext with the same size*.

Modern ciphering was inspired by mechanical ciphering machines such as Enigma, presented in Section 4.5. The most commonly used cyphers, called *block ciphers*, operate as follows (see [Figure 7.1](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0001)):

![Figure 7.1 Block-based ciphering.](images/c07f001.png)

[**Figure 7.1**](#c07.xhtml#rc07-fig-0001) Block-based ciphering.

*   The plaintext is divided into a series of fixed-length blocks ( <math alttext="upper P 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P 1](images/c07_1.png),  <math alttext="upper P 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P 2](images/c07_2.png), …,  <math alttext="upper P Subscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P Subscript m](images/c07_3.png)). In the standards currently in use, the block bit-length is of either 64 or 128.
*   An encryption key *K* (with a known length of 56, 128, 192, or 256 bits).
*   Encrypted blocks ( <math alttext="upper C 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 1](images/c07_4.png),  <math alttext="upper C 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msubmrow></math> ![upper C 2](images/c07_5.png), …,  <math alttext="upper C Subscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript m](images/c07_6.png)) are of a fixed length, which is the same than that of plaintext blocks.
*   Decryption is the inverse operation.

A block cipher is composed of two algorithms: encryption and decryption algorithms, which make use of the same secret key *K*. The algorithms are denoted  <math alttext="upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c07_7.png) and  <math alttext="upper D Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper D Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c07_8.png), which operate on input of fixed-length and produce output with the same length. Formally:

 <math alttext="upper E colon StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript k Baseline times StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n Baseline right-arrow StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>&#215;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper E colon StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript k Baseline times StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n Baseline right-arrow StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n](images/c07_9.png)

 <math alttext="upper D colon StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript k Baseline times StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n Baseline right-arrow StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>&#215;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8594;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper D colon StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript k Baseline times StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n Baseline right-arrow StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n](images/c07_10.png)

where *n* is the block bit-length and *k*, the key bit-length.

For any block plaintext *P*, the following property holds:  <math alttext="upper D Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper P right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![upper D Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper P right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper P](images/c07_11.png)

Encryption and decryption algorithms are based on iterated operations, mainly substitutions and permutations.

### 7.1.1 Confusion and Diffusion Properties

In the cryptography field, Claude Shannon proposed in the 1940s two fundamental properties of operation of secure ciphers called *confusion* and *diffusion* \[[1](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0001)\]. Both properties aim to make statistical-analysis-based attacks impracticable. With robust methods of confusion and diffusion, block ciphers appear as generating random ciphertexts, which are independent from the key and the plaintext.

***Definition 7.2 Confusion****: it is a cipher operation where each bit of the ciphertext should depend on several bits of the key. Therefore, the statistical relationship between the plaintext and ciphertext should be hidden*.

***Definition 7.3 Diffusion****: it is a cipher operation where when a single bit is changed in the plaintext, several bits in the ciphertext should change. Similarly, when a single bit changes in the ciphertext, several bits in the plaintext should change*.

***Definition 7.4 Avalanche effect****: changing a few bits in the plaintext (resp. in ciphertext) results in a lot of changes in the ciphertext (resp. in plaintext), which is known as avalanche effect; i.e. a small change in either the key or the plaintext should cause a drastic change in the ciphertext*.

Affine and Caesar ciphers, presented in Sections 4.2–4.3, do not make use of diffusion and confusion methods. Therefore, they are very easy to break. In block ciphers, the common techniques to achieve confusion and diffusion are: substitution boxes, permutations, and key expansion.

#### 7.1.1.1 Substitution Boxes

An S-Box is an array of *R* rows by *C* columns. It contains elements of a specific length; for example, TDEA S-Boxes are of a length of four bits, while those of AES are of a length of eight bits. In general, the number of rows or columns is at most 16.

The bit-length of the elements of an S-box depends on each cipher. For example, Elements of TDEA S-boxes are of a length of four bits, while those of AES are of a length of eight bits. The element space of an S-Box is at most equal to that of the input space; otherwise, some elements of the S-Box are never used. In some ciphers, such as TDEA, some elements may be repeated in an S-Box. [Figure 7.2](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0002) illustrates the access to an S-Box. The value to replace *D* is converted into two indexes, *r* and *c*. Then, the content of the cell,  <math alttext="upper D prime equals upper S bar upper B o x left-parenthesis r comma c right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper D prime equals upper S bar upper B o x left-parenthesis r comma c right-parenthesis](images/c07_12.png), is returned as the element to replace *D*.

![Figure 7.2 S-Box mapping.](images/c07f002.png)

[**Figure 7.2**](#c07.xhtml#rc07-fig-0002) S-Box mapping.

The following properties are expected not to compromise security and to enable decryption:

1.  S-Boxes include elements that appear as random sequences of elements; therefore, no relationship between elements could be inferred to design attacks. Such property is referred to as the nonlinearity of S-Boxes.
2.  S-Boxes are deterministic; i.e. the same input is always mapped to the same output.

#### 7.1.1.2 Permutation

***Definition 7.5 Permutation****: a function*  <math alttext="upper E colon StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n Baseline right-arrow StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n Baseline" Block ciphers make use of permutations to swap a part of a block with another, so that the diffusion is increased. In block ciphers addressed in this chapter, permutations are defined either by permutation tables or with shifting and mixing.

#### 7.1.1.3 Key Expansion

Block ciphers are iterated ciphers, which perform the same operations at all (with some exceptions) rounds. To increase confusion in the resulting ciphertexts, instead of using the same cipher key in all the rounds, each round has its own key called *round key*. The result is that the ciphers make use of *r* keys, where *r* is the number of rounds. The key expansion function, also called key schedule function, is the component of block ciphers that generates the round keys from the initial key (also called cipher key). In general, key expansion function makes use of permutations and s-boxes (see [Figure 7.3](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0003)).

![Figure 7.3 Key expansion.](images/c07f003.png)

[**Figure 7.3**](#c07.xhtml#rc07-fig-0003) Key expansion.

### 7.1.2 Feistel Structure

Many block ciphers (including DEA, Blowfish, CAST-128, and Kasumi) are based on *Feistel network*. The latter is also called *Feistel structure*.[¹](#c07.xhtml#c07-note-0001) The main component of a Feistel network is the *round function* *F*, which takes an input block and a *round key* and returns an output of the same length than that of the input block. The round function may be invertible or not. The number of rounds, denoted *n*, is a setting parameter of cryptosystems; often,  <math alttext="n equals 10 comma 12 comma 14 comma or 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>12</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>or</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>16</mn></mrow></math> ![n equals 10 comma 12 comma 14 comma or 16](images/c07_17.png). The number of rounds depends on the tradeoff between the desired security level and the efficiency. The latter is measured in terms of computation time or hardware implementation complexity.

When Feistel structure is used in cryptography, each round *i*,  <math alttext="1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>i</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to n](images/c07_18.png) makes use of a round key  <math alttext="upper K Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript i](images/c07_19.png) and performs a substitution and a permutation. Round keys are derived from the initial secret key by a key expansion function.

As shown on [Figure 7.4](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0004), the data block under processing (either for encryption or for decryption) is divided into two halves, denoted *L* (left) and *R* (right), and the cipher operates only on a single half in each round of encryption or decryption. Between rounds, the left and right halves are swapped.

![Figure 7.4 Feistel structure (encryption on the left and decryption on the right). Halves are indexed by the round number; and upper E and upper D denote encryption and decryption.](images/c07f004.png)

[**Figure 7.4**](#c07.xhtml#rc07-fig-0004) Feistel structure (encryption on the left and decryption on the right). Halves are indexed by the round number; and  <math alttext="upper E and upper D" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mtext>&#160;and&#160;</mtext><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> ![upper E and upper D](images/c07_20.png) denote encryption and decryption.

Below are the encryption and decryption procedures:

**Note**. The halves computed in the last round are concatenated in this order  <math alttext="upper R upper E Subscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper R upper E Subscript n](images/c07_27.png) followed by  <math alttext="upper L upper E Subscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper L upper E Subscript n](images/c07_28.png) to form the ciphertext block.

Decryption[²](#c07.xhtml#c07-note-0002) is the same as the encryption with one difference: the round keys used in encryption are used in the reverse order.

**Note**. The halves computed in the last round are concatenated in this order  <math alttext="upper R upper D Subscript n Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper R upper D Subscript n Baseline](images/c07_35.png) followed by  <math alttext="upper L upper D Subscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper L upper D Subscript n](images/c07_36.png) to form the plaintext block.

## 7.2 Triple Data Encryption Algorithm (TDEA)

The first version of TDEA was approved by the NIST in 2004; and the most recent revision of TDEA was published in 2017 \[[2](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0002)\]. Till now, TDEA is considered as a secure block cipher. It applies the DEA (Data Encryption Algorithm) cipher three times to each data block. To understand how TDEA works one must first understand the basics of DEA.

### 7.2.1 Data Encryption Algorithm (DEA)

It is worth noticing that DEA was originally specified in the Data Encryption Standard (DES[³](#c07.xhtml#c07-note-0003)), which became effective in 1977 and widely used for nearly three decades. DES was proposed by IBM researchers and its internals were covered by a patent.[⁴](#c07.xhtml#c07-note-0004) However, they became public afterward. DES is the most studied cipher; and the lessons learned from the vulnerabilities of DES contributed to the design of more secure ciphers.

However, since 2005, the last version of DES \[[3](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0003)\] is no longer recommended to be used alone, after some vulnerabilities were discovered. DES was withdrawn from NIST standards and DEA is specified as an engine of TDEA, i.e. DEA is repeated three times to encrypt or decrypt 64-bit blocks.

#### 7.2.1.1 DEA Encryption and Decryption

DEA is a block cipher with a block length of 64 bits and a key of a bit length of 56 bits (see [Figure 7.5](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0005)). DEA encryption and decryption transformations are very similar:

![Figure 7.5 Overall view of DEA.](images/c07f005.png)

[**Figure 7.5**](#c07.xhtml#rc07-fig-0005) Overall view of DEA.

*   Both encryption and decryption run in 16 rounds numbered from  <math alttext="1 to 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;to</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>16</mn></mrow></math> ![1 to 16](images/c07_37.png), forming a Feistel network (see [Figure 7.6](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0006)).
    
    ![Figure 7.6 DEA encryption and decryption diagrams.](images/c07f006.png)
    
    [**Figure 7.6**](#c07.xhtml#rc07-fig-0006) DEA encryption and decryption diagrams.
    
*   Each round takes a 64-bit input block and yields a 64-bit output block. Each input or output 64-bit block is split into two 32-bit halves, denoted *L* (left) and *R* (right). In encryption, the input halves of round *i* are denoted  <math alttext="upper L upper E Subscript i minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper L upper E Subscript i minus 1](images/c07_38.png) and  <math alttext="upper R upper E Subscript i minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper R upper E Subscript i minus 1](images/c07_39.png); and its output halves  <math alttext="upper L upper E Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper L upper E Subscript i](images/c07_40.png) and  <math alttext="upper R upper E Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper R upper E Subscript i](images/c07_41.png). In decryption, the input halves of round *i* are denoted  <math alttext="upper L upper D Subscript i minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper L upper D Subscript i minus 1](images/c07_42.png) and  <math alttext="upper R upper D Subscript i minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper R upper D Subscript i minus 1](images/c07_43.png); and its output halves  <math alttext="upper L upper D Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper L upper D Subscript i](images/c07_44.png) and  <math alttext="upper R upper D Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper R upper D Subscript i](images/c07_45.png).
*   Each round *i* makes use of its 48-bit round key, denoted  <math alttext="upper K Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript i](images/c07_46.png), which is derived from a DEA key, denoted  <math alttext="upper K upper E upper Y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K upper E upper Y](images/c07_47.png), using a key schedule function  <math alttext="upper K upper S" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K upper S](images/c07_48.png) (see [Section 7.2.2.3](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-03009));  <math alttext="upper K Subscript i Baseline equals upper K upper S left-parenthesis upper K upper E upper Y comma i right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>K</mi><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript i Baseline equals upper K upper S left-parenthesis upper K upper E upper Y comma i right-parenthesis](images/c07_49.png).
*   All the rounds use the same core function *f* (see [Section 7.2.1.3](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-03006)) to process the right half of their input.

#### 7.2.1.2 Initial Permutation and Its Inverse

The input and output of the initial permutation and of its inverse are 64-bit blocks. An input block is permuted according to a predefined rule to yield the output. Both permutations are keyless and deterministic. Therefore, they only aim at making bit transpositions. In literature, it is argued that the initial permutation and its inverse were introduced to be implemented in hardware to thwart the attacks against DEA by software.

*   *Initial permutation*  <math alttext="IP" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>IP</mtext></mrow></math> ![IP](images/c07_74.png)

Let  <math alttext="upper B left-bracket 1 colon 64 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>:</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper B left-bracket 1 colon 64 right-bracket](images/c07_75.png) and  <math alttext="upper B prime left-bracket 1 colon 64 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>'</mo><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>:</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper B prime left-bracket 1 colon 64 right-bracket](images/c07_76.png) be the input and output bit-vectors of permutation  <math alttext="IP" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>IP</mtext></mrow></math> ![IP](images/c07_77.png), respectively. Let  <math alttext="upper I upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![upper I upper P](images/c07_78.png) ([Table 7.1](#c07.xhtml#c07-tbl-0001)) be the table used by the permutation  <math alttext="IP" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>IP</mtext></mrow></math> ![IP](images/c07_79.png).
