     <math alttext="upper Z equals upper L upper R o t a t e left-parenthesis upper W left-bracket 3 right-bracket right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper Z equals upper L upper R o t a t e left-parenthesis upper W left-bracket 3 right-bracket right-parenthesis](images/c07_753.png);  <math alttext="upper Z equals left-bracket upper F upper F comma upper F upper F comma upper F upper F comma upper F upper F right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mi>F</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>F</mi><mi>F</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>F</mi><mi>F</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>F</mi><mi>F</mi></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper Z equals left-bracket upper F upper F comma upper F upper F comma upper F upper F comma upper F upper F right-bracket](images/c07_754.png), because  <math alttext="upper W left-bracket 3 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper W left-bracket 3 right-bracket](images/c07_755.png) has only 1-bits.

***Problem* *7.2***

Feistel cipher is correct, if  <math alttext="upper D e c left-parenthesis upper E n c left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ![upper D e c left-parenthesis upper E n c left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper B](images/c07_790.png), where *B* denotes a plaintext block.

***Problem* *7.3***

In Problem 7.2, we proved the correctness of Feistel cipher when the number of rounds is 1 or 2. In this problem, we address the correctness of Feistel cipher for an arbitrary number of rounds. To prove the correctness of Feistel cipher, we need to prove (by recurrence) that the computations in the decryption step have the following property:

 <math alttext="for-all i comma 1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8704;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![for-all i comma 1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to n](images/c07_816.png),  <math alttext="upper L upper D Subscript i Baseline equals upper R upper E Subscript n minus i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper L upper D Subscript i Baseline equals upper R upper E Subscript n minus i](images/c07_817.png) and  <math alttext="upper R upper D Subscript i Baseline equals upper L upper E Subscript n minus i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper R upper D Subscript i Baseline equals upper L upper E Subscript n minus i](images/c07_818.png)

The proof is made easy by the following fact: in encryption step, at round *i*, the right half is directly copied in left half used in round  <math alttext="i plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![i plus 1](images/c07_819.png). Hence, by Feistel design,  <math alttext="upper L upper E Subscript i Baseline equals upper R upper E Subscript i minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper L upper E Subscript i Baseline equals upper R upper E Subscript i minus 1](images/c07_820.png), for  <math alttext="i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c07_821.png).

The input of decryption is a ciphertext, which is equal to  <math alttext="upper R upper E Subscript n Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper L upper E Subscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>L</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper R upper E Subscript n Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper L upper E Subscript n](images/c07_822.png). Thus,

 <math alttext="upper L upper D 0 equals upper R upper E Subscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper L upper D 0 equals upper R upper E Subscript n](images/c07_823.png) and  <math alttext="upper R upper D 0 equals upper L upper E Subscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper R upper D 0 equals upper L upper E Subscript n](images/c07_824.png).

In the following, halves computed in encryption step are used in substitutions in the calculations of halves in decryption step.

The result of the last decryption round is  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper R upper E 0 comma upper L upper E 0 right-parenthesis period" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper R upper E 0 comma upper L upper E 0 right-parenthesis period](images/c07_830.png) Then, swapping the two halves yields  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper L upper E 0 comma upper R upper E 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>L</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>R</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper L upper E 0 comma upper R upper E 0 right-parenthesis](images/c07_831.png), which is the original plaintext.□

***Problem 7.4***

First, we address the correctness of DEA. Recall that DEA encryption and decryption are based on a Feistel network of 16 rounds. Let the 16-round Feistel network be modeled as a function ℱ that takes a 64-bit block and a set of 16 round keys; and it yields an output of the same bit-length. DEA encryption and decryption can be written using the function ℱ as follows:

***Problem*** *7.5*

1.  Proof of the complementarity property of DES
    
    We need the following lemma.
    
    *Lemma*: for any pair of *n*\-bit strings, *x* and *y*, the following holds:

    After the final permutation, the output of  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper K overbar comma upper M overbar right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>K</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>M</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper K overbar comma upper M overbar right-parenthesis](images/c07_873.png) is  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper R 16 overbar comma upper L 16 overbar right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper R 16 overbar comma upper L 16 overbar right-parenthesis](images/c07_874.png), which is the 1-complement of  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper K comma upper M right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis upper R 16 comma upper L 16 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper K comma upper M right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis upper R 16 comma upper L 16 right-parenthesis](images/c07_875.png). Therefore, we can conclude that:  <math alttext="upper C equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K comma upper M right-parenthesis right double arrow upper C overbar equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K overbar comma upper M overbar right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8658;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>K</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>M</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K comma upper M right-parenthesis right double arrow upper C overbar equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K overbar comma upper M overbar right-parenthesis](images/c07_876.png) □
    
2.  In general, when the naïve brute-force attack is applied against DES, the adversary, who knew a plaintext–ciphertext pair  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper M comma upper C right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper M comma upper C right-parenthesis](images/c07_877.png), needs to test each of the  <math alttext="2 Superscript 56" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>56</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 56](images/c07_878.png) keys to find a key, which matches the known pair. In this problem, we assume that the adversary knew two plaintext–ciphertext pairs,  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper M 1 comma upper C 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper M 1 comma upper C 1 right-parenthesis](images/c07_879.png) and  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper M 2 comma upper C 2 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper M 2 comma upper C 2 right-parenthesis](images/c07_880.png), such that  <math alttext="upper M 2 equals upper M 1 overbar" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></math> ![upper M 2 equals upper M 1 overbar](images/c07_881.png) and  <math alttext="upper C 2 equals upper C 1 overbar" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></math> ![upper C 2 equals upper C 1 overbar](images/c07_882.png); i.e.  <math alttext="upper C 2 equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K comma upper M 2 right-parenthesis equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K comma upper M 1 overbar right-parenthesis equals upper C 1 overbar equals ModifyingAbove upper E left-parenthesis upper K comma upper M 1 right-parenthesis With bar" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></math> ![upper C 2 equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K comma upper M 2 right-parenthesis equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K comma upper M 1 overbar right-parenthesis equals upper C 1 overbar equals ModifyingAbove upper E left-parenthesis upper K comma upper M 1 right-parenthesis With bar](images/c07_883.png).
    
    By the complementation property, which states that  <math alttext="upper C equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K comma upper M right-parenthesis upper C overbar equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K overbar comma upper M overbar right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>K</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>M</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K comma upper M right-parenthesis upper C overbar equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K overbar comma upper M overbar right-parenthesis](images/c07_884.png),
    
     <math alttext="upper C 2 overbar equals ModifyingAbove upper E left-parenthesis upper K comma upper M 2 right-parenthesis With bar equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K overbar comma upper M 2 overbar right-parenthesis equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K overbar comma upper M 1 right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>K</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>K</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C 2 overbar equals ModifyingAbove upper E left-parenthesis upper K comma upper M 2 right-parenthesis With bar equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K overbar comma upper M 2 overbar right-parenthesis equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K overbar comma upper M 1 right-parenthesis](images/c07_885.png)(a) 
    
    Let’s see the attack that takes advantage of the complementation property. The adversary tries all the  <math alttext="2 Superscript 55" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>55</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 55](images/c07_886.png) keys whose leftmost bit is 0 (notice that the other  <math alttext="2 Superscript 55" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>55</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 55](images/c07_887.png) keys are 1-complement of the tried keys). Let  <math alttext="upper K prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![upper K prime](images/c07_888.png) be one of the tried keys. The adversary makes an encryption,  <math alttext="upper C equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K prime comma upper M 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K prime comma upper M 1 right-parenthesis](images/c07_889.png). If  <math alttext="upper C 1 equals upper C" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C 1 equals upper C](images/c07_890.png), then  <math alttext="upper K prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![upper K prime](images/c07_891.png) is likely to be the real key *K*. Otherwise, if  <math alttext="upper C 2 overbar equals upper C" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C 2 overbar equals upper C](images/c07_892.png), then, by the double equality ([a](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0008)),  <math alttext="upper K prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![upper K prime](images/c07_893.png) is likely to be the 1-complement of the real key *K*, i.e.  <math alttext="upper K prime equals upper K overbar" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>K</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></math> ![upper K prime equals upper K overbar](images/c07_894.png), because  <math alttext="upper C 2 overbar equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K overbar comma upper M 1 right-parenthesis equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K prime comma upper M 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>K</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C 2 overbar equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K overbar comma upper M 1 right-parenthesis equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K prime comma upper M 1 right-parenthesis](images/c07_895.png). If neither  <math alttext="upper K prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> ![upper K prime](images/c07_896.png) nor  <math alttext="ModifyingAbove upper K prime With bar" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></math> ![ModifyingAbove upper K prime With bar](images/c07_897.png) can be the real key *K*, another key is picked and tested as above. We mentioned “likely to be the real key,” because false alarm may occur. Indeed, because the DES key space is of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 56" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>56</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 56](images/c07_898.png) and the ciphertext space is of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 64](images/c07_899.png), the same ciphertext may be yielded by more than one key. In particular, we may have  <math alttext="upper C equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K prime comma upper M 1 right-parenthesis equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K double-prime comma upper M 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8243;</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K prime comma upper M 1 right-parenthesis equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K double-prime comma upper M 1 right-parenthesis](images/c07_900.png), while  <math alttext="upper K prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> ![upper K prime](images/c07_901.png) and  <math alttext="upper K double-prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8243;</mo></msup></math> ![upper K double-prime](images/c07_902.png) are two distinct keys. To reduce the probability of false alarm, more than two plaintext–ciphertext pairs should be used. In conclusion, the complementation property of DES reduces the maximum number of encryptions to  <math alttext="2 Superscript 55" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>55</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 55](images/c07_903.png).
    

***Problem* *7.6***

1.  The algorithms of DEA encryption and decryption are the same with the exception of the use of the round keys. In the encryption, the rounds keys are used from  <math alttext="k 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![k 1](images/c07_904.png) to  <math alttext="k 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![k 16](images/c07_905.png), while they are used in the inverse order, from  <math alttext="k 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![k 16](images/c07_906.png) to  <math alttext="k 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![k 1](images/c07_907.png), in the decryption. If all the round keys are identical, the order does matter. Therefore, encrypting  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper K comma upper B right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper K comma upper B right-parenthesis](images/c07_908.png) is equivalent to a decryption. Hence,  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper K comma upper E left-parenthesis upper K comma upper B right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper K comma upper E left-parenthesis upper K comma upper B right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper B](images/c07_909.png). Notice that decrypting twice a ciphertext *C* results in the ciphertext *C*, i.e.  <math alttext="upper D left-parenthesis upper K comma upper D left-parenthesis upper K comma upper C right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper C" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> ![upper D left-parenthesis upper K comma upper D left-parenthesis upper K comma upper C right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper C](images/c07_910.png).
2.  Take  <math alttext="upper D left-parenthesis upper K comma upper D left-parenthesis upper K comma upper C right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper C" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> ![upper D left-parenthesis upper K comma upper D left-parenthesis upper K comma upper C right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper C](images/c07_911.png) and drop the odd[^(11)](#c07.xhtml#c07-note-0011) parity bits. The resulting 56-bit key is  <math alttext="upper K e y Subscript 1 left-parenthesis 56 right-parenthesis Baseline equals 00 0000 0000 0000 Subscript 16 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>56</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>00</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0000</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0000</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mrow><mn>0000</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K e y Subscript 1 left-parenthesis 56 right-parenthesis Baseline equals 00 0000 0000 0000 Subscript 16 Baseline](images/c07_912.png). Since all the bits of the input are 0 s in key schedule function, all the generated round keys are also 0 s. Permutation, rotation, and compression of s yield only 0 s.
    
    Take  <math alttext="upper K e y 2 equals FEFE FEFE FEFE FEFE Subscript 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mtext>FEFE&#160;FEFE&#160;FEFE&#160;FEFE</mtext></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K e y 2 equals FEFE FEFE FEFE FEFE Subscript 16](images/c07_914.png)      and remove the odd parity bits. The resulting 56-bit key is and  <math alttext="upper K e y Subscript 2 left-parenthesis 56 right-parenthesis Baseline equals FF FFFF FFFF FFFF Subscript 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>56</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mtext>FF&#160;FFFF&#160;FFFF&#160;FFFF</mtext></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K e y Subscript 2 left-parenthesis 56 right-parenthesis Baseline equals FF FFFF FFFF FFFF Subscript 16](images/c07_916.png). Since all the bits of the input are s, in key schedule function, all the generated round keys are also 1 s. Permutation, rotation, and compression of 1 s yield only 1 s. Taking into account the answer to the first question, both keys are weak and should be avoided, because an attacker can try all weak keys to decrypt twice an intercepted ciphertext and recover the key if the result is the same after two decryptions.

2.  Recall that the algorithms of DEA encryption and decryption differ only in the order in which the round keys are used. Let  <math alttext="upper K Subscript i Baseline comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript i Baseline comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma 16](images/c07_946.png) be the round keys generated by the key schedule function from a key  <math alttext="upper K e y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K e y](images/c07_947.png). The encryption algorithm makes use of *K*[1] in the 1^(st) round, …, and  <math alttext="upper K 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K 16](images/c07_948.png) in the 16^(th) round, while the decryption algorithm makes use of  <math alttext="upper K 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K 16](images/c07_949.png) in the 1^(st) round, …, and *K*[1] in the 16^(th) round. In the answer to question 1, the list of round keys generated from  <math alttext="upper K e y 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K e y 1](images/c07_950.png) is the reverse of that generated from  <math alttext="upper K e y 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K e y 2](images/c07_951.png). Therefore, encrypting  <math alttext="upper C equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K e y 2 comma upper M right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper C equals upper E left-parenthesis upper K e y 2 comma upper M right-parenthesis](images/c07_952.png) using  <math alttext="upper K e y 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K e y 1](images/c07_953.png) is equivalent to decrypting *C* with  <math alttext="upper K e y 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K e y 2](images/c07_954.png); i.e.  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper K e y 1 comma upper E left-parenthesis upper K e y 2 comma upper M right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper D left-parenthesis upper K e y 2 comma upper E left-parenthesis upper K e y 2 comma upper M right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper K e y 1 comma upper E left-parenthesis upper K e y 2 comma upper M right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper D left-parenthesis upper K e y 2 comma upper E left-parenthesis upper K e y 2 comma upper M right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper M](images/c07_955.png), for any plaintext *M*.

***Problem 7.8***

Using Table  <math alttext="upper P upper C soft hyphen 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>&#173;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper P upper C soft hyphen 1](images/c07_956.png), we build the first two 28-bit blocks,  <math alttext="upper C 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 0](images/c07_957.png) and  <math alttext="upper D 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper D 0](images/c07_958.png), used to generate the round keys. Let  <math alttext="upper K Superscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mi>j</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper K Superscript j](images/c07_959.png) denote the bit  <math alttext="j comma j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow></math> ![j comma j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma 64](images/c07_960.png) of the key *K* (“64”, because the key scheduling function starts with a 64-bit key and then drops odd parity bits).

 <math alttext="upper C 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 0](images/c07_962.png) and  <math alttext="upper D 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper D 0](images/c07_963.png) are concatenated to form a 56-bit block. The inspection of Table  <math alttext="upper P upper C soft hyphen 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>&#173;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![upper P upper C soft hyphen 2](images/c07_964.png) shows that at any round *i*,  <math alttext="i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>16</mn></mrow></math> ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma 16](images/c07_965.png), the following bits are not used to generate the round key  <math alttext="upper K Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript i](images/c07_966.png): bits 9, 18, 22, and 25, located in  <math alttext="upper C 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 0](images/c07_967.png); and bits 35, 38, 43, and 54, located in  <math alttext="upper D 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper D 0](images/c07_968.png) (because all those eight numbers are not included in Table  <math alttext="upper P upper C soft hyphen 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>&#173;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![upper P upper C soft hyphen 2](images/c07_969.png)).

The first round key, *K*[1], is computed as follows:  <math alttext="upper C 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 0](images/c07_970.png) and  <math alttext="upper D 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper D 0](images/c07_971.png) are one-bit-left-rotated to yield  <math alttext="upper C 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 1](images/c07_972.png) and  <math alttext="upper D 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper D 1](images/c07_973.png), which are concatenated and used in the compression permutation. Therefore, the key bits that are not used to generate *K*[1] are: <math alttext="upper K Superscript 50" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>50</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper K Superscript 50](images/c07_974.png),  <math alttext="upper K Superscript 43" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>43</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper K Superscript 43](images/c07_975.png),  <math alttext="upper K Superscript 11" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper K Superscript 11](images/c07_976.png),  <math alttext="upper K Superscript 52" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>52</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper K Superscript 52](images/c07_977.png),  <math alttext="upper K Superscript 7" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mn>7</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![upper K Superscript 7](images/c07_978.png),  <math alttext="upper K Superscript 46" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>46</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper K Superscript 46](images/c07_979.png),  <math alttext="upper K Superscript 6" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![upper K Superscript 6](images/c07_980.png), and  <math alttext="upper K Superscript 12" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper K Superscript 12](images/c07_981.png).

***Problem 7.9***

1.  With a key bit-length of 56, there exist  <math alttext="2 Superscript 56 Baseline asterisk 2 Superscript 56" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>56</mn></mrow></msup><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>56</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 56 Baseline asterisk 2 Superscript 56](images/c07_982.png) pairs of keys  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper K Subscript i Baseline comma upper K Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper K Subscript i Baseline comma upper K Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c07_983.png);  <math alttext="i comma j element-of left-bracket 0 comma 2 Superscript 56 Baseline minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>56</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![i comma j element-of left-bracket 0 comma 2 Superscript 56 Baseline minus 1 right-bracket](images/c07_984.png). Each pair is used to double-encrypt. We can do  <math alttext="2 Superscript 112" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>112</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 112](images/c07_985.png) double encryptions, but the final ciphertext is an element in  <math alttext="StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript 64](images/c07_986.png). Thus, in average, each element of the ciphertext space can be yielded by  <math alttext="StartFraction 2 Superscript 112 Baseline Over 2 Superscript 64 Baseline EndFraction equals 2 Superscript 48" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>112</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>48</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![StartFraction 2 Superscript 112 Baseline Over 2 Superscript 64 Baseline EndFraction equals 2 Superscript 48](images/c07_987.png) pairs. The probability to pick the real key pair is  <math alttext="1 slash 2 Superscript 48" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>48</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![1 slash 2 Superscript 48](images/c07_988.png). Therefore, the probability of false alarm is  <math alttext="1 minus 1 slash 2 Superscript 48" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>48</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![1 minus 1 slash 2 Superscript 48](images/c07_989.png), which is a very high probability.
2.  With a space of key pairs of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 48" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>48</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 48](images/c07_990.png) pairs, a maximum of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 48" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>48</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 48](images/c07_991.png) ciphertexts may be yielded. Thus, in average, the number key pairs, selected in the previous step, that encrypt the same plaintext to the same ciphertext is  <math alttext="StartFraction 2 Superscript 48 Baseline Over 2 Superscript 64 Baseline EndFraction equals 2 Superscript negative 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>48</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![StartFraction 2 Superscript 48 Baseline Over 2 Superscript 64 Baseline EndFraction equals 2 Superscript negative 16](images/c07_992.png); this probability is also the probability of false alarm. In other words, with two known plaintext-ciphertext pairs, the probability to find the real key pair is  <math alttext="1 minus 2 Superscript negative 16 Baseline almost-equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8776;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![1 minus 2 Superscript negative 16 Baseline almost-equals 1](images/c07_993.png).
3.  With three known plaintext-ciphertext pairs, the probability that three ciphertexts are yielded by the same key pair is  <math alttext="StartFraction 2 Superscript negative 16 Baseline Over 2 Superscript 64 Baseline EndFraction equals 2 Superscript negative 80" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>80</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![StartFraction 2 Superscript negative 16 Baseline Over 2 Superscript 64 Baseline EndFraction equals 2 Superscript negative 80](images/c07_994.png). The latter is the probability of false alarm. In conclusion, three known plaintext-ciphertext pairs are enough to break double DES.

***Problem* *7.10***

In SubBytes and SubBytes transformations, byte substitution is performed byte-by-byte, independently from each other. Therefore, to prove that InvSubBytes is the inverse of SubBytes, we need to prove that  <math alttext="upper I n v upper S bar upper B o x left-parenthesis upper S bar upper B o x left-parenthesis b right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![upper I n v upper S bar upper B o x left-parenthesis upper S bar upper B o x left-parenthesis b right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals b](images/c07_995.png) for any byte *b*. We use the matrix forms of substitution; i.e. ([7.2](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-2002)) and ([7.4](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-2004)):

 <math alttext="b prime equals upper S bar upper B o x left-parenthesis b right-parenthesis right double arrow b prime equals upper A dot b circled-plus c" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8658;</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> ![b prime equals upper S bar upper B o x left-parenthesis b right-parenthesis right double arrow b prime equals upper A dot b circled-plus c](images/c07_996.png), where  <math alttext="c equals left-bracket 63 right-bracket Subscript 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>63</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![c equals left-bracket 63 right-bracket Subscript 16](images/c07_997.png)

 <math alttext="x equals upper I n v upper S bar upper B o x left-parenthesis b Superscript prime Baseline right-parenthesis right double arrow x equals upper B dot b prime circled-plus d" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8658;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> ![x equals upper I n v upper S bar upper B o x left-parenthesis b Superscript prime Baseline right-parenthesis right double arrow x equals upper B dot b prime circled-plus d](images/c07_998.png), where  <math alttext="d equals left-bracket 05 right-bracket Subscript 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>05</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![d equals left-bracket 05 right-bracket Subscript 16](images/c07_999.png)

Then, by substitution:  <math alttext="x equals upper B dot left-parenthesis upper A dot b circled-plus c right-parenthesis circled-plus d equals left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper B dot upper A right-parenthesis dot b right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper B dot c right-parenthesis circled-plus d" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> ![x equals upper B dot left-parenthesis upper A dot b circled-plus c right-parenthesis circled-plus d equals left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper B dot upper A right-parenthesis dot b right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper B dot c right-parenthesis circled-plus d](images/c07_1000.png)

It is easy to check that  <math alttext="upper B dot upper A" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> ![upper B dot upper A](images/c07_1001.png) is the identity matrix.

Then, by substitution:  <math alttext="x equals b circled-plus left-parenthesis upper B dot c right-parenthesis circled-plus d" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> ![x equals b circled-plus left-parenthesis upper B dot c right-parenthesis circled-plus d](images/c07_1002.png)

As shown below,  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper B dot c right-parenthesis circled-plus d equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper B dot c right-parenthesis circled-plus d equals 0](images/c07_1003.png). Therefore,  <math alttext="x equals b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![x equals b](images/c07_1004.png), which confirms that  <math alttext="upper I n v upper S bar upper B o x left-parenthesis upper I n v upper S bar upper B o x left-parenthesis b right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper I n v upper S bar upper B o x left-parenthesis upper I n v upper S bar upper B o x left-parenthesis b right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c07_1005.png) for any byte *b*.

Let  <math alttext="normal upper A" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></math> ![normal upper A](images/c07_1012.png) and *B* be the matrices defined by ([7.5](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0003)) and ([7.6](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0004)). Using the matrix form of the MixColumns transformation, for any 4-byte column *c*,  <math alttext="c prime equals upper M i x upper C o l u m n s left-parenthesis c right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![c prime equals upper M i x upper C o l u m n s left-parenthesis c right-parenthesis](images/c07_1013.png) can be written as  <math alttext="c prime equals normal upper A c" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> ![c prime equals normal upper A c](images/c07_1014.png) and  <math alttext="d equals upper I n v upper M i x upper C o l u m n s left-parenthesis c prime right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![d equals upper I n v upper M i x upper C o l u m n s left-parenthesis c prime right-parenthesis](images/c07_1015.png) can be written as  <math alttext="d equals upper B c prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>c</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![d equals upper B c prime](images/c07_1016.png).
    
    Hence,  <math alttext="d equals left-parenthesis upper B upper A right-parenthesis c" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> ![d equals left-parenthesis upper B upper A right-parenthesis c](images/c07_1017.png). [**7**](#c07.xhtml#rc07-note-0007)  <math alttext="upper N k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> ![upper N k](images/c07_1024.png) denotes the number of 32-bit words of the key. That is,  <math alttext="upper N k equals 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![upper N k equals 4](images/c07_1025.png), 6, and 8 to denote keys of 128, 192, and 256 bits, respectively.
8.  [**8**](#c07.xhtml#rc07-note-0008) In the matrix forms discussed in the chapter, the usual addition is replaced by the XOR operation.
9.  [**9**](#c07.xhtml#rc07-note-0009) SubBytes and its inverse are the only non-linear transformation in AES.
10.  [**10**](#c07.xhtml#rc07-note-0010) “Indexed by *a*” means “*a* is split into two 4-bit halves to yield the indexes of a cell in the S-Box.”
11.  [**11**](#c07.xhtml#rc07-note-0011) Odd parity works as follows: for a given set of bits, if the count of bits with a value of 1 is even, the parity bit value is set to 1 making the total count of s in the entire set (including the parity bit) an odd number. If the count of bits with a value of 1 is odd, the count is already odd; hence, the parity bit value is 0.

# 8   
Block Cipher Modes of Operation for Confidentiality

In the previous chapter, two standard block ciphers, namely TDEA and AES, have been presented. A block cipher takes a fixed-size plaintext block and returns a ciphertext block of the same size. However, in many applications, a plaintext (for example an image) is composed of thousands of blocks or even more. It is not desirable to use a block cipher in such a way that the encryption of the individual plaintext blocks leaks some features about the whole plaintext. In addition, in many applications, the recipient of a message may need to authenticate the message sender.

Data protection refers to confidentiality of data in transit (i.e. data exchanged via a communication network) and data on storage devices (such as CD-ROMs and USB flash drives). Like messages that may be intercepted, while being transmitted form sender to recipient, storage devices may be stolen or copied, which would result in disclosing confidential data. In addition, the advent of storage area networks has made storage devices, which are directly connected to servers, vulnerable to attacks. Therefore, protecting storage devices is (often) required. Such a protection is commonly achieved using block ciphers. Overall, encryption of data on storage devices aims at providing: data confidentiality, fast data storage and retrieval, and optimization of storage space.

It should be noticed that the protection of data in transit (i.e. messages) and that of data on storage devices differ, which results in important implications for encryption, even though the core encryption algorithms are the same:

*   *Latency*: message transmission is ephemeral, while data storage is often used for a long time. In networks, the recipient follows a protocol for key establishment and authentication before encrypting/decrypting messages. Attacks against messages need that the attacker is present when messages are transmitted, while attacks against storage devices do not.
*   *Key management*: in networks, the encryption key changes from a message to another. Even the public key used for signature is renewed periodically. If a key is lost, the participants run a protocol to agree on a new key. In case of storage, if the encryption key is lost, the entire encrypted data is lost.

With the exception of one mode (XTS-AES), the modes of operation presented in this chapter can be used directly to protect messages or, with some adaptions, to protect data on storage devices. This chapter addresses the standard approaches to use block ciphers to encrypt and decrypt plaintexts, while considering plaintexts of a size longer than that of a single block.

It is worth noticing that encryption alone provides confidentiality guarantees but not data integrity guarantees. Indeed, in the event an adversary alters a message or the storage device content, the decryption operation cannot detect any alteration. Therefore, message authentication codes or other techniques are required to preserve data integrity. Modes of operation that provide data authenticity are addressed in the next chapter

## 8.1 Introduction

### 8.1.1 Definitions

***Definition 8.1 Mode of operation*** ***of block cipher****: it describes how to repeatedly apply a single-block cipher to provide confidentiality or authenticity. Alternatively, modes of operation are ways of using block ciphers for encrypting and decrypting multiple-block data or for providing authentication service*.

***Definition 8.2 Deterministic*** ***encryption****: given a key, an encryption is said to be deterministic if plaintext blocks with the same content are mapped to a same ciphertext block*.

***Definition 8.3 Probabilistic encryption****: given a key, an encryption is said to be probabilistic if any two plaintext blocks are (very likely) mapped to distinct ciphertext blocks* \[[1](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0001)\].

### 8.1.2 Overview of Standard Modes of Operation

To provide confidentiality and authenticity guarantees based on block ciphers, the NIST approved a set of modes of operation for block ciphers, which are presented and discussed in this chapter and the next one. They include (as shown on [Figure 8.1](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0001)):

![Figure 8.1 Block cipher modes of operations. (\*) Poly1305-AES is not yet approved as a block cipher mode of operation. (\*\*) ChaCha20 is a stream cipher, not a block cipher.](images/c08f001.png)

[**Figure 8.1**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-fig-0001) Block cipher modes of operations. (\*) Poly1305-AES is not yet approved as a block cipher mode of operation. (\*\*) ChaCha20 is a stream cipher, not a block cipher.

*   Eight modes of operation for confidentiality guarantees: Electronic Codebook (ECB), Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) and its variants, Cipher Feedback (CFB), Output Feedback (OFB), Counter (CTR), XTS-AES, FF1, and FF3 \[[2](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0002)[5](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0005)\].
*   Five modes of operation for confidentiality and authenticity guarantees: CCM, GCM, KW, KWP, and TKW.
    
    Two modes of operation for authenticity guarantees: CMAC and GMAC.
    

### 8.1.3 Notations and Common Basic Functions

Below are the notations and the basic functions used in the sequel to describe the modes of operation of block ciphers.

*   #: comment in algorithm description.
*    <math alttext="0 normal x" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> ![0 normal x](images/c08_1.png): prefix of a bit string, represented with hexadecimal characters.
*   ⌈*x*⌉:the least integer that is not less than the real number *x*.
*    <math alttext="left floor x right floor" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8970;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8971;</mo></mrow></math> ![left floor x right floor](images/c08_2.png): the greatest integer that is not greater than the real number *x*.
*    <math alttext="upper X StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper Y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> ![upper X StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper Y](images/c08_3.png): concatenation of bit strings *X* and <math alttext="upper Y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> ![upper Y](images/c08_4.png).
*    <math alttext="upper X circled-plus upper Y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> ![upper X circled-plus upper Y](images/c08_5.png): bitwise exclusive-OR of bit strings *X* and <math alttext="upper Y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> ![upper Y](images/c08_6.png) of the same length.

### 8.1.4 Common Aspects of Modes for Confidentiality

#### 8.1.4.1 Plaintext Length and Padding

In ECB and CBC modes, the total number of bits in a plaintext must be a multiple of the block length *b*, while in CBC variants, OFB, CTR, FF1, FF3-1, and XTS-AES modes, the total number of bits in a plaintext is arbitrary. In CFB mode, the total number of bits in a plaintext must be a multiple of a parameter *s*, with  <math alttext="s less-than-or-equal-to b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![s less-than-or-equal-to b](images/c08_17.png).

ECB and CBC modes require a padding mechanism to fill the last block, in such a way that the padded plaintext is of a length multiple of that of a block. The other modes do not require any data padding mechanism. In OFB, CTR, and CFB modes, the last plaintext block, which may be not fully filled, is XORed with a part of the ciphertext resulting from the encryption of an initialization vector or a counter.

When padding is required, there exist different techniques to generate padding bits. For example, start the padding field with a special bit (e.g. ”1”) or a combination of bits (e.g. “1010”), and then add a fixed bit sequence (e.g. add zero-bits).

#### 8.1.4.2 Initialization Vector

The objective of the initialization vector (IV) is to make the encryption probabilistic, i.e. two identical plaintexts are (very likely) to be mapped to two distinct ciphertexts. An IV must be generated for each plaintext encryption and the same IV is required in the corresponding decryption operation. Therefore, either the IV is sent to the recipient before the first ciphertext or both sides agree to use a specific function that generates the same IV for each message to encrypt/decrypt.

CBC, CFB, and OFB modes require the IV and the data block to be of the same bit-length. CTR mode requires a counter, which is similar to IV, but with some difference discussed in the sequel.

IV does not need to be secret. However, depending on the mode of operation of interest, IV must be either a nonce (i.e. an IV value should never be reused with the same key to encrypt two distinct plaintexts) or unpredictable (i.e. it must not be possible, for adversary, to predict the IV that will be associated with any plaintext). Two methods are recommended to generate unpredictable IVs:

1.  First method: generate a nonce, then encrypt and send it to recipient before the first ciphertext. Since the encrypted value is an encrypted nonce, the adversary cannot derive which IV will be used for the upcoming message.
2.  Second method: use a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) with a hidden seed.[¹](#c08.xhtml#c08-note-0001)

The simplest way to generate a nonce is to use a counter or use addresses and current time.

## 8.2 ECB Mode of Operation

In the Electronic Codebook[²](#c08.xhtml#c08-note-0002) (ECB) mode, the encryption and decryption operations are applied independently to each block (see [Figure 8.2](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0002)). ECB mode is the simplest mode of operation.

![Figure 8.2 Electronic CodeBook (ECB) mode of operation.](images/c08f002.png)

[**Figure 8.2**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-fig-0002) Electronic CodeBook (ECB) mode of operation.

Formally, ECB mode is defined by the following equations:

 <math alttext="upper B Subscript i Baseline equals upper D e c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i Baseline equals upper D e c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08_20.png),  <math alttext="for-all i comma 1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8704;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>i</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![for-all i comma 1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to m](images/c08_21.png)

The first advantage of ECB is that operations on distinct blocks may be performed in parallel. The second is that ECB is error-propagation free. That is, if a ciphertext block is altered,[³](#c08.xhtml#c08-note-0003) the encryption of the other ciphertext blocks is not affected (i.e. plaintexts whose ciphertexts are not altered are correctly recovered by the recipient).

However, ECB mode is not recommended, because of its vulnerability to statistical analysis and replay attacks. In ECB mode, attackers can easily find repetitions in a ciphertext and then use such a knowledge to disclose partially or entirely a plaintext.

## 8.3 CBC Modes of Operation

### 8.3.1 Basic CBC Mode

In the Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode, the encryption and decryption processes combine successive blocks. As shown in [Figure 8.3](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0003), the first block is encrypted/decrypted using a selected initialization vector, then each block  <math alttext="upper B Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i](images/c08_22.png) ( <math alttext="i ampersand gt semicolon 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#38;gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![i ampersand gt semicolon 1](images/c08_23.png)) is encrypted/decrypted using the ciphertext of block  <math alttext="upper B Subscript i minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i minus 1](images/c08_24.png) as an Initialization Vector. With the exception of the first block, each ciphertext block depends on its predecessor.

![Figure 8.3 Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode of operation.](images/c08f003.png)

[**Figure 8.3**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-fig-0003) Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode of operation.

Unlike ECB, in CBC and in other modes of operation, blocks with the same content are encrypted with distinct ciphertexts. In CBC, the encryption cannot be performed in parallel, but decryption can be. Indeed, when all ciphertext blocks are received, the recipient can perform parallel computations on them to recover the plaintext blocks.

CBC is not fully error-propagation free, because the decryption of ciphertext block *i* makes use of two ciphertext blocks *i* and  <math alttext="i minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![i minus 1](images/c08_26.png). In case some bits of ciphertext block *i* are altered, plaintext blocks *i* and  <math alttext="i plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![i plus 1](images/c08_27.png) cannot be recovered, but plaintext blocks with index greater than  <math alttext="i plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![i plus 1](images/c08_28.png) can be recovered correctly. CBC mode requires an initialization vector known to sender and recipient. In addition, the IV value should be unpredictable.

### 8.3.2 CBC Variants (CS1, CS2, CS3)

CBC is the most used mode of operation to provide confidentiality. However, padding is considered as a factor, which affects the performance[⁴](#c08.xhtml#c08-note-0004) of CBC-based cryptosystems. To overcome padding drawback, three variants of CBC mode named CBC-CS1, CBC-CS2, and CBC-CS3 have been added to the basic CBC \[[4](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0004)\]. CS stands for ciphertext stealing.

CBC variants encrypt plaintexts of arbitrary bit-length. A plaintext *B* is a concatenation of *m* blocks:  <math alttext="upper B equals upper B 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper B 2 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue ellipsis StartAbsoluteValue The encryption and decryption of complete blocks  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper B 1 comma ellipsis comma upper B Subscript m minus 2 Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper B 1 comma ellipsis comma upper B Subscript m minus 2 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08_33.png) and  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper C 1 comma ellipsis comma upper C Subscript m minus 2 Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper C 1 comma ellipsis comma upper C Subscript m minus 2 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08_34.png) are the same as in the basic CBC. CS variants differ only in how they order and process the two last ciphertext blocks  <math alttext="upper C Subscript m minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript m minus 1](images/c08_35.png) and  <math alttext="upper C Subscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript m](images/c08_36.png). Ciphertext stealing has no impact on security and block ordering is only used for implementation convenience. If  <math alttext="l e n left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![l e n left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis](images/c08_37.png) is a multiple of the block length *b*, then all three variants are equivalent to the basic CBC.

#### 8.3.2.1 CBC-CS1 Mode

In CBC-CS1 mode, padding[⁵](#c08.xhtml#c08-note-0005) is used to encrypt. Then, the ciphertext sent to recipient and the unpadded plaintext both have the same bit-length. Encryption and decryption of CBC-CS1 are as follows (see [Figure 8.4](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0004)):

![Figure 8.4 CBC-CS1 mode.](images/c08f004.png)

Hence, the idea of *ciphertext stealing*.

#### 8.3.2.2 CBC-CS2 and CBC-CS3 Modes

CBC-CS2 and CBC-CS3 are minor modifications of CBC-CS1 mode to swap the ciphertext blocks  <math alttext="upper C Subscript m minus 1 Superscript asterisk Baseline and upper C Subscript m Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\*</mo></msubsup><mtext>&#160;and&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript m minus 1 Superscript asterisk Baseline and upper C Subscript m Baseline](images/c08_65.png). The most popular variant is CBC-CS3, because the ciphertext is aligned on block boundary, which makes hardware implementations simpler.

*   *Encryption in CBC-CS2 mode*:

*   – Apply CBC-CS1 to produce a ciphertext  <math alttext="upper C equals upper C 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C 2 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue ellipsis StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C Subscript m minus 1 Superscript asterisk Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C Subscript m Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\*</mo></msubsup><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C equals upper C 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C 2 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue ellipsis StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C Subscript m minus 1 Superscript asterisk Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C Subscript m Baseline](images/c08_66.png).
*   – Conditional swapping:
