*   – Undo swapping:  <math alttext="upper C prime equals upper C 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C 2 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue ellipsis StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C Subscript m minus 1 Superscript asterisk Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C Subscript m Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\*</mo></msubsup><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C prime equals upper C 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C 2 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue ellipsis StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C Subscript m minus 1 Superscript asterisk Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C Subscript m Baseline](images/c08_77.png).
*   – Apply CBC-CS1 to decrypt  <math alttext="upper C prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![upper C prime](images/c08_78.png).

## 8.4 OFB Mode of Operation

OFB, CTR, and CFB modes of operation function like stream ciphers. Therefore, all of them use the same function to encrypt and decrypt. They do not directly encrypt the plaintext using the key. Instead, they compute a bit string, which is XORed with the plaintext block. The first plaintext block is XORed with the encrypted IV. Then, the latter is encrypted to produce a bit string, which is XORed with the second plaintext block, etc. (see [Figure 8.5](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0005)). OFB mode requires that the IV is a nonce.

![Figure 8.5 Output Feedback (OFB) mode of operation.](images/c08f005.png)

[**Figure 8.5**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-fig-0005) Output Feedback (OFB) mode of operation.

OFB mode does not require padding. Indeed, if the last plaintext block is of bit-length *u* less than *b* (the block length), only the most significant *u* bits of the last ciphertext block are XORed with the plaintext block and the least significant  <math alttext="b minus u" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow></math> ![b minus u](images/c08_79.png) bits are discarded. The same applies to decrypt if the last ciphertext block is of a length less than *b*. Such an operation is identical to that of a stream cipher.

Formally, the OFB mode is defined with the following equations:

![](images/c08_80.png)

With the exception of the first plaintext block, the encryption of a plaintext block depends on the encryption of the previous plaintext block. The same applies to decryption. Therefore, neither encryption nor decryption of blocks can be performed in parallel.

Like EBC, OFB mode is error-propagation free, because one ciphertext block is used to recover one plaintext block and ciphertext blocks are not recalculated at recipient. Only the plaintext block associated with the altered ciphertext block cannot be recovered.

## 8.5 CTR Mode of Operation

CTR mode is similar to OFB mode with the exception that a counter is used instead of an initialization vector (see [Figure 8.6](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0006)). In CTR, it is required that each plaintext block is encrypted with a distinct counter.

![Figure 8.6 Counter (CTR) mode of operation.](images/c08f006.png)

[**Figure 8.6**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-fig-0006) Counter (CTR) mode of operation.

One advantage of CTR over OFB is that encryption and decryption of distinct blocks can be performed in parallel. Formally, the OFB mode is defined by the following equations, where  <math alttext="upper C n t 1 comma upper C n t 2 comma ellipsis comma upper C n t Subscript m Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C n t 1 comma upper C n t 2 comma ellipsis comma upper C n t Subscript m Baseline](images/c08_98.png) denote the values of the counter:

![](images/c08_99.png)

Counter values can be generated by any function that returns a distinct value for each call. In addition, it is required that all counter values must be distinct for all messages encrypted with the same key. To fulfill the uniqueness of counter values used with a specific key, there exist several methods, including:

*   Sequential assignment of counter values, which is defined as follows: 
    *   –  <math alttext="upper C n t 1 Superscript 1 Baseline equals r a n d o m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi><msubsup><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C n t 1 Superscript 1 Baseline equals r a n d o m](images/c08_111.png)
    *   –  <math alttext="upper C n t Subscript i Superscript j Baseline equals upper C n t Subscript i minus 1 Superscript j Baseline plus 1 m o d 2 Superscript b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi><msubsup><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi><msubsup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>j</mi></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper C n t Subscript i Superscript j Baseline equals upper C n t Subscript i minus 1 Superscript j Baseline plus 1 m o d 2 Superscript b](images/c08_112.png), for  <math alttext="i equals 2 comma ellipsis comma m Subscript j Baseline comma j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper L" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> ![i equals 2 comma ellipsis comma m Subscript j Baseline comma j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper L](images/c08_113.png)
    *   –  <math alttext="upper C n t 1 Superscript j Baseline equals upper C n t Subscript m Sub Subscript j minus 1 Superscript j minus 1 Baseline plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi><msubsup><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>j</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi><msubsup><mi>t</mi><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper C n t 1 Superscript j Baseline equals upper C n t Subscript m Sub Subscript j minus 1 Superscript j minus 1 Baseline plus 1](images/c08_114.png) for  <math alttext="j equals 2 comma ellipsis comma upper L" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> ![j equals 2 comma ellipsis comma upper L](images/c08_115.png)
        
        where  <math alttext="upper C n t 1 Superscript 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi><msubsup><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C n t 1 Superscript 1](images/c08_116.png) denotes the first randomly selected counter value to use with a new key,  <math alttext="upper C n t 1 Superscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi><msubsup><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>j</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C n t 1 Superscript j](images/c08_117.png) the first counter value to use for message *j*,  <math alttext="upper C n t Subscript i Superscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi><msubsup><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C n t Subscript i Superscript j](images/c08_118.png), the counter value to use for block *i* of message *j*,  <math alttext="m Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![m Subscript j](images/c08_119.png) the number of blocks of message *j*, and *L* the number of messages, respectively.
        
*   Hybrid sequential assignment of counter values, which is defined as follows:
    
    *   – Divide the counter bits into two parts of *r* and  <math alttext="b minus r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> ![b minus r](images/c08_120.png) bits, where  <math alttext="r less-than b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![r less-than b](images/c08_121.png).
    *   – Assign to each message *j*, a nonce  <math alttext="n c Superscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>c</mi><mi>j</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![n c Superscript j](images/c08_122.png) in the interval  <math alttext="left-bracket 0 comma 2 Superscript r Baseline minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>r</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 0 comma 2 Superscript r Baseline minus 1 right-bracket](images/c08_123.png).
    *   – Assign to each block *i* of message *j* a counter block  <math alttext="upper C n t Subscript i Superscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi><msubsup><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C n t Subscript i Superscript j](images/c08_124.png) as follows:
        
         <math alttext="v 1 Superscript j Baseline equals r a n d o m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>j</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![v 1 Superscript j Baseline equals r a n d o m](images/c08_125.png) in  <math alttext="left-bracket 0 comma 2 Superscript b minus r Baseline minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 0 comma 2 Superscript b minus r Baseline minus 1 right-bracket](images/c08_126.png), <math alttext="j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper L" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper L](images/c08_127.png)
        
         <math alttext="v Subscript i Superscript j Baseline equals v Subscript i minus 1 Superscript j Baseline plus 1 m o d 2 Superscript b minus r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>j</mi></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![v Subscript i Superscript j Baseline equals v Subscript i minus 1 Superscript j Baseline plus 1 m o d 2 Superscript b minus r](images/c08_128.png), for  <math alttext="i equals 2 comma ellipsis comma m Subscript j Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![i equals 2 comma ellipsis comma m Subscript j Baseline](images/c08_129.png),  <math alttext="j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper L" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper L](images/c08_130.png)
        
         <math alttext="upper C n t Subscript i Superscript j Baseline equals n c Superscript j Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue v Subscript i Superscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi><msubsup><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>c</mi><mi>j</mi></msup><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C n t Subscript i Superscript j Baseline equals n c Superscript j Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue v Subscript i Superscript j](images/c08_131.png), for  <math alttext="i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma m Subscript j Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma m Subscript j Baseline](images/c08_132.png),  <math alttext="j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma](images/c08_133.png)
        

**Note**. When CTR mode is used, a maximum of  <math alttext="2 Superscript b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript b](images/c08_134.png) blocks can be encrypted with the same key.

## 8.6 CFB Mode of Operation

Like OFB, Cipher Feedback (CFB) mode operates as a stream cipher and makes use of an initialization vector and the same algorithm for encryption and decryption. In CFB mode, a feedback between successive plaintext blocks is used as in CBC mode, but in a different way (see [Figure 8.7](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0007)). CFB mode uses an initialization vector and a parameter *s*, which is an integer less than (or equal to) the block length *b*. The IV used in CFB must be unpredictable. Often, the name of CFB mode starts with the value of parameter *s*, such that  <math alttext="1 less-than-or-equal-to s less-than-or-equal-to b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![1 less-than-or-equal-to s less-than-or-equal-to b](images/c08_135.png). For example, CFB-8 and CFB-64 denote CFB with  <math alttext="s equals 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ![s equals 8](images/c08_136.png) and  <math alttext="s equals 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow></math> ![s equals 64](images/c08_137.png), respectively. CFB mode is said to be full-CFB if  <math alttext="s equals b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![s equals b](images/c08_138.png) (i.e. a block contains one and only one segment).

![Figure 8.7 Cipher Feedback (CFB) mode of operation.](images/c08f007.png)

[**Figure 8.7**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-fig-0007) Cipher Feedback (CFB) mode of operation.

CFB operates on plaintext/ciphertext segments of length  <math alttext="s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> ![s](images/c08_139.png) and not on blocks of length *b*. To distinguish segments from blocks, segments are upper-indexed with “#”. CFB does not directly encrypt (with operation  <math alttext="upper E n c Subscript upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper E n c Subscript upper K](images/c08_140.png)) the plaintext. Instead, it uses a bitstring (which results from either the encryption of IV or a previous ciphertext) and XORes it with the plaintext to get a ciphertext. Formally, CFB mode is defined by the following equations, where  <math alttext="m bar s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> ![m bar s](images/c08_141.png) denotes the number of segments of the plaintext,  <math alttext="upper L upper S upper B Subscript d Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper L upper S upper B Subscript d Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c08_142.png) and  <math alttext="upper M upper S upper B Subscript d Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper M upper S upper B Subscript d Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c08_143.png) denote the *d* least and most significant bits of integer *x*, respectively:

![](images/c08_144.png)

With the exception of the first block, in CFB mode, the encryption of a block depends on the previous one. Therefore, distinct blocks cannot be encrypted in parallel. However, once all the ciphertext blocks are received, the recipient can compute the input blocks ( <math alttext="upper I 2 comma upper I 3 comma ellipsis comma upper I Subscript m bar s Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>I</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper I 2 comma upper I 3 comma ellipsis comma upper I Subscript m bar s Baseline](images/c08_158.png)) and then perform in parallel the decryption of ciphertext blocks.

Like CBC, CFB mode is not fully error-propagation free. In case a ciphertext block *i* is altered, plaintext blocks *i* and  <math alttext="i plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![i plus 1](images/c08_159.png) cannot be recovered, but plaintext blocks with index greater than  <math alttext="i plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![i plus 1](images/c08_160.png) can be recovered correctly. It should be noticed that CFB mode is the slowest mode because it processes a small portion of the data to encrypt/decrypt at each step. The number of operations depends on segment size *s*.

## 8.7 Format-Preserving Encryption Modes of Operation

### 8.7.1 Common Aspects to FPE Modes

FF1 and FF3-1 modes[⁶](#c08.xhtml#c08-note-0006) of operation are called *Format-Preserving Encryption* (FPE) modes \[[3](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0003)\]. Both aim at preserving the format and the length of data in the ciphertext. For example, if the plaintext format is composed of credit card number (16 digits), CB holder name (20 characters), and expiry date (5 characters), the ciphertext must have the same format with three parts each corresponding to a CB field with the same length (see [Figure 8.8](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0008)).

![Figure 8.8 FPE encryption vs other modes of encryption (e.g. AES or TDEA).](images/c08f008.png)

[**Figure 8.8**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-fig-0008) FPE encryption vs other modes of encryption (e.g. AES or TDEA).

FPE modes are useful for applications that require data in specific format without need to change data models before encrypting or decrypting. Imagine that a semi-encrypted file contains the data of thousands of bank customers (where only names are in clear) and an application needs to check the expiry date of client John Taylor. Since the encryption of distinct fields are chained, it is required to decrypt a large portion of the file to retrieve the expiry date of interest, in most modes of operations. That may take a long time to decrypt. With FPE modes, applications can easily locate ciphertext portions of interest and decrypt only the required fields of data.

Currently, FF1 and FF3-1 modes are approved to be used only with AES block cipher with block length of 128 bits and key lengths of 128, 192, or 256 bits.

***Data representation***. FPE modes are designed to be adapted for any type of data. The number of symbols (also called characters) of an alphabet is called the base; it is denoted *radix*. The set of symbols[⁷](#c08.xhtml#c08-note-0007) of a base *radix* is  <math alttext="StartSet 0 comma 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma r a d i x minus 1 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 0 comma 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma r a d i x minus 1 EndSet](images/c08_161.png). A numeral is a nonnegative integer less than the base and a numeral string is a finite ordered sequence of numerals of the given base.

**Example 8.1**

*   – If  <math alttext="r a d i x equals 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>x</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ![r a d i x equals 8](images/c08_162.png), then the set of characters is  <math alttext="StartSet 0 comma 1 comma 2 comma 3 comma 4 comma 5 comma 6 comma 7 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 0 comma 1 comma 2 comma 3 comma 4 comma 5 comma 6 comma 7 EndSet](images/c08_163.png) in decimal representation and  <math alttext="StartSet 000 comma 001 comma 010 comma 011 comma 100 comma 101 comma 110 comma 111 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>000</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>001</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>010</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>011</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>100</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>101</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>110</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>111</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 000 comma 001 comma 010 comma 011 comma 100 comma 101 comma 110 comma 111 EndSet](images/c08_164.png) in binary representation.
*   – If  <math alttext="r a d i x equals 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow></math> ![r a d i x equals 16](images/c08_165.png), then the set of characters is  <math alttext="StartSet 0 comma 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma 14 comma 15 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>15</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 0 comma 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma 14 comma 15 EndSet](images/c08_166.png) in decimal representation and  <math alttext="StartSet 0 comma 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma upper E comma upper F EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>E</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>F</mi></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 0 comma 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma upper E comma upper F EndSet](images/c08_167.png) in hexadecimal representation.
*   – With  <math alttext="r a d i x equals 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow></math> ![r a d i x equals 16](images/c08_168.png),  <math alttext="upper X equals 12 13 5 7 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>13</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>5</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>7</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X equals 12 13 5 7 2](images/c08_169.png) is a string of five numerals (i.e. 12, 13, 5, 7, and 2) in decimal representation.
*   – With  <math alttext="r a d i x equals 2 Superscript 10" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![r a d i x equals 2 Superscript 10](images/c08_170.png),  <math alttext="upper X equals 125 978 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>125</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>978</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X equals 125 978 2](images/c08_171.png) is a string of three numerals (i.e. 125, 978, and 2) in decimal representation.

For simplicity, in the sequel, we focus only on numeral data represented with decimal characters. Texts and special characters should be converted into decimal symbols before applying FPE modes. For example, lower-case Latin letters may be represented with numbers 1 to 26, upper-case letters with numbers 27 to 52, etc. Another representation would be the well-known ASCII code.

The input data of FF1 and FF3-1 modes are numeral strings. If the base is greater than 10, then numerals of a string are separated by space character. FF1 and FF3-1 use different conventions for interpreting numeral strings as numbers. For FF1, numbers are represented by strings of numerals with *decreasing* order of significance (i.e. in big-endian); for FF3-1, numbers are represented by strings of numerals in the reverse order, i.e. with *increasing* order of significance (i.e. in little-endian). For example, “0125” is a string of decimal digits that represents the number “one hundred twenty-five” for FF1 and the number “five thousand two hundred ten” for FF3-1.

***Tweak***. To encrypt data, FPE modes make use of a secret key and a *tweak*. The latter does not need to be secret and intends the same as an initialization vector in other modes. In CBC, OFB, and CFB modes, the IV is used to encrypt and decrypt the first block. In FPE modes, the tweak[⁸](#c08.xhtml#c08-note-0008) is used inside a Feistel structure jointly with a key and can be regarded as a changeable part of a cipher key. Block ciphers that make use of tweaks are referred to as *tweakable block ciphers* \[[6](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0006)\]. One application of tweakable block ciphers is disk encryption, where each disc portion has an index, which is used as a tweak.

Encryption and decryption of FPE modes are based on Feistel structure presented in Section 7.1.2, with some adaptations. Specifically, instead of XOR operations in basic Feistel structure, in FPE modes, the operations are addition and subtraction modulo a power of the chosen base and the round function  <math alttext="upper F Subscript upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript upper K](images/c08_172.png) takes a key, the bit-length of the plaintext, the tweak, and the round number.

As shown in [Figure 8.9](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0009), the encryption and decryption are transformations in three steps: 1) the input is split into two parts *A* (left) and *B* (right) of lengths denoted  <math alttext="u" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math> ![u](images/c08_173.png) and *v*, respectively; 2) a keyed function is applied to one part of the input; and 3) the two parts are swapped and used as input of the next round.

![Figure 8.9 Feistel structure for building FF1 and FF3-1 modes.](images/c08f009.png)

[**Figure 8.9**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-fig-0009) Feistel structure for building FF1 and FF3-1 modes.

If the length of the plaintext is even, then  <math alttext="u equals l e n left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>u</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![u equals l e n left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis slash 2](images/c08_174.png). Otherwise, one half has one symbol more than the other.  <math alttext="u equals left-parenthesis l e n left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis minus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![u equals left-parenthesis l e n left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis minus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2](images/c08_175.png) and  <math alttext="v equals left-parenthesis l e n left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis plus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>v</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>(</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![v equals left-parenthesis l e n left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis plus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2](images/c08_176.png). The bit-lengths *u* and *v* are taken into account when swapping a half with the other.

The number of rounds, denoted *r*, is of 10 for FF1 and of 8 for FF3-1. Inputs of round *i* ( <math alttext="i equals 0 comma ellipsis comma r minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![i equals 0 comma ellipsis comma r minus 1](images/c08_177.png)) are denoted  <math alttext="upper A Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper A Subscript i](images/c08_178.png) and  <math alttext="upper B Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i](images/c08_179.png).

### 8.7.2 Encryption and Decryption in FF1 and FF3-1 Modes

*Common notations and basic functions*

*    <math alttext="r a d i x element-of left-bracket 2 period period 2 Superscript 16 Baseline right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>x</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>..</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r a d i x element-of left-bracket 2 period period 2 Superscript 16 Baseline right-bracket](images/c08_180.png): range of supported bases
*    <math alttext="upper X comma upper Y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> ![upper X comma upper Y](images/c08_181.png): numeral[⁹](#c08.xhtml#c08-note-0009) or bit strings. For example, 1101100010 is a bit string, while  <math alttext="15 154 13 19" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>15</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>154</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>13</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>19</mn></mrow></math> ![15 154 13 19](images/c08_182.png) is a numeral string in base 256 represented in base 10.
*    <math alttext="left-bracket m i n upper L e n Baseline period period m a x upper L e n right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mn>..</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left-bracket m i n upper L e n Baseline period period m a x upper L e n right-bracket](images/c08_183.png): range of supported plaintext length, such that  <math alttext="2 m i n upper L e n m a x upper L e n less-than 2 Superscript 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 m i n upper L e n m a x upper L e n less-than 2 Superscript 32](images/c08_184.png) and  <math alttext="r a d i x Superscript m i n upper L e n Baseline greater-than-or-equal-to 1 000 000" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>&#8805;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>000</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>000</mn></mrow></math> ![r a d i x Superscript m i n upper L e n Baseline greater-than-or-equal-to 1 000 000](images/c08_185.png).
*    <math alttext="m a x upper T upper L e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![m a x upper T upper L e n](images/c08_186.png): maximum supported tweak byte-length.
*    <math alttext="left-bracket x right-bracket Superscript c" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mi>c</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![left-bracket x right-bracket Superscript c](images/c08_187.png): representation of integer *x* as a string of *c* bytes. For example,  <math alttext="left-bracket 23 right-bracket Superscript 1 Baseline equals 00010111" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>23</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>00010111</mn></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 23 right-bracket Superscript 1 Baseline equals 00010111](images/c08_188.png).
*    <math alttext="l e n left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![l e n left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis](images/c08_189.png): number of bits/numerals of bit/numeral string *X*. For example, if  <math alttext="r a d i x equals 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![r a d i x equals 2](images/c08_190.png), then  <math alttext="l e n left-parenthesis 1101 right-parenthesis equals 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1101</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![l e n left-parenthesis 1101 right-parenthesis equals 4](images/c08_191.png); if  <math alttext="r a d i x equals 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow></math> ![r a d i x equals 16](images/c08_192.png), then  <math alttext="l e n left-parenthesis 11 13 7 2 right-parenthesis equals 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>11</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>13</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![l e n left-parenthesis 11 13 7 2 right-parenthesis equals 4](images/c08_193.png).
*    <math alttext="upper N u m left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper N u m left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis](images/c08_194.png): integer that a bit string *X* represents in base 10 when bits are in decreasing order of significance. For example,  <math alttext="upper N u m left-parenthesis 0100001 right-parenthesis equals 33" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>0100001</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>33</mn></mrow></math> ![upper N u m left-parenthesis 0100001 right-parenthesis equals 33](images/c08_195.png).
*   *Num[radix](x)*:integer that a numeral string *x* represents in base *radix* when numerals are in decreasing order of significance. For example,  <math alttext="upper N u m 8 left-parenthesis 0100001 right-parenthesis equals 1 asterisk 8 Superscript 5 Baseline plus 1 equals 32769" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>u</mi><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>8</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>0100001</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>8</mn><mn>5</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>32769</mn></mrow></math> ![upper N u m 8 left-parenthesis 0100001 right-parenthesis equals 1 asterisk 8 Superscript 5 Baseline plus 1 equals 32769](images/c08_196.png).
*   *(x)*: given a positive integer *x* less than  <math alttext="r a d i x Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![r a d i x Superscript m](images/c08_197.png), this function returns a string of numerals in base  <math alttext="r a d i x" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> ![r a d i x](images/c08_198.png). For example,  <math alttext="s t r 16 Superscript 4 Baseline left-parenthesis 1957 right-parenthesis equals 0 7 10 5" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow><mn>4</mn></msubsup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1957</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>10</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> ![s t r 16 Superscript 4 Baseline left-parenthesis 1957 right-parenthesis equals 0 7 10 5](images/c08_199.png), because  <math alttext="0 asterisk 16 cubed plus 7 asterisk 16 squared plus 10 asterisk 16 Superscript 1 Baseline plus 5 asterisk 16 Superscript 0 Baseline equals 1957" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>\*</mo><msup><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>\*</mo><msup><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>\*</mo><msup><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>\*</mo><msup><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow><mn>0</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1957</mn></mrow></math> ![0 asterisk 16 cubed plus 7 asterisk 16 squared plus 10 asterisk 16 Superscript 1 Baseline plus 5 asterisk 16 Superscript 0 Baseline equals 1957](images/c08_200.png).

### 8.7.3 FF1 Mode

FF1 mode makes use of a pseudorandom function  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis](images/c08_202.png), which takes an input multiple of 128 bits and produces a 128-bit block. It is similar to CBC mode, with the exception that CBC produces a ciphertext block for each plaintext block, while function *PRF* produces a single block for a set of blocks. Function  <math alttext="upper P upper R upper F left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>F</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper P upper R upper F left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis](images/c08_203.png) is defined as follows:

[Figure 8.10](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0010) depicts the computations performed in each round of FF1 mode. The encryption algorithm of FF1 mode is as follows:

![Figure 8.10 Round computations in FF1 mode. upper F upper B Subscript d Baseline left-parenthesis upper S right-parenthesis denotes the first d bytes of string S.](images/c08f010.png)

[**Figure 8.10**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-fig-0010) Round computations in FF1 mode.  <math alttext="upper F upper B Subscript d Baseline left-parenthesis upper S right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>F</mi><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper F upper B Subscript d Baseline left-parenthesis upper S right-parenthesis](images/c08_244.png) denotes the first *d* bytes of string *S*.

A right-parenthesis" display="inline" substring *A* has *u* or *v* symbols in base  <math alttext="r a d i x" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> ![r a d i x](images/c08_250.png); and  <math alttext="m equals u" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow></math> ![m equals u](images/c08_251.png) or  <math alttext="m equals v" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></math> ![m equals v](images/c08_252.png). To scramble *A* with *y*, without bias we need a value of *y* in which all bits are random. Therefore, for *y* to be a fully randomized number, it must be at least equal to  <math alttext="r a d i x Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![r a d i x Superscript m](images/c08_253.png). With a bit-string *S* of length *d*, with  <math alttext="d equals 4 left ceiling b slash 4 right ceiling plus 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mrow><mo>&#8968;</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mo>&#8969;</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![d equals 4 left ceiling b slash 4 right ceiling plus 4](images/c08_254.png), we can represent integers greater than  <math alttext="r a d i x Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![r a d i x Superscript m](images/c08_255.png). Indeed,  <math alttext="r a d i x Superscript m Baseline equals 2 Superscript l o g 2 left-parenthesis r a d i x right-parenthesis asterisk m Baseline 2 Superscript 8 asterisk b Baseline less-than 2 Superscript 8 asterisk d" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>\*</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msup><mo>&#60;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>\*</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![r a d i x Superscript m Baseline equals 2 Superscript l o g 2 left-parenthesis r a d i x right-parenthesis asterisk m Baseline 2 Superscript 8 asterisk b Baseline less-than 2 Superscript 8 asterisk d](images/c08_256.png).

Algorithm of FF1 decryption is similar to that of encryption. Both algorithms differ only in lines 4.1, 4.3, and 4.4. That is, the encryption algorithm makes use of half *B* to produce the bit string *Q* and it uses the half *A* and modular addition to yield *C*, which is copied in half *B*, while the decryption algorithm makes use of half *A* to produce the bit string *Q* and it uses the half *B* and modular subtraction to produce *C*, which is copied in half *A*.

**Example 8.2**

Below is a simple example to show how FF1 performs the encryption and decryption. To perform FF1 operations by hand, we need two simplifications: the number of rounds is limited to two and the  <math alttext="upper P upper R upper F upper P upper R upper F" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>F</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P upper R upper F upper P upper R upper F](images/c08_280.png) function returns six 0-bytes followed by the two rightmost bytes of input <math alttext="upper X" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> ![upper X](images/c08_282.png) followed by eight 0-bytes.

Let the plaintext be  <math alttext="upper X equals 28750457" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>28750457</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X equals 28750457](images/c08_283.png), a string of eight characters in base 10. Let the tweak be  <math alttext="upper T equals left-bracket 67 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>67</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper T equals left-bracket 67 right-bracket](images/c08_284.png), a string of one byte. Therefore,  <math alttext="t equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![t equals 1](images/c08_285.png).

*Encryption*

*   – Split the input:  <math alttext="u equals v equals eight-halves equals 4 semicolon upper A equals 2875 semicolon upper B equals 0457" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>8</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2875</mn><mo>;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0457</mn></mrow></math> ![u equals v equals eight-halves equals 4 semicolon upper A equals 2875 semicolon upper B equals 0457](images/c08_286.png)
*   –  <math alttext="b equals left ceiling left ceiling 4 asterisk l o g 2 left-parenthesis 10 right-parenthesis right ceiling slash 8 right ceiling equals 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>&#8968;</mo><mrow><mo>&#8968;</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>\*</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&#8969;</mo><mo>/</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo>&#8969;</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![b equals left ceiling left ceiling 4 asterisk l o g 2 left-parenthesis 10 right-parenthesis right ceiling slash 8 right ceiling equals 2](images/c08_287.png). Two bytes are required to represent in binary each of  <math alttext="2875 and 0457" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2875</mn><mtext>&#160;and&#160;</mtext><mn>0457</mn></mrow></math> ![2875 and 0457](images/c08_288.png) values.
*   –  <math alttext="d equals 4 left ceiling 2 slash 4 right ceiling plus 4 equals 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mrow><mo>&#8968;</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mo>&#8969;</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ![d equals 4 left ceiling 2 slash 4 right ceiling plus 4 equals 8](images/c08_289.png)

### 8.7.4 FF3-1 Mode

The main differences between FF1 and FF3-1 modes are the following:

*   FF3-1 is not flexible regarding the tweak length. In FF1, the tweak is an arbitrary string, which may be empty, while it must be of exactly 56 bits in FF3-1.
*   FF1 runs 10 rounds, while FF3-1 runs eight rounds.
*   If the length of the input string is odd, the length of the right half is one byte longer than the left half in FF1 mode and the inverse in FF3-1.
*   FF1 makes use of big-endian representation, while little-endian is used in FF3-1. Therefore, FF3-1 makes use of two functions to inverse strings before performing arithmetic operations:

*   –  <math alttext="upper R upper E upper V left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper R upper E upper V left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis](images/c08_333.png): given a character string *X*,  <math alttext="upper R upper E upper V left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper R upper E upper V left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis](images/c08_334.png) returns *X* in the reverse order. For example,  <math alttext="upper R upper E upper V left-parenthesis 1957 right-parenthesis equals 7591" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1957</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>7591</mn></mrow></math> ![upper R upper E upper V left-parenthesis 1957 right-parenthesis equals 7591](images/c08_335.png).
*   –  <math alttext="upper R upper E upper V upper B left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>V</mi><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper R upper E upper V upper B left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis](images/c08_336.png): given a byte string *B*,  <math alttext="upper R upper E upper V upper B left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>V</mi><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper R upper E upper V upper B left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis](images/c08_337.png) returns *B* in the reverse byte order. For example,  <math alttext="upper R upper E upper V upper B left-parenthesis left-bracket 1 right-bracket Superscript 1 Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue left-bracket 9 right-bracket Superscript 1 Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue left-bracket 5 right-bracket Superscript 1 Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue left-bracket 7 right-bracket Superscript 1 Baseline Algorithm of FF3-1 decryption is similar to that of encryption. Both algorithms differ only in lines 3.2 and 3.5. That is, the encryption algorithm makes use of half *B* to produce the bit string *P* and it uses the half *A* and modular addition to produce *C*, which is copied in half *B*, while the decryption algorithm makes use of half *A* to produce the bit string *P* and it uses the half *B* and modular subtraction to produce *C*, which is copied in half *A*.

## 8.8 XTS-AES Mode of Operation

### 8.8.1 Overview of XTS-AES

The standard algorithm to protect data on storage devices is the XTS-AES mode of operation. The latter was designed to provide data confidentiality on storage devices \[[5](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0005)\]. It was not designed to secure data in transit over networks. The acronym XTS stands for XEX (Xor-Encrypt-Xor) Tweakable block cipher with ciphertext Stealing. XTS-AES mode also is referred to as IEEE standard 1619. It is supported by many operating systems and platforms.

XTS-AES is a format-preserving encryption mode of operation. Hence, the length and the format of plaintext and ciphertext are the same (i.e. no disk space waste). Therefore, applications do not need to change data format to encrypt or decrypt. In addition, XTS-AES encrypts individual data units resulting in independent ciphertexts. Therefore, applications are not required to decrypt all ciphertexts to retrieve a specific item of data. Rather, XTS-AES provides support to fast data random access.

XTS-AES operates with keys of bit-length of either 256 or 512. If the XTS-AES key consists of 256 bits, the encrypt/decryption procedures use 128-bit AES; if the XTS-AES key consists of 512 bits, the procedures use 256-bit AES, which differ in term of number of rounds (see Section 7.3.3).

***Definition 8.4 Key scope*:** *it defines the stream of data encrypted by a particular key. The key scope is represented by three integers: tweak value corresponding the first data unit, the bit-length of data unit, and the number of units to be encrypted/decrypted under the control of this key*.

***Definition 8.5 Data unit***:[^(10)](#c08.xhtml#c08-note-0010) *it is a fixed-length bit-string within a key scope. The data unit length should be at least 128 bits. Each data unit is divided into 128-bit blocks*.

The total number[^(11)](#c08.xhtml#c08-note-0011) of 128-bit blocks of the entire data shall not exceed  <math alttext="2 Superscript 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 64](images/c08_385.png) and the maximum number[^(12)](#c08.xhtml#c08-note-0012) of 128-bit blocks in a data unit shall not exceed  <math alttext="2 Superscript 20" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 20](images/c08_386.png). Usually the length of data unit equals the sector length of storage devices, e.g. 512 or 4k bytes.

***Definition 8.6 XTS-AES Tweak value****: it is a 128-bit value representing the logical position of the data being encrypted or decrypted. Each data unit is assigned a tweak value*.

Tweak values are assigned consecutively, starting from an arbitrary value. An easy way to assign tweak values is to start with a random value  <math alttext="upper T 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper T 1](images/c08_387.png) and then increment it for each subsequent data unit; i.e.  <math alttext="upper T Subscript i Baseline equals upper T Subscript i minus 1 Baseline plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper T Subscript i Baseline equals upper T Subscript i minus 1 Baseline plus 1](images/c08_388.png) for  <math alttext="i ampersand gt semicolon 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#38;gt;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![i ampersand gt semicolon 1](images/c08_389.png). [Figure 8.12](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0012) illustrates the main items of XTS-AES mode of operation.

![Figure 8.12 Basic items of XTS-AES cipher.](images/c08f012.png)

[**Figure 8.12**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-fig-0012) Basic items of XTS-AES cipher.

***Modular multiplication***: input and output of XTS-AES encryption and decryption operations are bit-string of a length of 128 bits. Such operations perform multiplication, denoted ⊕, over an extension field  <math alttext="upper F 2 Superscript 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>128</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper F 2 Superscript 128](images/c08_390.png) (as below) with a reduction polynomial  <math alttext="f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 128 Baseline plus x Superscript 7 Baseline plus x squared plus x plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>7</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 128 Baseline plus x Superscript 7 Baseline plus x squared plus x plus 1](images/c08_391.png) and a primitive element α, which corresponds to polynomial *x* (i.e.  <math alttext="0000 ellipsis 0010 Subscript 2 Baseline equals 0002 Subscript 10 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0000</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>&#8230;</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mrow><mn>0010</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mrow><mn>0002</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![0000 ellipsis 0010 Subscript 2 Baseline equals 0002 Subscript 10 Baseline](images/c08_392.png) ). For more on extension fields, see Section 3.2.3.

### 8.8.3 Some Strengths and Weaknesses of XTS-AES

XTS-AES looks like ECB mode, because the ciphertexts are independent in both modes and encryption and decryption may be parallelized. However, with ECB, identical plaintext blocks are encrypted with the same ciphertext block, which provides some substrate for cryptanalysis attacks. With XTS-AES, due to block sequence number and tweaks, identical plaintext blocks are encrypted with distinct ciphertext blocks.

XTS-AES is more performant than CBC, when decrypting ciphertexts. In CBC, to access a specific field (or portion) in data on storage device, the decryption of the entire data is often required. With XTS-AES, only the searched field (or portion) requires decryption. Since XTS-AES is a format-preserving encryption only, it cannot provide support for data integrity. Indeed, because there is no hash or MAC (message authentication code) in the produced ciphertext, any alteration (modification, deletion or insertion), in the ciphertext, is decrypted as some (random) plaintext. There exist three main categories of potential attacks against XTS-AES:

*   Randomizing a sector: an adversary with write access to the encrypted storage device can change a sector to an arbitrary value, which results in invalid data used by legitimate applications.
*   Selective replay attack: an adversary with write access to the encrypted storage device can set the value of a sector to a specific value observed in past in order to corrupt some write operations. For example, consider a malicious store employee who has write access to a stock status file and who knows the index of a block, say  <math alttext="upper C Subscript x Superscript c u r r e n t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript x Superscript c u r r e n t](images/c08_444.png), associated with the number of articles  <math alttext="normal upper A" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></math> ![normal upper A](images/c08_445.png), of interest to him/her, in stock and he/she also knows that different versions of the file are encrypted with the same tweak, and finally, he/she has access to an older version of the same file. Under such conditions, the employee can replace block  <math alttext="upper C Subscript x Superscript c u r r e n t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript x Superscript c u r r e n t](images/c08_446.png) by an older block  <math alttext="upper C Subscript x Superscript o l d" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript x Superscript o l d](images/c08_447.png). Since  <math alttext="upper C Subscript x Superscript c u r r e n t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript x Superscript c u r r e n t](images/c08_448.png) and  <math alttext="upper C Subscript x Superscript o l d" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript x Superscript o l d](images/c08_449.png) ciphertext blocks have been encrypted by the same parameters (tweak, key, and bock index), the decryption of the modified block yields the stock status of interest to the malicious employee.
*   Traffic analysis: if an adversary can observe the communication between the encrypting device and the storage device, he/she can infer when some sectors are modified over time and then use such a knowledge to design an attack.

## 8.9 Comparison of Design Features of Modes for Confidentiality

[Table 8.1](#c08.xhtml#c08-tbl-0001) aims at summarizing some fundamental design features to compare block cipher modes of operation. The features of interest are the following:

*   *Encryption determinism*: is the same plaintext block always mapped to the same ciphertext block under the same key?
*   *Padding* is the plaintext length required to be a multiple of block length?
*   *Initialization vector*: is IV required? If Yes, should the IV be a nonce or unpredictable?
*   *Parallelization*: can the encryption or decryption of blocks be performed in parallel?
*   *Ciphertext error-propagation*: does a bit error in a ciphertext block prevent[^(13)](#c08.xhtml#c08-note-0013) the recovery of the remaining plaintext blocks? “No” means only the plaintext block associated with the altered ciphertext block is unlikely to be recovered correctly; “Yes” means the plaintext block associated with the altered ciphertext block and the plaintext block that follows are unlikely to be recovered correctly.
*   *IV and counter error-propagation*: in case the IV or counter is sent[^(14)](#c08.xhtml#c08-note-0014) to recipient, does bit alteration in the IV or counter impact the decryption?
*   *Diffusion* property: does a modification of a bit in a plaintext block propagate in the whole ciphertext?
*   *Block cipher (BC) decryption use*:[^(15)](#c08.xhtml#c08-note-0015) does the mode of operation make use of the decryption operation of the underlying block cipher to decrypt?
*   *Stream cipher*[^(16)](#c08.xhtml#c08-note-0016) *construction*: can the mode of operation be used as a stream cipher?

![Table 8.1 Comparison of modes of operation for confidentiality guaranteeing.](images/c08_450.png)

[**Table 8.1**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-tbl-0001) Comparison of modes of operation for confidentiality guaranteeing.

## 8.10 Security of Modes of Operation for Confidentiality

When a block cipher is used for confidentiality protection, the security goal is to prevent an eavesdropper with limited computational power to learn any information about the plaintext (except for maybe its length). This eavesdropper can apply the following attacks: known-plaintext attacks, chosen-plaintext attacks, and chosen-ciphertext attacks that should be prevented by the underlying cipher.

### 8.10.1 Vulnerability to Block Repetitions and Replay

In general, ECB is not recommended, because of the following vulnerabilities:

*   A block with a same content is encrypted with the same ciphertext, if it repeats in the same message or in distinct messages. ECB mode is the only mode, which does not hide repetitions in the plaintext, which may give advantage to adversary.
*   If an adversary replays ciphertexts, the recipient has no means to detect replays. For example, if a user is uploading a file on a storage server while using ECB, multiple portions of the file may be erroneously duplicated on the server in the event of a replay attack.

With the exception of ECB, the other modes (CBC, OFB, CTR, CFB, FF1, FF3-1, and XTS) do not suffer replay and plaintext repetition vulnerabilities due to the use of IV (which may be a nonce or unpredictable), counter (which is unique for each block), or tweak (which is a nonce) assuming that they are used correctly (i.e. the IV/counter/tweak is a nonce or unpredictable and the maximum number of plaintexts encrypted with the same key is not greater than the recommended limit).

### 8.10.2 Vulnerability to Predictable IV or Tweak

Remember that the ultimate goal for encryption algorithms is to provide confidentiality guarantees. With such a property, it is practically impossible for any adversary to infer any knowledge from the observed ciphertexts; i.e. all ciphertexts should appear as noise. For example, consider a scenario in which Alice sends a response Yes or No to answer a question from Bob. If the adversary can infer which response is sent without decrypting the response ciphertext, the secrecy is broken.

In some modes of operation, the IV (in CBC and CFB) or the tweak (in FF1, FF3-1, and XTS-AES) is required to be unpredictable because prediction of the IV/tweak may result in a break of the confidentiality property. Therefore, IV or tweak-based modes of operation are vulnerable to chosen-plaintext attacks as shown by the following attack scenario (see [Figure 8.15](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0015)) in which the adversary attacks a CBC oracle.

![Figure 8.15 Chosen-plaintext attack against CBC under predictable IV.](images/c08f015.png)

[**Figure 8.15**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-fig-0015) Chosen-plaintext attack against CBC under predictable IV.

Another example of vulnerability to predictable IV is considered in Problem 8.8.

### 8.10.3 Vulnerability to IV/Tweak that Is Not a Nonce

In OFB and CTR modes, if the IV is not a nonce, two messages may be encrypted with the same IV value, which may compromise confidentiality of encrypted plaintexts. Both modes are stream ciphers and the encryption of plaintext  <math alttext="upper B Subscript j" display="inline" Let this sequence be  <math alttext="upper O 1 comma upper O 2 comma ellipsis comma upper O Subscript upper L Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>O</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper O 1 comma upper O 2 comma ellipsis comma upper O Subscript upper L Baseline](images/c08_492.png).

The adversary can XOR the ciphertexts to find the following:

                 <math alttext="upper C Subscript i Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper C Subscript i Superscript 2 Baseline equals upper B Subscript i Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper O Subscript i Baseline circled-plus upper B Subscript i Superscript 2 Baseline circled-plus upper O Subscript i Baseline equals upper B Subscript i Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper B Subscript i Superscript 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper C Subscript i Superscript 2 Baseline equals upper B Subscript i Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper O Subscript i Baseline circled-plus upper B Subscript i Superscript 2 Baseline circled-plus upper O Subscript i Baseline equals upper B Subscript i Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper B Subscript i Superscript 2](images/c08_496.png), for  <math alttext="i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper L" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper L](images/c08_497.png).

Such a relationship may be used to disclose a plaintext if another is known, to find repetitions (at the same positions) in two plaintexts, or to infer other features of interest to the adversary.

Before encrypting plaintext blocks, FF1 and FF3-1 modes append to the plaintext other strings (tweak, plaintext length, round number, and constants), then a Feistel structure is applied, and bits are scrambled in each round. In the output of FF1 and FF3-1, applying  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper C Subscript i Superscript 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper C Subscript i Superscript 2](images/c08_498.png) does not help to derive  <math alttext="upper B Subscript i Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper B Subscript i Superscript 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper B Subscript i Superscript 2](images/c08_499.png).

In XTS-AES mode, the encryption of two plaintexts  <math alttext="upper M 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 1](images/c08_500.png) and  <math alttext="upper M 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 2](images/c08_501.png), with the same tweak, results in the following decryption, for  <math alttext="i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma min left-parenthesis l e n left-parenthesis upper M 1 right-parenthesis comma l e n left-parenthesis upper M 2 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>min</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma min left-parenthesis l e n left-parenthesis upper M 1 right-parenthesis comma l e n left-parenthesis upper M 2 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c08_502.png):
