Therefore, FF1, FF3-1, and XTS-AES modes are not vulnerable to attacks based on reuse of tweak value.

### 8.10.4 Vulnerability to Birthday Attacks

If the block bit-length of the underlying cipher (i.e. AES, TDEA, etc.) is *n*, then by birthday paradox, the adversary needs to intercept  <math alttext="2 Superscript StartFraction n Over 2 EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mfrac><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript StartFraction n Over 2 EndFraction](images/c08_507.png) ciphertext blocks to have (at a high probability) a collision. Such an interception is easy if the adversary has access to encrypted files. A collision may reveal some information useful to the adversary. For example, it may reveal repetition in the same plaintext or in distinct plaintexts. Notice that the exploitation of collisions in FF1 and FF3-1 modes is unlikely to help discovering any useful information about plaintexts due to the scrambling performed by modes.

In general, to avoid birthday attacks, it is recommended to encrypt less than  <math alttext="alpha asterisk 2 Superscript StartFraction n Over 2 EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mfrac><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![alpha asterisk 2 Superscript StartFraction n Over 2 EndFraction](images/c08_508.png) blocks by the same key, with α a small constant in magnitude of  <math alttext="10 Superscript negative 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![10 Superscript negative 3](images/c08_509.png) or even less.

### 8.10.5 Vulnerability to Bit-Flipping Attacks

The aim of bit-flipping attack is to change a ciphertext block at some positions in order to change the plaintext recovered by recipient at the same positions. In CBC mode, ciphertext block  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i](images/c08_510.png) is XORed with the decryption of block ciphertext  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i plus 1](images/c08_511.png) to recover plaintext  <math alttext="upper B Subscript i plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i plus 1](images/c08_512.png). OFB, CTR, and CFB modes are stream ciphers where the ciphertext block  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i](images/c08_513.png) is XORed with keystream block  <math alttext="upper O Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper O Subscript i](images/c08_514.png) to recover plaintext block  <math alttext="upper B Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i](images/c08_515.png). Therefore, changing a bit at position *j* in ciphertext block  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i](images/c08_516.png) results in a change of the bit at position *j* of plaintext block  <math alttext="upper B Subscript i plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i plus 1](images/c08_517.png), in case of CBC mode, or  <math alttext="upper B Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i](images/c08_518.png) in case of OFB, CTR, and CFB modes.

If the message format is known to adversary, this can cause devastating effects, especially if the important information is located at positions known to the adversary. For example, imagine an adversary who knows that the amount of money to transfer, denoted *v*, is less than 100 and it is encrypted alone in block  <math alttext="upper C 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 4](images/c08_519.png) using the AES-CTR. He/she can change  <math alttext="upper C 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 4](images/c08_520.png) so that the amount to transfer is increased by 1024 as follows:

The original plaintext block is recovered by the recipient as  <math alttext="upper B 4 equals upper C 4 circled-plus upper E n c Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis upper C n t 4 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>(</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper B 4 equals upper C 4 circled-plus upper E n c Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis upper C n t 4 right-parenthesis](images/c08_521.png).

Let  <math alttext="upper S equals 0 Superscript 117 Baseline double-vertical-bar 10000000000" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mn>117</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mrow><mo>&#8214;</mo><mrow><mn>10000000000</mn></mrow></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S equals 0 Superscript 117 Baseline double-vertical-bar 10000000000](images/c08_522.png) be the bit-string representing the integer 1024 on 128 bits.

The adversary changes  <math alttext="upper C 4 t o upper C prime Subscript 4 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>t</mi><mi>o</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><msup><mi>C</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 4 t o upper C prime Subscript 4 Baseline](images/c08_523.png) <math alttext="equals upper C 4 circled-plus upper S" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> ![equals upper C 4 circled-plus upper S](images/c08_524.png). Then, the recipient decrypts as follows:

upper B 4 circled-plus upper S period](images/c08_526.png)

Since the original amount *v* is less than 100, the bit-string  <math alttext="upper B prime Subscript 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><msup><mi>B</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B prime Subscript 4](images/c08_527.png) represents the integer  <math alttext="1024 plus v" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1024</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>v</mi></mrow></math> ![1024 plus v](images/c08_528.png).

ECB mode is not vulnerable to bit-flipping, because each ciphertext block is decrypted only with the decryption operation of the underlying block cipher, which is a pseudorandom permutation.

Given the scrambling performed in FF1 and FF3-1 rounds when encrypting or decrypting, the adversary has no control on which bits will flip in the recovered plaintext, if some bits are flipped in the ciphertext.

In the XTS-AES mode, block decryption is performed with AES-encryption followed by AES-decryption. Therefore, the adversary has no control on which bits will flip in the recovered plaintext, if some bits are flipped in the ciphertext.

### 8.11.1 List of Exercises and Problems

***Exercise 8.1***

Consider a block cipher *E*, defined by the pseudorandom permutation given by the table below. Each letter is a block. Then, consider ECB and CBC as modes of operation of the block cipher *E*. As the XOR operation (i.e. ⊕) is not defined on the set  <math alttext="left-brace upper A comma upper B comma ellipsis comma upper Z right-brace" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>&#8230;</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>Z</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left-brace upper A comma upper B comma ellipsis comma upper Z right-brace](images/c08_529.png), the following adaptations are used:

To encrypt a block  <math alttext="upper B Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i](images/c08_530.png), the ciphertext  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i minus 1](images/c08_531.png) (or the IV) is added  <math alttext="m o d u l o Baseline 26" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><mn>26</mn></mrow></math> ![m o d u l o Baseline 26](images/c08_532.png) to  <math alttext="upper B Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i](images/c08_533.png) (e.g.  <math alttext="upper B circled-plus upper C equals upper D" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> ![upper B circled-plus upper C equals upper D](images/c08_534.png),  <math alttext="upper K circled-plus upper I equals upper S" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>I</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K circled-plus upper I equals upper S](images/c08_535.png)).

1.  Decrypt the ciphertext OXBBJ, which was encrypted using ECB mode.
2.  Decrypt the ciphertext DOLYV, which was encrypted using CBC mode with IV=*K*.

![](images/c08_536.png)

***Exercise 8.2***

Discuss which of ECB, CBC, CTR, and FF1 modes could provide integrity guarantees.

***Exercise 8.3***

How many distinct counter blocks are required to encrypt a hard disk of 16 T bytes with AES-CTR?

***Exercise 8.4***

Let *s* denote the segment length parameter of CFB mode and *b* the block bit-length. Show that CFB mode is the same as OFB mode if  <math alttext="s equals b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![s equals b](images/c08_537.png).

***Exercise 8.5***

Show that ECB leaks information regarding plaintext-block repetition while CBC does not.

***Problem 8.1***

Consider a list of *N* names each of a length of 16 bytes. The name list is encrypted with four modes (ECB, CBC, OFB, and CTR) of operation of AES.

1.  On transit, a ciphertext block of index  <math alttext="i left-parenthesis 1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>i</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![i left-parenthesis 1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to upper N](images/c08_538.png)) is altered because of transmission errors changing some 0-bits to 1-bits and vice versa. What is the number of names that cannot be correctly recovered by the recipient for each mode of operation?
2.  On transit, a ciphertext block of index  <math alttext="i left-parenthesis 1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![i left-parenthesis 1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to upper N](images/c08_539.png)) is lost. What are the names that are missing in the recipient list and those that are not correctly recovered in each mode of operation?

***Problem 8.2***

Consider a plaintext, composed of *N* segments, encrypted with CFB mode.

1.  On transit, a ciphertext segment of index  <math alttext="i left-parenthesis 1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to upper N right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![i left-parenthesis 1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to upper N right-parenthesis](images/c08_540.png) is altered because of transmission errors changing some 0-bits to 1-bits and vice versa. What is the number of segments that cannot be correctly recovered by the recipient?
2.  On transit, a ciphertext segment of index  <math alttext="i left-parenthesis 1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![i left-parenthesis 1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to upper N](images/c08_541.png)) is lost. What are the plaintext segments that are missing in the recipient plaintext and those not correctly recovered? Without loss of generality, assume that the block length is a multiple of the segment length.

***Problem 8.3***

Show how CTR and OFB modes can be attacked if two plaintexts  <math alttext="upper M 1 and upper M 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;and&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 1 and upper M 2](images/c08_542.png) are encrypted with the same initial counter or IV, respectively.

***Problem 8.4***

Assume that a plaintext–ciphertext pair is known. Show that keeping the IV secret in OFB mode does not make an exhaustive key search more complex, if the number of plaintext blocks is at least 2.

***Problem 8.5***

Consider the following scenario: in a company, a group of engineers collaborate on a project including several tasks. Some engineers are task managers and they declare, on a weekly basis, the number of hours of participation of each engineer (including themselves) in the tasks assigned to them. Participation declarations are first securely sent to a server 1 by each task manager, and then server 1 encrypts, with ECB mode, a message for each engineer participation and sends the ciphertext to a server 2, which centralizes the engineers’ participation in the project. The key shared by servers is not known to engineers. The format of the messages between both servers is composed of three fields each represented on one block: Manager identifier, participating engineer identifier, and the number of hours of participation. One malicious task manager who participates in multiple tasks and who knows the format of ECB-encrypted messages and who can intercept and modify ciphertexts between servers, wants to increase his/her amount of participation hours. He/she observed that the task managers used to send participation declarations on Friday before 6:00 p.m., but the server 1 accepts declarations up to Friday midnight. How may the malicious engineer design the attack?

***Problem 8.6***

Prove the correctness of CBC-CS1 mode of operation.

***Problem 8.7***

Prove the correctness of XTS-AES block encryption.

***Problem 8.8***

Consider the following context: Alice and Bob agree to use CBC mode to protect their communications. Eve has the capacity to ask Alice to encrypt messages for her (i.e. Eve is able to mount chosen-plaintext attacks) and she is able to predict the IV that will be used by Alice to encrypt her next message. Bob asks Alice to do something and she has to reply just by “Yes” or “No” in one block. Alice encrypts her response  <math alttext="upper P Subscript upper A l i c e Baseline equals quotation-mark upper Y e s quotation-mark" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>"</mo><mi>Y</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>s</mi><mo>"</mo></mrow></math> ![upper P Subscript upper A l i c e Baseline equals quotation-mark upper Y e s quotation-mark](images/c08_543.png), using IV  <math alttext="upper I upper V 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper I upper V 0](images/c08_544.png), and sends a ciphertext  <math alttext="upper C Subscript t o upper B o b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript t o upper B o b](images/c08_545.png) to Bob. Eve intercepts  <math alttext="upper I upper V 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper I upper V 0](images/c08_546.png) and  <math alttext="upper C Subscript t upper B o b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript t upper B o b](images/c08_547.png) and she wants to know Alice’s response without any knowledge about the key. Show how Eve can discover Alice’s response.

### 8.11.2 Solutions to Exercises and Problems

***Exercise 8.1***

Let  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i](images/c08_548.png) be the ciphertext of plaintext block  <math alttext="upper B Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i](images/c08_549.png). Let *D* denote the decryption operation of block cipher *E*.

1.  Decryption of ciphertext OXBBJ using ECB mode
    
    The decryption using ECB mode is defined by:  <math alttext="upper B Subscript i Baseline equals upper D left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i Baseline equals upper D left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08_550.png).
    
    The plaintext associated with ciphertext OXBBJ is HELLO, because:
    
     <math alttext="upper D left-parenthesis upper O right-parenthesis equals upper H" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></math> ![upper D left-parenthesis upper O right-parenthesis equals upper H](images/c08_551.png),  <math alttext="upper D left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals upper E" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> ![upper D left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals upper E](images/c08_552.png),  <math alttext="upper D left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis equals upper L" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> ![upper D left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis equals upper L](images/c08_553.png),  <math alttext="upper D left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis equals upper L" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> ![upper D left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis equals upper L](images/c08_554.png),  <math alttext="upper D left-parenthesis upper J right-parenthesis equals upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>J</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> ![upper D left-parenthesis upper J right-parenthesis equals upper O](images/c08_555.png)
    
2.  Decryption of the ciphertext DOLYV, which was encrypted using CBC mode with IV=*K*
    
    The decryption using CBC mode is defined by:  <math alttext="upper B Subscript i Baseline equals upper D left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus upper C Subscript i minus 1 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i Baseline equals upper D left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus upper C Subscript i minus 1 Baseline](images/c08_556.png), with  <math alttext="upper C 0 equals upper I upper V" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C 0 equals upper I upper V](images/c08_557.png)
    
    Since ⊕ is not defined on the letters, the decryption is transformed as follows:
    
     <math alttext="upper B Subscript i Baseline equals upper L e t t e r left-parenthesis upper I n d left-parenthesis upper D left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis minus upper I n d left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i minus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis m o d Baseline 26 right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>I</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>26</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i Baseline equals upper L e t t e r left-parenthesis upper I n d left-parenthesis upper D left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis minus upper I n d left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i minus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis m o d Baseline 26 right-parenthesis](images/c08_558.png)
    
    Hence,

***Exercise 8.2***

ECB, CBC, CTR, and FF1 are algorithms aiming to provide confidentiality guarantees. As they do not make use of tags, no integrity guarantees could be provided. Any altered ciphertext is decrypted to a plaintext, which is very likely to be distinct from the original plaintext and the recipient has no means to check the integrity.

***Exercise 8.3***

We consider a disk of  <math alttext="16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>16</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![16](images/c08_564.png) T bytes encrypted with AES-CTR.  <math alttext="16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>16</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![16](images/c08_565.png) tera bytes are split into *m* 128-bit blocks, where  <math alttext="m equals StartFraction 2 Superscript 4 Baseline asterisk 2 Superscript 40 Baseline asterisk 2 cubed Over 2 Superscript 7 Baseline EndFraction equals 2 Superscript 40" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>40</mn></mrow></msup><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>7</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>40</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![m equals StartFraction 2 Superscript 4 Baseline asterisk 2 Superscript 40 Baseline asterisk 2 cubed Over 2 Superscript 7 Baseline EndFraction equals 2 Superscript 40](images/c08_566.png). The formulas above are the same as those of OFB encryption. The same apply to decryption. Therefore, CFB mode is identical to OFB mode if the segment length is the same as that of the block.

We can see that the same ciphertext block  <math alttext="upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis](images/c08_593.png) repeats three times in *C*. Therefore, ECB leaks information regarding plaintext repetition, while CBC does not.

***Problem 8.1***

1.  Error-propagation resistance
    
    *   – In ECB, OFB, and CTR modes, the decryption of a block is independent of that of other blocks. Therefore, if ciphertext block *i* is errored, only the name with index *i* is unlikely to be correctly recovered.
    *   – In CBC mode, the decryption of ciphertext block *k* depends on ciphertext blocks *k* and  <math alttext="k minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![k minus 1](images/c08_594.png). Therefore, if ciphertext block *i* is errored, there exist two cases: a) if  <math alttext="i equals upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![i equals upper N](images/c08_595.png), only the last name in the list is unlikely to be correctly recovered and b) if  <math alttext="i less-than upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![i less-than upper N](images/c08_596.png), the names with indices *i* and  <math alttext="i plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![i plus 1](images/c08_597.png) are is unlikely to be correctly recovered.
2.  Loss-propagation resistance
    
    *   – In ECB mode, the decryption of a block is independent of that of other blocks. Therefore, if ciphertext block  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i](images/c08_598.png) is lost, only the name with index *i* is missing in the recipient list.
    *   – In CTR mode, the encryption counter block  <math alttext="upper C t n Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>t</mi><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C t n Subscript j](images/c08_599.png) is used as a keystream string to encrypt the plaintext block  <math alttext="upper B Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript j](images/c08_600.png), for  <math alttext="j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper N](images/c08_601.png). In OFB and CFB modes, the encrypted block  <math alttext="upper I Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper I Subscript j](images/c08_602.png) is used as a keystream string to encrypt the plaintext block  <math alttext="upper B Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript j](images/c08_603.png), for  <math alttext="j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper N](images/c08_604.png). In all these three modes, if the ciphertext block  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i](images/c08_605.png) is lost, then the recipient makes use of block  <math alttext="upper C n t Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C n t Subscript i](images/c08_606.png) (for CTR) or  <math alttext="upper I Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper I Subscript i](images/c08_607.png) (for OFB and CFB) to decrypt ciphertext  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i plus 1](images/c08_608.png) for  <math alttext="i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper N minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper N minus 1](images/c08_609.png). Therefore, the name with index *i* is missing in the recipient list and all the subsequent names are very likely to be incorrectly recovered, if CTR, OFB, and CFB modes are used. Those three modes operate like stream ciphers where any loss in the keystream string results in a loss of synchronization.
    *   – In CBC mode, the encryption ciphertext block  <math alttext="upper C Subscript j minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript j minus 1](images/c08_610.png) is used to encrypt plaintext block  <math alttext="upper C Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript j](images/c08_611.png),  <math alttext="j equals 2 comma ellipsis comma upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![j equals 2 comma ellipsis comma upper N](images/c08_612.png). If ciphertext block  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i](images/c08_613.png) is lost, then the decryption of the subsequent ciphertext blocks is performed as:  <math alttext="upper B Subscript i Baseline equals upper D e c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i plus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus upper C Subscript i minus 1 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i Baseline equals upper D e c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i plus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus upper C Subscript i minus 1 Baseline](images/c08_614.png),  <math alttext="upper B Subscript i plus 1 Baseline equals upper D e c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i plus 2 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus upper C Subscript i plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> right-parenthesis circled-plus upper C Subscript upper N minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript upper N minus 1 Baseline equals upper D e c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C Subscript upper N Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus upper C Subscript upper N minus 1](images/c08_616.png). Because of a jump in ciphertexts,  <math alttext="upper B Subscript i Baseline equals upper D e c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i plus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus upper C Subscript i minus 1 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i Baseline equals upper D e c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i plus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus upper C Subscript i minus 1 Baseline](images/c08_617.png) is very likely to be an incorrect name. Therefore, the name with index *i* is missing in the recipient list and the names of index greater than *i* are unlikely to be correctly recovered, if CBC mode is used.

***Problem 8.2***

Recall that CFB mode processes segments of a bit-length *s*, which is not greater than that of a block denoted *b*. CFB mode operates like a stream cipher in which the leftmost *s* bits of keystream block  <math alttext="upper I Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper I Subscript j](images/c08_618.png) are XORed with plaintext segment  <math alttext="upper B Subscript j Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript j Superscript number-sign](images/c08_619.png) to produce the ciphertext segment  <math alttext="upper B Subscript j Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript j Superscript number-sign](images/c08_620.png). Assuming that *b* is a multiple of *s*, let  <math alttext="q equals b slash s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> ![q equals b slash s](images/c08_621.png). Keystream blocks are computed as follows:

 <math alttext="upper I 1 equals upper I upper V equals upper I upper V 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper I upper V 2 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue ellipsis StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper I upper V Subscript q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper I 1 equals upper I upper V equals upper I upper V 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper I upper V 2 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue ellipsis StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper I upper V Subscript q](images/c08_622.png), where  <math alttext="upper I upper V Subscript i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma q Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper I upper V Subscript i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma q Baseline](images/c08_623.png) are *s*\-bits segments of IV.

1.  Error-propagation resistance

In CFB mode, if the ciphertext segment  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign](images/c08_628.png) is altered, then the plaintext segment  <math alttext="upper B Subscript i Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i Superscript number-sign](images/c08_629.png) is unlikely to be correctly recovered. The keystream block  <math alttext="upper I Subscript i plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper I Subscript i plus 1](images/c08_630.png), used to decrypt the subsequent ciphertext segment  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i plus 1 Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i plus 1 Superscript number-sign](images/c08_631.png) is computed as:  <math alttext="upper I Subscript i plus 1 Baseline equals upper L upper S upper B Subscript b minus s Baseline left-parenthesis upper I Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper I Subscript i plus 1 Baseline equals upper L upper S upper B Subscript b minus s Baseline left-parenthesis upper I Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign](images/c08_632.png), which differs from the one used at encryption step. The segment decryptions are unlikely to produce the original plaintext segments as long as the errored ciphertext segment  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign](images/c08_633.png) is present inside keystream blocks subsequent to  <math alttext="upper I Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper I Subscript i](images/c08_634.png). Now, let us see how the segment  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign](images/c08_635.png) is left-shifted in the subsequent keystream blocks  <math alttext="upper I Subscript i plus 2 Baseline comma upper I Subscript i plus 3 comma Baseline ellipsis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo></mrow></msub><mo>&#8230;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper I Subscript i plus 2 Baseline comma upper I Subscript i plus 3 comma Baseline ellipsis](images/c08_636.png) until it disappears. Instead of string concatenation, integer representation of block is used for convenience.

In block  <math alttext="upper I Subscript i plus 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper I Subscript i plus 3](images/c08_642.png), the errored segment  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign](images/c08_643.png) is left-shifted with  <math alttext="2 s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> ![2 s](images/c08_644.png) positions. The shifting process continues until the segment  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign](images/c08_645.png) exits on the left. Let  <math alttext="q equals b slash s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> ![q equals b slash s](images/c08_646.png). After left-shifting with  <math alttext="q asterisk s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> ![q asterisk s](images/c08_647.png) positions, the ciphertext segment  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign](images/c08_648.png) is eliminated and the synchronization resumes. Therefore, all the ciphertext segments, from  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign](images/c08_649.png) to  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i plus q Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i plus q Superscript number-sign](images/c08_650.png), are unlikely to be correctly decrypted.

*   2\. Loss-propagation resistance

After decrypting ciphertext segment  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i minus 1 Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i minus 1 Superscript number-sign](images/c08_651.png), the recipient computes keystream block  <math alttext="upper I Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper I Subscript i](images/c08_652.png) as  <math alttext="upper I Subscript i Baseline equals upper L upper S upper B Subscript b minus s Baseline left-parenthesis upper I Subscript i minus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis asterisk 2 Superscript s Baseline plus upper C Subscript i minus 1 Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>s</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper I Subscript i Baseline equals upper L upper S upper B Subscript b minus s Baseline left-parenthesis upper I Subscript i minus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis asterisk 2 Superscript s Baseline plus upper C Subscript i minus 1 Superscript number-sign](images/c08_653.png). If the ciphertext segment  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign](images/c08_654.png) is lost, then the plaintext segment  <math alttext="upper B Subscript i Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i Superscript number-sign](images/c08_655.png) is missing in the plaintext recovered by recipient. Then, the recipient receives ciphertext segment  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i plus 1 Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i plus 1 Superscript number-sign](images/c08_656.png), while it was waiting for segment  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign](images/c08_657.png). Thus, it is unlikely to recover plaintext segment  <math alttext="upper B Subscript i plus 1 Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i plus 1 Superscript number-sign](images/c08_658.png). Then, keystream block  <math alttext="upper I Subscript i plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper I Subscript i plus 1](images/c08_659.png) is computed as:  <math alttext="upper I Subscript i plus 1 Baseline equals upper L upper S upper B Subscript b minus s Baseline left-parenthesis upper L upper S upper B Subscript b minus s Baseline left-parenthesis upper I Subscript i minus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis asterisk 2 Superscript s Baseline plus upper C Subscript i minus 1 Superscript number-sign Baseline right-parenthesis asterisk 2 Superscript s <math alttext="upper B Subscript i plus 1 Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i plus 1 Superscript After  <math alttext="q equals left ceiling b slash s right ceiling minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mrow><mo>&#8968;</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo>&#8969;</mo></mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8722;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![q equals left ceiling b slash s right ceiling minus 1](images/c08_664.png) incorrect decryptions, there is no ciphertext segment gap in subsequent keystream blocks and thus the resynchronization resumes on recipient side, ciphertext segment  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i Superscript number-sign](images/c08_665.png) is not treated (because it has not been received), ciphertext segments  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i plus 1 Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i plus 1 Superscript number-sign](images/c08_666.png) to  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i plus q Superscript number-sign" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>#</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i plus q Superscript number-sign](images/c08_667.png) are unlikely to decrypt to correct plaintext segments, and the decryption is one-segment behind the encryption, i.e.  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i plus q plus j ![upper C Subscript i plus q plus j Superscript number-sign](images/c08_668.png) is decrypted as it if was  <math alttext="upper B Subscript i plus q plus zero width space zero width space j minus 1 ***Problem 8.3***

Let  <math alttext="upper M Subscript j Superscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript j Superscript i](images/c08_670.png),  <math alttext="j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n Superscript 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>&#8230;</mn><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n Superscript 1](images/c08_671.png), and  <math alttext="upper M Subscript j Superscript 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript j Superscript 2](images/c08_672.png),  <math alttext="i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n squared comma" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>&#8230;</mn><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n squared comma](images/c08_673.png) denote blocks of plaintexts  <math alttext="upper M 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 1](images/c08_674.png) and  <math alttext="upper M 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 2](images/c08_675.png), respectively. Let  <math alttext="c Subscript j Superscript 1 Baseline comma" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mi>j</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> ![c Subscript j Superscript 1 Baseline comma](images/c08_676.png)  <math alttext="j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n Superscript 1 Baseline comma" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>&#8230;</mn><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n Superscript 1 Baseline comma](images/c08_677.png) and  <math alttext="c Subscript j Superscript 2 Baseline comma" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mi>j</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> ![c Subscript j Superscript 2 Baseline comma](images/c08_678.png) <math alttext="j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>&#8230;</mn><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n squared](images/c08_679.png), denote blocks of ciphertexts  <math alttext="c 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![c 1](images/c08_680.png) and  <math alttext="c 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![c 2](images/c08_681.png), respectively; Without loss of generality, assume that both plaintexts are of a length multiple of that of a block.

Recall that given a plaintext of *m* blocks, the ciphertext blocks are computed as follows:

If CTR is used,  <math alttext="upper C Subscript j Baseline equals upper B Subscript j Baseline circled-plus upper O Subscript j Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript j Baseline equals upper B Subscript j Baseline circled-plus upper O Subscript j Baseline](images/c08_686.png),  <math alttext="upper O Subscript j Baseline equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C n t Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper O Subscript j Baseline equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C n t Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08_687.png),  <math alttext="for-all j comma 1 less-than-or-equal-to j less-than-or-equal-to m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8704;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>j</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![for-all j comma 1 less-than-or-equal-to j less-than-or-equal-to m](images/c08_688.png).

Therefore, the ciphertext blocks in both modes are computed as  <math alttext="upper C Subscript j Baseline equals upper B Subscript j Baseline circled-plus upper O Subscript j Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript j Baseline equals upper B Subscript j Baseline circled-plus upper O Subscript j Baseline](images/c08_694.png),  <math alttext="for-all j comma 1 less-than-or-equal-to j less-than-or-equal-to m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8704;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>j</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![for-all j comma 1 less-than-or-equal-to j less-than-or-equal-to m](images/c08_695.png). Both modes differ only in how keystream blocks  <math alttext="upper O Subscript j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper O Subscript j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma m](images/c08_696.png) are computed.

If two plaintexts  <math alttext="upper M 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 1](images/c08_697.png) and  <math alttext="upper M 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 2](images/c08_698.png) are encrypted with the same counter or the same IV, then:

      <math alttext="upper C Subscript j Superscript 1 Baseline equals upper B Subscript j Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper O Subscript j Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>j</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript j Superscript 1 Baseline equals upper B Subscript j Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper O Subscript j Baseline](images/c08_699.png),   <math alttext="j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n Superscript 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n Superscript 1](images/c08_700.png)

      <math alttext="upper C Subscript j Superscript 2 Baseline equals upper B Subscript j Superscript 2 Baseline circled-plus upper O Subscript j Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>j</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript j Superscript 2 Baseline equals upper B Subscript j Superscript 2 Baseline circled-plus upper O Subscript j Baseline](images/c08_701.png),   <math alttext="j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n squared](images/c08_702.png).

Let  <math alttext="m equals min left-parenthesis n Superscript 1 Baseline comma n squared right-parenthesis period" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>min</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> ![m equals min left-parenthesis n Superscript 1 Baseline comma n squared right-parenthesis period](images/c08_703.png) XORing both plaintexts yields:

 <math alttext="upper C Subscript j Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper C Subscript j Superscript 2 Baseline equals left-parenthesis upper B Subscript j Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper O Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper B Subscript j Superscript 2 Baseline circled-plus upper O Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis equals upper B Subscript j Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper B Subscript j Superscript 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>j</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>j</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>j</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>j</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript j Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper C Subscript j Superscript 2 Baseline equals left-parenthesis upper B Subscript j Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper O Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper B Subscript j Superscript 2 Baseline circled-plus upper O Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis equals upper B Subscript j Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper B Subscript j Superscript 2](images/c08_704.png),  <math alttext="j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma m](images/c08_705.png)

Therefore, if CTR or OFB modes are used to encrypt two plaintexts with the same counter or the same IV, the adversary can derive the XOR of both plaintexts, which is particularly damaging, if plaintexts are messages in natural language.

***Problem 8.4***

In this problem, we consider a brute-force attack against OFB mode to disclose the key. The adversary is given a plaintext–ciphertext pair of at least two plaintext blocks.

By design of OFB,  <math alttext="upper C 1 equals upper B 1 circled-plus upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper I upper V right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C 1 equals upper B 1 circled-plus upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper I upper V right-parenthesis](images/c08_706.png),  <math alttext="upper C 2 equals upper B 2 circled-plus upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper I upper V right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript i equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis](images/c08_708.png) are plaintext blocks and  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis" display="inline" equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis](images/c08_709.png), the corresponding ciphertext blocks.

1.  Case 1: IV is known to the adversary

From the first ciphertext block and its ciphertext, the following is inferred:

 <math alttext="upper C 1 equals upper B 1 circled-plus upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper I upper V right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C 1 equals upper B 1 circled-plus upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper I upper V right-parenthesis](images/c08_710.png) <math alttext="upper C 1 circled-plus upper B 1 equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper I upper V right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C 1 circled-plus upper B 1 equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper I upper V right-parenthesis](images/c08_711.png)(a) 

Since the IV is known, the adversary has to find a key such that the encryption of the IV yields  <math alttext="upper C 1 circled-plus upper B 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 1 circled-plus upper B 1](images/c08_712.png), which is known. With a brute-force attack, a maximum of 2² keys may be tested, where *n* denotes the bit-length of the key.

*   b. Case 2: IV is unknown to the adversary

Using the second ciphertext block and its ciphertext, the following is inferred:

         <math alttext="upper C 2 equals upper B 2 circled-plus upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper I upper V right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C 2 equals upper B 2 circled-plus upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper I upper V right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c08_713.png)      <math alttext="upper C 2 circled-plus upper B 2 equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper I upper V right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C 2 circled-plus upper B 2 equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper I upper V right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c08_714.png)

Then, applying the block cipher decryption yields:

 <math alttext="upper D e c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C 2 circled-plus upper B 2 right-parenthesis equals upper D e c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper E n c left-parenthesis upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper I upper V right-parenthesis right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper I upper V right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper D e c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C 2 circled-plus upper B 2 right-parenthesis equals upper D e c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper E n c left-parenthesis upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper I upper V right-parenthesis right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper I upper V right-parenthesis](images/c08_715.png)(b) 

Substitution of (a) in (b) yields:

 <math alttext="upper D e c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C 2 circled-plus upper B 2 right-parenthesis equals upper C 1 circled-plus upper B 1" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper D e c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C 2 circled-plus upper B 2 right-parenthesis equals upper C 1 circled-plus upper B 1](images/c08_716.png)

Next, the adversary has to find a key such that the decryption of the  <math alttext="upper C 2 circled-plus upper B 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 2 circled-plus upper B 2](images/c08_717.png) yields  <math alttext="upper C 1 circled-plus upper B 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 1 circled-plus upper B 1](images/c08_718.png), which are known. With a brute-force attack, a maximum of 2² keys may be tested.

Consequently, making the IV secret does not result in a more complex brute-force attack to disclose the key in OFB mode.

***Problem 8.5***

The malicious task manager knows that the format of the ciphertext is composed of three blocks  <math alttext="upper C 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 1](images/c08_719.png), <math alttext="upper C 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 2](images/c08_720.png), and  <math alttext="upper C 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 3](images/c08_721.png), where  <math alttext="upper C 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 1](images/c08_722.png) is the encryption of the task manager ID,  <math alttext="upper C 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 2](images/c08_723.png) is the encryption of the participating engineer’s ID, and  <math alttext="upper C 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 3](images/c08_724.png) is the encryption of the number of hours. Since ECB mode is used, the encryption of any engineer’s ID produces the same ciphertext block in all the encrypted participation declarations. Let  <math alttext="upper C Subscript 2 bar m a l" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>\_</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript 2 bar m a l](images/c08_725.png) be the ciphertext of the malicious engineer’s ID. Such a ciphertext bock appear in all the encrypted messages related to the malicious engineer. With  <math alttext="upper C Subscript 2 bar m a l" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>\_</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript 2 bar m a l](images/c08_726.png) known, the malicious engineer has just to intercept ciphertexts, between servers, and replace the second ciphertext block of the intercepted ciphertexts by  <math alttext="upper C Subscript 2 bar m a l" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>\_</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript 2 bar m a l](images/c08_727.png) and the number of hours will count for him/her.

To discover the ciphertext associated with his/her ID, the malicious engineer knows that task managers used to send participation declarations on Friday before 6:00 p.m., but the server 1 accepts declarations up to Friday midnight. To exploit such a knowledge, he/she sends (for some weeks) his/her declarations late, say on Friday 11:00 p.m., and intercepts the ciphertexts between the servers. After some ciphertext interceptions, he/she can infer, at a high probability, the encryption of his/her ID, which is located in the first block of the ciphertexts. Then, he/she can change the second ciphertext blocks in some messages between servers.

***Problem 8.7***

We need to prove the correctness of XTS-AES at two levels: block and data unit encryption levels.

1.  Correctness of XTS-AES block encryption

In the encryption procedure, the ciphertext is produced as follows:

 <math alttext="upper C equals upper A upper E upper S bar upper E n c left-parenthesis upper K 1 comma upper P circled-plus upper A right-parenthesis circled-plus upper A" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C equals upper A upper E upper S bar upper E n c left-parenthesis upper K 1 comma upper P circled-plus upper A right-parenthesis circled-plus upper A](images/c08_743.png), where  <math alttext="upper A equals upper A upper E upper S bar upper E n c left-parenthesis upper K 2 comma upper T right-parenthesis alpha Superscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>j</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper A equals upper A upper E upper S bar upper E n c left-parenthesis upper K 2 comma upper T right-parenthesis alpha Superscript j](images/c08_744.png)

Assuming no alteration of the ciphertext block and given that *T* and *j* are the same on both sides,  <math alttext="upper A equals upper A upper E upper S bar upper E n c left-parenthesis upper K 2 comma upper T right-parenthesis circled-plus alpha Superscript j Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>j</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper A equals upper A upper E upper S bar upper E n c left-parenthesis upper K 2 comma upper T right-parenthesis circled-plus alpha Superscript j Baseline](images/c08_745.png) is the same on both sides.
