Therefore, the XTS-AES block encryption is correct.

*   2\. Correctness of XTS-AES data unit encryption 
    1.  – If the length of data unit *P* is a multiple of 128 bits, then *P* is split into *m* 128-bit blocks ( <math alttext="upper P 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P 0](images/c08_750.png), …,  <math alttext="upper P Subscript m minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P Subscript m minus 1](images/c08_751.png)) and an empty block  <math alttext="upper P Subscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P Subscript m](images/c08_752.png), such that  <math alttext="128 m equals l e n left-parenthesis upper P right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>128</mn><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![128 m equals l e n left-parenthesis upper P right-parenthesis](images/c08_753.png). From the data unit encryption algorithm, we can easily derive that each 128-bit plaintext block is encrypted as a 128-bit ciphertext block. The final ciphertext is  <math alttext="upper C 0 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue ellipsis StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C Subscript m minus 1 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>&#8230;</mn><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 0 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue ellipsis StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C Subscript m minus 1 Baseline](images/c08_754.png), with  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i Baseline equals upper X upper T upper S bar upper A upper E upper S bar upper B l o c k bar upper E n c r y t i o n left-parenthesis upper K comma upper P Subscript i Baseline comma upper T comma i right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>X</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i Baseline equals upper X upper T upper S bar upper A upper E upper S bar upper B l o c k bar upper E n c r y t i o n left-parenthesis upper K comma upper P Subscript i Baseline comma upper T comma i right-parenthesis](images/c08_755.png),  <math alttext="0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to m minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to m minus 1](images/c08_756.png). Since the XTS-AES block cipher is correct, the data unit decryption procedure returns the plaintext blocks  <math alttext="upper P 0 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue ellipsis StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P Subscript m minus 1 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>&#8230;</mn><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P 0 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue ellipsis StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P Subscript m minus 1 Baseline](images/c08_757.png), which is equal to the plaintext *P*.
    2.  – If the last block  <math alttext="upper P Subscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P Subscript m](images/c08_758.png) is not empty and of a bit-length *b*, less than 128, we need to prove the correctness of the algorithm for the last two blocks. The focus is on step 2.4 in encryption and decryption procedures.

Let  <math alttext="upper L upper M upper B Subscript b Baseline left-parenthesis upper A right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>M</mi><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper L upper M upper B Subscript b Baseline left-parenthesis upper A right-parenthesis](images/c08_759.png) and  <math alttext="upper R upper M upper B Subscript b Baseline left-parenthesis upper A right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper R upper M upper B Subscript b Baseline left-parenthesis upper A right-parenthesis](images/c08_760.png) denote the leftmost and the rightmost *d* bits of block *A*, respectively.

Let  <math alttext="upper B bar upper E n c left-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mo>(</mo><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper B bar upper E n c left-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c08_761.png) and  <math alttext="upper B bar upper D e c" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> ![upper B bar upper D e c](images/c08_762.png) be abbreviations of  <math alttext="upper X upper T upper S bar upper A upper E upper S bar upper B l o c k bar upper E n c r y t i o n left-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>(</mo><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper X upper T upper S bar upper A upper E upper S bar upper B l o c k bar upper E n c r y t i o n left-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c08_763.png) and  <math alttext="upper X upper T upper S bar upper A upper E upper S bar upper B l o c k bar upper D e c r y t i o n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper X upper T upper S bar upper A upper E upper S bar upper B l o c k bar upper D e c r y t i o n](images/c08_764.png), respectively.

Assuming no alteration of ciphertext,  <math alttext="b equals l e n left-parenthesis upper P Subscript m Baseline right-parenthesis equals l e n left-parenthesis upper C Subscript m Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![b equals l e n left-parenthesis upper P Subscript m Baseline right-parenthesis equals l e n left-parenthesis upper C Subscript m Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08_765.png);  <math alttext="0 less-than b less-than 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow></math> ![0 less-than b less-than 128](images/c08_766.png).

***Problem 8.8***

Eve’s chosen-plaintext attack may be performed as follows:

*   – Using CBC mode, the response  <math alttext="upper P Subscript upper A l i c e" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P Subscript upper A l i c e](images/c08_777.png) is encrypted as  <math alttext="upper C Subscript t o upper B o b Baseline equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper I upper V 0 circled-plus upper P Subscript upper A l i c e Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript t o upper B o b Baseline equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper I upper V 0 circled-plus upper P Subscript upper A l i c e Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08_778.png). Eve intercepts  <math alttext="upper C Subscript t o upper B o b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript t o upper B o b](images/c08_779.png) and  <math alttext="upper I upper V 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper I upper V 0](images/c08_780.png).
*   – Eve knows that the next IV to be used by Alice is  <math alttext="upper I upper V 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper I upper V 1](images/c08_781.png). She presumes that Alice’s response is “Yes” and she wants to confirm her suspicion. She prepares a message  <math alttext="m equals upper I upper V 1 circled-plus upper I upper V 0 circled-plus quotation-mark Yes quotation-mark" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#160;"Yes"&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![m equals upper I upper V 1 circled-plus upper I upper V 0 circled-plus quotation-mark Yes quotation-mark](images/c08_782.png) and asks Alice to encrypt the message *m*.
*   – Alice encrypts message *m* using IV  <math alttext="upper I upper V 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper I upper V 1](images/c08_783.png) and sends a ciphertext  <math alttext="upper C Subscript t o upper E v e Baseline equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper I upper V 1 circled-plus left-parenthesis upper I upper V 1 circled-plus upper I upper V 0 circled-plus quotation-mark Yes quotation-mark right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>(</mo><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mo>"</mo><mtext>Yes"</mtext></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript t o upper E v e Baseline equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper I upper V 1 circled-plus left-parenthesis upper I upper V 1 circled-plus upper I upper V 0 circled-plus quotation-mark Yes quotation-mark right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c08_784.png).
*   – On reception of  <math alttext="upper C Subscript t o upper E v e" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript t o upper E v e](images/c08_785.png), which is equal to <math alttext="upper C Subscript t o upper B o b Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript t o upper B o b Baseline](images/c08_786.png), Eve easily infers that Alice’s response was “Yes”, which is a break in confidentiality property.

## Notes

1.  [**1**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-note-0001) *Seed* is the initialization parameter of a PRNG. Pseudorandom number generation is addressed in [Chapter 16](#c16.xhtml).
2.  [**2**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-note-0002) In cryptography, a codebook is a lookup table for coding and decoding; each word has one string, which replaces it. Like a codebook, ECB mode associates a ciphertext to each plaintext block.
3.  [**3**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-note-0003) Block alteration means presence of bit transformations (e.g. “0” becomes “1” or “1” becomes “0 <math alttext="0 quotation-mark becomes quotation-mark 1 quotation-mark or quotation-mark 1 quotation-mark becomes quotation-mark 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>"</mo><mtext>&#160;becomes&#160;"</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>"</mo><mtext>&#160;or&#160;"</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>"</mo><mtext>&#160;becomes&#160;"</mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![0 quotation-mark becomes quotation-mark 1 quotation-mark or quotation-mark 1 quotation-mark becomes quotation-mark 0](images/c08_787.png)”).
4.  [**4**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-note-0004) Capacities required to save ciphertexts on storage devices or to transmit them.
5.  [**5**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-note-0005) Padding is used only to perform ciphertext computation and it does not impact the bit-length of the produced ciphertext.
6.  [**6**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-note-0006) FF2 has not been approved by NIST, because of its vulnerability. FF3-1 is a revision of FF3 mode.
7.  [**7**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-note-0007) It’s important to distinguish between symbols and their representation. The same symbol has several representations, depending on the chosen base.
8.  [**8**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-note-0008) The IV value is used once to encrypt/decrypt a set of blocks of the plaintext/ciphertext, while a (different) tweak value is used in each block encryption/decryption. That is a reason to use distinct terms.
9.  [**9**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-note-0009) When the chosen base is greater than 10, a space character is used to separate numerals.
10.  [**10**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-note-0010) “Data unit” as defined above is specific to XTS-AES mode. A data unit does not necessarily correspond to a physical or logical block on a storage device. The mapping between data units and data on storage device is implementation-dependent and is out of the scope of XTS-AES mode.
11.  [**11**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-note-0011)  <math alttext="2 Superscript 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 64](images/c08_788.png) limit is for thwarting birthday attack.
12.  [**12**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-note-0012)  <math alttext="2 Superscript 20" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 20](images/c08_789.png) limit is for interoperability of XTS-AES implementations.
13.  [**13**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-note-0013) For any mode of operation, if there are any bit errors in a ciphertext block, then the decryption of that ciphertext block is very unlikely to be correct.
14.  [**14**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-note-0014) Sending IVs or counters results in a vulnerability in the mode of operation.
15.  [**15**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-note-0015) Some modes of operation make use only of the encryption operation of the underlying block cipher to encrypt plaintexts and to decrypt ciphertexts.
16.  [**16**](#c08.xhtml#rc08-note-0016) Modes of operation, which generate a bit string that is XORed with the plaintext (respectively the ciphertext) to produce the ciphertext (respectively the plaintext), provide techniques (in addition to those presented in [Chapter 6](#c06.xhtml)) to build stream ciphers.

1.  **1** Goldwasser, S. and Micali, S. (1984). Probabilistic encryption. Journal of Computer and System Sciences 28: 270–299.
2.  **2** Dworkin, M. (2001). Recommendation for block cipher modes of operation methods and techniques, special publication 800-38A. NIST. National Institute for Standards and Technology.
3.  **3** Dworkin, M. (2019). Recommendation for block cipher modes of operation: methods for format-preserving encryption, special publication 800-38G. NIST. National Institute for Standards and Technology.
4.  **4** Dworkin, M. (2010). Recommendation for block cipher modes of operation: three variants of ciphertext stealing for CBC mode, addendum to NIST special publication 800-38A. NIST. National Institute of Standards and Technology.
5.  **5** IEEE. (2018). IEEE standard for cryptographic protection of data on block-oriented storage devices, IEEE Std 1619™-2018. Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers. IEEE.
6.  **6** Liskov, M., Rivest, R., and Wagner, D. (2002). Tweakable block ciphers. Journal of Cryptology 24: 588–613.

# 9   
Block Cipher Modes of Operation for Authentication and Confidentiality

In the previous chapter, we presented the modes of operation of block ciphers to provide confidentiality guarantees. Another security property of prime importance is integrity. Indeed, in the event an adversary alters a message or a storage device content, the decryption operation cannot detect any alteration. Therefore, message authentication codes or other techniques are required to preserve data integrity. To provide confidentiality and integrity guarantees based on block ciphers, the NIST approved a set of modes of operation for block ciphers, which are discussed in this chapter. They include (see [Figure 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0001)):

![Figure 9.1 Block cipher modes of operation for authentication and confidentiality.](images/c09f001.png)

[**Figure 9.1**](#c09.xhtml#rc09-fig-0001) Block cipher modes of operation for authentication and confidentiality.

*   Five modes of operation for confidentiality and authenticity guarantees: CCM, GCM, KW, KWP, and TKW.
*   Two modes of operation for authenticity guarantees only: CMAC and GMAC.

All these modes provide capabilities to generate and verify message tags. In addition to approved modes of operation of block ciphers, two other algorithms are useful to authenticate messages:

*   AES-GCM-SIV \[[1](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0001)\] is an extension of GCM, which is resistant to IV misuse.
*   ChaCha20-Poly1305 is a scheme recommended to build authenticated encryption for TLS implementation.

Notice that authentication, addressed in this chapter, means message authenticity and not the authentication of the entity sending a message. Entity authentication is addressed in [Chapter 15](#c15.xhtml).

## 9.1 Introduction

***Definition 9.1 Data authenticity**: it is a property to indicate that the data originated from its purported source.*

***Definition 9.2 Authenticated encryption**: it is a cryptography scheme that provides guarantees to data confidentiality and authenticity verification.*

***Definition 9.3 Associated data** (also called **additional authentication data**): it may be any bit string (including a MAC address, an IP addresses, a port numbers, a user name, an application name or a protocol title), which is used in data authenticity verification.*

***Definition 9.4 Authenticated encryption/decryption with associatedencryption/decryption with associated data”**[¹](#c09.xhtml#c09-note-0001) **data (AEAD)**: it is an authenticated encryption/decryption in which additional data is used to authenticity verification.*

**Definition 9.5 Nonce misuse-resistant AEAD**: it is an authenticated-encryption scheme in which encrypting different plaintexts with the same nonce will reveal nothing to adversary.

(\*) Poly1305-AES is not yet approved as a block cipher mode of operation.

(\*\*) ChaCha20 is a stream cipher, not a block cipher.

*Notations*: the same notations are used in [Chapters 8](#c08.xhtml) and [9](#c09.xhtml).

## 9.2 Block Cipher Modes of Operation for Confidentiality and Authentication

### 9.2.1 Authenticated Encryption and AEAD Algorithms

#### 9.2.1.1 Approaches to Data Authentication

When only confidentiality is provided (using the modes mentioned above), the recipient of a ciphertext performs the decryption whatever the ciphertext content may be. In the event, the ciphertext has been forged by an adversary, the recipient recovers a plaintext that has not been sent by his/her partner, which may result in making inappropriate decisions. Authenticated decryption is a means to verify the integrity of the plaintext before using it.

Dominant approaches to provide data authenticity guarantees make use of *authentication*[²](#c09.xhtml#c09-note-0002) *tag*, known as *Message Authentication Codes* (MACs). There also is another approach, which relies on spreading the authenticity information along the entire ciphertext (see Key-wrapping modes in [Section 9.2.7](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-02006)).

As illustrated by [Figure 9.2](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0002), there exist three basic approaches to authenticated encryption using a MAC, which differ in when the MAC is generated:

![Figure 9.2 Different approaches to authenticated encryption.](images/c09f002.png)

[**Figure 9.2**](#c09.xhtml#rc09-fig-0002) Different approaches to authenticated encryption.

*   *Encrypt-and-MAC* approach: a tag is produced using the plaintext and the latter is encrypted without the MAC. The same key is used both in encryption and in tag generation. Both operations may be performed in parallel. The recipient must decrypt the ciphertext and generate the MAC to know if the ciphertext has been altered or not. The MAC is generated only from the plaintext and it is not encrypted, it may leak information about the plaintext.
*   *MAC-then-Encrypt* approach: first, the MAC is generated, then the plaintext and the tag are encrypted together. Thus, the encrypted plaintext and tag are combined in a single ciphertext. This approach does not provide integrity to the ciphertext as does the MAC-and-Encrypt approach. Being encrypted together with a plaintext, the MAC does not leak information about the plaintext.
*   *Encrypt-then-MAC* approach: first, the plaintext is encrypted, then, a MAC is generated from the ciphertext. Often the encryption and authentication keys are distinct and derived from a master key. This approach provides integrity to both plaintext and ciphertext. The MAC does not leak information about the plaintext.

Standard algorithms for authenticated encryption (such as CMAC, CCM, and GCM), which are presented in the sequel, are Encrypt-then-MAC algorithms. In order to thwart attacks, it is recommended to always compute the MACs on the ciphertext and to use two distinct keys, one key for encryption and another for MAC generation.

#### 9.2.1.2 Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data Algorithms

The purpose of associated data in encrypted-authentication algorithms is to bind a ciphertext to the context where it is supposed to appear, so that the recipient can detect if a ciphertext is not used in the appropriate context and reject the ciphertext. The associated data does not necessarily have to be stored or transmitted with the ciphertext. Any context-dependent non-secret values (such as MAC address, IP address, TCP port number, user name, application name, or protocol title), that the both involved parties are able to correctly infer, can be used as associated data. In other words, the sender who can encrypt a plaintext and generate a MAC must know in which context the plaintext can be used on the recipient side and the recipient only makes use of the recovered plaintext in the agreed context and not in another. Therefore, a sender who shares a key with the recipient is prevented from accessing services or performing actions not agreed between both parties.

**Example 9.1**

An agenda management service is available to a group of staff members in a company. To secure communications between the members and the agenda server, a secret key is shared by all group members. To enable each group member access and update his/her agenda entry, an additional authentication data is associated to each member. Therefore, only the member holding the appropriate associated authentication data (say his/her chosen pseudo name) can encrypt and authenticate the data regarding his/her agenda entries.

#### 9.2.1.3 Limits of Authenticated-Decryption Modes

Given a plaintext  <math alttext="upper P Subscript s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P Subscript s](images/c09_1.png), the sender encrypts it to  <math alttext="upper C Subscript s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript s](images/c09_2.png) and computes a tag  <math alttext="upper T Subscript s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper T Subscript s](images/c09_3.png). On the recipient side, upon the reception of a ciphertext  <math alttext="upper C prime Subscript s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><msup><mi>C</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C prime Subscript s](images/c09_4.png) and its MAC  <math alttext="upper T prime Subscript s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><msup><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper T prime Subscript s](images/c09_5.png), the ciphertext is decrypted to produce a plaintext  <math alttext="upper P Subscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P Subscript r](images/c09_6.png) and then the recipient computes a tag  <math alttext="upper T Subscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper T Subscript r](images/c09_7.png) for the plaintext  <math alttext="upper P Subscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P Subscript r](images/c09_8.png). If  <math alttext="upper T prime Subscript s Baseline equals upper T Subscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><msup><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper T prime Subscript s Baseline equals upper T Subscript r](images/c09_9.png), then the recipient accepts the plaintext  <math alttext="upper P Subscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P Subscript r](images/c09_10.png). If  <math alttext="upper T prime Subscript s Baseline not-equals upper T Subscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><msup><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper T prime Subscript s Baseline not-equals upper T Subscript r](images/c09_11.png), then the recipient rejects the ciphertext, because  <math alttext="upper C prime Subscript s Baseline not-equals upper C Subscript s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><msup><mi>C</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C prime Subscript s Baseline not-equals upper C Subscript s](images/c09_12.png),  <math alttext="upper T Subscript r Baseline not-equals upper T Subscript s Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper T Subscript r Baseline not-equals upper T Subscript s Baseline](images/c09_13.png) or both. It is of paramount importance to keep in mind the following limitations when using any authenticated-encryption algorithm:

*   If the MAC verification fails, then the received plaintext is definitely distinct from the original plaintext (due to ciphertext alteration) or the ciphertext has not been issued by the legitimate sender holding the shared secret key *K*. However, if the MAC verification succeeds, it does not necessarily mean that the ciphertext is the original one. Indeed, an attacker can alter the ciphertext and then selects randomly a MAC, which matches the modified ciphertext.
*   MAC forgery attacks depend on  <math alttext="upper T l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper T l e n](images/c09_14.png), the bit-length of the MAC. The probability that the attacker randomly guesses the MAC, which matches the ciphertext he/she modified, is  <math alttext="2 Superscript minus upper T l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>T</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript minus upper T l e n](images/c09_15.png). The adversary could substitute a ciphertext for another without controlling the content by trying to find a collision (i.e. two distinct ciphertexts with the same MAC). By the birthday paradox, he/she needs to use (i.e. intercepts) at least  <math alttext="2 Superscript StartFraction upper T l e n Over 2 EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript StartFraction upper T l e n Over 2 EndFraction](images/c09_16.png).Therefore, the level of security is MAC-length-dependent. Standards recommend to use MACs with a length no smaller than 64 bits.
*   Another recommendation to prevent attacks is to limit the number of MACs generated with the same key, because in case a large number of tags are generated with the same key, collisions may be observed and their exploitation may be catastrophic. The maximum number of MACs per key depends on each authenticated-encryption algorithm, as discussed in the sequel.

### 9.2.2 CMAC Mode of Operation

CMAC (Cipher Message Authentication Code) is an algorithm to generate and validate MACs \[[2](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0002)\]. It makes use of a block cipher (TDEA or AES). Therefore, CMAC is considered as a mode of operation of block ciphers to provide authentication guarantees (and not confidentiality). CMAC is defined with three functions:

1.  *CMAC\_Subkey\_Generation*, which takes a block length *b* and a key *K* and returns two subkeys of bit-length *b* each. Parameter *b* is equal to 64 if TDEA cipher is used and 128 if AES is used.
2.  *CMAC\_MAC\_Generation*, which computes a tag *T* given a plaintext *M*. It looks like CBC encryption mode, but with a single block as output and a special treatment of the last block, using two subkeys.
3.  *CMAC\_MAC\_Verification*, which checks if the tag accompanying a plaintext is valid or not.

The algorithms of CMAC functions are given below. [Figure 9.3](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0003) depicts the MAC generation procedure of CMAC.

![Figure 9.3 Tag generation in CMAC mode of operation.](images/c09f003.png)

[**Figure 9.3**](#c09.xhtml#rc09-fig-0003) Tag generation in CMAC mode of operation.

### 9.2.3 CCM Mode of Operation

CCM (Counter with Cipher block chaining-Message authentication code) is an algorithm to provide confidentiality as well as authenticity of data \[[3](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0003)\]. It combines counter mode encryption (i.e. CTR mode) to provide confidentiality and cipher block chaining (CBC) to provide authenticity assurance. CCM processes blocks with a length of 128 bits. Therefore, it can be used jointly with AES, but not with TDEA whose block length is of 64 bits.

To encrypt, decrypt, and authenticate a set of plaintexts (such a set is called *key span*), CCM requires a secret key *K*, a block cipher, like AES, with an encryption primitive  <math alttext="upper E n c Subscript upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper E n c Subscript upper K](images/c09_59.png), and a MAC bit-length  <math alttext="upper T l e n less-than-or-equal-to 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow></math> ![upper T l e n less-than-or-equal-to 128](images/c09_60.png). To encrypt and produce a tag for a plaintext within a key span, CCM makes use of three inputs:

*   *p*: data that need to be encrypted and authenticated. Such data is called *payload*; its bit-length is denoted  <math alttext="upper P l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P l e n](images/c09_61.png), with  <math alttext="upper P l e n less-than 2 Superscript 67" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>67</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![upper P l e n less-than 2 Superscript 67](images/c09_62.png).
*   *A*: associated data, which includes some information known to the recipient and that does not need confidentiality, but is used in authentication step. The bit-length of the associated data is denoted  <math alttext="upper A l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper A l e n](images/c09_63.png), with  <math alttext="0 less-than-or-equal-to upper A l e n less-than 2 Superscript 67" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>A</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>67</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![0 less-than-or-equal-to upper A l e n less-than 2 Superscript 67](images/c09_64.png).
*   *N*: a nonce, which is a unique value associated with each plaintext; its bit-length is denoted  <math alttext="upper N l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper N l e n](images/c09_65.png).

#### 9.2.3.1 MAC Generation and Encryption

The tag generation and encryption algorithm is composed of four steps:

1.  Represent the inputs (i.e. payload *P*, associated data *A*, and nonce *N*) as 128-bits blocks. Such a formatting operation is described in 9.2.3.3. Let  <math alttext="upper B 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B 0](images/c09_66.png), …,  <math alttext="upper B Subscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript r](images/c09_67.png) be the blocks representing the inputs.

#### 9.2.3.2 MAC Verification and Decryption

MAC verification and decryption algorithm is composed of five steps:

1.  Check if the received ciphertext is valid regarding the tag length. If the length of the received ciphertext,  <math alttext="upper C l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C l e n](images/c09_98.png), is less or equal to that of a valid tag,  <math alttext="upper T l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper T l e n](images/c09_99.png), the received ciphertext is discarded, because it does not contain any encrypted data.
2.  Use the nonce value and counter indexes to produce formatted counter blocks  <math alttext="upper C t r 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>t</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C t r 0](images/c09_100.png), …,  <math alttext="upper C t r Subscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>t</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C t r Subscript m](images/c09_101.png), where *m* denotes the number of blocks of the payload;  <math alttext="m equals left-parenthesis upper C l e n minus upper T l e n right-parenthesis slash 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>T</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow></math> ![m equals left-parenthesis upper C l e n minus upper T l e n right-parenthesis slash 128](images/c09_102.png). The ciphertext is interpreted as  <math alttext="upper C equals upper C 1 StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper C 2 StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue period period period EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C Subscript m Baseline EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C Subscript m plus 1 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C equals upper C 1 StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper C 2 StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue period period period EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C Subscript m Baseline EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C Subscript m plus 1 Baseline](images/c09_103.png), where  <math alttext="upper C Subscript m plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript m plus 1](images/c09_104.png) denotes an encrypted tag with a bit-length of  <math alttext="upper T l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper T l e n](images/c09_105.png). Then, use CTR mode to produce a plaintext  <math alttext="upper P equals upper P 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P 2 StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue period period period EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P Subscript m Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P equals upper P 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P 2 StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue period period period EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P Subscript m Baseline](images/c09_106.png), such that  <math alttext="upper P Subscript i Baseline equals upper C Subscript i Baseline circled-plus upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C t r Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>t</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P Subscript i Baseline equals upper C Subscript i Baseline circled-plus upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C t r Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c09_107.png),  <math alttext="i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma m](images/c09_108.png). The last plaintext block may be incomplete to match the last ciphertext block.
3.  Decrypt the received tag as  <math alttext="upper T equals upper C Subscript m plus 1 Baseline circled-plus upper M upper S upper B Subscript upper T l e n Baseline left-parenthesis upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C t r 0 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis period" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>t</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> ![upper T equals upper C Subscript m plus 1 Baseline circled-plus upper M upper S upper B Subscript upper T l e n Baseline left-parenthesis upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C t r 0 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis period](images/c09_109.png)
4.  Represent the payload *P*, associated data *A*, and nonce *N* as 128-bits blocks, denoted  <math alttext="upper B 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B 0](images/c09_110.png), …,  <math alttext="upper B Subscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript r](images/c09_111.png), using the formatting function. Then, encrypt the blocks  <math alttext="upper B 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B 0](images/c09_112.png), …,  <math alttext="upper B Subscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript r](images/c09_113.png) and produce a tag  <math alttext="upper T prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> ![upper T prime](images/c09_114.png).
5.  Check if the received and computed tags are identical; and return either “Invalid” or “Valid” plus the payload.

MAC verification and decryption algorithm of CCM are given below.

#### 9.2.3.3 Information Formatting Function

The formatting function takes three bit-strings (a nonce  <math alttext="upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![upper N](images/c09_137.png), an associated data *A*, and a payload *P*) and a tag length and returns a sequence of *r* 128-bit blocks  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper B 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper B 0](images/c09_138.png), …,  <math alttext="upper B Subscript r Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript r Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c09_139.png) as depicted in [Figure 9.5](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0005). Let *n*, *a*, *p*, and *t* denote the byte-length of the nonce, the associated data, the payload, and the tag, respectively. Bit-lengths of all inputs of formatting function are multiple of 8. That is:  <math alttext="n equals upper N l e n slash 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ![n equals upper N l e n slash 8](images/c09_140.png),  <math alttext="a equals upper A l e n slash 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ![a equals upper A l e n slash 8](images/c09_141.png),  <math alttext="p equals upper P l e n slash 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals upper P l e n slash 8](images/c09_142.png), and  <math alttext="t equals upper T l e n slash 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>T</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ![t equals upper T l e n slash 8](images/c09_143.png). Let *Q* be a byte-string, which represents the payload byte-length and *q*, the byte-length of string *Q*. *q* is a parameter of the formatting function. For example, if  <math alttext="upper P l e n equals 8192" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8192</mn></mrow></math> ![upper P l e n equals 8192](images/c09_144.png) and  <math alttext="q equals 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![q equals 3](images/c09_145.png), then  <math alttext="upper Q equals 1024 equals 00000000 00000100 00000000" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1024</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>00000000</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>00000100</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>00000000</mn></mrow></math> ![upper Q equals 1024 equals 00000000 00000100 00000000](images/c09_146.png).

![Figure 9.5 Information formatting in CCM mode.](images/c09f005.png)

[**Figure 9.5**](#c09.xhtml#rc09-fig-0005) Information formatting in CCM mode.

*Formatting the nonce and control information*

The first byte of block  <math alttext="upper B 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B 0](images/c09_147.png) contains four flags: one reserved bit, one bit to indicate presence of associated data, three bits to encode the tag length as  <math alttext="left-bracket left-parenthesis t minus 2 right-parenthesis slash 2 right-bracket Subscript 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![left-bracket left-parenthesis t minus 2 right-parenthesis slash 2 right-bracket Subscript 3](images/c09_148.png), and three bits to encode the parameter *q* as  <math alttext="left-bracket q minus 1 right-bracket Subscript 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![left-bracket q minus 1 right-bracket Subscript 3](images/c09_149.png). For example, if the tag byte-length *t* is 16, it is represented as  <math alttext="left-bracket left-parenthesis 16 minus 2 right-parenthesis slash 2 right-bracket Subscript 3 Baseline equals 111" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>111</mn></mrow></math> ![left-bracket left-parenthesis 16 minus 2 right-parenthesis slash 2 right-bracket Subscript 3 Baseline equals 111](images/c09_150.png).

Notice that since  <math alttext="q minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![q minus 1](images/c09_151.png) is represented on three bits,  <math alttext="q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![q](images/c09_152.png) cannot be greater than 8. Therefore, the maximum byte-length of payload is  <math alttext="p less-than 2 Superscript 8 asterisk q Baseline less-than 2 Superscript 8 asterisk 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>\*</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msup><mo>&#60;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![p less-than 2 Superscript 8 asterisk q Baseline less-than 2 Superscript 8 asterisk 8](images/c09_153.png).

The remaining 15 bytes of block  <math alttext="upper B 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B 0](images/c09_154.png) are used to represent the nonce and the payload length. The nonce value is represented on  <math alttext="15 minus q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>15</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![15 minus q](images/c09_155.png) bytes. Notice that the parameter *q* bounds the nonce space, i.e. the number of distinct nonces is  <math alttext="2 Superscript 8 asterisk n Baseline less-than 2 Superscript 8 asterisk left-parenthesis 15 minus q right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>\*</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>&#60;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>\*</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>15</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 8 asterisk n Baseline less-than 2 Superscript 8 asterisk left-parenthesis 15 minus q right-parenthesis](images/c09_156.png).

*Formatting the associated data*

The second bit of the first byte of block  <math alttext="upper B 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B 0](images/c09_157.png) indicates whether associated data is present or not. If  <math alttext="a ampersand gt semicolon 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>&#38;gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![a ampersand gt semicolon 0](images/c09_158.png), then the associated data and its length are represented on *u* blocks  <math alttext="upper B 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B 1](images/c09_159.png), …,  <math alttext="upper B Subscript u" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>u</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript u](images/c09_160.png). The associated-data byte-length *a* is represented according to three cases:

1.  If  <math alttext="0 less-than a less-than 2 Superscript 16 Baseline minus 2 Superscript 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>8</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![0 less-than a less-than 2 Superscript 16 Baseline minus 2 Superscript 8](images/c09_161.png), then *a* is represented as  <math alttext="left-bracket a right-bracket Subscript 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![left-bracket a right-bracket Subscript 16](images/c09_162.png), i.e. on two bytes.
2.  If  <math alttext="2 Superscript 16 Baseline minus 2 Superscript 8 Baseline less-than-or-equal-to a less-than 2 Superscript 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>8</mn></msup><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 16 Baseline minus 2 Superscript 8 Baseline less-than-or-equal-to a less-than 2 Superscript 32](images/c09_163.png), then *a* is represented as  <math alttext="0 xff StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue 0 xfe EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue left-bracket a right-bracket Subscript 32 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mtext>xff</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mtext>xfe</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![0 xff StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue 0 xfe EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue left-bracket a right-bracket Subscript 32 Baseline](images/c09_164.png), i.e. on six bytes.
3.  If  <math alttext="2 Superscript 32 Baseline less-than-or-equal-to a less-than 2 Superscript 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 32 Baseline less-than-or-equal-to a less-than 2 Superscript 64](images/c09_165.png), then *a* is represented as  <math alttext="0 xff StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue 0 xff EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue left-bracket a right-bracket Subscript 64 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mtext>xff</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mtext>xff</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![0 xff StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue 0 xff EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue left-bracket a right-bracket Subscript 64 Baseline](images/c09_166.png), i.e. on ten bytes.

Then, *a* is followed by the associated data. If bytes used to represent the associated data and its length are not a multiple of 128 bits, then a string of 0-bits is appended to fill the last block  <math alttext="upper B Subscript u" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>u</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript u](images/c09_167.png).

*Formatting the payload*

The payload is represented as blocks denoted  <math alttext="upper B Subscript u plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript u plus 1](images/c09_168.png), …,  <math alttext="upper B Subscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B Subscript r](images/c09_169.png), where  <math alttext="r equals u plus left ceiling p slash 16 right ceiling" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo>&#8968;</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><mo>&#8969;</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r equals u plus left ceiling p slash 16 right ceiling](images/c09_170.png).

#### 9.2.3.4 Counter Formatting Function

The counter formatting function takes the nonce *N* and  <math alttext="m equals left ceiling StartFraction upper P l e n Over 128 EndFraction right ceiling" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>&#8968;</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>&#8969;</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![m equals left ceiling StartFraction upper P l e n Over 128 EndFraction right ceiling](images/c09_171.png), which is the number of blocks of the payload data, and returns  <math alttext="m plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![m plus 1](images/c09_172.png) 128-bit blocks  <math alttext="upper C t r 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>t</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C t r 0](images/c09_173.png),  <math alttext="upper C t r 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>t</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C t r 1](images/c09_174.png), …,  <math alttext="upper C t r Subscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>t</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C t r Subscript m](images/c09_175.png) formatted as follows:  <math alttext="upper C t r Subscript i Baseline equals upper F l a g s StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper N o n c e EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>t</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>F</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>s</mi><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C t r Subscript i Baseline equals upper F l a g s StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper N o n c e EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue i](images/c09_176.png) as depicted in [Figure 9.6](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0006). A counter index *i*,  <math alttext="i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma m](images/c09_177.png) is associated with each payload block *i*.  <math alttext="upper C t r 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>t</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C t r 0](images/c09_178.png) is used to encrypt/decrypt the tag. Counter formatting function makes use of the same formatting rules as those of information formatting described in [Section 9.2.3.3](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-03006).

### 9.2.4 GCM and GMAC Modes of Operation

GCM and GMAC are modes of operation of symmetric key block ciphers. Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) is an algorithm for authenticated encryption with associated data to be used jointly with a 128-bit block cipher such as AES \[[4](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0004)\]. GMAC makes use of the GCM operations to provide only data authenticity; it targets applications using non-confidential data, but with integrity requirements. GCM provides assurance of data confidentiality using a variation of counter mode (CTR) and it provides assurance of data authenticity using a hash function, which is defined over an extension field. Therefore, GCM and CCM differ regarding the generation and verification of tags.

#### 9.2.4.1 GCTR Encryption Mode

As mentioned previously, GCM encryption relies on a variation of CTR mode, called GCTR, with two distinguishing features compared to the basic CTR mode: 1) the plaintext is not required to be of a length multiple of that of a block and 2) counter values are computed using a special increment function modulo  <math alttext="2 Superscript s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>s</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript s](images/c09_179.png) defined as follows:

 <math alttext="upper I n c Subscript s Baseline left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals upper M upper S upper B Subscript l e n left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis minus s Baseline left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue left-bracket i n t left-parenthesis upper L upper S upper B Subscript s Baseline left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis right-parenthesis plus 1 m o d 2 Superscript s Baseline right-bracket Subscript s Baseline" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>s</mi></msup></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mi>s</mi></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper I n c Subscript s Baseline left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals upper M upper S upper B Subscript l e n left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis minus s Baseline left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue left-bracket i n t left-parenthesis upper L upper S upper B Subscript s Baseline left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis right-parenthesis plus 1 m o d 2 Superscript s Baseline right-bracket Subscript s Baseline](images/c09_180.png)

 <math alttext="upper I n c Subscript s Baseline left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper I n c Subscript s Baseline left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis](images/c09_181.png) increments the rightmost bits of bit string *X* and the leftmost  <math alttext="l e n left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis minus s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> ![l e n left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis minus s](images/c09_182.png) bits remain unchanged. In AES-GCM, the increment function is instantiated as  <math alttext="upper I n c 32 left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper I n c 32 left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis](images/c09_183.png).

GCTR algorithm is presented below and depicted in [Figure 9.7](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0007).

where *H* denotes the hash key; and ⊗ is the multiplication operation, defined over extension field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 128](images/c09_198.png), with the irreducible polynomial  <math alttext="f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 128 Baseline plus x Superscript 7 Baseline plus x squared plus x plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>7</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 128 Baseline plus x Superscript 7 Baseline plus x squared plus x plus 1](images/c09_199.png). (For more on multiplication over extension fields see Section 3.2.3).  <math alttext="upper D equals upper D Subscript 1 Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper D Subscript 2 Baseline StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue ellipsis EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper D Subscript m Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>&#8230;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper D equals upper D Subscript 1 Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper D Subscript 2 Baseline StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue ellipsis EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper D Subscript m Baseline](images/c09_200.png) where  <math alttext="upper D 1 comma upper D Subscript 2 Baseline comma ellipsis comma upper D Subscript m Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper D 1 comma upper D Subscript 2 Baseline comma ellipsis comma upper D Subscript m Baseline](images/c09_201.png) are 128-bit blocks and  <math alttext="m equals l e n left-parenthesis upper D right-parenthesis slash 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow></math> ![m equals l e n left-parenthesis upper D right-parenthesis slash 128](images/c09_202.png).

GCM standard provides an efficient method to implement the multiplication over the chosen finite field and its irreducible polynomial. As chosen below the multiplication algorithm only makes use of XOR and shift operations, which are very useful to speed the multiplication. The convention for interpreting strings as polynomials is little endian; i.e. the block  <math alttext="upper U equals u 0 u 1 ellipsis u 127 corresponds to the polynomial upper P left-parenthesis upper U right-parenthesis equals u 127 x Superscript 127 Baseline plus u 126 x Superscript 126 Baseline plus ellipsis plus u 1 x plus u 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8230;</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mn>127</mn></mrow></msub><mtext>&#160;corresponds&#160;to&#160;the&#160;polynomial&#160;</mtext><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>U</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mn>127</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>127</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mn>126</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>126</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper U equals u 0 u 1 ellipsis u 127 corresponds to the polynomial upper P left-parenthesis upper U right-parenthesis equals u 127 x Superscript 127 Baseline plus u 126 x Superscript 126 Baseline plus ellipsis plus u 1 x plus u 0](images/c09_203.png).

#### 9.2.4.3 Authenticated Encryption with GCM

To encrypt, decrypt, and authenticate a set of plaintexts (such a set is called *key span*), GCM requires a secret key *K*, a block cipher, like AES, with an encryption primitive  <math alttext="upper E n c Subscript upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper E n c Subscript upper K](images/c09_218.png), and a MAC bit-length  <math alttext="upper T l e n less-than-or-equal-to 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow></math> ![upper T l e n less-than-or-equal-to 128](images/c09_219.png). To encrypt and produce a tag for a plaintext in the key span, GCM makes use of three inputs:

*   *P*: data that needs to be encrypted and authenticated. Such data is called *payload* and its bit-length is denoted  <math alttext="upper P l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P l e n](images/c09_220.png). The standard requires that  <math alttext="upper P l e n less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript 39 Baseline minus 256" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>39</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>256</mn></mrow></math> ![upper P l e n less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript 39 Baseline minus 256](images/c09_221.png).
*   *A*: associated authenticated data, which includes some information known to the recipient and which does not need confidentiality, but it is used in the authentication step. The bit-length of the associated data is denoted  <math alttext="upper A l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper A l e n](images/c09_222.png). The associated data may be an empty bit-string. GCM requires that  <math alttext="upper A l e n less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript 64 Baseline minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper A l e n less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript 64 Baseline minus 1](images/c09_223.png).
*    <math alttext="upper I upper V" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> ![upper I upper V](images/c09_224.png): an initialization vector, which is a unique value (i.e. a nonce) associated with each plaintext; its bit-length is denoted  <math alttext="upper I upper V l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>V</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper I upper V l e n](images/c09_225.png). The latter may take a value of 64, 96, 128, or 160. The total number of invocations of the authenticated-encryption algorithm shall not exceed  <math alttext="2 Superscript 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 32](images/c09_226.png), including all IV lengths, with the same key.

The algorithm of encryption and Tag generation of GCM is given below and also depicted in [Figure 9.8](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0008).

![Figure 9.8 GCM authenticated encryption.](images/c09f008.png)

[**Figure 9.8**](#c09.xhtml#rc09-fig-0008) GCM authenticated encryption.

The operations of the authenticated decryption are similar to those of encryption. Below is the algorithm of the GCM authenticated decryption.

#### 9.2.4.5 GMAC Mode

When GCM is used for guaranteeing data authenticity only, the restricted GCM is called GMAC (Galois Message Authentication Code). The same functions are used in both modes as depicted in [Figure 9.9](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0009).

![Figure 9.9 GMAC tag generation.](images/c09f009.png)

[**Figure 9.9**](#c09.xhtml#rc09-fig-0009) GMAC tag generation.

#### 9.2.4.6 Forbidden Attack Against GCM with Repeated IV

GCM mode is vulnerable to an IV value repeated, by mistake, with the same key. The attack against GCM, known as *forbidden attack*, aims to recover the authentication key, denoted *H*, and then exploits such a finding to forge tags, which will be validated by the recipient. Recall *H* that is computed as  <math alttext="upper H equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis 0 Superscript 128 Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis 0 Superscript 128 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c09_260.png) and in consequence, it is assumed to be unknown to adversaries. Notice that the forbidden attack aims to recover the authentication key and not the encryption key. In order to simplify understanding of the attack, consider a scenario where the message sender makes use of AES-GCM to generate 128-bit tags for two one-block messages with the same IV and does not make use of associated data. Since AES is used as the underlying block cipher and the tag bit-length, denoted  <math alttext="upper T l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper T l e n](images/c09_261.png), is equal to 128, for any integer *J* and a bit string *S*:

 <math alttext="upper M upper S upper B Subscript upper T l e n Baseline left-parenthesis upper G upper C upper T upper R Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper J comma upper S right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper G upper C upper T upper R Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper J comma upper S right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>G</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper M upper S upper B Subscript upper T l e n Baseline left-parenthesis upper G upper C upper T upper R Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper J comma upper S right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper G upper C upper T upper R Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper J comma upper S right-parenthesis](images/c09_262.png)

If *S* is a one-block string, then  <math alttext="upper G upper C upper T upper R Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper J comma upper S right-parenthesis equals upper S circled-plus upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper J right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>J</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper G upper C upper T upper R Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper J comma upper S right-parenthesis equals upper S circled-plus upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper J right-parenthesis](images/c09_263.png)

Given two plaintexts  <math alttext="upper M Superscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper M Superscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis](images/c09_264.png) and  <math alttext="upper M Superscript left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper M Superscript left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis](images/c09_265.png), their encrypted tags  <math alttext="upper T Superscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper T Superscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis](images/c09_266.png) and  <math alttext="upper T Superscript left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper T Superscript left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis](images/c09_267.png) are computed as follows:
