It is worth noticing that in general,  <math alttext="upper G upper H a s h Subscript upper H" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>H</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper G upper H a s h Subscript upper H](images/c09_302.png) function yields a polynomial of degree *m*, which depends on the number of blocks in the plaintext and the associated data. In consequence, the number of roots of the polynomial inferred from  <math alttext="upper S Superscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Baseline circled-plus upper S Superscript left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#8853;</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper S Superscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Baseline circled-plus upper S Superscript left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis](images/c09_303.png) may be high, if messages are longer than one block and/or associated data is used; and the adversary may decide which root (i.e. which authentication key *H* to keep) among a large set to forge tags. To increase the chance of success in choosing the correct authentication key, the adversary may need to collect many pairs of messages encrypted with the same IV, each pair providing a set of roots. Then, combining the roots yielded by all pairs helps to find a single root (i.e. the valid authentication key) that matches all the pairs. Therefore, the forbidden attack against AES-GCM is likely to succeed only if the sender either encrypts plaintexts with small sizes or frequently makes use of the same IV to generate tags.

### 9.2.5 AES-GCM-SIV Mode

#### 9.2.5.1 What Does Nonce Misuse-resistance Mean?

In the nonce-based algorithms (OFB, CTR, and GCM) described above, it is assumed that the nonce value does not repeat with the same key. Such a requirement may not be fulfilled in practice because of weak randomness of some devices generating nonce values. For example, in CTR mode, if a counter value is repeated (because of a wrong counter value generation), the attacker can easily recover the XOR of two plaintexts. A second example of attack is the forbidden attack of AES-GCM (see [Section 9.2.4](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-02004)). Therefore, those algorithms suffer vulnerability when two distinct plaintexts are (wrongly) encrypted with the same[³](#c09.xhtml#c09-note-0003) key and nonce.

Nonce misuse-resistant AEADs, such as AES-GCM-SIV presented in the sequel, do not suffer the nonce-misuse vulnerability. For this class of AEADs, encrypting two plaintexts with the same nonce value only discloses whether the plaintexts were equal or not. Therefore, these algorithms are suggested in any situations where nonce uniqueness cannot be guaranteed. However, it is worth noticing that there does not yet exist a fully nonce misuse-resistant algorithm in which the nonce may repeat indefinitely without jeopardizing the security. Rather, there are bounds of nonce repetitions to provide some security levels (see Section 10.5.2).

#### 9.2.5.2 Overview of AES-GCM-SIV Mode

AES-GCM-SIV is a nonce-misuse resistant authenticated-encryption mode, which has the property that both privacy and integrity are preserved, even if nonces are repeated. It is an improvement of AES-GCM[⁴](#c09.xhtml#c09-note-0004) mode with the following main design differences:

*   In AES-GCM, a single key *K* is used to compute the tag and to encrypt, while in AES-GCM-SIV, the initial key *K*, called master key, is used to derive two keys,  <math alttext="upper K bar h a s h" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>h</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K bar h a s h](images/c09_304.png) (used to compute the tag) and  <math alttext="upper K bar m s g" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K bar m s g](images/c09_305.png) (used to encrypt the plaintext and the tag).
*   In AES-GCM, the initial counter value is computed only from the IV, while in AES-GCM-SIV, the encrypted tag is used as an initial counter value, thus providing more randomness.
*   While using the same extension field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript 128](images/c09_306.png), AES-GCM and AES-GCM-SIV use distinct irreducible polynomials. The authors of AES-GCM-SIV showed that the computations are faster with the irreducible polynomial they chose, in particular when operations are implemented in specific hardware.
*   The tag is computed with distinct hash functions:  <math alttext="upper G upper H a s h" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> ![upper G upper H a s h](images/c09_307.png) for AES-GCM and  <math alttext="upper P o l y v a l" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>y</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P o l y v a l](images/c09_308.png) for AES-GCM-SIV.
*   AES-GCM authenticates the encoded associated data and the ciphertext, while AES-GCM-SIV authenticates the encoded associated data and the plaintext. In other words, AES-GCM follows the Encrypt-then-MAC approach, while AES-GCM-SIV follows the MAC-then-Encrypt approach.

The principle of AES-GCM-SIV is as follows: two keys,  <math alttext="upper K bar h a s h" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>h</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K bar h a s h](images/c09_309.png) and  <math alttext="k bar m s g" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></math> ![k bar m s g](images/c09_310.png), are derived from a master key *K* and the initial nonce. The hash key  <math alttext="upper K bar h a s h" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>h</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K bar h a s h](images/c09_311.png) is applied to the associated data, the plaintext, and the data lengths to generate a hash, which is encrypted with the key  <math alttext="upper K bar m s g" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K bar m s g](images/c09_312.png) to produce a tag. The plaintext is encrypted with the CTR mode using the key  <math alttext="upper K bar m s g" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K bar m s g](images/c09_313.png) and the tag as the initial counter value. Therefore, the initial counter value is an effective nonce, which is distinct for every different initial-nonce/plaintext pair. In the event, the initial nonce repeats, the initial counter value will not repeat, if the plaintext does not repeat.

#### 9.2.5.3 Key Derivation and Hash Functions

*Key derivation function*: the encryption/decryption algorithm begins by deriving two keys, a hash key, denoted  <math alttext="upper K bar h a s h" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>h</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K bar h a s h](images/c09_314.png) and an encryption key, denoted  <math alttext="k bar m s g" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></math> ![k bar m s g](images/c09_315.png), from a master key *K* and the nonce *N*. As shown in the AES\_GCM\_SIV\_KeyDerivation function below, the length of the encryption key depends on the length of the master key (i.e. 128 or 256 bits).

***Hash function***  <math alttext="upper P o l y v a l" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>y</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P o l y v a l](images/c09_329.png)

Consider the polynomial  <math alttext="upper Q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 127 Baseline plus x Superscript 124 Baseline plus x Superscript 121 Baseline plus x Superscript 114 Baseline plus 1 period" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>127</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>124</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>121</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>114</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1.</mn></mrow></math> ![upper Q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x Superscript 127 Baseline plus x Superscript 124 Baseline plus x Superscript 121 Baseline plus x Superscript 114 Baseline plus 1 period](images/c09_372.png)  <math alttext="upper Q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper Q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c09_373.png) is represented as  <math alttext="01 00000000000000000000000000 04 92" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>01</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>00000000000000000000000000</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>04</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>92</mn></mrow></math> ![01 00000000000000000000000000 04 92](images/c09_374.png) in AES-GCM-SIV and as  <math alttext="80 0000000000000000000000000000 20 49" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>80</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0000000000000000000000000000</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>20</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>49</mn></mrow></math> ![80 0000000000000000000000000000 20 49](images/c09_375.png) in AES-GCM.

#### 9.2.5.4 Authenticated Encryption with AES-GCM-SIV

AES-GCM-SIV authenticated encryption takes a master key *K* of 128 or 256-bit length, a nonce *N* of 96-bit length, a plaintext *P*, and associated data *A*; *P* and *A* are byte strings of variable length. It returns a ciphertext *C* and a 128-bit tag,  <math alttext="upper T a g" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></math> ![upper T a g](images/c09_376.png). The AES-128 or AES-256 is used depending on the master key length. The authenticated encryption runs in three main steps:

1.  *Key derivation*: from the master key *K* and the nonce *N*, two keys are derived:  <math alttext="k bar h a s h" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>h</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> ![k bar h a s h](images/c09_377.png) of 128-bit length and  <math alttext="k bar m s g" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></math> ![k bar m s g](images/c09_378.png) of 128 or 256-bit length.
2.  *Hash generation*: the  <math alttext="upper P o l y v a l Subscript upper K bar upper H a s h Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>y</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>a</mi><msub><mi>l</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper P o l y v a l Subscript upper K bar upper H a s h Baseline](images/c09_379.png) hash function takes the hash key  <math alttext="upper K bar h a s h" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>h</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K bar h a s h](images/c09_380.png), the padded associated data, the padded plaintext, and the data lengths  <math alttext="l e n left-parenthesis upper A right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![l e n left-parenthesis upper A right-parenthesis](images/c09_381.png) and  <math alttext="l e n left-parenthesis upper P right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![l e n left-parenthesis upper P right-parenthesis](images/c09_382.png) and returns a hash. The generated hash is encrypted with the encryption key  <math alttext="upper K bar m s g" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K bar m s g](images/c09_383.png).
3.  *Plaintext encryption*: it is performed with a CTR encryption taking the key  <math alttext="upper K bar m s g" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K bar m s g](images/c09_384.png) and the encrypted tag as the initial counter value. The CTR mode used in AES-GCM-SIV is very similar to that used in AES-GCM; the minor difference is in counter incrementing due to integer encoding.

The authenticated encryption of AES-GCM-SIV algorithm is given below and is illustrated by [Figure 9.10](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0010).

![Figure 9.10 AES-GCM-SIV authenticated encryption.](images/c09f010.png)

#### 9.2.5.5 Authenticated Decryption with AES-GCM-SIV

The decryption algorithm below makes use of the same functions as the encryption algorithm.

### 9.2.6 Poly1305

Poly1305 is a fast algorithm to generate message tags. Initially Poly1305 was proposed under the name Poly1305-AES to be used jointly with AES \[[5](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0005)\]. Poly1305 is not yet approved by the NIST as a mode of operation of AES. However, it is recommended as one of the schemes to build AEAD algorithms used in TLS \[[6](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0006)\]. In TLS, the Poly1305 is used jointly with the stream cipher ChaCha20 (see Section 6.2.5); and their combination is referred to as ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD.

#### 9.2.6.1 Poly1305-AES

To generate a tag, Poly1305-AES makes use of:

*   One-time[⁵](#c09.xhtml#c09-note-0005) key of 32 bytes divided into two equal-size keys
*   an AES-128 key, denoted *s*, and an additional 128-bit key, denoted *r*;  <math alttext="r left-bracket 0 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 0 right-bracket](images/c09_436.png),  <math alttext="r left-bracket 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 1 right-bracket](images/c09_437.png), …,  <math alttext="r left-bracket 15 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 15 right-bracket](images/c09_438.png) denote the bytes of the additional key
*   a 128-bit nonce, *n*
*   a message *m* of variable byte-length

*Additional key* *r*

The additional key *r* is not used to encrypt or decrypt. It is an integer in little-endian encoding, i.e.  <math alttext="r equals r left-bracket 0 right-bracket plus 2 Superscript 8 Baseline r left-bracket 1 right-bracket plus 2 Superscript 16 Baseline r left-bracket 2 right-bracket plus ellipsis 2 Superscript 120 Baseline r left-bracket 15 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>8</mn></msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>120</mn></mrow></msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r equals r left-bracket 0 right-bracket plus 2 Superscript 8 Baseline r left-bracket 1 right-bracket plus 2 Superscript 16 Baseline r left-bracket 2 right-bracket plus ellipsis 2 Superscript 120 Baseline r left-bracket 15 right-bracket](images/c09_439.png). *r* must be a positive integer with the following restrictions:

*   The four most-significant bits of bytes  <math alttext="r left-bracket 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>\[</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 3](images/c09_440.png)\],  <math alttext="r left-bracket 7 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 7 right-bracket](images/c09_441.png),  <math alttext="r left-bracket 11 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 11 right-bracket](images/c09_442.png), and  <math alttext="r left-bracket 15 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 15 right-bracket](images/c09_443.png) must be zeros; i.e.  <math alttext="r left-bracket 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>\[</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 3](images/c09_444.png)\],  <math alttext="r left-bracket 7 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 7 right-bracket](images/c09_445.png),  <math alttext="r left-bracket 11 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 11 right-bracket](images/c09_446.png), and  <math alttext="r left-bracket 15 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 15 right-bracket](images/c09_447.png) take values smaller than 16.
*   The two least-significant bits of bytes  <math alttext="r left-bracket 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>\[</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 4](images/c09_448.png)\],  <math alttext="r left-bracket 8 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 8 right-bracket](images/c09_449.png), and  <math alttext="r left-bracket 12 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 12 right-bracket](images/c09_450.png) must be zeros; i.e.  <math alttext="r left-bracket 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>\[</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 4](images/c09_451.png)\],  <math alttext="r left-bracket 8 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 8 right-bracket](images/c09_452.png), and  <math alttext="r left-bracket 12 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 12 right-bracket](images/c09_453.png) take values divisible by 4.

*r* can be obtained by picking a random integer *z* in interval  <math alttext="left-bracket 0 comma 2 Superscript 128 Baseline left-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup><mo>(</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 0 comma 2 Superscript 128 Baseline left-parenthesis](images/c09_454.png) and applying the “and” operation (denoted ∧) to *z* in big-endian, using a mask as follows:

 <math alttext="r equals z" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></math> ![r equals z](images/c09_455.png) ∧  <math alttext="left-bracket 0 f ff ff fc 0 f ff ff fc 0 f ff ff fc 0 f ff ff ff right-bracket Subscript 16 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mtext>f&#160;ff&#160;ff&#160;fc&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mtext>f&#160;ff&#160;ff&#160;fc&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mtext>f&#160;ff&#160;ff&#160;fc&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mtext>f&#160;ff&#160;ff&#160;ff</mtext></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 0 f ff ff fc 0 f ff ff fc 0 f ff ff fc 0 f ff ff ff right-bracket Subscript 16 Baseline](images/c09_456.png)

*Message conversion and padding*

Let *m* be a message of a byte-length of *l*;  <math alttext="m left-bracket 0 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![m left-bracket 0 right-bracket](images/c09_457.png),  <math alttext="m left-bracket 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![m left-bracket 1 right-bracket](images/c09_458.png), …,  <math alttext="m left-bracket l minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![m left-bracket l minus 1 right-bracket](images/c09_459.png) denote the bytes of message *m*. Before computing the tag, conversion and padding operations are applied as follows:

1.  Split message *m* into segments of 16 bytes.
2.  Pad each 16-byte segment of message *m* to a 17-byte segment by appending one byte with the value 1.
3.  If the last segment of message *m* is of a byte-length less than 16, then append a byte with the value 1 and append bytes with the value 0, until the padded segment byte-length reaches 17. Padding with zeros does not affect the value of integers.

The pseudocode of the message conversion and padding is as follows:

*Tag generation*

Given a one-time key  <math alttext="left-parenthesis r comma k right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis r comma k right-parenthesis](images/c09_473.png), a nonce *n*, and a message *m*, which is transformed to a message *c*, the tag computation is defined by:

*Security of Poly1305-AES*

Poly1305-AES scheme is designed to ensure that a forged message is rejected with a probability of  <math alttext="1 minus left-parenthesis 14 StartFraction upper L Over 16 EndFraction right-parenthesis asterisk 2 Superscript negative 106 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>14</mn><mfrac><mi>L</mi><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>106</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![1 minus left-parenthesis 14 StartFraction upper L Over 16 EndFraction right-parenthesis asterisk 2 Superscript negative 106 Baseline](images/c09_475.png) for a *L*\-byte message, even after having observed  <math alttext="2 Superscript 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 64](images/c09_476.png) legitimate authenticated messages; thus, it is resistant against tag forgery attacks \[[5](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0005)\].

#### 9.2.6.2 ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD

Poly1305, used jointly with ChaCha20, is recommended as one of the building blocks of AEAD to implement TLS protocol. ChaCha20-Poly1305 is an adaptation of the original Poly1305-AES, where the 32-byte encryption key of Chacha20 is used to encrypt/decrypt data and to generate the one-time key  <math alttext="left-parenthesis r comma k right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis r comma k right-parenthesis](images/c09_477.png), used to generate the tag.

##### *9.2.6.2.1 Poly1305-mac*

To generate a tag for a plaintext *m*, Poly1305-mac takes the following inputs:

*   32-byte master key *K*, the key used to encrypt
*   96-bit nonce *n*
*   Message *m* of arbitrary byte-length

Tag generation follows three steps:

1.  One-time key generation: the master key *K*, the nonce *n*, and a counter with value 0 are used as input of ChaCha20 to produce a 64-byte keystream block *Y*. Only the leftmost 32 bytes of the block *Y* are used:  <math alttext="r equals upper Y left-bracket 0 period period 15 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r equals upper Y left-bracket 0 period period 15 right-bracket](images/c09_478.png) and  <math alttext="s equals upper Y left-bracket 16 period period 31 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mn>31</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![s equals upper Y left-bracket 16 period period 31 right-bracket](images/c09_479.png). Then, *r* is clamped to set to 0 some bits of bytes  <math alttext="r left-bracket 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>\[</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 3](images/c09_480.png),  <math alttext="r left-bracket 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>\[</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 4](images/c09_481.png),  <math alttext="r left-bracket 7 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 7 right-bracket](images/c09_482.png),  <math alttext="r left-bracket 8 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 8 right-bracket](images/c09_483.png),  <math alttext="r left-bracket 11 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 11 right-bracket](images/c09_484.png),  <math alttext="r left-bracket 12 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 12 right-bracket](images/c09_485.png), and  <math alttext="r left-bracket 15 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![r left-bracket 15 right-bracket](images/c09_486.png), exactly as in Poly1305-AES.
2.  Message *m* is converted and mapped as in Poly1305-AES to yield a padded plaintext *c*.
3.  Tag is computed according the following formula:

 <math alttext="t equals left-parenthesis left-parenthesis sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma q Endscripts left-parenthesis c Subscript i Baseline asterisk r Superscript left-parenthesis negative i plus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis m o d left-parenthesis 2 Superscript 130 Baseline minus 5 right-parenthesis plus s right-parenthesis right-parenthesis m o d 2 Superscript 128" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><munder><mstyle displaystyle="true" mathsize="140%"><mo>&#8721;</mo></mstyle><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>130</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![t equals left-parenthesis left-parenthesis sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma q Endscripts left-parenthesis c Subscript i Baseline asterisk r Superscript left-parenthesis negative i plus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis m o d left-parenthesis 2 Superscript 130 Baseline minus 5 right-parenthesis plus s right-parenthesis right-parenthesis m o d 2 Superscript 128](images/c09_487.png)

**Note**. Poly1305mac does not encrypt the nonce *n*, while Poly1305-AES does. Poly1305mac makes use of the nonce to generate a one-time key  <math alttext="left-parenthesis r comma s right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis r comma s right-parenthesis](images/c09_488.png), while Poly1305-AES assumes that the one-time key is given as input. In Poly1305mac, the component *s* of the one-time key is the half of a keystream block generated by ChaCha20; therefore, the encryption of the nonce in Poly1305-AES is equivalent to *s* in Poly1305mac.

##### *9.2.6.2.2 AEAD-ChaCha20-Poly1305*

ChaCha20 and Poly1305mac can be combined to build an AEAD, called AEAD-ChaCha20-Poly1305. To encrypt and generate a tag for a plaintext *P*, AEAD-ChaCha20-Poly1305 takes the following inputs:

*   256-bit encryption key *K*.
*   96-bit nonce *n*.
*   Plaintext *P* of arbitrary byte-length of at most (nearly) 256 G bytes.
*   Optional additional data *A* of at most  <math alttext="2 Superscript 64 Baseline minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 64 Baseline minus 1](images/c09_496.png) bytes.

It performs the following operations:

1.  Generate a one-time key  <math alttext="left-parenthesis r comma s right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis r comma s right-parenthesis](images/c09_497.png), using the encryption key *K* and the nonce *n*.
2.  Plaintext *P* is encrypted by ChaCha20, using key  <math alttext="upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K](images/c09_498.png); the ciphertext is denoted *C*.
3.  A tag *t* is produced by Poly1305mac, using a byte string  <math alttext="upper M a c upper D a t a" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M a c upper D a t a](images/c09_499.png) composed as follows:  <math alttext="upper M a c upper D a t a equals upper A StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue Append 16 left-parenthesis upper A right-parenthesis StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper C ### 9.2.7 Key Wrapping Modes

The authenticated-encryption algorithms presented in the previous subsections provide confidentiality and authentication guarantees. In addition to those algorithms, three modes of operation have been approved by NIST as modes to provide confidentiality and authentication guarantees to protect cryptographic keys when exchanged between two parties via an untrusted channel. Indeed, cryptographic keys are of prime importance in any cryptosystem; thus, they require more attention when exchanged. A key wrapping mode enables to encrypt a secret key with another secret key.

The key wrapping modes are stronger than the other modes, which target general data. However, the key protection is achieved at the cost of a lower performance compared to the other authenticated-encryption algorithms. That is the reason why key wrapping modes are only recommended to encrypt/decrypt keys and other highly-critical data.

***Definition 9.6 Key wrapping**: it is a symmetric cryptographic scheme, which provides confidentiality and integrity guarantees for cryptographic keys when exchanged between parties; i.e. it is a method of encrypting and decrypting keys using symmetric-key cryptography.*

Key wrapping modes differ from the other authenticated-encryption modes presented in previous subsections:

*   They do not generate a tag. Rather, they append (on the left of the plaintext) a constant-bit string, which is encrypted together with the plaintext, and then the decryption succeeds only if the constant-bit string is recovered at the beginning of the decryption output.
*   They do not provide capacity to use associated data.
*   They do not provide capacity to generate signatures. Recall that tags are required to generate signatures.

One may think about key wrapping as a mode of operation where the encryption of each bit of input is dependent on every other bits of input in all the blocks in a non-trivial way. In other words, key wrapping modes are based on the input diffusion.

The three key wrapping modes are called KW (AES Key Wrap), KWP (KW with Padding), and TKW (Triple DEA Key Wrap) \[[7](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0007)\]. For KW and KWP, the underlying block cipher is AES with the key length of 128, 192, or 256 bits. For TKW, the underlying block cipher is TDEA with the key length of 56 bits.

#### 9.2.7.1 KW and KWP Modes of Operation

KW and KWP are modes of operation of AES block cipher. Therefore, both modes process blocks of a length of 128 bits. Each block is split into two halves called semiblocks.[⁶](#c09.xhtml#c09-note-0006) As shown in the encryption and decryption algorithms of KW and KWP modes, the main components of KW mode are its functions denoted *W* and  <math alttext="upper W Superscript negative 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper W Superscript negative 1](images/c09_513.png); wrapping function *W* performs the encryption and unwrapping function  <math alttext="upper W Superscript negative 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper W Superscript negative 1](images/c09_514.png) the decryption. KWP is an extension of KW to process plaintexts of arbitrary length.

Wrapping function *W* takes a string *S* and splits it into *n* semiblocks. It makes use of internal variables  <math alttext="upper A Superscript t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper A Superscript t](images/c09_545.png) and  <math alttext="upper R Subscript i Superscript t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper R Subscript i Superscript t](images/c09_546.png) with  <math alttext="t equals 1 comma ellipsis comma s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> ![t equals 1 comma ellipsis comma s](images/c09_547.png),  <math alttext="s equals 6 left-parenthesis n minus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![s equals 6 left-parenthesis n minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c09_548.png),  <math alttext="i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c09_549.png). Wrapping function *W* runs *s* steps and in each step *t* ( <math alttext="t equals 1 comma ellipsis comma s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> ![t equals 1 comma ellipsis comma s](images/c09_550.png)), it performs an AES encryption and it updates variables  <math alttext="upper A Superscript t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper A Superscript t](images/c09_551.png) and  <math alttext="upper R Subscript n Superscript t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper R Subscript n Superscript t](images/c09_552.png). The variables  <math alttext="upper R Subscript k Superscript t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper R Subscript k Superscript t](images/c09_553.png), with  <math alttext="2 less-than-or-equal-to k less-than n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![2 less-than-or-equal-to k less-than n](images/c09_554.png), are updated using the values of the previous iteration as follows:  <math alttext="upper R Subscript k Superscript t Baseline equals upper R Subscript k plus 1 Superscript t minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper R Subscript k Superscript t Baseline equals upper R Subscript k plus 1 Superscript t minus 1](images/c09_555.png).

The complete algorithm is given below. Notice that: 1) the encryption starts with  <math alttext="upper A Superscript 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mn>0</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![upper A Superscript 0](images/c09_556.png), which is equal to the constant value  <math alttext="0 normal x upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> ![0 normal x upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6](images/c09_557.png), then the encryption output is propagated to the subsequent iterations, 2) the constant value is the only way to check the authenticity and its encryption is embedded in all the ciphertext bits. Therefore, no tag is generated. [Figure 9.12](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0012) depicts the operations of wrapping function *W* for encrypting four semiblocks  <math alttext="upper S 1 comma upper S 2 comma upper S 3 comma upper S 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S 1 comma upper S 2 comma upper S 3 comma upper S 4](images/c09_558.png). The wires on the top convey the most significant 64 bits and the wires on the bottom the least significant 64 bits of the input or the output of the AES encryption.

#### 9.2.7.3 Security of Key Wrapping Modes

First, wrapping key modes are deterministic; i.e. the ciphertext does not change, if the plaintext does not. Consequently, to prevent attacks based on repetitions of plaintext, it is recommended to include a nonce in each plaintext occurrence.

Second, as previously emphasized in other authenticated-encryption modes, if the authenticity verification fails when applying the key wrapping decryption, then there is no doubt, the ciphertext is not authentic. However, if the authenticity verification succeeds, there is no absolute assurance that the recovered plaintext is authentic, because of forgery attacks. The probability that an adversary would be able to forge a ciphertext that would be wrongly validated by the recipient should be addressed before using key wrapping modes. Recall that the authenticity verification in key wrapping modes is to check if the leftmost substring yielded by the decryption is equal to a constant bit-string (which equals  <math alttext="0 normal x upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> ![0 normal x upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6](images/c09_621.png) for KW,  <math alttext="0 normal x upper A Baseline 65959 upper A Baseline 6" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>A</mi><mn>65959</mn><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> ![0 normal x upper A Baseline 65959 upper A Baseline 6](images/c09_622.png) for KWP, and  <math alttext="0 normal x upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> ![0 normal x upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6 upper A Baseline 6](images/c09_623.png) for TKW). Recall also that KWP pads the plaintext bit-length on the right of the constant  <math alttext="0 normal x upper A Baseline 65959 upper A Baseline 6" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>A</mi><mn>65959</mn><mi>A</mi><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> ![0 normal x upper A Baseline 65959 upper A Baseline 6](images/c09_624.png), which results in a 64-bit string. Therefore, the probability to produce a valid ciphertext is  <math alttext="2 Superscript negative 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript negative 64](images/c09_625.png) for KW and KWP and  <math alttext="2 Superscript negative 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript negative 32](images/c09_626.png) for TKW. It is worth noticing that TKW mode is vulnerable to forgery attacks.

Third, cryptanalysis of key wrapping modes showed that these modes are vulnerable to attacks based on very long messages. In two very long messages, collisions located at some positions may occur and then may be used to design some attacks. To address such a vulnerability, the plaintext length is limited to  <math alttext="2 Superscript 60" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>60</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 60](images/c09_627.png),  <math alttext="2 Superscript 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 32](images/c09_628.png), and  <math alttext="2 Superscript 33" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>33</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 33](images/c09_629.png) bytes for KW, WP, and TKW, respectively.

### 9.2.8 Security of Authenticated-Encryption Modes

When a block cipher is used for confidentiality and/or authentication, the security goal is to prevent an adversary with limited computational power i) to learn any information on the plaintext, and/or ii) to alter the ciphertext or the plaintext while forging a valid MAC. Summarized below are the main vulnerabilities of authenticated-encryption modes addressed in literature.

#### 9.2.8.1 Block Repetitions and Replay

CMAC aims at providing message authenticity only. It is based on CBC, but without using an IV. Therefore, CMAC mode does not inherently protect against replay attacks. Indeed, the same message with its MAC may be re-sent multiple times by the attacker, and the recipient tag verification process validates all the (re)sent messages. However, since the plaintext is sent in clear, detection of plaintext repetitions does not matter in CMAC.

CCM, GCM, and AES-GCM-SIV are based on CTR and CBC mode with a nonce. Therefore, replay attacks can be easily detected. Since all those three modes make use of a nonce, they hide plaintext repetitions.

#### 9.2.8.2 Chosen-Ciphertext Attacks

With authenticated encryption, the task of adversary becomes (extremely) hard to disclose keys or plaintexts. It is worth noticing that the authenticated encryption can provide security against chosen-ciphertext attacks in which the adversary attempts to gain advantage (such as recovering the key) by submitting chosen ciphertexts to a decryption oracle. Authenticated decryption can easily recognize improperly built ciphertexts and do not decrypt them. Thus, adversary cannot select ciphertexts and receive their plaintexts.

#### 9.2.8.3 Birthday Attacks

MAC forgery attacks depend on  <math alttext="upper T l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper T l e n](images/c09_630.png), the bit-length of the tag. The probability that the attacker randomly guesses the MAC, which matches the ciphertext he/she modified, is  <math alttext="2 Superscript minus upper T l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>T</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript minus upper T l e n](images/c09_631.png). The adversary could substitute a ciphertext to another without controlling the content by trying the find a collision (i.e. two distinct ciphertexts with the same tag). By the birthday paradox, the adversary needs to use (i.e. intercepts) at least  <math alttext="2 Superscript StartFraction upper T l e n Over 2 EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript StartFraction upper T l e n Over 2 EndFraction](images/c09_632.png).

In case of CMAC and GMAC, which are two modes that do not provide confidentiality guarantees, the adversary may alter the plaintext (because it is in cleartext) and forge the tag using birthday attacks.

#### 9.2.8.4 Bit-flipping Attacks

When MACs are of concern, the aim of the bit-flipping attack would be to change a ciphertext or plaintext block and the MAC at some positions in order to change the plaintext recovered by recipient at the same positions. Such type of attacks is very unlikely to succeed in MAC generating modes, because the attacker has no means to know which bits will change in the recovered plaintext when bits are changed in the ciphertext or in the tag.

#### 9.2.8.5 Nonce Misuse

Recall that nonce misuse means that two or more plaintexts are encrypted with the same nonce by mistake. CMAC mode does not use any nonce; therefore, vulnerability to nonce misuse is not relevant. GCM mode is vulnerable to nonce misuse (see [Section 9.2.4.6](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-03013)). AES-GCM-SIV provides a solution to make GCM resistant to nonce misuse.

In CCM mode, if two plaintexts are encrypted with the same nonce, the same key and the same parameter *q* (the byte-length of the byte-length of plaintext), then counter blocks used to encrypt both messages are the same. Therefore, the forbidden attack may be mounted to derive the XOR of two plaintexts.

## 9.3 Exercises and Problems

## 9.3.1 List of Exercises and Problems

***Exercise 9.1***

Consider a user who encrypts and generates tags for files of 1 G bytes using CCM. How many files can he/she process before changing the key? Hint: observe the information formatting function.

**Problem *9.1***

CMAC is known to be an improvement of CBC-MAC[⁷](#c09.xhtml#c09-note-0007) algorithm. Both algorithms perform exactly the same operations until the last plaintext block  <math alttext="upper P Subscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P Subscript n](images/c09_633.png). In CBC-MAC, the last block  <math alttext="upper P Subscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P Subscript n](images/c09_634.png) is directly encrypted, while in CMAC, it is XORed with a subkey before being encrypted in step 4 of tag generation algorithm. CBC-MAC does not make use of subkeys *K*[1] and  <math alttext="upper K 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K 2](images/c09_635.png).

Assume that the tag bit-length is the same as that of a block and the plaintext length is a multiple of block length (i.e. we consider a tag generator without truncation of the final ciphertext and without padding the last plaintext block). Show that CBC-MAC is vulnerable to the following MAC forgery attack, while CMAC is not: given two plaintexts and their tags, the adversary can generate a forged plaintext with a valid tag without knowing the key.

***Problem 9.2***

In order to generate 128-bit tags for plaintexts of a bit-length multiple of 128, Bob modifies the standard CMAC by substituting addition mod 997 to XOR operations, i.e. instead of computing  <math alttext="upper A circled-plus upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ![upper A circled-plus upper B](images/c09_636.png), as in the original CMAC, he computes  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper A plus upper B right-parenthesis m o d Baseline 997" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>997</mn></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper A plus upper B right-parenthesis m o d Baseline 997](images/c09_637.png). Bob tries three MAC schemes:

1.  Scheme 1: Bob sends an encrypted 3-block message to the bank including an amount of money to transfer to Eve and the amount is encoded in the second block. Eve intercepts a message containing an amount of $25. How can Eve increase the amount she will receive, while the final tag does not change?
2.  Scheme 2: Bob sends an encrypted 3-block message to the bank including an amount of money to transfer to Eve and the amount is encoded in the third block (i.e. the last block). Eve intercepts a message containing an amount of $25. How can Eve increase the amount she will receive, while the final tag does not change?
3.  Scheme 3: Bob sends an encrypted 3-block message to the bank including an amount of money to transfer to Eve and the amount is encoded in an incomplete third block (i.e. only the five first bits of the third block are used in the plaintext). Eve intercepts a message containing an amount of $25. How can Eve increase the amount she will receive, while the final tag does not change?

***Problem 9.3***

Consider the following variant of CMAC intended to generate tags for messages of arbitrary lengths, which are multiples of the block length. The construction uses a block cipher  <math alttext="upper E colon StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript k Baseline times StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n Baseline right-arrow StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>&#215;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper E colon StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript k Baseline times StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n Baseline right-arrow StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n](images/c09_638.png), which is assumed to be secure, and computes a tag *T* for message *M* as  <math alttext="upper T equals upper M upper A upper C left-parenthesis upper M comma upper K right-parenthesis equals upper C upper B upper C Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper M StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue l right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>B</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper T equals upper M upper A upper C left-parenthesis upper M comma upper K right-parenthesis equals upper C upper B upper C Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper M StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue l right-parenthesis](images/c09_639.png), where *l* is the bit-length of *M* represented on *n* bits. Show that the construction is insecure under chosen-plaintext attack; i.e. an adversary who can get tags of some plaintexts can forge a tag.

***Problem 9.4***

Consider the following variant of CMAC intended to generate tags for messages of arbitrary lengths, which are multiples of the block length. The construction uses a block cipher  <math alttext="upper E colon StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript k Baseline times StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n Baseline right-arrow StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>&#215;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper E colon StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript k Baseline times StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n Baseline right-arrow StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n](images/c09_640.png), which is assumed to be secure. The secret key is a pair  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper K comma upper K prime right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper K comma upper K prime right-parenthesis](images/c09_641.png). The construction takes a message *M* and computes a tag *T* as follows:  <math alttext="upper T equals upper M upper A upper C left-parenthesis upper M comma left-parenthesis upper K comma upper K prime right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper C upper B upper C Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis circled-plus upper K prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>B</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></math> ![upper T equals upper M upper A upper C left-parenthesis upper M comma left-parenthesis upper K comma upper K prime right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper C upper B upper C Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis circled-plus upper K prime](images/c09_642.png).  <math alttext="upper K prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></math> ![upper K prime](images/c09_643.png) is of a block bit-length *n*, while *K* is of a bit-length of *k*, the cipher key bit-length. CBC is used with an IV of a fixed value 0. Show that the construction is insecure under the chosen-plaintext attack; i.e. an adversary who can get the tags of some plaintexts can forge a tag.

***Problem 9.5***

This problem addresses vulnerabilities of CMAC when a set of messages is processed with the same key assuming that the tag bit-length is the same as that of a block and the plaintext length is a multiple of block length (i.e. we consider a CMAC without performing truncation of the final ciphertext and without padding the last plaintext block).

1.  How many messages are required to have a collision (i.e. two distinct messages with the same tag) following the birthday paradox?
2.  Given two messages *M* and  <math alttext="upper M prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></math> ![upper M prime](images/c09_644.png), which have the same tag  <math alttext="upper T equals upper C upper M upper A upper C Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis equals upper C upper M upper A upper C Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper M prime right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper T equals upper C upper M upper A upper C Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis equals upper C upper M upper A upper C Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper M prime right-parenthesis](images/c09_645.png), how to build more collisions of the form  <math alttext="upper M StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper X" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>X</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper M StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper X](images/c09_646.png) and  <math alttext="upper M prime StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper X" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M prime StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper X](images/c09_647.png)? Such an attack is called length extension.
3.  Use answers to questions 1 and 2 to show how an adversary can forge a pair (message and tag) with an uncontrolled appended content.

***Problem 9.6***

This problem addresses message number limits in CMAC to prevent collision attacks. Hint: use birthday paradox.

1.  In page 13, the CMAC standard \[[2](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0002)\] recommends the following “the default recommendation is to limit the key to no more than  <math alttext="2 Superscript 48" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>48</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 48](images/c09_648.png) messages when the block size of the underlying block cipher is 128 bits, as with the AES algorithm, and  <math alttext="2 Superscript 21 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>21</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 21 Baseline](images/c09_649.png) messages when the block size is 64 bits, as with TDEA. Within these limits, the probability of a collision is expected to be less than one in a billion for the AES algorithm, and less than one in a million for TDEA.” How the recommended limits (i.e.  <math alttext="2 Superscript 48" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>48</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 48](images/c09_650.png) and  <math alttext="2 Superscript 21" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>21</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 21](images/c09_651.png)) can be substantiated?
2.  In most real-world systems, it is recommended that the adversary’s advantage should not be greater than  <math alttext="2 Superscript negative 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript negative 32](images/c09_652.png). In particular, the number of tags generated with the same key is such that the probability of tag collision should not be greater than  <math alttext="2 Superscript negative 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript negative 32](images/c09_653.png). What is the limit on message number to tag with AES-CMAC and TDEA-CMAC, both using the same key, such that collision risk does not exceed  <math alttext="2 Superscript negative 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript negative 32](images/c09_654.png)?

***Problem 9.7***

Show that ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD does not assure confidentiality protection, if the nonce is reused for two distinct messages.

***Problem 9.8***

In this problem, we want to show that Poly1305-AES is secure against forgery attacks, even if one-time key  <math alttext="left-parenthesis r comma s right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis r comma s right-parenthesis](images/c09_655.png) and nonce *n* are both reused to compute tags for two distinct plaintexts *m* and  <math alttext="m prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></math> ![m prime](images/c09_656.png), both of the same byte-length of 16. To simplify the problem, assume that  <math alttext="m prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></math> ![m prime](images/c09_657.png) is no less than *m*. Discuss why forging a plaintext *f* using *m*,  <math alttext="m prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></math> ![m prime](images/c09_658.png), and their tags cannot succeed. For example, try to find a tag for  <math alttext="f equals m prime minus m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![f equals m prime minus m](images/c09_659.png), assuming that one-time key  <math alttext="left-parenthesis r comma s right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis r comma s right-parenthesis](images/c09_660.png) and nonce *n* are unknown to the adversary.

Payload length is 1 G bytes. 1 G =  <math alttext="2 Superscript 30" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>30</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 30](images/c09_661.png); thus, *q* the byte-length of the payload length is 4. In formatting function, the nonce is represented on bytes 1 to  <math alttext="15 minus q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>15</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![15 minus q](images/c09_662.png) of the block  <math alttext="upper B 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper B 0](images/c09_663.png). Hence, the maximum distinct values of nonces is  <math alttext="2 Superscript 11 asterisk 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>11</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 11 asterisk 8](images/c09_665.png). Since each file requires a distinct nonce, the maximum number of files to encrypt and authenticate with the same key is  <math alttext="2 Superscript 88" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>88</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 88](images/c09_666.png).

***Problem 9.2***

1.  Scheme 1: the CMAC scheme designed by Bob to generate a 128-bit tag for each 3-block message  <math alttext="upper P equals left-parenthesis upper P 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P 2 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P 3 Superscript asterisk Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mn>3</mn><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P equals left-parenthesis upper P 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P 2 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P 3 Superscript asterisk Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c09_702.png) is as follows:

    Let  <math alttext="upper A m t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> ![upper A m t](images/c09_705.png) denote the amount included in the second block of *P*.
    
    By CMAC design,  <math alttext="upper P 3 equals left-parenthesis upper K 1 plus upper P 3 Superscript asterisk Baseline right-parenthesis m o d Baseline 997" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mn>3</mn><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>997</mn></mrow></math> ![upper P 3 equals left-parenthesis upper K 1 plus upper P 3 Superscript asterisk Baseline right-parenthesis m o d Baseline 997](images/c09_706.png), when  <math alttext="upper P 3 Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mn>3</mn><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper P 3 Superscript asterisk](images/c09_707.png) is a complete block

Scheme 2: the CMAC scheme designed by Bob to generate a 128-bit tag for each 3-block message  <math alttext="upper P equals left-parenthesis upper P 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P 2 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P 3 Superscript asterisk Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mn>3</mn><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P equals left-parenthesis upper P 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P 2 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper P 3 Superscript asterisk Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c09_717.png) is as follows:

     <math alttext="upper C 0 equals 0 Superscript b" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>0</mn><mi>b</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper C 0 equals 0 Superscript b](images/c09_722.png)

     <math alttext="upper T equals upper B o b bar upper M upper A upper C bar upper G e n e r a t i o n left-parenthesis upper K comma upper P right-parenthesis equals upper E n c Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper C 2 plus upper P 3 right-parenthesis m o d 997" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>b</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>G</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>(</mo><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>997</mn></mrow></math> ![upper T equals upper B o b bar upper M upper A upper C bar upper G e n e r a t i o n left-parenthesis upper K comma upper P right-parenthesis equals upper E n c Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper C 2 plus upper P 3 right-parenthesis m o d 997](images/c09_727.png) <math alttext="equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper C 2 plus upper A m t plus upper K 1 right-parenthesis m o d 997 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>A</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>997</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper C 2 plus upper A m t plus upper K 1 right-parenthesis m o d 997 right-parenthesis](images/c09_728.png)

3.  Scheme 3: the amount of money is included in the third block and encoded, so that it contains only the amount; i.e. the last block of the plaintext is incomplete. That is, Bob’s MAC scheme becomes: <math alttext="upper B o b bar upper M upper A upper C bar upper G e n e r a t i o n left-parenthesis upper K comma upper P right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>b</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>G</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper B o b bar upper M upper A upper C bar upper G e n e r a t i o n left-parenthesis upper K comma upper P right-parenthesis](images/c09_731.png):
    
     <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper K 1 comma upper K 2 right-parenthesis equals upper C upper M upper A upper C bar upper S u b k e y bar upper G e n e r a t i o n left-parenthesis upper K comma 128 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>S</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>b</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>G</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>128</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper K 1 comma upper K 2 right-parenthesis equals upper C upper M upper A upper C bar upper S u b k e y bar upper G e n e r a t i o n left-parenthesis upper K comma 128 right-parenthesis](images/c09_732.png)
    
    Let  <math alttext="upper A m t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> ![upper A m t](images/c09_733.png) denote the amount included in the third block of *P* denoted  <math alttext="upper P 3 Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mn>3</mn><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper P 3 Superscript asterisk](images/c09_734.png).
    
     <math alttext="j equals 128 minus l e n left-parenthesis upper P 3 Superscript asterisk Baseline right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mn>3</mn><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![j equals 128 minus l e n left-parenthesis upper P 3 Superscript asterisk Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c09_735.png) <math alttext="upper P 3 equals upper K 2 circled-plus left-parenthesis upper P 3 Superscript asterisk Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue 0 Superscript j Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mo>(</mo><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mn>3</mn><mo>\*</mo></msubsup><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><msup><mn>0</mn><mi>j</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper P 3 equals upper K 2 circled-plus left-parenthesis upper P 3 Superscript asterisk Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue 0 Superscript j Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c09_736.png) <math alttext="upper C 0 equals 0 Superscript b" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>0</mn><mi>b</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper C 0 equals 0 Superscript b](images/c09_737.png)
    
    for  <math alttext="i equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![i equals 1](images/c09_738.png) to  <math alttext="3 colon upper C Subscript i Baseline equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i minus 1 Baseline plus upper P Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis m o d Baseline 997 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>997</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![3 colon upper C Subscript i Baseline equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i minus 1 Baseline plus upper P Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis m o d Baseline 997 right-parenthesis](images/c09_739.png)

    The tag generated by Bob is:

    If Eve increases the amount by *x*, then:

    The conclusion is that the modulo operator is not appropriate to design MAC schemes, as suggested by Bob.
    

***Problem 9.3***

As a solution to the problem, we discuss a forgery attack with a 3-block message.

By construction of the proposed MAC scheme:

***Problem 9.4***

The tag forgery attack may be designed as follows:

1.  The adversary gets two tags:
