***Problem 9.5***

1.  With a tag bit-length of *b*, the number of distinct tags is  <math alttext="2 Superscript b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript b](images/c09_766.png). From the birthday paradox (in Section 3.4), we can deduce that if the number of messages (for which the tags have been produced with the same key *K*) known to the adversary is close to  <math alttext="2 Superscript b slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript b slash 2](images/c09_767.png), then there exists a high probability that two distinct messages *M* and  <math alttext="upper M prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></math> ![upper M prime](images/c09_768.png) have the same tag; i.e.  <math alttext="upper C upper M upper A upper C Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis equals upper C upper M upper A upper C Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis upper M prime right-parenthesis equals upper T" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C upper M upper A upper C Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis equals upper C upper M upper A upper C Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis upper M prime right-parenthesis equals upper T](images/c09_769.png).
    
2.  Assume that two messages *M* and  <math alttext="upper M prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> ![upper M prime](images/c09_770.png) are known and they have the same tag under the key in use; i.e.  <math alttext="upper T equals upper C upper M upper A upper C Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis equals upper C upper M upper A upper C Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper M prime right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper T equals upper C upper M upper A upper C Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis equals upper C upper M upper A upper C Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper M prime right-parenthesis](images/c09_771.png). Let *n* and  <math alttext="n prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></math> ![n prime](images/c09_772.png) denote the number of blocks of messages *M* and  <math alttext="upper M prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></math> ![upper M prime](images/c09_773.png), respectively. Let  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i](images/c09_774.png),  <math alttext="i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c09_775.png), and  <math alttext="upper C prime Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C prime Subscript j](images/c09_776.png),  <math alttext="j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></math> ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n prime](images/c09_777.png), denote the ciphertext blocks computed for messages *M* and  <math alttext="upper M prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></math> ![upper M prime](images/c09_778.png), respectively. Since any plaintext block is of length *b*, only the subkey *K*[1] is used. The tag of both messages is computed as follows:
    
     <math alttext="upper T equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C Subscript n minus 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K 1 circled-plus upper M Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C prime Subscript n prime minus 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K Subscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper M prime Subscript n Sub Superscript prime Subscript right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>M</mi><msup><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper T equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C Subscript n minus 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K 1 circled-plus upper M Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C prime Subscript n prime minus 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K Subscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper M prime Subscript n Sub Superscript prime Subscript right-parenthesis](images/c09_779.png)

Thus,  <math alttext="upper C Subscript n minus 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K 1 circled-plus upper M Subscript n Baseline equals upper C prime Subscript n prime minus 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K Subscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper M Subscript n Sub Superscript prime Subscript Superscript prime Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>M</mi><msup><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript n minus 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K 1 circled-plus upper M Subscript n Baseline equals upper C prime Subscript n prime minus 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K Subscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper M Subscript n Sub Superscript prime Subscript Superscript prime Baseline](images/c09_780.png)

 <math alttext="upper C Subscript n minus 1 Baseline circled-plus upper M Subscript n Baseline equals upper C Subscript n prime minus 1 Superscript prime Baseline circled-plus upper M prime Subscript n Sub Superscript prime Subscript" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>M</mi><msup><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript n minus 1 Baseline circled-plus upper M Subscript n Baseline equals upper C Subscript n prime minus 1 Superscript prime Baseline circled-plus upper M prime Subscript n Sub Superscript prime Subscript](images/c09_781.png)(a) 

Now, extend both messages with the same bit string *X* of *p* blocks.

 <math alttext="upper M Superscript 1 Baseline equals upper M StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper X" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M Superscript 1 Baseline equals upper M StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper X](images/c09_782.png) and  <math alttext="upper M squared equals upper M prime StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper X" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M squared equals upper M prime StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper X](images/c09_783.png)

Let  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i Superscript 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i Superscript 1](images/c09_784.png),  <math alttext="i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n plus l e n left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n plus l e n left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis](images/c09_785.png), and  <math alttext="upper C Subscript j Superscript 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript j Superscript 2](images/c09_786.png),  <math alttext="j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n prime plus l e n left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis comma" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n prime plus l e n left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis comma](images/c09_787.png) denote the ciphertext blocks computed for messages  <math alttext="upper M Superscript 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![upper M Superscript 1](images/c09_788.png) and  <math alttext="upper M squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![upper M squared](images/c09_789.png), respectively.

Then, continuing the encryption of  <math alttext="upper M Superscript 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![upper M Superscript 1](images/c09_793.png) and  <math alttext="upper M squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![upper M squared](images/c09_794.png) blocks, yields:

 <math alttext="upper C Subscript n plus d Superscript 1 Baseline equals upper C Subscript n prime plus d Superscript 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript n plus d Superscript 1 Baseline equals upper C Subscript n prime plus d Superscript 2](images/c09_795.png), for  <math alttext="d equals 1 comma ellipsis comma l e n left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![d equals 1 comma ellipsis comma l e n left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis](images/c09_796.png)

Thus,  <math alttext="upper C upper M upper A upper C Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper M StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper X right-parenthesis equals upper C upper M upper A upper C Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper M prime StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper X right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C upper M upper A upper C Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper M StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper X right-parenthesis equals upper C upper M upper A upper C Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper M prime StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper X right-parenthesis](images/c09_797.png). Any value of *X* results in a collision discovery.

*   3) According to the birthday paradox, the attacker needs  <math alttext="2 Superscript b slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript b slash 2](images/c09_798.png) messages and their MACs to observe a collision  <math alttext="upper T equals upper C upper M upper A upper C Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis equals upper C upper M upper A upper C Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper M prime right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper T equals upper C upper M upper A upper C Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis equals upper C upper M upper A upper C Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper M prime right-parenthesis](images/c09_799.png). Next, he/she needs to get a message  <math alttext="upper M double-prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8243;</mo></msup></math> ![upper M double-prime](images/c09_800.png) starting with either *M* or  <math alttext="upper M prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> ![upper M prime](images/c09_801.png) and its tag is  <math alttext="upper T double-prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8243;</mo></msup></math> ![upper T double-prime](images/c09_802.png). Using the answer to question 2, the attacker makes a substitution in the first part of  <math alttext="upper M double-prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8243;</mo></msup></math> ![upper M double-prime](images/c09_803.png). If  <math alttext="upper M double-prime equals upper M StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper X" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8243;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M double-prime equals upper M StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper X](images/c09_804.png), then the forged pair is  <math alttext="left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper M prime StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper X right-parenthesis comma upper T prime prime right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo><mo>&#8242;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper M prime StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper X right-parenthesis comma upper T prime prime right-parenthesis](images/c09_805.png). Otherwise, it is  <math alttext="left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper M StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper X right-parenthesis comma upper T prime prime right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo><mo>&#8242;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper M StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper X right-parenthesis comma upper T prime prime right-parenthesis](images/c09_806.png). The forged pair will be validated by the recipient, because it has a valid tag.

***Problem 9.6***

If one generates tags for  <math alttext="2 Superscript 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 128](images/c09_807.png) messages with AES-CMAC or  <math alttext="2 Superscript 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 64](images/c09_808.png) messages with TDEA-CMAC, the probability of collision (i.e. two messages map to the same tag) is 1. In general, when tag generation is of concern, the number of messages processed with the same key should not exceed a specific limit to make the risk of collision below some desired threshold.

Recall that the generalization of the birthday paradox (see Section 3.4) states that: given any set of *M* values with a uniform distribution, the probability  <math alttext="upper P r left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper P r left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis](images/c09_809.png) two values among *n* values from the set are identical is given by:  <math alttext="n almost-equals StartRoot 2 asterisk upper M asterisk upper P r left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis EndRoot" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8776;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><mi>M</mi><mtext>\*</mtext><mi>P</mi><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> ![n almost-equals StartRoot 2 asterisk upper M asterisk upper P r left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis EndRoot](images/c09_810.png). We apply the birthday paradox formula to prove the validity of the statement included in the CMAC standard. In this problem, *M* is the number of distinct tags and *n* the number of messages required for a collision to occur at a probability of  <math alttext="upper P r left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P r left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis](images/c09_811.png).

1.  Proof of statement in CMAC standard

The birthday paradox formula can be rewritten as:  <math alttext="upper P r left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis almost-equals StartFraction n squared Over 2 upper M EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8776;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>M</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![upper P r left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis almost-equals StartFraction n squared Over 2 upper M EndFraction](images/c09_812.png). Given a collision risk threshold of *P* the number *n* of messages tagged with the same key should be such that  <math alttext="upper P r left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis less-than upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P r left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis less-than upper P](images/c09_813.png). So, the following inequality must hold:

 <math alttext="StartFraction n squared Over 2 upper M EndFraction less-than upper P" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>M</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![StartFraction n squared Over 2 upper M EndFraction less-than upper P](images/c09_814.png)(a) 

*   – Case 1: If AES-CMAC is used, then the tag space is of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 128](images/c09_815.png). One billion can be approximated by  <math alttext="2 Superscript 30" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>30</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 30](images/c09_816.png); thus, “less than one in a billion” may be replaced by “ <math alttext="less-than 2 Superscript negative 30" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#60;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![less-than 2 Superscript negative 30](images/c09_817.png)” and the collision risk threshold becomes  <math alttext="upper P equals 2 Superscript negative 30" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper P equals 2 Superscript negative 30](images/c09_818.png). By making substitutions in inequality (a):  <math alttext="StartFraction left-parenthesis 2 Superscript 48 Baseline right-parenthesis squared Over 2 asterisk 2 Superscript 128 Baseline EndFraction equals StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript 33 Baseline EndFraction less-than StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript 30 Baseline EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>48</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>33</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#60;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>30</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![StartFraction left-parenthesis 2 Superscript 48 Baseline right-parenthesis squared Over 2 asterisk 2 Superscript 128 Baseline EndFraction equals StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript 33 Baseline EndFraction less-than StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript 30 Baseline EndFraction](images/c09_819.png).
*   – Case 2: If TDEA-CMAC is used, then the tag space is of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 64](images/c09_820.png). One million can be approximated by  <math alttext="2 Superscript 20" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 20](images/c09_821.png); thus, “less than one in a million” may be replaced by “ <math alttext="less-than 2 Superscript negative 20" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#60;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![less-than 2 Superscript negative 20](images/c09_822.png)” and the collision risk threshold becomes  <math alttext="upper P equals 2 Superscript negative 20" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper P equals 2 Superscript negative 20](images/c09_823.png). By making substitutions in inequality (a):  <math alttext="StartFraction left-parenthesis 2 Superscript 21 Baseline right-parenthesis squared Over 2 asterisk 2 Superscript 64 Baseline EndFraction equals StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript 23 Baseline EndFraction less-than StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript 20 Baseline EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>21</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>23</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#60;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![StartFraction left-parenthesis 2 Superscript 21 Baseline right-parenthesis squared Over 2 asterisk 2 Superscript 64 Baseline EndFraction equals StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript 23 Baseline EndFraction less-than StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript 20 Baseline EndFraction](images/c09_824.png).

In both cases, the bound on the collision risk is not exceeded, if the limit on the number of messages is fulfilled. Therefore, the statement in CMAC standard is valid.

*   2) Limit of message to tag with a collision risk not greater than =  <math alttext="2 Superscript negative 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript negative 32](images/c09_825.png)

Rearrange inequality (a) as  <math alttext="n less-than StartRoot 2 asterisk upper M asterisk upper P EndRoot" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mtext>\*</mtext><mi>M</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> ![n less-than StartRoot 2 asterisk upper M asterisk upper P EndRoot](images/c09_826.png), then make substitutions.

*   – Case 1: AES-CMAC:  <math alttext="n less-than StartRoot 2 asterisk 2 Superscript 128 Baseline asterisk 2 Superscript negative 32 Baseline EndRoot equals StartRoot 2 EndRoot asterisk 2 Superscript 48" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mtext>\*</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msqrt><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>48</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![n less-than StartRoot 2 asterisk 2 Superscript 128 Baseline asterisk 2 Superscript negative 32 Baseline EndRoot equals StartRoot 2 EndRoot asterisk 2 Superscript 48](images/c09_827.png)
*   – Case 2: TDEA-CMAC:  <math alttext="n less-than StartRoot 2 asterisk 2 Superscript 64 Baseline asterisk 2 Superscript negative 32 Baseline EndRoot equals StartRoot 2 EndRoot asterisk 2 Superscript 21" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mtext>\*</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msqrt><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>21</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![n less-than StartRoot 2 asterisk 2 Superscript 64 Baseline asterisk 2 Superscript negative 32 Baseline EndRoot equals StartRoot 2 EndRoot asterisk 2 Superscript 21](images/c09_828.png)

In conclusion, the statement given in CMAC standard is an undersizing of limits yielded for a collision risk not greater than  <math alttext="2 Superscript negative 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript negative 32](images/c09_829.png) in order to provide an easy way to appreciate the impact of message number on the tag collision occurrence.□

***Problem 9.7***

Assume that an encryption key *K* and nonce *n* are reused to encrypt two plaintexts *m* and  <math alttext="m prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></math> ![m prime](images/c09_830.png) of the same byte-length *l*. If the key *K* and the nonce *n* are used twice, the generated keystream string is the same for both executions of ChaCha20. Let *Y* denote the generated keystream string, using key *K* and nonce *n*. Since ChaCha20 is a stream cipher, the produced ciphertexts are  <math alttext="upper C equals m circled-plus upper Y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C equals m circled-plus upper Y](images/c09_831.png) and  <math alttext="upper C prime equals m prime circled-plus upper Y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C prime equals m prime circled-plus upper Y](images/c09_832.png). From  <math alttext="upper C circled-plus upper C prime equals m circled-plus m prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></math> ![upper C circled-plus upper C prime equals m circled-plus m prime](images/c09_833.png), one can derive useful information regarding the plaintexts; thus, confidentiality is compromised.

***Problem 9.8***

The lengths of both messages *m* and  <math alttext="m prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></math> ![m prime](images/c09_834.png) are of 16 bytes. Therefore, the conversion and padding operations result in adding  <math alttext="2 Superscript 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 128](images/c09_835.png) to each plaintext (we omit the little-endian encoding). Two padded plaintexts *c* and  <math alttext="c prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>c</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> ![c prime](images/c09_836.png) are yielded; then, two tags *t* and  <math alttext="t prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></math> ![t prime](images/c09_837.png) are computed. Since both initial plaintexts are of a 16-byte-length, tags are computed as:

Since *r*, *s*, and *n* are unknown to the adversary, he/she cannot compute the second component of right part of the last equality. Therefore, Poly1305-AES is secure against the suggested forgery attack.

## Notes

1.  [**1**](#c09.xhtml#rc09-note-0001) In literature, the acronym AEAD is expanded as either “Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data” or “Authenticated Encryption with Additional Data,” which are the same notion.
2.  [**2**](#c09.xhtml#rc09-note-0002) It is worth noticing that in this chapter, *authentication* refers to *data authenticity* and not to *user authentication* (e.g. with a password or biometrics), which is another aspect of security.
3.  [**3**](#c09.xhtml#rc09-note-0003) Notice that to be standard-complying, applications should not use the same key and nonce to process distinct messages.
4.  [**4**](#c09.xhtml#rc09-note-0004) AES-GCM means GCM mode of operation of AES bock cipher.
5.  [**5**](#c09.xhtml#rc09-note-0005) For each tag to compute, a distinct 32-byte key is used. So, the sender and recipient of tagged messages must agree on a procedure (e.g. a key derivation function) to generate one-time keys from a session key.
6.  [**6**](#c09.xhtml#rc09-note-0006) A *semiblock* is the half of a block, i.e. a 64-bit substring, if AES is used and a 32-bit substring, if TDEA is used.
7.  [**7**](#c09.xhtml#rc09-note-0007) CBC-MAC has not been approved as standard because of its vulnerabilities.

# 10   
Introduction to Security Analysis of Block Ciphers

Modern cryptography security relies on the computational difficulty[¹](#c10.xhtml#c10-note-0001) to break ciphers rather than on the theoretical impossibility to break them. If adversaries have enough resources and time, they can break any cipher. The security analysis of block ciphers and their modes of operation is a wide field in cryptography. One approach to address the security of ciphers is to show how it is hard for adversaries to break ciphers given the resources they can use. The adversaries have access to black boxes (called oracles) associated with the ciphers to attack and they try to guess some information through the exploitation of chosen plaintexts and ciphertexts. Consequently, information inference is probabilistic. The information inferred through querying a black-box is measured in terms of *adversary advantage*. Secure ciphers are those ciphers for which the advantage of adversaries is negligible if their resources and time remain below some limits. The analysis of different scenarios of attacks is an approach to assess the security of ciphers from a probabilistic point of view. In particular, security analysis aims to define bounds beyond which the use of some ciphers may become insecure.

Security analysis is based on oracles, in particular oracles modeling the encryption, decryption, MAC generation, and MAC verification operations. The cipher to analyze is put in the worst conditions; i.e. the adversaries can choose any plaintexts to encrypt or ciphertexts to decrypt or the adversaries choose MACs and then ask the oracle to verify their validity. Therefore, the interception of true plaintexts and ciphertexts is not an issue.

In general, block cipher analysis is defined using two parameters relating to the following questions:

*   What is the goal of the adversary: decrypt a ciphertext, learn something about the plaintext from the ciphertext or recover the key?
*   What is the amount of resources available to the adversary? The resources are described in terms of computation time and known plaintexts, ciphertexts, and plaintext–ciphertext pairs. In addition, the memory required to store data may be a critical issue.

Security analysis of modes of operation of block ciphers addresses two issues:

*   *Privacy*: it should be computationally infeasible for an adversary to derive any information from the ciphertexts unless the key is known. Such a property is called *perfect secrecy* \[[1](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0001)\].
*   *Authenticity*: it should be computationally infeasible for an adversary to forge a valid pair ciphertext–tag unless the key is known.

As mentioned in other chapters, cryptographic standards specify limits for the number of plaintexts to encrypt to not compromise the security. This chapter aims at introducing some security bounds, which link the plaintext limit and the expected security in terms of privacy and authenticity preserving. It is worth noticing that this chapter is far from covering the field of probabilistic security analysis.

## 10.1 Pseudorandom Functions and Permutations

Pseudorandom functions (PRFs) and pseudorandom permutations (PRPs) are basic tools in cryptography. One of the primary motivations of PRFs and PRPs is to enable the security analysis of block ciphers and their modes of operation \[[2](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0002)–[4](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0004)\]. This section presents basic definitions relevant to PRFs and PRPs.

### 10.1.1 Definitions of Random and Pseudorandom Functions and Permutations

***Definition 10.1 Function****: a function*  <math alttext="f colon German script upper M German right-arrow German script upper R" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo mathvariant="fraktur">&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8475;</mi></mrow></math> ![f colon German script upper M German right-arrow German script upper R](images/c10_1.png) *from a set*  <math alttext="German script upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi></math> ![German script upper M](images/c10_2.png)*, called function domain*, *to a set* ℛ*, called function range or codomain, assigns to each element of*  <math alttext="German script upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi></math> ![German script upper M](images/c10_3.png) *one element of* ℛ.

***Definition 10.2 Permutation***: *a permutation*  <math alttext="pi colon German script upper M right-arrow German script upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi></mrow></math> ![pi colon German script upper M right-arrow German script upper M](images/c10_4.png) *from a set*  <math alttext="German script upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi></math> ![German script upper M](images/c10_5.png)*, called permutation domain, to the set*  <math alttext="German script upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi></math> ![German script upper M](images/c10_6.png)*, is a bijective function that uniquely assigns to each element of*  <math alttext="German script upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi></math> ![German script upper M](images/c10_7.png) *one element of*  <math alttext="German script upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi></math> ![German script upper M](images/c10_8.png).

***Definition 10.3 Function family***: *a function family* *Fis a map*  <math alttext="upper F colon script upper K times German script upper M right-arrow script upper R" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8475;</mi></mrow></math> ![upper F colon script upper K times German script upper M right-arrow script upper R](images/c10_9.png)*, where*  <math alttext="script upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi></math> ![script upper K](images/c10_10.png) *denotes the key space*,  <math alttext="German script upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi></math> ![German script upper M](images/c10_11.png) *the domain of* *F, and* ℛ *its range, which also is called co-domain of* *F*.

When functions are used in cryptographic algorithm analysis, the elements (or points) of  <math alttext="script upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi></math> ![script upper K](images/c10_12.png),  <math alttext="German script upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi></math> ![German script upper M](images/c10_13.png), and ℛ are bit strings. That is,  <math alttext="script upper K equals StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![script upper K equals StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript k](images/c10_14.png),  <math alttext="German script upper M equals StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![German script upper M equals StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n](images/c10_15.png), and  <math alttext="script upper R equals StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript upper L" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#8475;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>L</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![script upper R equals StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript upper L](images/c10_16.png), where *k* denotes the key bit-length; *n* and *L* denote the bit-length of function input and output, respectively.

***Definition 10.4 Instance of a function family*:** *given a key*  <math alttext="upper K element-of script upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K element-of script upper K](images/c10_17.png)*, an instance of a function family* *F, denoted*  <math alttext="upper F Subscript upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript upper K](images/c10_18.png)*, is a map from each point*  <math alttext="x element-of German script upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi></mrow></math> ![x element-of German script upper M](images/c10_19.png) *to a point*  <math alttext="y element-of script upper R" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>&#8475;</mi></mrow></math> ![y element-of script upper R](images/c10_20.png) *such that*  <math alttext="upper F Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis right-arrow y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8594;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis right-arrow y](images/c10_21.png).

***Definition 10.5 Permutation family***: *a permutation family* *P* *is a collection of permutations with the same domain and range; i.e*.  <math alttext="upper P colon script upper K times German script upper M right-arrow German script upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P colon script upper K times German script upper M right-arrow German script upper M](images/c10_22.png).

and a permutation family  <math alttext="upper P colon script upper K times German script upper M right-arrow German script upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P colon script upper K times German script upper M right-arrow German script upper M](images/c10_34.png) is a collection of permutations  <math alttext="upper P 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P 1](images/c10_35.png),  <math alttext="upper P 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P 2](images/c10_36.png), …,  <math alttext="upper P Subscript 2 Sub Superscript k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P Subscript 2 Sub Superscript k](images/c10_37.png), each with a key in the key space  <math alttext="script upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi></math> ![script upper K](images/c10_38.png).

The collection of all functions of  <math alttext="German script upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi></math> ![German script upper M](images/c10_39.png) to ℛ is denoted  <math alttext="upper F u n c left-parenthesis German script upper M comma script upper R right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8475;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper F u n c left-parenthesis German script upper M comma script upper R right-parenthesis](images/c10_40.png); and the collection of all permutations of  <math alttext="German script upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi></math> ![German script upper M](images/c10_41.png) to  <math alttext="German script upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi></math> ![German script upper M](images/c10_42.png) is denoted  <math alttext="upper P e r m left-parenthesis German script upper M right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P e r m left-parenthesis German script upper M right-parenthesis](images/c10_43.png).

Notice the massive difference in size between *F* and  <math alttext="upper F u n c left-parenthesis German script upper M comma script upper R right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8475;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper F u n c left-parenthesis German script upper M comma script upper R right-parenthesis](images/c10_44.png) sets and between *P* and  <math alttext="upper P e r m left-parenthesis German script upper M right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P e r m left-parenthesis German script upper M right-parenthesis](images/c10_45.png) sets (see Problem 10.1):

*    <math alttext="StartAbsoluteValue upper F EndAbsoluteValue equals StartAbsoluteValue script upper K EndAbsoluteValue equals 2 Superscript k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>F</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![StartAbsoluteValue upper F EndAbsoluteValue equals StartAbsoluteValue script upper K EndAbsoluteValue equals 2 Superscript k](images/c10_46.png) and  <math alttext="StartAbsoluteValue upper F u n c left-parenthesis German script upper M comma script upper R right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue equals StartAbsoluteValue script upper R EndAbsoluteValue Superscript StartAbsoluteValue German script upper M EndAbsoluteValue Baseline equals 2 Superscript upper L asterisk 2 Super Superscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8475;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>&#8475;</mi><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![StartAbsoluteValue upper F u n c left-parenthesis German script upper M comma script upper R right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue equals StartAbsoluteValue script upper R EndAbsoluteValue Superscript StartAbsoluteValue German script upper M EndAbsoluteValue Baseline equals 2 Superscript upper L asterisk 2 Super Superscript n](images/c10_47.png)
*    <math alttext="StartAbsoluteValue upper P EndAbsoluteValue equals StartAbsoluteValue script upper K EndAbsoluteValue equals 2 Superscript k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![StartAbsoluteValue upper P EndAbsoluteValue equals StartAbsoluteValue script upper K EndAbsoluteValue equals 2 Superscript k](images/c10_48.png) and  <math alttext="StartAbsoluteValue upper P e r m left-parenthesis German script upper M right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue equals StartAbsoluteValue German script upper M EndAbsoluteValue factorial equals 2 Superscript n Baseline factorial" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>!</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>!</mo></mrow></math> ![StartAbsoluteValue upper P e r m left-parenthesis German script upper M right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue equals StartAbsoluteValue German script upper M EndAbsoluteValue factorial equals 2 Superscript n Baseline factorial](images/c10_49.png)

**Example 10.1**

AES-128 block cipher is a family of permutations that make use of 128-bit keys and 128-bit plaintext to produce 128-bit ciphertext blocks. Therefore, it is a family of permutations with  <math alttext="script upper K equals StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![script upper K equals StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript 128](images/c10_50.png) and  <math alttext="German script upper M equals StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![German script upper M equals StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript 128](images/c10_51.png).

AES-128-CMAC is a function family of algorithms that produce tags (i.e. message authentication codes) of  <math alttext="upper T l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper T l e n](images/c10_52.png)\-bit length for messages of arbitrary bit-length. Therefore, it is a function family with  <math alttext="script upper K equals StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![script upper K equals StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript 128](images/c10_53.png),  <math alttext="German script upper M equals StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo></msup></mrow></math> ![German script upper M equals StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript asterisk](images/c10_54.png), and  <math alttext="script upper R equals StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript upper T l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#8475;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![script upper R equals StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript upper T l e n](images/c10_55.png).

***Definition 10.7 Random function***: *given an element* *x* *of a domain*  <math alttext="German script upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi></math> ![German script upper M](images/c10_56.png)*, a random function*  <math alttext="normal phi" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#966;</mi></math> ![normal phi](images/c10_57.png) <math alttext="colon German script upper M right-arrow script upper R" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8475;</mi></mrow></math> ![colon German script upper M right-arrow script upper R](images/c10_58.png)*is a black-box, which returns a random element* *y* *in codomain* ℛ*. If the same input* *x* *is given to a random function φ, at multiple times, the same output* *y* *is returned. Given any distinct inputs* *x*[1] *and* *x*[2]*, the output*  <math alttext="y 1 equals phi left-parenthesis x 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![y 1 equals phi left-parenthesis x 1 right-parenthesis](images/c10_59.png) *and*  <math alttext="y 2 equals phi left-parenthesis x 2 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![y 2 equals phi left-parenthesis x 2 right-parenthesis](images/c10_60.png) *are independent*.

***Definition 10.8 Random permutation***: *given an element* *x* *of a domain*  <math alttext="German script upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi></math> ![German script upper M](images/c10_61.png)*, a random permutation*  <math alttext="pi colon German script upper M right-arrow German script upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi></mrow></math> ![pi colon German script upper M right-arrow German script upper M](images/c10_62.png) *is a black-box, which returns a random element* *y* *of*  <math alttext="German script upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi></math> ![German script upper M](images/c10_63.png)*. If an input* *x* *is given to a random permutation* π*, for the first time, the returned output is distinct from all previously returned outputs. If the same input* *x* *is given to a random permutation*  <math alttext="normal pi" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#960;</mi></math> ![normal pi](images/c10_64.png)*, at multiple times, the same output* *y* *is returned. Given any distinct inputs* *x*[1] *and* *x*[2]*, the outputs*  <math alttext="y 1 equals normal pi left-parenthesis x 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">&#960;</mi><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![y 1 equals normal pi left-parenthesis x 1 right-parenthesis](images/c10_65.png) *and*  <math alttext="y 2 equals normal pi left-parenthesis x 2 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">&#960;</mi><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![y 2 equals normal pi left-parenthesis x 2 right-parenthesis](images/c10_66.png) *are independent and distinct*.

***Definition 10.9 Pseudorandom function*** *(****PRF****): a PRF*  <math alttext="upper F colon script upper K times German script upper M right-arrow script upper R" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8475;</mi></mrow></math> ![upper F colon script upper K times German script upper M right-arrow script upper R](images/c10_67.png) *a is family of functions whose any instance is computationally indistinguishable from a random function of the function*  <math alttext="f a m i l y upper F u n c left-parenthesis upper M comma upper R right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>y</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>F</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>R</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![f a m i l y upper F u n c left-parenthesis upper M comma upper R right-parenthesis](images/c10_68.png).

***Definition 10.10 Pseudorandom permutation*** *(****PRP****): a PRP*  <math alttext="upper F colon script upper K times German script upper M right-arrow German script upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi></mrow></math> ![upper F colon script upper K times German script upper M right-arrow German script upper M](images/c10_69.png) *is a family of permutations whose any instance is computationally indistinguishable from a random instance of the permutation family*  <math alttext="upper P e r m left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>m</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper P e r m left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis](images/c10_70.png)*. A PRP* *P* *is required to be bijective, and to have an efficient inversion function*  <math alttext="upper P Superscript negative 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper P Superscript negative 1](images/c10_71.png)*; i.e*.  <math alttext="for-all upper K element-of script upper K comma" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8704;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>K</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> ![for-all upper K element-of script upper K comma](images/c10_72.png) <math alttext="upper P Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis normal k comma upper P comma left-parenthesis k comma x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals x" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis normal k comma upper P comma left-parenthesis k comma x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals x](images/c10_73.png).

A pseudorandom function family *F* (resp. PRP *P*) is *computationally indistinguishable* from a random function (resp. permutation), if an adversary that has practical computational resources and given access to an instance of the PRF *F* (resp. PRP *p*) and to a random function (resp. permutation), with the same domain and codomain; he/she cannot distinguish between the outputs of the PRF (resp. PRP) and those of the random function (resp. permutation).

### 10.1.2 Indistinguishability and Security of PRFs

***Definition 10.11 Oracle***: *an oracle of a function* *fis a (theoretical) black box that responds to every unique query with a (truly) random response chosen uniformly from the output domain of the function*.

The most commonly used approach to evaluate the security (i.e. indistinguishability) of PRFs (and also PRPs) is based on a probabilistic analysis and referred to as *Real-Or-Random* (ROR), which works as a game between a *distinguisher* *A* (called hereafter *adversary*) of a PRF *F* and a challenger (see [Figure 10.1](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0001)).

![Figure 10.1 General framework for PRF indistinguishability analysis.](images/c10f001.png)

[**Figure 10.1**](#c10.xhtml#rc10-fig-0001) General framework for PRF indistinguishability analysis.

Adversary *A* is given an interface to access two oracles and it submits one or more queries and receives answers. Before processing the first query, the game challenger, whose strategy is unknown to the adversary, uniformly selects at random a key *k* from the key space  <math alttext="script upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi></math> ![script upper K](images/c10_74.png) and a random binary *b*. For each submitted query, if  <math alttext="b equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![b equals 1](images/c10_75.png), then the query is processed with the instance function  <math alttext="upper F Subscript upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript upper K](images/c10_76.png) (i.e. processed with the oracle of *F*); and if  <math alttext="b equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![b equals 0](images/c10_77.png), then the query is processed with a random function φ selected function from the family  <math alttext="upper F u n c left-parenthesis German script upper M comma script upper R right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8475;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper F u n c left-parenthesis German script upper M comma script upper R right-parenthesis](images/c10_78.png). Upon reception of an answer, the adversary tries to guess which oracle processed its query, i.e. which value was chosen for *b*. The adversary outputs 1, if it thinks that the query was processed by an instance of PRF *F* (i.e. the received bit string is a valid ciphertext); and 0 otherwise (i.e. the received bit string is random).

Each adversary query and guess is called *experiment*. For each experiment, a quantity called *PRF-advantage* is computed to measure how the adversary is able to distinguish between the PRF and a random function:
