***Problem 10.5***

An adaptive CPA-adversary is the one that exploits the results of past queries  <math alttext="1 comma ellipsis comma q minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![1 comma ellipsis comma q minus 1](images/c10_713.png) to decide which plaintext  <math alttext="upper M Subscript q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript q](images/c10_714.png) to submit in the query *q*. For each query *i*, it receives  <math alttext="f left-parenthesis upper M Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![f left-parenthesis upper M Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c10_715.png), which is computed using either an instance of permutation family or a random permutation. A non-adaptive adversary is the one that prepares in advance a set of plaintexts  <math alttext="upper M 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 1](images/c10_716.png),  <math alttext="upper M 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 2](images/c10_717.png), …,  <math alttext="upper M Subscript q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript q](images/c10_718.png) and then queries the accessible oracle. The adversary gets a set of ciphertexts  <math alttext="f left-parenthesis upper M 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![f left-parenthesis upper M 1 right-parenthesis](images/c10_719.png),  <math alttext="f left-parenthesis upper M 2 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![f left-parenthesis upper M 2 right-parenthesis](images/c10_720.png) , …,  <math alttext="f left-parenthesis upper M Subscript q Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![f left-parenthesis upper M Subscript q Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c10_721.png), which have been computed either with an instance of a permutation family or by a random permutation.

1.  Show that a 128-bit block cipher, with 128-bit key, defined by  <math alttext="upper E Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals upper K circled-plus x" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> ![upper E Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals upper K circled-plus x](images/c10_722.png) is insecure for an adaptive adversary as well as for a non-adaptive one.
2.  Show that a 128-bit block cipher, with 128-bit key, defined by  <math alttext="upper E Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals upper K circled-plus Rotate left-parenthesis x comma upper K m o d Baseline 128 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>Rotate</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>128</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals upper K circled-plus Rotate left-parenthesis x comma upper K m o d Baseline 128 right-parenthesis](images/c10_723.png) is insecure for an adaptive adversary as well as for a non-adaptive one.  <math alttext="Rotate left-parenthesis x comma m right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>Rotate</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![Rotate left-parenthesis x comma m right-parenthesis](images/c10_724.png) is a function, which performs an *m*\-bit left-rotation of *x*.

Use the Real-or-Random security analysis model.

***Problem 10.6***

Consider an adversary against ECB that submits a pair of plaintexts  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper M 1 comma upper M 2 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper M 1 comma upper M 2 right-parenthesis](images/c10_725.png) each of two blocks,  <math alttext="upper M 1 equals left-bracket 0 right-bracket Subscript n Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue left-bracket 0 right-bracket Subscript n Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 1 equals left-bracket 0 right-bracket Subscript n Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue left-bracket 0 right-bracket Subscript n Baseline](images/c10_726.png) and  <math alttext="upper M 2 equals left-bracket 0 right-bracket Subscript n Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue left-bracket 1 right-bracket Subscript n Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 2 equals left-bracket 0 right-bracket Subscript n Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue left-bracket 1 right-bracket Subscript n Baseline](images/c10_727.png). Show that ECB is insecure (i.e. the advantage of an adversary is very high). Use the Right-or-Left security analysis model.

***Problem 10.7***

Consider an adversary against CBC that submits two queries:  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper M 0 Superscript 1 Baseline equals 0 comma upper M 1 Superscript 1 Baseline equals 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>M</mi><mn>0</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper M 0 Superscript 1 Baseline equals 0 comma upper M 1 Superscript 1 Baseline equals 0 right-parenthesis](images/c10_728.png) and  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper M 0 squared equals 0 comma upper M 1 squared equals 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>M</mi><mn>0</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper M 0 squared equals 0 comma upper M 1 squared equals 1 right-parenthesis](images/c10_729.png), where all  <math alttext="upper M Subscript i equals 0 comma 1 Superscript j equals 1 comma 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript i equals 0 comma 1 Superscript j equals 1 comma 2](images/c10_730.png) are one-block each. Show that CBC is insecure (i.e. the advantage of an adversary is high), if the IV is predictable. Use the Right-or-Left security analysis model.

***Problem 10.8***

Consider the case of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 48" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>48</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 48](images/c10_731.png) messages of a length of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 16](images/c10_732.png) blocks each. All the messages are encrypted with the same nonce. What is the adversary’s advantage in this case? Use Gueron and Y. Lindell’s bound (see [Section 10.5.2.3](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-03009)).

***Problem 10.9***

This problem aims to show that AES-GCM-SIV outperforms AES-GCM in terms of the amount of data that can be encrypted. Consider a user encrypting a collection of data with length multiple of 128 bits, while guaranteeing an adversary’s advantage bound no greater than  <math alttext="2 Superscript negative 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript negative 32](images/c10_733.png). What is the maximum byte-length of data that can be encrypted with the same key in the following scenarios? Use Gueron and Lindell’s bound (see [Section 10.5.2.3](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-03009)).

1.  A single IV is used to encrypt with the AES-GCM mode.
2.   <math alttext="2 Superscript 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 32](images/c10_734.png) distinct IVs are used to encrypt with the AES-GCM mode. Notice that for AES-GCM standard compliance, the maximum number of IV values used under the same key with AES-GCM should not exceed  <math alttext="2 Superscript 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 32](images/c10_735.png).
3.  A single nonce is used to encrypt with the AES-GCM-SIV mode, assuming that data are fragmented into messages of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 30" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>30</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 30](images/c10_736.png) 128-bit blocks.
4.   <math alttext="2 Superscript 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 32](images/c10_737.png) distinct nonces are used to encrypt with the AES-GCM-SIV mode, assuming that data are fragmented into messages of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 30" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>30</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 30](images/c10_738.png) 128-bit blocks.
5.   <math alttext="2 Superscript 62" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>62</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 62](images/c10_739.png) distinct nonces are used to encrypt with the AES-GCM-SIV mode, assuming that data are fragmented into messages of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>8</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 8](images/c10_740.png) 128-bit blocks and the maximum nonce repetition is  <math alttext="2 Superscript 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>8</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 8](images/c10_741.png) for all nonces.

In general, the number of permutations of a set of *N* distinct elements is  <math alttext="upper N factorial" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow></math> ![upper N factorial](images/c10_779.png). Therefore, the number of permutations of  <math alttext="upper P e r m left-parenthesis German script upper M right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P e r m left-parenthesis German script upper M right-parenthesis](images/c10_780.png) is  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 2 Superscript n Baseline right-parenthesis factorial" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>)</mo><mo>!</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 2 Superscript n Baseline right-parenthesis factorial](images/c10_781.png)

***Problem 10.2***

When the adversary queries the oracle of *E* with a value *x*, the challenger selects a random key, which is not used to compute  <math alttext="y equals upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![y equals upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c10_782.png). Therefore, upon reception of *y*, the adversary has no information in *y* to help it find the used key. Even though the number of queries is large, no useful information will be inferred by the adversary from the returned results. Therefore, the probability that the adversary guesses the key is  <math alttext="StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript n Baseline EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript n Baseline EndFraction](images/c10_783.png); i.e.  <math alttext="upper A upper D upper V Subscript upper E Superscript k r Baseline left-parenthesis period right-parenthesis equals StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript n Baseline EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>D</mi><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![upper A upper D upper V Subscript upper E Superscript k r Baseline left-parenthesis period right-parenthesis equals StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript n Baseline EndFraction](images/c10_784.png). Hence, the block cipher is very secure against key-recovery attacks. However, with a single query, because the adversary knows that  <math alttext="upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> ![upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x](images/c10_785.png), upon reception of *y*, if  <math alttext="y equals x" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> ![y equals x](images/c10_786.png), the adversary strategy is to output 1 with a probability of 1. With a probability of  <math alttext="StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript n Baseline EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript n Baseline EndFraction](images/c10_787.png), the adversary outputs 1 while a random function is used and the returned value is such that  <math alttext="y equals x" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> ![y equals x](images/c10_788.png). Therefore,  <math alttext="upper A upper D upper V Subscript upper E Superscript p r f minus c p a Baseline left-parenthesis q comma t right-parenthesis equals 1 minus StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript n Baseline EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>D</mi><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>a</mi></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![upper A upper D upper V Subscript upper E Superscript p r f minus c p a Baseline left-parenthesis q comma t right-parenthesis equals 1 minus StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript n Baseline EndFraction](images/c10_789.png), which means that the block cipher *E* is insecure against chosen-plaintext attacks.

***Problem 10.3***

The adversary asks the oracle of  <math alttext="upper E prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![upper E prime](images/c10_790.png) with a pair  <math alttext="left-parenthesis x 1 comma 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis x 1 comma 0 right-parenthesis](images/c10_791.png) and receives *y*. If an instance  <math alttext="upper E prime Subscript upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi>K</mi><mo>'</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper E prime Subscript upper K](images/c10_792.png) of  <math alttext="upper E prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![upper E prime](images/c10_793.png) is used, then  <math alttext="y equals upper E prime Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis x StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue 0 right-parenthesis equals upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper E Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis x circled-plus 0 right-parenthesis equals upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis period" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi>K</mi><mo>'</mo></msubsup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> ![y equals upper E prime Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis x StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue 0 right-parenthesis equals upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis StartAbsoluteValue StartAbsoluteValue upper E Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis x circled-plus 0 right-parenthesis equals upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis period](images/c10_794.png) Therefore, the strategy of the adversary would be to output 1, if the two halves of *y* are identical. If the adversary has access to a random permutation, then there is a probability of  <math alttext="StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript n Baseline EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript n Baseline EndFraction](images/c10_795.png) that  <math alttext="y equals y 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue y 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![y equals y 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue y 1](images/c10_796.png),  <math alttext="y 1 element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![y 1 element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n](images/c10_797.png) has been picked at random. Hence,  <math alttext="upper A upper D upper V Subscript upper E prime Superscript p r p minus c p a Baseline left-parenthesis q comma t right-parenthesis equals 1 minus StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript n Baseline EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>D</mi><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>a</mi></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8722;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![upper A upper D upper V Subscript upper E prime Superscript p r p minus c p a Baseline left-parenthesis q comma t right-parenthesis equals 1 minus StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript n Baseline EndFraction](images/c10_798.png), which is very high. Therefore,  <math alttext="upper E prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![upper E prime](images/c10_799.png) is an insecure PRP.

***Problem 10.4***

Twofold cascade of *E* is also called double-encryption of *E*. There are two cases to address:  <math alttext="upper K 1 equals upper K 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K 1 equals upper K 2](images/c10_800.png) and  <math alttext="upper K 1 not-equals upper K 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8800;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K 1 not-equals upper K 2](images/c10_801.png).

Case:  <math alttext="upper K 1 equals upper K 2 equals upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K 1 equals upper K 2 equals upper K](images/c10_802.png)

The adversary asks the oracle with any point  <math alttext="x element-of left-brace 0 comma 1 right-brace Superscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![x element-of left-brace 0 comma 1 right-brace Superscript n](images/c10_803.png) and gets a point  <math alttext="y element-of left-brace 0 comma 1 right-brace Superscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![y element-of left-brace 0 comma 1 right-brace Superscript n](images/c10_804.png). Since *E* is a secure PRP, the adversary cannot distinguish between an instance  <math alttext="upper E Subscript k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper E Subscript k](images/c10_805.png) and a random permutation π. Then, *y* is submitted to the oracle and the adversary gets a point  <math alttext="y prime element-of left-brace 0 comma 1 right-brace Superscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![y prime element-of left-brace 0 comma 1 right-brace Superscript n](images/c10_806.png). Once again, since *E* is a secure PRP, the adversary cannot distinguish between an instance  <math alttext="upper E Subscript upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper E Subscript upper K](images/c10_807.png) and a random permutation π. Hence, after two queries, the adversary cannot distinguish between  <math alttext="pi left-parenthesis pi left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![pi left-parenthesis pi left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c10_808.png) and  <math alttext="upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c10_809.png). Therefore,  <math alttext="upper E Superscript left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper E Superscript left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis](images/c10_810.png) is a secure PRP.

Case:  <math alttext="upper K 1 not-equals upper K 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K 1 not-equals upper K 2](images/c10_811.png)

In this case, the test runs in two sessions, each with a (distinct) key. The adversary asks the oracle with any point  <math alttext="x element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![x element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n](images/c10_812.png) and gets a point  <math alttext="y element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![y element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n](images/c10_813.png). Since *E* is a secure PRP, the adversary cannot distinguish between an instance  <math alttext="upper E Subscript upper K 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper E Subscript upper K 2](images/c10_814.png) and a random permutation  <math alttext="pi 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![pi 2](images/c10_815.png). Then, *y* is submitted to the oracle and the adversary gets a point  <math alttext="y prime element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>'</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![y prime element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript n](images/c10_816.png). Since *E* is a secure PRP, the adversary cannot distinguish between an instance  <math alttext="upper E Subscript upper K 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper E Subscript upper K 1](images/c10_817.png) and a random permutation  <math alttext="pi 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![pi 1](images/c10_818.png). Hence, after two queries, the adversary cannot distinguish between  <math alttext="pi 1 left-parenthesis pi 2 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![pi 1 left-parenthesis pi 2 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c10_819.png) and  <math alttext="upper E Subscript upper K 1 Baseline left-parenthesis upper E Subscript upper K 2 Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E Subscript upper K 1 Baseline left-parenthesis upper E Subscript upper K 2 Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c10_820.png). Therefore,  <math alttext="upper E Superscript left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper E Superscript left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis](images/c10_821.png) is a secure PRP.

***Problem 10.5***

*   Consider a block cipher  <math alttext="upper E colon StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript 128 Baseline times StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript 128 Baseline right-arrow StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#215;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper E colon StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript 128 Baseline times StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript 128 Baseline right-arrow StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript 128](images/c10_822.png) such that  <math alttext="upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals upper K circled-plus x" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> ![upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals upper K circled-plus x](images/c10_823.png).
    
    First, consider an adaptive adversary, which chooses  <math alttext="upper M 1 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper M 1 equals 1](images/c10_824.png) and queries the oracle and gets *y*. Then, it asks the oracle with  <math alttext="upper M 2 equals y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M 2 equals y](images/c10_825.png) and gets *z*. If the adaptive adversary has access to the oracle of *E*, then:

    Therefore, if  <math alttext="z equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![z equals 1](images/c10_827.png), then the adversary outputs 1 with a probability of 1. The probability that  <math alttext="z equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![z equals 1](images/c10_828.png) is returned by a random permutation, for the second query, is  <math alttext="StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript 128 Baseline EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript 128 Baseline EndFraction](images/c10_829.png). Hence,  <math alttext="upper A upper D upper V Subscript upper E Superscript p r p minus c p a Baseline left-parenthesis t comma 2 right-parenthesis equals 1 minus StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript 128 Baseline EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>D</mi><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>a</mi></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![upper A upper D upper V Subscript upper E Superscript p r p minus c p a Baseline left-parenthesis t comma 2 right-parenthesis equals 1 minus StartFraction 1 Over 2 Superscript 128 Baseline EndFraction](images/c10_830.png); and the block cipher *E* is insecure against an adaptive adversary.

    Therefore, if  <math alttext="y 1 circled-plus y 2 equals 1 Superscript left-parenthesis 128 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![y 1 circled-plus y 2 equals 1 Superscript left-parenthesis 128 right-parenthesis](images/c10_852.png), the adversary outputs 1 with a probability of 1. The probability that a random permutation returns two images  <math alttext="y 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![y 1](images/c10_853.png) and  <math alttext="y 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![y 2](images/c10_854.png), such that  <math alttext="y 1 circled-plus y 2 equals 1 Superscript left-parenthesis 128 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![y 1 circled-plus y 2 equals 1 Superscript left-parenthesis 128 right-parenthesis](images/c10_855.png), is of  <math alttext="1 slash 2 Superscript 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![1 slash 2 Superscript 128](images/c10_856.png). Therefore, the adversary advantage is close to 1, which makes the block cipher insecure.

It gets *q* integers:  <math alttext="y Subscript i Baseline equals upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![y Subscript i Baseline equals upper E Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c10_858.png) or  <math alttext="y Subscript i Baseline equals left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![y Subscript i Baseline equals left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c10_859.png), for all  <math alttext="i element-of left-bracket 1 comma q right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![i element-of left-bracket 1 comma q right-bracket](images/c10_860.png), where π is a random permutation. If the adversary is given access to the permutation family *E*, then for any pair  <math alttext="i comma j element-of left-bracket 1 comma q right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![i comma j element-of left-bracket 1 comma q right-bracket](images/c10_861.png),  <math alttext="i not-equals j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8800;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>j</mi></mrow></math> ![i not-equals j](images/c10_862.png),

    Then, the adversary takes any pair  <math alttext="left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline comma x Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline comma x Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c10_866.png) and checks if  <math alttext="y Subscript i Baseline circled-plus y Subscript j Baseline equals Rotate left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline comma r right-parenthesis circled-plus Rotate left-parenthesis x Subscript j Baseline comma r right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>Rotate</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>Rotate</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![y Subscript i Baseline circled-plus y Subscript j Baseline equals Rotate left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline comma r right-parenthesis circled-plus Rotate left-parenthesis x Subscript j Baseline comma r right-parenthesis](images/c10_867.png), for  <math alttext="r equals 0 comma ellipsis comma 127" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>127</mn></mrow></math> ![r equals 0 comma ellipsis comma 127](images/c10_868.png). If the test is positive, then the adversary outputs 1 with a probability of 1. The probability that a random permutation returns a pair of values, which matches the previous condition, is very low. Therefore, the adversary advantage is close to 1, which makes the block cipher insecure even for a non-adaptive adversary.
    

***Problem 10.6***

The security analysis model to use in this problem is the Right-or-Left model.

After querying with a pair of plaintexts  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper M 0 comma upper M 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper M 0 comma upper M 1 right-parenthesis](images/c10_869.png), the adversary receives a two-block-ciphertext,  <math alttext="upper C equals upper C 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C equals upper C 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper C 2](images/c10_870.png).

If  <math alttext="b equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![b equals 0](images/c10_871.png), then  <math alttext="upper C 1 equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis left-bracket 0 right-bracket Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C 1 equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis left-bracket 0 right-bracket Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c10_872.png) and  <math alttext="upper C 2 equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis left-bracket 0 right-bracket Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C 2 equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis left-bracket 0 right-bracket Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c10_873.png); i.e.  <math alttext="upper M 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 0](images/c10_874.png) is encrypted by the oracle.

If  <math alttext="b equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![b equals 1](images/c10_875.png), then  <math alttext="upper C 1 equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis left-bracket 0 right-bracket Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C 1 equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis left-bracket 0 right-bracket Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c10_876.png) and  <math alttext="upper C 2 equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis left-bracket 1 right-bracket Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C 2 equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis left-bracket 1 right-bracket Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c10_877.png); i.e.  <math alttext="upper M 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 1](images/c10_878.png) is encrypted by the oracle.

Thus, after receiving the ciphertext *C*, if  <math alttext="upper C 1 not-equals upper C 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8800;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 1 not-equals upper C 2](images/c10_879.png), the adversary outputs 1 at a probability of 1; and if it receives  <math alttext="upper C 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 2](images/c10_880.png) such that  <math alttext="upper C 1 equals upper C 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 1 equals upper C 2](images/c10_881.png), it outputs 0 at a probability of 1. Since the underlying block cipher is a pseudorandom permutation, the probability that  <math alttext="upper C 1 equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis equals upper C 2 equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C 1 equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis equals upper C 2 equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis](images/c10_882.png) is 0. Hence, the probability that the adversary outputs 1, while the left (i.e.  <math alttext="b equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![b equals 0](images/c10_883.png)) oracle was accessed, is 0. Therefore, the ECB-CPA-adversary advantage is  <math alttext="1 minus 0 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![1 minus 0 equals 1](images/c10_884.png), which means that EBC is insecure.

***Problem 10.7***

The security analysis model to use in this problem is the Right-or-Left model.

Assume that the adversary can predict that the IV to encrypt the first message is  <math alttext="upper I upper V 1 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper I upper V 1 equals 0](images/c10_887.png) and that to encrypt the second is  <math alttext="upper I upper V 2 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper I upper V 2 equals 1](images/c10_888.png). Thus, after the second query, if the adversary receives  <math alttext="upper C 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 2](images/c10_899.png) such that  <math alttext="upper C 1 equals upper C 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 1 equals upper C 2](images/c10_900.png), it outputs 1 at a probability of 1; and if the adversary receives  <math alttext="upper C 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 2](images/c10_901.png) such that  <math alttext="upper C 1 not-equals upper C 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 1 not-equals upper C 2](images/c10_902.png), it outputs 0 at a probability of 1. Since the underlying block cipher is a pseudorandom permutation, the probability that  <math alttext="upper C 1 equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis equals upper C 2 equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C 1 equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis equals upper C 2 equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis](images/c10_903.png) is 0. Thus, the probability that the adversary outputs 1, while the left (i.e.  <math alttext="b equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![b equals 0](images/c10_904.png)) oracle was accessed, is 0. Therefore, the CBC-CPA-adversary advantage is  <math alttext="1 minus 0 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![1 minus 0 equals 1](images/c10_905.png), which means that CBC is insecure, if the IV can be predicted.

## Notes

1.  [**1**](#c10.xhtml#rc10-note-0001) The computational difficulty refers to the fact that given practical resources that adversaries can use, the time for an attack to succeed is too long (in centuries or more) to attempt the attack.
2.  [**2**](#c10.xhtml#rc10-note-0002) A random-access machine model is an abstract CPU model used to do some computations.
3.  [**3**](#c10.xhtml#rc10-note-0003) Each key check requires more than  <math alttext="10 cubed" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![10 cubed](images/c10_950.png) (which is very optimistic) processor operations. The fastest computer in 2022 has a speed of  <math alttext="442 asterisk 10 Superscript 15" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>442</mn><mo>\*</mo><msup><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![442 asterisk 10 Superscript 15](images/c10_951.png) operations per second.
4.  [**4**](#c10.xhtml#rc10-note-0004) Notice that the total amount of encrypted bits is  <math alttext="e Superscript slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![e Superscript slash 2](images/c10_952.png), because each query takes two equal-length plaintexts and only one of them is encrypted.
5.  [**5**](#c10.xhtml#rc10-note-0005) *q* shall not exceed 2² blocks encrypted with the same key; otherwise, a collision occurs. Indeed, attack, after encrypting 2² blocks with the same key, the adversary can collect twice a ciphertext, which is known as collision.
6.  [**6**](#c10.xhtml#rc10-note-0006) It is assumed that the adversary does not query the oracle twice with the same value either for tag generation or for tag verification, because querying twice with the same input does not provide new knowledge to the adversary.
7.  [**7**](#c10.xhtml#rc10-note-0007) Notice that the computation time *t* is specified in terms of encryption and decryption operations of the underlying block cipher, because those operations are the most time-consuming.
8.  [**8**](#c10.xhtml#rc10-note-0008) A hash function, which makes use of a compression function that is iterated on each block, is referred to *iterated hash function*.
9.  [**9**](#c10.xhtml#rc10-note-0009) Some proposed bounds include the total length of associated data in μ.
10.  [**10**](#c10.xhtml#rc10-note-0010) According to the *Multiplication counting principle*, if one event can occur in *u* ways and a second event can occur in *v* ways after the first event has occurred, then the two events can occur in  <math alttext="u asterisk v" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></math> ![u asterisk v](images/c10_953.png) ways. In the considered problem, each point of  <math alttext="German script upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="fraktur">&#8499;</mi></math> ![German script upper M](images/c10_954.png) may have up to  <math alttext="2 Superscript upper L" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript upper L](images/c10_955.png) images in  <math alttext="script upper R" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#8475;</mi></mrow></math> ![script upper R](images/c10_956.png) independently of the other points.

# 11   
Introduction to Cryptanalysis Attacks on Symmetric Ciphers

Cryptanalysis is the science and techniques of analyzing and breaking cryptographic algorithms and protocols. There exist hundreds of cryptanalysis attack variants. Cryptanalysis is a very exciting field; and improvements of existing attacks are proposed every year. Cryptanalysis attacks can be categorized according to various criteria, such as:

*   Nongeneric vs generic attacks: in the first category, attackers take advantage of vulnerabilities of internal components of attacked ciphers, while they do not in the second category. In general, nongeneric attacks are more efficient than generic ones, as attackers know the internal vulnerabilities of attacked ciphers.
*   Statistical vs deterministic attacks: in the first category, the attackers derive some properties of attacked ciphers that can hold with some probabilities and exploit such statistical knowledge to partially or entirely recover keys. In the second category, attackers design models of ciphers in form of equations. Models are used to reduce the search space of keys. Linear and differential cryptanalyses are examples of statistical attacks, while algebraic attacks are deterministic. Linear cryptanalysis together with differential cryptanalysis are the most widely used attacks against block ciphers.
*   Known vs chosen information: there exist four main types (or models) of attacks: ciphertext-only, known-plaintext, chosen-plaintext, and chosen-ciphertext attacks.

In Section 2.4.2, a general categorization of cryptanalysis methods is provided to show the main categories of attacks. This chapter aims at introducing some common methods used to attack symmetric ciphers, namely:

*   Memory-time trade-off attacks, including Hellman’s tables and rainbow chains
*   Linear cryptanalysis
*   Differential cryptanalysis
*   Algebraic cryptanalysis
*   Cube attacks
*   Divide-and-conquer attacks
*   Correlation attacks

This chapter introduces only the basic version of each mentioned attacks. All the basic attacks have been improved and specialized (to address specific ciphers) in literature and many variants exist for each attack. The chapter is not a comprehensive survey.

Examples are used to show how a key can be partially or entirely recovered. It is worth noticing that only simple ciphers (or toy ciphers) are used in examples below. The parameters of our toy-ciphers are such that the reader could check the attacks “by hand.” Recovering key bits of real ciphers requires a lot of formulas and time-consuming experimentations.

Three metrics are commonly used to assess the complexities of attacks: computation time, memory to store data (plaintexts, ciphertexts, and others), and the number of known/chosen plaintexts and/or ciphertexts. Those metrics are briefly discussed in this chapter, because huge parameters are often required to describe attack complexities. It is worth noticing that almost all cryptanalysis attacks are academic and cannot be performed, in practice, by normal attackers against real ciphers, because of the huge amount of required resources. However, some security and intelligence agencies could have resources to perform them.

## 11.1 Memory-Time Trade-off Attacks

In general, we can regard Memory-Time Trade-Off (MTTO) attacks as methods searching for a preimage of a one-way function by utilizing a significant memory prepared in a precomputation phase to reduce the time complexity. The latter is decreased by increasing the memory complexity and vice versa. Common MTTO attacks rely on Hellman’s and Rainbow tables and their extensions. MTTO attacks may be used under known plaintext, chosen plaintext, or ciphertext-only assumptions.

### 11.1.1 Hellman’s Table-based Attacks

Hellman proposed a table design for inverting one-way functions \[[1](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0001)\]. In particular, Hellman’s tables have been used to break DES cipher. Cryptographic attacks based on Hellman’s tables are categorized as MTTO attacks. Hellman’s table design is a solution to deploy a probabilistic dictionary attack while taking into account the memory-time trade-off. Hellman’s table (HT) design is based on two principles:

1.  partially store a reduced attack dictionary,
2.  decide a trade-off between two parameters, *m* (the memory space) and *t* (the number of table lookup operations).

Therefore, HT-based MTTO attacks in cryptography are probabilistic in nature. Below is described the design of an HT-based MTTO attack to recover a secret key *K* of *n*\-bit-length, assuming a pair plaintext–ciphertext, ( <math alttext="upper P 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P 0](images/c11_1.png),  <math alttext="upper C 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 0](images/c11_2.png)) of bit-length of *l* each, is known. If  <math alttext="l ampersand gt semicolon n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#38;gt;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![l ampersand gt semicolon n](images/c11_3.png), then a reduction function *R* is used to reduce the length of ciphertext (for example delete the last  <math alttext="l minus n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![l minus n](images/c11_4.png) bits of the ciphertext).

Let  <math alttext="upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper P 0 right-parenthesis equals upper C 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper P 0 right-parenthesis equals upper C 0](images/c11_5.png) denote the encryption of plaintext  <math alttext="upper P 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P 0](images/c11_6.png) using key *K*. A one-way function *f* is defined by  <math alttext="f left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis equals upper R left-bracket upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper P 0 right-parenthesis right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![f left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis equals upper R left-bracket upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper P 0 right-parenthesis right-bracket](images/c11_7.png). Computing  <math alttext="f left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![f left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis](images/c11_8.png), given *K*, is equivalent to  <math alttext="upper R left-bracket upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper P 0 right-parenthesis right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper R left-bracket upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper P 0 right-parenthesis right-bracket](images/c11_9.png), with known *K* and  <math alttext="upper P 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P 0](images/c11_10.png). Therefore, it is easy to compute. However, computing *K* given  <math alttext="upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper P 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper P 0 right-parenthesis](images/c11_11.png) and *R* is equivalent to cryptanalysis. An HT-based attack is composed of two phases: offline precomputation and key search.

### 11.1.2 Offline Precomputation

First, the attacker selects the value of two trade-off parameters *m* (memory space) and *t* (computation time). Then, he/she chooses *m* start points,  <math alttext="upper S upper P 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S upper P 1](images/c11_12.png),  <math alttext="upper S upper P 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S upper P 2](images/c11_13.png), …,  <math alttext="upper S upper P Subscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S upper P Subscript m](images/c11_14.png), randomly in  <math alttext="StartSet 0 comma 1 comma ellipsis comma upper N EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 0 comma 1 comma ellipsis comma upper N EndSet](images/c11_15.png), where  <math alttext="upper N equals 2 Superscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper N equals 2 Superscript n](images/c11_16.png) and *n* is the key bit-length, computed as follows (illustrated by [Figure 11.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0001)):

![Figure 11.1 (a) Matrix of images under f and (b) Hellman table.](images/c11f001.png)

[**Figure 11.1**](#c11.xhtml#rc11-fig-0001) (a) Matrix of images under *f* and (b) Hellman table.

Therefore, chain *i* contains *t* encryption keys. With the exception of the start point, a key  <math alttext="x Subscript i comma k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![x Subscript i comma k](images/c11_19.png) is the result of two operations, encryption using key  <math alttext="x Subscript i comma k minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![x Subscript i comma k minus 1](images/c11_20.png), followed by a reduction.

Such a case is referred to as *false alarm*. A false alarm means that when online key search is performed, both chains may be inspected and only one chain will (probably) contribute to find the secret key and the other chain is a wrong track. Notice that false alarms may concern more than two chains.

### 11.1.3 Key Search

Recall that row *i* is computed according to formula (11.1). Given a ciphertext  <math alttext="upper C 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 0](images/c11_39.png) associated with plaintext  <math alttext="upper P 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P 0](images/c11_40.png), the key search is performed column by column:

*   Test if key *K* is in the column  <math alttext="t minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![t minus 1](images/c11_41.png):
    
    If there exists a row *i*,  <math alttext="0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to m](images/c11_42.png), such that  <math alttext="upper E upper P Subscript i Baseline equals upper R left-bracket upper C 0 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E upper P Subscript i Baseline equals upper R left-bracket upper C 0 right-bracket](images/c11_43.png), then  <math alttext="upper E upper P Subscript i Baseline equals x Subscript i comma t Baseline equals upper R left-bracket upper E n c Subscript x Sub Subscript i comma t minus 1 Subscript Baseline left-parenthesis upper P 0 right-parenthesis right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E upper P Subscript i Baseline equals x Subscript i comma t Baseline equals upper R left-bracket upper E n c Subscript x Sub Subscript i comma t minus 1 Subscript Baseline left-parenthesis upper P 0 right-parenthesis right-bracket](images/c11_44.png). Hence,  <math alttext="upper C 0 equals upper E n c Subscript x Sub Subscript i comma t minus 1 Baseline left-parenthesis upper P 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C 0 equals upper E n c Subscript x Sub Subscript i comma t minus 1 Baseline left-parenthesis upper P 0 right-parenthesis](images/c11_45.png) and maybe  <math alttext="upper K equals x Subscript i comma t minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K equals x Subscript i comma t minus 1](images/c11_46.png). Check if the guessed key is correct: if  <math alttext="upper E n c Subscript x Sub Subscript i comma t minus 1 Baseline left-parenthesis upper P 0 right-parenthesis not-equals upper C 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8800;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper E n c Subscript x Sub Subscript i comma t minus 1 Baseline left-parenthesis upper P 0 right-parenthesis not-equals upper C 0](images/c11_47.png), then try another row, until a correct key is found or all rows are tested.
    
*   If the key is not in the column  <math alttext="t minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![t minus 1](images/c11_48.png), then test if it is in column  <math alttext="t minus 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![t minus 2](images/c11_49.png):
    
    If there exists a row *i*,  <math alttext="0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![0 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to m](images/c11_50.png), such that  <math alttext="x Subscript i comma t minus 1 Baseline equals upper R left-bracket upper E n c Subscript x Sub Subscript i comma t minus 2 Subscript Baseline left-parenthesis upper P 0 right-parenthesis right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![x Subscript i comma t minus 1 Baseline equals upper R left-bracket upper E n c Subscript x Sub Subscript i comma t minus 2 Subscript Baseline left-parenthesis upper P 0 right-parenthesis right-bracket](images/c11_51.png), then  <math alttext="upper C 0 equals upper E n c Subscript x Sub Subscript i comma t minus 2 Baseline left-parenthesis upper P 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline"
