Subscript i comma t minus 2](images/c11_53.png). If the guessed key is not correct, then try another row until a correct key is found or all rows are tested.
    
*   Iteratively, until all the columns are tried or the correct key is found, try columns  <math alttext="t minus 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![t minus 3](images/c11_54.png),  <math alttext="t minus 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![t minus 4](images/c11_55.png), …, 1.

The pseudocode for key HT-based search is as follows:

*   *Attack success probability*

Hellman showed that if all the  <math alttext="m asterisk t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> ![m asterisk t](images/c11_85.png) elements in the matrix in the 0^(th) to  <math alttext="t minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![t minus 1](images/c11_86.png)^(th) columns are distinct and the secret key *K* is chosen randomly, the probability of success is  <math alttext="m asterisk t slash upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![m asterisk t slash upper N](images/c11_87.png), where *N* is the cardinality of the key space. Unfortunately, two or several matrix rows starting with distinct points merge and yield common keys. The larger a table, the higher the probability that chains merge with each other. The probability of attack success with a table of *m* rows and *t* columns, given in \[[1](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0001)\], is as follows:

 <math alttext="upper P r Subscript upper S i n g l e upper T a b l e Baseline left-parenthesis m comma t right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript m Endscripts sigma-summation Underscript j equals 0 Overscript t minus 1 Endscripts left-parenthesis 1 minus StartFraction i asterisk t Over upper N EndFraction right-parenthesis Superscript j plus 1" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8805;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mstyle displaystyle="true" mathsize="140%"><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover></mstyle><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mstyle displaystyle="true" mathsize="140%"><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover></mstyle><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript upper S i n g l e upper T a b l e Baseline left-parenthesis m comma t right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript m Endscripts sigma-summation Underscript j equals 0 Overscript t minus 1 Endscripts left-parenthesis 1 minus StartFraction i asterisk t Over upper N EndFraction right-parenthesis Superscript j plus 1](images/c11_88.png)

Hellman showed that:

*   For a fixed value of *N*, there is not much to be gained by increasing *m* or *t* beyond the point at which  <math alttext="m asterisk t squared equals upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![m asterisk t squared equals upper N](images/c11_89.png).
*   A typical setting would be  <math alttext="m equals t equals upper N Superscript 1 slash 3 Baseline period" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> ![m equals t equals upper N Superscript 1 slash 3 Baseline period](images/c11_90.png)
*   If  <math alttext="m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![m](images/c11_91.png) is very small compared to *N*, then  <math alttext="upper P r Subscript upper S i n g l e upper T a b l e Baseline left-parenthesis m comma t right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to StartFraction m asterisk t Over upper N EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8805;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript upper S i n g l e upper T a b l e Baseline left-parenthesis m comma t right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to StartFraction m asterisk t Over upper N EndFraction](images/c11_92.png).

**Note**. A single HT results in a maximum of  <math alttext="m asterisk t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> ![m asterisk t](images/c11_93.png) distinct keys among *N* possible keys, with  <math alttext="upper N greater-than-or-equal-to m asterisk t squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![upper N greater-than-or-equal-to m asterisk t squared](images/c11_94.png). To increase the probability of attack success, it is recommended to use *t* tables with a distinct reduction function for each table. Using *t* reduction functions ( <math alttext="upper R 1 comma upper R 2 comma ellipsis comma upper R Subscript t Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper R 1 comma upper R 2 comma ellipsis comma upper R Subscript t Baseline](images/c11_95.png)) results in a probability of success of:

 <math alttext="upper P r Subscript t upper T a b l e s Baseline left-parenthesis m comma t right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to 1 minus left-parenthesis 1 minus StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript m Endscripts sigma-summation Underscript j equals 0 Overscript t minus 1 Endscripts left-parenthesis 1 minus StartFraction i asterisk t Over upper N EndFraction right-parenthesis Superscript j plus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript t" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mstyle displaystyle="true" mathsize="140%"><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover></mstyle><mstyle displaystyle="true" mathsize="140%"><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover></mstyle><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>t</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript t upper T a b l e s Baseline left-parenthesis m comma t right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to 1 minus left-parenthesis 1 minus StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript m Endscripts sigma-summation Underscript j equals 0 Overscript t minus 1 Endscripts left-parenthesis 1 minus StartFraction i asterisk t Over upper N EndFraction right-parenthesis Superscript j plus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript t](images/c11_96.png)

*   *Complexity of HT-based attacks*

Hellman’s table is composed of *m* rows each of two columns (start and end points). With *t* tables of *m* chains each and with  <math alttext="m equals t equals upper N Superscript 1 slash 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![m equals t equals upper N Superscript 1 slash 3](images/c11_97.png), the memory complexity is  <math alttext="upper N Superscript 2 slash 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper N Superscript 2 slash 3](images/c11_98.png). If *n* is the key bit-length, then  <math alttext="t asterisk 2 m asterisk n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>\*</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![t asterisk 2 m asterisk n](images/c11_99.png) bits are required to store the start and end points of *t* tables. The key search is performed column by column. A key search operation is composed of  <math alttext="y Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![y Subscript i](images/c11_100.png) calculation (i.e. encryption and reduction), test if  <math alttext="y Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![y Subscript i](images/c11_101.png) is in the last column of the HT, and if  <math alttext="y Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![y Subscript i](images/c11_102.png) is an endpoint, test if the key in the column  <math alttext="t minus i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> ![t minus i](images/c11_103.png) is the secret key. Assume[¹](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0001) that the false alarm rate is not enough high to dominate the computation. Under such an assumption, the number of encryption and reduction operations for one table is *t*. Since HT-based attacks make use of *t* tables, the attack time complexity is  <math alttext="t squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![t squared](images/c11_104.png). If  <math alttext="t equals upper N Superscript 1 slash 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![t equals upper N Superscript 1 slash 3](images/c11_105.png), then the time complexity is  <math alttext="upper N Superscript 2 slash 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper N Superscript 2 slash 3](images/c11_106.png).

Brute-force attack to recover a key of 100-bit-length has a complexity time of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 100" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>100</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 100](images/c11_107.png), thus computationally infeasible. With MTTO attack, the time complexity is  <math alttext="t equals left-parenthesis 2 Superscript 100 Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript 2 slash 3 Baseline almost-equals 2 Superscript 67" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>100</mn></mrow></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8776;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>67</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![t equals left-parenthesis 2 Superscript 100 Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript 2 slash 3 Baseline almost-equals 2 Superscript 67](images/c11_108.png), thus computationally feasible.

**Example 11.1** The following is a simple example to show how Hellman’s table-based attack works. Let the key space size be  <math alttext="upper N equals 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow></math> ![upper N equals 64](images/c11_109.png). Choose a simple encryption, say  <math alttext="upper E n c Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis upper P right-parenthesis equals upper P asterisk k m o d 2 upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>k</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![upper E n c Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis upper P right-parenthesis equals upper P asterisk k m o d 2 upper N](images/c11_110.png). Plaintexts and ciphertexts are of 7-bit length.

Assume that the known plaintext is  <math alttext="upper P 0 equals 57" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>57</mn></mrow></math> ![upper P 0 equals 57](images/c11_111.png).

1.  *Building of Hellman’s tables*
    
    According to Hellman’s recommendation (i.e.  <math alttext="m equals t equals upper N Superscript 1 slash 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![m equals t equals upper N Superscript 1 slash 3](images/c11_112.png)), let  <math alttext="m equals t equals" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> ![m equals t equals](images/c11_113.png) 4. Four reduction functions are needed to build four HTs. Let the reduction functions be:
    
     <math alttext="upper R 1 left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals left floor StartFraction z Over 2 EndFraction right floor" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>&#8970;</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>&#8971;</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper R 1 left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals left floor StartFraction z Over 2 EndFraction right floor](images/c11_114.png)        <math alttext="upper R 2 left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis left-parenthesis z m o d 16 right-parenthesis asterisk 16 plus left-parenthesis left floor StartFraction z Over 16 EndFraction right floor right-parenthesis right-parenthesis m o d upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>z</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>16</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>\*</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>&#8970;</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>&#8971;</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R 2 left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis left-parenthesis z m o d 16 right-parenthesis asterisk 16 plus left-parenthesis left floor StartFraction z Over 16 EndFraction right floor right-parenthesis right-parenthesis m o d upper N](images/c11_115.png)
    
     <math alttext="upper R 3 left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals StartAbsoluteValue 3 z minus 11 EndAbsoluteValue m o d upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>z</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R 3 left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals StartAbsoluteValue 3 z minus 11 EndAbsoluteValue m o d upper N](images/c11_116.png)  <math alttext="upper R 4 left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis colon left floor StartFraction z Over 2 EndFraction right floor minus left floor StartFraction z Over 7 EndFraction right floor" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mrow><mo>&#8970;</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>&#8971;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mrow><mo>&#8970;</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>z</mi><mn>7</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>&#8971;</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper R 4 left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis colon left floor StartFraction z Over 2 EndFraction right floor minus left floor StartFraction z Over 7 EndFraction right floor](images/c11_117.png)
    
    Let the random start points be:
    
     <math alttext="StartSet 15 comma 32 comma 17 comma 36 comma 24 comma 11 comma 48 comma 61 comma 57 comma 10 comma 4 comma 42 comma 63 comma 19 comma 54 comma 26 EndSet period" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>15</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;&#160;</mtext><mn>32</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;&#160;</mtext><mn>36</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;&#160;</mtext><mn>24</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;&#160;</mtext><mn>48</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;&#160;</mtext><mn>61</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;&#160;</mtext><mn>57</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;&#160;</mtext><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;&#160;</mtext><mn>42</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;&#160;</mtext><mn>63</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;&#160;</mtext><mn>19</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;&#160;</mtext><mn>54</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;&#160;</mtext><mn>26</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mo>}</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 15 comma 32 comma 17 comma 36 comma 24 comma 11 comma 48 comma 61 comma 57 comma 10 comma 4 comma 42 comma 63 comma 19 comma 54 comma 26 EndSet period](images/c11_118.png)
    
    The HT matrices are shown in [Table 11.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-tbl-0001).
    
    Notice that there exist collisions in HTs 1, 2, and 4 (e.g. chains 3 and 4 in HT 1 have three common values). All endpoints are distinct in all HTs, which makes higher the probability of key search success.
    
2.  *Key search in HTs*
    
    Three scenarios are considered.
    
    1.  Scenario 1: plaintext encrypted with  <math alttext="upper K equals 36" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>36</mn></mrow></math> ![upper K equals 36](images/c11_119.png)
        
        Hence,  <math alttext="upper C 0 equals 57 asterisk 36 m o d 128 equals 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>57</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>36</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>128</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper C 0 equals 57 asterisk 36 m o d 128 equals 4](images/c11_120.png)
        
        *   Table 1 exploration
            
             <math alttext="y 1 equals upper R 1 left-parenthesis upper C 0 right-parenthesis equals upper R 1 left-parenthesis 4 right-parenthesis equals 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![y 1 equals upper R 1 left-parenthesis upper C 0 right-parenthesis equals upper R 1 left-parenthesis 4 right-parenthesis equals 2](images/c11_121.png). 2 is the endpoint in chain 2 in table 1.  <math alttext="x Subscript 2 comma 3 Superscript 1 Baseline equals 36" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>36</mn></mrow></math> ![x Subscript 2 comma 3 Superscript 1 Baseline equals 36](images/c11_122.png) is the correct key.
            
    2.  Scenario 2: plaintext encrypted with  <math alttext="upper K equals 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![upper K equals 17](images/c11_123.png)
        
        Hence,  <math alttext="upper C 0 equals 57 asterisk 17 m o d 128 equals 73" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>57</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>17</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>128</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>73</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper C 0 equals 57 asterisk 17 m o d 128 equals 73](images/c11_124.png)
        
        *   Table 1 exploration
            
             <math alttext="y 1 equals upper R 1 left-parenthesis upper C 0 right-parenthesis equals upper R 1 left-parenthesis 73 right-parenthesis equals 36" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>73</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>36</mn></mrow></math> ![y 1 equals upper R 1 left-parenthesis upper C 0 right-parenthesis equals upper R 1 left-parenthesis 73 right-parenthesis equals 36](images/c11_125.png). 36 is not an endpoint in table 1.
            
             <math alttext="y 2 equals f 1 left-parenthesis y 1 right-parenthesis equals upper R 1 left-parenthesis 57 asterisk 36 m o d 128 right-parenthesis equals 2" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>57</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>36</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>128</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![y 2 equals f 1 left-parenthesis y 1 right-parenthesis equals upper R 1 left-parenthesis 57 asterisk 36 m o d 128 right-parenthesis equals 2](images/c11_126.png)

Since  <math alttext="57 asterisk 8 m o d 128 equals 72 not-equals upper C 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>57</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>8</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>128</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>72</mn><mo>&#8800;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![57 asterisk 8 m o d 128 equals 72 not-equals upper C 0](images/c11_128.png),  <math alttext="x Subscript 2 comma 2 Superscript 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> ![x Subscript 2 comma 2 Superscript 1](images/c11_129.png) is not the correct key.
            
             <math alttext="y 3 equals f 1 left-parenthesis y 2 right-parenthesis equals upper R 1 left-parenthesis 57 asterisk 2 m o d 128 right-parenthesis equals 57" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>57</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>2</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>128</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>57</mn></mrow></math> ![y 3 equals f 1 left-parenthesis y 2 right-parenthesis equals upper R 1 left-parenthesis 57 asterisk 2 m o d 128 right-parenthesis equals 57](images/c11_130.png). 57 is not an endpoint in table 1.
            
             <math alttext="y 4 equals f 1 left-parenthesis y 3 right-parenthesis equals upper R 1 left-parenthesis 57 asterisk 57 m o d 128 right-parenthesis equals 24" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>57</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>57</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>128</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>24</mn></mrow></math> ![y 4 equals f 1 left-parenthesis y 3 right-parenthesis equals upper R 1 left-parenthesis 57 asterisk 57 m o d 128 right-parenthesis equals 24](images/c11_131.png). 24 is the endpoint in chain 3 of table 1. Since table 1 has no false alarms, the key is  <math alttext="x Subscript 3 comma 0 Superscript 1 Baseline equals 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![x Subscript 3 comma 0 Superscript 1 Baseline equals 17](images/c11_132.png), which is the correct key.

*Conclusion*: no correct key is recovered in scenario 3. If one visually inspects the four tables, no element equal to 23 is present. Therefore, there is no chance that the correct key can be found in the used tables.

*   *Distinguished points*

![Table 11.1 Example of Hellman’s tables.](images/c11-5.png)

[**Table 11.1**](#c11.xhtml#rc11-tbl-0001) Example of Hellman’s tables.

Rivest suggested an improvement of the original Hellman’s tables, cited in \[[2](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0002)\]. Rivest observed that the number of table lookups (and consequently the attack time) is drastically reduced if the endpoints have some property; for example, endpoints beginning with a fixed number of 0s. Such endpoints are called *distinguished points*. Therefore, instead of performing exactly *t* computations for each start point, computations continue until an endpoint with the appropriate property is found for each start point. Then, the improved table is used in the online key search as in the original Hellman’s algorithm.

### 11.1.4 Rainbow Chains

Oechslin proposed an improvement to Hellman’s tables called *rainbow chains* to reduce the effect of chain collisions \[[3](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0003)\]. In HTs, when two chains collide at some point, they merge and yield redundant keys. In most cases, rainbow chains do not merge even if they collide.

*   *Rainbow table* *precomputation*

A rainbow table is equivalent to *t* HTs. Recall that in the Hellman’s tables, each table has its own reduction function. Rainbow chains make use of *t* distinct reduction functions denoted  <math alttext="upper R 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper R 1](images/c11_168.png),  <math alttext="upper R 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper R 2](images/c11_169.png), …,  <math alttext="upper R Subscript t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper R Subscript t](images/c11_170.png) in every chain. Therefore, *t* one-way functions are defined by:

*M* start points are randomly selected in key space. Let  <math alttext="upper S upper P 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S upper P 1](images/c11_172.png),  <math alttext="upper S upper P 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S upper P 2](images/c11_173.png), …,  <math alttext="upper S upper P Subscript upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>M</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S upper P Subscript upper M](images/c11_174.png) be the selected start points. *   *Key search in rainbow table*

It is worth noticing that lookup in a rainbow table is a little bit more complex than that in Hellman’s table, because *t* reduction functions are used in every rainbow chain, while the same reduction function is used in all the chains of the same HT.

*   Iteratively, the condition for key *K* to be in column *d*,  <math alttext="0 less-than-or-equal-to d less-than t minus 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![0 less-than-or-equal-to d less-than t minus 3](images/c11_195.png), is:

From the previous conditions, the iterative search in the rainbow table is constructed according to the following pseudocode:

*   *Attack success probability*

When two rainbow chains *i* and *j* collide at points  <math alttext="k 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![k 1](images/c11_227.png) and  <math alttext="k 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![k 2](images/c11_228.png), they merge only if  <math alttext="k 1 equals k 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![k 1 equals k 2](images/c11_229.png). Therefore, the probability for two chains of length *t* to merge is  <math alttext="StartFraction 1 Over t EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>t</mi></mfrac></mrow></math> ![StartFraction 1 Over t EndFraction](images/c11_230.png). Hence, the probability of attack success, given in \[[3](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0003)\], is:

 <math alttext="upper P Subscript r Baseline left-parenthesis upper M comma t right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to 1 minus product Underscript i equals 1 Overscript t Endscripts left-parenthesis 1 minus StartFraction upper M Subscript i Baseline Over upper N EndFraction right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true" mathsize="140%"><munderover><mo>&#8719;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>t</mi></munderover></mstyle><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P Subscript r Baseline left-parenthesis upper M comma t right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to 1 minus product Underscript i equals 1 Overscript t Endscripts left-parenthesis 1 minus StartFraction upper M Subscript i Baseline Over upper N EndFraction right-parenthesis](images/c11_231.png)

where  <math alttext="upper M 1 equals upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M 1 equals upper M](images/c11_232.png) and  <math alttext="upper M Subscript k plus 1 Baseline equals upper N left-parenthesis 1 minus e Superscript minus StartFraction upper M Super Subscript k Superscript Over upper N EndFraction Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>N</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript k plus 1 Baseline equals upper N left-parenthesis 1 minus e Superscript minus StartFraction upper M Super Subscript k Superscript Over upper N EndFraction Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c11_233.png).

If  <math alttext="upper M equals m asterisk t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M equals m asterisk t](images/c11_234.png) and *t* distinct reductions functions are used in both table types, then the success probability of a rainbow table of size  <math alttext="upper M asterisk t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M asterisk t](images/c11_235.png) is equivalent to that of *t* HTs of size  <math alttext="m asterisk t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> ![m asterisk t](images/c11_236.png).

*   *Complexity of rainbow-chain-based attacks*

With one table of  <math alttext="upper M equals m asterisk t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M equals m asterisk t](images/c11_237.png) chains and  <math alttext="m equals t equals upper N Superscript 1 slash 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![m equals t equals upper N Superscript 1 slash 3](images/c11_238.png), the memory complexity of attack is of  <math alttext="upper N Superscript 2 slash 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper N Superscript 2 slash 3](images/c11_239.png); the same as that of Hellman’s tables. In the worst case, all *t* columns of the rainbow table have to be tested when searching a secret key. Assume that false alarm rate is not high enough to dominate computation. To test if the secret key is in column  <math alttext="t minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![t minus 1](images/c11_240.png),  <math alttext="y 1 equals upper R 1 left-bracket upper C 0 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![y 1 equals upper R 1 left-bracket upper C 0 right-bracket](images/c11_241.png) is calculated, which requires one reduction. To test if it is in column  <math alttext="t minus 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![t minus 2](images/c11_242.png),  <math alttext="y 2 equals f Subscript t Baseline left-parenthesis upper R Subscript t minus 1 Baseline left-bracket upper C 0 right-bracket right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![y 2 equals f Subscript t Baseline left-parenthesis upper R Subscript t minus 1 Baseline left-bracket upper C 0 right-bracket right-parenthesis](images/c11_243.png) is calculated, which requires one encryption-reduction operation. To test if it is in column 0,  <math alttext="y Subscript t Baseline equals f Subscript t Baseline left-parenthesis f Subscript t minus 1 Baseline left-parenthesis f Subscript t minus 2 Baseline ellipsis left-parenthesis f 2 left-parenthesis upper R 1 left-bracket upper C 0 right-bracket right-parenthesis right-parenthesis right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8230;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![y Subscript t Baseline equals f Subscript t Baseline left-parenthesis f Subscript t minus 1 Baseline left-parenthesis f Subscript t minus 2 Baseline ellipsis left-parenthesis f 2 left-parenthesis upper R 1 left-bracket upper C 0 right-bracket right-parenthesis right-parenthesis right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c11_244.png) is calculated, which requires  <math alttext="t minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![t minus 1](images/c11_245.png) encryption-reduction operations. To compute each <math alttext="y Subscript d Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![y Subscript d Baseline](images/c11_246.png),  <math alttext="d equals 1 comma ellipsis comma t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> ![d equals 1 comma ellipsis comma t](images/c11_247.png),  <math alttext="StartFraction t left-parenthesis t minus 1 right-parenthesis Over 2 EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></math> ![StartFraction t left-parenthesis t minus 1 right-parenthesis Over 2 EndFraction](images/c11_248.png) encryption-reduction operations are required, which is the half of that needed for Hellman’s tables.

In addition to encryption-reduction operations, *t* table lookup operations are needed to check if each <math alttext="y Subscript i Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![y Subscript i Baseline](images/c11_249.png) is an endpoint; and *t* chain reconstruction operations to check if each <math alttext="y Subscript i Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![y Subscript i Baseline](images/c11_250.png) is the correct key. Since encryption-reduction operation dominate in computation, the complexity of rainbow-table-based attack, with  <math alttext="t equals upper N Superscript 1 slash 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![t equals upper N Superscript 1 slash 3](images/c11_251.png), is  <math alttext="StartFraction t left-parenthesis t minus 1 right-parenthesis Over 2 EndFraction asterisk upper N Superscript 1 slash 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![StartFraction t left-parenthesis t minus 1 right-parenthesis Over 2 EndFraction asterisk upper N Superscript 1 slash 3](images/c11_252.png).

**Example 11.2** The following is a simple example to show how a rainbow chain-based attack works. Let the key space size be  <math alttext="upper N equals 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow></math> ![upper N equals 64](images/c11_253.png). Choose a simple encryption, say  <math alttext="upper E n c Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis upper P right-parenthesis equals upper P asterisk k m o d 2 upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>k</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![upper E n c Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis upper P right-parenthesis equals upper P asterisk k m o d 2 upper N](images/c11_254.png). Plaintexts and ciphertexts are of 7-bit length.

Assume that the known plaintext is  <math alttext="upper P 0 equals 57" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>57</mn></mrow></math> ![upper P 0 equals 57](images/c11_255.png).

1.  *Building of rainbow table*
    
    According to Hellman’s recommendation (i.e.  <math alttext="m equals t equals upper N Superscript 2 slash 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![m equals t equals upper N Superscript 2 slash 3](images/c11_256.png)), let  <math alttext="m equals t equals" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> ![m equals t equals](images/c11_257.png) 4.
    
    Four reduction functions are needed to build the rainbow table. The reduction functions and start points are the same as those used in Example 11.2:
    
     <math alttext="upper R 1 left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals left floor StartFraction z Over 2 EndFraction right floor" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>&#8970;</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>&#8971;</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper R 1 left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals left floor StartFraction z Over 2 EndFraction right floor](images/c11_258.png)     <math alttext="upper R 2 left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis left-parenthesis z m o d 16 right-parenthesis asterisk 16 plus left-parenthesis left floor StartFraction z Over 16 EndFraction right floor right-parenthesis right-parenthesis m o d upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>z</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>16</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>\*</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>&#8970;</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>&#8971;</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R 2 left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis left-parenthesis z m o d 16 right-parenthesis asterisk 16 plus left-parenthesis left floor StartFraction z Over 16 EndFraction right floor right-parenthesis right-parenthesis m o d upper N](images/c11_259.png)
    
     <math alttext="upper R 3 left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals StartAbsoluteValue 3 z minus 11 EndAbsoluteValue m o d upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>z</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R 3 left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals StartAbsoluteValue 3 z minus 11 EndAbsoluteValue m o d upper N](images/c11_260.png)  <math alttext="upper R 4 left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis colon left floor StartFraction z Over 2 EndFraction right floor minus left floor StartFraction z Over 7 EndFraction right floor" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mrow><mo>&#8970;</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>&#8971;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mrow><mo>&#8970;</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>z</mi><mn>7</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>&#8971;</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper R 4 left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis colon left floor StartFraction z Over 2 EndFraction right floor minus left floor StartFraction z Over 7 EndFraction right floor](images/c11_261.png)
    
    The start point set is  <math alttext="StartSet 10 comma 63 comma 54 comma 19 comma 4 comma 32 comma 48 comma 57 comma 15 comma 42 comma 24 comma 61 comma 17 comma 36 comma 26 comma 11 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>63</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>54</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>19</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>32</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>48</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>57</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>15</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>42</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>24</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>61</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>36</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>26</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 10 comma 63 comma 54 comma 19 comma 4 comma 32 comma 48 comma 57 comma 15 comma 42 comma 24 comma 61 comma 17 comma 36 comma 26 comma 11 EndSet](images/c11_262.png).
    
    The rainbow table is shown in [Table 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-tbl-0002):
    
    ![Table 11.2 Example of rainbow table.](images/c11-9.png)
    
    [**Table 11.2**](#c11.xhtml#rc11-tbl-0002) Example of rainbow table.
    
    Merges and false alarms are highlighted in gray. For example, chains 2 and 3 merge, because a collision occurred in position  <math alttext="j equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![j equals 1](images/c11_263.png) for both chains, while chains 15 and 16 merge, because a collision occurred in position  <math alttext="j equals 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![j equals 2](images/c11_264.png) for both chains.
    
    Endpoint 1 has four inverse images, while endpoints 16, 41, and 43 all have two inverse images. Merges and false alarms are frequent when the key space is small, which is the case of this example ( <math alttext="upper N equals 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow></math> ![upper N equals 64](images/c11_265.png)).
    
2.  *Key search in rainbow table*
    
    Three scenarios are considered.
    
    1.  Scenario 1: plaintext encrypted with  <math alttext="upper K equals 27" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>27</mn></mrow></math> ![upper K equals 27](images/c11_266.png)
        
         <math alttext="upper C 0 equals 57 asterisk 27 m o d 128 equals 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>57</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>27</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>128</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![upper C 0 equals 57 asterisk 27 m o d 128 equals 3](images/c11_267.png).
        
         <math alttext="y 1 equals upper R 4 left-parenthesis upper C 0 right-parenthesis equals left floor three-halves right floor minus left floor three-sevenths right floor equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>&#8970;</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>&#8971;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mrow><mo>&#8970;</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>7</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>&#8971;</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![y 1 equals upper R 4 left-parenthesis upper C 0 right-parenthesis equals left floor three-halves right floor minus left floor three-sevenths right floor equals 1](images/c11_268.png). 1 is the endpoint of chains 1, 2, 3, and 4. Key is  <math alttext="x Subscript 2 comma 3 Baseline equals x Subscript 3 comma 3 Baseline equals 27" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>27</mn></mrow></math> ![x Subscript 2 comma 3 Baseline equals x Subscript 3 comma 3 Baseline equals 27](images/c11_269.png), which is the correct key.
        
        Testing keys  <math alttext="x Subscript 1 comma 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![x Subscript 1 comma 3](images/c11_270.png) and  <math alttext="x Subscript 4 comma 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![x Subscript 4 comma 3](images/c11_271.png) (both equal to 18) results in incorrect key.
        
    2.  Scenario 2: plaintext encrypted with  <math alttext="upper K equals 5" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> ![upper K equals 5](images/c11_272.png)
        
        Hence,  <math alttext="upper C 0 equals 57 asterisk 5 m o d 128 equals 29" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>57</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>5</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>128</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>29</mn></mrow></math> ![upper C 0 equals 57 asterisk 5 m o d 128 equals 29](images/c11_273.png).
        
         <math alttext="y 1 equals upper R 4 left-parenthesis upper C 0 right-parenthesis equals left floor StartFraction 29 Over 2 EndFraction right floor minus left floor StartFraction 29 Over 7 EndFraction right floor equals 10" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>&#8970;</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>29</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>&#8971;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mrow><mo>&#8970;</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>29</mn></mrow><mn>7</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>&#8971;</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math> ![y 1 equals upper R 4 left-parenthesis upper C 0 right-parenthesis equals left floor StartFraction 29 Over 2 EndFraction right floor minus left floor StartFraction 29 Over 7 EndFraction right floor equals 10](images/c11_274.png), which is not an endpoint.
        
         <math alttext="y 2 equals f 4 left-parenthesis upper R 3 left-bracket upper C 0 right-bracket right-parenthesis equals f 4 left-parenthesis StartAbsoluteValue left-parenthesis 3 asterisk 29 minus 11 right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue m o d 64 right-parenthesis equals f 4 left-parenthesis 12 right-parenthesis equals upper R 4 left-parenthesis upper E n c 12 left-parenthesis upper P 0 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>29</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>64</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow></math> ![y 2 equals f 4 left-parenthesis upper R 3 left-bracket upper C 0 right-bracket right-parenthesis equals f 4 left-parenthesis StartAbsoluteValue left-parenthesis 3 asterisk 29 minus 11 right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue m o d 64 right-parenthesis equals f 4 left-parenthesis 12 right-parenthesis equals upper R 4 left-parenthesis upper E n c 12 left-parenthesis upper P 0 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals 16](images/c11_275.png), which is the endpoint of chains 7 and 8.

*Conclusion*: no correct key is recovered in scenario 3. If one visually inspects the rainbow table, no element equal to 6 is present. Therefore, there is no chance that the correct key can be found in the table.

## 11.2 Linear Cryptanalysis

Linear cryptanalysis technique was first introduced by Mitsuru Matsui, who applied it to DES cipher \[[4](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0004)\]. Using CPU technology of the 1990s, 12-round DES was broken in 50 hours using  <math alttext="2 Superscript 33" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>33</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 33](images/c11_287.png) known plaintexts; and 16-round DES was broken, using  <math alttext="2 Superscript 47" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>47</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 47](images/c11_288.png) known plaintexts.

Linear cryptanalysis is applied to key-alternating block ciphers to either disclose some plaintexts or to recover the cipher key \[[5](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0005)\]. It may be used in known-plaintext attacks or only-ciphertext attacks. In the following, we only focus on known-plaintext attacks. The probability of attack success depends on the number of known plaintext‒ciphertext pairs; in general, this number is large. The basic ideas of linear cryptanalysis are:

*   Find relationships, in form of linear approximations, between bits of plaintext, ciphertext, and key.
*   Use each linear approximation as distinguisher to predict one bit of information about an unknown plaintext, the cipher key or the last-round key.

Linear cryptanalysis is suitable against key-alternating block ciphers (such as DES and AES) where the key of round *i* is XORed with the round input to yield the round output, using a transformation function (as shown on [Figure 11.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0004)). The relationships are associated with one round, some rounds, or the full cipher. Specifically, linear cryptanalysis tries to linearly approximate the nonlinear components of a block cipher. Recall that s-boxes are the main nonlinear functions used in block ciphers.

![Figure 11.4 Key-iterating block cipher diagram.](images/c11f004.png)

[**Figure 11.4**](#c11.xhtml#rc11-fig-0004) Key-iterating block cipher diagram.

### 11.2.2 Constructing Linear Approximation Expressions

First of all, notice that for a given cipher and a set of plaintext‒ciphertext pairs, there may or may not exist linear relationships, whose exploitation results in deduction of bit-information about the key. Linear attack success depends on the selected linear approximations and on the randomness in known plaintexts.

Let *P* and *C* denote a plaintext and its ciphertext, and *K*, the cipher key, such that  <math alttext="upper C equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper P right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C equals upper E n c Subscript upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper P right-parenthesis](images/c11_329.png). #### 11.2.2.1 Finding Linear Approximations Associated with an s-box

The main nonlinear components of block ciphers are s-boxes. Therefore, linear cryptanalysis focuses essentially on s-boxes. For simplicity, assume that the input and output of s-boxes are of the same bit-length. The quality of linear expressions combining input and output bits is analyzed and the good ones are kept. Good linear approximations are those which result in a high probability of attack success. To understand how linear expressions can be identified, let us consider the following example.

**Example 11.4** Consider an s-box, which takes four bits and outputs four bits, according to the table in [Figure 11.5](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0005). As you may see the s-box is not a linear function.

![Figure 11.5 Simple s-box and its table.](images/c11f005.png)

[**Figure 11.5**](#c11.xhtml#rc11-fig-0005) Simple s-box and its table.

Three linear expressions are tried:  <math alttext="upper X 1 circled-plus upper X 4 equals upper Y 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper X 1 circled-plus upper X 4 equals upper Y 4](images/c11_348.png),  <math alttext="upper X 2 circled-plus upper X 3 equals upper Y 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper X 2 circled-plus upper X 3 equals upper Y 4](images/c11_349.png), and  <math alttext="upper X 2 circled-plus upper X 3 equals upper Y 1 circled-plus upper Y 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper X 2 circled-plus upper X 3 equals upper Y 1 circled-plus upper Y 2](images/c11_350.png).

In [Table 11.3](#c11.xhtml#c11-tbl-0003), incorrect approximations are highlighted in gray.

![Table 11.3 Evaluation of linear expressions.](images/c11_358.png)

The bias is 0.
