The bias is  <math alttext="StartFraction 12 Over 16 EndFraction minus one-half equals one-fourth" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow></math> ![StartFraction 12 Over 16 EndFraction minus one-half equals one-fourth](images/c11_355.png).

The first and third linear approximations of the s-box are more likely to be correct than the second one. They are good linear approximations; they are written as follows:

 <math alttext="left-bracket 1 0 0 1 right-bracket dot upper X circled-plus left-bracket 0 0 0 1 right-bracket dot upper Y equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 1 0 0 1 right-bracket dot upper X circled-plus left-bracket 0 0 0 1 right-bracket dot upper Y equals 0](images/c11_356.png) (first approximation)

 <math alttext="left-bracket 0 1 1 0 right-bracket dot upper X circled-plus left-bracket 1 1 0 0 right-bracket dot upper Y equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 0 1 1 0 right-bracket dot upper X circled-plus left-bracket 1 1 0 0 right-bracket dot upper Y equals 0](images/c11_357.png) (third approximation)

#### 11.2.2.2 Measuring Quality of Linear Approximations

If *b* is the bit-length of the input and output of an s-box, we can try  <math alttext="2 Superscript b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript b](images/c11_420.png) masks for each random variable *X* (input) or *Y* (output). Therefore, the number of linear approximations is  <math alttext="2 Superscript 2 b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 2 b](images/c11_421.png). However, only a few linear approximations are good. The idea of linear cryptanalysis is to keep expressions with a large or low probability of occurrence; i.e. keep expressions with a large (or low) bias; the larger the bias, the better the quality of approximation. Expressions that occur with a probability of ½ (or very close to ½) do not provide information useful to perform linear attacks, because those expressions may hold or not with the same probability of ½; their bias is (close to) 0. Expressions with a bias of  <math alttext="minus-or-plus one-half" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8723;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></math> ![minus-or-plus one-half](images/c11_422.png) are perfect. In summary:

*   If  <math alttext="epsilon equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![epsilon equals 0](images/c11_423.png), nothing can be learned.
*   If  <math alttext="epsilon ampersand gt semicolon 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>&#38;gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![epsilon ampersand gt semicolon 0](images/c11_424.png), approximation  <math alttext="left-parenthesis alpha dot upper X right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis beta dot upper Y right-parenthesis equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis alpha dot upper X right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis beta dot upper Y right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c11_425.png) is good.
*   If  <math alttext="epsilon less-than 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![epsilon less-than 0](images/c11_426.png), approximation  <math alttext="left-parenthesis alpha dot upper X right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis beta dot upper Y right-parenthesis circled-plus 1 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis alpha dot upper X right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis beta dot upper Y right-parenthesis circled-plus 1 equals 0](images/c11_427.png) is good.

The common method to measure the quality of linear approximations is the *linear approximation table* (LAT), which is a  <math alttext="2 Superscript b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript b](images/c11_428.png)\-by- <math alttext="2 Superscript b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript b](images/c11_429.png) matrix, where  <math alttext="upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis](images/c11_430.png) denotes the number of correct matchings (i.e.  <math alttext="left-parenthesis alpha dot upper X right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis beta dot upper Y right-parenthesis equals 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis alpha dot upper X right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis beta dot upper Y right-parenthesis equals 0 right-parenthesis](images/c11_431.png) of the expression using α and β values, minus  <math alttext="2 Superscript b minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript b minus 1](images/c11_432.png). Formally, the LAT is defined by:

 <math alttext="upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis equals 2 Superscript b Baseline asterisk epsilon left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></msup><mo>\*</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis equals 2 Superscript b Baseline asterisk epsilon left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis](images/c11_433.png)(11.8) 

Equation ([11.8](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0008)) is equivalent to  <math alttext="upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis equals StartAbsoluteValue upper X comma upper Y element-of upper F 2 Superscript b Baseline vertical-bar left-brace alpha dot upper X equals beta dot upper Y right-brace EndAbsoluteValue minus 2 Superscript b minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis equals StartAbsoluteValue upper X comma upper Y element-of upper F 2 Superscript b Baseline vertical-bar left-brace alpha dot upper X equals beta dot upper Y right-brace EndAbsoluteValue minus 2 Superscript b minus 1](images/c11_434.png).

**Note**. The sum of all elements of a LAT is 0. The sum of all elements of any column or row is either  <math alttext="2 Superscript b minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript b minus 1](images/c11_435.png) or  <math alttext="minus 2 Superscript b minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![minus 2 Superscript b minus 1](images/c11_436.png).

 <math alttext="upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis](images/c11_437.png) equal zero means that the approximation is as good as a random approximation. Therefore, we do not learn anything form zero-elements of a LAT. The larger is the absolute value of a LAT element, the more the linear approximation tells us about the approximated function. Positive elements mean that linear approximation is frequently correct, while negative elements mean that linear approximation is rarely correct. Adding 1 to a linear expression that is rarely correct results in a linear expression that is frequently correct; i.e. if  <math alttext="alpha dot upper X circled-plus beta dot upper Y equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![alpha dot upper X circled-plus beta dot upper Y equals 0](images/c11_438.png) is rarely correct, then  <math alttext="alpha dot upper X circled-plus beta dot upper Y circled-plus 1 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![alpha dot upper X circled-plus beta dot upper Y circled-plus 1 equals 0](images/c11_439.png) is frequently correct.

**Note**. Designers of block ciphers need to use s-boxes with low values in their LATs, while attackers prefer them with large values. Therefore, to design ciphers resistant against linear cryptanalysis, s-boxes with low LAT values are needed.

**Example 11.5**  [Table 11.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-tbl-0004) is the LAT corresponding to the s-box specified in [Figure 11.5](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0005).

![Table 11.4 Example of linear approximation table of an s-box.](images/c11-14.png)

[**Table 11.4**](#c11.xhtml#rc11-tbl-0004) Example of linear approximation table of an s-box.

#### 11.2.2.3 Finding Linear Expressions Associated with an s-box and a Key

Consider the toy-cipher, illustrated by [Figure 11.6](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0006), which makes use of the s-box defined in [Figure 11.5](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0005). The key is XORed with the plaintext to yield the input bits of the s-box. Therefore, a linear approximation involving the plaintext, the ciphertext, and the key has the following form:

 <math alttext="left-parenthesis alpha dot left-parenthesis upper P circled-plus upper K right-parenthesis right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis beta dot upper C right-parenthesis equals 0" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis alpha dot left-parenthesis upper P circled-plus upper K right-parenthesis right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis beta dot upper C right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c11_440.png)![Figure 11.6 Example of a toy-cipher with one round.](images/c11f006.png)

[**Figure 11.6**](#c11.xhtml#rc11-fig-0006) Example of a toy-cipher with one round.

The form above is equivalent to  <math alttext="left-parenthesis alpha dot upper P right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis beta dot upper C right-parenthesis equals alpha dot upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis alpha dot upper P right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis beta dot upper C right-parenthesis equals alpha dot upper K](images/c11_441.png), meaning that if some information is known about some bits of the plaintext and ciphertext, then some information could be deduced about some bits of the key. For example, if  <math alttext="left-parenthesis left-bracket 0 1 1 0 right-bracket dot upper P right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis left-bracket 0 0 0 1 right-bracket dot upper C right-parenthesis equals 0 equals left-parenthesis left-bracket 0 0 1 1 right-bracket dot upper K right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis left-bracket 0 1 1 0 right-bracket dot upper P right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis left-bracket 0 0 0 1 right-bracket dot upper C right-parenthesis equals 0 equals left-parenthesis left-bracket 0 0 1 1 right-bracket dot upper K right-parenthesis](images/c11_442.png), then  <math alttext="upper K 3 circled-plus upper K 4 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper K 3 circled-plus upper K 4 equals 0](images/c11_443.png). Therefore, the 3^(rd) and 4^(th) bits of the key are both equal either to 1 or to 0.

#### 11.2.2.4 Finding Linear Expressions Associated with Two s-boxes and a Key

Consider the toy-cipher, illustrated by [Figure 11.7](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0007), which makes use of two s-boxes. The cipher has two rounds. Let  <math alttext="upper K Superscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mi>r</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper K Superscript r](images/c11_444.png) denote the key of round *r* and  <math alttext="k Subscript i equals 1 ellipsis comma 4 Superscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mi>r</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![k Subscript i equals 1 ellipsis comma 4 Superscript r](images/c11_445.png), the four bits of  <math alttext="k Superscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![k Superscript r](images/c11_446.png). We can express linear expressions of the form:

 <math alttext="alpha dot left-parenthesis upper P circled-plus upper K Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis equals beta Superscript 1 Baseline dot upper Y Superscript 1" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>&#183;</mo><msup><mi>Y</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![alpha dot left-parenthesis upper P circled-plus upper K Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis equals beta Superscript 1 Baseline dot upper Y Superscript 1](images/c11_447.png)(11.9)  <math alttext="beta Superscript 1 Baseline dot left-parenthesis upper Y Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K squared right-parenthesis equals beta squared dot upper C" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>&#183;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>Y</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> ![beta Superscript 1 Baseline dot left-parenthesis upper Y Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K squared right-parenthesis equals beta squared dot upper C](images/c11_448.png)(11.10) ![Figure 11.7 Example of a toy-cipher with two rounds.](images/c11f007.png)

[**Figure 11.7**](#c11.xhtml#rc11-fig-0007) Example of a toy-cipher with two rounds.

where,  <math alttext="upper Y Superscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>Y</mi><mi>r</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper Y Superscript r](images/c11_449.png),  <math alttext="beta Superscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>r</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![beta Superscript r](images/c11_450.png), and  <math alttext="upper K Superscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mi>r</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper K Superscript r](images/c11_451.png) denote the output, the output mask, and the key of round *r*, respectively. Combining equations ([11.9](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0009)) and ([11.10](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0010)) yields:

 <math alttext="alpha dot upper P circled-plus beta squared dot upper C equals alpha dot upper K Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus beta Superscript 1 Baseline dot upper K squared" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><msup><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>&#8853;</mo><msup><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>&#183;</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![alpha dot upper P circled-plus beta squared dot upper C equals alpha dot upper K Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus beta Superscript 1 Baseline dot upper K squared](images/c11_452.png)(11.11) 

The last linear expression is referred to as *linear full-cipher approximation*. By Piling-up lemma, its bias is  <math alttext="epsilon Subscript 1 comma 2 Baseline equals 2 asterisk epsilon 1 asterisk epsilon 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![epsilon Subscript 1 comma 2 Baseline equals 2 asterisk epsilon 1 asterisk epsilon 2](images/c11_453.png), where  <math alttext="epsilon 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![epsilon 1](images/c11_454.png) and  <math alttext="epsilon 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![epsilon 2](images/c11_455.png) are biases of expressions (11.9) and (11.10), respectively.

**Note**. The output of the first round and the input of the second round make use of the same mask. Otherwise, in the approximation, some input bits of the second rounds have no relationship with the plaintext and the key of the first round.

We use the LAT illustrated in [Table 11.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-tbl-0004), to find the biases.

For the first linear approximation:  <math alttext="upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis 9 comma 1 right-parenthesis equals 4 equals 2 Superscript 4 Baseline asterisk epsilon 1 right double arrow epsilon 1 equals 1 slash 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8658;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis 9 comma 1 right-parenthesis equals 4 equals 2 Superscript 4 Baseline asterisk epsilon 1 right double arrow epsilon 1 equals 1 slash 4](images/c11_468.png). Hence, the first expression holds with a probability of  <math alttext="upper P 1 equals one-half plus one-fourth equals three-fourths" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow></math> ![upper P 1 equals one-half plus one-fourth equals three-fourths](images/c11_469.png).

For the second linear approximation:  <math alttext="upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis 1 comma 5 right-parenthesis equals negative 4 equals 2 Superscript 4 Baseline asterisk epsilon 2 right double arrow epsilon 2 equals negative one-fourth" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8658;</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow></math> ![upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis 1 comma 5 right-parenthesis equals negative 4 equals 2 Superscript 4 Baseline asterisk epsilon 2 right double arrow epsilon 2 equals negative one-fourth](images/c11_470.png). Hence, the second expression holds with a probability of  <math alttext="upper P 2 equals one-half minus one-fourth equals one-fourth" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow></math> ![upper P 2 equals one-half minus one-fourth equals one-fourth](images/c11_471.png).

For the third linear approximation, we use Piling-up lemma applied to two random binary variables in  <math alttext="upper L Superscript 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![upper L Superscript 1](images/c11_472.png) and  <math alttext="upper L squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![upper L squared](images/c11_473.png):  <math alttext="epsilon Subscript 1 comma 2 Baseline equals 2 asterisk epsilon 1 asterisk epsilon 2 equals negative one-eighth" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>8</mn></mfrac></mrow></math> ![epsilon Subscript 1 comma 2 Baseline equals 2 asterisk epsilon 1 asterisk epsilon 2 equals negative one-eighth](images/c11_474.png). Hence, the third expression holds with a probability of  <math alttext="upper P 3 equals one-half minus one-eighth equals three-eighths" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>8</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>8</mn></mfrac></mrow></math> ![upper P 3 equals one-half minus one-eighth equals three-eighths](images/c11_475.png).

#### 11.2.2.5 Finding Linear Expressions Associated with a Full Cipher

When the cipher is composed of more than two rounds, each using several s-boxes and permutation, the linear expressions can be selected among a large set of combinations. Using Piling-up lemma and LAT of each s-box, the selected s-boxes should be such that the biases of linear full-cipher approximation are the largest. Each linear full-cipher approximation contributes to infer a bit of information on the cipher key (i.e. a relationship between some bits of the cipher key). S-boxes selected to perform linear cryptanalysis are referred to as active s-boxes. Below, we show how to find a linear full-cipher approximation associated with a toy-cipher.

**Example 11.7** *Notations*

*   *b*: bit-length of plaintext, ciphertext, and key
*    <math alttext="upper P Subscript i Baseline comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P Subscript i Baseline comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma b](images/c11_476.png): plaintext bits;  <math alttext="upper C Subscript i Baseline comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript i Baseline comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma b](images/c11_477.png): ciphertext bits
*   *R*: number of rounds
*   *d*: number of s-boxes per round; *m*: number of input (or output) bits per s-box
*    <math alttext="upper K Superscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mi>r</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper K Superscript r](images/c11_478.png): key of round  <math alttext="r comma r equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper R" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> ![r comma r equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper R](images/c11_479.png);  <math alttext="upper K Subscript i Superscript r Baseline comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>r</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript i Superscript r Baseline comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma b](images/c11_480.png): bits of  <math alttext="upper K Superscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mi>r</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper K Superscript r](images/c11_481.png)
*    <math alttext="upper Y Superscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>Y</mi><mi>r</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper Y Superscript r](images/c11_482.png): output of round  <math alttext="r semicolon upper Y Subscript i Superscript r Baseline comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>Y</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>r</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![r semicolon upper Y Subscript i Superscript r Baseline comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma b](images/c11_483.png): bits of  <math alttext="upper Y Superscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>Y</mi><mi>r</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper Y Superscript r](images/c11_484.png)
*    <math alttext="upper U Subscript l comma j Superscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>U</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>r</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper U Subscript l comma j Superscript r](images/c11_485.png),  <math alttext="l equals 1 comma ellipsis comma d comma j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![l equals 1 comma ellipsis comma d comma j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma m](images/c11_486.png): input bits of s-box  <math alttext="upper S Subscript l Superscript r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>r</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript l Superscript r](images/c11_487.png)

*    <math alttext="upper L upper A upper T Superscript l Baseline left-parenthesis i comma j right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>A</mi><msup><mi>T</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper L upper A upper T Superscript l Baseline left-parenthesis i comma j right-parenthesis](images/c11_491.png): value of the LAT of s-box *l* at row *i* and column *j*.

Consider the cipher illustrated by [Figure 11.8](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0008), where  <math alttext="b equals 16 comma upper R equals 5" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> ![b equals 16 comma upper R equals 5](images/c11_492.png), and  <math alttext="d equals m equals 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![d equals m equals 4](images/c11_493.png). In each round *r*, with the exception of the first and last rounds, the output of round  <math alttext="r minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![r minus 1](images/c11_494.png) is permuted and then XORed with the key of round *r* to feed s-boxes of round *r*. A single permutation is used in the entire cipher, with the following mapping:

![Figure 11.8 Cipher with four rounds, four s-boxes per round, and a permutation.](images/c11f008.png)

[**Figure 11.8**](#c11.xhtml#rc11-fig-0008) Cipher with four rounds, four s-boxes per round, and a permutation.

![](images/c11_495.png)

where  <math alttext="i right-arrow left-parenthesis l comma j right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![i right-arrow left-parenthesis l comma j right-parenthesis](images/c11_511.png) denotes connection of bit *i* of permutation input to input bit *j* of s-box *l*. In [Figure 11.8](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0008), thick lines highlight how bits are used to form linear approximation corresponding to rounds. To simplify, all the s-boxes are identical to the one with LAT shown in [Table 11.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-tbl-0004).

Using mask notation,  <math alttext="upper L Superscript 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![upper L Superscript 4](images/c11_564.png) can be rewritten as:

where  <math alttext="normal upper Omega Subscript upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#937;</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![normal upper Omega Subscript upper K](images/c11_566.png) is a binary constant that depends on the cipher key.

However, when we want to recover one bit-information about the cipher key (using Matsui’s algorithm 1, described in the sequel), we need a linear expression of the form  <math alttext="pi dot upper P circled-plus sigma dot upper C circled-plus kappa dot upper K equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>&#954;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![pi dot upper P circled-plus sigma dot upper C circled-plus kappa dot upper K equals 0](images/c11_567.png). Therefore, another analysis work must be done. That is, using the key scheduling algorithm of cipher, cryptanalyst needs to express  <math alttext="normal upper Omega Subscript upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#937;</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![normal upper Omega Subscript upper K](images/c11_568.png) (which is a sum of bits of key rounds) as a sum of bits of the first-round key (i.e. the cipher key). That is, he/she needs to find a mask κ such that  <math alttext="normal upper Omega Subscript upper K Baseline equals kappa dot upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#937;</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#954;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> ![normal upper Omega Subscript upper K Baseline equals kappa dot upper K](images/c11_569.png). When the key scheduling yields round keys using key permutation, it is easy to find the mask κ (as shown in Example 11.8).

### 11.2.3 General Methodology for Performing Linear Cryptanalysis

General methodology for performing linear cryptanalysis follows three steps:

1.  Compute linear approximation tables (LATs) of s-boxes and associate linear expressions to linear components (e.g. permutation tables) of the cipher.
2.  Using LATs of s-boxes and Piling-up lemma, 
    *   – Select good linear approximations for each round. There may exist several good linear approximations.
    *   – Select[²](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0002) good full-cipher or partial[³](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0003)\-cipher linear approximations. There may exist several good linear approximations.
3.  Use each linear approximation of a full or a partial cipher and known plaintext–ciphertext pairs to deduce a bit of information about the cipher key, to partially recover the last-round key, or to disclose plaintexts.

There exist two basic algorithms to perform linear cryptanalysis attacks, which were both proposed in the seminal Matsui’s paper: deduction of a bit-information about cipher key or recovery of bits of last-round key.

#### 11.2.3.1 Algorithm 1: Deduction of a Bit-information about Cipher Key

In this algorithm, the adversary selects a good full-cipher linear approximation of the form  <math alttext="pi dot upper P circled-plus sigma dot upper C circled-plus kappa dot upper K equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>&#954;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![pi dot upper P circled-plus sigma dot upper C circled-plus kappa dot upper K equals 0](images/c11_570.png). The selected linear approximation takes into account all rounds and with a large (positive or negative) bias.

The set of known plaintext–ciphertext pairs should be as large as possible, and with random plaintexts. The number of known plaintexts and their randomness have an impact on the probability of correctly guessing one bit-information about the cipher key.

A bit-information means  <math alttext="kappa dot upper K equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#954;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![kappa dot upper K equals 0](images/c11_571.png) or  <math alttext="kappa dot upper K equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#954;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![kappa dot upper K equals 1](images/c11_572.png), depending on the bias. Each linear full-cipher approximation provides one bit of the cipher key (if the mask κ has only one 1-bit) or a relationship between some bits of the key (if the mask κ has more than one 1-bit). For example, if we learn that two bits of the key are either 1 or 0, we reduce the exhaustive search by a factor of 2. Several linear full-cipher approximations are needed to recover the entire cipher key. Matsui’s algorithm 1 works as follows:

**Example 11.8** Consider the toy-cipher illustrated by [Figure 11.9](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0009). All arguments are of a bit-length of 4. The cipher runs in two rounds, which make use of the same s-box. The linear approximation table of the used s-box is identical to that given in [Table 11.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-tbl-0004). The key of the first round is the cipher key; and that of the second round is yielded by a permutation of the first key. The encryption of all plaintexts using all keys is shown in [Table 11.5](#c11.xhtml#c11-tbl-0005).

*   *Selection and use of the first linear full-cipher approximation*

From the LAT of chosen s-box, we select  <math alttext="upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis 10 comma 11 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis 10 comma 11 right-parenthesis](images/c11_587.png). Therefore, the linear approximation for the first round is  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 10 dot left-parenthesis upper P circled-plus upper K Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis 11 dot upper Y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>11</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 10 dot left-parenthesis upper P circled-plus upper K Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis 11 dot upper Y right-parenthesis](images/c11_588.png), which has a bias of  <math alttext="negative 1 slash 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![negative 1 slash 4](images/c11_589.png). In bit representation, linear approximation for the first round is:

 <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper P 1 circled-plus upper K 1 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper P 3 circled-plus upper K 3 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus upper Y Subscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper Y 3 circled-plus upper Y 4 equals 0" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>3</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper P 1 circled-plus upper K 1 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper P 3 circled-plus upper K 3 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus upper Y Subscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper Y 3 circled-plus upper Y 4 equals 0](images/c11_590.png)

For the second round, we select  <math alttext="upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis 11 comma 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>11</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis 11 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c11_591.png). Hence, the linear approximation for the second round is  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 11 dot left-parenthesis upper Y circled-plus upper K squared right-parenthesis right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis 1 dot upper C right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>11</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 11 dot left-parenthesis upper Y circled-plus upper K squared right-parenthesis right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis 1 dot upper C right-parenthesis](images/c11_592.png), which corresponds to a bias of  <math alttext="negative 1 slash 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![negative 1 slash 4](images/c11_593.png). In bit representation, linear approximation for the second round is:

 <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper Y 1 circled-plus upper K 1 squared right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper Y 3 circled-plus upper K 3 squared right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper Y 4 circled-plus upper K 4 squared right-parenthesis circled-plus upper C 4 equals 0" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>4</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper Y 1 circled-plus upper K 1 squared right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper Y 3 circled-plus upper K 3 squared right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper Y 4 circled-plus upper K 4 squared right-parenthesis circled-plus upper C 4 equals 0](images/c11_594.png)

By substitutions and using key permutation, where  <math alttext="upper K 1 squared equals upper K 3 Superscript 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>3</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper K 1 squared equals upper K 3 Superscript 1](images/c11_595.png),  <math alttext="upper K 3 squared equals upper K 4 Superscript 1 Baseline comma upper K 4 squared equals upper K 1 Superscript 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>4</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>4</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper K 3 squared equals upper K 4 Superscript 1 Baseline comma upper K 4 squared equals upper K 1 Superscript 1](images/c11_596.png),

 <math alttext="left-parenthesis left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper P 1 circled-plus upper K 1 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper P 3 circled-plus upper K 3 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis circled-plus upper K 3 Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K 4 Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K 1 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus upper C 4 equals 0" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>3</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>3</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>4</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper P 1 circled-plus upper K 1 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper P 3 circled-plus upper K 3 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis circled-plus upper K 3 Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K 4 Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K 1 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus upper C 4 equals 0](images/c11_597.png)

which can be rewritten as  <math alttext="10 dot upper P circled-plus 1 dot upper C equals upper K 4 Superscript 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>P</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>C</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>4</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> ![10 dot upper P circled-plus 1 dot upper C equals upper K 4 Superscript 1](images/c11_598.png); it has a bias of  <math alttext="2 left-parenthesis negative one-fourth right-parenthesis left-parenthesis negative one-fourth right-parenthesis equals one-eighth" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>8</mn></mfrac></mrow></math> ![2 left-parenthesis negative one-fourth right-parenthesis left-parenthesis negative one-fourth right-parenthesis equals one-eighth](images/c11_599.png)

We apply Matsui’s algorithm 1, with *N*, the number of known plaintexts, of 7:

*   Computation of  <math alttext="upper V left-parenthesis upper P comma upper C right-parenthesis equals 10 dot upper P circled-plus 1 dot upper C" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>P</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> ![upper V left-parenthesis upper P comma upper C right-parenthesis equals 10 dot upper P circled-plus 1 dot upper C](images/c11_600.png), for known plaintexts
    
     <math alttext="upper V left-parenthesis 1 comma 12 right-parenthesis equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V left-parenthesis 1 comma 12 right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c11_601.png)   <math alttext="upper V left-parenthesis 2 comma 8 right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V left-parenthesis 2 comma 8 right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c11_602.png)    <math alttext="upper V left-parenthesis 4 comma 9 right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V left-parenthesis 4 comma 9 right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c11_603.png)   <math alttext="upper V left-parenthesis 5 comma 13 right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V left-parenthesis 5 comma 13 right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c11_604.png)
    
     <math alttext="upper V left-parenthesis 8 comma 10 right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V left-parenthesis 8 comma 10 right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c11_605.png)   <math alttext="upper V left-parenthesis 12 comma 11 right-parenthesis equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V left-parenthesis 12 comma 11 right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c11_606.png)   <math alttext="upper V left-parenthesis 15 comma 14 right-parenthesis equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>15</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>14</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V left-parenthesis 15 comma 14 right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c11_607.png)
    
*   The bias is positive and the count *T* is equal to 3, which is less than  <math alttext="7 slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![7 slash 2](images/c11_608.png). Hence, we guess that  <math alttext="upper K 4 Superscript 1 Baseline equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>4</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper K 4 Superscript 1 Baseline equals 1](images/c11_609.png).

*   *Selection and use of the second linear full-cipher approximation*

From the LAT of chosen s-box, we select  <math alttext="upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis 15 comma 7 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>15</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis 15 comma 7 right-parenthesis](images/c11_610.png). Therefore, the linear approximation for the first round is  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 15 dot left-parenthesis upper P circled-plus upper K Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis 7 dot upper Y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>15</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 15 dot left-parenthesis upper P circled-plus upper K Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis 7 dot upper Y right-parenthesis](images/c11_611.png), which has a bias of  <math alttext="negative 1 slash 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ![negative 1 slash 8](images/c11_612.png). In bit representation, linear approximation for the first round is:

 <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper P 1 circled-plus upper K 1 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper P 2 circled-plus upper K 2 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper P 3 circled-plus upper K 3 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper P 4 circled-plus upper K 4 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus upper Y 2 circled-plus upper Y 3 circled-plus upper Y 4 equals 0" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo> <mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>3</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>4</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper P 1 circled-plus upper K 1 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper P 2 circled-plus upper K 2 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper P 3 circled-plus upper K 3 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper P 4 circled-plus upper K 4 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus upper Y 2 circled-plus upper Y 3 circled-plus upper Y 4 equals 0](images/c11_613.png)

For the second round, we use  <math alttext="upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis 7 comma 3 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis 7 comma 3 right-parenthesis](images/c11_614.png). Hence, the linear approximation for the second round is  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 7 dot left-parenthesis upper Y circled-plus upper K squared right-parenthesis right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis 3 dot upper C right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 7 dot left-parenthesis upper Y circled-plus upper K squared right-parenthesis right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis 3 dot upper C right-parenthesis](images/c11_615.png), which corresponds to a bias of  <math alttext="1 slash 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![1 slash 4](images/c11_616.png).

In bit representation, linear approximation for the second round is:

 <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper Y 2 circled-plus upper K 2 squared right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper Y 3 circled-plus upper K 3 squared right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper Y 4 circled-plus upper K 4 squared right-parenthesis circled-plus upper C 3 circled-plus upper C 4 equals 0" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo> <mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>4</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper Y 2 circled-plus upper K 2 squared right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper Y 3 circled-plus upper K 3 squared right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper Y 4 circled-plus upper K 4 squared right-parenthesis circled-plus upper C 3 circled-plus upper C 4 equals 0](images/c11_617.png)

The combination of the linear approximations of both rounds yields the second full-linear approximation:

 <math alttext="upper P 1 circled-plus upper P 2 circled-plus upper P 3 circled-plus upper P 4 circled-plus upper C 3 circled-plus upper C 4 equals upper K 1 Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K 2 Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K 3 Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K 4 Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K 2 squared circled-plus upper K 3 squared circled-plus upper K 4 squared" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi> <mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>4</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>4</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper P 1 circled-plus upper P 2 circled-plus upper P 3 circled-plus upper P 4 circled-plus upper C 3 circled-plus upper C 4 equals upper K 1 Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K 2 Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K 3 Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K 4 Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K 2 squared circled-plus upper K 3 squared circled-plus upper K 4 squared](images/c11_618.png)

Using key permutation, where  <math alttext="upper K 2 squared equals upper K 2 Superscript 1 Baseline comma upper K 3 squared equals upper K 4 Superscript 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>4</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper K 2 squared equals upper K 2 Superscript 1 Baseline comma upper K 3 squared equals upper K 4 Superscript 1](images/c11_619.png), and  <math alttext="upper K 4 squared equals upper K 1 Superscript 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>4</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper K 4 squared equals upper K 1 Superscript 1](images/c11_620.png), the linear approximation becomes:  <math alttext="upper P 1 circled-plus upper P 2 circled-plus upper P 3 circled-plus upper P 4 circled-plus upper C 3 circled-plus upper C 4 equals upper K 3 Superscript 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper P 1 circled-plus upper P 2 circled-plus upper P 3 circled-plus upper P 4 circled-plus upper C 3 circled-plus upper C 4 equals upper K 3 Superscript 1](images/c11_621.png); and its bias is  <math alttext="2 left-parenthesis negative one-eighth right-parenthesis left-parenthesis one-fourth right-parenthesis equals negative one-sixteenth period" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>8</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> ![2 left-parenthesis negative one-eighth right-parenthesis left-parenthesis one-fourth right-parenthesis equals negative one-sixteenth period](images/c11_622.png)

We apply Matsui’s algorithm 1, with *N*, the number of known plaintexts, of 7:

*   Computation of  <math alttext="upper V left-parenthesis upper P comma upper C right-parenthesis equals 15 dot upper P circled-plus 3 dot upper C" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> ![upper V left-parenthesis upper P comma upper C right-parenthesis equals 15 dot upper P circled-plus 3 dot upper C](images/c11_623.png), for known plaintexts
    
     <math alttext="upper V left-parenthesis 1 comma 12 right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V left-parenthesis 1 comma 12 right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c11_624.png)  <math alttext="upper V left-parenthesis 2 comma 8 right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V left-parenthesis 2 comma 8 right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c11_625.png)  <math alttext="upper V left-parenthesis 4 comma 9 right-parenthesis equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V left-parenthesis 4 comma 9 right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c11_626.png)  <math alttext="upper V left-parenthesis 5 comma 13 right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V left-parenthesis 5 comma 13 right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c11_627.png)
    
     <math alttext="upper V left-parenthesis 8 comma 10 right-parenthesis equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V left-parenthesis 8 comma 10 right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c11_628.png)  <math alttext="upper V left-parenthesis 12 comma 11 right-parenthesis equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V left-parenthesis 12 comma 11 right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c11_629.png)  <math alttext="upper V left-parenthesis 15 comma 14 right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>15</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>14</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V left-parenthesis 15 comma 14 right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c11_630.png)
    
*   The bias is negative and the count *T* is equal to 3, which is less than  <math alttext="7 slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![7 slash 2](images/c11_631.png). Therefore, we guess that  <math alttext="upper K 3 Superscript 1 Baseline equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>3</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper K 3 Superscript 1 Baseline equals 0](images/c11_632.png).

*   *Selection and use of the third linear full-cipher approximation*

From the LAT of chosen s-box, we select  <math alttext="upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis 11 comma 14 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>11</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis 11 comma 14 right-parenthesis](images/c11_633.png). Thus, the linear approximation for the first round is  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 11 dot left-parenthesis upper P circled-plus upper K Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis 14 dot upper Y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>11</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>14</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 11 dot left-parenthesis upper P circled-plus upper K Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis 14 dot upper Y right-parenthesis](images/c11_634.png), which has a bias of  <math alttext="1 slash 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ![1 slash 8](images/c11_635.png). In bit representation, linear approximation for the first round is:

 <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper P 1 circled-plus upper K 1 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper P 3 circled-plus upper K 3 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper P 4 circled-plus upper K 4 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus upper Y 1 circled-plus upper Y 2 circled-plus upper Y 3 equals 0" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo> <mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>3</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>4</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper P 1 circled-plus upper K 1 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper P 3 circled-plus upper K 3 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper P 4 circled-plus upper K 4 Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis circled-plus upper Y 1 circled-plus upper Y 2 circled-plus upper Y 3 equals 0](images/c11_636.png)

For the second round, we use  <math alttext="upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis 14 comma 5 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>14</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis 14 comma 5 right-parenthesis](images/c11_637.png). Thus, the linear approximation for the second round is  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 14 dot left-parenthesis upper Y circled-plus upper K squared right-parenthesis right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis 5 dot upper C right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>14</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 14 dot left-parenthesis upper Y circled-plus upper K squared right-parenthesis right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis 5 dot upper C right-parenthesis](images/c11_638.png), which corresponds to a bias of  <math alttext="1 slash 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![1 slash 4](images/c11_639.png). In bit representation, linear approximation for the second round is:

 <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper Y 1 circled-plus upper K 1 squared right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper Y 2 circled-plus upper K 2 squared right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper Y 3 circled-plus upper K 3 squared right-parenthesis circled-plus upper C 2 circled-plus upper C 4 equals 0" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper Y 1 circled-plus upper K 1 squared right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper Y 2 circled-plus upper K 2 squared right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper Y 3 circled-plus upper K 3 squared right-parenthesis circled-plus upper C 2 circled-plus upper C 4 equals 0](images/c11_640.png)

The combination of the linear approximations of both rounds yields the third full-linear approximation:

upper K 3 Superscript 1](images/c11_642.png),  <math alttext="upper K 2 squared equals upper K 2 Superscript 1 Baseline comma upper K 3 squared equals upper K 4 Superscript 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>4</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> K 4 squared equals upper K 1 Superscript 1](images/c11_644.png), the linear approximation becomes:  <math alttext="upper P 1 circled-plus upper P 3 circled-plus upper P 4 circled-plus upper C 2 circled-plus upper C 4 equals upper K 1 Superscript 1 Baseline circled-plus upper K 2 Superscript 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>8</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> We apply Matsui’s algorithm 1, with *N*, the number of known plaintexts, of 7:

*   Computation of  <math alttext="upper V left-parenthesis upper P comma upper C right-parenthesis equals 11 dot upper P circled-plus 5 dot upper C" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>P</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> ![upper V left-parenthesis upper P comma upper C right-parenthesis equals 11 dot upper P circled-plus 5 dot upper C](images/c11_647.png), for known plaintexts
    
     <math alttext="upper V left-parenthesis 1 comma 12 right-parenthesis equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V left-parenthesis 1 comma 12 right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c11_648.png)   <math alttext="upper V left-parenthesis 2 comma 8 right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V left-parenthesis 2 comma 8 right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c11_649.png)    <math alttext="upper V left-parenthesis 4 comma 9 right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V left-parenthesis 4 comma 9 right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c11_650.png)   <math alttext="upper V left-parenthesis 5 comma 13 right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V left-parenthesis 5 comma 13 right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c11_651.png)
