***Problem 11.5***

By definition,  <math alttext="upper T upper A upper L left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper T upper A upper L left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis](images/c11_1291.png) is the number of correct matchings (i.e.  <math alttext="alpha dot upper X equals beta dot upper Y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> ![alpha dot upper X equals beta dot upper Y](images/c11_1292.png)) of the linear expression, using α and β values, minus  <math alttext="2 Superscript b minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript b minus 1](images/c11_1293.png). *m*, the number of correct matchings for a fixed pair  <math alttext="left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis](images/c11_1294.png), is defined by:

 <math alttext="m equals StartAbsoluteValue StartSet upper X comma upper Y element-of upper F 2 Superscript b Baseline vertical-bar alpha upper X plus beta upper Y equals 0 EndSet EndAbsoluteValue" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msubsup><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>X</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mo>}</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![m equals StartAbsoluteValue StartSet upper X comma upper Y element-of upper F 2 Superscript b Baseline vertical-bar alpha upper X plus beta upper Y equals 0 EndSet EndAbsoluteValue](images/c11_1295.png)

With a bit-length of *b*, there exist  <math alttext="2 Superscript b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript b](images/c11_1296.png) linear equations. Therefore, the probability  <math alttext="upper P r left-parenthesis alpha dot upper X plus beta dot upper Y equals 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P r left-parenthesis alpha dot upper X plus beta dot upper Y equals 0 right-parenthesis](images/c11_1297.png) is  <math alttext="m slash 2 Superscript b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>/</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![m slash 2 Superscript b](images/c11_1298.png) and the bias  <math alttext="epsilon left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![epsilon left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis](images/c11_1299.png) is  <math alttext="StartFraction m Over 2 Superscript b Baseline EndFraction minus one-half" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mi>m</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></math> ![StartFraction m Over 2 Superscript b Baseline EndFraction minus one-half](images/c11_1300.png). Then, by substitutions:

 <math alttext="2 Superscript b Baseline asterisk epsilon left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis equals 2 Superscript b Baseline left-parenthesis StartFraction m Over 2 Superscript b Baseline EndFraction minus one-half right-parenthesis equals m minus 2 Superscript b minus 1 Baseline equals upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></msup><mo>\*</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>m</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript b Baseline asterisk epsilon left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis equals 2 Superscript b Baseline left-parenthesis StartFraction m Over 2 Superscript b Baseline EndFraction minus one-half right-parenthesis equals m minus 2 Superscript b minus 1 Baseline equals upper L upper A upper T left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis](images/c11_1301.png)□

     <math alttext="alpha dot upper X circled-plus beta dot upper Y equals alpha dot upper X circled-plus beta dot left-parenthesis lamda dot upper X circled-plus mu right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis alpha circled-plus beta dot lamda right-parenthesis dot upper X circled-plus beta dot lamda" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> ![alpha dot upper X circled-plus beta dot upper Y equals alpha dot upper X circled-plus beta dot left-parenthesis lamda dot upper X circled-plus mu right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis alpha circled-plus beta dot lamda right-parenthesis dot upper X circled-plus beta dot lamda](images/c11_1304.png)

Once α, β, λ, and μ are fixed,  <math alttext="left-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis beta Subscript i Baseline mu Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>&#8230;</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis beta Subscript i Baseline mu Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c11_1306.png) is a constant  <math alttext="c 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![c 0](images/c11_1307.png), either 0 or 1;  <math alttext="alpha Subscript i Baseline beta Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![alpha Subscript i Baseline beta Subscript i](images/c11_1308.png) is a constant denoted  <math alttext="a Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![a Subscript i](images/c11_1309.png), either 0 or 1, for  <math alttext="i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma b](images/c11_1310.png). Therefore, the bias of linear expression (a) is 0. By Piling-up lemma, if a random binary variable *Z* has a bias of 0, the bias of any variable combination including *Z* also is 0. We can conclude that linear cryptanalysis cannot be applied to break ciphers using linear s-boxes.

*   By Piling-up lemma, the bias of a linear expression involving 16 s-boxes, all with a bias of ¼, is  <math alttext="2 Superscript 15 Baseline asterisk left-parenthesis one-fourth right-parenthesis Superscript 16 Baseline equals 2 Superscript negative 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></msup><mo>\*</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>17</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 15 Baseline asterisk left-parenthesis one-fourth right-parenthesis Superscript 16 Baseline equals 2 Superscript negative 17](images/c11_1314.png).

1.  Consider any differential  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 0 less-than-or-equal-to beta less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript m Baseline minus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 0 less-than-or-equal-to beta less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript m Baseline minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c11_1323.png). For any s-box input *X*, if  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper X comma upper X circled-plus alpha right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper X comma upper X circled-plus alpha right-parenthesis](images/c11_1324.png) is such that  <math alttext="upper S left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis circled-plus upper S left-parenthesis upper X circled-plus alpha right-parenthesis equals beta" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math> ![upper S left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis circled-plus upper S left-parenthesis upper X circled-plus alpha right-parenthesis equals beta](images/c11_1325.png), then also  <math alttext="upper S left-parenthesis upper X circled-plus alpha right-parenthesis circled-plus upper S left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals beta" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math> ![upper S left-parenthesis upper X circled-plus alpha right-parenthesis circled-plus upper S left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals beta](images/c11_1326.png). Therefore, if  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper X comma upper X circled-plus alpha right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper X comma upper X circled-plus alpha right-parenthesis](images/c11_1327.png) is included in set  <math alttext="normal upper Delta Subscript alpha comma beta Superscript upper S" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mi>S</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![normal upper Delta Subscript alpha comma beta Superscript upper S](images/c11_1328.png), then  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper X circled-plus alpha comma upper X right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper X circled-plus alpha comma upper X right-parenthesis](images/c11_1329.png) also is included. Thus, the cardinality of the set  <math alttext="normal upper Delta Subscript alpha comma beta Superscript upper S" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mi>S</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![normal upper Delta Subscript alpha comma beta Superscript upper S](images/c11_1330.png), in equation (a), is even. In other words, the elements of each DDT are even positive integers.
2.  Consider any row α in DDT. The bit-length of variable *X* and of α is of *n*. Therefore, we can build  <math alttext="2 Superscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript n](images/c11_1331.png) ordered pairs  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper X comma upper X circled-plus alpha right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper X comma upper X circled-plus alpha right-parenthesis](images/c11_1332.png). A difference  <math alttext="upper S left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper X circled-plus alpha right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8853;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis circled-plus left-parenthesis upper X circled-plus alpha right-parenthesis](images/c11_1333.png) is associated with each pair  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper X comma upper X circled-plus alpha right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper X comma upper X circled-plus alpha right-parenthesis](images/c11_1334.png). Therefore, the number of s-box output differences associated with row α is  <math alttext="2 Superscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript n](images/c11_1335.png). Therefore, the element sum of each DDT row is  <math alttext="2 Superscript n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript n](images/c11_1336.png).

***Problem 11.8***

First step: compute the bits of the keystream until the last intercepted bit. Since the considered LFSR has a primitive feedback polynomial, it has seven distinct states. Assume that the initial state is  <math alttext="s Subscript 0 Baseline equals left-parenthesis k Subscript 0 comma Baseline comma k 1 comma k 2 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 1 comma 1 comma 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![s Subscript 0 Baseline equals left-parenthesis k Subscript 0 comma Baseline comma k 1 comma k 2 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 1 comma 1 comma 0 right-parenthesis](images/c11_1337.png). Then,

# 12   
Public-Key Cryptosystems  
RSA and Finite Field Cryptography-based Schemes

## 12.1 Introduction to Public-Key Cryptosystems

In symmetric cryptosystems, the message sender and recipient must share a common secret (i.e. a ciphering key) before encrypting and decrypting messages. The big question is: how to agree on the secret key in first place, particularly if sender and receiver never met? It looks like the “The chicken or egg” dilemma. Trust is required before exchanging the secret key in a secure way. Therefore, symmetric cryptosystems are limited to use in cases where both parties know and trust each other.

The turning point in modern cryptography occurred in 1976‒1977, when Diffie and Hellman \[[1](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0001)\] on one side and Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman \[[2](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0002)\], on the other, proposed original schemes to secure systems without requiring a unique cipher shared by both parties. The proposed schemes were and are still used to design public-key cryptosystems. The latter provide support to secure communications worldwide between people who do not a priori know each other. The first and still most widely used public-key cryptosystem is with no doubt is the RSA.

Modern cryptography is founded on the idea that the key used to encrypt messages can be made public, while the key used to decrypt messages must be kept private. As such, these systems are known as public-key cryptographic systems (also called asymmetric cryptosystems) and are based on operations easy to process in one direction, but difficult to invert.

Public-key algorithms provide support for confidentiality through message encryption and authentication through message signature (see [Figure 12.1](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0001)). Public-key encryption is founded on the idea that the key used to encrypt messages is made public, while the key used to decrypt is kept private. Public-key signature is based on the idea that the key used to sign messages is private, while the key used to verify signature is made public.

![Figure 12.1 Overall scheme of public-key cryptosystems.](images/c12f001.png)

[**Figure 12.1**](#c12.xhtml#rc12-fig-0001) Overall scheme of public-key cryptosystems.

There exist hundreds (or even more) algorithms in the symmetric cryptography world, while there exist only three families of public key algorithms, namely RSA, discrete logarithm-based, and elliptic curve schemes. The first generation of public-key cryptosystems, including RSA, Diffie-Hellman key exchange, Menezes-Qu-Vanstone, and ElGamal cryptosystems are addressed in this chapter. The security of those cryptosystems is based on either integer factorization problem (addressed in [Section 12.2.4](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-02005)) or discrete logarithm problem (DLP) in cyclic groups  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c12_1.png) (addressed in [Section 12.3.1](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-02008)). Those problems are known to be computationally infeasible for large numbers. The second generation of public-key cryptosystems is based on elliptic curve theory. They are more powerful than the first generation and are on the way to dominate in the future. The security of elliptic curve cryptosystems is based on discrete logarithm problem in finite fields *F[p]* (addressed in Section 3.2.2).

Public-key cryptography is fundamentally based on the theory of numbers and not on a shared secret without worrying about adversaries listening in the exchanged messages via an insecure network. The strong idea behind the public-key cryptography is a challenge to attackers, which may be phrased as follows: *you, the potential attackers, know the key used to encrypt the messages sent to me, but you cannot decrypt them unless you have algorithms to solve factoring or DLP problems*.

Public-key cryptography makes use of one-way functions, also called trapdoor functions. A one-way function is a function easy to compute if the input is given, but it is computationally infeasible to find the input if the output is given (i.e. given the function image). For example, RSA is based on integer factoring. Computing the product  <math alttext="n equals p asterisk q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![n equals p asterisk q](images/c12_2.png) given *p* and *q* is easy. However, finding *p* and *q* given *n* is computationally infeasible when *n* is a product of two large random primes.

In summary public-key cryptography is divided into two classes: IFC (Integer Factorization Cryptography) and DLC (Discrete Logarithm Cryptography). The latter is divided into two subclasses: Finite Field Cryptography (FFC) and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC). DSA is an example of FFC algorithms; ECDSA is an example of ECC algorithms. Other examples of DLC algorithms are the Diffie-Hellman and MQV key agreement algorithms, which have both FFC and ECC forms. The difference between those three classes is the underlying used math. IFC and FFC algorithms are discussed in this chapter and the ECC algorithms in the next one.

[Table 12.1](#c12.xhtml#c12-tbl-0001) summarizes the services provided by public-key algorithms:

[**Table 12.1**](#c12.xhtml#rc12-tbl-0001) Security services provided by public-key-algorithms.

|  || *Algorithm family* |
| --- | --- |
| *Service* || *IFC* || *FFC* || *ECC* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Key exchange || RSA || DHKE, MQV || ECDH, ECMQV |
| Encryption || RSA || ElGamal || ECIES |
| Signature || RSA || DSA, ElGamal || ECDSA, EdDSA |
| DHKE: Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange, DSA: Digital Signature Algorithm, ECDH: Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman key agreement protocol, ECIES: Elliptic Curve Integrated Encryption Scheme, MQV: Menezes-Qu-Vanstone, ECMQV: Elliptic Curve MQV, ECDSA: Elliptic Curve Digital Signature, EdDSA: Edwards-curve DSA. |

*   Encryption service is for guaranteeing confidentiality. In general, public-key cryptosystems are not recommended to encrypt large amounts of data.
*   Signature service is for authentication of message origin.
*   Key exchange service is the way to use public keys to generate a shared secret between parties. Then, the shared secret is used to derive a symmetric key; and then, parties make use of a symmetric cipher, such as AES, to encrypt and decrypt their messages.
    

**Note**. RSA and DLP-based schemes rely on cyclic groups. To address those cryptographic schemes the fundamentals of modular arithmetic and cyclic groups are reminded with examples in [Chapter 3](#c03.xhtml).

### 12.1.1 Attacks Against Public-Key Cryptosystems

Since public-key cryptosystems reveal a part of data used in the encryption or signature schemes, they are vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. For decades, attackers and cryptanalysts have addressed a lot of vulnerabilities to recover the hidden part of those cryptosystems. Identified vulnerabilities have been taken into account to provide a high level of security in the current public-key cryptosystems.

Public-key cryptosystems are considered safe at multiple levels of security strength depending on the length (in bits) of the keys. Public-key standards provide useful guides to select parameter values for each cryptographic algorithm. As discussed in the sequel, when public-key algorithms are used correctly, they are secure enough to prevent all known attacks. However, if a cryptosystem is not complying with standards, it becomes a target for attackers, which, in particular, can easily lead to recovering the private key. Even a brute-force attack, which is inefficient in general, can succeed if the algorithm is not parameterized correctly. The potential attacks depend on the mathematical foundations of each algorithm. In the next sections, some well-known attacks are discussed.

#### 12.1.1.1 Attacks Against Encryption Schemes

Attacks against encryption schemes aim at recovering the private key, disclosing the plaintext or generating illegitimate messages. When used correctly, the standard public-key encryption algorithms are known to be resistant to attacks aiming to recover private keys or plaintexts. Correct use of algorithms mainly includes selection of large prime numbers, padding of messages, and single use of keys to encrypt.

However, the third type of attack, known as existential forgery attack, cannot be thwarted by public-key algorithms. Given the public key and/or some encrypted messages intercepted by the adversary, the latter can forge and encrypt a message without controlling the content of the message. Such an attack may lead the recipient to receive data, which tamper its functions. As the adversary cannot choose the content of the message, his/her objective is jeopardizing the recipient availability.

#### 12.1.1.2 Attacks Against Digital Signature Schemes

In the cyberspace, digital signature is a cryptographic transformation. Consequently, the difficulty in forging signatures is linked to the mathematical foundations used to design digital signature schemes. The latter are far more difficult to forge than hand signatures.

Attacks against digital signature may be categorized into three groups:

1.  *Universal forgery*: adversary is able to recover the private key of the signer and then sign any message.
2.  *Selective forgery*: adversary is able to create valid signatures on messages of his/her choice.
3.  *Existential forgery*: adversary can generate a pair composed of a signature and a message without controlling the message content.

When used correctly, standard public-key signature algorithms are known to be resistant to the first and second types of attacks. Public-key signature algorithms presented in this chapter and the next make signature forgery computationally infeasible even if the signatures of some messages are known to adversary. However, the existential forgery attack remains a threat to public-key cryptosystems. In this type of attack, the adversary intercepts the public key of the signer and some signed messages, then he/she generates a forged signature and derives the message content that matches the forged signature (see an example in [Section 12.3.4.3](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-03013)). Notice that the content of the message depends on the forged signature and cannot be controlled by the adversary. The recipient validates the signature and makes use of the received content, which may jeopardize its functions.

Last but not least, potential attacks against digital signatures are identity and private-key theft, which are both out of the scope of algorithms presented in this chapter and the next one. In the first type of attack, the adversary sends his own public key to recipient pretending he/she is the legitimate party and then signs messages. To thwart identity theft, a certificate authority, which acts as a notary, provides assurance regarding the validity of the public key. Certification authority is addressed in Section 15.2. Consequently, in operational cryptosystems, public-key cryptographic algorithms are used jointly with certificate authorities. Private-key theft is a more challenging issue. Either the private key has been really stolen or the malicious owner tries to deny sending a particular message. The solutions to real or alleged private-key theft are not addressed in this book.

## 12.2 RSA Cryptosystem

The seminal asymmetric ciphering was patented[¹](#c12.xhtml#c12-note-0001) by Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman in 1977 and published in \[[2](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0002)\]. Named after its coauthors, RSA was the first radically different approach in which the sender and receiver do not need to share a secret key. RSA is based on two keys: a private key known only to its owner and a public key, as the name suggests, known to all. In the last four decades, vulnerabilities of RSA have been intensively addressed and the proposed countermeasures were included in operational RSA cryptosystems. Most of clients and servers in the today’s Internet make use of RSA to secure their communications.

Let us consider a scenario in which Bob needs to receive messages from Alice and both partners agree to use the RSA cryptosystem to make their messages confidential. To do so, the steps to follow are:

1.  Bob computes two keys (public and private keys).
2.  Bob sends his public key to Alice.
3.  When Alice has a message to send, she encrypts the message using Bob’s public key.
4.  When Bob receives the encrypted message, he uses his private key to retrieve the plaintext.

To provide secure systems, RSA must address fundamental questions:

*   How Bob can compute public and private keys?
*   How Bob can share his public key with Alice?
*   A more challenging question: how to make it *computationally infeasible* to derive the private key from the public key (assuming a known key computation algorithm)?

Answers to the first and third questions take their roots in the modular arithmetic (a sub-branch of arithmetic), which is the basis of RSA. However, RSA by itself does not address the second question. It only assumes that the network is reliable, but insecure. Public-key distribution is provided by public-key infrastructures (PKIs), which are addressed in Section 15.2. First, RSA operations (i.e. key generation and distribution, encryption, and decryption) are described, then security and correctness proof are addressed.

The computations and exchanges to achieve an RSA-based secure communication between Alice and Bob are illustrated by [Figure 12.2](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0002).

![Figure 12.2 Illustration of RSA-based communication.](images/c12f002.png)

### 12.2.2 Implementation Issues

#### 12.2.2.1 Fast Modular Exponentiation Methods

RSA encryption and decryption are modular exponentiation operations, which are time consuming in operational RSA cryptosystems and complex to do by hand. Imagine you have  <math alttext="1918 Superscript 24367 Baseline m o d 669984751" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>1918</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>24367</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>669984751</mn></mrow></math> ![1918 Superscript 24367 Baseline m o d 669984751](images/c12_36.png) to compute. A naïve method would be to apply an iterative method to compute powers of 1918 from 1 to 24367, and then compute the modulo 669984751. That would take a huge amount of time. Hopefully, there exist fast methods for modular exponentiation computation, which are based on the exploitation of intermediate computations. The most commonly used methods to optimize the RSA computation time are:

*   Square-and-multiply method, which may be used for encryption, or decryption, or for both.
*   Chinese-remainder-theorem-based method, which may be used for decryption.

The reader should refer to Section 3.3.2 to learn how the square-and-multiply method, called right-to-left binary exponentiation, works. The CRT-based decryption is specific to RSA and is described below.

#### 12.2.2.2 Chinese Remainder Theorem-based RSA Decryption

Chinese remainder theorem (CRT) is a powerful tool to solve congruence equation systems. The CRT is independent of RSA and it is presented in Section 3.3.4. The reader should first learn how the CRT works in general before applying it to implement RSA decryption. As previously described, the decryption of a ciphertext *C* requires a modular exponentiation:  <math alttext="upper M identical-to upper C Superscript d Baseline m o d upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M identical-to upper C Superscript d Baseline m o d upper N](images/c12_37.png), where *M* is the plaintext,  <math alttext="d" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> ![d](images/c12_38.png) the private key, and *N* the RSA modulus. Recall that  <math alttext="upper N equals p q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper N equals p q](images/c12_39.png) and *d* is the modular inverse of the public key *e* modulo  <math alttext="left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis q minus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis q minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c12_40.png).

To make RSA decryption faster, the idea of the CRT-based RSA decryption method is to perform two exponentiations  <math alttext="upper C Superscript d Super Subscript p Superscript Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C Superscript d Super Subscript p Superscript Baseline m o d p](images/c12_41.png) and  <math alttext="upper C Superscript d Super Subscript q Superscript Baseline m o d q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C Superscript d Super Subscript q Superscript Baseline m o d q](images/c12_42.png) instead of  <math alttext="upper C Superscript d Baseline m o d p q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C Superscript d Baseline m o d p q](images/c12_43.png) and then make use of CRT to produce a result, which is the plaintext *M*.

Below is the principle of CRT-based RSA decryption method:

*   Since *p* and *q* are primes, for any integer  <math alttext="upper M less-than upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M less-than upper N](images/c12_44.png), if  <math alttext="upper M identical-to upper C Superscript d Baseline m o d p q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M identical-to upper C Superscript d Baseline m o d p q](images/c12_45.png), then  <math alttext="upper M identical-to upper C Superscript d Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M identical-to upper C Superscript d Baseline m o d p](images/c12_46.png) and  <math alttext="upper M identical-to upper C Superscript d Baseline m o d q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M identical-to upper C Superscript d Baseline m o d q](images/c12_47.png) (application of Lemma 3.2).
*   Since *p* and *q* are primes, they are either coprime to *C* or one of them (not both) is not coprime to *C*. The application of the CRT requires at least two congruence equations. Therefore, the CRT-based RSA decryption is used only if both *p* and *q* are coprime to *C*. If *p* and *q* are coprime to *C*, then by Fermat’s little theorem:
    
     <math alttext="1 identical-to upper C Superscript p minus 1 Baseline m o d p and 1 identical-to upper C Superscript q minus 1 Baseline m o d q period" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext>&#160;and&#160;</mtext></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![1 identical-to upper C Superscript p minus 1 Baseline m o d p and 1 identical-to upper C Superscript q minus 1 Baseline m o d q period](images/c12_48.png)
    
*   Exponent *d* can be written as:  <math alttext="d equals i 1 left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis Superscript i 2 Baseline plus d Subscript p Baseline equals k 1 left-parenthesis q minus 1 Exponent  <math alttext="d Subscript p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![d Subscript p](images/c12_60.png) is bounded by  <math alttext="p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p minus 1](images/c12_61.png) and  <math alttext="d Subscript q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![d Subscript q](images/c12_62.png), by  <math alttext="q minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![q minus 1](images/c12_63.png).

     <math alttext="left-brace StartLayout 1st Row upper M identical-to upper C Superscript d Super Subscript p Superscript Baseline m o d p 2nd Row upper M identical-to upper C Superscript d Super Subscript q Superscript Baseline m o d q EndLayout" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo> <mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow></math> ![left-brace StartLayout 1st Row upper M identical-to upper C Superscript d Super Subscript p Superscript Baseline m o d p 2nd Row upper M identical-to upper C Superscript d Super Subscript q Superscript Baseline m o d q EndLayout](images/c12_64.png)

    Let  <math alttext="upper C Superscript d Super Subscript p Superscript Baseline m o d p identical-to upper M Subscript p Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Superscript d Super Subscript p Superscript Baseline m o d p identical-to upper M Subscript p Baseline](images/c12_66.png), such that  <math alttext="upper M Subscript p Baseline less-than p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript p Baseline less-than p](images/c12_67.png), and  <math alttext="upper C Superscript d Super Subscript q Superscript Baseline m o d q identical-to upper M Subscript q Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Superscript d Super Subscript q Superscript Baseline m o d q identical-to upper M Subscript q Baseline](images/c12_68.png), such that  <math alttext="upper M Subscript q Baseline less-than q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript q Baseline less-than q](images/c12_69.png).
    
*   By virtue of the Chinese remainder theorem, there exists a unique integer  <math alttext="upper M less-than p asterisk q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M less-than p asterisk q](images/c12_70.png) such that both congruence equations are fulfilled. By Gauss’s algorithm (see Section 3.3.4), *M* is computed as:
    
     <math alttext="upper M identical-to left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper M Subscript p Baseline asterisk q asterisk left-parenthesis q Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d p right-parenthesis right-parenthesis plus left-parenthesis upper M Subscript q Baseline asterisk p asterisk left-parenthesis p Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d q right-parenthesis right-parenthesis right-parenthesis m o d p q" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>\*</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M identical-to left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper M Subscript p Baseline asterisk q asterisk left-parenthesis q Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d p right-parenthesis right-parenthesis plus left-parenthesis upper M Subscript q Baseline asterisk p asterisk left-parenthesis p Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d q right-parenthesis right-parenthesis right-parenthesis m o d p q](images/c12_71.png)

The pseudocode of the CRT-based decryption is as follows:

**Example 12.2** Let  <math alttext="p equals 37" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>37</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 37](images/c12_84.png),  <math alttext="q equals 89" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>89</mn></mrow></math> ![q equals 89](images/c12_85.png),  <math alttext="d equals 2987" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2987</mn></mrow></math> ![d equals 2987](images/c12_86.png), and  <math alttext="upper C equals 2494" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2494</mn></mrow></math> ![upper C equals 2494](images/c12_87.png).

The plaintext *M* is such that  <math alttext="upper M identical-to 2494 Superscript 2987 Baseline m o d 37 asterisk 89" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mrow><mn>2494</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2987</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>37</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>89</mn></mrow></math> ![upper M identical-to 2494 Superscript 2987 Baseline m o d 37 asterisk 89](images/c12_88.png) and by Lemma 3.2,  <math alttext="upper M identical-to 2494 Superscript 2987 Baseline m o d 37" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mrow><mn>2494</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2987</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>37</mn></mrow></math> ![upper M identical-to 2494 Superscript 2987 Baseline m o d 37](images/c12_89.png) and  <math alttext="upper M identical-to 2494 Superscript 2987 Baseline m o d 89" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mrow><mn>2494</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2987</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>89</mn></mrow></math> ![upper M identical-to 2494 Superscript 2987 Baseline m o d 89](images/c12_90.png).

To find the plaintext *M* using the CRT-based RSA decryption, we proceed as follows:

1.  – Reduce the bases of both congruences as follows:
    
     <math alttext="2494 equals 67 asterisk 37 plus 15 equals 28 asterisk 89 plus 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2494</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>67</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>37</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>28</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>89</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![2494 equals 67 asterisk 37 plus 15 equals 28 asterisk 89 plus 2](images/c12_91.png)
    
     <math alttext="upper C Subscript p Baseline identical-to 2494 m o d 37 identical-to left-parenthesis 67 asterisk 37 plus 15 right-parenthesis m o d 37 identical-to 15" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>2494</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>37</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>67</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>37</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>37</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript p Baseline identical-to 2494 m o d 37 identical-to left-parenthesis 67 asterisk 37 plus 15 right-parenthesis m o d 37 identical-to 15](images/c12_92.png)
    
     <math alttext="upper C Subscript q Baseline identical-to 2494 m o d 89 identical-to left-parenthesis 28 asterisk 89 plus 2 right-parenthesis m o d 89 identical-to 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>2494</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>89</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>28</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>89</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>89</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>2</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript q Baseline identical-to 2494 m o d 89 identical-to left-parenthesis 28 asterisk 89 plus 2 right-parenthesis m o d 89 identical-to 2](images/c12_93.png)
    
2.  – Reduce the exponents:
    
     <math alttext="2987 equals 82 left-parenthesis 37 minus 1 right-parenthesis plus 35 equals 33 left-parenthesis 89 minus 1 right-parenthesis plus 83" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2987</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>82</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>37</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>35</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>33</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>89</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>83</mn></mrow></math> ![2987 equals 82 left-parenthesis 37 minus 1 right-parenthesis plus 35 equals 33 left-parenthesis 89 minus 1 right-parenthesis plus 83](images/c12_94.png)
    
     <math alttext="d Subscript p Baseline equals 2987 m o d left-parenthesis 37 minus 1 right-parenthesis equals 35" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2987</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>37</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>35</mn></mrow></math> ![d Subscript p Baseline equals 2987 m o d left-parenthesis 37 minus 1 right-parenthesis equals 35](images/c12_95.png)
    
     <math alttext="d Subscript p Baseline equals 2987 m o d left-parenthesis 89 minus 1 right-parenthesis equals 83" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2987</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>89</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>83</mn></mrow></math> ![d Subscript p Baseline equals 2987 m o d left-parenthesis 89 minus 1 right-parenthesis equals 83](images/c12_96.png)
    
3.  – Exponentiation in  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z 37" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>&#8484;</mi><mrow><mn>37</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z 37](images/c12_97.png) and  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z 89" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>&#8484;</mi><mrow><mn>89</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z 89](images/c12_98.png):
    
     <math alttext="15 Superscript 8 asterisk 4 Baseline m o d 37 identical-to left-parenthesis 7 right-parenthesis Superscript 4 Baseline m o d 37 identical-to 33 15 cubed m o d 37 identical-to 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>37</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>4</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>37</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>33</mn></mrow><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>37</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ![15 Superscript 8 asterisk 4 Baseline m o d 37 identical-to left-parenthesis 7 right-parenthesis Superscript 4 Baseline m o d 37 identical-to 33 15 cubed m o d 37 identical-to 8](images/c12_99.png)
    
     <math alttext="2 Superscript 11 Baseline m o d 89 identical-to 1 2 Superscript 6 Baseline m o d 89 identical-to 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>89</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>6</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>89</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>64</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 11 Baseline m o d 89 identical-to 1 2 Superscript 6 Baseline m o d 89 identical-to 64](images/c12_100.png)
    
     <math alttext="upper M Subscript p Baseline equals upper C Subscript p Superscript d Super Subscript p Superscript Baseline m o d p equals 15 Superscript 35 Baseline m o d 37 identical-to left-parenthesis 15 Superscript 8 asterisk 4 Baseline right-parenthesis left-parenthesis 15 cubed right-parenthesis m o d 37 identical-to 5" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>p</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>35</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>37</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>37</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>5</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript p Baseline equals upper C Subscript p Superscript d Super Subscript p Superscript Baseline m o d p equals 15 Superscript 35 Baseline m o d 37 identical-to left-parenthesis 15 Superscript 8 asterisk 4 Baseline right-parenthesis left-parenthesis 15 cubed right-parenthesis m o d 37 identical-to 5](images/c12_101.png)
    
     <math alttext="upper M Subscript q Baseline equals upper C Subscript q Superscript d Super Subscript q Superscript Baseline m o d q equals 116 Superscript 93 Baseline m o d 131 identical-to 30" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>q</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></msubsup><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>116</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>93</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>131</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow></math> ![upper M Subscript q Baseline equals upper C Subscript q Superscript d Super Subscript q Superscript Baseline m o d q equals 116 Superscript 93 Baseline m o d 131 identical-to 30](images/c12_102.png)
    
4.  – CRT-based solution to decryption
    
     <math alttext="89 Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d 37 identical-to 5 37 Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d 89 identical-to 77" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>89</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>37</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>37</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>89</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>77</mn></mrow></math> ![89 Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d 37 identical-to 5 37 Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d 89 identical-to 77](images/c12_103.png)
    
     <math alttext="upper M equals left-parenthesis left-parenthesis 5 asterisk 89 asterisk left-parenthesis 89 Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d 37 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis plus left-parenthesis 64 asterisk 37 asterisk left-parenthesis 37 Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d 89 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis right-parenthesis m o d 37 asterisk 89" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>89</mn><mo>\*</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>89</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>37</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>64</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>37</mn><mo>\*</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>37</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>89</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>37</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>89</mn></mrow></math> ![upper M equals left-parenthesis left-parenthesis 5 asterisk 89 asterisk left-parenthesis 89 Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d 37 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis plus left-parenthesis 64 asterisk 37 asterisk left-parenthesis 37 Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d 89 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis right-parenthesis m o d 37 asterisk 89](images/c12_104.png)
    
    Therefore, the plaintext is 153.
    

*   *Decryption time reduction*

If the decryption  <math alttext="upper M identical-to upper C Superscript d Baseline m o d p q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M identical-to upper C Superscript d Baseline m o d p q](images/c12_105.png) is carried out with the exponent *d* using the right-to-left binary exponentiation method,  <math alttext="left ceiling l o g 2 d right ceiling" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8968;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo>&#8969;</mo></mrow></math> ![left ceiling l o g 2 d right ceiling](images/c12_106.png) iterations[⁴](#c12.xhtml#c12-note-0004) are performed. *d* is less than *N*, but it may have the same bit-length than that of the modulus *N*. Therefore, exponentiation  <math alttext="upper C Superscript d" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper C Superscript d](images/c12_107.png) requires at most  <math alttext="left ceiling l o g 2 p q right ceiling" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8968;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>&#8969;</mo></mrow></math> ![left ceiling l o g 2 p q right ceiling](images/c12_108.png) iterations.

If the CRT-RSA decryption method is used jointly with the right-to-left binary exponentiation method to decrypt,  <math alttext="left ceiling l o g 2 d Subscript p Baseline right ceiling plus left ceiling l o g 2 d Subscript q Baseline right ceiling" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8968;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>&#8969;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>&#8968;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow><mo>&#8969;</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left ceiling l o g 2 d Subscript p Baseline right ceiling plus left ceiling l o g 2 d Subscript q Baseline right ceiling](images/c12_109.png) iterations are performed. Since  <math alttext="d Subscript p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![d Subscript p](images/c12_110.png) and  <math alttext="d Subscript q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![d Subscript q](images/c12_111.png) are bounded by *p* and *p* respectively,  <math alttext="left ceiling l o g 2 d Subscript p Baseline right ceiling plus left ceiling l o g 2 d Subscript q Baseline right ceiling less-than left ceiling l o g 2 p right ceiling plus left ceiling l o g 2 q right ceiling equals left ceiling l o g 2 p q right ceiling" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8968;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>&#8969;</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo>&#8968;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow><mo>&#8969;</mo></mrow><mo>&#60;</mo><mrow><mo>&#8968;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>&#8969;</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo>&#8968;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>&#8969;</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>&#8968;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>&#8969;</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left ceiling l o g 2 d Subscript p Baseline right ceiling plus left ceiling l o g 2 d Subscript q Baseline right ceiling less-than left ceiling l o g 2 p right ceiling plus left ceiling l o g 2 q right ceiling equals left ceiling l o g 2 p q right ceiling](images/c12_112.png). Therefore, there is no gain in terms of iterations in the right-to-left binary exponentiation method. However, CRT-RSA method may result in a reduction of computation time by a factor of 4 if the primes *p* and *q* have the same bit-length (which is often the case in operational cryptosystems). Indeed, the regular decryption performs operations over  <math alttext="p q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![p q](images/c12_113.png) while in CRT-RSA decryption performs operations over ℤ[p] and  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript q](images/c12_114.png), which have nearly the same cardinality. In the right-to-left binary exponentiation method, the most time-consuming operation is the modular multiplication. Consider a computer, which has a basic unsigned multiplication operation, which takes two 32-bit words and returns a 64-bit result. The product  <math alttext="a asterisk b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![a asterisk b](images/c12_115.png), with *a* and *b* integers less than <math alttext="2 Superscript 32 Baseline minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 32 Baseline minus 1](images/c12_116.png), requires a single multiplication operation. Now, consider that *a* and *b* are less than  <math alttext="2 Superscript 64 Baseline minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 64 Baseline minus 1](images/c12_117.png). Therefore, they may be represented as  <math alttext="a equals 2 Superscript 32 Baseline asterisk a 1 plus a 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![a equals 2 Superscript 32 Baseline asterisk a 1 plus a 2](images/c12_118.png) and  <math alttext="b equals 2 Superscript 32 Baseline asterisk b 1 plus b 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![b equals 2 Superscript 32 Baseline asterisk b 1 plus b 2](images/c12_119.png), with  <math alttext="a 2 equals a m o d 2 Superscript 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![a 2 equals a m o d 2 Superscript 32](images/c12_120.png) and  <math alttext="b 2 equals b m o d 2 Superscript 32" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![b 2 equals b m o d 2 Superscript 32](images/c12_121.png). To compute  <math alttext="upper C equals a asterisk b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C equals a asterisk b](images/c12_122.png) we need four multiplications:  <math alttext="a 1 asterisk b 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![a 1 asterisk b 1](images/c12_123.png),  <math alttext="a 1 asterisk b 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![a 1 asterisk b 2](images/c12_124.png),  <math alttext="a 2 asterisk b 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![a 2 asterisk b 1](images/c12_125.png), and  <math alttext="a 2 asterisk b 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![a 2 asterisk b 2](images/c12_126.png) and then do some additions and storage in two 64-bit long words. That is why CRT-RSA decryption may reduce the decryption time by a factor of 4 at least.

#### 12.2.2.3 Why  <math alttext="e equals 65537" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>65537</mn></mrow></math> ![e equals 65537](images/c12_127.png) **Is Often Used in RSA Cryptosystems?**

Since the public key exponent *e* is public, the security of RSA does not rely on the exponent value provided that *e* is greater or equal to 3 and coprime with  <math alttext="phi left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#981;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![phi left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis](images/c12_128.png) and the *padding* technique is used. See Problem 12.1, which shows why *e* must be different of 1 and 2. However, it is recommended that the exponent selection should be done in such a way that encryption computation is minimized. Recall that encryption is a modular exponentiation. 65537 is the exponent value the most used in operational RSA cryptosystems. First, 65537 is prime and there is no need to check if  <math alttext="upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis e comma phi left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#981;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis e comma phi left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c12_129.png) holds. Second, and more important, 65537 is equal to  <math alttext="2 Superscript 16 Baseline plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 16 Baseline plus 1](images/c12_130.png), which makes modular exponentiation faster.

### 12.2.3 Proof of Correctness of RSA

RSA is correct if the decryption of a ciphertext  <math alttext="upper C equals upper M Superscript e Baseline m o d n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>M</mi><mi>e</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C equals upper M Superscript e Baseline m o d n](images/c12_131.png) returns the original plaintext *M*. Formally, the following must hold:

 <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper M Superscript e Baseline m o d n right-parenthesis Superscript d Baseline m o d n identical-to upper M m o d n equals upper M comma for-all upper M less-than-or-equal-to n minus 1" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mi>e</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>d</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mi>M</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper M Superscript e Baseline m o d n right-parenthesis Superscript d Baseline m o d n identical-to upper M m o d n equals upper M comma for-all upper M less-than-or-equal-to n minus 1](images/c12_132.png)(a) 

By the modular arithmetic rule (Lemma 3.1), which states:  <math alttext="a Superscript q Baseline m o d p identical-to left-parenthesis a m o d p right-parenthesis Superscript q Baseline m o d n comma" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>q</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>q</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![a Superscript q Baseline m o d p identical-to left-parenthesis a m o d p right-parenthesis Superscript q Baseline m o d n comma](images/c12_133.png) in which *a* is replaced by  <math alttext="upper M Superscript e Baseline m o d n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mi>e</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M Superscript e Baseline m o d n](images/c12_134.png), (a) is rewritten as:

 <math alttext="upper M Superscript e d Baseline m o d n identical-to upper M m o d n for-all m less-than-or-equal-to n" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8801;</mo><mi>M</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8704;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M Superscript e d Baseline m o d n identical-to upper M m o d n for-all m less-than-or-equal-to n](images/c12_135.png)(b) 

Below is the method most used in literature to prove (b); it is based on Fermat’s little theorem.

By definition:  <math alttext="e asterisk d identical-to 1 m o d left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis q minus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![e asterisk d identical-to 1 m o d left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis q minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c12_136.png). Therefore, there exists an integer *k* such that:

 <math alttext="e asterisk d equals 1 plus k left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis q minus 1 right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![e asterisk d equals 1 plus k left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis q minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c12_137.png)

By substitution:

If  <math alttext="upper M equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper M equals 0](images/c12_140.png) then  <math alttext="0 Superscript e asterisk d Baseline m o d identical-to 0 m o d upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![0 Superscript e asterisk d Baseline m o d identical-to 0 m o d upper N](images/c12_141.png).

Let us consider  <math alttext="upper M ampersand gt semicolon 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#38;gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper M ampersand gt semicolon 0](images/c12_142.png). Since  <math alttext="upper M less-than n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M less-than n](images/c12_143.png) and *n* is a product of two primes *p* and *q*, *M* can have common dividers with *p* or with *q*, but not with both. Thus, three cases are to consider:

Case 1: *M* is coprime with *p* and with *q*.

Case 2: *M* is coprime with *p* and not with *q*.

Case 3: *M* is coprime with *q* and not with *p*.

Cases 2 and 3 are identical.

1.  Case 1: *M* is coprime with *p* and with *q*.
    
    If *M* is coprime with *p*, by Fermat’s little theorem:
