*    <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper P upper H s a l t right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis 10 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue 77 right-parenthesis equals upper E upper H period upper H a s h" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>H</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>10</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>77</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>H</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper P upper H s a l t right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis 10 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue 77 right-parenthesis equals upper E upper H period upper H a s h](images/c12_338.png). Thus, the signature is valid.

## 12.3 Finite Field-based Cryptography

### 12.3.1 Discrete Logarithm Problem

#### 12.3.1.1 What Is the Discrete Logarithm Problem?

Recall that in classic mathematics, given two real numbers *a* and *b*,  <math alttext="l o g Subscript b Baseline left-parenthesis a right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![l o g Subscript b Baseline left-parenthesis a right-parenthesis](images/c12_343.png), the logarithm of *a* to base *b*, is a real number *c* such that:  <math alttext="b Superscript c Baseline equals a" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> ![b Superscript c Baseline equals a](images/c12_344.png).  <math alttext="l o g left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![l o g left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c12_345.png) is the inverse function of  <math alttext="e Superscript x" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![e Superscript x](images/c12_346.png). Analogously, in any cyclic group  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c12_347.png) with generator *g*, powers  <math alttext="g Superscript k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>k</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![g Superscript k](images/c12_348.png) can be defined for all integers *k*, and  <math alttext="l o g Subscript g Baseline left-parenthesis h right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![l o g Subscript g Baseline left-parenthesis h right-parenthesis](images/c12_349.png), the discrete algorithm of an element  <math alttext="h element-of double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![h element-of double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c12_350.png), is an integer *k* such that:  <math alttext="g Superscript k Baseline identical-to h m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mi>h</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![g Superscript k Baseline identical-to h m o d p](images/c12_351.png).

**Example 12.5** Let us consider  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z 11 Superscript asterisk Baseline equals StartSet 1 comma 2 comma 3 comma 4 comma 5 comma 6 comma 7 comma 8 comma 9 comma 10 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow><mo>\*</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>10</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z 11 Superscript asterisk Baseline equals StartSet 1 comma 2 comma 3 comma 4 comma 5 comma 6 comma 7 comma 8 comma 9 comma 10 EndSet](images/c12_352.png)

Element 2 is a generator of  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z 11 Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z 11 Superscript asterisk](images/c12_353.png), since:

 <math alttext="2 Superscript 0 Baseline equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>0</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 0 Baseline equals 1](images/c12_354.png)              <math alttext="2 Superscript 1 Baseline equals 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 1 Baseline equals 2](images/c12_355.png)        <math alttext="2 squared equals 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![2 squared equals 4](images/c12_356.png)    <math alttext="2 cubed equals 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![2 cubed equals 8](images/c12_357.png)

 <math alttext="2 Superscript 4 Baseline equals 16 identical-to 5 m o d 11" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 4 Baseline equals 16 identical-to 5 m o d 11](images/c12_358.png)        <math alttext="2 Superscript 5 Baseline equals 32 identical-to 10 m o d 11" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>5</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>10</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 5 Baseline equals 32 identical-to 10 m o d 11](images/c12_359.png)     <math alttext="2 Superscript 6 Baseline equals 64 identical-to 9 m o d 11" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>6</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>9</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 6 Baseline equals 64 identical-to 9 m o d 11](images/c12_360.png)

Find *k* such that  <math alttext="2 Superscript k Baseline identical-to 3 m o d 11" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>3</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript k Baseline identical-to 3 m o d 11](images/c12_364.png). It is easy to find *k* when the powers of 2 calculated a priori;  <math alttext="k equals 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ![k equals 8](images/c12_365.png).

#### 12.3.1.2 Attacks Against DLP

One naïve way (also called brute-force attack) to solve the discrete logarithm is to prepare the table of powers of the generator element for all the elements of the cyclic group  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk Baseline left-parenthesis normal i period normal e period StartAbsoluteValue double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk Baseline EndAbsoluteValue" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mo>.</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mo>.</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk Baseline left-parenthesis normal i period normal e period StartAbsoluteValue double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk Baseline EndAbsoluteValue](images/c12_366.png) powers of the generator should be calculated and stored). Therefore, the complexity (in computation or memory capacity) of the brute-force attack is  <math alttext="upper O left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper O left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c12_367.png). With today’s computers, it is recommended to use cyclic groups with cardinality higher that  <math alttext="2 Superscript 90" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>90</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 90](images/c12_368.png) to make brute-force attack computationally infeasible.

The best known attack algorithms against DLP, which work in arbitrary groups, have a complexity of  <math alttext="upper O left-parenthesis StartRoot p EndRoot right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msqrt><mi>p</mi></msqrt></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper O left-parenthesis StartRoot p EndRoot right-parenthesis](images/c12_369.png) and include *Baby-step giant-step* algorithm and *Pollard’s rho* algorithm. For both attack algorithms, the set of elements of the cyclic group is partitioned before testing candidate solutions.

Other efficient DLP attacks algorithms exist, under some assumptions, including *Pohlig-Hellman* algorithm (which assumes that the order of the group has a small number of prime factors) and *Index calculus* algorithm (which requires an efficient procedure to select a relatively small subset of elements of the group, in such a way that a significant fraction of elements can be efficiently expressed as products of elements of the selected subset). For more detail on DLP attacks, refer to \[[7](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0007)\].

In general, DLP is considered computationally intractable. That is, no feasible algorithm is known for computing discrete logarithms when large cyclic fields are used, because the modular exponentiation  <math alttext="g Superscript k Baseline equals h m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![g Superscript k Baseline equals h m o d p](images/c12_370.png) is a one-way function . Considering current and near-future CPU technologies, it is recommended to use groups with cardinality higher than  <math alttext="2 Superscript 2 asterisk 80" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>80</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 2 asterisk 80](images/c12_371.png) to make the best known DLP attacks computationally infeasible. In practice, cryptosystems make use of groups with cardinality higher than  <math alttext="2 Superscript 1024" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>1024</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 1024](images/c12_372.png).

The most recent record on solving DLP in cyclic groups  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c12_373.png) was announced in late 2019. Researchers computed the discrete logarithm modulo for 795 bits. The computation took approximately 3100 core-years, using Intel Xeon Gold 6130 CPUs (2.1GHz). Another record on solving DLP in extension fields  <math alttext="upper G upper F left-parenthesis 2 Superscript m Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>F</mi><mo>(</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper G upper F left-parenthesis 2 Superscript m Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c12_374.png) was announced in late 2019. Researchers computed the discrete logarithm modulo for  <math alttext="upper G upper F left-parenthesis 2 Superscript 30750 Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>F</mi><mo>(</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>30750</mn></mrow></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper G upper F left-parenthesis 2 Superscript 30750 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c12_375.png) using 25 481 219 core hours on clusters based on Intel Xeon architecture.

In the sequel, the most known finite field-based cryptographic algorithms (namely, DHKE, ElGamal, and MQV), are presented.

### 12.3.2 Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange

The Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange (DHKE[⁷](#c12.xhtml#c12-note-0007)) scheme is the first important application of DLP to design a cryptography scheme \[[1](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0001)\]. In order to describe the DHKE protocol, let us consider a use case in which Alice and Bob generate a shared secret (see Fiure [12.5](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0005)).

![Figure 12.5 Illustration of Diffie-Hellman key exchange protocol.](images/c12f005.png)

[**Figure 12.5**](#c12.xhtml#rc12-fig-0005) Illustration of Diffie-Hellman key exchange protocol.

The main purpose of the DHKE protocol is the key exchange between communicating parties. DHKE does not explicitly address how the shared secret can be used for encryption or for digital signature. Therefore, in practice, it is not used for encryption or signature. Other schemes, such as ElGamal encryption and signature algorithms, extended DHKE. It is worth noticing that the encryption with DHKE may be easily implemented as follows:

*   Encryption:  <math alttext="upper C equals upper M period upper S m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>S</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C equals upper M period upper S m o d p](images/c12_391.png); (*M* is the message to encrypt)
*   Decryption:  <math alttext="upper M equals upper C period upper S Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>.</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M equals upper C period upper S Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d p](images/c12_392.png)
    
    *   where: *M* is the message to encrypt, *C* the ciphertext, *S* the shared secret, and  <math alttext="upper S Superscript negative 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper S Superscript negative 1](images/c12_393.png) is the inverse of element *S* in the multiplicative group  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c12_394.png).
        

**Example 12.6** Alice and Bob decide to compute a shared secret using DHKE protocol with  <math alttext="p equals 227" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>227</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 227](images/c12_395.png), which is prime, and  <math alttext="g equals 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![g equals 2](images/c12_396.png).

Alice chooses her private key to be  <math alttext="upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline equals 175" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>175</mn></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline equals 175](images/c12_397.png). Then, she computes her public key:  <math alttext="upper P u Subscript upper A Baseline equals 2 Superscript 175 Baseline m o d 227 equals 2 Superscript 3 asterisk 44 plus 43 Baseline m o d 227 equals left-parenthesis 171 cubed asterisk 199 right-parenthesis m o d 227 equals 201" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>175</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>227</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>44</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>43</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>227</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><msup><mrow><mn>171</mn></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>\*</mo><mn>199</mn><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>227</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>201</mn></mrow></math> ![upper P u Subscript upper A Baseline equals 2 Superscript 175 Baseline m o d 227 equals 2 Superscript 3 asterisk 44 plus 43 Baseline m o d 227 equals left-parenthesis 171 cubed asterisk 199 right-parenthesis m o d 227 equals 201](images/c12_398.png).

Bob chooses his private key to be  <math alttext="upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline equals 44" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>44</mn></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline equals 44](images/c12_399.png). Then, he computes his public key:  <math alttext="upper P u Subscript upper B Baseline equals 2 Superscript 44 Baseline m o d 227 equals 171" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>44</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>227</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>171</mn></mrow></math> ![upper P u Subscript upper B Baseline equals 2 Superscript 44 Baseline m o d 227 equals 171](images/c12_400.png).

Then, public keys are exchanged between Alice and Bob.

The shared secret computed by Alice is:

*   *Resistance to attacks*

Given the public parameters (*g*, *p*,  <math alttext="upper P u Subscript upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P u Subscript upper B](images/c12_408.png), and  <math alttext="upper P u Subscript upper A" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P u Subscript upper A](images/c12_409.png)), breaking the Diffie-Hellman key exchange scheme means revealing the session key *S*, which requires solving a problem known as Diffie-Hellman problem.

Since the session key *S* is derived from a couple of public and private keys, from either  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper P u Subscript upper B Baseline comma upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper P u Subscript upper B Baseline comma upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c12_415.png) or  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper P u Subscript upper A Baseline comma upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper P u Subscript upper A Baseline comma upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c12_416.png), the adversary should[⁹](#c12.xhtml#c12-note-0009) reveal one of private keys ( <math alttext="upper P r Subscript upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript upper B](images/c12_417.png) or  <math alttext="upper P r Subscript upper A" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript upper A](images/c12_418.png)). Unfortunately, for the adversary, revealing a private key, which is defined by a modular exponentiation, requires the adversary to solve the DLP problem, which is known to be computationally infeasible. In such a case, the DHP is equivalent to the DLP. Therefore, solving the Diffie-Hellman problem (DHP) also is computationally infeasible for large values of cyclic group size.

### 12.3.3 Menezes-Qu-Vanstone Key-exchange Protocol

MQV (Menezes-Qu-Vanstone) key-agreement is one of the numerous extensions to the original Diffie-Hellman key-exchange protocol \[[8](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0008)–[10](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0010)\]. MQV is designed to work in an arbitrary finite group, either in FFC context or in ECC context. In both cases, MQV provides a countermeasure to some attacks against the DHKE, including the small group attack, discussed in 13.5.3.1. MQV makes use of two key-pairs for each party: a static (i.e. long-term) key-pair and an ephemeral key-pair. The protocol run by Alice and Bob to generate a shared secret is shown in [Figure 12.6](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0006).

![Figure 12.6 Illustration of MQV key exchange protocol.](images/c12f006.png)

[**Figure 12.6**](#c12.xhtml#rc12-fig-0006) Illustration of MQV key exchange protocol.

### 12.3.4 ElGamal Cryptosystem

ElGamal cryptosystem makes use of the DHKE protocol to provide a complete cryptosystem \[[11](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0011)\]. From the cryptographic foundation point of view, ElGamal scheme is just a reordering of DH communications between parties to implement encryption and signature. The security of ElGamal scheme is equivalent to that of DHKE scheme.

#### 12.3.4.1 ElGamal Encryption

Consider a use case in which Bob needs to receive confidential messages from Alice. The calculations and exchanges are illustrated by [Figure 12.7](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0007).

![Figure 12.7 Illustration of ElGamal encryption.](images/c12f007.png)

[**Figure 12.7**](#c12.xhtml#rc12-fig-0007) Illustration of ElGamal encryption.

    From the public information ( <math alttext="upper C 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 1](images/c12_480.png),  <math alttext="upper C 2 comma p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C 2 comma p](images/c12_481.png)) and the intercepted message  <math alttext="upper M 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 1](images/c12_482.png), the adversary can easily discover  <math alttext="upper M 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 2](images/c12_483.png):  <math alttext="upper M 2 equals upper M 1 asterisk upper C 2 asterisk upper C 1 Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>\*</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M 2 equals upper M 1 asterisk upper C 2 asterisk upper C 1 Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d p](images/c12_484.png).
    
    In general, if the sender does not change the private key, the adversary has just to capture the plaintext of any message to learn the content of all messages of a session.
    
*   – The consequence of encrypting a single message by each private key value is that when the sender transmits, at different times, the same data (for example a password or PIN code), the ciphertexts are different and the adversary will not be able to detect that the same data is sent multiple times.

#### 12.3.4.2 ElGamal Signature

Consider a use case in which Bob sends signed messages, using ElGamal signature scheme, to Alice who checks the authenticity of messages sent by Bob. The calculations and exchanges are illustrated by [Figure 12.8](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0008).

![Figure 12.8 Illustration of ElGamal signature protocol.](images/c12f008.png)

[**Figure 12.8**](#c12.xhtml#rc12-fig-0008) Illustration of ElGamal signature protocol.

*   *Proof of correctness of ElGamal digital signature*

A digital signature service is correct if the result of the verification of a valid signature is “valid signature”. The proof of correctness of ElGamal signature may be proven by substitutions as follows:

First, we introduce the following lemma:

**Lemma 12.1**  <math alttext="quotation-mark m o d p left-right-arrow m o d p minus 1 quotation-mark" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>"</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8596;</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>"</mo></mrow></math> ![quotation-mark m o d p left-right-arrow m o d p minus 1 quotation-mark](images/c12_498.png): for any positive integers *a*, *p*, and *k*, the following holds:  <math alttext="a Superscript k Baseline m o d p identical-to a Superscript k m o d left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![a Superscript k Baseline m o d p identical-to a Superscript k m o d left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline m o d p](images/c12_499.png)

#### 12.3.4.3 ElGamal Digital Signature Security and Potential Attacks

##### *12.3.4.3.1 Security*

If the signature scheme is implemented properly (i.e. compliance with single-use of per-message-signature keys), most attacks (including trying to derive private keys from a set of messages with their signatures or trying to generate a valid signature without signer’s private key or trying to generate a message given the signatures of other messages) are equivalent to solving the Discrete logarithm problem.

##### *12.3.4.3.2 Potential Attacks Against ElGamal Signature*

*Attack aiming to disclose signer’s private key*: a per-message-signature key must be used to sign a single message and must not be reused (in conjunction with the same public key). Otherwise, the adversary will be able to derive the private key of the signer as shown in Problem 12.22.

*Attack aiming to forge a signature*: the attack also is called *existential forgery*. In the signature scheme presented previously, an adversary can generate legitimate signatures without knowledge of the private key of the legitimate signer, but he/she cannot decide (or control) which content to include in the message. Therefore, there is no potential impact in terms of security, except of denial of service, because the adversary always tries to send specific content such as “send money” or “apply an action on an asset” to win something. Problem 12.23 shows how signature forging may be designed.

## 12.4 Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA)

The original digital signature scheme of ElGamal results in signatures composed of two items (*r* and *s*), each of which has a size of *p* bits. Consequently, the size of the digital signature is twice the message size. Thus, signing long size messages (such as pictures, scanned documents, and videos) results in significant consumption of resources (bandwidth and memory), which are limited in some mobile and embedded devices. To alleviate such a drawback of ElGamal signature scheme, it is recommended to sign the hash of the message and not the entire message. This recommendation led to the DSA[^(14)](#c12.xhtml#c12-note-0014) (Digital Signature Algorithm) standard, which is currently one of the three techniques mostly used to sign documents online. The main adaptions of ElGamal signature scheme to yield the DSA standard are addressed in this section. For specific details regarding the implementations of the DSA standard (including how parameters are selected and checked), refer to \[[12](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0012)\] and [Chapter 14](#c14.xhtml).

### 12.4.1 DSA Domain Parameters

A digital signature is computed using the following domain parameters that should be agreed upon by the two parties before signing:

*   *p*: a prime modulus
*   *g*: a subgroup generator, of order *q*, in the multiplicative group  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c12_538.png)
*   *q*: the order of generator *g* (*q* is a prime divisor[^(15)](#c12.xhtml#c12-note-0015) of  <math alttext="p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p minus 1](images/c12_539.png)). In other words,  <math alttext="g Superscript q Baseline m o d p equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>q</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![g Superscript q Baseline m o d p equals 1](images/c12_540.png) (see Problem 12.25).

DSA standard specifies four security strength levels and their associated pairs  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper L comma upper N right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper L comma upper N right-parenthesis](images/c12_541.png), where *L* and *N* are the length (in bits) of *p* and  <math alttext="q comma" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> ![q comma](images/c12_542.png) respectively:

 <math alttext="StartLayout 1st Row 1st Column upper L equals 1024 comma upper N equals 160 2nd Column 3rd Column upper L equals 2048 comma upper N equals 224 2nd Row 1st Column upper L equals 2048 comma upper N equals 256 2nd Column 3rd Column upper L equals 3072 comma upper N equals 256 EndLayout" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtable columnalign="left"><mtr columnalign="left"><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1024</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>160</mn></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2048</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>224</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr columnalign="left"><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2048</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>256</mn></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3072</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>256</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math> ![StartLayout 1st Row 1st Column upper L equals 1024 comma upper N equals 160 2nd Column 3rd Column upper L equals 2048 comma upper N equals 224 2nd Row 1st Column upper L equals 2048 comma upper N equals 256 2nd Column 3rd Column upper L equals 3072 comma upper N equals 256 EndLayout](images/c12_543.png)

To make infeasible the known attacks against the DSA, the minimum security strength requires to make use of a generator *g* that generates a subgroup of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 160" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>160</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 160](images/c12_544.png) elements from a larger group of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 1024" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>1024</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 1024](images/c12_545.png). In addition to domain parameters, the two parties should agree on a hash function, which should have at least a security strength equivalent to the one of the agreed pair  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper L comma upper N right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper L comma upper N right-parenthesis](images/c12_546.png).

### 12.4.2 DSA-Keys Generation

As in DHKE and ElGamal schemes, the private and public keys of the signer are generated using domain parameters and an approved random bit generator. However, it should be noticed that the DSA private-keys and the per-message-signature keys are picked in the range  <math alttext="left-bracket 1 comma q minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 1 comma q minus 1 right-bracket](images/c12_547.png) and not in  <math alttext="left-bracket 1 comma p minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 1 comma p minus 1 right-bracket](images/c12_548.png) as DHKE and ElGamal schemes.

### 12.4.3 DSA Signature Generation

DSA signature generation is an adaptation of ElGamal signature generation in which the message hash is signed instead of signing the entire message. Formally, DSA signature  <math alttext="left-parenthesis r comma s right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis r comma s right-parenthesis](images/c12_549.png) of a message *M* is defined as follows:

*    <math alttext="r equals left-parenthesis g Superscript upper K Baseline m o d p right-parenthesis m o d q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>)</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![r equals left-parenthesis g Superscript upper K Baseline m o d p right-parenthesis m o d q](images/c12_550.png)   (*K* is the per-message-signature key)
*    <math alttext="upper Z equals l e f t m o s t left-parenthesis min left-parenthesis upper N comma o u t l e n right-parenthesis comma upper H upper A upper S upper H left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>min</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>H</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper Z equals l e f t m o s t left-parenthesis min left-parenthesis upper N comma o u t l e n right-parenthesis comma upper H upper A upper S upper H left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c12_551.png)
*    <math alttext="s equals upper K Superscript negative 1 Baseline asterisk left-parenthesis upper Z plus upper P r Subscript s Baseline asterisk r right-parenthesis m o d q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msup><mo>\*</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![s equals upper K Superscript negative 1 Baseline asterisk left-parenthesis upper Z plus upper P r Subscript s Baseline asterisk r right-parenthesis m o d q](images/c12_552.png)   ( <math alttext="upper P r Subscript s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript s](images/c12_553.png) is the private key of the signer)

 <math alttext="min left-parenthesis upper N comma o u t l e n right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>min</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![min left-parenthesis upper N comma o u t l e n right-parenthesis](images/c12_554.png) denotes the minimum of the *N* (the order of the generator) and  <math alttext="o u t l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![o u t l e n](images/c12_555.png) (the bit length of the hash function output).

If  <math alttext="r equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![r equals 0](images/c12_556.png) or  <math alttext="s equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![s equals 0](images/c12_557.png), a new value of *r* shall be recalculated and tried.

### 12.4.4 DSA Signature Verification

The intended recipient, or any other party (since the message content is not encrypted), verifies the signature to determine the authenticity of the signer. First, the verifier should receive and agree on the DSA domain parameters, the identity of the hash function, and the public key of the signer  <math alttext="upper P u Subscript s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P u Subscript s](images/c12_558.png), before any signature verification. Upon reception of a message  <math alttext="upper M prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![upper M prime](images/c12_559.png) and its signature  <math alttext="left-parenthesis r prime comma s prime right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis r prime comma s prime right-parenthesis](images/c12_560.png), the verification is as follows:

*    <math alttext="upper Z equals l e f t m o s t left-parenthesis min left-parenthesis upper N comma o u t l e n right-parenthesis comma upper H upper A upper S upper H left-parenthesis upper M prime right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>min</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>H</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>H</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper Z equals l e f t m o s t left-parenthesis min left-parenthesis upper N comma o u t l e n right-parenthesis comma upper H upper A upper S upper H left-parenthesis upper M prime right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c12_561.png)
    
     <math alttext="w equals s prime Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>s</mi><msup><mo>'</mo><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![w equals s prime Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d q](images/c12_562.png)
    
     <math alttext="u 1 equals upper Z asterisk w m o d q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>w</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![u 1 equals upper Z asterisk w m o d q](images/c12_563.png)
    
     <math alttext="u 2 equals r prime asterisk w m o d q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>\*</mo><mi>w</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![u 2 equals r prime asterisk w m o d q](images/c12_564.png)
    
     <math alttext="v equals left-parenthesis left-parenthesis g Superscript u 1 Baseline right-parenthesis asterisk left-parenthesis upper P u Subscript s Superscript Super Superscript u 2 Superscript Baseline right-parenthesis m o d p right-parenthesis m o d q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>\*</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mi>s</mi><mrow><msup><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>q</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext></mrow></math> ![v equals left-parenthesis left-parenthesis g Superscript u 1 Baseline right-parenthesis asterisk left-parenthesis upper P u Subscript s Superscript Super Superscript u 2 Superscript Baseline right-parenthesis m o d p right-parenthesis m o d q](images/c12_565.png)
    
    If  <math alttext="v equals r prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> ![v equals r prime](images/c12_566.png) the signature is Valid. Otherwise, the message is rejected.
    

### 12.4.5 Advantages of DSA over ElGamal Signature Scheme

Both schemes are based on the discrete logarithm problem. Therefore, their security is the same. From a mathematical point of view, both schemes have the same foundations. The elements (private and per-message-signature keys) to keep secret and the way they are changed are the same in both schemes. However, the schemes mainly differ from the performance point of view. [Table 12.2](#c12.xhtml#c12-tbl-0002) summarizes the main differences between ElGamal signature and DSA.

![Table 12.2 Differences between ElGamal and DSA schemes.](images/c12_567.png)

[**Table 12.2**](#c12.xhtml#rc12-tbl-0002) Differences between ElGamal and DSA schemes.

DSA standard specifies four security strength levels (see DSA domain parameters in [Section 12.4.1](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-02012)) and the ratio between  <math alttext="p and q varies from StartFraction 1024 Over 160 EndFraction equals 6.4 to StartFraction 3072 Over 256 EndFraction equals 12" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mtext>&#160;and&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi><mtext>&#160;varies&#160;from&#160;</mtext><mfrac><mrow><mn>1024</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>160</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>6.4</mn><mtext>&#160;to&#160;</mtext><mfrac><mrow><mn>3072</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>256</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow></math> ![p and q varies from StartFraction 1024 Over 160 EndFraction equals 6.4 to StartFraction 3072 Over 256 EndFraction equals 12](images/c12_572.png). Thus, DSA produces signatures, which are six times smaller, resulting in less memory and less bandwidth than ElGamal scheme. In general, the calculations of modular exponentiations are the slowest parts of the cryptographic systems. DSA signature generation is at least six times faster than ElGamal signature generation. In addition, DSA verification requires two exponentiations rather than three in ElGamal scheme. Thus, DSA signature verification is faster.

The definition of the first component of the signature, *r*, differs. In DSA, two moduli are applied. In ElGamal scheme, the magnitude of *r* is at least six times the one of DSA. Therefore, in DSA, *r* only carries a partial information about the per-message-signature key *K*. Thus, deriving the per-message-signature key from intercepted signatures would be harder in DSA than in ElGamal scheme.

In DSA, the selection of the generator *g* fulfills a specific condition, i.e.  <math alttext="g Superscript q Baseline m o d p equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>q</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![g Superscript q Baseline m o d p equals 1](images/c12_573.png). With such a condition, some  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c12_574.png) generator candidates are discarded when selecting the generator *g*. It is known in cryptanalysis that some attacks, such as Pohlig-Hellman attack, can efficiently compute logarithms is subgroups whose generators have some properties. Thus, by design, DSA is more resistant to attacks than ElGamal scheme.

***Exercise 12.4***

Let RSA parameters be:  <math alttext="p equals 101" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>101</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 101](images/c12_590.png),  <math alttext="q equals 113" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>113</mn></mrow></math> ![q equals 113](images/c12_591.png), and  <math alttext="e equals 6747" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6747</mn></mrow></math> ![e equals 6747](images/c12_592.png).

***Problem 12.2***

Use the following statements to prove the correctness of RSA:

*   Euler’s theorem (Theorem 3.4) states that if *a* and *z* are two coprime positive integers, then  <math alttext="a Superscript phi left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis Baseline identical-to 1 m o d z" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>&#981;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>z</mi></mrow></math> ![a Superscript phi left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis Baseline identical-to 1 m o d z](images/c12_616.png), where is  <math alttext="phi left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#981;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![phi left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis](images/c12_617.png) the Euler’s totient.[^(16)](#c12.xhtml#c12-note-0016)
*   If *z* is prime, then  <math alttext="phi left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals z minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#981;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![phi left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals z minus 1](images/c12_618.png).
*   Given three integers *x*, *y*, and *z*, if  <math alttext="z equals x asterisk y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ![z equals x asterisk y](images/c12_619.png), then  <math alttext="phi left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals phi left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis asterisk phi left-parenthesis y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#981;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>&#981;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo><mi>&#981;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![phi left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals phi left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis asterisk phi left-parenthesis y right-parenthesis](images/c12_620.png).

Prove that the attacker can generate a valid signature.

***Problem 12.11***

1.  Show that the product of two RSA ciphertexts is equal to the encryption of the product of the two respective plaintexts. In other words, show that RSA has a multiplicative property.
2.  Assume that Bob, Alice, and Eve share a public key  <math alttext="left-parenthesis e comma n right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis e comma n right-parenthesis](images/c12_648.png) and Bob owns the private key *d*. The ciphertexts are known to the three partners. Alice and Bob exchange plaintexts that Eve should not read. To check that Bob possesses the right private key, Eve encrypts messages, using Bob’s public key, and asks Bob to decrypt them and return the plaintext. If Bob decrypts correctly the ciphertexts, Eve concludes that he owns the appropriate private key. Unfortunately, such a challenge-based authentication protocol has a weakness. Design an attack based on RSA multiplicative property, which enables Eve to disclose messages sent by Alice.

***Problem 12.23***

Assume that an adversary forges a legitimate ElGamal signature, without controlling the content of the generated fake message as follows:

*g* (generator), *p* (modulus), and  <math alttext="upper P u Subscript upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P u Subscript upper B](images/c12_696.png) (public key of the legitimate signer) are public parameters known to the adversary.

The adversary’s actions are:

1.  Select two positive integers *a* and *b* such that:
    
     <math alttext="a comma b less-than p minus 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![a comma b less-than p minus 2](images/c12_697.png) and (thus,  <math alttext="b Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![b Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c12_698.png) exists).
    
2.  Calculate the signature components:
    
     <math alttext="r equals g Superscript a Baseline asterisk left-parenthesis upper P u Subscript upper B Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript b Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>a</mi></msup><mo>\*</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>b</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![r equals g Superscript a Baseline asterisk left-parenthesis upper P u Subscript upper B Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript b Baseline m o d p](images/c12_699.png)
    
     <math alttext="s equals negative r asterisk b Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![s equals negative r asterisk b Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c12_700.png)
    
3.  Compute the (fake) message:
    
     <math alttext="upper M identical-to s asterisk a m o d left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mi>s</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>\*</mo><mi>a</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper M identical-to s asterisk a m o d left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c12_701.png)
    
    Notice that the message generated by the adversary depends on *a* and *b* and cannot be controlled by the adversary to include a specific content.
    
4.  Send  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper M comma left-parenthesis r comma s right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper M comma left-parenthesis r comma s right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c12_702.png)

How many distinct first-components (i.e. *r*) of ElGamal signature can be generated for a message *x* given a modulus *p*, which is a safe prime, and *g* an element of  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c12_708.png).

## 12.5.2 Solutions to Exercises and Problems

***Exercise 12.1***

Given two primes, *p* and *q*, an RSA public key *e* is chosen such that  <math alttext="upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis e comma phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis e comma phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c12_713.png). <math alttext="p equals 19 and q equals 11 right double arrow phi left-parenthesis 19 asterisk 11 right-parenthesis equals 180" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>19</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>and</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>&#8658;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>19</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>180</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 19 and q equals 11 right double arrow phi left-parenthesis 19 asterisk 11 right-parenthesis equals 180](images/c12_714.png)

 <math alttext="upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis 11 comma 180 right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>11</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>180</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis 11 comma 180 right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c12_715.png). Hence,  <math alttext="e 1 equals 11" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow></math> ![e 1 equals 11](images/c12_716.png) is a valid RSA public key.

 <math alttext="upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis 4 comma 180 right-parenthesis equals 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>180</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis 4 comma 180 right-parenthesis equals 4](images/c12_717.png). Hence,  <math alttext="e 2 equals 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![e 2 equals 4](images/c12_718.png) is not a valid RSA public key.

 <math alttext="upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis 120 comma 180 right-parenthesis equals 60" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>120</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>180</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>60</mn></mrow></math> ![upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis 120 comma 180 right-parenthesis equals 60](images/c12_719.png). Hence,  <math alttext="e 3 equals 60" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>60</mn></mrow></math> ![e 3 equals 60](images/c12_720.png) is not a valid RSA public key.

 <math alttext="upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis 15311 comma 180 right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>15311</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>180</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis 15311 comma 180 right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c12_721.png). Hence,  <math alttext="e 4 equals 15311" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>15311</mn></mrow></math> ![e 4 equals 15311](images/c12_722.png) is a valid RSA public key.

***Exercise 12.2***

 <math alttext="p equals 7" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 7](images/c12_723.png),  <math alttext="q equals 13" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow></math> ![q equals 13](images/c12_724.png)

![](images/c12_725.png)

***Exercise 12.3***

Recall that given two primes *p* and *q*, the RSA private key *d* is the multiplicative inverse of the public exponent *e*. Formally:

 <math alttext="e asterisk d identical-to 1 m o d phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![e asterisk d identical-to 1 m o d phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis](images/c12_736.png), where  <math alttext="phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis q minus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis q minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c12_737.png) <math alttext="e asterisk d identical-to 1 m o d phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis right double arrow there-exists k element-of double-struck upper N vertical-bar e asterisk d equals 1 plus k asterisk phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8658;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8707;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>&#8469;</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>\*</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![e asterisk d identical-to 1 m o d phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis right double arrow there-exists k element-of double-struck upper N vertical-bar e asterisk d equals 1 plus k asterisk phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis](images/c12_738.png)

Thus, the following property holds:

 <math alttext="left-parenthesis e asterisk d right-parenthesis plus left-parenthesis negative k asterisk phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis e asterisk d right-parenthesis plus left-parenthesis negative k asterisk phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c12_739.png)

Let  <math alttext="k prime equals negative k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> ![k prime equals negative k](images/c12_740.png)

By RSA design, *e* is coprime with  <math alttext="phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis](images/c12_741.png), i.e.  <math alttext="upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis comma e right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis comma e right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c12_742.png). Thus, the problem to solve becomes

 <math alttext="left-parenthesis phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis asterisk k prime right-parenthesis plus left-parenthesis e asterisk d right-parenthesis equals upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis comma e right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>G</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis asterisk k prime right-parenthesis plus left-parenthesis e asterisk d right-parenthesis equals upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis comma e right-parenthesis](images/c12_743.png), where *d* and  <math alttext="k prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![k prime](images/c12_744.png) are the variables to find.

The Extended Euclidean Algorithm (EEA) enables to solve the equation  <math alttext="a upper X plus b upper Y equals upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis a comma b right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>X</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>G</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![a upper X plus b upper Y equals upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis a comma b right-parenthesis](images/c12_745.png). When RSA private key computation is of concern, the EEA is used to find *d*, the private key, and  <math alttext="k prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![k prime](images/c12_746.png) such that:

 <math alttext="phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis asterisk k prime plus e asterisk d equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis asterisk k prime plus e asterisk d equals 1](images/c12_747.png)

In this exercise, only *d* is of interest.

1.   <math alttext="p equals 13" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 13](images/c12_748.png),  <math alttext="q equals 11" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow></math> ![q equals 11](images/c12_749.png), and  <math alttext="e equals 7" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> ![e equals 7](images/c12_750.png)

 <math alttext="phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 13 minus 1 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis 11 minus 1 right-parenthesis equals 120" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>13</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>11</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>120</mn></mrow></math> ![phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 13 minus 1 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis 11 minus 1 right-parenthesis equals 120](images/c12_751.png)

The problem to solve is  <math alttext="120 asterisk k prime plus 7 asterisk d equals upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis 120 comma 7 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>120</mn><mo>\*</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>\*</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>G</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>120</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![120 asterisk k prime plus 7 asterisk d equals upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis 120 comma 7 right-parenthesis](images/c12_752.png)

First, even if  <math alttext="g c d left-parenthesis 120 comma 7 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>120</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![g c d left-parenthesis 120 comma 7 right-parenthesis](images/c12_753.png) is known, the steps of EEA to find  <math alttext="upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis 120 comma 7 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>120</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis 120 comma 7 right-parenthesis](images/c12_754.png) are required to find *d*. In this scenario, there are two steps to find  <math alttext="upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis 120 comma 7 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>120</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis 120 comma 7 right-parenthesis](images/c12_755.png):

1^(st) step:  <math alttext="120 equals 7 asterisk 17 plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>120</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![120 equals 7 asterisk 17 plus 1](images/c12_756.png)

2^(nd) step:  <math alttext="17 equals 17 asterisk 1 plus 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>17</mn><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![17 equals 17 asterisk 1 plus 0](images/c12_757.png)

Second, to find the values of EEA variables *d* and  <math alttext="k prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![k prime](images/c12_758.png), do substitutions starting from the equality of the step whose remainder is 1.

 <math alttext="1 equals 120 asterisk 1 minus 7 asterisk 17 equals 120 asterisk 1 plus 7 asterisk left-parenthesis negative 17 right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>120</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>120</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>\*</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>17</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![1 equals 120 asterisk 1 minus 7 asterisk 17 equals 120 asterisk 1 plus 7 asterisk left-parenthesis negative 17 right-parenthesis](images/c12_759.png)

Thus,  <math alttext="d equals negative 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![d equals negative 17](images/c12_760.png). In modulo 120,  <math alttext="d equals 103" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>103</mn></mrow></math> ![d equals 103](images/c12_761.png).

2)  <math alttext="p equals 7" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 7](images/c12_762.png),  <math alttext="q equals 11" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow></math> ![q equals 11](images/c12_763.png), and  <math alttext="e equals 13" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow></math> ![e equals 13](images/c12_764.png)

 <math alttext="phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 7 minus 1 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis 11 minus 1 right-parenthesis equals 60" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>11</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>60</mn></mrow></math> ![phi left-parenthesis p asterisk q right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 7 minus 1 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis 11 minus 1 right-parenthesis equals 60](images/c12_765.png)

First, the steps of EEA to find  <math alttext="upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis 10200 comma 19 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>10200</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>19</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis 10200 comma 19 right-parenthesis](images/c12_766.png) are required to find *d*. In this scenario, there are six steps:

1^(st) step:  <math alttext="60 equals 13 asterisk 4 plus 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>60</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ![60 equals 13 asterisk 4 plus 8](images/c12_767.png)  2^(nd) step:  <math alttext="13 equals 8 asterisk 1 plus 5" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>13</mn><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>8</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> ![13 equals 8 asterisk 1 plus 5](images/c12_768.png)

3^(rd) step:  <math alttext="8 equals 5 asterisk 1 plus 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![8 equals 5 asterisk 1 plus 3](images/c12_769.png)  4^(th) step:  <math alttext="5 equals 3 asterisk 1 plus 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![5 equals 3 asterisk 1 plus 2](images/c12_770.png)

5^(th) step:  <math alttext="3 equals 2 asterisk 1 plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![3 equals 2 asterisk 1 plus 1](images/c12_771.png)  6^(th) step:  <math alttext="2 equals 2 asterisk 1 plus 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![2 equals 2 asterisk 1 plus 0](images/c12_772.png)

Second, to find the values of EEA variables *d* and  <math alttext="k prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![k prime](images/c12_773.png), do substitutions starting from the equality of the 5^(th) step:
