**Problem 12.15**

*   A private key used in DHKE protocol must be distinct from 1, because of the following:

If one side, say Bob, picks 1 as his private key, then his public key is  <math alttext="upper P u Subscript upper B Baseline identical-to g Superscript 1 Baseline m o d p identical-to g" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>g</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P u Subscript upper B Baseline identical-to g Superscript 1 Baseline m o d p identical-to g](images/c12_1183.png).

The other side, say Alice, picks a private key  <math alttext="upper P r Subscript upper A" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript upper A](images/c12_1184.png) distinct from 1, then her public key is  <math alttext="upper P u Subscript upper A Baseline identical-to g Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper A Superscript Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P u Subscript upper A Baseline identical-to g Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper A Superscript Baseline m o d p](images/c12_1185.png).

Next, the shared secret key is computed as  <math alttext="upper K Subscript upper A upper B Baseline identical-to left-parenthesis g Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper A Superscript Baseline identical-to g Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper A Superscript Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript upper A upper B Baseline identical-to left-parenthesis g Superscript 1 Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper A Superscript Baseline identical-to g Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper A Superscript Baseline m o d p](images/c12_1186.png). Therefore, the shared secret key is the same as Alice’s public key, which is insecure.

*   A private key used in DHKE protocol must be distinct from  <math alttext="p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p minus 1](images/c12_1187.png), because of the following:

If Bob picks  <math alttext="p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p minus 1](images/c12_1188.png) as his private key, then his public key is  <math alttext="upper P u Subscript upper B Baseline identical-to g Superscript p minus 1 Baseline m o d p identical-to 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper P u Subscript upper B Baseline identical-to g Superscript p minus 1 Baseline m o d p identical-to 1](images/c12_1189.png) (by Fermat’s little theorem). Alice picks a private key  <math alttext="upper P r Subscript upper A" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript upper A](images/c12_1190.png) distinct from  <math alttext="p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p minus 1](images/c12_1191.png), then her public key is  <math alttext="upper P u Subscript upper A Baseline identical-to g Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper A Superscript Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P u Subscript upper A Baseline identical-to g Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper A Superscript Baseline m o d p](images/c12_1192.png).

Next, the shared secret key computed by Bob is  <math alttext="upper K Subscript upper B upper A Baseline identical-to left-parenthesis upper P u Subscript upper A Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript p minus 1 Baseline m o d p identical-to left-parenthesis g Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper A Superscript Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript p minus 1 Baseline m o d p identical-to 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>A</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript upper B upper A Baseline identical-to left-parenthesis upper P u Subscript upper A Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript p minus 1 Baseline m o d p identical-to left-parenthesis g Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper A Superscript Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript p minus 1 Baseline m o d p identical-to 1](images/c12_1193.png); the shared secret key computed by Alice is  <math alttext="upper K Subscript upper A upper B Baseline identical-to left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper A Superscript Baseline m o d p identical-to 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript upper A upper B Baseline identical-to left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper A Superscript Baseline m o d p identical-to 1](images/c12_1194.png).

Hence, if a participant uses  <math alttext="p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p minus 1](images/c12_1195.png) as private key, then both sides would generate a shared secret key equal to 1, which is equivalent to not using any cipher.

***Problem 12.16***

The shared secret key generated by the DHKE protocol is defined by:

 <math alttext="upper K Subscript upper A upper B Baseline identical-to left-parenthesis g Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper A Superscript Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper B Superscript Baseline m o d p identical-to g Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper A Superscript asterisk upper P r Super Subscript upper B Superscript Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript upper A upper B Baseline identical-to left-parenthesis g Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper A Superscript Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper B Superscript Baseline m o d p identical-to g Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper A Superscript asterisk upper P r Super Subscript upper B Superscript Baseline m o d p](images/c12_1196.png), where  <math alttext="upper P r Subscript upper A" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript upper A](images/c12_1197.png),  <math alttext="upper P r Subscript upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript upper B](images/c12_1198.png), *g*, and *p* denote party private keys, the generator, and the modulus, respectively.

If the private keys are chosen such that  <math alttext="upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline asterisk upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline equals k asterisk left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>\*</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline asterisk upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline equals k asterisk left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c12_1199.png), with *k* a positive integer, then  <math alttext="upper K Subscript upper A upper B Baseline identical-to g Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper A Superscript asterisk upper P r Super Subscript upper B Superscript Baseline m o d p identical-to left-parenthesis g Superscript p minus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript k Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript upper A upper B Baseline identical-to g Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper A Superscript asterisk upper P r Super Subscript upper B Superscript Baseline m o d p identical-to left-parenthesis g Superscript p minus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript k Baseline m o d p](images/c12_1200.png).

Since *g* is coprime to *p*, by Fermat’s little theorem,  <math alttext="upper K Subscript upper A upper B Baseline identical-to left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Superscript k Baseline m o d p equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript upper A upper B Baseline identical-to left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Superscript k Baseline m o d p equals 1](images/c12_1201.png).

For example, if  <math alttext="p equals 47" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>47</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 47](images/c12_1202.png),  <math alttext="upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline equals 23" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>23</mn></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline equals 23](images/c12_1203.png), and  <math alttext="upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline equals 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline equals 2](images/c12_1204.png), then  <math alttext="upper K Subscript upper A upper B Baseline identical-to g Superscript 23 asterisk 2 Baseline m o d 47 identical-to 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mn>23</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>47</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript upper A upper B Baseline identical-to g Superscript 23 asterisk 2 Baseline m o d 47 identical-to 1](images/c12_1205.png).

***Problem 12.17***

1.  Given a group  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c12_1206.png), by definition of element order (see Section 3.2.1)), if an element *g* has an order of  <math alttext="upper Omega left-parenthesis g right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#937;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper Omega left-parenthesis g right-parenthesis](images/c12_1207.png), then  <math alttext="g Superscript upper Omega left-parenthesis g right-parenthesis Baseline m o d p identical-to 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>&#937;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![g Superscript upper Omega left-parenthesis g right-parenthesis Baseline m o d p identical-to 1](images/c12_1208.png). Hence, for any positive integers *k* and α, with  <math alttext="alpha less-than upper Omega left-parenthesis g right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>&#937;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![alpha less-than upper Omega left-parenthesis g right-parenthesis](images/c12_1209.png),  <math alttext="g Superscript k asterisk upper Omega left-parenthesis g right-parenthesis plus alpha Baseline m o d p identical-to g Superscript alpha Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>&#937;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>&#945;</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![g Superscript k asterisk upper Omega left-parenthesis g right-parenthesis plus alpha Baseline m o d p identical-to g Superscript alpha Baseline m o d p](images/c12_1210.png).

In DHKE protocol, the computation of the shared secret key  <math alttext="upper K Subscript upper A upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript upper A upper B](images/c12_1211.png) from two private keys  <math alttext="upper P r Subscript upper A" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript upper A](images/c12_1212.png) and  <math alttext="upper P r Subscript upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript upper B](images/c12_1213.png) is as follows:  <math alttext="upper K Subscript upper A upper B Baseline equals g Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper A Superscript asterisk upper P r Super Subscript upper B Superscript Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript upper A upper B Baseline equals g Superscript upper P r Super Subscript upper A Superscript asterisk upper P r Super Subscript upper B Superscript Baseline m o d p](images/c12_1214.png).

display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![alpha prime](images/c12_1218.png), two positive integers less than  <math alttext="upper Omega left-parenthesis g right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#937;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper Omega left-parenthesis g right-parenthesis](images/c12_1219.png), then  <math alttext="upper K Subscript upper A upper B Baseline equals g Superscript alpha asterisk alpha prime Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript upper A upper B Baseline equals g Superscript alpha asterisk alpha prime Baseline m o d p](images/c12_1220.png).

Increasing a private key value by a multiple of  <math alttext="upper Omega left-parenthesis g right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#937;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper Omega left-parenthesis g right-parenthesis](images/c12_1221.png) does not change the resulting shared secret key. Therefore, if a generator *g* has an order of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 256" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>256</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 256](images/c12_1222.png), then the maximum value that private keys can have is  <math alttext="2 Superscript 256 Baseline minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>256</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 256 Baseline minus 1](images/c12_1223.png).

*   2\. In DHKE, the security strength depends on the private key value range, which in turn is limited by the order of the generator. Therefore, to provide a security strength of 256 bits to DHKE protocol, the generator should have an order of at least  <math alttext="2 Superscript 256" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>256</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 256](images/c12_1224.png).
*   First, the generator used in DHKE protocol is public, thus known to the adversary. Second, to recover a private key *K*, one has to solve a discrete logarithm problem either “find *K* such that  <math alttext="2 Superscript upper K Baseline identical-to h m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mi>h</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript upper K Baseline identical-to h m o d p](images/c12_1225.png)” or “find *K* such that  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 2 Superscript 16 Baseline plus 1 right-parenthesis Superscript upper K Baseline identical-to h m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mi>h</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 2 Superscript 16 Baseline plus 1 right-parenthesis Superscript upper K Baseline identical-to h m o d p](images/c12_1226.png)”, with known *p* and *h*. Therefore, from the security point of view, the value of the generator (excluding 1 and  <math alttext="p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p minus 1](images/c12_1227.png)) does not matter. Therefore, it is customary to select a generator *g*, which makes public and shared key computations easier, usually  <math alttext="g equals 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![g equals 2](images/c12_1228.png) or  <math alttext="g equals 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![g equals 3](images/c12_1229.png).

1. Hence,  <math alttext="left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis Superscript k Baseline identical-to left-parenthesis left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis squared right-parenthesis Superscript k 1 Baseline asterisk left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis Superscript k 2 Baseline identical-to left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Superscript k 1 Baseline asterisk left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis Superscript k 2 Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></msup><mo>\*</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></msup><mo>\*</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis Superscript k Baseline identical-to left-parenthesis left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis squared right-parenthesis Superscript k 1 Baseline asterisk left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis Superscript k 2 Baseline identical-to left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Superscript k 1 Baseline asterisk left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis Superscript k 2 Baseline m o d p](images/c12_1238.png).

Therefore,  <math alttext="g equals p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![g equals p minus 1](images/c12_1239.png) generates only two elements; its order is 2.

*   Let  <math alttext="g equals p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![g equals p minus 1](images/c12_1240.png) be the generator used in HDKE protocol. The answer to question 1, shows that  <math alttext="left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis Superscript k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis Superscript k](images/c12_1241.png) is either 1 or <math alttext="p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p minus 1](images/c12_1242.png). Therefore, the shared secret key generated by DHKE is either 1 or  <math alttext="p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p minus 1](images/c12_1243.png) whatever are the chosen private keys. Therefore, the shared secret key is easy to recover from observing the public parameters *p* and *g*.

***Problem 12.19***

1.  Lagrange’s theorem states that if *G* is a group and *H* is a subgroup of *G*, then  <math alttext="StartAbsoluteValue upper H EndAbsoluteValue" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow></math> ![StartAbsoluteValue upper H EndAbsoluteValue](images/c12_1244.png) divides  <math alttext="StartAbsoluteValue upper G EndAbsoluteValue" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow></math> ![StartAbsoluteValue upper G EndAbsoluteValue](images/c12_1245.png). In addition, any element  <math alttext="a element-of normal upper G" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></mrow></math> ![a element-of normal upper G](images/c12_1246.png), with order denoted  <math alttext="upper Omega left-parenthesis a right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#937;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper Omega left-parenthesis a right-parenthesis](images/c12_1247.png) generates a subgroup of  <math alttext="normal upper G" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></math> ![normal upper G](images/c12_1248.png); thus,  <math alttext="upper Omega left-parenthesis a right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#937;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper Omega left-parenthesis a right-parenthesis](images/c12_1249.png) divides  <math alttext="StartAbsoluteValue upper G EndAbsoluteValue" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow></math> ![StartAbsoluteValue upper G EndAbsoluteValue](images/c12_1250.png).

If *p* is a prime, then  <math alttext="StartAbsoluteValue double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk Baseline EndAbsoluteValue equals p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![StartAbsoluteValue double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk Baseline EndAbsoluteValue equals p minus 1](images/c12_1251.png). If *p* is a safe prime, then  <math alttext="p minus 1 equals 2 q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![p minus 1 equals 2 q](images/c12_1252.png), with *q* prime. Hence, dividers of  <math alttext="p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p minus 1](images/c12_1253.png) are  <math alttext="StartSet 1 comma 2 comma q comma p minus 1 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 1 comma 2 comma q comma p minus 1 EndSet](images/c12_1254.png). Therefore, any element in  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c12_1255.png) has an order of 1, 2,  <math alttext="q equals StartFraction p minus 1 Over 2 EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></math> ![q equals StartFraction p minus 1 Over 2 EndFraction](images/c12_1256.png), or  <math alttext="p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p minus 1](images/c12_1257.png).

Element 1 generates a subgroup of a single element, which is 1 itself, because  <math alttext="1 Superscript k Baseline equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>1</mn><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![1 Superscript k Baseline equals 1](images/c12_1258.png), for any positive integer *k*.

Therefore, any element in  <math alttext="StartSet 3 comma 4 comma ellipsis comma p minus 2 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 3 comma 4 comma ellipsis comma p minus 2 EndSet](images/c12_1266.png) has an order of either  <math alttext="StartFraction p minus 1 Over 2 EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></math> ![StartFraction p minus 1 Over 2 EndFraction](images/c12_1267.png) or  <math alttext="p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p minus 1](images/c12_1268.png), if *p* is a safe prime.

*   When DHKE protocol is of concern, parties agree on a generator *g* to compute a shared secret key. If *p* is a safe prime, any element *g* of  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk Baseline minus left-brace 1 comma p minus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo>{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk Baseline minus left-brace 1 comma p minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c12_1269.png) has an order of either  <math alttext="StartFraction p minus 1 Over 2 EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></math> ![StartFraction p minus 1 Over 2 EndFraction](images/c12_1270.png) or  <math alttext="p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p minus 1](images/c12_1271.png). Hence, depending on the shown generator, either  <math alttext="StartFraction p minus 1 Over 2 EndFraction minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![StartFraction p minus 1 Over 2 EndFraction minus 1](images/c12_1272.png) or  <math alttext="p minus 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![p minus 2](images/c12_1273.png) distinct private keys may be chosen. Therefore, a safe prime *p* provides a security strength of nearly  <math alttext="2 Superscript l o g 2 left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript l o g 2 left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c12_1274.png).

***Problem 12.20***

Yes, the basic DHKE protocol, as defined in this chapter, is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attack. Let us show a scenario: Alice and Bob cooperate to generate a shared secret key. Eve intercepts the messages sent by Alice and Bob. Then, instead of the legitimate Alice’s public key, Eve makes use of her private key and sends her public key to Bob. Then, the generated shared secret key is known to Eve. Therefore, she can recover the messages sent by Bob to Alice and then either not forward them to Alice or modify them before sending them. To let Alice decrypt the messages, Eve sends her public key to Alice instead of Bob’s public key. In this scenario, there are two shared secret keys, one between Bob and Eve and another between Eve and Alice. To prevent DHKE protocol from man-in-the-middle attack, a third trusted party must be used to authenticate the public keys used to generate a shared secret key.

***Problem 12.21***

1.  If the initialization value  <math alttext="pi left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![pi left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis](images/c12_1275.png) used by a party *B* and the public key of partner *A* are known to adversary who can intercept ciphertexts, then the adversary can easily derive the per-message keys used for encrypting the plaintexts, because she/he knows the PRNG in use. Also, if the adversary knows the *k*^(th) pair ciphertext-plaintext, he/she can use *k* to obtain per-message keys used for plaintexts encrypted before and after the *k*^(th) plaintext, because the PRNG in use is deterministic.
2.  The primary technique to make a known PRNG secure when used in a cryptosystem, is to make its seed (i.e. initial value) confidential. Another technique is to randomly discard some returned results of the PRNG before using a value as a private key. For example, use in tandem two PRNGs, one is public and another is private. The second PRNG is periodically used to pick a random integer, which indicates the number of PRNG results to discard before selecting one result as a per-message key. Since the number and the positions of discarded values of the PRNG are unknown to the adversary, he/she cannot reconstruct the series of per-message keys from the construction of the public PRNG.
3.  As conclusion, we can say that the security of ElGamal cryptosystem depends not only on the subgroup used to pick private keys but also on the security of the PRNG used to generate random private keys.

Then, Alice tests if  <math alttext="v equals g Superscript upper M Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>M</mi></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![v equals g Superscript upper M Baseline m o d p](images/c12_1303.png).

By construction:  <math alttext="upper M identical-to s asterisk a m o d left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>a</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper M identical-to s asterisk a m o d left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c12_1304.png).

By substitution of *v* and *M*, the test becomes:

 <math alttext="g Superscript s asterisk a Baseline m o d p equals g Superscript s asterisk a m o d left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline m o d p" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>a</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![g Superscript s asterisk a Baseline m o d p equals g Superscript s asterisk a m o d left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline m o d p](images/c12_1305.png)

Using Lemma 12.1 “ <math alttext="m o d p left-right-arrow m o d p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8596;</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![m o d p left-right-arrow m o d p minus 1](images/c12_1306.png)”, the test becomes:

 <math alttext="g Superscript s asterisk a Baseline m o d p equals g Superscript s asterisk a Baseline m o d p" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![g Superscript s asterisk a Baseline m o d p equals g Superscript s asterisk a Baseline m o d p](images/c12_1307.png)

Therefore, the signature is considered valid.

***Problem 12.24***

1.  According to ElGamal’s signature design, the signer must select an ephemeral key *k* such that  <math alttext="2 less-than-or-equal-to k less-than-or-equal-to p minus 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![2 less-than-or-equal-to k less-than-or-equal-to p minus 2](images/c12_1308.png) and  <math alttext="GCD left-parenthesis k comma p minus 1 right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>GCD</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![GCD left-parenthesis k comma p minus 1 right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c12_1309.png). Thus, if  <math alttext="p equals 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 17](images/c12_1310.png), then ephemeral keys are selected from  <math alttext="StartSet 3 comma 5 comma 7 comma 9 comma 11 comma 13 comma 15 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>15</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 3 comma 5 comma 7 comma 9 comma 11 comma 13 comma 15 EndSet](images/c12_1311.png). Compute the first-component (*r*) of signature for each candidate ephemeral-key, using  <math alttext="g equals 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![g equals 3](images/c12_1312.png):

 <math alttext="r 1 equals 3 Superscript 3 Baseline m o d 17 equals 10" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>3</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math> ![r 1 equals 3 Superscript 3 Baseline m o d 17 equals 10](images/c12_1313.png)    <math alttext="r 2 equals 3 Superscript 5 Baseline m o d 17 equals 5" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>5</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> ![r 2 equals 3 Superscript 5 Baseline m o d 17 equals 5](images/c12_1314.png)

 <math alttext="r 3 equals 3 Superscript 7 Baseline m o d 17 equals 11" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>7</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow></math> ![r 3 equals 3 Superscript 7 Baseline m o d 17 equals 11](images/c12_1315.png)    <math alttext="r 4 equals 3 Superscript 9 Baseline m o d 17 equals 14" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>9</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn></mrow></math> ![r 4 equals 3 Superscript 9 Baseline m o d 17 equals 14](images/c12_1316.png)

 <math alttext="r 5 equals 3 Superscript 11 Baseline m o d 17 equals 7" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> ![r 5 equals 3 Superscript 11 Baseline m o d 17 equals 7](images/c12_1317.png)    <math alttext="r 6 equals 3 Superscript 13 Baseline m o d 17 equals 12" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>13</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow></math> ![r 6 equals 3 Superscript 13 Baseline m o d 17 equals 12](images/c12_1318.png)

 <math alttext="r 7 equals 3 Superscript 15 Baseline m o d 17 equals 6" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>7</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>15</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> ![r 7 equals 3 Superscript 15 Baseline m o d 17 equals 6](images/c12_1319.png)

Therefore, the number of distinct first-components of signature that can be associated with a message *x*, under the given parameters, is 7. Notice that the order of element 3 is 16; thus, it is a generator of the group  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z 17 Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z 17 Superscript asterisk](images/c12_1320.png).

*   2\.  <math alttext="p equals 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 17](images/c12_1321.png): as in previous case, ephemeral keys are selected from  <math alttext="StartSet 3 comma 5 comma 7 comma 9 comma 11 comma 13 comma 15 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>15</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 3 comma 5 comma 7 comma 9 comma 11 comma 13 comma 15 EndSet](images/c12_1322.png). Compute the first-component of signature for each candidate ephemeral-key, using  <math alttext="g equals 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![g equals 2](images/c12_1323.png):

 <math alttext="r 1 equals 2 Superscript 3 Baseline m o d 17 equals 2 Superscript 11 Baseline m o d 17 equals 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>3</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ![r 1 equals 2 Superscript 3 Baseline m o d 17 equals 2 Superscript 11 Baseline m o d 17 equals 8](images/c12_1324.png)

 <math alttext="r 2 equals 2 Superscript 5 Baseline m o d 17 equals 2 Superscript 13 Baseline m o d 17 equals 15" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>5</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>13</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow></math> ![r 2 equals 2 Superscript 5 Baseline m o d 17 equals 2 Superscript 13 Baseline m o d 17 equals 15](images/c12_1325.png)

 <math alttext="r 3 equals 2 Superscript 7 Baseline m o d 17 equals 2 Superscript 15 Baseline m o d 17 equals 9" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>7</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></math> ![r 3 equals 2 Superscript 7 Baseline m o d 17 equals 2 Superscript 15 Baseline m o d 17 equals 9](images/c12_1326.png)

 <math alttext="r 4 equals 2 Superscript 9 Baseline m o d 17 equals 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>9</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![r 4 equals 2 Superscript 9 Baseline m o d 17 equals 2](images/c12_1327.png)

Therefore, the number of distinct first-components of signature that can be associated with a message *x*, under the given parameters, is 4. Notice that the order of element 2 is 8 (because  <math alttext="2 Superscript 8 Baseline m o d 17 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>8</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 8 Baseline m o d 17 equals 1](images/c12_1328.png)). Hence, 2 is a generator of the subgroup of  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z 17 Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z 17 Superscript asterisk](images/c12_1329.png).

*   3) If *p* is a safe prime, then the number of nonzero elements in  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c12_1330.png) is  <math alttext="2 q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![2 q](images/c12_1331.png), with  <math alttext="p equals 2 q plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 2 q plus 1](images/c12_1332.png) and *q* a prime. Any ephemeral key in  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c12_1333.png) is coprime to  <math alttext="p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p minus 1](images/c12_1334.png), i.e. coprime to  <math alttext="2 q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![2 q](images/c12_1335.png). Since *q* is prime, any odd element in  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c12_1336.png) is coprime to  <math alttext="2 q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![2 q](images/c12_1337.png). Therefore, the number of elements that can be used as ephemeral keys is  <math alttext="StartFraction p minus 1 Over 2 EndFraction minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![StartFraction p minus 1 Over 2 EndFraction minus 1](images/c12_1338.png), “ <math alttext="negative 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![negative 1](images/c12_1339.png)” is to exclude element 1, which cannot be used as ephemeral key. Since *g* is a generator of  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c12_1340.png), no distinct keys  <math alttext="k 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![k 1](images/c12_1341.png) and  <math alttext="k 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![k 2](images/c12_1342.png), with  <math alttext="2 less-than k 1 less-than k 2 less-than p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 less-than k 1 less-than k 2 less-than p minus 1](images/c12_1343.png), could result in the same signature first-component, because  <math alttext="g Superscript k 1 Baseline CrossOut identical-to EndCrossOut g Superscript k 2 Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></msup><menclose notation="updiagonalstrike"><mo>&#8801;</mo></menclose><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![g Superscript k 1 Baseline CrossOut identical-to EndCrossOut g Superscript k 2 Baseline m o d p](images/c12_1344.png). Hence, the number of distinct first-components of signature that can be generated for the same message, under the given conditions, is  <math alttext="StartFraction p minus 1 Over 2 EndFraction minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![StartFraction p minus 1 Over 2 EndFraction minus 1](images/c12_1345.png).

**Problem 12.25**

*g* is a generator of a subgroup, of order *q* of the multiplicative group  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c12_1364.png) and *q* is a prime divisor of  <math alttext="p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p minus 1](images/c12_1365.png). Since *g* is an element of  <math alttext="double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![double-struck upper Z Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c12_1366.png) of order *q*, by the definition of the element order (see Section 3.2.1),  <math alttext="g Superscript q Baseline m o d p identical-to 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![g Superscript q Baseline m o d p identical-to 1](images/c12_1367.png).

The property can also be proven otherwise as follows:

If *q* is a prime divisor of  <math alttext="p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p minus 1](images/c12_1368.png), then there exists a unique positive integer *i* such that:  <math alttext="p minus 1 equals i asterisk q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![p minus 1 equals i asterisk q](images/c12_1369.png).

Generator *g* can be rewritten as:  <math alttext="g identical-to h Superscript i Baseline m o d p identical-to h Superscript left-parenthesis StartFraction p minus 1 Over q EndFraction right-parenthesis Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>q</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![g identical-to h Superscript i Baseline m o d p identical-to h Superscript left-parenthesis StartFraction p minus 1 Over q EndFraction right-parenthesis Baseline m o d p](images/c12_1370.png), with *h* a positive integer less than *p*. Then,

***Problem 12.26***

DSA scheme is correct if the verification of a legitimate signed message accompanied with its signature results is “Valid signature”.

Assume that the received data are *p*, *g*,  <math alttext="upper P u b Subscript s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>u</mi><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P u b Subscript s](images/c12_1373.png), *M*, and  <math alttext="left-parenthesis r comma s right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis r comma s right-parenthesis](images/c12_1374.png) generated by the legitimate signer. If *M* is the authentic message, then the hash computed by the verifier is *Z*, which is the same as the one computed by the signer. To prove DSA correctness, we make substitutions in the formulas used by the verifier as follows:

To do so, the following Lemma is needed:

*Proof*: Since  <math alttext="a m o d q equals b m o d q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![a m o d q equals b m o d q](images/c12_1381.png), *a* can be written as:  <math alttext="a equals b plus j asterisk q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![a equals b plus j asterisk q](images/c12_1382.png) (*j* is an integer).

Since  <math alttext="upper K m o d q equals left-parenthesis upper K m o d q right-parenthesis m o d q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K m o d q equals left-parenthesis upper K m o d q right-parenthesis m o d q](images/c12_1384.png), replace in lemma 12.3 *a* by  <math alttext="upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K](images/c12_1385.png) and *b* by  <math alttext="upper K m o d q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K m o d q](images/c12_1386.png). Then, from lemma 12.3:

 <math alttext="StartLayout 1st Row g Superscript upper K Baseline m o d p equals g Superscript upper K m o d q Baseline m o d p 2nd Row v equals left-parenthesis g Superscript upper K Baseline m o d p right-parenthesis m o d q equals left-parenthesis g Superscript upper K m o d q Baseline m o d p right-parenthesis m o d q EndLayout" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mtable><mtr><mtd><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>)</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> ![StartLayout 1st Row g Superscript upper K Baseline m o d p equals g Superscript upper K m o d q Baseline m o d p 2nd Row v equals left-parenthesis g Superscript upper K Baseline m o d p right-parenthesis m o d q equals left-parenthesis g Superscript upper K m o d q Baseline m o d p right-parenthesis m o d q EndLayout](images/c12_1387.png)

Then:  <math alttext="v equals left-parenthesis g Superscript upper K m o d q Baseline m o d p right-parenthesis m o d q equals r equals left-parenthesis g Superscript upper K Baseline m o d p right-parenthesis m o d q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>)</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![v equals left-parenthesis g Superscript upper K m o d q Baseline m o d p right-parenthesis m o d q equals r equals left-parenthesis g Superscript upper K Baseline m o d p right-parenthesis m o d q](images/c12_1388.png), which means that the signature verification is correct.□

***Problem 12.27***

In block ciphers, the key length is chosen enough long to be resistant to brute-force attack, while in RSA, the modulus and private key have to be enough large to be resistant against factoring. Naïve brute-force attack against AES is of a complexity of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 128](images/c12_1389.png). Using the complexity bound proven in \[[3](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0003)\], the complexity of factoring RSA-2048 modulus is of

 <math alttext="exp left-parenthesis left-parenthesis left-parenthesis StartFraction 64 Over 9 EndFraction right-parenthesis Superscript one-third Baseline right-parenthesis left-parenthesis left-parenthesis l n 2 Superscript 2048 Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript one-third Baseline left-parenthesis l n l n 2 Superscript 2048 Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript two-thirds Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis almost-equals 2 Superscript 117" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow><mn>9</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>2048</mn></mrow></msup><mo>)</mo><msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo>(</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>2048</mn></mrow></msup><mo>)</mo><msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8776;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>117</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![exp left-parenthesis left-parenthesis left-parenthesis StartFraction 64 Over 9 EndFraction right-parenthesis Superscript one-third Baseline right-parenthesis left-parenthesis left-parenthesis l n 2 Superscript 2048 Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript one-third Baseline left-parenthesis l n l n 2 Superscript 2048 Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript two-thirds Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis almost-equals 2 Superscript 117](images/c12_1390.png)

Both complexities result in computationally infeasible attacks. Therefore, RSA keys are much larger than AES keys.

## Notes

1.  [**1**](#c12.xhtml#rc12-note-0001) The patent for the RSA algorithm (US patent n° 4405829) was issued on September 1983, exclusively licensed to RSA Security Inc. This patent expired in 2000.
2.  **2** By definition of multiplicative inverse,  <math alttext="d identical-to e Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![d identical-to e Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d n](images/c12_1391.png).
3.  **3** The value of *M* must be an integer between 0 and  <math alttext="n minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![n minus 1](images/c12_1392.png), because the encryption and the description functions are  <math alttext="m o d u l o n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>u</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![m o d u l o n](images/c12_1393.png). In case the message to send has a value greater than  <math alttext="n minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![n minus 1](images/c12_1394.png), it must be fragmented into a series of segments and each segment is encrypted separately.
4.  [**4**](#c12.xhtml#rc12-note-0004) An iteration is composed of a test, a multiplication, a division, and a squaring (see the algorithm of the right-to-left binary exponentiation method in Section 3.3.2).
5.
