# 13   
Public-Key Cryptosystems  
Elliptic Curve Cryptography

## 13.1 Introduction

### 13.1.1 What Is Elliptic Curve Cryptography?

First, notice that Elliptic curves (EC) have nothing to do with ellipses. Elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC) is a high performance alternative approach to RSA for asymmetric algorithms. Elliptic curve cryptography algorithms entered wide use in 2004. After a slow start, elliptic curve-based algorithms are gaining popularity and the pace of adoption is accelerating. EC cryptosystems have been adopted by Amazon, Google, and many others to secure communications with their customers.

As shown in [Table 13.1](#c13.xhtml#c13-tbl-0001) (from RFC 5349 \[[1](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0001)\]), EC cryptosystems amply outperform RSA-based cryptosystems. The table compares the level of security (i.e. resistance to attacks) of symmetric, ECC, and RSA systems depending on the length of keys. We can conclude, at least, that: i) with a key size of *2L* bits, ECC provides a comparable level of security to symmetric systems with a key size of *L* bits without the need to share the same secret key, as required by symmetric systems, and ii) ECCs with less than 255-bit keys provide comparable security level to RSA-2048 systems (i.e. RSA with the key size currently in use). RSA-2048 requires eight times bits than ECC with comparable security level. Even more significantly, RSA-512 requires 30 times bits than ECC with comparable security level.

[**Table 13.1**](#c13.xhtml#rc13-tbl-0001) Comparable key sizes (in bits).

 
| *Symmetric* || *ECC* || *RSA* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 80112128192256 || 160–223224–255256–383384–511512+ || 102420483072768015360 |
| --- | --- | --- |

Until 2015, the NSA (National Security Agency, US) recommended 256-bit ECC for protecting classified information up to the secret level and 384-bit for Top secret level. Since 2015, the NSA recommended 384-bit for all classified information. IETF standards have been proposed to support ECC for SSL and TLS \[[2](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0002)–[4](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0004)\]. In most applications such as OpenSSL and OpenSSH, the key length is 256 bits.

ECC ensures fast encryption speed with a high complexity of decryption to ensure data confidentiality and authentication. Shorter ECC encryption keys use fewer memory and CPU resources. However, the ECC comes with a drawback, which is its complexity of design. ECC uses fairly more difficult mathematical operations based on elliptic curves on finite fields, which are addressed in this chapter.

*Public keys* in the ECC are *elliptic curve points*, which are pairs of integer coordinates  <math alttext="left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis](images/c13_1.png), laying on elliptic curve over a finite field *F[p]*, while RSA public keys are integers within  <math alttext="z Subscript p Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![z Subscript p Baseline](images/c13_2.png).

ECC provides three groups of algorithms, which share the same foundations, the elliptic curves over finite fields:

*   ECC key-agreement like EC cofactor Diffie-Hellman (see [Section 13.5.3](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-1031)) and EC Menezes-Qu-Vanstone (see [Section 13.5.4](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-1033)).
*   ECC digital-signature algorithms like the well-known ECDSA (see [Section 13.5.5](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-1034)) and EdDSA (see [Section 13.5.6](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-1039)).
*   ECC encryption algorithms including the ECIES and EEEC (see [Section 13.5.7](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-1044)).

First, the foundations of ECC algorithms are addressed and then the three types of algorithms are presented.

### 13.1.2 What Is an Elliptic Curve?

The idea of elliptic curves in cryptography was suggested independently by Neal Koblitz \[[5](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0005)\] and Victor Miller \[[6](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0006)\].

***Definition 13.1: An* *elliptic curve*** *over a set* *S* *(real numbers, integer numbers, etc.), denoted*  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper S right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper S right-parenthesis](images/c13_3.png)*, is the set of solutions*  <math alttext="left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis element-of upper S squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis element-of upper S squared](images/c13_4.png) *to the equation*:[¹](#c13.xhtml#c13-note-0001)

 <math alttext="y squared plus d x y plus e y equals x cubed plus c x squared plus a x plus b" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![y squared plus d x y plus e y equals x cubed plus c x squared plus a x plus b](images/c13_5.png)(13.1) 

*where*  <math alttext="a comma b comma c comma d" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> ![a comma b comma c comma d](images/c13_6.png)*, and* *e* *are constants*.

[Figure 13.1](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0001) shows some examples of shape of elliptic curves over real numbers.

![Figure 13.1 Examples of EC with associated equations.](images/c13f001.png)

[**Figure 13.1**](#c13.xhtml#rc13-fig-0001) Examples of EC with associated equations.

The *elliptic curve cryptography* uses elliptic curves over finite fields. This means that the points on the curve are limited to integer coordinates within the field. There are two types of fields to build ECs: prime fields, denoted *F[p]*, where *p* is a prime, and extension fields, denoted  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c13_7.png), where the number of elements is a prime power.

ECs over prime fields and ECs over extension fields differ in their EC equations and in their operations on curve points. The former are not easy to grasp quickly; the latter are still a bit more complex, but they are recommended by the standards of public key cryptosystems like ECDSA (elliptic curve digital signature algorithm).

### 13.1.3 Order and Point Set of an Elliptic Curve

***Definition 13.2:** The* ***order*** *of an EC* *is the number of points on the EC including a virtual point called point to infinity*.

*Notations:*

*   An elliptic curve is denoted  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_8.png) in case of a prime field and  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m Subscript Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m Subscript Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_9.png) in case of an extension field.
*   The EC order is denoted  <math alttext="number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis or number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m Subscript Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>#</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;or&#160;</mtext><mo>#</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis or number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m Subscript Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_10.png) depending on the field type.

The role of the point to infinity is addressed in the sequel.

**Note.** Elliptic curves are based on finite fields. To address easily EC-based cryptosystems, the basics of finite fields are reminded with examples and exercises in [Chapter 3](#c03.xhtml) (see Section 3.2.2).

## 13.2 **Elliptic Curve Cryptography over Prime Field** ***F**[**p**]*

### 13.2.1 **Definition of Elliptic Curves over Prime Fields:** ***E(F***[***p***]***)***

***Definition 13.3 Elliptic curve*:**[²](#c13.xhtml#c13-note-0002) *it is denoted*  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_11.png) *and formed by the set of solutions*  <math alttext="left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis element-of upper F Subscript p Baseline squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><msup><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis element-of upper F Subscript p Baseline squared](images/c13_12.png) *to the* equation [13.2](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-2002) *under the condition* [13.3](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-2003).

 <math alttext="upper E colon y squared identical-to x cubed plus a x plus b m o d p" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper E colon y squared identical-to x cubed plus a x plus b m o d p](images/c13_13.png)(13.2)  <math alttext="left-parenthesis a comma b element-of upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis logical-and left-parenthesis 4 a cubed plus 27 b squared CrossOut identical-to EndCrossOut 0 m o d p right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8743;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>27</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><menclose notation="updiagonalstrike"><mo>&#8801;</mo></menclose><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis a comma b element-of upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis logical-and left-parenthesis 4 a cubed plus 27 b squared CrossOut identical-to EndCrossOut 0 m o d p right-parenthesis](images/c13_14.png)(13.3) 

*F[p]* *is the set of positive integers:*  <math alttext="upper F Subscript p Baseline equals StartSet 0 comma 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma p minus 1 EndSet equals double-struck upper Z Subscript p Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>&#8484;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript p Baseline equals StartSet 0 comma 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma p minus 1 EndSet equals double-struck upper Z Subscript p Baseline](images/c13_15.png).

**Note**. The equation  <math alttext="y squared identical-to x cubed plus a x plus b m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![y squared identical-to x cubed plus a x plus b m o d p](images/c13_16.png) is called Weierstrass equation. Hence, the elliptic curves defined by the equation are called Weierstrass curves.

*   ***Point to infinity***

A special point called *point at infinity*, denoted  <math alttext="script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></math> ![script upper O](images/c13_17.png), is associated with any elliptic curve. It is used to tell that addition of two points cannot lead to a third point (see *vertical point addition* below). Point to infinity (also called *zero element*) is the neutral element of elliptic curve arithmetic. Adding point to infinity to any point *P* results in that other point, including adding point to infinity to itself:  <math alttext="upper P plus script upper O equals upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P plus script upper O equals upper P](images/c13_18.png),  <math alttext="script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></math> ![script upper O](images/c13_19.png) *+*  <math alttext="script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></math> ![script upper O](images/c13_20.png) *\=*  <math alttext="script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></math> ![script upper O](images/c13_21.png).

Point to infinity is an artificial point of the curve; it is introduced to fill gaps in the table for addition of points on the curve, and it acts as the group neutral element. When two points have the same x-coordinate, their addition results in a point to infinity

**Example 13.1** The equation of the elliptic curve used in Bitcoin (denoted *secp256k1*) is  <math alttext="y squared equals x cubed plus 7" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> ![y squared equals x cubed plus 7](images/c13_22.png). When we limit the use of the EC to  <math alttext="upper F 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F 17](images/c13_23.png); i.e. the equation becomes:  <math alttext="y squared identical-to left-parenthesis x cubed plus 7 right-parenthesis m o d 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![y squared identical-to left-parenthesis x cubed plus 7 right-parenthesis m o d 17](images/c13_24.png). The points are shown on [Figure 13.2](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0002).[³](#c13.xhtml#c13-note-0003) Notice that condition 13.5 is fulfilled since:  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 4 asterisk 0 cubed plus 27 asterisk 7 squared right-parenthesis m o d 17 CrossOut identical-to EndCrossOut 0 m o d 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>27</mn><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>7</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><menclose notation="updiagonalstrike"><mo>&#8801;</mo></menclose><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 4 asterisk 0 cubed plus 27 asterisk 7 squared right-parenthesis m o d 17 CrossOut identical-to EndCrossOut 0 m o d 17](images/c13_25.png).

![Figure 13.2 Points of elliptic curve upper E colon y squared identical-to left-parenthesis x cubed plus 7 right-parenthesis m o d 17.](images/c13f002.png)

[**Figure 13.2**](#c13.xhtml#rc13-fig-0002) Points of elliptic curve  <math alttext="upper E colon y squared identical-to left-parenthesis x cubed plus 7 right-parenthesis m o d 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![upper E colon y squared identical-to left-parenthesis x cubed plus 7 right-parenthesis m o d 17](images/c13_35.png).

*   – Point  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 3 comma 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 3 comma 0 right-parenthesis](images/c13_26.png) belongs to  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F 17 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F 17 right-parenthesis](images/c13_27.png), because  <math alttext="3 cubed plus 7 minus 0 equals 34 identical-to 0 m o d 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>34</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![3 cubed plus 7 minus 0 equals 34 identical-to 0 m o d 17](images/c13_28.png).
*   – Point  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 8 comma 3 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 8 comma 3 right-parenthesis](images/c13_29.png) belongs to  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F 17 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F 17 right-parenthesis](images/c13_30.png), because  <math alttext="8 cubed plus 7 minus 3 squared equals 510 equals 17 asterisk 30 identical-to 0 m o d 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>8</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>510</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![8 cubed plus 7 minus 3 squared equals 510 equals 17 asterisk 30 identical-to 0 m o d 17](images/c13_31.png).
*   – Point  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 3 comma 3 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 3 comma 3 right-parenthesis](images/c13_32.png) does not belong to  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F 17 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F 17 right-parenthesis](images/c13_33.png), because  <math alttext="3 cubed plus 7 minus 3 squared equals 7 identical-to 7 m o d 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>7</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![3 cubed plus 7 minus 3 squared equals 7 identical-to 7 m o d 17](images/c13_34.png).

**Notes**

*   – The shape of the curve given by  <math alttext="y squared identical-to x cubed plus a x plus b m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![y squared identical-to x cubed plus a x plus b m o d p](images/c13_36.png) over a prime field *F[p]* differs from that of the curve  <math alttext="y squared identical-to x cubed plus a x plus b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![y squared identical-to x cubed plus a x plus b](images/c13_37.png) (i.e. without specifying a field). For example, the shapes of the curves of the first EC in [Figures 13.1](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0001) and [13.2](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0002) are distinct although they have the same equation  <math alttext="y squared equals x cubed plus 7" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> ![y squared equals x cubed plus 7](images/c13_38.png). The reason is that when the field is finite, say *F[p]*, the points of the initial curve are mapped  <math alttext="m o d u l o p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![m o d u l o p](images/c13_39.png) on a curve where the points have integer coordinates in a square *p* by *p*. Let  <math alttext="left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis](images/c13_40.png) be the coordinates of any point on the infinite elliptic curve. Rewrite *x* and *y* as  <math alttext="y equals y 1 plus k 1 p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![y equals y 1 plus k 1 p](images/c13_41.png) and  <math alttext="x equals x 1 plus k 2 p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![x equals x 1 plus k 2 p](images/c13_42.png), where *x*[1] and  <math alttext="y 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![y 1](images/c13_43.png) are two positive integers less than *p*. Equation 13.4 may be rewritten as  <math alttext="left-parenthesis y 1 plus k 1 p right-parenthesis squared identical-to left-parenthesis x 1 plus k 2 p right-parenthesis cubed plus a left-parenthesis x 1 plus k 2 p right-parenthesis plus b m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis y 1 plus k 1 p right-parenthesis squared identical-to left-parenthesis x 1 plus k 2 p right-parenthesis cubed plus a left-parenthesis x 1 plus k 2 p right-parenthesis plus b m o d p](images/c13_44.png), which can be simplified (using modular arithmetic rules) as  <math alttext="y 1 squared identical-to x 1 cubed plus a x 1 plus b m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msup><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msup><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![y 1 squared identical-to x 1 cubed plus a x 1 plus b m o d p](images/c13_45.png). Consequently, all the points whose coordinates differ by a multiple of the modulus *p* have the same image point on the EC. For example, all points of EC defined by  <math alttext="y squared equals x cubed plus 7" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> ![y squared equals x cubed plus 7](images/c13_46.png) with coordinates  <math alttext="x equals 3 plus 17 k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>17</mn><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> ![x equals 3 plus 17 k](images/c13_47.png) (*k* is integer) and  <math alttext="y equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![y equals 0](images/c13_48.png) are mapped to a single point with coordinates  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 3 comma 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 3 comma 0 right-parenthesis](images/c13_49.png) on the  <math alttext="upper E upper C left-parenthesis upper F 17 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E upper C left-parenthesis upper F 17 right-parenthesis](images/c13_50.png).
*   – The number of points on the elliptic curve over a finite field *F[p]* is different from the number of elements in the field *F[p]*. Since points on the curve  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_51.png) have their coordinates in a square *p* by *p*, the number of points may be larger than *p*. Exercise 13.1 shows an example of  <math alttext="EC left-parenthesis upper F 23 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>EC&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>23</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![EC left-parenthesis upper F 23 right-parenthesis](images/c13_52.png), which has 27 points plus the point to infinity.

### 13.2.2 Operations on Elliptic Curves

A single basic operation can be applied to elliptic curve points, the addition, with four forms: point addition, point doubling, point multiplication by a scalar, and vertical point addition. Note that all operations are  <math alttext="m o d u l o p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![m o d u l o p](images/c13_53.png).

*   *Point addition*

 <math alttext="upper R 1 equals upper P plus upper Q semicolon upper R 2 equals upper P plus upper R 1 semicolon upper R 3 equals upper P plus upper R 2" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo>;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper R 1 equals upper P plus upper Q semicolon upper R 2 equals upper P plus upper R 1 semicolon upper R 3 equals upper P plus upper R 2](images/c13_62.png)![Figure 13.3 Point addition.](images/c13f003.png)

[**Figure 13.3**](#c13.xhtml#rc13-fig-0003) Point addition.

To locate point  <math alttext="upper R 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper R 1](images/c13_63.png) on the curve; first, a line is drawn between points *P* and  <math alttext="upper Q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper Q](images/c13_64.png). The intersection of the line  <math alttext="upper P upper Q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P upper Q](images/c13_65.png) with the curve is the point  <math alttext="minus upper R 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![minus upper R 1](images/c13_66.png). Then, the intersection of the vertical line including point  <math alttext="minus upper R 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![minus upper R 1](images/c13_67.png) with the curve results in the point  <math alttext="minus upper R 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![minus upper R 1](images/c13_68.png).  <math alttext="minus upper R 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![minus upper R 1](images/c13_69.png) and  <math alttext="upper R 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper R 1](images/c13_70.png) are symmetrical with respect to the x-axis.

*   *Point doubling*

Let  <math alttext="upper P equals left-parenthesis x Subscript upper P Baseline comma y Subscript upper P Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>P</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>P</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P equals left-parenthesis x Subscript upper P Baseline comma y Subscript upper P Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_71.png) be a point on the elliptic curve  <math alttext="upper E colon y squared identical-to left-parenthesis x cubed plus a x plus b right-parenthesis m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper E colon y squared identical-to left-parenthesis x cubed plus a x plus b right-parenthesis m o d p](images/c13_72.png). The point doubling results in a point  <math alttext="upper R equals upper P plus upper P equals 2 upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R equals upper P plus upper P equals 2 upper P](images/c13_73.png), such that  <math alttext="upper R equals left-parenthesis x Subscript upper R Baseline comma y Subscript upper R Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>R</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper R equals left-parenthesis x Subscript upper R Baseline comma y Subscript upper R Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_74.png) where:

 <math alttext="x Subscript upper R Baseline equals lamda squared minus 2 x Subscript upper P Baseline comma y Subscript upper R Baseline equals lamda left-parenthesis x Subscript p Baseline minus x Subscript upper R Baseline right-parenthesis minus y Subscript upper P Baseline comma lamda equals StartFraction 3 x Subscript upper P Superscript 2 Baseline plus a Over 2 y Subscript upper P Baseline EndFraction" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>P</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8195;</mtext><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>R</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>P</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8195;</mtext><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>P</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![x Subscript upper R Baseline equals lamda squared minus 2 x Subscript upper P Baseline comma y Subscript upper R Baseline equals lamda left-parenthesis x Subscript p Baseline minus x Subscript upper R Baseline right-parenthesis minus y Subscript upper P Baseline comma lamda equals StartFraction 3 x Subscript upper P Superscript 2 Baseline plus a Over 2 y Subscript upper P Baseline EndFraction](images/c13_75.png)

As there is no second point to add when point doubling, to locate the point  <math alttext="2 upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![2 upper P](images/c13_76.png), a tangent to the curve is drawn at point *P*. Then, from the intersection between tangent and curve, draw a vertical line to locate the point  <math alttext="2 upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![2 upper P](images/c13_77.png) (see [Figure 13.4](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0004)).

![Figure 13.4 Point multiplication by a scalar.](images/c13f004.png)

[**Figure 13.4**](#c13.xhtml#rc13-fig-0004) Point multiplication by a scalar.

*   *Addition of vertical points (addition of negative point)*

Equation  <math alttext="y squared equals x cubed plus a x plus b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![y squared equals x cubed plus a x plus b](images/c13_78.png) yields a symmetric curve. A point with the same x-coordinate has two y-coordinates. If  <math alttext="upper P equals left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P equals left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis](images/c13_79.png), its negative is denoted  <math alttext="en-dash upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8211;</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![en-dash upper P](images/c13_80.png), and defined as  <math alttext="negative upper P equals minus left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis x comma negative y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![negative upper P equals minus left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis x comma negative y right-parenthesis](images/c13_81.png).[⁴](#c13.xhtml#c13-note-0004)

Addition of point *P* and its negative results in point to infinity:  <math alttext="upper P plus left-parenthesis negative upper P right-parenthesis equals script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P plus left-parenthesis negative upper P right-parenthesis equals script upper O](images/c13_82.png).

Using the graphical representation of the elliptic curve, one can easily observe that when two points *P* and *Q* have the same x-coordinate, there is no other point on the line  <math alttext="upper P upper Q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P upper Q](images/c13_83.png) that intersects with the curve, that is why their addition results in point to infinity. For example, in [Figure 13.3](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0003),  <math alttext="upper R 1 plus left-parenthesis minus upper R 1 right-parenthesis equals script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R 1 plus left-parenthesis minus upper R 1 right-parenthesis equals script upper O](images/c13_84.png).

*   *Point multiplication by a scalar*

Let *P* be a point over the EC and *k* an integer, multiplying *P* by *k* results in a point  <math alttext="upper R equals k dot upper P equals upper P plus upper P plus dot dot dot plus upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R equals k dot upper P equals upper P plus upper P plus dot dot dot plus upper P](images/c13_85.png). Scalar multiplication is achieved by repeated addition. Notice that a direct multiplication does not exist for elliptic curves, which makes the EC-based cryptography secure (see [section 13.4](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-1027)). [Figure 13.4](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0004) shows an example of multiplication  <math alttext="upper R equals 4 dot upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R equals 4 dot upper P](images/c13_86.png). Multiplying any EC point by 0 returns the point to infinity  <math alttext="script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></math> ![script upper O](images/c13_87.png); and multiplying  <math alttext="script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></math> ![script upper O](images/c13_88.png) by any positive integer *k* returns  <math alttext="script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></math> ![script upper O](images/c13_89.png).

**Note**. In literature, two notations exist to denote scalar multiplication: either with a symbol “⋅” between the scalar and the point (e.g.  <math alttext="8 dot upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![8 dot upper P](images/c13_90.png)) or without the symbol (e.g.  <math alttext="8 upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>8</mn><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![8 upper P](images/c13_91.png)). In the sequel, the first notation is used to denote point multiplication and “\*” to denote integer multiplication.

### 13.2.3 Generator and Cofactor of EC

Every EC over a field *F[p]* is a cyclic group. Consequently, there exists a point  <math alttext="upper G element-of upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper G element-of upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_92.png), such that all the points of the EC are multiples of *G*.

***Definition 13.4:** An element* *G* *on an elliptic curve*  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_93.png) *is a* ***generator*** *(also called* ***primitive*** ***element***) *if and only if any point on the elliptic curve is a multiple of* *G. Formally:*

*G* *is a generator of*  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis right double arrow for-all upper P element-of upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis comma there-exists k element-of double-struck upper N Superscript asterisk Baseline vertical-bar k dot upper G equals upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8658;</mo><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8707;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>&#8469;</mi><mo>\*</mo></msup><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis right double arrow for-all upper P element-of upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis comma there-exists k element-of double-struck upper N Superscript asterisk Baseline vertical-bar k dot upper G equals upper P](images/c13_94.png).

In general, not any points on an elliptic curve can generate all the points of the EC. Rather, each point of an EC can generate a subset of points. In group theory, we say that the EC is a group, and the subset of points, a subgroup.

An elliptic curve is a group with *N* points. If *N* is prime, then there is only one subgroup that is the same than the entire group. If *N* is not a prime, then to each integer *d* that divides *N* is associated a subgroup of  <math alttext="upper N slash d" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> ![upper N slash d](images/c13_95.png) points. For example, if *N* is divisible only by 2, 4, and 8, there exist subgroups with 2, 4, 8,  <math alttext="upper N slash 8" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ![upper N slash 8](images/c13_96.png),  <math alttext="upper N slash 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![upper N slash 4](images/c13_97.png),  <math alttext="upper N slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![upper N slash 2](images/c13_98.png), and *N* points.

By Lagrange’s theorem (Theorem 3.11), all the orders of the subgroups of a group are dividers of the order of the group. If the group order is prime, then any element of the group, with the exception of the neutral element, are generators of the group.

***Definition 13.5:** The* ***order of a point*** *P* *on an EC, denoted*  <math alttext="o r d left-parenthesis upper P right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![o r d left-parenthesis upper P right-parenthesis](images/c13_99.png)*, is the number of points, including the point to infinity, which can be generated starting from point* *P*.

***Definition 13.6:** The* ***cofactor****, denoted* *h, of a point* *P* *is the ratio between the cardinality of the elliptic curve and the order of point* *P. Formally*,  <math alttext="h equals StartFraction number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis Over o r d left-parenthesis upper P right-parenthesis EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>#</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![h equals StartFraction number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis Over o r d left-parenthesis upper P right-parenthesis EndFraction](images/c13_100.png).

In other words, Lemma 13.1 means that taking a point *Q* on a curve and multiplying it by the cofactor necessarily yields a point in a subgroup of prime order *d*. Therefore, that Lemma is important when selecting a base point in elliptic curve cryptography. A base point is a point that can generate all points in a subgroup of the curve. The simplified procedure to select a base point is:

1.  Select a prime *p* and the parameters of the elliptic curve
2.  Compute the order of the elliptic curve, denoted  <math alttext="number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>#</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_103.png)
3.  Choose *n*, the prime order of the curve subgroup
4.  Compute the cofactor  <math alttext="h equals StartFraction number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis Over n EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>#</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mrow></math> ![h equals StartFraction number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis Over n EndFraction](images/c13_104.png)
5.  Choose a random point *Q* on the curve
6.  If  <math alttext="h dot upper Q not-equals script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></mrow></math> ![h dot upper Q not-equals script upper O](images/c13_105.png), then *Q* is a basepoint (of prime order *n* and cofactor *h*). Otherwise, go to step 5 and try another point.

In cryptography, we use a base point *B*, which can generate a subset of *n* points, such that *n* is a prime and it divides *N*, the order of the curve. The cofactor of *B* is  <math alttext="h equals StartFraction upper N Over n EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>N</mi><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mrow></math> ![h equals StartFraction upper N Over n EndFraction](images/c13_106.png).

If the cofactor is 1, then the used subgroup is the entire group. Any nonzero point on the curve is an elliptic curve generator and any point that satisfies the curve equation is an element of the subgroup. If the cofactor is greater than 1, then the used subgroup of order *n* is strictly included in the group. A point that satisfies the curve equation belongs to some subgroups and does not belong to other subgroups. Therefore, EC-based cryptographic algorithms must consider this property.

**Notes**

*   – Notice there may exist more than one generator for the same elliptic curve.
*   – If point *P* is a generator of an elliptic curve, then its cofactor is 1. EC cryptosystems with cofactor larger than 4 are more susceptible to attacks and are undesirable when the size of the subgroups is small.
*   – In EC-based algorithms, a base point is used to compute the public keys. To face attacks against EC-based cryptosystems, the ideal value of base-point cofactor is 1 (see [Section 13.4](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-1027)).

### 13.2.4 Montgomery and Edwards Curves

Montgomery and Edwards curves are two special categories of EC \[[7](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0007)\]. Since 2019, both EC categories are recommended by the NIST for digital signature \[[8](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0008), [9](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0009)\]. Those curves are claimed to have better performance and increased side-channel resistance compared to traditional curves described in previous sections.

***Definition 13.7 Edwards curve****: it is an elliptic curve over a finite field *F[p], denoted*  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_107.png)*, with prime* *p, formed by the set of solutions*  <math alttext="left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis element-of upper F Subscript p Baseline squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><msup><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis element-of upper F Subscript p Baseline squared](images/c13_108.png) *to the* equation ([13.4](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-2007)) under the condition (13.5).*

 <math alttext="upper E colon y squared plus a x squared equals 1 plus d x squared y squared m o d p" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper E colon y squared plus a x squared equals 1 plus d x squared y squared m o d p](images/c13_109.png)(13.4)  <math alttext="left-parenthesis d not-equals 0 right-parenthesis logical-and left-parenthesis d not-equals a right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8743;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis d not-equals 0 right-parenthesis logical-and left-parenthesis d not-equals a right-parenthesis](images/c13_110.png)(13.5) 

Currently, two Edwards curves exist:

1.  Edwards25519 curve, with  <math alttext="p equals 2 Superscript 255 Baseline minus 19" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>255</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>19</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 2 Superscript 255 Baseline minus 19](images/c13_111.png),  <math alttext="a equals negative 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![a equals negative 1](images/c13_112.png),  <math alttext="d equals negative 121665 slash 121666" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>121665</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>121666</mn></mrow></math> ![d equals negative 121665 slash 121666](images/c13_113.png), and a cofactor of 8.
2.  Edwards448 curve, with  <math alttext="p equals 2 Superscript 448 Baseline minus 2 Superscript 224 Baseline minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>448</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>224</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 2 Superscript 448 Baseline minus 2 Superscript 224 Baseline minus 1](images/c13_114.png),  <math alttext="a equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![a equals 1](images/c13_115.png),  <math alttext="d equals negative 39081" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>39081</mn></mrow></math> ![d equals negative 39081](images/c13_116.png) and a cofactor of 4.

***Definition 13.8 Montgomery curve****: it is an elliptic curve over a finite field* *F[p], denoted*  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_117.png)*, with prime* *p, formed by the set of solutions*  <math alttext="left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis element-of upper F Subscript p Baseline squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><msup><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis element-of upper F Subscript p Baseline squared](images/c13_118.png) *to the equation (13.6) under the condition (13.7)*.

 <math alttext="upper E colon upper B y squared equals x cubed plus upper A x squared plus x m o d p" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>B</mi><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>A</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper E colon upper B y squared equals x cubed plus upper A x squared plus x m o d p](images/c13_119.png)(13.6)  <math alttext="upper B left-parenthesis upper A squared minus 4 right-parenthesis not-equals 0" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8800;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper B left-parenthesis upper A squared minus 4 right-parenthesis not-equals 0](images/c13_120.png)(13.7) 

Currently, two Montgomery curves exist:

1.  Curve25519 curve, with  <math alttext="p equals 2 Superscript 255 Baseline minus 19" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>255</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>19</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 2 Superscript 255 Baseline minus 19](images/c13_121.png),  <math alttext="upper A equals 486662" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>486662</mn></mrow></math> ![upper A equals 486662](images/c13_122.png),  <math alttext="upper B equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper B equals 1](images/c13_123.png), and a cofactor of 8.
2.  Curve448 curve, with  <math alttext="p equals 2 Superscript 448 Baseline minus 2 Superscript 224 Baseline minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>448</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>224</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 2 Superscript 448 Baseline minus 2 Superscript 224 Baseline minus 1](images/c13_124.png),  <math alttext="upper A equals 156326" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>156326</mn></mrow></math> ![upper A equals 156326](images/c13_125.png),  <math alttext="upper B equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper B equals 1](images/c13_126.png), and a cofactor of 8.

The operations applicable to traditional EC are redefined to match Montgomery and Edwards EC models.

*   *Identity element and negative of a point*

Point to infinity  <math alttext="script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></math> ![script upper O](images/c13_161.png) is the identity element; it does not appear on the Montgomery curve (the same as in the traditional ECs).

If  <math alttext="upper P equals left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P equals left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis](images/c13_162.png) is a point on a Montgomery curve, its negative is denoted  <math alttext="en-dash upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8211;</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![en-dash upper P](images/c13_163.png), and defined as  <math alttext="negative upper P equals minus left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis x comma negative y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![negative upper P equals minus left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis x comma negative y right-parenthesis](images/c13_164.png).

## 13.3 Elliptic Curve Cryptography over Extension Fields

Prime power fields, of the form  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c13_165.png), also are called extension fields (or extended binary fields); their basics and useful properties of are presented in Section 3.2.4.

It is worth noticing that some cryptographic standards based on finite fields recommended the utilization of extension fields,  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c13_166.png), to make computations faster. In 2013, NIST recommended fifteen elliptic curves to support signature with ECDSA among which ten are based on  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c13_167.png) fields \[[10](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0010)\].

### 13.3.1 Definition of EC over Extension Fields

ECDSA, which is the most likely standard to dominate in future cryptosystems, recommends the use of elliptic curves over extension fields \[[10](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0010)–[12](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0012)\]. The latter provide a foundation to more efficient cryptosystems than those provided by EC over prime fields. However, extension fields come with more complexity in calculations.

***Definition 13.9:** An elliptic curve over an extension field*  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c13_168.png)*, denoted*  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m Subscript Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m Subscript Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_169.png)*, is the set of points*  <math alttext="left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis](images/c13_170.png)*, which are solutions to* equation ([13.8](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-2008)*) under condition (*[13.9](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-2009)*)*:

 <math alttext="upper E colon y squared plus x y equals x cubed plus a x squared plus b" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![upper E colon y squared plus x y equals x cubed plus a x squared plus b](images/c13_171.png)(13.8)  <math alttext="left-parenthesis a comma b element-of upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m Subscript Baseline right-parenthesis logical-and left-parenthesis b not-equals 0 logical-and i s bar p r i m e left-parenthesis m right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8743;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8743;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>i</mi><mi>s</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis a comma b element-of upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m Subscript Baseline right-parenthesis logical-and left-parenthesis b not-equals 0 logical-and i s bar p r i m e left-parenthesis m right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c13_172.png)(13.9) 

**Note**. The elliptic curves defined by the equality ([13.8](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-2008)) and condition ([13.9](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-2009)) are also referred to as binary Weierstrass curves or simply by binary curves.

Examples of elliptic curves under equation ([13.8](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-2008)) over ℝ (real numbers) are shown in [Figure 13.5](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0005). Notice that, unlike curves over prime fields, the curves over  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c13_173.png) fields are not symmetrical regarding the x-axis.

![Figure 13.5 Examples of EC over real numbers with associated equations.](images/c13f005.png)

    The field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 squared](images/c13_187.png) has four elements, i.e.  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 squared Baseline equals StartSet left-parenthesis 00 right-parenthesis comma left-parenthesis 01 right-parenthesis comma left-parenthesis 10 right-parenthesis comma left-parenthesis 11 right-parenthesis EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>00</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>01</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 squared Baseline equals StartSet left-parenthesis 00 right-parenthesis comma left-parenthesis 01 right-parenthesis comma left-parenthesis 10 right-parenthesis comma left-parenthesis 11 right-parenthesis EndSet](images/c13_188.png)
    
*   Find EC points over  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 squared](images/c13_189.png). Given that the number of points  <math alttext="left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis](images/c13_190.png) to test is low,  <math alttext="StartAbsoluteValue upper F Subscript 2 squared Baseline StartAbsoluteValue asterisk EndAbsoluteValue upper F Subscript 2 squared Baseline EndAbsoluteValue equals 4 asterisk 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>\*</mo><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![StartAbsoluteValue upper F Subscript 2 squared Baseline StartAbsoluteValue asterisk EndAbsoluteValue upper F Subscript 2 squared Baseline EndAbsoluteValue equals 4 asterisk 4](images/c13_191.png), one naïve method is to check every couple regarding the EC equation. Let us list every point and check if equation ([13.8](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-2008)) is satisfied. In [Table 13.2](#c13.xhtml#c13-tbl-0002), rows in gray denote points on the curve.

![Table 13.2 Example of EC point computation.](images/c13_192.png)

[**Table 13.2**](#c13.xhtml#rc13-tbl-0002) Example of EC point computation.

#### 13.3.1.1 Operations on Points of Curve  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m Subscript Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m Subscript Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_258.png)

Rules for point operations are defined for elliptic curves over  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c13_259.png). The formulas differ from the ones defined for curves over prime fields (*F[p]*), because the EC equations differ (see equations 13.2, 13.4, 13.6, [13.8](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-2008)).

**Note**. Operations on EC points, over an extension field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c13_260.png), are done modulo the irreducible polynomial selected for the field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c13_261.png).

*   *Point addition*

![upper P equals left-parenthesis x Subscript upper P Baseline comma y Subscript upper P Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_262.png) and  <math alttext="upper Q equals left-parenthesis x Subscript upper Q Baseline comma y Subscript upper Q Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" x Subscript upper Q](images/c13_264.png)), on the elliptic curve  <math alttext="upper E colon y squared plus x y equals x cubed plus a x squared plus b period" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> ![upper E colon y squared plus x y equals x cubed plus a x squared plus b period](images/c13_265.png) The addition results in a point  <math alttext="upper R equals upper P plus upper Q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R equals upper P plus upper Q](images/c13_266.png), such that ![upper R equals left-parenthesis x Subscript upper R Baseline comma y Subscript upper R Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_267.png) where:
