*   *Point doubling*

Let  <math alttext="upper P equals left-parenthesis x Subscript upper P Baseline comma y Subscript upper P Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>P</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>P</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P equals left-parenthesis x Subscript upper P Baseline comma y Subscript upper P Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_271.png) be a point on the elliptic curve  <math alttext="upper E colon y squared plus x y equals x cubed plus a x squared plus b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![upper E colon y squared plus x y equals x cubed plus a x squared plus b](images/c13_272.png). Point doubling results in a point  <math alttext="upper R equals upper P plus upper P equals 2 dot upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R equals upper P plus upper P equals 2 dot upper P](images/c13_273.png), such that  <math alttext="upper R equals left-parenthesis x Subscript upper R Baseline comma y Subscript upper R Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>R</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper R equals left-parenthesis x Subscript upper R Baseline comma y Subscript upper R Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_274.png) where:

 <math alttext="x Subscript upper R Baseline equals lamda squared plus lamda plus a" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> ![x Subscript upper R Baseline equals lamda squared plus lamda plus a](images/c13_275.png) <math alttext="y Subscript upper R Baseline equals x Subscript upper P Baseline squared plus left-parenthesis plus 1 right-parenthesis x Subscript upper R" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>P</mi></msub><msup><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mo>(</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>R</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![y Subscript upper R Baseline equals x Subscript upper P Baseline squared plus left-parenthesis plus 1 right-parenthesis x Subscript upper R](images/c13_276.png)  <math alttext="lamda equals x Subscript upper P Baseline plus StartFraction y Subscript upper P Baseline Over x Subscript upper P Baseline EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>P</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>P</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>P</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![lamda equals x Subscript upper P Baseline plus StartFraction y Subscript upper P Baseline Over x Subscript upper P Baseline EndFraction](images/c13_277.png)

*   *Addition of vertical points (addition of negative point)*

Under the equation  <math alttext="y squared plus x y equals x cubed plus a x squared plus b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![y squared plus x y equals x cubed plus a x squared plus b](images/c13_278.png), the negative of point *P* is denoted  <math alttext="en-dash upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8211;</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![en-dash upper P](images/c13_279.png), and defined as  <math alttext="negative upper P equals minus left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis x comma x plus y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![negative upper P equals minus left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis x comma x plus y right-parenthesis](images/c13_280.png). As for EC over prime fields, addition of point *P* and its negative results in point to infinity:  <math alttext="upper P plus left-parenthesis negative upper P right-parenthesis equals script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P plus left-parenthesis negative upper P right-parenthesis equals script upper O](images/c13_281.png).

*   *Point multiplication by a scalar*

Let *P* be a point over the EC and *k* a scalar, multiplying *P* by *k* results in a point  <math alttext="upper R equals k dot upper P equals upper P plus upper P plus dot dot dot plus upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R equals k dot upper P equals upper P plus upper P plus dot dot dot plus upper P](images/c13_282.png) (*k* times). As for EC over prime fields, scalar multiplication of points of  <math alttext="normal upper E left-parenthesis normal upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript normal m Subscript Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![normal upper E left-parenthesis normal upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript normal m Subscript Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_283.png) is achieved by repeated addition. Multiplying an EC point by 0 returns the point to infinity  <math alttext="script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></math> ![script upper O](images/c13_284.png) and multiplying point to infinity by a scalar returns the point to infinity. That is:

 <math alttext="for-all upper P element-of normal upper E left-parenthesis normal upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript normal m Subscript Baseline right-parenthesis comma 0 dot upper P equals script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></mrow></math> ![for-all upper P element-of normal upper E left-parenthesis normal upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript normal m Subscript Baseline right-parenthesis comma 0 dot upper P equals script upper O](images/c13_285.png), and  <math alttext="k dot script upper O equals script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></mrow></math> ![k dot script upper O equals script upper O](images/c13_286.png) for every integer *k*.

**Example 13.4**

Consider again the curve  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript 2 squared Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript 2 squared Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_287.png) with equation  <math alttext="y squared plus x y equals x cubed plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![y squared plus x y equals x cubed plus 1](images/c13_288.png) (parameter *a* of the equation is equal to 0) over the field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 squared](images/c13_289.png) with reduction polynomial  <math alttext="f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x squared plus x plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x squared plus x plus 1](images/c13_290.png) and generator  <math alttext="g equals x" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> ![g equals x](images/c13_291.png). The order of  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript 2 squared Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript 2 squared Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_294.png) is 8 and the four points  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 2 comma 0 right-parenthesis comma left-parenthesis 2 comma 2 right-parenthesis comma left-parenthesis 3 comma 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 2 comma 0 right-parenthesis comma left-parenthesis 2 comma 2 right-parenthesis comma left-parenthesis 3 comma 0 right-parenthesis](images/c13_295.png), and  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 3 comma 3 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 3 comma 3 right-parenthesis](images/c13_296.png) are generators of  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript 2 squared Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript 2 squared Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_297.png).

#### 13.3.1.2 Fast Scalar Multiplication

Multiplication of a point *P* by a scalar *k* is defined by repeated point addition. There is no direct multiplication by a scalar as for real or integer numbers. In the previous subsections, a naïve method to calculate  <math alttext="k dot upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![k dot upper P](images/c13_298.png) is used: apply one point doubling operation followed by  <math alttext="k minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![k minus 1](images/c13_299.png) point additions. Such a method is time consuming, especially when *k* is a large value, which is used in practice to secure communications (*k* is of order  <math alttext="2 Superscript 256" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>256</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 256](images/c13_300.png) in current EC implementations). To optimize the computation time of scalar multiplication, fast methods have been proposed taking advantage of the associativity property of cyclic groups. For example:

 <math alttext="23 dot upper P equals upper P plus 22 dot upper P equals upper P plus 2 left-parenthesis 11 right-parenthesis dot upper P equals upper P plus 2 left-parenthesis 1 plus 2 left-parenthesis 1 plus 2 left-parenthesis 2 dot upper P right-parenthesis right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>23</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>22</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![23 dot upper P equals upper P plus 22 dot upper P equals upper P plus 2 left-parenthesis 11 right-parenthesis dot upper P equals upper P plus 2 left-parenthesis 1 plus 2 left-parenthesis 1 plus 2 left-parenthesis 2 dot upper P right-parenthesis right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c13_301.png)

To calculate  <math alttext="23 dot upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>23</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![23 dot upper P](images/c13_302.png), four point doublings and three point additions are required instead of one point doubling followed by 22 point additions under the naïve method. Among the proposed algorithms for fast scalar multiplication in EC cryptosystems, two algorithms are presented below: *left-to-right binary method for point multiplication* and *recursive method for point multiplication*. Many other variations of fast scalar multiplication of EC points do exist \[[13](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0013)\]. The first point multiplication method is based on the binary representation of the scalar *k*; its pseudocode is as follows:

### 13.3.2 Set and Number of Points of an EC

#### 13.3.2.1 Finding the Set of Points on an EC

Given the EC equation parameters (i.e. *a* and *b*) and the cardinality of the field (i.e. *p* or  <math alttext="2 Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript m](images/c13_318.png)), finding the set of all points on an elliptic curve in case of low values of *p* or *m* is not a hard problem. One naïve approach is to test every couple of integers  <math alttext="left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis](images/c13_319.png) regarding the EC equation. That is,  <math alttext="p squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![p squared](images/c13_320.png) or  <math alttext="2 Superscript 2 m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 2 m](images/c13_321.png)  <math alttext="left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis](images/c13_322.png)\-couples have to be tested and if the equations verified for a given couple, the latter is a point on the EC. However, when the value of *p* or *m* is large (the magnitude of *p* and  <math alttext="2 Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript m](images/c13_323.png) is  <math alttext="2 Superscript 256" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>256</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 256](images/c13_324.png) for standard-based cryptosystems), calculation of all points becomes complex. Luckily, EC-based public key protocols do not require to know all the EC points; rather they need to select one random point, called *base point*, on the elliptic curve. EC-based cryptosystems include functions that return a random point on an EC given the EC equation parameters and field cardinality. The examples of sets of EC points given in this chapter are used only for educational purpose.

#### 13.3.2.2 Finding the Exact Number of Points on an EC

Given the EC equation parameters (i.e. *a* and *b*) and the field cardinality *q* (*q* is either a prime *p* or a power prime  <math alttext="2 Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript m](images/c13_325.png)), finding the exact number of points on an elliptic curve is a hard problem (in term of complexity) in the general case. Many methods to approximate the exact number of points on an EC have been proposed in the literature. Hasse’s theorem is the most commonly used way to know the lower and upper bounds of the number of EC points, given the cardinality of the finite field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript q](images/c13_326.png). It states the following:

 <math alttext="StartAbsoluteValue number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript q Baseline right-parenthesis minus q minus 1 EndAbsoluteValue less-than-or-equal-to 2 StartRoot q EndRoot" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mo>#</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mi>q</mi></msqrt></mrow></math> ![StartAbsoluteValue number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript q Baseline right-parenthesis minus q minus 1 EndAbsoluteValue less-than-or-equal-to 2 StartRoot q EndRoot](images/c13_328.png)(13.10) 

Hasse’s theorem tells us that  <math alttext="number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript q Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>#</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript q Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_329.png) is in the interval  <math alttext="left-parenthesis q plus 1 minus 2 StartRoot q EndRoot comma q plus 1 plus 2 StartRoot q EndRoot right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mi>q</mi></msqrt><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mi>q</mi></msqrt></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis q plus 1 minus 2 StartRoot q EndRoot comma q plus 1 plus 2 StartRoot q EndRoot right-parenthesis](images/c13_330.png).  <math alttext="number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript q Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>#</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript q Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_331.png) is roughly equal to the size of  <math alttext="upper F Subscript q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript q](images/c13_332.png). In case of prime fields only, Theorem [13.2](#c13.xhtml#c13-feafxd-0002) gives the exact number of points of an elliptic curve over a prime field.

 <math alttext="number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis equals p plus 1 plus sigma-summation Underscript x element-of upper F Subscript p Baseline Endscripts left-parenthesis StartFraction x cubed plus a x plus b Over p EndFraction right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>#</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><msub><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mi>p</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mstyle></mrow></math> ![number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis equals p plus 1 plus sigma-summation Underscript x element-of upper F Subscript p Baseline Endscripts left-parenthesis StartFraction x cubed plus a x plus b Over p EndFraction right-parenthesis](images/c13_333.png)(13.11) 

where  <math alttext="left-parenthesis StartFraction x cubed plus a x plus b Over p EndFraction right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mi>p</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis StartFraction x cubed plus a x plus b Over p EndFraction right-parenthesis](images/c13_334.png) denotes Legendre symbol (see Section 3.1.7.1), which is equal to 1 if there exists  <math alttext="y element-of upper F Subscript p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![y element-of upper F Subscript p](images/c13_335.png) such that  <math alttext="y squared equals x cubed plus a x plus b m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![y squared equals x cubed plus a x plus b m o d p](images/c13_336.png) and  <math alttext="negative 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![negative 1](images/c13_337.png), otherwise, with one exception, if  <math alttext="x cubed plus a x plus b identical-to 0 m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![x cubed plus a x plus b identical-to 0 m o d p](images/c13_338.png), Legendre symbol is equal to 0.

The idea of Theorem [13.2](#c13.xhtml#c13-feafxd-0002) is to consider  <math alttext="u equals left-parenthesis x cubed plus a x plus b right-parenthesis m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![u equals left-parenthesis x cubed plus a x plus b right-parenthesis m o d p](images/c13_339.png) for each  <math alttext="x element-of upper F Subscript p Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![x element-of upper F Subscript p Baseline](images/c13_340.png) and check if *u* is a square residue (i.e. there exists  <math alttext="v element-of upper F Subscript p Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>v</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![v element-of upper F Subscript p Baseline](images/c13_341.png) such that  <math alttext="v squared identical-to u m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>v</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mi>u</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![v squared identical-to u m o d p](images/c13_342.png)). Therefore, Theorem [13.2](#c13.xhtml#c13-feafxd-0002) comes with a high cost to compute the number of points.

## 13.4 Security of EC Cryptosystems

Breaking an EC cryptosystem is equivalent to solving the computational problem known as elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem, which is stated as follows:

In regular algebra, when a product  <math alttext="upper A asterisk upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ![upper A asterisk upper B](images/c13_346.png) is given and *A* is known, inferring *B* is easy. In EC, point  <math alttext="upper Q equals k dot upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![upper Q equals k dot upper P](images/c13_347.png) is equal to the addition of point  <math alttext="left-parenthesis k minus 1 right-parenthesis dot upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis k minus 1 right-parenthesis dot upper P](images/c13_348.png) to point *P*. Therefore, to use a point  <math alttext="upper Q equals k dot upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![upper Q equals k dot upper P](images/c13_349.png), point  <math alttext="left-parenthesis k minus 1 right-parenthesis dot upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis k minus 1 right-parenthesis dot upper P](images/c13_350.png) must be calculated, and so on until  <math alttext="2 dot upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![2 dot upper P](images/c13_351.png). Multiplication of an EC point by a scalar *k* is performed through repeated addition:

 <math alttext="k dot upper P equals upper Q Subscript k Baseline vertical-bar upper Q Subscript j Baseline equals upper Q Subscript j minus 1 Baseline plus upper P comma left-parenthesis 2 less-than j less-than-or-equal-to k right-parenthesis comma upper Q 1 equals upper P" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8195;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![k dot upper P equals upper Q Subscript k Baseline vertical-bar upper Q Subscript j Baseline equals upper Q Subscript j minus 1 Baseline plus upper P comma left-parenthesis 2 less-than j less-than-or-equal-to k right-parenthesis comma upper Q 1 equals upper P](images/c13_352.png)

In addition, since ECs are cyclic groups, if the order of *P* is *n*, the following holds:

 <math alttext="left-parenthesis d asterisk n plus k right-parenthesis dot upper P equals k dot upper P equals upper Q comma for-all d element-of double-struck upper N comma k element-of double-struck upper N comma k less-than n" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>&#8469;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>&#8469;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis d asterisk n plus k right-parenthesis dot upper P equals k dot upper P equals upper Q comma for-all d element-of double-struck upper N comma k element-of double-struck upper N comma k less-than n](images/c13_353.png)

Therefore, the attacker should not only find and exploit a single value of *k*, but a set of values modulo *n*. To deduce which value of *k* matches the product  <math alttext="k dot upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![k dot upper P](images/c13_354.png) and recover the private key *k*, one needs to calculate all multiples modulo *n* of the given point *P*.

To intuitively understand the complexity of inferring *k* from  <math alttext="k dot upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![k dot upper P](images/c13_355.png), let us make the analogy with points on a circle. From a point *P* on the circle move left or right, with a given angle, to a new point  <math alttext="upper P prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![upper P prime](images/c13_356.png), then repeat the moving on the circle until a point *Q* is reached, then, from point *Q*, make a large number *d* of rotations (each rotation is a series of shifting on the circle) over the circle and then stop. Determining the exact number of shifting, given the start point *P* and finish point *Q*, is computationally intractable if the variation of shifting angle and the number of rotations are large.

Consequently, “inferring *k* given  <math alttext="k dot upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![k dot upper P](images/c13_357.png)” problem becomes computationally infeasible to break operational EC cryptosystems where the bit-length of the order of the chosen base point *P* and that of the field cardinality are of 256 or more.

At the time of writing this chapter, the last known breaking of EC cryptosystem was made by mathematicians in 2004. A message encrypted with an elliptic curve key algorithm using a 109-bit long key was broken. The effort required 2600 computers and took 17 months.

[Table 13.3](#c13.xhtml#c13-tbl-0003), from \[[14](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0014)\], illustrates the computing power needed to solve the EC discrete logarithm problem, with the most efficient method known at the time of writing this chapter, depending on the size of the underlying finite field.

[**Table 13.3**](#c13.xhtml#rc13-tbl-0003) Computing power required to solve the EC discrete logarithm problem.

| *Bit-length of the order of base point*  || *Computing power needed (in MIPS years)* |
| --- | --- |
| 162224256384521 || 1.1 × 10^(12)2.3 × 10^(21)1.5 × 10^(26)2.9 × 10^(45)8.4 × 10^(65) |
| --- | --- |
| *(1 MIPS year = the amount of work performed, in one year, by a computer operating at the rate of one million instructions per second)*. |

**Note**. To not jeopardize the security of EC cryptosystems (i.e. to make the key discovery attacks computationally infeasible), the cofactor of the base point *G*, which is used as parameter in ECC-based algorithms, should be as small as possible, i.e. close to 1. Recall that the cofactor is  <math alttext="h equals StartFraction number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis Over o r d left-parenthesis upper G right-parenthesis EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>#</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![h equals StartFraction number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis Over o r d left-parenthesis upper G right-parenthesis EndFraction](images/c13_358.png), where  <math alttext="number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>#</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_359.png) is that cardinality of the EC and  <math alttext="o r d left-parenthesis upper G right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![o r d left-parenthesis upper G right-parenthesis](images/c13_360.png) is the number of points generated starting from *P*. If  <math alttext="h equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![h equals 1](images/c13_361.png), then the selected base point is a generator of the EC, and consequently all the points of the curve may be used to generate public keys, thus making the space of search too wide, which prevents attacks.

## 13.5 Elliptic Curve-based Algorithms

The elliptic curve-based algorithms used in cryptosystems are categorized as key-agreement, message signature, and message encryption algorithms. First, the common features are presented, then how ECs is used for each category of algorithms is addressed.

### 13.5.1 Security Strength Levels of EC Algorithms

The level of security is measured in bits. It represents the capacity of the EC algorithms to resist to attacks. Each extra bit of security doubles the amount of computation needed by an attacker to compromise security. ECC standards specify four security strength levels and the requirements regarding the parameter  <math alttext="n left-parenthesis the order of the base point upper G" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>the&#160;order&#160;of&#160;the&#160;base&#160;point&#160;</mtext><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> ![n left-parenthesis the order of the base point upper G](images/c13_362.png)):

*   Security strength 112:  <math alttext="2 Superscript 223 Baseline less-than n less-than 2 Superscript 256 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>223</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>256</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 223 Baseline less-than n less-than 2 Superscript 256 Baseline](images/c13_363.png)
*   Security strength 128:  <math alttext="2 Superscript 255 Baseline less-than n less-than 2 Superscript 384 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>255</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>384</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 255 Baseline less-than n less-than 2 Superscript 384 Baseline](images/c13_364.png)
*   Security strength 192:  <math alttext="2 Superscript 383 Baseline less-than n less-than 2 Superscript 512 Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>383</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>512</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 383 Baseline less-than n less-than 2 Superscript 512 Baseline](images/c13_365.png)
*   Security strength 256:  <math alttext="2 Superscript 511 Baseline less-than n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>511</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 511 Baseline less-than n](images/c13_366.png)

### 13.5.2 Domain Parameters

All EC-based algorithms require the selection of domain parameters. Domain parameters are public information exchanged via an insecure network. They are:

*   *q*: the order (or cardinality) of the underlying field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript q](images/c13_367.png). *q* is either a prime *p* or a prime power  <math alttext="2 Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript m](images/c13_368.png) (with prime *m*).
*    <math alttext="upper F upper R" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> ![upper F upper R](images/c13_369.png): field representation, if  <math alttext="q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![q](images/c13_370.png)\= <math alttext="2 Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript m](images/c13_371.png) (i.e. the underlying field is an extension field).  <math alttext="upper F upper R" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> ![upper F upper R](images/c13_372.png) includes the degree and coefficients of the reduction polynomial  <math alttext="f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c13_373.png) associated with the field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m](images/c13_374.png).
*   *a* and *b*: coefficients of elliptic curve equation. Both are elements of  <math alttext="upper F Subscript q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript q](images/c13_375.png). There are four EC equations:
    
    *   Basic curves over prime fields:  <math alttext="y squared equals x cubed plus a x plus b m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![y squared equals x cubed plus a x plus b m o d p](images/c13_376.png).
    *   Edwards curves:  <math alttext="y squared plus a x squared equals 1 plus d x squared y squared m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![y squared plus a x squared equals 1 plus d x squared y squared m o d p](images/c13_377.png).
    *   Montgomery curves:  <math alttext="upper B y squared equals x cubed plus upper A x squared plus x m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>A</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper B y squared equals x cubed plus upper A x squared plus x m o d p](images/c13_378.png).
    *   Basic curves over extension fields:  <math alttext="y squared plus x y equals x cubed plus a x squared plus b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![y squared plus x y equals x cubed plus a x squared plus b](images/c13_379.png).
*    <math alttext="left-parenthesis x Subscript upper G Baseline comma y Subscript upper G Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>G</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>G</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis x Subscript upper G Baseline comma y Subscript upper G Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_380.png): coordinates of the base point *G*.
*   *n*: order of base point *G* (the order of *G* is the number of points generated by *G*). It is the smallest prime number *n* such that:  <math alttext="n period upper G equals script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></mrow></math> ![n period upper G equals script upper O](images/c13_381.png)).
*   *h*: the cofactor associated with the base point:  <math alttext="h equals StartFraction StartAbsoluteValue upper E left-parenthesis upper F p right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue Over n EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mrow></math> ![h equals StartFraction StartAbsoluteValue upper E left-parenthesis upper F p right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue Over n EndFraction](images/c13_382.png)

ANSI and IETF standards provide approved guidelines to select all domain parameters and to verify their validity regarding the required level of security strength \[[2](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0002)–[4](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0004), [7](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0007), [14](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0014)\]. It is worth noticing that the parameters selection is of paramount importance to comply with the needed level of security strength. It is highly recommended for EC-based algorithms implementers to use the standard domain parameters.

### 13.5.3 EC Diffie–Hellman (ECDH) Key-Agreement Protocol

One of the most important variation of the original Diffie-Hellman scheme \[[15](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0015)\], which is presented in Section 12.3.2, is its combination with elliptic curves over finite fields to provide powerful protocol, the ECDH, to share public keys. ECDH (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman) protocol is recommended as a standard for key-agreement protocol by NIST. The readers interested in detail regarding the protocol may refer to the ANSI standard X9-63 \[[16](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0016)\]. In sequel, only the principle of the ECDH is described.

ECDH is a key-agreement protocol that enables two parties to generate a shared secret, while using an elliptic curve. The execution of ECDH protocol by two parties, Alice and Bob, is as illustrated by [Figure 13.6](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0006).

![Figure 13.6 Elliptic-Curve Diffie-Hellman key-agreement.](images/c13f006.png)

[**Figure 13.6**](#c13.xhtml#rc13-fig-0006) Elliptic-Curve Diffie-Hellman key-agreement.

*Proof of ECDH correctness*:

*   Bob computes:  <math alttext="upper S Subscript upper B Baseline equals upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline dot upper A equals left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline asterisk upper P Subscript upper A Baseline right-parenthesis m o d n right-parenthesis dot upper G" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript upper B Baseline equals upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline dot upper A equals left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline asterisk upper P Subscript upper A Baseline right-parenthesis m o d n right-parenthesis dot upper G](images/c13_383.png).
*   Alice computes:  <math alttext="upper S Subscript upper A Baseline equals upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline dot upper B equals left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline asterisk upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline right-parenthesis m o d n right-parenthesis dot upper G" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript upper A Baseline equals upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline dot upper B equals left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline asterisk upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline right-parenthesis m o d n right-parenthesis dot upper G](images/c13_384.png).
*   Since multiplication is commutative over integers,  <math alttext="upper S Subscript upper B Baseline equals upper S Subscript upper A" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript upper B Baseline equals upper S Subscript upper A](images/c13_385.png). Thus, both parties compute the same shared secret. Notice that the modulus in the equations above is *n* (the order of base point *G*) and not *q*, the modulus of the field  <math alttext="upper F Subscript q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript q](images/c13_386.png).□

The shared information may be used as a symmetric key to encrypt messages exchanged between Alice and Bob.

**Note**. The shared secret is the *x*\-coordinate of point *S*. The *y*\-coordinate ( <math alttext="y Subscript upper S" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>S</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![y Subscript upper S](images/c13_387.png)) is not a second secret, because if  <math alttext="x Subscript upper S" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>S</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![x Subscript upper S](images/c13_388.png) is known,  <math alttext="y Subscript upper S" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>S</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![y Subscript upper S](images/c13_389.png) is calculated using the EC equation whose parameters (*a* and *b*) are public.

**Example 13.5**

Let us consider the elliptic curve  <math alttext="upper E colon y squared equals left-parenthesis x cubed plus 2 x plus 2 right-parenthesis m o d Baseline 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![upper E colon y squared equals left-parenthesis x cubed plus 2 x plus 2 right-parenthesis m o d Baseline 17](images/c13_390.png).

*   – Check that  <math alttext="upper F 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F 17](images/c13_391.png) is a prime field: 
    *   17 is a prime number.
    *    <math alttext="upper F 17 equals StartSet 0 comma 1 comma 2 comma 3 comma 4 comma 5 comma 6 comma 7 comma 8 comma 9 comma 10 comma 11 comma 12 comma 13 comma 14 comma 15 comma 16 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>12</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>15</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>16</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper F 17 equals StartSet 0 comma 1 comma 2 comma 3 comma 4 comma 5 comma 6 comma 7 comma 8 comma 9 comma 10 comma 11 comma 12 comma 13 comma 14 comma 15 comma 16 EndSet](images/c13_392.png)
    *   0 is the neutral element for addition and each element in  <math alttext="upper F 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F 17](images/c13_393.png) has an additive inverse in  <math alttext="upper F 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F 17](images/c13_394.png):  <math alttext="0 plus 0 identical-to 0 m o d Baseline 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![0 plus 0 identical-to 0 m o d Baseline 17](images/c13_395.png),  <math alttext="1 plus 16 identical-to 0 m o d Baseline 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![1 plus 16 identical-to 0 m o d Baseline 17](images/c13_396.png)
    *    <math alttext="2 plus 15 identical-to 0 m o d Baseline 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>15</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![2 plus 15 identical-to 0 m o d Baseline 17](images/c13_397.png), …,  <math alttext="16 plus 1 identical-to 0 m o d Baseline 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![16 plus 1 identical-to 0 m o d Baseline 17](images/c13_398.png)
    *   1 is the neutral element for multiplication and each nonzero element in  <math alttext="upper F 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F 17](images/c13_399.png) has a multiplicative inverse in  <math alttext="upper F 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F 17](images/c13_400.png):
    *    <math alttext="1 Superscript negative 1 Baseline equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![1 Superscript negative 1 Baseline equals 1](images/c13_401.png);  <math alttext="2 Superscript negative 1 Baseline equals 9" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript negative 1 Baseline equals 9](images/c13_402.png), because  <math alttext="2 asterisk 9 identical-to 1 m o d Baseline 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>9</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![2 asterisk 9 identical-to 1 m o d Baseline 17](images/c13_403.png), …
    *    <math alttext="16 Superscript negative 1 Baseline equals 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow></math> ![16 Superscript negative 1 Baseline equals 16](images/c13_404.png), because  <math alttext="16 asterisk 16 equals 255 identical-to 1 m o d Baseline 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>255</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![16 asterisk 16 equals 255 identical-to 1 m o d Baseline 17](images/c13_405.png)
    *    <math alttext="upper F 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F 17](images/c13_406.png) is a cyclic group for addition and for multiplication operations.
    *    <math alttext="upper F 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F 17](images/c13_407.png) is a prime field.

*   – Select a base point *G*
    
    It is recommended to select the point with the highest order. In this example, all points have the same order equal to 19. The check has been done with an ad hoc program. Below are the scalar multiplications for point  <math alttext="upper G equals left-parenthesis 7 comma 6 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>6</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper G equals left-parenthesis 7 comma 6 right-parenthesis](images/c13_412.png). #### 13.5.3.1 Small-Subgroup Attack Against ECDH

Some attacks have been reported in literature and focused mainly on domain parameter selection and not directly on the design of ECDH. In particular, the small subgroup attack is of interest, because it resulted in ECDH extensions including the ECMQV agreement protocol described in next subsection. It works as follows: assume that an active attacker, say Eve, can intercept and modify messages exchanged between Alice and Bob while running the ECDH protocol and assume that  <math alttext="n comma the order of the subgroup comma is n equals c asterisk m comma where c" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;the&#160;order&#160;of&#160;the&#160;subgroup</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;is&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;where&#160;</mtext><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> ![n comma the order of the subgroup comma is n equals c asterisk m comma where c](images/c13_430.png) is a small value:

1.  Eve intercepts  <math alttext="upper A equals upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline dot upper G" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> ![upper A equals upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline dot upper G](images/c13_431.png), the public key of Alice, and replaces it by  <math alttext="m dot upper A" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> ![m dot upper A](images/c13_432.png), then sends it to Bob.
2.  Eve intercepts  <math alttext="upper B equals upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline dot upper G" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> ![upper B equals upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline dot upper G](images/c13_433.png), the public key of Bob, and replaces it by  <math alttext="m dot upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ![m dot upper B](images/c13_434.png), then sends it to Alice.
3.  Alice computes  <math alttext="upper S Subscript upper A Baseline equals upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline dot m upper B equals left-parenthesis upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline asterisk m asterisk upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline right-parenthesis dot upper G" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript upper A Baseline equals upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline dot m upper B equals left-parenthesis upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline asterisk m asterisk upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline right-parenthesis dot upper G](images/c13_435.png)
4.  Bob computes  <math alttext="upper S Subscript upper B Baseline equals upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline dot m upper A equals left-parenthesis upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline asterisk m asterisk upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline right-parenthesis dot upper G" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript upper B Baseline equals upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline dot m upper A equals left-parenthesis upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline asterisk m asterisk upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline right-parenthesis dot upper G](images/c13_436.png)

Eve impacts the agreement as follows:

*   Minor impact: the shared secret is not exactly the one the parties were expecting to generate. Indeed, Alice and Bob agree on  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline asterisk upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline asterisk m right-parenthesis dot upper G" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline asterisk upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline asterisk m right-parenthesis dot upper G](images/c13_437.png) and not on  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline asterisk upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline right-parenthesis dot upper G" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline asterisk upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline right-parenthesis dot upper G](images/c13_438.png).
*   Dramatic impact: the attack forces the shared secret to be one of a small and known subset of EC points, which makes an exhaustive search of the shared secret computationally feasible. Indeed,

Varying  <math alttext="k prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> ![k prime](images/c13_442.png) from 1 to *c* results in a set of points  <math alttext="StartSet upper G comma 2 dot upper G comma ellipsis comma left-parenthesis c minus 1 right-parenthesis dot upper G EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>G</mi></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet upper G comma 2 dot upper G comma ellipsis comma left-parenthesis c minus 1 right-parenthesis dot upper G EndSet](images/c13_443.png) points. Thus, Alice and Bob agree on a shared point in a tight set when *c* is a small value.

Example 13.6 shows how the small-subgroup attack may limit the set of shared secret values.

Eve intercepts  <math alttext="upper B equals upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline dot upper G" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> ![upper B equals upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline dot upper G](images/c13_453.png), the public key of Bob, and replaces it by  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline asterisk 9 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><mn>9</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline asterisk 9 right-parenthesis](images/c13_454.png), then sends it to Alice.

Alice computes  <math alttext="upper S Subscript upper A Baseline equals upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline dot left-parenthesis 9 dot upper B right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline asterisk 9 asterisk upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline right-parenthesis dot upper G" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>9</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>B</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>\*</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript upper A Baseline equals upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline dot left-parenthesis 9 dot upper B right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis upper P r Subscript upper A Baseline asterisk 9 asterisk upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline right-parenthesis dot upper G](images/c13_455.png)

 <math alttext="upper S Subscript upper A Baseline equals upper S Subscript upper B Baseline equals upper Z prime prime dot left-parenthesis 18 dot upper G right-parenthesis plus 18 dot upper G equals script upper O period" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>'</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>18</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>G</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>18</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></mrow><mo>.</mo></math> ![upper S Subscript upper A Baseline equals upper S Subscript upper B Baseline equals upper Z prime prime dot left-parenthesis 18 dot upper G right-parenthesis plus 18 dot upper G equals script upper O period](images/c13_463.png)

Alice and Bob have no choice; the only valid shared secret is point  <math alttext="9 dot upper G" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>9</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> ![9 dot upper G](images/c13_464.png). Therefore, Eve can easily disclose confidential messages.

### 13.5.4 EC Menezes-Qu-Vanstone (ECMQV) Key-Agreement Protocol

MQV (Menezes-Qu-Vanstone) \[[17](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0017), [18](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0018)\] key-agreement is one of the numerous extensions to the original Diffie-Hellman key-exchange protocol. MQV is designed to work in an arbitrary finite group and, in particular, elliptic curve groups. It is recommended by the NIST \[[19](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0019)\].

ECMQV provides a countermeasure to some attacks against the ECDH, including the small group attack discussed in previous subsection. MQV makes use of two key-pairs for each party: a static (i.e. long-term) key-pair and an ephemeral (i.e. a key-pair used only in the key-agreement transaction) key-pair. The protocol run by Alice and Bob to generate a shared secret is depicted in [Figure 13.7](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0007).

![Figure 13.7 Elliptic Curve MQV agreement protocol.](images/c13f007.png)
