#### 13.5.6.4 Comment on EdDSA Signature Verification Procedure

The signature verification is based on the test of the condition  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 2 Superscript c Baseline asterisk v right-parenthesis dot upper G equals 2 Superscript c Baseline dot upper R prime plus left-parenthesis 2 Superscript c Baseline asterisk t right-parenthesis dot upper Q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>c</mi></msup><mo>\*</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>c</mi></msup><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>R</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>c</mi></msup><mo>\*</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 2 Superscript c Baseline asterisk v right-parenthesis dot upper G equals 2 Superscript c Baseline dot upper R prime plus left-parenthesis 2 Superscript c Baseline asterisk t right-parenthesis dot upper Q](images/c13_626.png), where  <math alttext="2 Superscript c" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>c</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript c](images/c13_627.png) is the cofactor of the used curve. This signature verification is referred to as batch verification. Another verification condition referred to as cofactor-less verification (or also unbatched verification) may be used; the verifier tests  <math alttext="v dot upper G equals upper R prime plus t dot upper Q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>v</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>t</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> ![v dot upper G equals upper R prime plus t dot upper Q](images/c13_628.png). Any signature that passes the factor-less verification passes the batched verification. However, not all signatures that pass the batched verification pass the factor-less verification as shown by the following example.

To simply, we omit the encoding. Let  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper R prime comma upper S right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>S</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper R prime comma upper S right-parenthesis](images/c13_629.png) be a signature and let *U* be a point[^(15)](#c13.xhtml#c13-note-0015) with an order of  <math alttext="2 Superscript c" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>c</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript c](images/c13_630.png) (thus,  <math alttext="2 Superscript c Baseline dot upper U equals script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>c</mi></msup><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>U</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript c Baseline dot upper U equals script upper O](images/c13_631.png)). Replace  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper R prime comma v right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper R prime comma v right-parenthesis](images/c13_632.png) by  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper R prime plus upper U comma v right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>U</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper R prime plus upper U comma v right-parenthesis](images/c13_633.png). In the batched verification, the check is:

However, it should be noticed that the second part  <math alttext="h equals StartFraction StartAbsoluteValue upper E left-parenthesis upper F p right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue Over n EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mrow></math> ![h equals StartFraction StartAbsoluteValue upper E left-parenthesis upper F p right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue Over n EndFraction](images/c13_636.png) can only be produced by the (dishonest) signer that owns the private key. Thus, this signature modification has no impact on security, because the second part of the signature is computed by the private key owner. In the cofactor-less verification, the check is:

Therefore, the signature  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper R prime plus upper U comma v right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>U</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>v</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper R prime plus upper U comma v right-parenthesis](images/c13_638.png) does not pass the cofactor-based test.

Because multiplication by  <math alttext="2 Superscript c" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>c</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript c](images/c13_639.png) eliminates the  <math alttext="2 Superscript c" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>c</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript c](images/c13_640.png)\-torsion component, the batch verification, can be thought of as checking validity only in the prime-order subgroup (i.e. it checks only signatures generated by honest private-key owners), while the cofactor-less can be thought of as checking validity in the full group and rejects signatures modified by dishonest private-key owners. It is argued in literature that under specific implementations of the verification test, the batch verification can speed up the verification.

### 13.5.7 Elliptic Curve Encryption Algorithms

EC encryption algorithms provide public-key-based mechanisms to encrypt messages exchanged over an insecure network. EC encryption schemes are designed, so that it is hard for an attacker to recover plaintexts from their ciphertexts.

A variety of EC-based encryption algorithms have been proposed in literature. In particular, two EC-based encryption schemes are of interest to cryptosystem designers and users: Elliptic Curve Integrated Encryption Scheme (ECIES), which is specified in ANSI X9-63 standard, and the EC-based ElGamal encryption scheme.

#### 13.5.7.1 ECIES Framework

The best known encryption scheme based on elliptic curves is ECIES. ECIES provides capabilities for encryption, key exchange, and digital signature. Hence, it is called *Integrated Encryption Scheme*. Notice there exist different versions of ECIES depending on the standards such as ANSI X9-63 \[[16](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0016)\], IEEE 1363 \[[20](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0020)\], and ISO 18033-2 \[[21](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0021)\]. Differences may prevent interoperability between ECIES implementations. In this chapter, we focus on the common principles of ECIES versions.

The basic idea of the ECIES is as follows: the two parties share elliptic curve domain parameters. Then, each party generates a key pair (private and public keys). From the key pairs and the base point *G*, both parties calculate the shared secret *Z*. Then, from the shared secret, the same key derivation function is used to generate two keys one for symmetric encryption and the other for authentication. The messages are encrypted and decrypted with a symmetric cipher. Thus, ECIES is a hybrid scheme that uses a public key system to transport a session key to be used by a symmetric cipher.

##### *13.5.7.1.1 ECIES Functions*

As the “I” in the name indicates, ECIES integrates a set of functions: Key-Agreement function (KA), hash function, message authentication code function, Key-Derivation Function (KDF), and symmetric encryption/decryption functions

*   *Key-Agreement* function (KA): it is used to exchange the ECC domain parameters and public keys between parties and to compute the shared secret. The most commonly used KA, in current ECIES implementations, is the ECDH protocol (see [Section 13.5.3](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-1031)). Other protocols may also be used.
*   *Hash function*: it is used to produce hashes in KDF and in MAC function. SHA-256 and SHA-512 functions dominate in current ECIES implementations.
*   *Message Authentication Code* (MAC): a MAC accompanying each message is used for authentication. Consequently, ECIES includes mechanisms to provide data integrity as well as message authentication. HMAC-SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-512, CMAC-AES-128, CMAC-AES-192, and CMAC-AES-256 schemes dominate in current ECIES implementations. The key used in MAC scheme is denoted  <math alttext="k 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![k 2](images/c13_641.png) and it is computed by KDF function.
*   *Symmetric Encryption/decryption* scheme: it is used to encrypt and decrypt messages. The most commonly used symmetric scheme, in current ECIES implementations, is the AES standard. The symmetric encryption (and decryption) key, denoted  <math alttext="k 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![k 1](images/c13_642.png), is computed by KDF function.
*   *Key Derivation Function* (KDF): the role of this function is to compute, from the shared secret, a string[^(16)](#c13.xhtml#c13-note-0016) *K* composed of two keys: symmetric encryption key ( <math alttext="k 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![k 1](images/c13_643.png)) and MAC key ( <math alttext="k 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![k 2](images/c13_644.png)). The most commonly used KDF is the one defined in the ANSI X9-63 standard \[[16](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0016)\], which operates as follows \[[22](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0022)\]:

##### *13.5.7.1.2 ECIES Operation*

ECIES is composed of three processes: Setup, encryption, and decryption.

*   *Setup process*

Before starting ECIES to encrypt/decrypt messages, the two parties should prepare (using a protocol not a part of ECIES) the context of use. The message recipient selects the following items and sends them to the message sender:

*   The hash function  <math alttext="upper H upper A upper S upper H" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>H</mi></mrow></math> ![upper H upper A upper S upper H](images/c13_656.png) and its output bit-length ( <math alttext="h a s h l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![h a s h l e n](images/c13_657.png)), the KDF function, the MAC scheme and its bit-length of the MAC key ( <math alttext="m a c k e y l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![m a c k e y l e n](images/c13_658.png)), and the symmetric cipher to encrypt/decrypt data.
*   Domain parameters:  <math alttext="upper T equals StartSet q comma a comma b comma upper G comma upper F upper R comma n comma h EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>F</mi><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>h</mi></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper T equals StartSet q comma a comma b comma upper G comma upper F upper R comma n comma h EndSet](images/c13_659.png).([^(17)](#c13.xhtml#c13-note-0017))
*   The public key of the recipient  <math alttext="upper P u Subscript upper R Baseline equals upper P r Subscript upper R Baseline dot upper G" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P u Subscript upper R Baseline equals upper P r Subscript upper R Baseline dot upper G](images/c13_660.png). The recipient key-pair is a long-term pair (i.e. can be used to decrypt a set a messages).

In case the sender does not agree on the ECIES parameters selected by the recipient, the setup process fails.

*   *ECIES decryption*

##### *13.5.7.1.3 Security and Proof of Correctness of ECIES Algorithm*

Breaking ECIES is equivalent to solving the EC discrete logarithm problem. Thus, ECIES is considered secure when used with a base point of a large order. The proof of correctness is easy to establish. First, recall that the domain parameters and all the functions (hash, key derivation, and key encryption/decryption) and their inputs are the same for both parties. Second, the KDF returns the same couple of keys for both parties, because the secret *Z* used is the same.

The recipient computes (line 1 of pseudocode) the shared secret as  <math alttext="upper Z Subscript upper R Baseline equals upper P r Subscript upper R Baseline dot upper P u Subscript upper S Superscript e" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>e</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper Z Subscript upper R Baseline equals upper P r Subscript upper R Baseline dot upper P u Subscript upper S Superscript e](images/c13_697.png) and the message sender computes it (line 2 in pseudocode) as  <math alttext="upper Z Subscript upper S Baseline equals upper P r Subscript upper S Superscript e Baseline dot upper P u Subscript upper R Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>e</mi></msubsup><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>R</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper Z Subscript upper S Baseline equals upper P r Subscript upper S Superscript e Baseline dot upper P u Subscript upper R Baseline](images/c13_698.png).

Since  <math alttext="upper P u Subscript upper R Baseline equals upper P r Subscript upper R Baseline dot upper G" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P u Subscript upper R Baseline equals upper P r Subscript upper R Baseline dot upper G](images/c13_699.png) and  <math alttext="upper P u Subscript upper S Superscript e Baseline equals upper P r Subscript upper S Superscript e Baseline dot upper G" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>e</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>e</mi></msubsup><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> ![upper P u Subscript upper S Superscript e Baseline equals upper P r Subscript upper S Superscript e Baseline dot upper G](images/c13_700.png),  <math alttext="upper Z Subscript upper R Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>R</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper Z Subscript upper R Baseline](images/c13_701.png) =  <math alttext="upper Z Subscript upper S Baseline equals upper Z" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow></math> ![upper Z Subscript upper S Baseline equals upper Z](images/c13_702.png).

If the encrypted message *C* and the associate tag *T* have been generated by the legitimate message sender, then  <math alttext="upper T equals upper M upper A upper C left-parenthesis upper C comma k 2 right-parenthesis equals upper T prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> ![upper T equals upper M upper A upper C left-parenthesis upper C comma k 2 right-parenthesis equals upper T prime](images/c13_703.png). By definition of symmetric ciphering, we have  <math alttext="upper D upper E upper C left-parenthesis upper C comma k 1 right-parenthesis equals upper D upper E upper C left-parenthesis upper E upper N upper C left-parenthesis upper M comma k 1 right-parenthesis comma k 1 right-parenthesis equals upper M" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>N</mi><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper D upper E upper C left-parenthesis upper C comma k 1 right-parenthesis equals upper D upper E upper C left-parenthesis upper E upper N upper C left-parenthesis upper M comma k 1 right-parenthesis comma k 1 right-parenthesis equals upper M](images/c13_704.png)

#### 13.5.7.2 ElGamal Encryption Using EC Cryptography

The ElGamal Encryption using elliptic curve (EEEC) is an adaptation of the original ElGamal encryption scheme \[[23](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0023)\] to the elliptic curve context. The core of the EEEC is that the message to encrypt is hidden in an EC point coordinate. It is worth noticing that EEEC is fully-based on public key cryptography, while ECIES makes use of public key cryptography and symmetric cryptography. In other words, EEEC is a pure public key scheme, while ECIES is a hybrid one.

##### *13.5.7.2.1 Mapping Messages to EC Points*

EEEC scheme applies operations on EC points to encrypt and decrypt messages. Unlike the encryption schemes presented in previous sections and chapters (in which a message is handled as an integer), EEEC requires that the message to encrypt is in the form a point on an elliptic curve. Mapping integers to EC points adds complexity to the encryption scheme. The mapping should be done in such a way that the plaintext is uniquely recovered from the ciphertext.

One naïve method to do mapping is as follows: given a message, represented by an integer *M*, and a point *G* on the considered elliptic curve, map *M* to  <math alttext="upper M dot upper G" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M dot upper G](images/c13_705.png), which is an EC point. Such a mapping can be used if the size of the message is small. However, this type of mapping obviously makes the EC discrete logarithm problem easy to solve.

In general, there is no known polynomial deterministic algorithm for mapping integers to points on an arbitrary elliptic curve. However, there exist some fast probabilistic methods for mapping. In particular, Koblitz proposed some methods, called embedding plaintext methods, to map integers to EC points \[[5](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0005)\]. The method to choose depends on the cardinality of the field (i.e.  <math alttext="upper F Subscript p Baseline or upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mtext>&#160;or&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript p Baseline or upper F Subscript 2 Sub Superscript m Baseline](images/c13_706.png)). Below is the most known mapping method, which is called *probabilistic mapping method*.

The probabilistic mapping method can be used for elliptic curves over *F[p]*, with *p* a prime, to embed a message *M* in the x-coordinate of an EC point as follows:

1.  Select an integer *K* smaller than  <math alttext="l o g 2 left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![l o g 2 left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c13_707.png).
    
2.  Any message to encode is represented by an integer  <math alttext="0 less-than-or-equal-to upper M plus 1 less-than StartFraction p Over upper K EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mfrac><mi>p</mi><mi>K</mi></mfrac></mrow></math> ![0 less-than-or-equal-to upper M plus 1 less-than StartFraction p Over upper K EndFraction](images/c13_708.png) such that:
    
      <math alttext="0 less-than-or-equal-to upper M plus 1 less-than StartFraction p Over upper K EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mfrac><mi>p</mi><mi>K</mi></mfrac></mrow></math> ![0 less-than-or-equal-to upper M plus 1 less-than StartFraction p Over upper K EndFraction](images/c13_709.png).
    
3.  Pick an integer *x*, such that:  <math alttext="h equals StartFraction StartAbsoluteValue upper E left-parenthesis upper F p right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue Over n EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mrow></math> ![h equals StartFraction StartAbsoluteValue upper E left-parenthesis upper F p right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue Over n EndFraction](images/c13_710.png).
4.  If  <math alttext="f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x cubed plus a x plus b left-parenthesis m o d p right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x cubed plus a x plus b left-parenthesis m o d p right-parenthesis](images/c13_711.png) is a square in *F[p]*, then  <math alttext="left-parenthesis x comma StartRoot f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis EndRoot right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis x comma StartRoot f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis EndRoot right-parenthesis](images/c13_712.png) is a point on the elliptic curve  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_713.png). Otherwise, try another integer *x* until the test is positive or all the values of *x* in the range have been tested.
5.  If *M* is embedded in *x*, then, *M* is easily retrieved from *x*:  <math alttext="h equals StartFraction StartAbsoluteValue upper E left-parenthesis upper F p right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue Over n EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mrow></math> ![h equals StartFraction StartAbsoluteValue upper E left-parenthesis upper F p right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue Over n EndFraction](images/c13_714.png).

**Notes**

*   – The probabilistic mapping method may fail in finding an *x* value, which represents the x-coordinate of a point on the elliptic curve.
*   – The *x* value yielded by the mapping (if it succeeds) is  <math alttext="x equals upper K asterisk upper M plus c" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> ![x equals upper K asterisk upper M plus c](images/c13_715.png) (*c* is an integer,  <math alttext="0 less-than-or-equal-to c less-than upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>c</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> ![0 less-than-or-equal-to c less-than upper K](images/c13_716.png)). Since *x* represents the coordinate of a point on  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_717.png), *x* is less than *p*. Thus, the value of any message *M* to encrypt should be less than  <math alttext="left floor StartFraction upper P Over upper K EndFraction right floor" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8970;</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>P</mi><mi>K</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>&#8971;</mo></mrow></math> ![left floor StartFraction upper P Over upper K EndFraction right floor](images/c13_718.png).
*   – To speed the computations, *K* should be a power of 2. If  <math alttext="upper K equals 2 Superscript upper L" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![upper K equals 2 Superscript upper L](images/c13_719.png) (*L* is an integer), then *x* is yielded by *L* left-bit shifts of the integer *M*. The plaintext *L* can be decoded simply by dropping the *M* rightmost bits of *x*. That is:  <math alttext="upper M equals StartFraction x Over 2 Superscript upper L Baseline EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>x</mi><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![upper M equals StartFraction x Over 2 Superscript upper L Baseline EndFraction](images/c13_720.png).
*   – On one hand, the value of *K* should be as low as possible, because it impacts the amount of data embedded in plaintexts; the higher the value of *K* is, the lower the size of messages that can be mapped to EC points is. On the other hand, the lower the value of *K* is, the lower probability to find an EC point is. The probability of mapping failure is  <math alttext="2 Superscript negative upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript negative upper K](images/c13_721.png). See Problem 13.7.

**Example 13.8** Let  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F 113 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>113</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F 113 right-parenthesis](images/c13_722.png) be an elliptic curve of equation  <math alttext="y squared equals x cubed plus 7" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> ![y squared equals x cubed plus 7](images/c13_723.png).

Let *K* be 8. Consequently, any message *M* to map should be such that:

 <math alttext="0 less-than-or-equal-to upper M less-than-or-equal-to left floor StartFraction upper P Baseline 113 Over 8 EndFraction right floor negative 1 equals 13" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mrow><mo>&#8970;</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mn>113</mn></mrow><mn>8</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>&#8971;</mo></mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow></math> ![0 less-than-or-equal-to upper M less-than-or-equal-to left floor StartFraction upper P Baseline 113 Over 8 EndFraction right floor negative 1 equals 13](images/c13_724.png)

Let the message to map be 7 ⇒  <math alttext="8 asterisk 7 less-than-or-equal-to x less-than 8 asterisk left-parenthesis 7 plus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>7</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>x</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>8</mn><mo>\*</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![8 asterisk 7 less-than-or-equal-to x less-than 8 asterisk left-parenthesis 7 plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c13_725.png).

 <math alttext="x equals 60" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>60</mn></mrow></math> ![x equals 60](images/c13_726.png) fulfills the EC equation:  <math alttext="60 cubed plus 7 m o d 113 equals 64 equals 8 squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msup><mrow><mn>60</mn></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>8</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![60 cubed plus 7 m o d 113 equals 64 equals 8 squared](images/c13_727.png). Thus, point

 <math alttext="left-parenthesis 60 comma 8 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>60</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 60 comma 8 right-parenthesis](images/c13_728.png) is a solution to map message 7. In binary representation,  <math alttext="60 equals 111100 Subscript 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>60</mn><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mn>111100</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![60 equals 111100 Subscript 2](images/c13_729.png). The value of first three bits forms the value of *M*, which is  <math alttext="7 equals 111 Subscript 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mn>111</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![7 equals 111 Subscript 2](images/c13_730.png).

*   – Let  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F 113 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>113</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F 113 right-parenthesis](images/c13_731.png) be an elliptic curve of equation  <math alttext="y squared equals x cubed plus 7" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> ![y squared equals x cubed plus 7](images/c13_732.png).

Let *K* be 16. Consequently, any message *M* to map should be such that:

 <math alttext="y squared equals x cubed plus 7 period" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>7</mn><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> ![y squared equals x cubed plus 7 period](images/c13_733.png)

As shown by the following table, some messages have more than one EC point candidates to be embedded, while two messages (0 and 6) have no EC point to be mapped; therefore, they cannot be encrypted under the selected elliptic curve and the probabilistic mapping method.

![](images/c13_734.png)

##### *13.5.7.2.2 Encryption and Decryption*

Below is the operation sequence followed by Alice and Bob to secure their communication, while using the EEEC algorithm.

![](images/c13_745.png)

**Example 13.9**

Alice and Bob use the elliptic curve  <math alttext="upper E colon y squared identical-to left-parenthesis x cubed plus x plus 1 right-parenthesis m o d 23" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8801;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>23</mn></mrow></math> ![upper E colon y squared identical-to left-parenthesis x cubed plus x plus 1 right-parenthesis m o d 23](images/c13_761.png). Points of  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F 23 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>23</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F 23 right-parenthesis](images/c13_762.png) are the following:

 <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F 23 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>23</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F 23 right-parenthesis](images/c13_763.png)

Any of the following points can be used as generator of the chosen EC:

Alice encrypts and Bob decrypts as follows:

*   – Bob’s parameter selection: 
    *   Field cardinality:  <math alttext="p equals 23" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>23</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 23](images/c13_765.png).
    *   Elliptic curve:  <math alttext="upper E colon y squared left-parenthesis x cubed plus x plus 1 right-parenthesis m o d 23 comma left-parenthesis a equals b equals 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>23</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ![upper E colon y squared left-parenthesis x cubed plus x plus 1 right-parenthesis m o d 23 comma left-parenthesis a equals b equals 1 right-parenthesis](images/c13_766.png).
    *   Base point:  <math alttext="upper G equals left-parenthesis 9 comma 16 right-parenthesis period upper G is a generator semicolon hence comma o r d left-parenthesis upper G right-parenthesis equals StartAbsoluteValue upper E left-parenthesis upper F 23 right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue equals 28 period" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>16</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>G</mi><mtext>&#160;is&#160;a&#160;generator</mtext><mo>;</mo><mtext>hence</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>23</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>28.</mn></mrow></math> ![upper G equals left-parenthesis 9 comma 16 right-parenthesis period upper G is a generator semicolon hence comma o r d left-parenthesis upper G right-parenthesis equals StartAbsoluteValue upper E left-parenthesis upper F 23 right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue equals 28 period](images/c13_767.png)
    *   Bob’s private key:  <math alttext="upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline equals 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline equals 3](images/c13_768.png).
    *   Bob’s public key:  <math alttext="upper P u Subscript upper B Baseline equals 3 dot upper G equals 3 dot left-parenthesis 9 comma 16 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 1 comma 16 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#8901;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P u Subscript upper B Baseline equals 3 dot upper G equals 3 dot left-parenthesis 9 comma 16 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 1 comma 16 right-parenthesis](images/c13_769.png).
    *   Send  <math alttext="left-parenthesis a comma b comma p comma upper G comma n comma upper P u Subscript upper B Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis a comma b comma p comma upper G comma n comma upper P u Subscript upper B Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_770.png).
*   Alice’s encryption 
    *   Message to send is  <math alttext="upper M equals 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![upper M equals 3](images/c13_771.png).
    *   Parameter for integer to point mapping:  <math alttext="upper K equals 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![upper K equals 4](images/c13_772.png)
    *   Mapping of integer 3 onto the selected EC, with  <math alttext="upper K equals 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![upper K equals 4](images/c13_773.png), yields point  <math alttext="mu equals left-parenthesis 12 comma 4 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![mu equals left-parenthesis 12 comma 4 right-parenthesis](images/c13_774.png)\# (because  <math alttext="4 squared equals left-parenthesis 12 squared plus 12 plus 1 right-parenthesis m o d Baseline 23" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>4</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>23</mn></mrow></math> ![4 squared equals left-parenthesis 12 squared plus 12 plus 1 right-parenthesis m o d Baseline 23](images/c13_775.png)).
    *   Pick  <math alttext="k prime equals 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![k prime equals 4](images/c13_776.png).
    *   Alice’s public key:  <math alttext="upper P u Subscript upper A Baseline equals 4 dot upper G equals 4 dot left-parenthesis 9 comma 16 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 13 comma 7 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>&#8901;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P u Subscript upper A Baseline equals 4 dot upper G equals 4 dot left-parenthesis 9 comma 16 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 13 comma 7 right-parenthesis](images/c13_777.png).
    *   Compute ciphertext:  <math alttext="y squared equals x cubed plus 7" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> ![y squared equals x cubed plus 7](images/c13_778.png).
    *   Send  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper P u Subscript upper A Baseline comma upper C comma upper K right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper P u Subscript upper A Baseline comma upper C comma upper K right-parenthesis](images/c13_779.png).
*   Bob’s decryption
    
    *   Receive  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper P u Subscript upper A Baseline comma upper C comma upper K right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper P u Subscript upper A Baseline comma upper C comma upper K right-parenthesis](images/c13_780.png).
    *    <math alttext="mu prime equals left-parenthesis 6 comma 4 right-parenthesis minus left-parenthesis 3 dot left-parenthesis 13 comma 7 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 6 comma 4 right-parenthesis minus left-parenthesis 17 comma 3 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>&#8901;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>17</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![mu prime equals left-parenthesis 6 comma 4 right-parenthesis minus left-parenthesis 3 dot left-parenthesis 13 comma 7 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 6 comma 4 right-parenthesis minus left-parenthesis 17 comma 3 right-parenthesis](images/c13_781.png).
    *   By definition, if  <math alttext="upper P equals left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P equals left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis](images/c13_782.png), the negative point of *P*, in a prime field, is  <math alttext="negative upper P equals left-parenthesis x comma negative y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![negative upper P equals left-parenthesis x comma negative y right-parenthesis](images/c13_783.png).
    *   Thus,  <math alttext="mu prime equals left-parenthesis 6 comma 4 right-parenthesis plus left-parenthesis 17 comma negative 3 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 6 comma 4 right-parenthesis plus left-parenthesis 17 comma 20 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 12 comma 4 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>17</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>17</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>20</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![mu prime equals left-parenthesis 6 comma 4 right-parenthesis plus left-parenthesis 17 comma negative 3 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 6 comma 4 right-parenthesis plus left-parenthesis 17 comma 20 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 12 comma 4 right-parenthesis](images/c13_784.png).
    *   Then,  <math alttext="upper M prime equals left floor StartFraction x Subscript mu prime Baseline Over upper K EndFraction right floor equals left floor StartFraction 12 Over 4 EndFraction right floor equals 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>&#8970;</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></msub></mrow><mi>K</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>&#8971;</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>&#8970;</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>&#8971;</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![upper M prime equals left floor StartFraction x Subscript mu prime Baseline Over upper K EndFraction right floor equals left floor StartFraction 12 Over 4 EndFraction right floor equals 3](images/c13_785.png), which is the message encrypted by Alice.

##### *13.5.7.2.3 EEEC Security*

Breaking EEEC is equivalent to solving the EC discrete logarithm problem. Thus, EEEC is considered secure when used with large size fields.

##### *13.5.7.2.4 Proof of Correctness*

To retrieve the EC point generated by the sender, the recipient computes

 <math alttext="mu prime equals upper C prime minus upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline dot upper P u Subscript upper A Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![mu prime equals upper C prime minus upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline dot upper P u Subscript upper A Baseline](images/c13_786.png), which, by substitutions, becomes:

 <math alttext="mu prime equals mu plus k prime dot upper P u Subscript upper B Baseline minus upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline dot upper P u Subscript upper A Baseline equals mu plus left-parenthesis k prime dot upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline dot upper G right-parenthesis minus left-parenthesis upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline dot k prime dot upper G right-parenthesis equals mu" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><msup><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>&#956;</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext></mrow></math> ![mu prime equals mu plus k prime dot upper P u Subscript upper B Baseline minus upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline dot upper P u Subscript upper A Baseline equals mu plus left-parenthesis k prime dot upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline dot upper G right-parenthesis minus left-parenthesis upper P r Subscript upper B Baseline dot k prime dot upper G right-parenthesis equals mu](images/c13_787.png)

Then, from x-coordinate of point  <math alttext="mu prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></math> ![mu prime](images/c13_788.png), the recipient extracts the message  <math alttext="mu prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></math> ![mu prime](images/c13_789.png).□

***Problem 13.5*** Prove Theorem 13.2.

***Problem 13.6*** In December 2010, the ECDSA private key used by Sony to sign the software for PlayStation 3 console was discovered. The attack worked, because Sony used a static value for *k* in the signature generation procedure. In this problem, you are asked to design an attack to discover Alice’s private key assuming that, by mistake, Alice makes use of the same value of *k* for all her signed messages.

***Problem 13.7*** Alice and Bob use the elliptic curve  <math alttext="y squared equals x cubed plus x plus 1 m o d 23" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>23</mn></mrow></math> ![y squared equals x cubed plus x plus 1 m o d 23](images/c13_889.png). The EC points are shown in example 13.9.

1.  Can Alice and Bob agree to use point  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 4 comma 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 4 comma 0 right-parenthesis](images/c13_890.png) as value for parameter *G*?
2. 3.  With the selected parameters (i.e. *a* =  <math alttext="b equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![b equals 1](images/c13_892.png) and  <math alttext="equals 23" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>23</mn></mrow></math> ![equals 23](images/c13_893.png)), what are the messages that Alice can encrypt using the probabilistic mapping method?

    Let  <math alttext="x Subscript k upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![x Subscript k upper P](images/c13_897.png) denote the x-coordinate of point  <math alttext="k dot upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![k dot upper P](images/c13_898.png) and  <math alttext="y Subscript k upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![y Subscript k upper P](images/c13_899.png) its y-coordinate. *P* is point  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 5 comma 8 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 5 comma 8 right-parenthesis](images/c13_900.png). The formula of point doubling yields:

    Then, try to add to *P* to  <math alttext="2 upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![2 upper P](images/c13_905.png) using formula of point addition:
    
     <math alttext="lamda equals StartFraction y Subscript 2 upper P Baseline minus y Subscript 1 upper P Baseline Over x Subscript 2 upper P Baseline minus x Subscript 1 upper P Baseline EndFraction equals StartFraction 9 minus 8 Over 5 minus 5 EndFraction equals StartFraction 1 Over 0 EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>9</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>0</mn></mfrac></mrow></math> ![lamda equals StartFraction y Subscript 2 upper P Baseline minus y Subscript 1 upper P Baseline Over x Subscript 2 upper P Baseline minus x Subscript 1 upper P Baseline EndFraction equals StartFraction 9 minus 8 Over 5 minus 5 EndFraction equals StartFraction 1 Over 0 EndFraction](images/c13_906.png)⇒  <math alttext="upper P plus 2 upper P equals 3 upper P equals script upper O left-parenthesis point to infinity right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mtext>point&#160;to&#160;infinity</mtext></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P plus 2 upper P equals 3 upper P equals script upper O left-parenthesis point to infinity right-parenthesis](images/c13_907.png)
    
     <math alttext="3 upper P" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> ![3 upper P](images/c13_908.png) cannot be calculated. Consequently,  <math alttext="upper P equals left-parenthesis 5 comma 8 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper P equals left-parenthesis 5 comma 8 right-parenthesis](images/c13_909.png) is not a generator for points of  <math alttext="upper E left-parenthesis upper F 17 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper E left-parenthesis upper F 17 right-parenthesis](images/c13_910.png).

All the EC points are multiple of point  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 6 comma 6 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>6</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 6 comma 6 right-parenthesis](images/c13_920.png); hence, it is a generator of the EC. The order of the generator  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 6 comma 6 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 6 comma 6 right-parenthesis](images/c13_921.png) is  <math alttext="number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis equals 18" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>#</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>18</mn></mrow></math> ![number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis equals 18](images/c13_922.png).
    

![Table 13.4 Calculations of multiple points of point (6,6).](images/c13_923.png)
