    5^(th) function call:  <math alttext="upper R upper P upper M left-parenthesis left-parenthesis 2 comma 2 right-parenthesis comma 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>M</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper R upper P upper M left-parenthesis left-parenthesis 2 comma 2 right-parenthesis comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c13_1371.png)
    
     <math alttext="k equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![k equals 1](images/c13_1372.png) ⇒ Return  <math alttext="left-parenthesis left-parenthesis 2 comma 2 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis left-parenthesis 2 comma 2 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c13_1373.png)
    
    Starting from the bottom, the substitution of the result returned by the *i*^(th) call of RPM in the *i-1*^(th) RPM call yields the final result, which is  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 2 comma 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 2 comma 0 right-parenthesis](images/c13_1374.png).
    

***Problem 13.4*** Given the elliptic curve  <math alttext="upper E colon y squared equals x cubed plus 2 x plus 2 m o d 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![upper E colon y squared equals x cubed plus 2 x plus 2 m o d 17](images/c13_1375.png), why all points of the elliptic are generators?

Recall that the order of a point *P* of an elliptic curve is the smallest *k* such that  <math alttext="k dot upper P equals script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></mrow></math> ![k dot upper P equals script upper O](images/c13_1376.png) and a point *G* is a generator, if the order of *G* is equal to the number of points of the curve including the point  <math alttext="script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></math> ![script upper O](images/c13_1377.png). In general, with the exception of point  <math alttext="script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></math> ![script upper O](images/c13_1378.png), which has an order of 1 (because  <math alttext="1 dot script upper O equals script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></mrow></math> ![1 dot script upper O equals script upper O](images/c13_1379.png)), the elements of a group *E* associated with an elliptic curve have orders in  <math alttext="left-bracket 2 comma StartAbsoluteValue upper E EndAbsoluteValue right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>E</mi><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 2 comma StartAbsoluteValue upper E EndAbsoluteValue right-bracket](images/c13_1380.png). By Lagrange theorem and its corollary, any element of a group has an order, which divides the cardinality of the group. Since the cardinality of the group associated with the elliptic curve  <math alttext="y squared equals x cubed plus 2 x plus 2 m o d 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![y squared equals x cubed plus 2 x plus 2 m o d 17](images/c13_1381.png) is equal to 19, which is a prime, the order of all elements, distinct from  <math alttext="script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></math> ![script upper O](images/c13_1382.png) is 19. Therefore, by definition of a group generator, all points of the elliptic curve, with the exception of  <math alttext="script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></math> ![script upper O](images/c13_1383.png), are generators.

***Problem 13.5*** *(Proof of Theorem 13.2)* Let  <math alttext="upper E colon y squared identical-to x cubed plus a x plus b m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper E colon y squared identical-to x cubed plus a x plus b m o d p](images/c13_1384.png) be an elliptic curve over prime field *F[p]*. A prime field has exactly *p* elements. For any  <math alttext="u element-of upper F Subscript p Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>u</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![u element-of upper F Subscript p Baseline](images/c13_1385.png), if  <math alttext="left-parenthesis u cubed plus a u plus b right-parenthesis m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>u</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis u cubed plus a u plus b right-parenthesis m o d p](images/c13_1386.png) is a square residue, then there exists two points  <math alttext="left-parenthesis u comma w right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis u comma w right-parenthesis](images/c13_1388.png) on the elliptic curve such that  <math alttext="left-parenthesis plus-or-minus w right-parenthesis squared identical-to left-parenthesis u cubed plus a u plus b right-parenthesis m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>&#177;</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>u</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis plus-or-minus w right-parenthesis squared identical-to left-parenthesis u cubed plus a u plus b right-parenthesis m o d p](images/c13_1389.png), with the exception that if  <math alttext="left-parenthesis u cubed plus a u plus b right-parenthesis m o d p equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>u</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis u cubed plus a u plus b right-parenthesis m o d p equals 0](images/c13_1390.png), there exists a single point  <math alttext="left-parenthesis u comma 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis u comma 0 right-parenthesis](images/c13_1391.png). Therefore, the number of points associated with any  <math alttext="u upper F Subscript p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>u</mi><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![u upper F Subscript p](images/c13_1392.png) is  <math alttext="1 plus left-parenthesis StartFraction u cubed plus a u plus b Over p EndFraction right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>u</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mi>p</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![1 plus left-parenthesis StartFraction u cubed plus a u plus b Over p EndFraction right-parenthesis](images/c13_1393.png), where  <math alttext="left-parenthesis StartFraction u cubed plus a u plus b Over p EndFraction right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>u</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mi>p</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis StartFraction u cubed plus a u plus b Over p EndFraction right-parenthesis](images/c13_1394.png) is Legendre symbol (see Section 3.1.7.1) of integer  <math alttext="left-parenthesis u cubed plus a u plus b right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>u</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis u cubed plus a u plus b right-parenthesis](images/c13_1395.png) and *p*. Recall that, given two integers *a* and *p*, with  <math alttext="a less-than-or-equal-to p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![a less-than-or-equal-to p](images/c13_1396.png), Legendre symbol  <math alttext="left-parenthesis StartFraction a Over p EndFraction right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>a</mi><mi>p</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis StartFraction a Over p EndFraction right-parenthesis](images/c13_1397.png) is equal to 1, if *a* is a square residue modulo *p*; it is equal to –1, if *a* is a square nonresidue modulo *p*; and it is equal to 0, if  <math alttext="a m o d p equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![a m o d p equals 0](images/c13_1398.png). Therefore, considering all the elements of *F[p]*, the number of points on the elliptic curve, denoted  <math alttext="number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>#</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![number-sign upper E left-parenthesis upper F Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13_1399.png), is given by:

The “1” after sign “=” is used to include the point to infinity  <math alttext="script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></math> ![script upper O](images/c13_1401.png).□

***Problem 13.6*** Alice signed two messages  <math alttext="upper M 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 1](images/c13_1402.png) and  <math alttext="upper M 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 2](images/c13_1403.png). Let  <math alttext="left-parenthesis r 1 comma s 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis r 1 comma s 1 right-parenthesis](images/c13_1404.png) and  <math alttext="left-parenthesis r 2 comma s 2 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis r 2 comma s 2 right-parenthesis](images/c13_1405.png) be ECDSA signatures of messages  <math alttext="upper M 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 1](images/c13_1406.png) and  <math alttext="upper M 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 2](images/c13_1407.png) respectively.

If Alice used the same point  <math alttext="upper Q equals k dot upper G" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> ![upper Q equals k dot upper G](images/c13_1408.png) to sign both messages, then  <math alttext="r 1 equals r 2 equals x Subscript upper Q Baseline m o d n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![r 1 equals r 2 equals x Subscript upper Q Baseline m o d n](images/c13_1409.png) (recall that the component *r* in signature is the x-coordinate of point *Q*).

In messages  <math alttext="upper M 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 1](images/c13_1410.png) and  <math alttext="upper M 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 2](images/c13_1411.png), signatures  <math alttext="left-parenthesis r 1 comma s 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis r 1 comma s 1 right-parenthesis](images/c13_1412.png) and  <math alttext="left-parenthesis r 2 comma s 2 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis r 2 comma s 2 right-parenthesis](images/c13_1413.png), point *Q*, and the hash function are public. Therefore, the attacker can use them.

First, the attacker calculates the hashes:  <math alttext="upper H 1 equals h a s h left-parenthesis upper M 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H 1 equals h a s h left-parenthesis upper M 1 right-parenthesis](images/c13_1414.png) and  <math alttext="upper H 2 equals h a s h left-parenthesis upper M 2 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H 2 equals h a s h left-parenthesis upper M 2 right-parenthesis](images/c13_1415.png).

Second, using the definition of the component *s* of signature, the attacker can write:

1.  Alice and Bob should not use point  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 4 comma 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 4 comma 0 right-parenthesis](images/c13_1423.png) as parameter *G*, because the order of point (4, 0) is 2. Point  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 4 comma 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 4 comma 0 right-parenthesis](images/c13_1424.png) can only generate itself and  <math alttext="script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></math> ![script upper O](images/c13_1425.png) (because the y-coordinate is 0). With  <math alttext="upper G equals left-parenthesis 4 comma 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper G equals left-parenthesis 4 comma 0 right-parenthesis](images/c13_1426.png), both public keys are the same and equal to  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 4 comma 0 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 4 comma 0 right-parenthesis](images/c13_1427.png), because the single value that Bob can choose as private key and that Alice can choose as ephemeral key  <math alttext="k prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![k prime](images/c13_1428.png) is 1.
2.  If Bob selects point  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 13 comma 7 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 13 comma 7 right-parenthesis](images/c13_1429.png) for parameter *G*, he cannot use a private key higher than 6, because  <math alttext="7 dot left-parenthesis 13 comma 7 right-parenthesis equals script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>7</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo>&#8901;</mo><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></mrow></math> ![7 dot left-parenthesis 13 comma 7 right-parenthesis equals script upper O](images/c13_1430.png) (the order of point  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 13 comma 7 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 13 comma 7 right-parenthesis](images/c13_1431.png) is 7).
3.  The messages that Alice can encrypt depend only on parameters *K* and *p*. Since  <math alttext="p equals 23" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>23</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 23](images/c13_1432.png), the messages that can be encrypted are in the range  <math alttext="left-bracket 0 comma 22 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>22</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 0 comma 22 right-bracket](images/c13_1433.png). In addition, the messages, which will be encrypted, depend on the success of the probabilistic mapping method. The table below gives, for each *K* value, the range of message values that can be tested for mapping, the message values for which the mapping succeeded to find EC points, the mapping success ratio, and the ratio of the numbers *l* of integers less than *p* that can be encrypted.

![](images/c13_1434.png)

As you may notice, the higher the value of *K* is, the higher the probability of mapping success is. Conversely, the higher the value of *K* is, the lower the number of message values to map is.

## Notes

1.  [**1**](#c13.xhtml#rc13-note-0001) Elliptic curves used in cryptography are a simplified form of the general equation of elliptic curves. This book is limited to ECs for cryptography.
2.  [**2**](#c13.xhtml#rc13-note-0002) This is the definition of the traditional ECs over finite fields *F[p]* with prime  <math alttext="p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![p](images/c13_1435.png).
3.  [**3**](#c13.xhtml#rc13-note-0003) The EC points were calculated using a few-lines python code.
4.  [**4**](#c13.xhtml#rc13-note-0004) Note that the same sign “–” is used with different meanings. “–” before a point means the inverse point within the underlying field (it comes from a field operation), while “–” before a y-coordinate means the inverse regarding the y-axis (it comes from the usual interpretation of “minus”).
5.  **5** For both parties, the generation of private keys shall use standard random number generator, which has been approved to be attack-resistant (see [Chapter 16](#c16.xhtml)).
6.  [**6**](#c13.xhtml#rc13-note-0006) Points may be calculated with a simple program, given *a* and *b* (the coefficients of the curve equation) and *p* (the modulus of the field).
7.  [**7**](#c13.xhtml#rc13-note-0007) The randomness of selection of *k* must be approved and *k* must be kept secret. The values of *k* have the same security requirements as the private key. If an attacker retrieves two or more messages signed with the same value of *k*, he/she can derive the private key of the signer.
8.  [**8**](#c13.xhtml#rc13-note-0008) The calculations in the signing process are made  <math alttext="m o d u l o n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![m o d u l o n](images/c13_1436.png). Consequently, the bit size of the hash *H* must not be greater than the bit size of *n* (the order of the base point *G*). In case, the bit size of the hash *H* is greater than the bit size of *n*, only the leftmost  <math alttext="left ceiling l o g 2 left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis right ceiling" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>&#8968;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8969;</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left ceiling l o g 2 left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis right ceiling](images/c13_1437.png) bits of the hash are used in signing and also in verification.
9.  [**9**](#c13.xhtml#rc13-note-0009) The probability that  <math alttext="r equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![r equals 0](images/c13_1438.png) (or that  <math alttext="s equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![s equals 0](images/c13_1439.png)) is approximately  <math alttext="1 slash n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![1 slash n](images/c13_1440.png).
10.  [**10**](#c13.xhtml#rc13-note-0010) SHAKE256 is a variant of the SHA3 family.  <math alttext="upper S upper H upper A upper K upper E Baseline 256 left-parenthesis upper D a t a comma 912 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mi>H</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>K</mi><mi>E</mi><mn>256</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>912</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S upper H upper A upper K upper E Baseline 256 left-parenthesis upper D a t a comma 912 right-parenthesis](images/c13_1441.png) has an output of  <math alttext="912 slash 2 equals 456" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>912</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>456</mn></mrow></math> ![912 slash 2 equals 456](images/c13_1442.png) bits.
11.  [**11**](#c13.xhtml#rc13-note-0011) The randomness of selection of *k* must be approved and *k* must be kept secret.
12.  [**12**](#c13.xhtml#rc13-note-0012) Encoding an EC point is the transformation of point coordinates into a bit-string.
13.  [**13**](#c13.xhtml#rc13-note-0013) For example, use  <math alttext="c o n t e x t equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![c o n t e x t equals 1](images/c13_1443.png), to sign emails,  <math alttext="c o n t e x t equals 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![c o n t e x t equals 2](images/c13_1444.png), to sign pictures, and  <math alttext="c o n t e x t equals 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![c o n t e x t equals 3](images/c13_1445.png), to sign videos.
14.  [**14**](#c13.xhtml#rc13-note-0014) *s* is the same in Key-pair generation and Signature generation.
15. # 14   
Key Management

In previous chapters, we discussed how cryptographic keys might be used. More precisely, symmetric keys are mainly used for data encryption and decryption and for message authentication code generation and verification. Private and public key pairs are mainly used for digital signature generation and verification, for shared secret generation, and for encryption and decryption of keys and data. In addition to those usages of keys, in this chapter, we discuss how existing keys may be used to derive new keys.

Keys are owned and used by entities (e.g. devices, individuals or organizations) that interact with other entities to conduct specific operations in different fields of activities (e.g. e-commerce, e-government services, e-health, etc.). These keys are analogous to the combination of a safe. If adversaries know the combination of a safe, the latter does not provide any security against attacks, even it is very complex. Keys are the most valuable items in computer security; thus, their protection (i.e. confidentiality, integrity, and availability) is of paramount importance. During its lifetime, the key is either in transit (i.e. exchanged between parties), in use (to encrypt, to decrypt, to sign, etc.), or in storage. Key protection[¹](#c14.xhtml#c14-note-0001) shall address all those steps in the key lifetime cycle.

Key management provides the functions for a secure management of cryptographic keys throughout their lifetime. It mainly includes key generation, storage, distribution, recovery, suspension, and withdrawal. This chapter aims at introducing the main mechanisms and protocols for key generation, key agreement, key transport, and key distribution.

Public-key infrastructures (PKIs) are essential services for distribution of public keys. The latter are included in certificates delivered by trusted authorities enabling the recipient to have assurance regarding the holder of a public key. PKIs maintain coherent and valid lists of public keys. PKIs are discussed in Section 15.2.

Randomness is of prime importance to generate robust keys (i.e. keys very difficult to guess with statistical analysis methods). In [Chapter 16](#c16.xhtml), we introduce the recommended pseudorandom bit generators.

It is worth noticing that the protocols and functions presented in this chapter are specified in NIST recommendations and RFCs (Request for comments) and used in current secured applications and services.

## 14.1 Key-Management-related Notions

### 14.1.1 Types, Security Strengths, and Cryptoperiod of Keys

#### 14.1.1.1 Key Types

Keys are used for providing different forms of services, mainly including:

*   Data confidentiality
*   Data integrity
*   Entity authentication (i.e. provide assurance of the identity of a party)
*   Non-repudiation
*   Authorization to access protected physical or logical resources
*   Support services (e.g. key establishment, key agreement, random number generation, etc.)

Thus, keys may be categorized into several types depending on their use. More precisely, the following key types are used to categorize keys \[[1](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0001)\]:

*   *Symmetric encryption and decryption keys*: they are used with symmetric-key algorithms to provide confidentiality guarantees.
*   *Symmetric key-wrapping keys*: they are used to encrypt other keys when they are in transit.
*   *Symmetric master/key-derivation keys*: they are used to derive other symmetric keys.
*   *Symmetric authentication keys*: they are used with symmetric-key algorithms to provide identity authentication and integrity.
*   *Symmetric key-agreement keys*: they are used to establish symmetric keys.
*   *Symmetric DRBG*[²](#c14.xhtml#c14-note-0002) *keys*: they are used to generate random bits or numbers.
*   *Symmetric authorization keys*: they are used to provide privileges to an entity using a symmetric cryptographic algorithm.
*   *Private signature-generation keys*: they are used by public-key algorithms to generate digital signatures intended for long-term use.
*   *Public signature-verification keys*: they are used by public-key algorithms to verify digital signatures.
*   *Private authentication keys*: they are used with public-key algorithms to provide evidence of the sender identity, when establishing an authenticated session or performing some action.
*   *Public authentication keys*: they are used with public-key algorithms to verify the identity of the sender, when establishing an authenticated session or performing some action.
*   *Private key-transport keys*: they are the private keys of asymmetric-key algorithms and are used to decrypt keys that have been encrypted with the corresponding public key, when establishing symmetric keys.

*   *Public key-transport keys*: they are the public keys of asymmetric-key algorithms and are used to encrypt keys when establishing symmetric-keys.
*   *Private static key-agreement keys*: they are the long-term private-keys of asymmetric-key algorithms and are used to establish symmetric keys.
*   *Public static key-agreement keys*: they are long-term public keys of asymmetric-key algorithms. They are used to establish symmetric keys.
*   *Private ephemeral key-agreement keys*: they are the short-term private keys of asymmetric-key algorithms. They are used only once to establish one or more symmetric keys.
*   *Public ephemeral key-agreement keys*: they are the short-term public keys of asymmetric-key algorithms. They are used in a single key-establishment transaction to establish one or more symmetric keys.
*   *Private authorization keys*: they are the private keys of asymmetric-key algorithms and are used to prove the owner’s right to privileges.
*   *Public authorization keys*: they are the public keys of asymmetric-key algorithms and are used to verify privileges for an entity that knows the associated private authorization-key.

*Usage uniqueness*

In general, each key should be used for only one purpose (e.g. confidentiality, integrity authentication, or digital signature), because of, at least, the following two reasons:

1.  The use of the same key for two distinct cryptographic applications may weaken the security provided by one or both of the applications.
2.  Limiting the use of a key limits the damage that could be done if the key is compromised.

#### 14.1.1.2 Security Strengths

Cryptographic algorithms can provide different security strengths depending mainly on the bit-length of the used keys. Recall that the security strength (also called security level) is defined as a number associated with the amount of operations that is required to break a cryptographic algorithm. The commonly used numbers of security strengths are 80, 112, 128, 192, and 256 bits.

**Note**. The security strength of 80 bits is no more secure with the current technologies that can be used by attackers. Therefore, the lowest recommended security strength is of 112 bits.

[Tables 14.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-tbl-0001) and [14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-tbl-0002) provide the security strength of the cryptographic algorithms (i.e. ciphers, digital signature generation, hash functions, MAC generation, etc.) discussed in previous chapters. As you may see, algorithms have comparable security strengths with different key bit-lengths; e.g. RSA with a key bit-length of 3072 has a security strength comparable to that of AES with a key of 128 bits.

[**Table 14.1**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-tbl-0001) Security strengths of common ciphers. Adapted from \[[1](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0001)\].

|  ||  || DSA, DH, MQV || RSA[³](#c14.xhtml#c14-note-0003) || ECC-based algorithms |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 112 || 3TDEA || *L* = 2048, *N* = 224 || *K* = 2048 || *F* = 224-255 |
| 128 || AES-128 || *L* = 3072, *N* = 256 || *K* = 3072 || *F* = 256-383 |
| 192 || AES-192 || *L* =7680, *N* = 384 || *K* = 7680 || *F* = 384-511 |
| 256 || AES-256 || *L* = 15,360, *N* = 512 || *K* = 15,360 || *F* ≥ 512 |
| DSA: Digital Signature Algorithm, DH: Diffie-Hellman, MQV: Menezes-Qu-Vanstone, ECC: Elliptic Curve Cryptography, *L*: public-key bit-length, *N*: private key bit-length, *K*: RSA modulus bit-length, *F*: key bit-length. |

| Security strength || Hash functions for applications requiring collision resistance (e.g. digital signatures) || Hash functions for HMAC, KMAC, KDF, and DRBG |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 112 || SHA-224, SHA-512/224, SHA3-224 ||  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 128 || SHA-256, SHA-512/256, SHA3-256 || SHA-1, KMAC128 |
| 192 || SHA-384, SHA3-384 || SHA-224, SHA-512/224, SHA3-224 |
| ≥ 256 || SHA-512, SHA3-512 || SHA-256, SHA-512/256, SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA3-256, SHA3-384, SHA-512, KMAC-256 |
| HMAC: Hash-based Message Authentication Code, KDF: Key-Derivation Function, KMAC: Keccak-based Message Authentication Code, DRBG: Deterministic Random Bit Generator. |

Many applications require multiple cryptographic services (e.g. key establishment, confidentiality protection, integrity protection, digital signature, etc.). A different algorithm and key could be used to provide each service or multiple services could be provided by the same algorithm using the same or different keys. In addition, many services can be provided by more than one algorithm (e.g. digital signature can be provided by either RSA or ECDSA). Some algorithms are inherently efficient by design to perform some specific services, e.g. HMAC is efficient to provide data integrity protection. Therefore, a cryptosystem designer may have to choose a variety of algorithms and their appropriate key bit-lengths. It is worth noticing that the higher the security strength is, the higher the computation time and amount of other resources required to perform security operations are. Therefore, a trade-off between security strength and performance is to be considered when selecting the bit-length of keys.

#### 14.1.1.3 Cryptoperiod

***Definition 14.1 Cryptoperiod****: it is the time span during which a specific key is authorized for use by legitimate entities.*

The security provided by a key may be reduced or completely lost with time, because of the progress in cryptanalysis or simply the key becomes suspect (i.e. potential attackers might know some information about the key). The cryptoperiod of a key may be defined in terms of time between the generation of the key and its end of use or in terms of the maximum amount of data protected by the key. An adequately defined key cryptoperiod has the following properties:

1.  It limits the number of plaintext and ciphertext pairs encrypted with the same key; and therefore, it limits the amount of information available to attackers to recover the key.
2.  It limits the time for attackers to access resources protected with a key.

In general, short cryptoperiods enhance security. However, frequent changes of keys result in an overhead (due to key generation and distribution) and key-distribution methods are subject to human errors, which might actually increase the risk of key exposure. Therefore, a trade-off between cryptoperiod, overhead, and risk is to be considered by security-system administrators. [Table 14.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-tbl-0003) summarizes the key types and their respective cryptoperiods suggested by the NIST \[[1](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0001)\]. Notice that the cryptoperiod may be different, depending on the entity using the key, the originator (i.e. the entity that starts the information exchange) or the recipient.

| --- | --- | --- |

| Public signature-verification key || Authentication, Integrity, non-repudiation || Several |

### 14.1.2 Key-Management Phases and Functions

As illustrated by [Figure 14.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0001), a cryptographic key follows a series of steps, among which the following are the most addressed in cryptosystems:

![Figure 14.1 Main steps in the life cycle of a cryptographic key.](images/c14f001.png)

[**Figure 14.1**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-fig-0001) Main steps in the life cycle of a cryptographic key.

*   The key is generated using a specific key generation scheme.
*   In case of public-key cryptosystems, the public key is registered at a trusted authority.
*   The key is stored on a permanent and failure-resistant device.
*   The key is made available to legitimate users.
*   The key is used to perform cryptographic actions (encryption, decryption, signature generation and verification, etc.).
*   The key is suspended, because its cryptoperiod is exceeded or it became compromised.
*   The key is archived; and it is no more used in cryptographic operations.
*   The key is destroyed and its material is completely removed from the operational cryptosystem.

The key management encompasses a set of functions along with requirements that depend on the characteristics of data protected by each key. For example, top-secret data do not require the same severity level of key management than nonclassified data.

In this chapter, we focus on two fundamental functions: key generation and key establishment. Both functions are present in almost all key management systems. Overall, the key life cycle can be divided into four phases:

1.  *Pre-operational phase*: the key is not yet available to perform cryptographic operations. Two main functions compose this phase: key generation and secure key distribution. In addition, for public-key algorithms, a third function is required, the key registration at some trusted authority.
2.  *Operational phase*: the key is available for use to encrypt, decrypt, sign, etc. The key shall be stored on a safe device, often including key backup capabilities.
3.  *Post-operational phase*: the key is no longer used to encrypt or sign data. Key-related information is archived on separate devices, and may be processed to recover some keys or other information. The keys, at this phase, are archived until no longer needed to authenticate data or entities or to decrypt data, previously encrypted with these keys. Public keys should be de-registered.
4.  *Destruction phase*: the key is no longer available for any cryptographic operation.

## 14.2 Key-Generation Schemes

***Definition 14.2 Shared secret****: it is a secret value that has been computed using a key-agreement scheme and is used as input to a key-derivation function.*

***Definition 14.3 Key generation****: it is a procedure by which a new key is created.*

***Definition 14.4 Key derivation***: *it is a procedure by which one or more keys are derived from a shared secret.*

***Definition 14.5 Key owner***: *in the symmetric systems, any entity, which is authorized to share and use a key, is an owner of that key. In asymmetric systems, the party, which creates a pair of keys (private and public keys), is the owner of the private key.*

***Definition 14.6 Static key***: *a key that is intended for use for a relatively long period (in years) and is typically intended for use in many key-establishment operations.*

***Definition 14.7 Ephemeral key***: *a cryptographic key that is generated for each execution of a cryptographic process (e.g. key-agreement or key-transport) and that meets other requirements of the key type (e.g. unique to each message or session).*

### 14.2.1 Key Generation for Symmetric-Key Systems

A symmetric key can be generated by one party and then is communicated to the other party or generated by both parties using a key-agreement protocol. A key can be generated using an approved DRBG, from a password, by combining multiple keys, or by using a key-derivation function. Keys may also be generated using approved key-agreement protocols. [Figure 14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0002) depicts the main methods to generate keys. Those methods are addressed in more detail in the subsequent sections. In all cases, the key generation shall be based directly or indirectly on an approved DRBG, which guarantees randomness.

![Figure 14.2 Different techniques of key generation for symmetric-key algorithms.](images/c14f002.png)

[**Figure 14.2**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-fig-0002) Different techniques of key generation for symmetric-key algorithms.

#### 14.2.1.1 Key Generation Using DRBGs

Approved DRBGs (Deterministic random bit generators) may be used to generate symmetric keys or inputs for asymmetric-key-generation algorithms. Approved DRBGs are discussed in [Chapter 16](#c16.xhtml). The random bit string, say *B*, of a bit-length  <math alttext="upper B l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper B l e n](images/c14_1.png), required for the generation of a key *K*, is obtained as follows \[[2](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0002)\]:

 <math alttext="upper B equals upper U circled-plus upper V" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>U</mi><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> ![upper B equals upper U circled-plus upper V](images/c14_2.png)

> where: *U* is a bit string of  <math alttext="upper B l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper B l e n](images/c14_3.png) bits obtained as the output of an approved DRBG, which shall have at least the security strength of the algorithm/application that will use key *K*. *V* is a bit string of  <math alttext="upper B l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper B l e n](images/c14_4.png) bits, which could be all zeroes. *U* and *V* are statistically independent of each other. Bit string *V* may be another key or computed by a hash function or any other function that can increase the randomness of pair  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper U comma upper V right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper U comma upper V right-parenthesis](images/c14_5.png).

The bit-length  <math alttext="upper B l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper B l e n](images/c14_6.png) depends on the algorithm/application that will use the key (see [Table 14.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-tbl-0001)).

#### 14.2.1.2 Key Derived from a Password

In some popular applications (including encryption of data on storage devices), keys are generated from passwords. However, in general, user-generated passwords are less random than is required for cryptographic keys; that is, the number of passwords that are likely to be used to derive a key is significantly smaller than the number of keys that are possible for a given key bit-length. Therefore, passwords shall not be used directly as cryptographic keys.

To enable users generate keys from their passwords, the NIST approved a family of key derivation functions to transform a password into a key \[[3](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0003)\]. Each password-based key derivation function, denoted PBKDF, is defined by the selection of a pseudorandom function (see [Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml) for more on PRFs) and a fixed iteration count *C*. More precisely, a PBKDF is an HMAC parameterized with a hash function (e.g. SHA-256 or SHA3-384) and a hash bit-length  <math alttext="upper H l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper H l e n](images/c14_7.png). The PBKDF takes a password *P*, a salt *S*, a key bit-length  <math alttext="upper K l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K l e n](images/c14_8.png); and outputs a key *K* of the desired bit-length  <math alttext="upper K l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K l e n](images/c14_9.png). The salt is used as a part of the key in HMAC and it shall be generated using an approved DRBG with a bit-length of at least 128. The number of iterations, *C*, shall be as large as possible; 1000 is the minimum recommended value for *C*. For critical keys, *C* should be in millions. [Figure 14.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0003) illustrates the generic structure of a PBKDF; and the pseudocode is as follows.

![Figure 14.3 General structure of a PBKDF.](images/c14f003.png)

[**Figure 14.3**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-fig-0003) General structure of a PBKDF.

**Note**. Some functions are generic; and they need specific elements (such as a hash function or some bit-lengths) to build them before any usage. The elements used one time to instantiate a generic function are specified in **parameters** clause. The **input** clause specifies the values used in each function call.

**Notes**

*   – The process of key generation described above is public. Therefore, when passwords are used to generate cryptographic keys, it is assumed that an attacker is able to perform search attacks (e.g. dictionary attack) on the key generation process. Therefore, the password entropy is a critical issue. To make attacks computationally infeasible, it is recommended i) to use randomly generated passwords instead of user-chosen passwords, ii) the typical password length is of 20 to 30 characters.
*   – The salt of bit-length  <math alttext="upper S l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper S l e n](images/c14_22.png) allows generating a set of  <math alttext="2 Superscript upper S l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>S</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript upper S l e n](images/c14_23.png) keys corresponding to each password, for a fixed iteration count. Using a salt makes it difficult for attackers to prepare a table of potential keys. To make attacks computationally infeasible, the bit-length of the salt should be as large as possible.

#### 14.2.1.3 Key-Generation by Key-Derivation Methods

Two key derivation methods[⁵](#c14.xhtml#c14-note-0005) (KDM) are recommended \[[4](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0004)\], one-step and two-step methods. The second method provides more randomness in the generated key compared to the first method, but it requires more computation time.

##### *14.2.1.3.1 One-Step Key Derivation Method*

In one-step key-derivation method, the KDM is parameterized with an auxiliary function, denoted *H*, which can be a hash function  <math alttext="upper H a s h" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> ![upper H a s h](images/c14_24.png), HMAC defined by its hash function, or KMAC. The KDM takes a shared secret *Z*, a key bit-length, a salt (only if options 2 or 3 are used), and optional fixed data; and yields a key of the desired key bit-length (see [Figure 14.4](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0004)). Auxiliary function *H* may be defined by one of the following options:

[**Figure 14.4**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-fig-0004) General structure of one-step key-derivation method.

##### *14.2.1.3.2 Two-Step Key Derivation Functions*

As illustrated by [Figure 14.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0005), two-step key-derivation method makes use of two functions: randomness extraction and key expansion. In addition to the shared secret and the key bit-length, the two-step KDM requires a salt and an IV, when the KDF is in feedback mode (see [Section 14.2.1.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-03008)).

![Figure 14.5 General structure of the two-step key derivation method.](images/c14f005.png)

[**Figure 14.5**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-fig-0005) General structure of the two-step key derivation method.

The randomness-extraction function makes use of either HMAC or AES-CMAC mode of operation to generate a tag, which serves as a key-derivation key, denoted  <math alttext="upper K d k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K d k](images/c14_52.png), in the second step. The required *Salt* is used as a MAC key in HMAC or in the AES-CMAC. The second step is similar to that of the one-step KDM and it makes use of one of the basic key-derivation functions described in [Section 14.2.1.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-03008).

When HMAC is used in the two-step KDM, the recommended hash functions are the same as for the one-step KDM (see [Section 14.2.1.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-03008)). When AES-CMAC is used to generate the tag, the security strength is of 128 bits regardless of the AES variant used (i.e. 128, 192, or 256), because the output of AES is always of 128 bits.

#### 14.2.1.4 **Key Generated by Combining Multiple Other Keys and** Data

A symmetric key can be generated from other existing symmetric keys. Let  <math alttext="upper K 1 comma upper K 2 comma ellipsis comma upper K Subscript n Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper K 1 comma upper K 2 comma ellipsis comma upper K Subscript n Baseline](images/c14_65.png) be a list of independently generated keys and  <math alttext="upper D 1 comma upper D 2 comma ellipsis comma upper D Subscript n Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper D 1 comma upper D 2 comma ellipsis comma upper D Subscript n Baseline](images/c14_66.png) be a list of additional data, which are not required to be secret. The list of keys and additional data can be combined in different ways to generate a new key *K* as follows \[[2](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0002)\]:

*   Key concatenating:  <math alttext="upper K equals upper K 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper K 2 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue ellipsis StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper K Subscript n Baseline period" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> ![upper K equals upper K 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper K 2 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue ellipsis StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper K Subscript n Baseline period](images/c14_67.png)
*   Key-data XORing:  <math alttext="upper K equals upper K 1 circled-plus upper K 2 circled-plus ellipsis circled-plus upper K Subscript n Baseline circled-plus upper D 1 circled-plus upper D 2 circled-plus ellipsis circled-plus upper D Subscript n Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K equals upper K 1 circled-plus upper K 2 circled-plus ellipsis circled-plus upper K Subscript n Baseline circled-plus upper D 1 circled-plus upper D 2 circled-plus ellipsis circled-plus upper D Subscript n Baseline](images/c14_68.png).
*   Key extracting:  <math alttext="upper K equals upper T r u n c left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper H upper M upper A upper C Subscript upper H a s h Baseline left-parenthesis upper S a l t comma upper K 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper K 2 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue ellipsis StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper K Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis comma upper K l e n right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>T</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>H</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mo>(</mo><mi>S</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper K equals upper T r u n c left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper H upper M upper A upper C Subscript upper H a s h Baseline left-parenthesis upper S a l t comma upper K 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper K 2 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue ellipsis StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper K Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis comma upper K l e n right-parenthesis](images/c14_69.png);  <math alttext="upper H a s h" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> ![upper H a s h](images/c14_70.png) is a hash function. The function  <math alttext="upper T r u n c" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper T r u n c](images/c14_71.png) is applied to keep  <math alttext="upper K l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper K l e n](images/c14_72.png) bits from the produced tag.  <math alttext="upper S a l t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> ![upper S a l t](images/c14_73.png) is used as a key for the HMAC function.

The keys, which are combined, may be generated using any other method of key generation.

#### 14.2.1.5 Key-Derivation Functions

A pseudorandom function (PRF) is the core component for building key-derivation functions. A PRF is computationally indistinguishable from a random function for those observers without knowledge of the key used by the PRF. For more on PRF properties, the reader should refer to [Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml). The commonly used PRFs to build KDFs include HMAC, KMAC, and CMAC mode of operation.

Given a PRF, there exist three modes of function for generating a key from another shared key \[[5](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0005)\]:

*   KDF in counter mode, where the distinctive input of the PRF is a counter value used to produce a portion of the final output.
*   KDF in feedback mode, where the output of the PRF in each iteration is used in the next iteration to produce a portion of the final output.
*   KDF in double-pipelined mode, where the outputs of the PRF in feedback and counter modes are pipelined.

[Figure 14.7](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0007) illustrates the three modes of KDF. The secret used as input to KDFs is called *key-derivation key*, and denoted  <math alttext="upper K Subscript i n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript i n](images/c14_74.png). The desired key bit-length is denoted  <math alttext="upper K l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K l e n](images/c14_75.png). In addition, an IV, which is used in the feedback mode, and other fixed data may be used.

![Figure 14.7 Variants of KDFs.](images/c14f007.png)

[**Figure 14.7**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-fig-0007) Variants of KDFs.

**Note**. All KDFs discussed in this chapter are parametrized with an auxiliary function, which can be a hash function or a keyed-MAC algorithm (i.e. HMAC or KMAC). Therefore, a KDF is a family of functions that mainly differ in their auxiliary functions.

### 14.2.2 Key Generation for Asymmetric-Key Cryptosystems

Pairs of public and private keys are generated using the mathematical specifications of the involved algorithms. Recall that the security of public-key-based algorithms relies on the difficulty either to factorize large integers (as mentioned in [Chapter 12](#c12.xhtml)) or to find the discrete logarithm for large integers (as mentioned in [Chapters 12](#c12.xhtml) and [13](#c13.xhtml)). Thus, public-key-based cryptography is divided into two categories:

*   Integer Factorization Cryptography (IFC); RSA is the most known and used algorithm in IFC.
*   Discrete logarithm Cryptography (DLC), which is divided into two subcategories, Finite-Field Cryptography (FFC) and Elliptic-Curve Cryptography (ECC). The most known and commonly used DLC algorithms are Diffie-Hellman (DH) and Menezes-Qu-Vanstone (MQV) algorithms, which can be used under either FFC or ECC.

In this subsection, we present the methods for generating key-pairs (i.e. public and private key pairs); and in the next subsection, we address how IFC- and DLC-based algorithms can be used to build key-agreement protocols.

#### 14.2.2.1 RSA Key-Pair Generation

RSA is presented in Section 12.2. An RSA key-pair is denoted  <math alttext="left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper N comma d right-parenthesis comma left-parenthesis upper N comma e right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper N comma d right-parenthesis comma left-parenthesis upper N comma e right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c14_122.png), where *N* is the modulus, *d*, the private exponent, and *e*, the public exponent.  <math alttext="upper N b equals left ceiling l o g 2 upper N right ceiling" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>&#8968;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo>&#8969;</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper N b equals left ceiling l o g 2 upper N right ceiling](images/c14_123.png) denotes the bit-length of the modulus *N*. The commonly used RSA modulus bit-lengths vary from  <math alttext="2048" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2048</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![2048](images/c14_124.png) to 8192. Currently, the maximum value of  <math alttext="upper N b" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ![upper N b](images/c14_125.png), which is suggested by the RSA standard for the protection of critical data, is of 15,360.

The parameters used to generate RSA key-pairs should meet the following requirements \[[6](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0006), [7](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0007)\]:

1.  Public exponent  <math alttext="e colon 2 Superscript 16 Baseline less-than e less-than 2 Superscript 256" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>256</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![e colon 2 Superscript 16 Baseline less-than e less-than 2 Superscript 256](images/c14_126.png) and  <math alttext="upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis e comma upper L upper C upper M left-parenthesis p minus 1 comma q minus 1 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>M</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis e comma upper L upper C upper M left-parenthesis p minus 1 comma q minus 1 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c14_127.png).
2.  Private exponent *d*:  <math alttext="2 Superscript StartFraction upper N b Over 2 EndFraction Baseline less-than-or-equal-to d less-than upper L upper C upper M left-parenthesis p minus 1 comma q minus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>M</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript StartFraction upper N b Over 2 EndFraction Baseline less-than-or-equal-to d less-than upper L upper C upper M left-parenthesis p minus 1 comma q minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c14_128.png) and  <math alttext="d asterisk e equals 1 m o d left-parenthesis left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis q minus 1 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![d asterisk e equals 1 m o d left-parenthesis left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis q minus 1 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c14_129.png).
3. RSA key-pair generators (RSAKPGs) make use of an approved DRBG. Two families of RSAKPGs are recommended \[[7](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0007)\]: RSAKPG1 (with a fixed exponent *e*) and RSAKPG2 (with a random exponent *e*). Each family has three variants, which differ only in the format of the output representation: in the basic format, the output is  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper N comma d right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper N comma d right-parenthesis](images/c14_131.png); in the prime-factor variant, the output is  <math alttext="left-parenthesis p comma q comma d right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis p comma q comma d right-parenthesis](images/c14_132.png); and in the CRT (Chinese[⁷](#c14.xhtml#c14-note-0007) remainder theorem), the output is  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper N comma e comma d comma p comma q comma d upper P comma d upper Q comma q upper I n v right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>Q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mi>I</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>v</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper N comma e comma d comma p comma q comma d upper P comma d upper Q comma q upper I n v right-parenthesis](images/c14_134.png), where  <math alttext="d upper P equals d m o d left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![d upper P equals d m o d left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c14_135.png),  <math alttext="d upper Q equals d m o d left-parenthesis q minus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![d upper Q equals d m o d left-parenthesis q minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c14_136.png), and  <math alttext="q upper I n v equals q Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mi>I</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![q upper I n v equals q Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d p](images/c14_137.png). If the verification fails, an indication of “Inconsistency” is returned and the key-pair generation operation shall be re-run.

#### 14.2.2.2 Key-Pair Generation for DH and MQV

Diffie-Hellman (DF) and Menezes-Qu-Vanstone (MQV) are the most used cryptographic algorithms based on prime finite fields (see Sections 12.2–12.3).

##### *14.2.2.2.1 FFC Domain Parameter Selection*

The selection of domain parameters is of prime importance for the security of finite-field cryptography-based schemes as well as for elliptic-curve cryptography based schemes. A finite field with *p* elements  <math alttext="StartSet 0 comma 1 comma ellipsis comma p minus 1 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 0 comma 1 comma ellipsis comma p minus 1 EndSet](images/c14_162.png) is denoted  <math alttext="upper F Subscript p Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript p Baseline](images/c14_163.png)(see mathematical notations and notions relating to prime finite fields in Section 3.2.2).  <math alttext="upper F Subscript p Baseline minus StartSet 0 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript p Baseline minus StartSet 0 EndSet](images/c14_164.png) is denoted  <math alttext="upper F Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c14_165.png).

Public keys recommended to perform key establishment using finite-field cryptography are restricted to a cyclic subgroup of  <math alttext="upper F Subscript p Superscript asterisk Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript p Superscript asterisk Baseline](images/c14_166.png) with prime order *q*, such that *q* divides  <math alttext="p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p minus 1](images/c14_167.png). An element  <math alttext="g element-of upper F Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><msubsup><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![g element-of upper F Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c14_168.png) is a generator of  <math alttext="upper F Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c14_169.png) if any element  <math alttext="a element-of upper F Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><msubsup><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![a element-of upper F Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c14_170.png) can be written as a power of *g* modulo *p*; i.e.  <math alttext="for-all a upper F Subscript p Superscript asterisk Baseline comma there-exists k element-of double-struck upper N vertical-bar a identical-to g Superscript k Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>a</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msubsup><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8707;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>&#8469;</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![for-all a upper F Subscript p Superscript asterisk Baseline comma there-exists k element-of double-struck upper N vertical-bar a identical-to g Superscript k Baseline m o d p](images/c14_171.png).

Domain parameters required in FFC-based schemes are the following:

*   *p*: a safe prime denoting the size of the finite field *F[p]*.
*   *g*: a subgroup generator of the cyclic group  <math alttext="upper F Subscript p Superscript asterisk" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>F</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>\*</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper F Subscript p Superscript asterisk](images/c14_172.png).
*   *q*: a prime denoting the order of the subgroup generated by *g*.
*   Optional parameters used in some specific prime and generator selection procedures.

Testing integer primality is addressed in Section 16.3.2. There does not exist an algorithm, which can test the primality of any large integer in a reasonable time, but there exist probabilistic algorithms that can test if an integer is not prime. If an integer is not confirmed (at a given probability) to be non-prime, it is probably prime. Hence the notion of probable primes used in cryptographic algorithms (see Section 16.3.2.2).

Two methods are recommended to select FFC domain parameters:

1.  *Generation of domain parameters using recommended safe-primes*: the first method to select domain parameters is as follows:
    
    *   – Choose *p* out of the same primes[⁸](#c14.xhtml#c14-note-0008) recommended in \[[8](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0008)–[10](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0010)\] and shown in [Table 14.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-tbl-0005).
    *   – Choose  <math alttext="q equals left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![q equals left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2](images/c14_173.png); since *p* is a safe prime, *q* is a prime.
    *   – Choose  <math alttext="g equals 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![g equals 2](images/c14_174.png), which makes implementation efficient.
2.  *Generation of domain parameters using ad hoc probable or provable primes*: the second method to select domain parameters is summarized as follows \[[6](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0006)\]:
    
    *   – Probable primes can be generated using a hash function *H*, such as SHA-256, a *Counter*, which specifies the number of repetitions of the hash function, and a *Seed* (a random integer, which must be unique for each set of parameter domain).
    *   – Provable primes can be generated using Shawe-Taylor’s algorithm \[[11](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0011)\], as discussed in Section 16.3.4.1.
    *   – Once two primes *p* and *p* are generated, select a generator *g* using the following algorithm.

2.  Key-pair generation by testing candidates (ECC-KPGTC), which picks a random number and then checks whether it can produce a valid private key.
