## 14.3 Key-Establishment Schemes

### 14.3.1 Overall View of Key-Establishment Schemes

The key establishment is the process by which two (or more) parties establish shared keys. As shown in [Figure 14.8](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0008), there are two categories of key-establishment protocols: generate-then-send approach or follow-key-agreement approach. In the first category, the key is generated by one party, using methods discussed in [Section 14.2.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-02003) (for symmetric keys) and [Section 14.2.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-02004) (for asymmetric keys); and, then, transmits (or distributes) the generated key to the other party. In case of a symmetric key, the latter is securely transmitted to the other party manually or using a key-wrapping or a key-transport protocol. In case of a public key, the latter is not secret and it is directly sent to the other party or embedded in a digital certificate delivered by a trusted party. Digital certificates are discussed in Section 15.1.

![Figure 14.8 Main building-blocks of key-establishment protocols.](images/c14f008.png)

[**Figure 14.8**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-fig-0008) Main building-blocks of key-establishment protocols.

In the second category, both parties provide to information, which jointly establish a shared secret key. A key derivation function is then used to derive a secret key from the shared secret. Key-derivation functions are discussed in [Section 14.2.1.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-03008).

***Definition 14.8 Key establishment***: it is the process by which two (or more) parties establish a shared secret key. The execution of the key-establishment scheme is referred to as key-establishment transaction.

***Definition 14.9 Key agreement***: it is the process by which the resultant secret key is obtained from the information contributed by both parties. The execution of the key-agreement scheme is referred to as key-agreement transaction.

***Definition 14.10 Key transport***: it is the process by which one party (the sender) selects and encrypts or wraps a key and then distributes it to another party (the recipient). The execution of the key-transport scheme is referred to as key transaction.

***Definition 14.11 Key distribution***: it is the process by which a key, from an entity that either owns, generates, or otherwise acquires the key is transmitted to another entity that is intended to use the key. The process may be either manual or by using a key transport protocol.

***Definition 14.12 Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS)***: it is a property of key agreement protocols that change the session key for each user-initiated session, so that if one session key is compromised, only the data encrypted with such a key is vulnerable; and the data encrypted with any other session key will not be affected.

In the public-key-based key-establishment schemes, the following actions should be performed before starting a key-establishment process:

*   Selection of the FFC or ECC domain parameters to use (for recommended values of domain parameters, see [Section 14.2.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-02004)).
*   Generation (and maybe registration) and distribution of the public keys.
*   Selection of a key-derivation function and its parameters (see [Section 14.2.1.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-03008)).
*   Selection of a hash function or a MAC algorithm and the associated parameters (tag bit-length, MAC key bit-length, and maybe additional fixed data), when a key-confirmation is required (see [Section 14.3.3.1.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-04009)).

One usual approach is that the initiator of a key-establishment transaction selects and validates all the parameters; and the other party accepts the proposed parameters.

The output of a key-establishment transaction, called *Keying material*, is either a secret key or a bit-string from which a secret key and other information are extracted.

**Note**. The key-establishment schemes aim to establish keys and other cryptographic elements (e.g. initialization vectors, etc.), the whole is called *keying material*. The focus in this chapter is on the shared keys. Thus, by default, the keying material is limited to a secret key *K*, which may be used for providing confidentiality assurance and authentication, and a MAC key,  <math alttext="upper M a c upper K e y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M a c upper K e y](images/c14_299.png), which is used only during the agreement process to confirm the possession of private keys. Thus, in subsequent pseudocodes,  <math alttext="upper K e y i n g upper M a t e r i a l equals left-parenthesis upper K comma upper M a c upper K e y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper K e y i n g upper M a t e r i a l equals left-parenthesis upper K comma upper M a c upper K e y right-parenthesis](images/c14_300.png).

*Symmetric-key distribution*

There exist two main solutions:

1.  *Peer-based generation and distribution*: once a symmetric key is generated by one party, it is made available to other party either manually[^(16)](#c14.xhtml#c14-note-0016) or using an automated key-transport protocol. The latter may be either a key-wrapping protocol such as KW or KWP, which are addressed in detail in Section 9.2.6, or a public-key key-transport protocol, such as RSA-KTS-OAEP, which is addressed in [Section 14.3.3.2.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-04012).
2.  *Use of a key* *distribution center*: a server is used to generate and distribute (session) keys to end-users associated with the server (see [Section 14.3.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-02006)).

*Public-key distribution*

For security reasons, the following two recommendations shall be observed when using public-key-based schemes to protect data or services:

*   One key-pair shall be used for one usage.
*   To be trusted, a public key shall have a certificate associated with it. It is highly recommended that public keys should be distributed by a trusted third-party. This issue is addressed in Section 15.2.

The distribution of the public key shall provide assurance to the recipient that:

*   The public key is valid (e.g. the public key satisfies the required mathematical properties).
*   The purpose/usage of the public key is known (e.g. for RSA digital signatures or for elliptic-curve key-agreement).
*   All the domain parameters associated with the public key are known and the recipient agrees to use them.
*   The public-key owner actually possesses the corresponding private key. This last requirement may be checked by the recipient through a key-confirmation procedure (see [Section 14.3.3.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-03012)).

### 14.3.2 Key-Establishment Using a Key Distribution Center

***Definition 14.13** **Key distribution center (KDC):** it is a solution to generate and distribute keys to entities that need to communicate with each other but do not share keys except with the center. Entities that have a keying relationship with a KDC are called **subscribers**.*

A KDC may have two or more levels. At the bottom of the hierarchy, there are entities, called subscribers, that need to securely exchange data. At the top, a central server is used. When the number of subscribers is large or when fault tolerance is an issue or for other organizational or security reasons, there may exist intermediate servers. Without loss of generality, we focus, in the sequel, on two-level KDCs, i.e. subscribers are connected to one server. Each subscriber shares a key with the server. To enable establishing a secure session between two subscribers, a session key is generated by the server and distributed to the subscribers. Therefore, the KDC is a solution to simplify the key management when the subscribers cannot generate and distribute their public keys or when using a symmetric key for each pair of subscribers, which would result in a huge number of symmetric keys. For example, the KDC-based approach would be appropriate in a virtual private network or in an IoT network where the *things* cannot (because of their limited computation resources) make use of public keys.

As illustrated in [Figure 14.9](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0009), each subscriber  <math alttext="upper S Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript i](images/c14_301.png) shares two keys with the server \[[13](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0013)\]:

1.  A key-wrapping key  <math alttext="upper K upper W upper K Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>W</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K upper W upper K Subscript i](images/c14_302.png), which is used to wrap (i.e. protect) a session key generated by the server when the key is transmitted to the subscriber *s*;
2.  A data-authentication key  <math alttext="upper D upper A upper K Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>A</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper D upper A upper K Subscript i](images/c14_303.png), which is used by the server and the subscriber  <math alttext="upper S Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript i](images/c14_304.png) to send authenticated-messages and to authenticate received messages.

![Figure 14.9 Relationships between the server of KDC and its subscribers.](images/c14f009.png)

[**Figure 14.9**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-fig-0009) Relationships between the server of KDC and its subscribers.

In general, key-wrapping and data-authentication keys are configured manually on the server and the subscribers. Key-wrapping keys are used by algorithms, such as AES key wrap, AES key wrap with padding, and Triple DEA key wrap (see Section 9.2.7). Data-authentication keys are used by algorithms such as CMAC and GMAC, which are discussed in [Chapter 9](#c09.xhtml). There exist two approaches to select the authentication and wrapping algorithms. In the first approach, the authentication and wrapping algorithms are fixed on all the components of the KDC (i.e. the server and subscribers) before requesting any session key generation. In the second approach, the subscriber that requests a new session key includes, in its request, information to indicate which algorithms (out of those available) to use and their parameters (e.g. the key bit-length and the hash output bit-length). Then, the provided inputs are either accepted or rejected by the KDC server or by the other subscriber(s). Notice that the second approach is more flexible than the first one, but it is more complex to implement. Without loss of generality, we assume in the sequel that the first approach is used.

**Notes**

*   – All subscribers must trust the KDC server. The latter must be protected against attacks. If the KDC server is compromised, all messages can be easily discovered.
*   – The availability of the KDC server is an issue. If the KDC server becomes faulty or inaccessible to some subscribers, some or all subscribers cannot establish session keys.

*Session key establishment*

When a subscriber  <math alttext="upper S Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript i](images/c14_305.png) needs to securely communicate with another subscriber  <math alttext="upper S Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript j](images/c14_306.png), and it does not share a session key with  <math alttext="upper S Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript j](images/c14_307.png) or needs to change the current session key shared with  <math alttext="upper S Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript j](images/c14_308.png), the following operations are performed:

1.  Subscriber  <math alttext="upper S Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript i](images/c14_309.png) sends an authenticated message  <math alttext="upper M 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 1](images/c14_310.png) to request a session key. The message  <math alttext="upper M 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 1](images/c14_311.png) includes, at least, the IDs of subscribers  <math alttext="upper S Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript i](images/c14_312.png) and  <math alttext="upper S Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript j](images/c14_313.png) and a tag computed by the subscriber  <math alttext="upper S Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript i](images/c14_314.png) using the key  <math alttext="upper D upper A upper K Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>A</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper D upper A upper K Subscript i](images/c14_315.png), which it shared with the server.
2.  The server receives the message  <math alttext="upper M 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 1](images/c14_316.png) and authenticates it, using the key  <math alttext="upper D upper A upper K Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>A</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper D upper A upper K Subscript i](images/c14_317.png) that it shares with subscriber  <math alttext="upper S Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript i](images/c14_318.png). If the authentication succeeds, the process continues; otherwise, no session key is delivered to subscriber  <math alttext="upper S Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S Subscript i](images/c14_319.png), an error notification is returned and the process is stopped.
3.  The server makes use of derivation function to generate a new session key  <math alttext="upper S upper K Subscript i comma j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S upper K Subscript i comma j](images/c14_320.png).
4.  The server makes use of a key-wrapping algorithm and the key-wrapping keys  <math alttext="upper K upper W upper K Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>W</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K upper W upper K Subscript i](images/c14_321.png) and  <math alttext="upper K upper W upper K Subscript j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>W</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K upper W upper K Subscript j](images/c14_322.png) to protect two copies of the session key  <math alttext="upper S upper K Subscript i comma j" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S upper K Subscript i comma j](images/c14_323.png). Depending on the implantation of the KDC, there are two options[^(17)](#c14.xhtml#c14-note-0017) to continue the process.
5.  Option 1 (illustrated in [Figure 14.10a](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0010)):

**Note**. One of the most known and currently used KDCs is with no doubt Kerberos. The latter is presented in Section 15.4.

### 14.3.3 Key-Establishment Using Public-Key-based Schemes

As previously mentioned, key-establishment includes key-agreement and key-transport. As shown in [Figure 14.11](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0011), there exist only two recommended schemes for key-transport (namely, KTS-OAEP and key-wrapping modes KW and KWP), while there exist several key-agreement schemes: two schemes are based on RSA, ten on Diffie-Hellman protocol, and four on Menezes-Qu-Vanstone protocol.

![Figure 14.11 Recommended public-key-based key-establishment schemes.](images/c14f011.png)

[**Figure 14.11**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-fig-0011) Recommended public-key-based key-establishment schemes.

Key-establishment may involve two or more parties. Without loss of generality, we assume, in the sequel, that only two parties are involved. The party, which starts the key-establishment process, is called the *initiator* of the key-establishment transaction; and the other party, the *recipient*.

In all the key-agreement and key-transport schemes described in this chapter, the key-pair (i.e. private and public keys) of a party is generated either by that party or by a trusted party. Then, the public key of each partner may be distributed to the other party either directly by the public-key owner or included in a certificate issued by an authority trusted by both parties. Thus, in the diagrams that will follow, the terms *Distribute* and *Obtain* public keys and dashed arrows are used in instead of *Send*, *Receive*, and solid arrows.

**Notes**

*   – To prevent attacks against implementations of cryptographic algorithms, it is recommended to destroy any sensitive copies of secrets and other parameters used during the execution of key-establishment transactions.
*   – The static (also referred to as long-term) public keys of the parties involved in key-agreement schemes are assumed to be generated and distributed (directly or via a trusted party) before starting agreement transactions.
*   – Once a shared secret *Z* is generated, it is provided as input to a key-derivation function to yield a shared key. Thus, any key-agreement transaction includes the agreed KDF and its parameters.

#### 14.3.3.1 Common Mechanisms and Functions

##### *14.3.3.1.1 Key-Confirmation*

In all the public-key based key-establishment schemes, the recipient may trust or not the public key of the other party. To provide assurance about the public key used in a key-establishment scheme, an operation, called *key-confirmation*, may be required. Using the key-confirmation, one party (or both) get(s) assurance that the other party has generated the shared secret using its private key, which must correspond to the public key used in the transaction. In other words, using the key-confirmation, the recipient has assurance that its partner effectively owns the key-pair used in the key-agreement or key-transport transaction. The key-confirmation may be unilateral (i.e. only one party requires the verification of key-pair possession) or bilateral (both parties require the verification key-pair possession). A bilateral key-confirmation is composed of two instances of the unilateral key-confirmation; thus, both parties can detect an error in the key-agreement process. Key-confirmation makes use of a MAC algorithm among the recommended algorithms (see [Table 14.4](#c14.xhtml#c14-tbl-0004)).

##### *14.3.3.1.2 Common Conversion Functions*

The following conversion functions are common to many schemes.

MAC algorithms recommended in key-establishment schemes are shown in [Table 14.7](#c14.xhtml#c14-tbl-0007).

#### 14.3.3.2 Key-Establishment Schemes Using RSA

##### *14.3.3.2.1 Key-Agreement Schemes Using RSA*

Two main families of key-agreement schemes (KASs) are recommended to establish a key between two parties  <math alttext="upper X and upper Y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mtext>&#160;and&#160;</mtext><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> ![upper X and upper Y](images/c14_402.png) \[[7](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0007)\]. Both KAS families may be used with or without key-confirmation. They differ mainly in the number, one or two, of key-pairs that are used.

Before starting the key-agreement, both parties must agree on the key-derivation function to use and its associated hash function. In addition, if a confirmation is required, the parties must agree on a MAC algorithm and the parameters to use (i.e. bit-lengths of the MAC key and MAC tag). The agreement on the MAC parameters to use is out of the scope of the KASs. Both KASs make use of two operations, *RSASVE\_GENERATE* (RSA Secret-Value Encapsulation) and  <math alttext="upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period r e c o v e r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>V</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period r e c o v e r](images/c14_403.png):

1.   <math alttext="upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period g e n e r a t e left-parenthesis upper N comma e right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>V</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period g e n e r a t e left-parenthesis upper N comma e right-parenthesis](images/c14_404.png): this operation enables one party to generate a shared secret *Z*, and to encrypt it with the public key of the other party. The operation makes use of a DRBG to produce a random bit-string with the same bit-length than that of the modulus *N*. The output of this operation is a pair  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper Z comma upper C right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper Z comma upper C right-parenthesis](images/c14_405.png), a shared secret and its ciphertext.
2.   <math alttext="upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period r e c o v e r left-parenthesis upper N comma d right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>V</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period r e c o v e r left-parenthesis upper N comma d right-parenthesis](images/c14_406.png): this operation enables the ciphertext recipient to decrypt the received message with its private key in order to recover the shared secret *Z*.

The pseudocode of  <math alttext="upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period g e n e r a t e and upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period r e c o v e r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>V</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mtext>&#160;and</mtext><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>V</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period g e n e r a t e and upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period r e c o v e r](images/c14_407.png) operations is the following:

###### 14.3.3.2.1.1 Key-Agreement Scheme #1 (KAS1)

KAS1 makes use of a single key-pair. KAS1 family consists of two variants: basic-KAS1 (without key-confirmation) and Uni-Cnf-KAS1 (with unilateral key-confirmation). Both variants are depicted in [Figure 14.12](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0012).

![](images/c14f012.png)

[**Figure 14.12**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-fig-0012) Flow diagram of key-agreement scheme #1 (KAS1).

**Note.** In Tables 14.12-14.28, some steps are included without any performed operation; they aim to provide symmetry in party’s behavior.

Let *X* denote the party, which initiates the key agreement and *Y*, the recipient. Let  <math alttext="upper P r Subscript upper Y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript upper Y](images/c14_445.png) and  <math alttext="upper P u Subscript upper Y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P u Subscript upper Y](images/c14_446.png) denote the static private and public keys of the party *Y*, respectively.

The steps of the agreement scheme Basic-KAS1 are as follows:

1.  Party *X* generates a secret *Z* and encrypts it using  <math alttext="upper P u Subscript upper Y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P u Subscript upper Y](images/c14_447.png); the encrypted secret is denoted *C*; i.e. (*Z, C*) =  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper Z comma upper C right-parenthesis equals upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period g e n e r a t e left-parenthesis upper N comma e right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>V</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper Z comma upper C right-parenthesis equals upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period g e n e r a t e left-parenthesis upper N comma e right-parenthesis](images/c14_448.png)
2.  *C* is exchanged between the parties.
3.  Party *Y* recovers the shared secret using the operation  <math alttext="upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period r e c o v e r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>V</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period r e c o v e r](images/c14_449.png) and its private key  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper N comma d right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper N comma d right-parenthesis](images/c14_450.png); i.e. Z = RSASVE\_  <math alttext="upper Z equals upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period r e c o v e r left-parenthesis upper C comma upper N comma d right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>V</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper Z equals upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period r e c o v e r left-parenthesis upper C comma upper N comma d right-parenthesis](images/c14_451.png)
4.  Party *Y* generates[^(19)](#c14.xhtml#c14-note-0019) a nonce  <math alttext="upper N o n c e Subscript upper Y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper N o n c e Subscript upper Y](images/c14_452.png) and sends it to party *X*.
5.  Both parties use the shared secret *Z*, the nonce  <math alttext="upper N o n c e Subscript upper Y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper N o n c e Subscript upper Y](images/c14_453.png), and an agreed key-derivation function KDF (and may be other additional parameters depending on the KDF) to derive a new key *K* and a MAC key, if the key-confirmation is required. That is,
    
     <math alttext="upper K e y i n g upper M a t e r i a l equals left-parenthesis upper K left-bracket comma upper M a c upper K e y right-bracket right-parenthesis equals upper K upper D upper F left-parenthesis upper Z comma upper N o u n c e Subscript upper Y Baseline comma ellipsis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>K</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper K e y i n g upper M a t e r i a l equals left-parenthesis upper K left-bracket comma upper M a c upper K e y right-bracket right-parenthesis equals upper K upper D upper F left-parenthesis upper Z comma upper N o u n c e Subscript upper Y Baseline comma ellipsis right-parenthesis](images/c14_454.png) ([^(20)](#c14.xhtml#c14-note-0020))
    
6.  The shared secret *Z* is destroyed by both parties.

In Uni-Cnf-KAS1 variant, a MAC algorithm, a MAC bit-length,  <math alttext="upper T a g upper L e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper T a g upper L e n](images/c14_455.png), and the IDs of parties are included in key-agreement transaction. After Basic-KAS1, the following steps are performed:

Otherwise, the key-confirmation succeeds.

###### 14.3.3.2.1.2 Key-Agreement Scheme #2 (KAS2)

KAS2 makes use of two key-pairs; thus, both parties equally contribute to the shared secret construction, which is used to generate a new key. KAS2 family consists of three variants: BasicKAS2 (without key-confirmation), Uni-Cnf-KAS2 (with key-confirmation by one party), and Bil-Cnf-KAS2 (with bilateral key-confirmation). KAS2 variants are depicted in [Figure 14.13](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0013). Basic-KAS2 steps are as follows:

![](images/c14f013.png)

[**Figure 14.13**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-fig-0013)  Flow diagram of key-agreement scheme #2 (KAS2).

1.  Party *X* generates the first part of the shared secret, denoted  <math alttext="upper Z Subscript upper X" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>X</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper Z Subscript upper X](images/c14_471.png), and encrypts it using  <math alttext="upper P u Subscript upper Y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P u Subscript upper Y](images/c14_472.png); the encrypted secret is denoted  <math alttext="upper C Subscript upper X" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>X</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript upper X](images/c14_473.png); i.e.  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper Z Subscript upper X Baseline comma upper C Subscript upper X Baseline right-parenthesis equals upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period g e n e r a t e left-parenthesis upper N Subscript upper Y Baseline comma e Subscript upper Y Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>X</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>V</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper Z Subscript upper X Baseline comma upper C Subscript upper X Baseline right-parenthesis equals upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period g e n e r a t e left-parenthesis upper N Subscript upper Y Baseline comma e Subscript upper Y Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c14_474.png).
2.   <math alttext="upper C Subscript upper X" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>X</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript upper X](images/c14_475.png) is exchanged between the parties.
3.  Party *Y* recovers the first part of shared secret using the operation  <math alttext="upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period r e c o v e r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>V</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period r e c o v e r](images/c14_476.png) and its private key  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper N Subscript upper Y Baseline comma d right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper N Subscript upper Y Baseline comma d right-parenthesis](images/c14_477.png); i.e.  <math alttext="upper Z Subscript upper X Baseline equals upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period r e c o v e r left-parenthesis upper C Subscript upper Y Baseline comma upper N Subscript upper Y Baseline comma d Subscript upper Y Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>V</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper Z Subscript upper X Baseline equals upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period r e c o v e r left-parenthesis upper C Subscript upper Y Baseline comma upper N Subscript upper Y Baseline comma d Subscript upper Y Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c14_478.png).
    
4.  Party *Y* generates the second part of the shared secret, denoted  <math alttext="upper Z Subscript upper Y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper Z Subscript upper Y](images/c14_479.png), and encrypts it using  <math alttext="upper P u Subscript upper X" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>X</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P u Subscript upper X](images/c14_480.png); the encrypted secret is denoted  <math alttext="upper C Subscript upper Y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript upper Y](images/c14_481.png); i.e.  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper Z Subscript upper Y Baseline comma upper C Subscript upper Y Baseline right-parenthesis equals upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period g e n e r a t e left-parenthesis upper N Subscript upper X Baseline comma e Subscript upper X Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>V</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>X</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper Z Subscript upper Y Baseline comma upper C Subscript upper Y Baseline right-parenthesis equals upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period g e n e r a t e left-parenthesis upper N Subscript upper X Baseline comma e Subscript upper X Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c14_482.png).

6.  Party *X* recovers the shared secret using the operation  <math alttext="upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period r e c o v e r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>V</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period r e c o v e r](images/c14_484.png) and its private key  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper N Subscript upper X Baseline comma d Subscript upper X Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>X</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper N Subscript upper X Baseline comma d Subscript upper X Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c14_485.png); i.e.  <math alttext="upper Z Subscript upper Y Baseline equals upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period r e c o v e r left-parenthesis upper C Subscript upper Y Baseline comma upper N Subscript upper X Baseline comma d Subscript upper X Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>V</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>X</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper Z Subscript upper Y Baseline equals upper R upper S upper A upper S upper V upper E period r e c o v e r left-parenthesis upper C Subscript upper Y Baseline comma upper N Subscript upper X Baseline comma d Subscript upper X Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c14_486.png).
7.  Both parties form the shared secret *Z*, as  <math alttext="upper Z equals upper Z Subscript upper X Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper Z Subscript upper Y Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper Z equals upper Z Subscript upper X Baseline StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper Z Subscript upper Y Baseline](images/c14_487.png).
8.  Both parties use the shared secret *Z* and an agreed key-derivation function KDF (and may be other additional parameters depending on the KDF) to derive a new key *K*. They derive a MAC key, if the key-confirmation is required;  <math alttext="upper K e y i n g upper M a t e r i a l equals upper K upper D upper F left-parenthesis upper Z comma ellipsis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>K</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper K e y i n g upper M a t e r i a l equals upper K upper D upper F left-parenthesis upper Z comma ellipsis right-parenthesis](images/c14_488.png).
9.  The shared secrets  <math alttext="upper Z comma upper Z Subscript upper X Baseline comma and upper Z Subscript upper Y Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;and&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper Z comma upper Z Subscript upper X Baseline comma and upper Z Subscript upper Y Baseline](images/c14_489.png) are destroyed.

Unilateral or bilateral confirmation may be added to the basic KAS2 to build the Uni-Cnf-KAS2 and Bil-Cnf-KAS2 respectively. Bil-Cnf-KAS2 is the double instantiation of Uni-Cnf-KAS1 steps. The key-confirmation steps are depicted in [Figure 14.14](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0014).

![](images/c14f014.png)

[**Figure 14.14**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-fig-0014)  Flow diagram of key-confirmation alternatives for KAS2.

##### *14.3.3.2.2 Key-Transport Schemes Using RSA*

In the key-transport schemes (KTSs), the initiator of the transaction selects a key and then sends it to the recipient. It is recommended to use the Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding (OAEP) procedure to encrypt the key and the additional inputs \[[7](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0007)\]. The OAEP procedure is described in Section 12.2.5. Therefore, OAEP is added as a suffix to RSA-based KTS. KTS-OAEP family has two variants, Basic-KTS-OAEP (without key-confirmation) and Uni-Cnf-KTS-OAEP (with unilateral key-confirmation). KTS-OAEP specifies only a unilateral key-confirmation, because a single key-pair is used in the transaction. The material used to perform key-confirmation in KTS is the same as in KASs.

The keying material (i.e. the secret key and the MAC key, if a key-confirmation is required) is encrypted with *RSA-OAEP-Encrypt* operation and decrypted with *RSA-OAEP-Decrypt*. Notice that the modulus *N* of the key-pair of the transaction initiator must be at least equal to the key to transport, because the ciphertext of the key is yielded  <math alttext="m o d u l o upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![m o d u l o upper N](images/c14_555.png).

Both KTS-OAEP variants are depicted in [Figure 14.15](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0015). The steps of Basic KTS-OAEP scheme are as follows:

![](images/c14f015.png)

[**Figure 14.15**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-fig-0015) Flow diagram of Key-transport scheme (KTS-OAEP).

1.  Party *X* selects the key *K* to transport and the optional input *A*.
2.  Party *X* encrypts the key *K* and optional input *A* using public key  <math alttext="upper P u Subscript upper Y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P u Subscript upper Y](images/c14_556.png). The encrypted secret is denoted *C*; i.e.  <math alttext="upper C equals upper R upper S upper A soft hyphen upper O upper A upper E upper P soft hyphen upper E n c r y p t left-parenthesis upper P u Subscript upper Y Baseline comma upper K comma upper A right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>&#173;</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>&#173;</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>y</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper C equals upper R upper S upper A soft hyphen upper O upper A upper E upper P soft hyphen upper E n c r y p t left-parenthesis upper P u Subscript upper Y Baseline comma upper K comma upper A right-parenthesis](images/c14_557.png).
3.  Ciphertext *C* is exchanged between parties.
4.  Party *Y* recovers the key *K*; it recovers the  <math alttext="upper M a c upper K e y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M a c upper K e y](images/c14_558.png), if a unilateral key-confirmation is required.  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper K comma upper M a c upper K e y right-parenthesis equals upper R upper S upper A soft hyphen upper O upper A upper E upper P soft hyphen upper D e c r y p t left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper N comma d right-parenthesis comma upper C right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>&#173;</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>&#173;</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>y</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper K comma upper M a c upper K e y right-parenthesis equals upper R upper S upper A soft hyphen upper O upper A upper E upper P soft hyphen upper D e c r y p t left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper N comma d right-parenthesis comma upper C right-parenthesis](images/c14_559.png)

#### 14.3.3.3 DLC-based Key-Agreement Schemes

##### *14.3.3.3.1 DLC-based Primitives for Shared-Secret Generation*

Four primitives are used to compute a shared secret based either on FFC or on ECC:

*   Primitive FFC-DH: computes a shared secret using Diffie-Hellman algorithm based on the finite-field cryptography (see Section 12.3.2).
*   Primitive ECC-CDH: computes a shared secret using EC cofactor Diffie-Hellman algorithm based on the elliptic-curve cryptography (see Section 13.5.3).
*   Primitive FFC-MQV: computes a shared secret using Menezes-Qu-Vanstone algorithm based on the finite-field cryptography (see Section 12.3.3).
*   Primitive ECC-MQV: computes a shared secret using Menezes-Qu-Vanstone algorithm based on the elliptic-curve cryptography (see Section 13.5.4).

The four primitives are used in the next subsection to build key-agreement schemes. Before calling these primitives, the domain parameters should be selected and the required key-pairs generated. The output of the primitives is a shared secret that will be used in a subsequent step to generate a secret key and, when needed, other keying material.

Pseudocodes of the primitives are as follows:

##### *14.3.3.3.2 Key-Agreement Categories and Common Steps*

Fourteen DLC-based key-agreement schemes (KASs) are recommended \[[14](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0014)\]: ten Diffie-Hellman-based schemes and four Menezes-Qu-Vanstone-based schemes. DLC-based KASs are grouped into two categories: agreement schemes based on FFC (Finite Field Cryptography) and those based on ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography). Another distinctive feature of DLC-based KASs is the number of static and ephemeral keys that are used (see [Figure 14.16](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0016)). The most robust (but the most resource consuming) schemes are the ones in which each partner participates in the key-agreement with its static and ephemeral keys. The lightest schemes are those in which only ephemeral keys are used; hence, trust between parties is required before performing key-agreement transactions. As shown in [Figure 14.17](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0017), DLC-based KASs are built using six steps (not all the steps are required in all key-agreement schemes):

![Figure 14.16 Categorization of DLC-based key-agreement schemes.](images/c14f016.png)

[**Figure 14.16**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-fig-0016) Categorization of DLC-based key-agreement schemes.

![Figure 14.17 Main steps of DLC-based key-agreement schemes.](images/c14f017.png)

[**Figure 14.17**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-fig-0017) Main steps of DLC-based key-agreement schemes.

*   Selection of the (FFC or ECC) domain parameters and a key-derivation function and its parameters. This step is out of the scope of the key-agreement transaction.
*   Generation and distribution of the static public key(s), if required. This step is out of the scope of the key-agreement transaction.
*   Generation and exchange of ephemeral public key(s), if required.
*   Computation of a shared secret. This step is mandatory.
*   Derivation of keying material, which includes a secret shared key and a MAC key (to generate tags used in key-confirmation step). This step is mandatory.
*   Key-confirmation, which enables one party to provide to the other party assurance about its used public key.

##### *14.3.3.3.3 Key-Confirmation*

Key-confirmation may be included in most of the DLC-based key-agreement transactions to provide assurance that a party possesses the static private key associated with the static public key used in the key-agreement process. Like RSA-based KASs, DLC-based KASs can specify unilateral (when only a single static public key is used) or bilateral (if a pair of static public keys are used) key-confirmation.

The parameters (MAC algorithm and MAC bit-length) and operations (generation and exchange of tags) used in key-confirmation in DLC-based KASs are the same than those used in RSA-based KASs ([Section 14.2.2.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-03009)). The only difference is in the values used in tag generation. The MAC key (denoted  <math alttext="upper M a c upper K e y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M a c upper K e y](images/c14_626.png)) used to generate the tags is extracted from the output of the KDF by both parties. There exist four key-confirmation schemes:

1.  2e-2s key-confirmation scheme is applicable when two ephemeral and two static public keys are used. Each of the parties participates with an ephemeral key, denoted  <math alttext="upper E p h e m Subscript upper X Baseline or upper E p h e m Subscript upper Y Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>h</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mtext>&#160;or&#160;</mtext><mi>E</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>h</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper E p h e m Subscript upper X Baseline or upper E p h e m Subscript upper Y Baseline](images/c14_627.png). The 2e-2s key-confirmation scheme is depicted in [Figure 14.18](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0018).
    
    ![Figure 14.18  Flow diagrams of key-confirmation in 2ephemeral-2static KASs.](images/c14f018.png)
    
    [**Figure 14.18**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-fig-0018)  Flow diagrams of key-confirmation in 2ephemeral-2static KASs.
    
2.  1e-2s key-confirmation scheme is applicable when only one party, say *X*, makes use of an ephemeral public key and two static public keys are used. Party *Y* participates in the key-confirmation by a nonce, instead of an ephemeral key. The 1e-2s key-confirmation is depicted in [Figure 14.19](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0019).
    
    ![Figure 14.19  Flow diagrams of key-confirmation in 1-ephemeral-2static KASs.](images/c14f019.png)
    
    [**Figure 14.19**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-fig-0019)  Flow diagrams of key-confirmation in 1-ephemeral-2static KASs.
    
3.  1e-1s key-confirmation scheme is applicable when the party *X* has an ephemeral public key and the party *Y* has a static public key. No bilateral key-confirmation is provided, because there is a single static public key in this scheme. Party *X* participates with a nonce. The 1e-1s key-confirmation is depicted in [Figure 14.20](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0020).
    
    ![Figure 14.20  Flow diagram of key-confirmation in 1-ephemeral-1static KASs.](images/c14f020.png)
    
    [**Figure 14.20**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-fig-0020)  Flow diagram of key-confirmation in 1-ephemeral-1static KASs.
    
4.  0e-2s key-confirmation scheme is applicable when no ephemeral public key is used and two static public keys are used. The 0e-2s key-confirmation is depicted in [Figure 14.21](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0021).

![Figure 14.21 Flow diagrams of key-confirmation in 0-ephemeral-2static KASs.](images/c14f021.png)

[**Figure 14.21**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-fig-0021) Flow diagrams of key-confirmation in 0-ephemeral-2static KASs.

Each key-confirmation scheme may have three alternatives: unilateral key-confirmation provided by party *X*, unilateral key-confirmation provided by party *Y*, or a bilateral key-confirmation.

## 14.4 Problems and Solutions

### 14.4.1 List of Problems

***Problem 14.1***

Bob needs to generate two RSA key-pairs to communicate with Alice and Charlie. He selects two moduli  <math alttext="upper N 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper N 1](images/c14_911.png) and  <math alttext="upper N 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper N 2](images/c14_912.png), which have a common factor. Show that such a strategy is extremely dangerous.

***Problem 14.2***

Assume that Alice and Bob are members of a private network in which all the RSA public keys have a modulus in the interval  <math alttext="left-bracket 2 Superscript 2047 Baseline comma 2 Superscript 2048 Baseline minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>2047</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>2048</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 2 Superscript 2047 Baseline comma 2 Superscript 2048 Baseline minus 1 right-bracket](images/c14_913.png) and the same public exponent  <math alttext="e equals 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![e equals 3](images/c14_914.png). Alice decides to use the following scheme to generate a 256-bit AES key to encrypt/decrypt data exchanged with Bob:

*   – Alice selects a random integer  <math alttext="upper K contains-as-member left-bracket 0 comma 2 Superscript 256 Baseline minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8715;</mo><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>256</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![upper K contains-as-member left-bracket 0 comma 2 Superscript 256 Baseline minus 1 right-bracket](images/c14_915.png).
*   – She computes  <math alttext="upper C equals upper K Superscript e Baseline m o d upper N Subscript upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C equals upper K Superscript e Baseline m o d upper N Subscript upper B](images/c14_916.png), where  <math alttext="upper N Subscript upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper N Subscript upper B](images/c14_917.png) denotes the modulus of Bob’s public key; and she sends *C* to Bob.
*   – Upon receipt of message *C*, Bob decrypts the message to obtain the key *K*;  <math alttext="upper K equals upper C Superscript d Super Subscript upper B Baseline m o d upper N Subscript upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K equals upper C Superscript d Super Subscript upper B Baseline m o d upper N Subscript upper B](images/c14_918.png), where  <math alttext="d Subscript upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![d Subscript upper B](images/c14_919.png) denotes the private key of Bob.
*   – Then, both parties send and receive messages, encrypted and decrypted using AES-256 with the key *K*.

1.  Show that, using the encrypted message *C*, a malicious member in the private network can recover the AES key generated by Alice.
2.  Suggest an idea to Alice to make her protocol secure.

***Problem 14.3***

Discuss why it is recommended, when using RSA, to select large primes *p* and *q* such that  <math alttext="StartAbsoluteValue p minus q EndAbsoluteValue ampersand gt semicolon 2 Superscript StartFraction l e n left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis Over 2 EndFraction minus 100" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#38;gt;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![StartAbsoluteValue p minus q EndAbsoluteValue ampersand gt semicolon 2 Superscript StartFraction l e n left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis Over 2 EndFraction minus 100](images/c14_920.png).

***Problem 14.4***

Consider a virtual network of 1000 hosts, which need to secure their communications using symmetric keys. The first solution is to associate a permanent symmetric key with each pair of hosts; the second is to use a KDC to generate session keys, on-demand. Assume that any host can exchange data simultaneously with at most two other peers.

1.  What is the number of permanent and session keys in both solution?
2.  Discuss the advantages of the second solution compared to the first one.
3.  Assume that all hosts include two encryption algorithms, AES-CBC and AES-GCM. Which algorithm do you recommend to secure communications between hosts?

***Problem 14.5***

In this problem, we discuss some properties and weaknesses of the KDC-based establishment scheme described in [Section 14.3.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-02006).

1.  Can Eve obtain a session key on behalf of Bob; and then communicate with Alice who does not trust her?
2.  Is the scheme vulnerable to replay attacks? If yes, suggest a solution to prevent replay attacks.

***Problem*** ***14.6***

Alice and Bob receive from a third party a key *K*, of *m* bits, to secure their exchanges. They make use of a dedicated protocol to guarantee that they effectively share the same key. Alice generates an *m*\-bit random integer  <math alttext="upper N Subscript upper A" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper N Subscript upper A](images/c14_921.png); then, she computes and sends to Bob a message including the integer  <math alttext="upper C Subscript upper A Baseline equals upper N Subscript upper A Baseline circled-plus upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript upper A Baseline equals upper N Subscript upper A Baseline circled-plus upper K](images/c14_922.png). Then, upon reception of the integer  <math alttext="upper C Subscript upper A" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript upper A](images/c14_923.png), Bob XORes  <math alttext="upper C Subscript upper A" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript upper A](images/c14_924.png) with the shared key and sends the  <math alttext="upper C Subscript upper B Baseline equals upper C Subscript upper A Baseline circled-plus upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript upper B Baseline equals upper C Subscript upper A Baseline circled-plus upper K](images/c14_925.png). Next, Alice makes the verification. Then, Bob initiates the same key verification operation than that of Alice.

1.  Show that the protocol above enables both parties to confirm that they share the same key.
2.  Show that the protocol used by Alice and Bob enables Eve, who passively listens to communications between Alice and Bob, to easily recover their secret key.

***Problem 14.7***

Alice and Bob agree to use the Diffie-Hellman protocol with prime *p* and generator *g*. They perform the following actions:

*   – Alice generates a random integer *x* and computes her public key  <math alttext="upper K u Subscript upper A Baseline equals g Superscript x Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K u Subscript upper A Baseline equals g Superscript x Baseline m o d p](images/c14_926.png); and sends it to Bob.
*   – Bob generates a random integer *y* and computes his public key  <math alttext="upper K u Subscript upper B Baseline equals g Superscript y Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>y</mi></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K u Subscript upper B Baseline equals g Superscript y Baseline m o d p](images/c14_927.png); and sends it to Alice.
*   – Upon receiving Bob’s public key, Alice computes the shared key  <math alttext="upper K equals upper K u Subscript upper B Superscript x Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>K</mi><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>x</mi></msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K equals upper K u Subscript upper B Superscript x Baseline m o d p](images/c14_928.png).
*   – Upon receiving Alice’s public key, Bob computes the shared key  <math alttext="upper K equals upper K u Subscript upper A Superscript y Baseline m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>K</mi><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>y</mi></msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K equals upper K u Subscript upper A Superscript y Baseline m o d p](images/c14_929.png).
*   – Then, Alice and Bob exchange messages encrypted using the key *K*.
*   – Which of security properties are guaranteed: confidentiality, integrity, or/and authenticity?
