***Problem 14.12***

In 1979, Shamir proposed an original secret sharing scheme to enable a group of members to share a secret, which is represented by *n* pieces. Notice that the pieces are not fragments of the secret. At least  <math alttext="k comma k less-than n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>k</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![k comma k less-than n](images/c14_947.png), pieces are required to reconstruct the secret. Less than *k* pieces cannot reconstruct the secret. Shamir’s secret sharing scheme works as follows:

*   – *Let* *D* *be the data representing the secret*.
*   – *D* *is represented by n pieces, denoted*  <math alttext="upper D 1 comma upper D 2 comma ellipsis comma upper D Subscript n Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper D 1 comma upper D 2 comma ellipsis comma upper D Subscript n Baseline](images/c14_948.png).
*   – *Pick a random prime* *p* *bigger than both* *D* *and* *n*.
*   – *Pick a polynomial*  <math alttext="upper Q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper Q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c14_949.png) *of degree*  <math alttext="k minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![k minus 1](images/c14_950.png)
    
     <math alttext="upper Q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals a 0 plus a 1 x plus a 2 x squared plus period period plus a Subscript left-parenthesis k minus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline x Superscript left-parenthesis k minus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>..</mn><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper Q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals a 0 plus a 1 x plus a 2 x squared plus period period plus a Subscript left-parenthesis k minus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline x Superscript left-parenthesis k minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c14_951.png)
    
    – where all the coefficients  <math alttext="a Subscript i Baseline s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> ![a Subscript i Baseline s](images/c14_952.png) are integers.  <math alttext="a 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![a 0](images/c14_953.png) is required to be equal to *D* and the other coefficients are randomly chosen in the interval  <math alttext="left-bracket 0 comma p minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 0 comma p minus 1 right-bracket](images/c14_954.png).
    
*   – *The pieces are computed as follows*:
*    <math alttext="upper D 1 equals upper Q left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper D 1 equals upper Q left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis m o d p](images/c14_955.png),  <math alttext="upper D 2 equals upper Q left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper D 2 equals upper Q left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis m o d p](images/c14_956.png)*, …*,  <math alttext="upper D Subscript n Baseline equals upper Q left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper D Subscript n Baseline equals upper Q left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis m o d p](images/c14_957.png)
*   – *The pieces and their indices are distributed among the group members; i.e. each group member holds one or several pairs*  <math alttext="left-parenthesis upper D Subscript i Baseline comma i right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis upper D Subscript i Baseline comma i right-parenthesis](images/c14_958.png). *The same piece may be held by one or more members*.
*   – *Reconstitution of the secret*:

The correctness of Shamir’s relies on the fact that given *k* points  <math alttext="left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline comma y Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline comma y Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c14_961.png), with distinct  <math alttext="x Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![x Subscript i](images/c14_962.png)’s, there exists one and only one polynomial  <math alttext="upper Q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper Q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c14_963.png), of degree *k*, such that  <math alttext="y Subscript i Baseline equals upper Q left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> ![y Subscript i Baseline equals upper Q left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma k](images/c14_964.png). Shamir showed that by using  <math alttext="n equals 2 k minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![n equals 2 k minus 1](images/c14_965.png), one gets a very robust scheme.

Consider that the staff members in a bank make use of Shamir’s scheme to share the combination of a safe, say  <math alttext="upper D equals 1723" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1723</mn></mrow></math> ![upper D equals 1723](images/c14_966.png). To compute the pieces, the following values are chosen:  <math alttext="n equals 6" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> ![n equals 6](images/c14_967.png),  <math alttext="k equals 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![k equals 3](images/c14_968.png), and  <math alttext="p equals 1999" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1999</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 1999](images/c14_969.png). The chosen polynomial  <math alttext="upper Q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper Q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c14_970.png) is of degree 2 and is defined by  <math alttext="1723 plus 1500 x plus 1001 x squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1723</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1500</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1001</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![1723 plus 1500 x plus 1001 x squared](images/c14_971.png).

1.  Show how the piece values are computed.
2.  Take three pieces and their indices, then reconstruct the safe combination.

### 14.4.2 Solutions to Problems

***Problem 14.1***

Given two moduli  <math alttext="upper N 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper N 1](images/c14_972.png) and  <math alttext="upper N 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper N 2](images/c14_973.png), it is easy to find their greatest common divider,  <math alttext="upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis upper N 1 comma upper N 2 right-parenthesis equals p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper G upper C upper D left-parenthesis upper N 1 comma upper N 2 right-parenthesis equals p](images/c14_974.png). Since any RSA modulus is a product of only two primes, if the first prime is found, then it is very easy to find the second. Therefore, any observer who has access to Bob’s public keys can easily disclose the private keys he is using.

***Problem 14.2***

1.  The malicious member in the network knows that the modulus of any public key is in the interval  <math alttext="left-bracket 2 Superscript 2047 Baseline comma 2 Superscript 2048 Baseline minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>2047</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>2048</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 2 Superscript 2047 Baseline comma 2 Superscript 2048 Baseline minus 1 right-bracket](images/c14_975.png) and its public exponent is  <math alttext="e equals 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![e equals 3](images/c14_976.png). Any key *K*, randomly selected by Alice, has a value less than  <math alttext="2 Superscript 256" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>256</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 256](images/c14_977.png). Thus,  <math alttext="upper K cubed less-than 2 Superscript 256 asterisk 3 Baseline less-than 2 Superscript 2047 Baseline less-than-or-equal-to upper N Subscript upper B Baseline less-than 2 Superscript 2048 Baseline upper K cubed m o d upper N Subscript upper B Baseline equals upper K cubed equals upper C" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>&#60;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>256</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#60;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>2047</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>2048</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>K</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K cubed less-than 2 Superscript 256 asterisk 3 Baseline less-than 2 Superscript 2047 Baseline less-than-or-equal-to upper N Subscript upper B Baseline less-than 2 Superscript 2048 Baseline upper K cubed m o d upper N Subscript upper B Baseline equals upper K cubed equals upper C](images/c14_978.png). Therefore, using *C*, the attacker can derive the secret key shared by Alice and Bob, i.e.  <math alttext="upper K equals upper C Superscript one-third" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper K equals upper C Superscript one-third](images/c14_979.png).
2.  To make Alice’s protocol secure, one suggestion would be to generate a random integer *n* in the interval  <math alttext="left-bracket 1 comma 2 Superscript 2048 Baseline minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>2048</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 1 comma 2 Superscript 2048 Baseline minus 1 right-bracket](images/c14_980.png). Then, she computes and sends  <math alttext="upper C equals n Superscript e Baseline m o d upper N Subscript upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C equals n Superscript e Baseline m o d upper N Subscript upper B](images/c14_981.png). Next, *n* is recovered by Bob. Then, Alice and Bob use the rightmost 256 bits of *n* as their AES-256 key.

***Problem 14.3***

Let RSA modulus  <math alttext="upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![upper N](images/c14_982.png) be of large bit-length, say 2048. Imagine an attacker who assumes that one of the primes, <math alttext="p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![p](images/c14_983.png) or *q*, say *p*, is of a short bit-length, say *m* bits. Then, the attacker can test a maximum of  <math alttext="2 Superscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript m](images/c14_984.png) integers to factorize *N*; and then discloses the second prime and the private key. The attack succeeds using reasonable resources, if *m* is less than 80; even if the bit-length of the modulus is very large, it does not prevent the recovery of the private key if one of the primes is small. When the modulus *N* is of a bit-length of 2048 or even more (e.g. 3072 or 4096) and *p* and *q* primes are selected such that  <math alttext="StartAbsoluteValue p minus q EndAbsoluteValue ampersand gt semicolon 2 Superscript StartFraction l e n left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis Over 2 EndFraction minus 100" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#38;gt;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![StartAbsoluteValue p minus q EndAbsoluteValue ampersand gt semicolon 2 Superscript StartFraction l e n left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis Over 2 EndFraction minus 100](images/c14_985.png), the bit-lengths of both primes is in magnitude of 1000 or even more, which makes the attack above computationally infeasible.

Lenstra’s elliptic curve factorization method is the most efficient method to factorize large integers, when one of their prime factors is small.

***Problem 14.4***

1.  In the first solution,  <math alttext="1000 asterisk 999 slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1000</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>999</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![1000 asterisk 999 slash 2](images/c14_986.png) permanent keys are required.
    
    In the second solution, 1000 authentication keys and 1000 wrapping keys are required; in total, 2000 permanent keys are required. Wrapping keys are used to transport session keys. Since each host can exchange at most with two other peers, a maximum of 1000 session keys may be used.
    
2.  In the first solution, the number of keys (keys to configure, store, and communicate to all parties) is large. In addition, if a key shared between two parties is compromised, all the plaintexts exchanged between the parties can be recovered and a manual reconfiguration of the key is required to protect the future exchanges. In the second solution, there are less keys to store, to change manually, and to secure. Session keys are generated on-demand and hosts can change them to prevent attacks making exploitation of a huge plaintexts encrypted with the same key. If the *i*^(th) session key is compromised, only the plaintexts encrypted with the *i*^(th) session key can be recovered.
3.  AES-CBC provides only confidentiality guarantees, while AES-GCM provides authenticity and confidentiality. In both solutions, to prevent attacks that alter the ciphertexts, we recommend the use of AES-GCM. In general, when a KDC is used, it is recommended that subscribers use session keys with authenticated-encryption algorithms to preserve confidentiality and integrity.

***Problem 14.5***

1.  The session-key request includes the IDs of the parties that need to obtain a session key and a tag computed with the authentication key shared between the request-originator and the server. In addition, the session key is wrapped using the wrapping-key of the request originator. Therefore, unless Eve knows the authentication and wrapping keys of Bob, she cannot impersonate Bob to generate a session key, shared with Alice, with Bob being the originator of the request.
2.  The KDC scheme is vulnerable to replay attacks as shown by the following example. Bob establishes a first session key with Alice. To limit the amount of data encrypted with the same session key, Bob requests a new session key for each data block to send to Alice. Eve intercepts the first authenticated message containing the first wrapped session-key. Then, each time Bob requests a new session key, Eve intercepts the request and replies with the message that contains the first session key. Notice that Eve cannot know the value of the session key, but she compels Alice and Bob to use the same session key for a long time and maybe she can infer some information about the ciphertexts she intercepts. To prevent replay attacks, one solution is to use a nonce in each key request; the same nonce is included in the message returned by the server. Since both messages (i.e. the request and the response) are authenticated and they include a nonce, the replay attack cannot succeed.

2.  The protocol used by Alice and Bob is insecure when their exchanges can be intercepted. If Eve receives the messages  <math alttext="upper C Subscript upper A" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript upper A](images/c14_993.png) and  <math alttext="upper C Subscript upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript upper B](images/c14_994.png), she derives the secret key by: <math alttext="upper C Subscript upper A Baseline circled-plus upper C Subscript upper B Baseline equals upper N Subscript upper A Baseline circled-plus upper K circled-plus upper N Subscript upper A Baseline equals upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><mi>K</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8853;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> ![upper C Subscript upper A Baseline circled-plus upper C Subscript upper B Baseline equals upper N Subscript upper A Baseline circled-plus upper K circled-plus upper N Subscript upper A Baseline equals upper K](images/c14_995.png).

***Problem 14.7***

No security properties are guaranteed with the proposed actions, because of the man-in-the-middle-attack. An attacker who can intercept the first message (which contains a public key) sent by Alice or Bob, can reply to the sender using his own public key, which results in a shared key computed between a legitimate party and the attacker.

***Problem 14.8***

In general, static public keys are distributed by a trusted third party or each static public key is included in the sender’s digital certificate to prove that the name of the entity on the certificate owns the private key associated with the public key. A key-agreement is a process to establish a secret key between two parties to exchange confidential data. If no static public key is used, both parties cannot trust each other. Therefore, it is not recommended to use a key-agreement without static public keys. Otherwise, any interested attacker can apply a man-in-the-middle attack and compromise the confidentiality of transmitted data. For example, consider the following scenario:

*   Bob wants to establish a secret key with Alice. He generates an ephemeral key-pair and sends his ephemeral public key to Alice. Eve intercepts the message sent by Bob and replies with her ephemeral public key. Then, Bob and Eve compute a shared secret, which contains a secret key *K*. Next, Bob encrypts his messages using the key *K*, which is known to Eve. Therefore, no transmitted data by Bob remains confidential to Eve.
    

***Problem 14.9***

Since the hash function *H* is not invertible, Eve cannot recover any session key before session *m*, whatever the key-derivation method from the three.

In Derivation 1, once the key of session *m* is recovered, Eve can derive the session keys of all the subsequent sessions, because the hash function is public. The same applies to Derivation 2, because the <math alttext="upper S upper K Subscript m plus 1 Baseline equals upper H left-parenthesis upper S upper K Subscript m Baseline circled-plus left-parenthesis m plus 1 right-parenthesis m o d 2 Superscript upper H l e n Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8853;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>H</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S upper K Subscript m plus 1 Baseline equals upper H left-parenthesis upper S upper K Subscript m Baseline circled-plus left-parenthesis m plus 1 right-parenthesis m o d 2 Superscript upper H l e n Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c14_996.png), where all elements (i.e.  <math alttext="upper S upper K Subscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S upper K Subscript m](images/c14_997.png), *m*,  <math alttext="upper H l e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper H l e n](images/c14_998.png), and *H*) are known to Eve.

In Derivation 3, once the key of session *m* is recovered, Eve cannot derive the session keys of the subsequent sessions, because the key  <math alttext="upper S upper K Subscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S upper K Subscript m](images/c14_999.png) is XORed with  <math alttext="upper K m s t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K m s t](images/c14_1000.png) before hashing. Therefore, Eve cannot recover  <math alttext="upper S upper K Subscript m plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S upper K Subscript m plus 1](images/c14_1001.png) only from  <math alttext="upper S upper K Subscript m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S upper K Subscript m](images/c14_1002.png); she needs  <math alttext="upper K m s t" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K m s t](images/c14_1003.png).

***Problem 14.10***

1.  There are mainly two reasons, which are extensively discussed in literature. The first is that for the same security strength, the asymmetric encryption is known to be very slow compared to symmetric encryption, in particular when symmetric encryption is achieved by hardware. The second reason is that the symmetric encryption preserves the length of the plaintext, while some asymmetric encryption algorithms, such as RSA-OAEP, need to extend the original plaintext with padding bits to prevent some attacks, when the very short messages are encrypted (see Problem 12.5).
2.  If only the recipient public key is available, the sender encrypts data using this public key and the recipient decrypts using his/her private key. Alternatively, the sender can generate a symmetric key *K*, encrypts it with the recipient public key, and sends it to the data recipient. Then, the sender encrypts the data using the symmetric key *K*, which is known to the recipient.

***Problem 14.11***

When Alice and Bob use the Diffie-Hellman scheme with a modulus *p* of 1024, they establish a session key of a bit-length of 1024, which is larger than the keys used by AES or DEA. Therefore, only a piece of the session key can be used to encrypt with either AES or DEA. There exist many ways to derive a block cipher key from a session key. In practice, key-derivation functions are used. Let us focus on the methods suggested in this problem.

1.  Use of AES: it is admitted that brute-force attack against AES-128 is computationally infeasible using the current technologies. Since the session key  <math alttext="upper K Subscript upper A comma upper B" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript upper A comma upper B](images/c14_1004.png) is unknown to Eve, the three proposed methods provide the same security strength. From the known plaintext, Eve cannot recover the AES key to disclose other plaintexts. Notice that the third method makes use of a hash function, which does not increase the security strength.
2.  Use of DEA: it is known that DEA key recovery using brute-force attack is computationally feasible, because  <math alttext="2 Superscript 56" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>56</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 56](images/c14_1005.png) keys can be tested with an acceptable
3.  computation time. 
    1.  The first method enables to change the DEA key after 100 blocks, which seems introducing unpredictability in DEA keys. When ciphertext, at the position of the known plaintext, is intercepted, Eve runs a brute-force attack (i.e. she tests a maximum of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 56" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>56</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 56](images/c14_1006.png) keys) to recover the DEA key used to encrypt the known plaintext. Since the formula of DEA key updating is linear and known to Eve, she can recover the previous (by modular subtraction) and the next (by modular addition) DEA keys. Therefore, she can disclose all the plaintexts. Therefore, this method is insecure.
    2.  When the second method is used, Eve can recover the key, which served to encrypt the plaintext she knew; let this key be  <math alttext="upper K Subscript p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript p](images/c14_1007.png). Then, since the key of the  <math alttext="i t h" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></math> ![i t h](images/c14_1008.png) group of 100 blocks is yielded from the previous key plus one, Eve can disclose the keys before and after the key  <math alttext="upper K Subscript p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript p](images/c14_1009.png). The hash function does not help to secure the messages.
    3.  When the third method is used, Eve can recover the key  <math alttext="upper K Subscript p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript p](images/c14_1010.png), which served to encrypt the plaintext she knew. Then, she can decrypt a maximum of 100 consecutive plaintexts that have been encrypted using the key  <math alttext="upper K Subscript p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript p](images/c14_1011.png). However, even if the DEA-key updating formula is known to Eve, she cannot recover the other keys, because the hash function is not invertible. From  <math alttext="upper K Subscript p Baseline equals upper H left-parenthesis upper K Subscript upper A comma upper B Baseline plus p right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript p Baseline equals upper H left-parenthesis upper K Subscript upper A comma upper B Baseline plus p right-parenthesis](images/c14_1012.png), Eve cannot derive  <math alttext="upper K Subscript upper A comma upper B Baseline plus p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript upper A comma upper B Baseline plus p](images/c14_1013.png) in order to compute  <math alttext="upper K Subscript upper A comma upper B Baseline plus p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript upper A comma upper B Baseline plus p minus 1](images/c14_1014.png) or  <math alttext="upper K Subscript upper A comma upper B Baseline plus p plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript upper A comma upper B Baseline plus p plus 1](images/c14_1015.png); and then disclose the keys after and before key  <math alttext="upper K Subscript p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript p](images/c14_1016.png). Therefore, the third method can be considered as partially secure.

***Problem 14.12***

Take three pieces and their indices, say  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 731 comma 2 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>731</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 731 comma 2 right-parenthesis](images/c14_1023.png),  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 1239 comma 3 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1239</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 1239 comma 3 right-parenthesis](images/c14_1024.png), and  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 265 comma 5 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>265</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 265 comma 5 right-parenthesis](images/c14_1025.png). Build the following equation system:
    
     <math alttext="731 equals a 0 plus 2 a 1 plus 4 a 2 m o d Baseline 1999" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>731</mn><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>1999</mn></mrow></math> ![731 equals a 0 plus 2 a 1 plus 4 a 2 m o d Baseline 1999](images/c14_1026.png)(a)  <math alttext="1239 equals a 0 plus 3 a 1 plus 9 a 2 m o d Baseline 1999" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1239</mn><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>1999</mn></mrow></math> ![1239 equals a 0 plus 3 a 1 plus 9 a 2 m o d Baseline 1999](images/c14_1027.png)(b)  <math alttext="265 equals a 0 plus 5 a 1 plus 25 a 2 m o d Baseline 1999" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>265</mn><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>25</mn><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>1999</mn></mrow></math> ![265 equals a 0 plus 5 a 1 plus 25 a 2 m o d Baseline 1999](images/c14_1028.png)(c) 
    
    Then, we get:

    Then, from (d) and (e), we get:
    
     <math alttext="508 asterisk 2 plus 974 equals minus 6 a 2 m o d Baseline 1999" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>508</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>974</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>6</mn><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>1999</mn></mrow></math> ![508 asterisk 2 plus 974 equals minus 6 a 2 m o d Baseline 1999](images/c14_1031.png) <math alttext="a 2 equals negative 1990 asterisk 6 Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d Baseline 1999 equals negative 1990 asterisk 1666 m o d Baseline 1999 equals 1001" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1990</mn><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>6</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>1999</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1990</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>1666</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>1999</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1001</mn></mrow></math> ![a 2 equals negative 1990 asterisk 6 Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d Baseline 1999 equals negative 1990 asterisk 1666 m o d Baseline 1999 equals 1001](images/c14_1032.png)
    
    Then, from (d), we get:
    
     <math alttext="508 equals a 1 plus 1001 asterisk 5 m o d Baseline 1999" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>508</mn><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1001</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>1999</mn></mrow></math> ![508 equals a 1 plus 1001 asterisk 5 m o d Baseline 1999](images/c14_1033.png) <math alttext="a 1 equals 508 minus 1001 asterisk 5 m o d Baseline 1999 equals 1500" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>508</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1001</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>1999</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1500</mn></mrow></math> ![a 1 equals 508 minus 1001 asterisk 5 m o d Baseline 1999 equals 1500](images/c14_1034.png)
    
    Finally, from (a), we get:
    
     <math alttext="upper D equals a 0 equals 731 minus 2 asterisk 1500 minus 4 asterisk 1001 m o d Baseline 1999 equals 1723" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>731</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>1500</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>1001</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>1999</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1723</mn></mrow></math> ![upper D equals a 0 equals 731 minus 2 asterisk 1500 minus 4 asterisk 1001 m o d Baseline 1999 equals 1723](images/c14_1035.png)
    
    Therefore, the entire safe combination is reconstructed.
    

## Notes

1.  [**1**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0001) Protection may be provided manually, in an automated fashion, or by some combination of manual and automated methods. This book does not focus on manual protection of keys (including trusted courier, bags, safes, etc.).
2.  [**2**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0002) DRBG stands for Deterministic Random Bit Generator. [Chapter 16](#c16.xhtml) addresses in detail the approved DRBGs.
3.  [**3**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0003) The following formula is useful to compute  <math alttext="upper S left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis](images/c14_1036.png), the maximum security strength of RSA with a modulus of a bit-length of *n*:  <math alttext="upper S left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 1.923 asterisk RootIndex 3 StartRoot n asterisk ln left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis EndRoot asterisk RootIndex 3 StartRoot left-bracket ln left-parenthesis n asterisk ln left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis right-bracket squared EndRoot minus 4.69 right-parenthesis slash ln left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis period upper S left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1.923</mn><mo>\*</mo><mroot><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>ln</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>3</mn></mroot><mo>\*</mo><mroot><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mn>3</mn></mroot><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4.69</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>ln</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 1.923 asterisk RootIndex 3 StartRoot n asterisk ln left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis EndRoot asterisk RootIndex 3 StartRoot left-bracket ln left-parenthesis n asterisk ln left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis right-bracket squared EndRoot minus 4.69 right-parenthesis slash ln left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis period upper S left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis](images/c14_1037.png) is rounded to a standard value (i.e. 112, 128, 192, …).
4.  [**4**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0004) Support services mainly include key-agreement, key-transport, and random number generation.
5.  [**5**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0005) Sometimes, “key derivation method” and “key derivation function” are used interchangeably.
6.  [**6**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0006) The security strength is the same whether the hash function is used in option 1 or in option 2. It also is the same when used in the two-step key derivation method.
7.  [**7**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0007) The Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) is presented in Section 3.3.4 and the RSA-CRT-based decryption is described in Section 12.2.2.2. RSA implementations are faster when the CRT is used for decryption.
8.  [**8**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0008) *p* is a safe prime if  <math alttext="left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2](images/c14_1038.png) is also a prime.
9.  [**9**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0009) Parameters *a* and *b* are used in traditional elliptic curves. Edwards and Montgomery curves make use of other parameters (see Section 13.2.4).
10.  [**10**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0010) Other names may be used in Internet RFCs, but the specification is the same.
11.  [**11**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0011) P224, P-256, P-384, P-521, W-25519, and W-448 are names of Weierstrass (i.e. traditional) curves. Curve25519 and Curve448 are names of Montgomery curves. E488 is an Edwards curve.
12.  [**12**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0012) The number of EC points that can be generated by the selected base point is the number of points  <math alttext="left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis](images/c14_1039.png) that match the EC equation divided by the cofactor.
13.  [**13**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0013) Curves E448 and Edwards-448 differ in the value of parameter *d* .
14.  [**14**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0014) Since 2019, binary curves are deprecated, because of their limited adoption in industry \[[12](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0012), [15](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0015)\].
15.  [**15**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0015) Some ECs have the same irreducible polynomial, but differ in other domain parameters.
16.  [**16**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0016) “Manual key-transport” refers to a variety of methods to let the other party know the key, including face-to-face exchange, suitcase, email, phone, etc. In general, all those methods are not recommended.
17.  [**17**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0017) Option 1 results in more activities performed by the KDC server, while option 2 results in more activities by the subscriber that originates a session-key transaction.
18.  [**18**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0018) KMAC generates tags of variable bit-length. In practice, the bit-length should be close to either 128 or 256.
19.  [**19**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0019) Notice that in KAS1, the party *X* generates the shared secret *Z*, while the party *Y* generates the nonce  <math alttext="upper N o n c e Subscript upper Y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper N o n c e Subscript upper Y](images/c14_1040.png). Therefore, both parties do not equally contribute to the shared secret, which is used to generate a new secret key.
20.  [**20**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0020) The output of the KDF is split into two parts: a shared key *K* and a MAC key  <math alttext="upper M a c upper K e y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ![upper M a c upper K e y](images/c14_1041.png) (used to generate tags when required).  <math alttext="quotation-mark left-bracket comma right-bracket quotation-mark" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>"</mo><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>"</mo></mrow></math> ![quotation-mark left-bracket comma right-bracket quotation-mark](images/c14_1042.png) means optional.
21.  **21**  <math alttext="quotation-mark ellipsis quotation-mark" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>"</mo><mn>&#8230;</mn><mo>"</mo></mrow></math> ![quotation-mark ellipsis quotation-mark](images/c14_1043.png) means that other optional parameters may be used.
22.  [**22**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0022) “\*” denotes integer multiplication, while “⋅” denotes the multiplication of an EC point by a scalar.
23.  [**23**](#c14.xhtml#rc14-note-0023)  <math alttext="script upper O" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></math> ![script upper O](images/c14_1044.png) denotes the point to infinity.
24.  **24**  <math alttext="upper N o n c e Subscript upper X" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>X</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper N o n c e Subscript upper X](images/c14_1045.png) used in 0e-2s key-confirmation alternatives is the same as the one used in KDF.
