xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![upper S r e a l m](images/c15_62.png) and  <math alttext="upper S n a m e" alttext="upper S n a m e" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></math> ![upper S n a m e](images/c15_63.png) are those of the TGS.

*   – Send the message  <math alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper S bar upper R e p" alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper S bar upper R e p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper S bar upper R e p](images/c15_64.png) to the client. 
    *   Upon receiving a message  <math alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper S bar upper R e p" alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper S bar upper R e p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper S bar upper R e p](images/c15_65.png), the client decrypts the encrypted part of the message using its key  <math alttext="upper K Subscript upper C" alttext="upper K Subscript upper C" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>C</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript upper C](images/c15_66.png). If one of the values of  <math alttext="upper N o n c e" alttext="upper N o n c e" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></math> ![upper N o n c e](images/c15_67.png),  <math alttext="upper S t a r t upper T i m e" alttext="upper S t a r t upper T i m e" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></math> ![upper S t a r t upper T i m e](images/c15_68.png), and  <math alttext="upper E n d upper T i m e" alttext="upper E n d upper T i m e" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></math> ![upper E n d upper T i m e](images/c15_69.png) is not identical to one included in the  <math alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper S bar upper R e q" alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper S bar upper R e q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper S bar upper R e q](images/c15_70.png), an error in raised. Otherwise, the client concludes that the sender of  <math alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper S bar upper R e p" alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper S bar upper R e p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper S bar upper R e p](images/c15_71.png) knows its key. Then, the client saves the TGT and the session key  <math alttext="upper S upper K" alttext="upper S upper K" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> ![upper S upper K](images/c15_72.png). The authentication of the client by the KAS is finished.

##### *15.4.2.2.2 Second Step: Getting an Application Server Ticket*

When the client needs to access an application server, the following actions are performed to get an application server ticket.

*   1\. The client prepares and sends to the TGS a request  <math alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper T upper G upper S bar upper R e q" alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper T upper G upper S bar upper R e q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>T</mi><mi>G</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K upper R upper B bar upper T upper G upper S bar upper R e q](images/c15_73.png) that includes the client name, the server name and realm, the not-before and not-after dates desired by the client to use the application server ticket, the block cipher desired by the client, and the TGT received in step 1. That is,

*   2\. Upon reception of a  <math alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper T upper G upper S bar upper R e q" alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper T upper G upper S bar upper R e q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>T</mi><mi>G</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K upper R upper B bar upper T upper G upper S bar upper R e q](images/c15_75.png) message, the TGS performs the following:

*   – Decrypt the TGT and compare its values with those included in the  <math alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper T upper G upper S bar upper R e q" alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper T upper G upper S bar upper R e q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>T</mi><mi>G</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K upper R upper B bar upper T upper G upper S bar upper R e q](images/c15_76.png). Then, check the validity period of the TGT. If any test fails, an error indication is returned.
*   – Retrieve in the database the key of the application server requested by the client. Let  <math alttext="upper K Subscript s" alttext="upper K Subscript s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript s](images/c15_77.png) denote the application server key.
*   – Generate an application server ticket  <math alttext="upper A upper S upper T" alttext="upper A upper S upper T" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> ![upper A upper S upper T](images/c15_78.png), then build a three-part TGS response  <math alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper T upper G upper S bar upper R e p" alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper T upper G upper S bar upper R e p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>T</mi><mi>G</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K upper R upper B bar upper T upper G upper S bar upper R e p](images/c15_79.png) in a similar way than for  <math alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper S bar upper R e p" alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper S bar upper R e p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper S bar upper R e p](images/c15_80.png); i.e.

those of the application server requested by the client.

*   3\. Upon receiving a message  <math alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper T upper G upper S bar upper R e p" alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper T upper G upper S bar upper R e p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>T</mi><mi>G</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K upper R upper B bar upper T upper G upper S bar upper R e p](images/c15_91.png), the client decrypts the encrypted part of the message using the session key. If one of the values of  <math alttext="upper N o n c e" alttext="upper N o n c e" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></math> ![upper N o n c e](images/c15_92.png),  <math alttext="upper S t a r t upper T i m e" alttext="upper S t a r t upper T i m e" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></math> ![upper S t a r t upper T i m e](images/c15_93.png), and  <math alttext="upper E n d upper T i m e" alttext="upper E n d upper T i m e" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></math> ![upper E n d upper T i m e](images/c15_94.png) is not identical to one included in the  <math alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper T upper G upper S bar upper R e q" alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper T upper G upper S bar upper R e q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>T</mi><mi>G</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K upper R upper B bar upper T upper G upper S bar upper R e q](images/c15_95.png), an error is raised. Otherwise, the client concludes that the sender of  <math alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper T upper G upper S bar upper R e p" alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper T upper G upper S bar upper R e p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>T</mi><mi>G</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K upper R upper B bar upper T upper G upper S bar upper R e p](images/c15_96.png) is the TGS. Then, the client saves the application server ticket  <math alttext="upper A upper S upper T period" alttext="upper A upper S upper T period" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>T</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> ![upper A upper S upper T period](images/c15_97.png)

##### *15.4.2.2.3 Third Step: Mutual Client/Server Authentication*

In the third step, the following actions are performed.

*   1\. The client prepares a server request  <math alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e q" alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e q](images/c15_98.png), which includes the ticket  <math alttext="upper A upper S upper T" alttext="upper A upper S upper T" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> ![upper A upper S upper T](images/c15_99.png) and an authenticator using the session key; i.e.

 <math alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e q equals left-parenthesis upper A upper S upper T comma upper A u t h e n t i c a t o r right-parenthesis" alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e q equals left-parenthesis upper A upper S upper T comma upper A u t h e n t i c a t o r right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>A</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e q equals left-parenthesis upper A upper S upper T comma upper A u t h e n t i c a t o r right-parenthesis](images/c15_100.png)

where  <math alttext="upper A u t h e n t i c a t o r equals upper E Subscript upper K Sub Subscript upper S upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C r e a l m comma upper C n a m e comma upper C t i m e upper S t a m p comma upper S e q upper N u m b e r comma ellipsis right-parenthesis" alttext="upper A u t h e n t i c a t o r equals upper E Subscript upper K Sub Subscript upper S upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C r e a l m comma upper C n a m e comma upper C t i m e upper S t a m p comma upper S e q upper N u m b e r comma ellipsis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mi>K</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>C</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>S</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>q</mi><mi>N</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>b</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper A u t h e n t i c a t o r equals upper E Subscript upper K Sub Subscript upper S upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C r e a l m comma upper C n a m e comma upper C t i m e upper S t a m p comma upper S e q upper N u m b e r comma ellipsis right-parenthesis](images/c15_101.png)

*   2\. Upon reception of a request  <math alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e q" alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e q](images/c15_102.png), the application server performs the following actions:

*   – Decrypt the ticket  <math alttext="upper A upper S upper T" alttext="upper A upper S upper T" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> ![upper A upper S upper T](images/c15_103.png) using its key  <math alttext="upper K Subscript upper S" alttext="upper K Subscript upper S" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>S</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper K Subscript upper S](images/c15_104.png).
*   – From the ticket, get the session key and the name and realm of the sender.
*   – Decrypt the authenticator using the session key.
*   – If the data (i.e. client name and realm and other information) included in the authenticator is not identical to that included in the ticket  <math alttext="upper A upper S upper T" alttext="upper A upper S upper T" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> ![upper A upper S upper T](images/c15_105.png), an error is returned to the client. Otherwise, the application server successfully authenticates the client.
*   – The application server builds a response message  <math alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e p" alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e p](images/c15_106.png), which includes the timestamp and sequence number from the  <math alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e q" alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e q](images/c15_107.png) message, all encrypted using the session key:

 <math alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e p equals upper E Subscript upper K Sub Subscript upper S upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C t i m e upper S t a m p comma upper S e q upper N u m b e r comma ellipsis right-parenthesis" alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e p equals upper E Subscript upper K Sub Subscript upper S upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C t i m e upper S t a m p comma upper S e q upper N u m b e r comma ellipsis right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mi>K</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>q</mi><mi>N</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>b</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e p equals upper E Subscript upper K Sub Subscript upper S upper K Baseline left-parenthesis upper C t i m e upper S t a m p comma upper S e q upper N u m b e r comma ellipsis right-parenthesis](images/c15_108.png)

*   3\. Upon reception of a response message  <math alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e p" alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e p](images/c15_109.png), the client decrypts the message using the session key. If the content of the message matches the data included in the request message  <math alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e q" alttext="upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e q" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K upper R upper B bar upper A upper P bar upper R e q](images/c15_110.png), the mutual authentication successfully terminates.

### 15.4.3 Advantages, Limits, and Security of Kerberos

**Advantages**. There are many advantages in using Kerberos, in particular the following:

*   Kerberos enables secured exchanges between principals that do not trust each other.
*   Kerberos separates authentication from services. The application servers do not know, or ask for, the client passwords.
*   A single client authentication to Kerberos server is enough to access all Kerberos-authenticated services. Therefore, Kerberos provides a *Single sign-on* service to clients.
*   Protecting user information is simplified, since all user authentication information is stored on one centralized authentication server.
*   Kerberos concentrates the maintenance of secrets (i.e. stored keys) in a small number of places (that can be protected appropriately) rather than distributing them all over the network.

**Limits.** The following issues should be considered when using Kerberos:

*   The names of all the principals are registered in the database. They must be unique in each realm. The clients must know the names of the application servers they need to access. Any change in names may result in authentication failures. Consider for example, a client that received a ticket to access an application server *S* for a period of one year. Then, the server name is changed to  <math alttext="upper S prime" alttext="upper S prime" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>'</mo></mrow></math> ![upper S prime](images/c15_111.png). After the name change, the client is no more authenticated by the server, because the ticket became invalid.The database is the main vulnerability point of Kerberos. It must be protected using appropriate procedures that are not part of Kerberos.

*   Any denial-of-service attack against Kerberos results in a denial-of-service attack against all the principals using Kerberos.
*   Kerberos generates and securely transmits the session key to the client and server. Once obtained, the session key must be protected by the client and the server without actions from Kerberos. In particular, clients may be attacked to recover the session key and then attackers disclose the private communications.
*   Validity check of ticket period relies on synchronized clocks in the whole system. Clock synchronization is required, but not provided by Kerberos. Any desynchronization (at some drift) may result in invalid tickets. Therefore, any participants (clients, application servers, and Kerberos) must use the appropriate time services (e.g. Network Time Protocol).
*   As an authentication service, Kerberos provides a means of verifying the identity of principals on a network. Authentication is usually useful primarily as a first step in the process of authorization, determining whether a client may use a service, which objects the client is allowed to access, and the type of access allowed for each object. Kerberos does not, by itself, provide authorization. Possession of an application server ticket provides only authentication of the client to that service, and not how the client can use the resources of the application server (i.e. read, write, delete, … objects).
*   Kerberos does not, by itself, provide integrity and confidentiality of data exchanged between a client and an application server. Additional mechanisms (such as HMAC or authenticated-encryption algorithms) should be agreed between the parties before sending data.

**Security**. Researchers have been investigating Kerberos since it was first published. Weaknesses have been discovered in specific Kerberos implementations, as well as in the protocol itself. Those weaknesses have been addressed, and Kerberos remains fundamental for authentication in the private networks. Kerberos has been widely implemented for decades, and it is considered a mature and safe protocol for authenticating users. Kerberos uses strong cryptography, including secret-key encryption, to protect sensitive data. Therefore, Kerberos protocol is currently considered secure.

## 15.5 Exercises and Problems

### 15.5.1 List of Exercises and Problems

***Exercise 15.1***

Consider a PKI with a single CA, which acts as root-CA and issuing CA. It signs and sends three certificates to three collaborative users  <math alttext="upper U 1" alttext="upper U 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper U 1](images/c15_112.png),  <math alttext="upper U 2" alttext="upper U 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper U 2](images/c15_113.png), and  <math alttext="upper U 3" alttext="upper U 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper U 3](images/c15_114.png). User  <math alttext="upper U 1" alttext="upper U 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper U 1](images/c15_115.png) wants to send a signed document to user  <math alttext="upper U 2" alttext="upper U 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper U 2](images/c15_116.png). Then, user  <math alttext="upper U 2" alttext="upper U 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper U 2](images/c15_117.png) updates the document, signs it, and then sends it to user  <math alttext="upper U 3" alttext="upper U 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper U 3](images/c15_118.png). The hash function used by the collaborating users is known before the start of the document update. Explain how the digital certificates are used to protect the integrity of the document.

***Exercise 15.2***

Is a registration authority an intermediate CA?

***Exercise 15.3***

1.  Imagine that Eve knew Bob’s public key and certificate. Can she use the known information to exchange data with Alice pretending to be Bob?
2.  Can Eve change Bob’s certificate and include her public key in place of that of Bob, and then sends the certificate to Alice?

***Exercise 15.4***

Alice and Bob obtained digital certificates from a CA. Then, they authenticated to each other and exchanged some data encrypted with a session key established using the Diffie-Hellman protocol, and stopped their session. Eve intercepted all the ciphertexts exchanged between Alice and Bob; and she recovered the private key used by the CA to generate Alice and Bob’s certificates.

1.  Can Eve disclose plaintexts exchanged between Alice and Bob in the closed session?
2.  Can Eve disclose plaintexts to be exchanged in a future session?

***Exercise 15.5***

Users in domains  <math alttext="upper D 1" alttext="upper D 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper D 1](images/c15_119.png) and  <math alttext="upper D 2" alttext="upper D 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper D 2](images/c15_120.png) have CA  <math alttext="upper C 1" alttext="upper C 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 1](images/c15_121.png) and CA  <math alttext="upper C 2" alttext="upper C 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 2](images/c15_122.png) as trust anchors, respectively. Both domains are acquired by a company, which owns a domain  <math alttext="upper D 3" alttext="upper D 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper D 3](images/c15_123.png) and has CA  <math alttext="upper C 3" alttext="upper C 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper C 3](images/c15_124.png) as trust anchor. What are the steps that the users in the three domains must follow to communicate with each other?

***Exercise 15.6***

1.  Can Kerberos protect against denial-of-service attacks?
2.  Can Kerberos protect against replay attacks?
3.  Can Kerberos guarantee the integrity of data exchanged between principals?
4.  Can Kerberos protect application server resources against unauthorized accesses?

***Problem 15.1***

Some people may be attacked, because they consider that any website with HTTPS and a padlock icon belongs to an honest entity. In addition, some people do not carefully read, letter by letter, the names of secured websites. Suggest a use case of fraudulent website where an attacker owning an authentic digital certificate, delivered by a trusted authority, can obtain confidential data from un-warned or naïve people.

***Problem 15.2***

Assume that the secret keys of Kerberos clients are derived from their passwords, which are entered securely in the database, i.e. passwords cannot be intercepted during transfer. Show a scenario where an attacker can obtain tickets to access application servers.

***Problem 15.3***

This problem aims to discuss a simple way to include public keys into Kerberos. Consider a modification of Kerberos, which provides a two-step validation: the Kerberos authentication server delivers application-server tickets to clients. Instead of using private keys stored on Kerberos database, each principal has a certificate delivered by an authority trusted by Kerberos. The modified Kerberos frees principals from checking the validity of certificates. Suggest a public-key-based protocol to deliver tickets and session keys. List some of the drawbacks of public-key-based Kerberos.

### 15.5.2 Solutions to Exercises and Problems

***Exercise 15.1***

Steps to update the document:

*   The three users exchange their certificates. Certificate validation is immediate, because all users trust the same root-CA, which signed their certificates.
*   User  <math alttext="upper U 1" alttext="upper U 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper U 1](images/c15_125.png) computes a hash  <math alttext="upper H 1" alttext="upper H 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper H 1](images/c15_126.png) of the document  <math alttext="upper D 1" alttext="upper D 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper D 1](images/c15_127.png); encrypts  <math alttext="upper H 1" alttext="upper H 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper H 1](images/c15_128.png) with his/her private key; obtains a signature  <math alttext="upper S 1" alttext="upper S 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S 1](images/c15_129.png); and sends a message  <math alttext="upper M 1" alttext="upper M 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 1](images/c15_130.png) containing  <math alttext="upper D 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper S 1" alttext="upper D 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper S 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper D 1 StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue upper S 1](images/c15_131.png) to user  <math alttext="upper U 2" alttext="upper U 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper U 2](images/c15_132.png).
*   User  <math alttext="upper U 2" alttext="upper U 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper U 2](images/c15_133.png) receives the message  <math alttext="upper M 1" alttext="upper M 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper M 1](images/c15_134.png). He/she extracts the public key of user  <math alttext="upper U 1" alttext="upper U 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper U 1](images/c15_135.png) from  <math alttext="upper U 1" alttext="upper U 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper U 1](images/c15_136.png)’s certificate. He/she decrypts the signature  <math alttext="upper S 1" alttext="upper S 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper S 1](images/c15_137.png) using  <math alttext="upper U 1" alttext="upper U 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper U 1](images/c15_138.png)’s public key and obtains a bit-string  <math alttext="upper H prime 1" alttext="upper H prime 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn><mo>'</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H prime 1](images/c15_139.png). He/she computes a hash  <math alttext="upper H double-prime 1" alttext="upper H double-prime 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>'</mo><mo>'</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H double-prime 1](images/c15_140.png) of the document  <math alttext="upper D 1" alttext="upper D 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper D 1](images/c15_141.png). If  <math alttext="upper H prime 1 equals upper H double-prime 1" alttext="upper H prime 1 equals upper H double-prime 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn><mo>'</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>'</mo><mo>'</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper H prime 1 equals upper H double-prime 1](images/c15_142.png), then the collaboration continues. Otherwise, the document has been altered during transfer; and the collaboration is stopped.

No. An intermediate CA is a CA that is not a root-CA and it issues certificates to lower level CAs or end-entities. An RA assists a CA to check and validate the information included in certificate requests submitted by end-entities.

***Exercise 15.3***

1.  No. Bob’s public key as well as his certificate is not secret. To decrypt the data encrypted by Alice using Bob’s public key, Eve needs Bob’s private key.
2.  No. Recall that the CA signature is a signed hash of the user public key plus other data. Bob’s certificate is signed using the CA’s private key. If Bob’s public key is changed, the signature on the certificate becomes invalid.

***Exercise 15.4***

1.  Certificates do not include private keys. Therefore, the session key established by Alice and Bob using their private keys cannot be recovered by Eve with the help of the CA private-key. Thus, she cannot disclose the plaintexts exchanged in the closed session.
2.  Using the CA private-key, Eve can generate and sign on behalf of the CA a certificate with Bob as the owner name, but with her public key. Then, when the new session is to be setup between Alice and Bob, Eve can mount a man-in-the-middle attack and replace Bob’s messages by her messages. Alice will receive a valid certificate with Bob’s name. Then, Alice will encrypt her messages with Eve’s public key and not with that of Bob.

***Exercise 15.6***

1.  No. Kerberos is not resistant to denial-of-service. DoS are common attacks against systems and are out of the scope of Kerberos.
2.  Yes. Each client request includes a nonce and/or a timestamp, which are checked by Kerberos to prevent replay attacks.
3.  No. Kerberos provides a session key to be used by the principals (i.e. client and server) to encrypt their messages. However, the encryption alone cannot provide integrity guarantees; other mechanisms are required (e.g. use of HMAC of authenticated-encryption algorithms as those discussed in [Chapter 9](#c09.xhtml)).
4.  No. Kerberos provides assurance to application servers that the clients who received tickets have been authenticated. The authentication does not specify which type of access (i.e. read, write, append, delete, etc.) is granted to clients when accessing server resources.

***Problem 15.1***

We suggest the following scenario. An attacker legally obtains a certificate for a domain bnpparisbas.com, and mounts a website identical to that of https//:bnpparibas.com, a French bank. Then, he sends messages using some emailing list, asking customers of BNP Paribas to use an included link to do some operations on their accounts. People who have no accounts at BNP Paribas ignore the message, but some of the BNP Paribas customers may click on the link provided in the email and perform the requested operations. If they check the certificate, they can see the name of bnpparisbas.com and they do not pay attention to the “s” after “pari”, which does not exist in the authentic domain name of BNP Paribas. Therefore, a digital certificate plus a secured website do not necessarily mean an honest website.

***Problem 15.2***

It is known that Kerberos is vulnerable to attacks based on password guessing. If the passwords used by clients are weak, attackers can disclose them, using dictionary attacks, derive their secret keys (because the derivation function of keys from passwords is known), and then can authenticate to Kerberos and obtain application server tickets. Therefore, it is recommended to use strong passwords and change them periodically.

***Problem 15.3***

The suggested protocol is as follows:

*   The client obtains the certificate of the application server, then sends a ticket request including his/her certificate and that of the application server.
*   The modified Kerberos checks the validity of both certificates (maybe asking the authority, which delivered the certificates).
*   Modified Kerberos generates a random session key and a ticket (that includes the session key and client name) encrypted with the public key of the application server. The session key is encrypted using the public key of the client. Then, a message, including the encrypted session key and the ticket, is sent to the client.
*   The client decrypts the first part of the message to recover the session key. Then, he/she prepares an authenticator (which includes authentication-data, e.g. a timestamp and/or a name) encrypted using the session key. Then, he/she sends a request to the application server. The request includes some of authentication data (in cleartext), the authenticator, and the ticket.
*   Upon reception of a client request, the application server decrypts the ticket using his/her private key and recovers the session key. Then, he/she decrypts the authenticator to confirm that the sender knows the session key. Finally, a response is sent to the client. The response includes some of the authentication data of the client encrypted with the session key.
*   The client receives the server response and decrypts the message to confirm that the responding server holds the appropriate private key used to encrypt the ticket.

Drawbacks of public-key-based Kerberos include:

*   Public-key cryptography is a relatively expensive operation.
*   Checking the validity of certificates requires much more work than checking just if a principal is registered in the local database of Kerberos.
*   Principals are required to pay to receive and renew their certificates.

## Notes

1.  [**1**](#c15.xhtml#rc15-note-0001) The issuer and subject names are commonly represented using an X.500 or Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) format.
2.  [**2**](#c15.xhtml#rc15-note-0002) It may take time before an invalid certificate is added to the CRL. The period of CRL updating may be an hour, a day, a week …; it depends on each CA and the usages of the public-keys certified by that CA.
3.  [**3**](#c15.xhtml#rc15-note-0003) Since 2015, all SSL versions are deprecated. Today, when people use the term SSL, they talk about TLS. The reason of still using SSL or SSL/TLS is that the term SSL persists in minds as it was a guarantee of security over Internet.
4.  [**4**](#c15.xhtml#rc15-note-0004) Forward secrecy is a feature of key agreement schemes, which provide the property that session keys are not compromised if the private keys used in the key agreement become compromised.
5.  [**5**](#c15.xhtml#rc15-note-0005) AES-128-CCM and AES-128- CCM-8 are identical with an exception: AES-128- CCM-8 uses eight octets for authentication, instead of the full 16 octets used by AES-128-CCM.
6.  [**6**](#c15.xhtml#rc15-note-0006) The name of the hash function is not specified, because implicitly Edwards’s curve 25519 is used with SHA512 and the curve with SHAKE256.
7.  [**7**](#c15.xhtml#rc15-note-0007) The name *Kerberos* was derived from the Greek mythology; it is a name of a three-head dog that protected the gates of hells.
8.  [**8**](#c15.xhtml#rc15-note-0008) The term *realm* is used to make the analogy between the protection of digital systems and that of the realms in the spirit of the Greek mythology of the three-head dog.
9.  [**9**](#c15.xhtml#rc15-note-0009) In the two-step authentication, the client must authenticate to the Kerberos authentication server for each application server to access.
10.  [**10**](#c15.xhtml#rc15-note-0010) It is a symmetric key; therefore, “private” is omitted in the sequel.
11.  [**11**](#c15.xhtml#rc15-note-0011) The TGT (also called initial ticket) generated by Kerberos is similar to the certificate issued by a certificate authority when a public key is used. It is used to prove that the client holding the TGT was authenticated and it can share, with the application server, the session key included in the TGT to encrypt and decrypt messages.
12.  [**12**](#c15.xhtml#rc15-note-0012) Kerberos makes use of absolute time. So, the clocks of the entities (Kerberos, clients, and application servers) must be synchronized (with a bounded difference between clocks).

# 16   
Generation of Pseudorandom and Prime Numbers for Cryptographic Applications

As emphatically underlined in previous chapters, random numbers (RNs) and prime numbers (PNs) play a fundamental role in cryptography. In particular, cryptographic keys and nonces used in some cryptographic algorithms shall appear as entirely random bit-strings for observers (i.e. attackers).

In general, there exist two basic strategies for generating random numbers: non-deterministic and deterministic strategies. In the first category, a physical process is used to generate bit sequences, while in the second category, an algorithm is used. Non-deterministic RN generators produce true RNs, while deterministic RN generators produce pseudo RNs. The second category of RN generators is the most dominant in computer-based systems and are built using deterministic random bit generators (DRBGs). The latter are algorithms that output random bit-strings, which mainly depend on an initial input called *seed*. Therefore, the outputs of DRBGs are pseudorandom bit-strings instead of true random ones. Even if the algorithm of a DRBG is known, when the seed is picked from a (very) large set and kept secret, the DRBG output is very likely to be unpredictable and looks like a random value.

Pseudorandom bit-strings are also called pseudorandom numbers and DRBGs are referred to as Pseudo Random Number Generators (PRNGs). The first part of this chapter addresses basic and recommended algorithms to generate pseudo RNs.

The security of IFC (Integer Factorization Cryptography) and DLC (Discrete Logarithm Cryptography)-based algorithms fundamentally relies on prime numbers. Unlike for PRNs, there does not exist algorithms that deterministically generate, with certainty, large prime numbers. A practical alternative to true primes is to use integers that are not proven to be composite. The second part of this chapter presents the recommended algorithms to support prime number generation based on primality testing.

It is worth noticing that since the security of cryptographic algorithms depends on PRNGs, if a PRNG can be made predictable for attackers, it can be used as a backdoor to compromise confidentiality and integrity of protected data. The same threat applies to the algorithms used to select prime numbers.

## 16.1 Introduction to Pseudorandom Number Generation

### 16.1.1 Basic Notions and Definitions

***Definition 16.1 Ideal random bit-string***: *it is a bit-string in which each bit is unpredictable and unbiased, with a value that is independent on the values of the other bits in the sequence.*

***Definition 16.2 Random number sequence***: *it is a random sequence of numbers, which has no order and does not follow an intelligible pattern or combination. For external observers, a random sequence of numbers appears like a digitalization of noise.*

***Definition 16.3 Random number generator***: *it is an algorithm (or a circuit) which outputs a sequence of statistically independent and unbiased numbers.*

***Definition 16.4 Truly random number generator (TRNG**): it is a process, which relies on physical observations (e.g. coin flipping, lottery, thermal noise of an equipment, natural phenomena, etc.) to generate numbers.*

*Properties of truly random numbers*

TRNs are characterized by two fundamental properties:

1.  *Uniform distribution*: i.e. all the numbers in a required range often occur with the same probability.
2.  *Independence*: if one knows some or all the numbers up to a certain point in a random number sequence, he/she should not be able to predict the next one(s).

TRNGs have some limitations, including:

*   They require extra hardware, which has a cost.
*   In general, they are not fast enough to generate RNs at a high rate required by some applications or services.
*   Their output is not reproducible to support the testing of cryptographic applications and algorithms.
*   If attackers have access to the physical phenomenon used by a TRNG, the entire security of a system may be compromised.

***Definition 16.5 Seed****: it is the initial value provided to a random number (or bits) generator to output a sequence of* pseudorandom numbers (or bit-strings).

In practice, TRNGs are used only to generate seeds (i.e. initial inputs) for software pseudorandom number generators, which are capable of generating RNs at high rates.

***Definition 16.6 Pseudorandom number generator*** *(PRNG): it is a deterministic algorithm which, given a truly random number, called *seed*, outputs a sequence of numbers, which appear as being random.*

***Definition 16.7 Pseudorandom*** ***Bit Generator** (PRBG)* *(also called ***Deterministic Random Bit Generator*** (DRBG)): it is a deterministic¹ algorithm which, given a truly random binary sequence of length *k*, called seed, outputs a binary sequence of length *L* which appears to be random. The output of a PRBG is called a pseudorandom bit sequence.*

A DRBG can be used to generate (uniformly distributed) random numbers. For example, a random integer in the interval  <math alttext="left-bracket 0 comma n right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 0 comma n right-bracket](images/c16_1.png) can be obtained by generating a random bit sequence of length  <math alttext="l o g 2 left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![l o g 2 left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis plus 1](images/c16_2.png), and converting it to an integer; if the resulting integer exceeds *n*, one option is to discard it and generate a new random bit sequence. The other option is to pick the  <math alttext="m o d u l o n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![m o d u l o n](images/c16_3.png) of the DRBG output.

***Definition 16.8 Period*** *of a PRNG/PRBG: any PRNG/PRBG repeats a specific pattern of random numbers (or bits). The period* *of a PRNG/PRBG* *measures the number of output numbers (or bits) after which the PRNG/PRBG begins to repeat itself.*

### 16.1.2 Entropy

In cryptography, the unpredictability of secrets (such as cryptographic keys) is essential. If *X* is a random variable associated with a secret, then the probability that a secret value is guessed correctly is related to the entropy of the random variable *X*. If a process used to generate secret items has a small entropy (i.e. it is so poor that it can only generate a small number of different random numbers), the cryptographic items (such as session keys, nonces, and initialization vectors) become predictable. Therefore, entropy is of paramount importance to design secrets. Basics of entropy are presented in this section.

***Definition 16.9 Entropy*:** *it is the amount of information provided by an observation of a random variable. It reflects the uncertainty associated with predicting the variable value. The larger the value of entropy, the greater the uncertainty in predicting the value of an observation.*

#### 16.1.2.1 Source of Entropy

An entropy source is a combination of an analogue noise source (e.g. thermal noise or device vibration noise), a conditioner, and a health testing, which together generate random bit-strings to be used as seeds by pseudorandom bit generators. [Figure 16.1](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0001) illustrates the components of an entropy source:

*   *Analogue noise source*: an analogue signal is sampled and digitalized. Notice that without a genuine noise, adding other deterministic components in the chain of random bit generation would not help in producing unpredictable numbers, because the algorithms used in number generation are public, in general.
*   *Conditioning component*: it is an optional deterministic function responsible for reducing bias and/or increasing the entropy rate of the resulting output bits. In general, keyed-hash and encryption functions are used as conditioning components.
*   *Health testing* of a noise source aims to detect failures of the noise source (e.g. no change in the signal due to a hardware failure) or to detect a deviation from the expected output during the correct operation of the noise source (e.g. no variation in a physical phenomenon as expected).

![Figure 16.1 Generic model of entropy source.](images/c16f001.png)

[**Figure 16.1**](#c16.xhtml#rc16-fig-0001) Generic model of entropy source.

Noise sources can be divided into two categories: physical and digital noise sources. The following physical phenomena may be used as physical noise sources:

*   The sound from a microphone or a video input from a camera.
*   The air turbulence within a sealed disk drive, which causes random fluctuations in read latency times of disk drive sector.
*   The frequency instability of a free running oscillator.
*   Elapsed time between emission of particles during radioactive decay.
*   Thermal noise from a semiconductor diode or resistor.

The following may be used as digital noise sources:

*   The system time measured at a fine granularity.
*   The current value of a portion of the random access memory.
*   The position of a PC mouse.
*   A portion of a file (e.g. in Linux, the file /dev/random contains information collected from device drivers, which can be used to generate random numbers).

#### 16.1.2.2 Entropy from a Statistical Point of View

There are many possible measures of entropy, but the central notion of information theory for expressing the uncertainty about a random variable is the Shannon’s entropy \[[1](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0001)\].

***Definition 16.10 Shannon’s entropy*:** *it is a measure of the average uncertainty of a random variable *X*. Formally, the Shannon’s entropy is defined as follows: let *X* be a random variable, which takes its values in a set  <math alttext="upper S equals StartSet x 1 comma x 2 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript upper N Baseline EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S equals StartSet x 1 comma x 2 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript upper N Baseline EndSet](images/c16_4.png), with probability  <math alttext="probability left-parenthesis upper X equals x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis equals p Subscript i Baseline comma i left-bracket 1 comma upper N right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>Pr</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![probability left-parenthesis upper X equals x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis equals p Subscript i Baseline comma i left-bracket 1 comma upper N right-bracket](images/c16_5.png), the entropy of the random variable *X*, denoted  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis](images/c16_6.png), is defined by \[[1](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0001)\]:*

 <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals minus sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper N Endscripts left-parenthesis p Subscript i Baseline asterisk l o g 2 left-parenthesis p Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true" mathsize="140%"><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover></mstyle><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals minus sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper N Endscripts left-parenthesis p Subscript i Baseline asterisk l o g 2 left-parenthesis p Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c16_7.png)

It also is the minimum number of bits required on the average to describe a value  <math alttext="x Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![x Subscript i](images/c16_8.png) of the random variable *X*.

**Example 16.1**

*   – Let  <math alttext="normal upper X" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi></math> ![normal upper X](images/c16_9.png) be a random variable that takes its values in the Latin alphabet. If all the letters are equiprobable, then  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals l o g 2 left-parenthesis 26 right-parenthesis equals 4.70" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>26</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4.70</mn></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals l o g 2 left-parenthesis 26 right-parenthesis equals 4.70](images/c16_10.png). Therefore, five bits are required to represent each value of the variable *X*.
*   – Let *Y* bet a random variable, which takes its values in a set of passwords. Assume that a password is composed of eight equiprobable characters: five letters (upper or lower cases)  <math alttext="StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow></math> ![StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue](images/c16_11.png) two decimal digits  <math alttext="StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow></math> ![StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue](images/c16_12.png) one special character out of eight. There exist  <math alttext="52 Superscript 5" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>52</mn></mrow><mn>5</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![52 Superscript 5](images/c16_13.png) arrangements of 5 letters out of 52,  <math alttext="10 squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> ![10 squared](images/c16_14.png) arrangements of two digits out of 10, and eight arrangements of one special character out of eight. Therefore, the cardinality *N* of the distinct passwords is  <math alttext="upper N equals 52 Superscript 5 Baseline asterisk 10 squared asterisk 8 equals 304 1 almost-equals 63 225 600 2 Superscript 38.14" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>52</mn></mrow><mn>5</mn></msup><mo>\*</mo><msup><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>\*</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>304</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8776;</mo><mn>63</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>225</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>600</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>38.14</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper N equals 52 Superscript 5 Baseline asterisk 10 squared asterisk 8 equals 304 1 almost-equals 63 225 600 2 Superscript 38.14](images/c16_15.png). Hence,

 <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals minus sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper N Endscripts StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction left-parenthesis l o g 2 left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals l o g 2 left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis equals 38.14" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true" mathsize="140%"><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover></mstyle><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>38.14</mn></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals minus sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper N Endscripts StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction left-parenthesis l o g 2 left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals l o g 2 left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis equals 38.14](images/c16_16.png)

***Definition 16.11 Joint entropy*** *of two random variables *X* and *Y*: it measures the uncertainty of a joint event “*X* and *Y*.” It is denoted  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper X comma upper Y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper X comma upper Y right-parenthesis](images/c16_17.png) and defined by:*

 <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper X comma upper Y right-parenthesis equals minus sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper N Endscripts sigma-summation Underscript j equals 1 Overscript upper M Endscripts left-parenthesis p Subscript i comma j Baseline asterisk l o g 2 left-parenthesis p Subscript i comma j Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true" mathsize="140%"><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover></mstyle><mstyle displaystyle="true" mathsize="140%"><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></munderover></mstyle><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>\*</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper X comma upper Y right-parenthesis equals minus sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper N Endscripts sigma-summation Underscript j equals 1 Overscript upper M Endscripts left-parenthesis p Subscript i comma j Baseline asterisk l o g 2 left-parenthesis p Subscript i comma j Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c16_18.png)

*where  <math alttext="p Subscript i comma j Baseline equals probability left-parenthesis upper X equals x Subscript i Baseline comma upper Y equals y Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>Pr</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![p Subscript i comma j Baseline equals probability left-parenthesis upper X equals x Subscript i Baseline comma upper Y equals y Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c16_19.png) and *N* and *M* are the numbers of values of *X* and *Y*, respectively.*

***Definition 16.12 Conditional entropy***: *it quantifies the amount of information needed to describe the outcome of a random variable *Y* given the value of a random variable *X* is known. It is written as  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper Y vertical-bar upper X right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper Y vertical-bar upper X right-parenthesis](images/c16_20.png) and defined by:*

 <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper Y vertical-bar upper X right-parenthesis equals minus sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper N Endscripts sigma-summation Underscript j equals 1 Overscript upper M Endscripts p Subscript i comma j Baseline asterisk l o g 2 left-parenthesis StartFraction p Subscript i comma j Baseline Over p Subscript i Baseline EndFraction right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true" mathsize="140%"><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover></mstyle><mstyle displaystyle="true" mathsize="140%"><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></munderover></mstyle><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>\*</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper Y vertical-bar upper X right-parenthesis equals minus sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper N Endscripts sigma-summation Underscript j equals 1 Overscript upper M Endscripts p Subscript i comma j Baseline asterisk l o g 2 left-parenthesis StartFraction p Subscript i comma j Baseline Over p Subscript i Baseline EndFraction right-parenthesis](images/c16_21.png)

*where  <math alttext="StartFraction p Subscript i comma j Baseline Over p Subscript i Baseline EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![StartFraction p Subscript i comma j Baseline Over p Subscript i Baseline EndFraction](images/c16_22.png) is the conditional probability*. The conditional entropy of *Y* if  <math alttext="upper X equals x Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper X equals x Subscript i](images/c16_23.png) is defined by:

 <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper Y vertical-bar upper X equals x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis equals minus sigma-summation Underscript j equals 1 Overscript upper M Endscripts mathsize="140%"><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></munderover></mstyle><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>Pr</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\*</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>Pr</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ***Properties of entropy***

Let  <math alttext="normal upper X" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi></math> ![normal upper X](images/c16_25.png) and  <math alttext="normal upper Y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">Y</mi></math> ![normal upper Y](images/c16_26.png) be two random variables, which take *N* and *M* distinct values, respectively. The following properties hold:

1.   <math alttext="0 upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![0 upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis](images/c16_27.png), which means that there is an upper bound to the entropy.
2.   <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c16_29.png), if and only if  <math alttext="there-exists i element-of left-bracket 1 comma upper N right-bracket vertical-bar p Subscript i Baseline equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8707;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![there-exists i element-of left-bracket 1 comma upper N right-bracket vertical-bar p Subscript i Baseline equals 1](images/c16_30.png).  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c16_31.png) means that we are certain of the variable value that will be observed.
3.   <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals minus left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction right-parenthesis sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts l o g 2 left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction right-parenthesis equals l o g 2 upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>N</mi></mrow></mstyle></mrow></math> Endscripts l o g 2 left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction right-parenthesis equals l o g 2 upper N](images/c16_32.png), if and only if  <math alttext="p Subscript i Baseline equals p Subscript j Baseline equals StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow></math> ![p Subscript i Baseline equals p Subscript j Baseline equals StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction](images/c16_33.png),  <math alttext="for-all i comma for-all j element-of left-bracket 1 comma upper N right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![for-all i comma for-all j element-of left-bracket 1 comma upper N right-bracket](images/c16_34.png), which is the most uncertain situation to predict the value of the random variable.
4.  Any change toward equalization of the probabilities  <math alttext="p 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![p 1](images/c16_35.png),  <math alttext="p 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![p 2](images/c16_36.png) ,…,  <math alttext="p Subscript upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![p Subscript upper N](images/c16_37.png) increases the entropy  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis](images/c16_38.png).  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis](images/c16_39.png) reaches it maximal value when all the probabilities are equal.
5.   <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper X comma upper Y right-parenthesis upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis plus upper H left-parenthesis upper Y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper X comma upper Y right-parenthesis upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis plus upper H left-parenthesis upper Y right-parenthesis](images/c16_40.png). The uncertainty of a joint event is less than or equal to the sum of the individual uncertainties.
6.   <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper Y vertical-bar upper X right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis upper X comma upper Y right-parenthesis minus upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper Y vertical-bar upper X right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis upper X comma upper Y right-parenthesis minus upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis](images/c16_41.png) or alternatively,  <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper X comma upper Y right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis plus upper H left-parenthesis upper Y vertical-bar upper X right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper X comma upper Y right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis plus upper H left-parenthesis upper Y vertical-bar upper X right-parenthesis](images/c16_42.png).
7.   <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper Y vertical-bar upper X right-parenthesis equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper Y vertical-bar upper X right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c16_43.png), if and only if the value of *Y* is completely determined by the value of *X*.  <math alttext="normal upper H left-parenthesis upper Y vertical-bar upper X right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis upper Y right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![normal upper H left-parenthesis upper Y vertical-bar upper X right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis upper Y right-parenthesis](images/c16_44.png), if and only if *Y* and *X* are independent. Uncertainty of *Y* is never increased, if *X* is known.

***Definition 16.13 Min-entropy*** *of a random variable *X* that takes values from a set  <math alttext="upper S equals StartSet x 1 comma x 2 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript upper N Baseline
