![upper H bar m i n left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals min Underscript i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper N Endscripts left-parenthesis minus l o g 2 p Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis equals minus l o g 2 m a x Subscript i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper N Baseline p Subscript i](images/c16_49.png).*

The min-entropy is the negative logarithm of the probability that *X* is determined correctly with only one guess of the form “is *X* equal to  <math alttext="x Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![x Subscript i](images/c16_50.png)?”

***Properties of min-entropy***

1.  The maximum possible value for the min-entropy of a random variable with *N* distinct values is  <math alttext="l o g 2 upper N" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> ![l o g 2 upper N](images/c16_51.png) that is reached when the random variable has a uniform probability distribution.
2.  If a random variable *X* has a min-entropy of *h*, then the probability of observing (or guessing) any particular value of *X* is no greater than  <math alttext="2 Superscript negative h" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript negative h](images/c16_52.png).

***Definition 16.14 Hartley’s entropy***: *it is also called max-entropy; and it is a simple measurement that only relies on the cardinality of the set of possible values of the variable. Let *N* denote the cardinality of the values of a variable *X*. The Hartley’s entropy of *X* is defined by:*  <math alttext="upper H upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals l o g 2 left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals l o g 2 left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis](images/c16_53.png).

Hartley’s entropy assumes the distribution of values of the random variable is uniform. Therefore, the Shannon’s entropy is a generalization of that of Hartley, because when all the values are identically distributed, i.e.  <math alttext="p Subscript i Baseline equals p Subscript j Baseline equals StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction comma for-all i element-of left-bracket 1 comma upper N right-bracket comma for-all j element-of left-bracket 1 comma upper N right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mrow><mo>\]</mo><mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![p Subscript i Baseline equals p Subscript j Baseline equals StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction comma for-all i element-of left-bracket 1 comma upper N right-bracket comma for-all j element-of left-bracket 1 comma upper N right-bracket](images/c16_54.png), the Shannon’s entropy formula becomes:

 <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals minus sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper N Endscripts left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction asterisk l o g 2 left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals negative upper N asterisk StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction asterisk l o g 2 left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction right-parenthesis equals l o g 2 left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true" mathsize="140%"><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover></mstyle><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo>\*</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>\*</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo>\*</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals minus sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper N Endscripts left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction asterisk l o g 2 left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals negative upper N asterisk StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction asterisk l o g 2 left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction right-parenthesis equals l o g 2 left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis](images/c16_55.png)

**Note.** The most used model of entropy in cryptography is the min-entropy, which measures the lower bound on the entropy. The min-entropy is never greater than the Shannon’s entropy, which measures the average unpredictability of the outcomes.

### 16.1.3 Some Popular PRNGs (not to use in Cryptography)

The following three PRNGs are well known and used, in particular in simulation and testing applications. However, they are not used in cryptography field, because the prediction of the PRNG output is easy.

#### 16.1.3.1 Middle-Square Algorithm

Take a first random number  <math alttext="upper X 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper X 0](images/c16_56.png) (generated by an entropy source) of *n* digits, square it, and then pick the *n* digits in the middle of  <math alttext="upper X 0 squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper X 0 squared](images/c16_57.png) and obtain a new random number  <math alttext="upper X 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper X 1](images/c16_58.png), then square  <math alttext="upper X 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper X 1](images/c16_59.png) and pick the *n* digits in the middle of  <math alttext="upper X 1 squared" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> ![upper X 1 squared](images/c16_60.png) and obtain  <math alttext="upper X 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper X 2](images/c16_61.png), etc. The sequence of numbers generated by the Middle-square algorithm is defined by:

 <math alttext="upper X Subscript i Baseline equals upper M i d d l e bar d i g i t s bar o f left-parenthesis upper X Subscript n minus 1 Superscript 2 Baseline comma n right-parenthesis comma i ampersand gt semicolon 0" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>s</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>o</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>(</mo><msubsup><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#38;gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X Subscript i Baseline equals upper M i d d l e bar d i g i t s bar o f left-parenthesis upper X Subscript n minus 1 Superscript 2 Baseline comma n right-parenthesis comma i ampersand gt semicolon 0](images/c16_62.png)

where  <math alttext="upper X 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper X 0](images/c16_63.png) is a selected seed. If some  <math alttext="upper X Subscript i" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper X Subscript i](images/c16_64.png) has less than  <math alttext="2 n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![2 n](images/c16_65.png) digits, it is padded, on the left, with 0s to get a number with  <math alttext="2 n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![2 n](images/c16_66.png) digits. The generated sequence of numbers in the interval  <math alttext="left-bracket 0 comma 10 Superscript n Baseline minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 0 comma 10 Superscript n Baseline minus 1 right-bracket](images/c16_67.png) appear as a sequence of random numbers.

**Example 16.2**

*   – Let  <math alttext="upper X 0 equals 89" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>89</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 0 equals 89](images/c16_68.png).
    
*    <math alttext="upper X 0 Superscript 1 Baseline equals 7921" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>7921</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 0 Superscript 1 Baseline equals 7921](images/c16_69.png); hence,  <math alttext="upper X 1 equals 92" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>92</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 1 equals 92](images/c16_70.png).     <math alttext="upper X 1 squared equals 8464" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>8464</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 1 squared equals 8464](images/c16_71.png); hence,  <math alttext="upper X 2 equals 46" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>46</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 2 equals 46](images/c16_72.png).
    
*    <math alttext="upper X 2 squared equals 2116" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>X</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>2116</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 2 squared equals 2116](images/c16_73.png); hence,  <math alttext="upper X 3 equals 11" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 3 equals 11](images/c16_74.png).     <math alttext="upper X 3 squared equals 0121" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>X</mi><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>0121</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 3 squared equals 0121](images/c16_75.png); hence,  <math alttext="upper X 4 equals 12" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>12</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 4 equals 12](images/c16_76.png).
    
*   The sequence continues as follows:  <math alttext="14 comma 19 comma 36 comma 29 comma 84 comma 5 comma 2 comma 0 comma 0 comma 0 ellipsis comma 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>14</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>19</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>36</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>29</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>84</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![14 comma 19 comma 36 comma 29 comma 84 comma 5 comma 2 comma 0 comma 0 comma 0 ellipsis comma 0](images/c16_77.png).
    
*   The PRNG stops producing distinct values when it reach  <math alttext="upper X 12 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 12 equals 0](images/c16_78.png).
    
*   ● Let  <math alttext="upper X 0 equals 2916" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2916</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 0 equals 2916](images/c16_79.png)
    

*    <math alttext="upper X 0 squared equals 2916 squared equals 08503056" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>2916</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>08503056</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 0 squared equals 2916 squared equals 08503056](images/c16_80.png); thus,  <math alttext="upper X 1 equals 5030" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>5030</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 1 equals 5030](images/c16_81.png).
    
*    <math alttext="upper X 1 squared equals 5030 squared equals 25300900" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>5030</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>25300900</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 1 squared equals 5030 squared equals 25300900](images/c16_82.png); thus,  <math alttext="upper X 2 equals 3009" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3009</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 2 equals 3009](images/c16_83.png).
    
*    <math alttext="upper X 2 squared equals 3009 squared equals 09054081" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>X</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>3009</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>09054081</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 2 squared equals 3009 squared equals 09054081](images/c16_84.png); thus,  <math alttext="upper X 3 equals 0540" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0540</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 3 equals 0540](images/c16_85.png).
    
*    <math alttext="upper X 3 squared equals 0540 squared equals 00291600" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msubsup><mi>X</mi><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>0540</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>00291600</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 3 squared equals 0540 squared equals 00291600](images/c16_86.png); thus,  <math alttext="upper X 4 equals 2916 equals upper X 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2916</mn><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper X 4 equals 2916 equals upper X 0](images/c16_87.png).
    
*   Therefore, the second PRNG has a period of 4, which is a very low value.
    

#### 16.1.3.2 Linear Congruential Generator

The current golden standard for the generation of random numbers is the linear congruential generator (LCG). The LCG has four inputs: the modulus *m*, the multiplier *a*, the increment *b*, and the seed  <math alttext="upper X 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper X 0](images/c16_88.png). The LCG random number sequence is defined by:

 <math alttext="upper X Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis a upper X Subscript i minus 1 Baseline plus b right-parenthesis m o d m comma i ampersand gt semicolon 0" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#38;gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis a upper X Subscript i minus 1 Baseline plus b right-parenthesis m o d m comma i ampersand gt semicolon 0](images/c16_89.png)

One of the most known and used LCGs was proposed by Park and Miller in 1988; it is referred to as MINSTD. The original version of Park and Miller’s LCG was defined by a modulus  <math alttext="m equals 2 Superscript 31 Baseline minus 1 equals 2 147 483 647" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>31</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>147</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>483</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>647</mn></mrow></math> ![m equals 2 Superscript 31 Baseline minus 1 equals 2 147 483 647](images/c16_90.png), a multiplier  <math alttext="a equals 7 Superscript 5 Baseline equals 16807" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>7</mn><mn>5</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>16807</mn></mrow></math> ![a equals 7 Superscript 5 Baseline equals 16807](images/c16_91.png), and an increment  <math alttext="b equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![b equals 0](images/c16_92.png). Some implementations use  <math alttext="a equals 48 comma 271" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>48</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>271</mn></mrow></math> ![a equals 48 comma 271](images/c16_93.png) or  <math alttext="a equals 69621" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>69621</mn></mrow></math> ![a equals 69621](images/c16_94.png). Park and Miller’s LCG has a (full) period of  <math alttext="m minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![m minus 1](images/c16_95.png). It is worth noticing that the rand() function of ISO C standard is based on Park and Miller’s LCG.

Another known LCG is the one used by the drand48() function of Linux (complying with POSIX 1.-2001), where the random number sequence is defined by:  <math alttext="upper X Subscript i Baseline equals left-parenthesis 25214903917 asterisk upper X Subscript i minus 1 Baseline plus 11 right-parenthesis m o d 2 Superscript 48" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>25214903917</mn><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>48</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![upper X Subscript i Baseline equals left-parenthesis 25214903917 asterisk upper X Subscript i minus 1 Baseline plus 11 right-parenthesis m o d 2 Superscript 48](images/c16_96.png). The values returned by drand48() are nonnegative double-precision, floating-point values uniformly distributed over the interval  <math alttext="left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c16_97.png).

**Example 16.3**

Let LCG parameters be  <math alttext="upper X 0 equals 19" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>19</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 0 equals 19](images/c16_98.png),  <math alttext="m equals 101" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>101</mn></mrow></math> ![m equals 101](images/c16_99.png),  <math alttext="a equals 13" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow></math> ![a equals 13](images/c16_100.png), and  <math alttext="b equals 11" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow></math> ![b equals 11](images/c16_101.png). The numbers generated with the selected parameters are:

19, 56, 32, 23, 7, 1, 24, 20, 69, 100, 99, 86, 18, 43, 65, 48, 29, 85, 5, 76, 90, 70, 12, 66, 61, 97, 60, 84, 93, 8, 14, 92, 96, 47, 16, 17, 30, 98, 73, 51, 68, 87, 31, 10, 40, 26, 46, 3, 50, 55, 19, 56, 32, 23, 7, 1, 24, 20, 69, 100, 99, 86, 18, 43, 65, 48, 29, 85, 5, 76, 90, 70, 12, 66, 61, 97, 60, 84, 93, 8, 14, 92, 96, 47, 16, 17, 30, 98, 73, 51, 68, 87, 31, 10, 40, 26, 46, 3, 50, 55.

First, notice that all the numbers appear in double. Therefore, they are uniformly distributed. Second, notice that when the seed (i.e. 19) repeats, all the following numbers repeat. Therefore, the generated sequence has a cycle of 50 numbers; and it should not be used when more than 50 random numbers are required.

**Notes**

*   In general, LCGs have greater cycle periods than Middle-square algorithms, which makes them preferred PRNGs.
*   The period of an LCG may be the same than that of its modulus.
*   Because of their predictability, LCGs should not be used as building blocks of cryptosystems (see Problem 16.1).

#### 16.1.3.3 Mersenne Twister PRNG

Currently, the most respected PRNG is called Mersenne Twister (MT); it was proposed by Matsumoto and Nishimura in 1998 \[[2](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0002)\]. Its period is of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 19937 Baseline minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>19937</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 19937 Baseline minus 1](images/c16_102.png), which means that approximately  <math alttext="10 Superscript 5980" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5980</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![10 Superscript 5980](images/c16_103.png) random numbers may be generated without sequence repetition. There exist standard implementations of the MT19937 in many programming languages (such as Python) and libraries (such as C++, Mathematica, and Statistical Package for the Social Sciences).

**Note**. For interested readers, Park and Miller discussed some properties to design and implement good random number generators \[[3](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0003)\].

### 16.1.4 PRNGs for Cryptography: Notions and Design Principles

#### 16.1.4.1 Properties of PRNGs for Cryptography

***Definition 16.15 Cryptographically secure PRNG (CSPRNG)***: *it is a PRNG suitable to cryptographic applications and services. Numbers generated by a CSPRNG shall be statistically indistinguishable from pure random numbers and unpredictable for an adversary that does not know the seed.*

In other words, a pseudorandom number sequence is cryptographically secure, if it is difficult for an attacker, with limited computational resources, to predict the next number(s) from the numbers already in his/her possession. A minimum security requirement for PRNG is that the length  <math alttext="k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> ![k](images/c16_104.png) of the random seed should be sufficiently large, so that a search over  <math alttext="2 Superscript k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript k](images/c16_105.png) elements (i.e. the entire seed space of possible seeds) is computationally infeasible, which prevents brute-force attacks.

#### 16.1.4.2 General Guidelines for the Design of PRBGs for Cryptography

In practice, different approaches can be used to build a CSPRNG:

*   Block ciphers running in some suitable modes such as CTR.
*   Stream ciphers[²](#c16.xhtml#c16-note-0002) (with an adequate period).
*   Hash functions and keyed-hash functions.
*   Combination of the above building blocks.

The NIST recommendation is to use Deterministic Random Bit Generators (DRBGs) to generate PRNs, as discussed in the next section. A DRBG generates bit-strings that are converted into numbers. Therefore, in the context of this chapter, DRBGs are equivalent to PRNGs. In \[[4](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0004)–[6](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0006)\], useful recommendations are provided to help DRBG developers. Below is a summary of the proposed guidelines. For more detail, refer to the complete recommendations.

##### *16.1.4.2.1 Entropy Input*

A DRBG takes an entropy input and other inputs (personalized string, nonce, etc.) to generate a sequence of pseudorandom bit strings. As shown in [Figure 16.2](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0002), there exist three main alternatives to deliver an entropy input depending on noise source quality:

![Figure 16.2 Main alternatives for entropy input.](images/c16f002.png)

[**Figure 16.2**](#c16.xhtml#rc16-fig-0002) Main alternatives for entropy input.

*   A single source of noise is used (see [Figure 16.2a](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0002)): when a noise source delivers outputs, which are close to true-random bit-strings, the outputs of noise source can be directly used as input to the DRBG.
*   A single source of noise is used jointly with conditioning function (see [Figure 16.2b](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0002)): when a noise source delivers outputs, which are not close to true-random bit-strings, the outputs are processed by a conditioning function to reduce the bias in the noise and then the outputs of the conditioning function are used as input to the DRBG. Recall that a conditioning function can be an encryption or a hash function.
*   Multiple sources are used jointly with a conditioning function (see [Figure 16.2c](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0002)): when the entropy of a single noise source is not enough to deliver entropy input with the required length, multiple noise sources can be used and their outputs are concatenated to form an entropy bit-string, with a sufficient length, which then is processed with a conditioning function to generate the entropy input to the DRBG.

When DRBGs recommended by the NIST are considered, the conditioning function may be one of the following:

*   HMAC algorithm (see Section 5.3.2.1)
*   AES-CMAC (see Section 9.2.2)
*   AES-CBC-MAC[³](#c16.xhtml#c16-note-0003)
*   An approved hash function (see [Table 16.1](#c16.xhtml#c16-tbl-0001))
*   Hash\_DerivationFunction (see [Section 16.2.2](#c16.xhtml#c16-sec-02004))
*   BC\_DerivationFunction (see [Section 16.2.4](#c16.xhtml#c16-sec-02006))

![Table 16.1 Recommended values and hash functions for DRBGs.](images/c16_106.png)

[**Table 16.1**](#c16.xhtml#rc16-tbl-0001) Recommended values and hash functions for DRBGs.

##### *16.1.4.2.2 Validation of Entropy Noise*

In order to design an entropy source that provides an adequate amount of entropy per output bit-string, the developer must be able to accurately estimate the amount of entropy that can be provided by sampling the used noise source. The validation of an entropy source presents many challenges, because it depends on the environment of the security system and details of implementation. The general approach to validate a source of a DRBG is to sample the noise source and use statistical tests, such as Chi-square test, to assess the IID property of the outputs. The samples from a noise source are independent and identically distributed (IID), if each sample has the same probability distribution as every other sample, and all samples are mutually independent. The IID assumption significantly simplifies the process of entropy estimation. When the IID assumption does not hold, i.e. the samples are either not identically distributed or are not independently distributed (or both), estimating entropy is more difficult and requires other advanced methods. The recommended solution to reduce the imperfection (i.e. the bias) of a source of noise is to include a conditioning function. For more detail on recommended methods for testing entropy sources, refer to \[[5](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0005)\].

##### *16.1.4.2.3 Full Entropy*

It is recommended that the bit-strings used as entropy input of DRBGs are full entropy bit-strings. A bit-string has the full entropy property, if the amount of entropy is essentially the same as its length.

***Definition 16.16 Full entropy bit-string*** : *it is a bit-string in which each bit is with a uniform distribution and independent of every other bits of that bit-string. A bit-string of *n* bits is said to have full entropy, if the bit-string is estimated to contain at least  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 1 minus right-parenthesis n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 1 minus right-parenthesis n](images/c16_111.png) bits of entropy, where ε is a very small value (e.g.  <math alttext="epsilon less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript negative 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![epsilon less-than-or-equal-to 2 Superscript negative 64](images/c16_112.png)), which represents the upper bound on bias.*

In \[[6](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0006)\], it is considered that when a process (which may be a noise source, a noise source with conditioning function, or a combination of multiple noise sources) has an input with an entropy of at least  <math alttext="2 n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![2 n](images/c16_113.png), the process is sufficient to generate full entropy bit-strings of  <math alttext="n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![n](images/c16_114.png) bits.

##### *16.1.4.2.4 Reseeding DRBGs*

In general, in cryptography, the period of a PRNG is not an issue, if it is large (e.g. in magnitude of  <math alttext="2 Superscript 64" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 64](images/c16_115.png)). However, in CSPRBGs, it is recommended to reseed the generation process (i.e. change the seed), for the following reasons:

1.  Prevent against attackers being able to figure out numbers that were output before the internal state of the PRBG becomes compromised. Reseeding, is an efficient operation (with no extra cost), which protects against backtracking attacks. When entropy source is available on-demand, the DRBG is said to support *prediction resistance*.
2.  To include fresh signals from the current source of entropy or to add new sources of entropy to the system in order to improve the randomness of the seed.

Reseeding is optional, but recommended, and it may be

*   Explicitly requested by a consuming cryptographic application or service.
*   Performed when prediction resistance is requested by a consuming application.
*   Triggered when a predetermined number of pseudorandom outputs have been produced or a predetermined number of *generate* requests have been made (i.e. at the end of the seed life).
*   Triggered by external events (e.g. whenever a new entropy is available).

As discussed in the next section, the NIST recommends to reseed a DRBG after some amount of generated bit-strings (see [Tables 16.1](#c16.xhtml#c16-tbl-0001) and [16.2](#c16.xhtml#c16-tbl-0002)).

![Table 16.2 Recommended values for block-cipher-based DRBGs.](images/c16_116.png)

[**Table 16.2**](#c16.xhtml#rc16-tbl-0002) Recommended values for block-cipher-based DRBGs.

##### *16.1.4.2.5 Other Inputs of DRBGs*

DRBGs used in practice are standard; and the sources of entropy rely on public algorithms. Therefore, most operational cryptographic applications and services make use of the same components to generate random numbers, which may result in a backdoor. In addition to entropy input, it is highly recommended to add other user-chosen inputs to DRBGs used in cryptography to enforce their resistance to attacks. In particular, DRBGs recommended by the NIST have three optional parameters: a personalization string, a nonce, and an additional input.

*   *Personalization string*: it is intended to introduce additional input into the initialization of a DRBG. This personalization string might contain values unknown to attackers or values that tend to differentiate a DRBG instance from all others. Ideally, a personalization string is set to some bit string that is as unique as possible. Appropriate contents for the personalization bit-string include: device serial numbers, user identification, network addresses, protocol version identifiers, per-module or per-device values, random numbers generated with other PRNGs, and timestamps. A combination of the previous items can be used to form a personalization bit-string. The personalization string is used during the instantiation of the DRBG.
*   *Nonce*: a nonce may be required in the construction of a seed during a DRBG instantiation in order to provide a security cushion to block certain attacks. Each nonce shall be unique to the cryptographic module in which instantiation is performed, but need not be secret. When used, the nonce shall be considered to be a critical security parameter. A nonce may be composed of one (or more) of the following components (other components may also be appropriate): a random value that is generated anew for each nonce, using an approved random bit generator; a timestamp of sufficient resolution, so that it is different each time it is used; a monotonically increasing sequence number; or combination of a timestamp and a monotonically increasing sequence number. When provided, the nonce is used in the DRBG instantiation and reseeding operations.
*   *Additional input*: it is an optional input provided to reseeding operations and random bit-string generation requests and it aims to add randomness to the current state of the DRBG, so that each bit-string is generated using internal state of the DRBG and a user randomly-selected input.

##### *16.1.4.2.6 Conversion of a Bit-String into Integers*

DRBGs generate bit-strings with a required bit-length of *L*, while algorithms (such as Diffie-Hellman) need random numbers in a range of  <math alttext="left-bracket 1 comma n minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 1 comma n minus 1 right-bracket](images/c16_124.png) to generate keying material. As depicted in [Figure 16.3](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0003), to generate a random number from the output of a DRBG, a conversion operation is required. Currently, two conversion methods are recommended \[[7](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0007)\]: modular reduction and discard method.

![Figure 16.3 PRNG = DRBG + conversion function.](images/c16f003.png)

[**Figure 16.3**](#c16.xhtml#rc16-fig-0003) PRNG = DRBG + conversion function.

###### *16.1.4.2.6.1* *Modular Reduction*

DRBG output, a value in  <math alttext="left-bracket 0 comma 2 Superscript upper L Baseline minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 0 comma 2 Superscript upper L Baseline minus 1 right-bracket](images/c16_125.png), is reduced to an integer in the interval  <math alttext="left-bracket 1 comma n minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 1 comma n minus 1 right-bracket](images/c16_126.png), while ensuring that any bias introduced in the conversion is negligible, using the following procedure:

###### *16.1.4.2.6.2* *Discard Method*

This method converts a probability distribution on  <math alttext="left-bracket 0 comma n minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 0 comma n minus 1 right-bracket](images/c16_142.png) into a probability distribution on  <math alttext="left-bracket 0 comma 2 Superscript upper L Baseline minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 0 comma 2 Superscript upper L Baseline minus 1 right-bracket](images/c16_143.png) and accepts an output value only if it is in both intervals,  <math alttext="left-bracket 0 comma n minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 0 comma n minus 1 right-bracket](images/c16_144.png) and  <math alttext="left-bracket 0 comma upper N minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 0 comma upper N minus 1 right-bracket](images/c16_145.png), using the following procedure:

##### *16.1.4.2.7 Conceptual Interface*

Conceptually, a DRBG can be viewed as a black-box that can be accessed by users[⁴](#c16.xhtml#c16-note-0004) requesting random bit-strings through an interface defined by at least four operations:

1.  Instantiate function: it initializes the internal status of the DRBG, using the entropy input, the personalization string, and, optionally, a nonce. It builds the seed.
2.  Reseed function: it acquires a new entropy input and combines it with the current internal state and any additional input that is provided to create a new seed and a new internal state.
3.  Generate function: it enables the consuming application to query the DRBG to obtain a new rand bit-string.
4.  Health testing function: it provides useful information to check if the DRBG continues to operate correctly or not.

## 16.2 Pseudorandom Bit Generators Recommended for Cryptography

In \[[4](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0004)\], the NIST recommends three models of DRBGs: hash-function-based, HMAC-based, and block-cipher-based DRBGs. The three models share common notions: inputs, internal state (i.e. variables that represent the current state of the DRBG), and access interface functions.

### 16.2.1 Common Mechanisms and Processes

#### 16.2.1.1 Security Strength

If the seed is kept secret, the bits generated by the DRBG will be unpredictable, up to the instantiated security strength of the DRBG. The three specified DRBGs support four security strengths: 112, 128, 192, or 256 bits. The security strength is requested during the DRBG instantiation, and the Instantiate function obtains the appropriate amount of entropy for the requested security strength (see values in [Tables 16.1](#c16.xhtml#c16-tbl-0001) and [16.2](#c16.xhtml#c16-tbl-0002)). If the available entropy input does not have the required security strength, the instantiation fails. The maximum security strength supported by a specific DRBG instantiation depends on the DRBG implementation and on the amount of entropy used to feed the DRBG. In order to provide a security strength of *S* bits, the bit-length of the entropy input shall be of at least *S*. Once instantiated, a DRBG *G* is called to generate bit-strings with a bit-length *L* specified by the consuming application. The security strength of the output of a bit-length *L* is  <math alttext="upper S upper L left-parenthesis upper G comma upper L right-parenthesis equals m i n left-parenthesis upper L comma upper D upper R upper B upper G bar upper S upper L left-parenthesis upper G right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>G</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>S</mi><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper S upper L left-parenthesis upper G comma upper L right-parenthesis equals m i n left-parenthesis upper L comma upper D upper R upper B upper G bar upper S upper L left-parenthesis upper G right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c16_159.png), where  <math alttext="upper D upper R upper B upper G bar upper S upper L left-parenthesis upper G right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>G</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>S</mi><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper D upper R upper B upper G bar upper S upper L left-parenthesis upper G right-parenthesis](images/c16_160.png) denotes the maximum security strength level that the DRBG *G* can provide. Therefore, applications that require a certain security strength must request random bit-strings of a bit-length at least equal to the required security strength.

**Note.** Using a random bit-string yielded by a concatenation of *m* outputs, each of *L* bits, of a DRBG with a maximum strength level of 128 bits, will not result in a security strength of  <math alttext="m asterisk 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>\*</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow></math> ![m asterisk 128](images/c16_161.png) bits, but of  <math alttext="m i n left-parenthesis 128 comma m asterisk upper L right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>128</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![m i n left-parenthesis 128 comma m asterisk upper L right-parenthesis](images/c16_162.png).

#### 16.2.1.2 Instantiating a DRBG

Any DRBG shall be instantiated before requesting random bit-strings. The instantiation process performs the following actions:

*   If the security strength required by the consuming application is greater than the maximum security strength that can be provided by the DRBG, then return an error. Otherwise, set the  <math alttext="upper D upper R upper B upper G bar i n s t a n c e bar s e c u r i t y bar s t r e n g t h" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>G</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>s</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> ![upper D upper R upper B upper G bar i n s t a n c e bar s e c u r i t y bar s t r e n g t h](images/c16_163.png) to the lowest security strength greater than or equal to the required security strength from the set  <math alttext="StartSet 112 comma 128 comma 192 comma 256 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>112</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>128</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>192</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>256</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 112 comma 128 comma 192 comma 256 EndSet](images/c16_164.png).  <math alttext="upper D upper R upper B upper G bar i n s t a n c e bar s e c u r i t y bar s t r e n g t h" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>G</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>s</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> ![upper D upper R upper B upper G bar i n s t a n c e bar s e c u r i t y bar s t r e n g t h](images/c16_165.png) is one of the constants of the internal state of the DRBG.
*   If the lengths of some parameters do not comply with the limits (as specified in [Tables 16.1](#c16.xhtml#c16-tbl-0001) and [16.2](#c16.xhtml#c16-tbl-0002)), then return an error.
*   Get the entropy input from the entropy source. If the used source of entropy does not have the capacity to deliver outputs with a bit-length that can provide the  <math alttext="upper D upper R upper B upper G bar i n s t a n c e bar s e c u r i t y bar s t r e n g t h" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>G</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>s</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> ![upper D upper R upper B upper G bar i n s t a n c e bar s e c u r i t y bar s t r e n g t h](images/c16_167.png), then return an error.
*   When the Instantiate function makes use of a nonce, obtain a nonce with a security strength of at least  <math alttext="upper D upper R upper B upper G bar i n s t a n c e bar s e c u r i t y bar s t r e n g t h slash 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>G</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>s</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![upper D upper R upper B upper G bar i n s t a n c e bar s e c u r i t y bar s t r e n g t h slash 2](images/c16_168.png).
*   Use the Instantiate function to compute the initial state of the DRBG.

#### 16.2.1.3 Reseeding a DRBG

Reseeding a DRBG does not change its  <math alttext="upper D upper R upper B upper G bar i n s t a n c e bar s e c u r i t y bar s t r e n g t h" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>G</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>s</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> ![upper D upper R upper B upper G bar i n s t a n c e bar s e c u r i t y bar s t r e n g t h](images/c16_169.png). The reseeding process performs the following actions:

*   If the lengths of some parameters do not comply with the limits (as specified in [Tables 16.1](#c16.xhtml#c16-tbl-0001) and [16.2](#c16.xhtml#c16-tbl-0002)), then return an error.
*   Get the entropy input from the entropy source. If the used source of entropy does not have the capacity to deliver outputs with a bit-length that can provide the  <math alttext="upper D upper R upper B upper G bar i n s t a n c e bar s e c u r i t y bar s t r e n g t h" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>G</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>s</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> ![upper D upper R upper B upper G bar i n s t a n c e bar s e c u r i t y bar s t r e n g t h](images/c16_170.png), then return an error.
*   Use the Reseed function to compute the new internal state of the DRBG.

#### 16.2.1.4 Internal State of a DRBG

Any DRBG instance has an internal state, which, in general, includes two categories of elements: common elements and specific elements. Elements common to all the three DRBG models include:

*   Constants: the maximum security strength that can be provided by the DRBG instance (denoted  <math alttext="upper D upper R upper B upper G bar i n s t a n c e bar s e c u r i t y bar s t r e n g t h" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>G</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>s</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>\_</mo><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> ![upper D upper R upper B upper G bar i n s t a n c e bar s e c u r i t y bar s t r e n g t h](images/c16_171.png)), the bit-length of the seed (denoted  <math alttext="upper S e e d upper L e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper S e e d upper L e n](images/c16_173.png)), the maximum bits per generate request, and the maximum number of generate requests before reseeding.
*   Variable  <math alttext="upper R e s e e d upper C o u n t e r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R e s e e d upper C o u n t e r](images/c16_174.png), which indicates the number of random bit-strings generated since the instantiation of the DRBG or since the last reseeding action. It is reinitialized to 1 when the DRBG is reseeded.

#### 16.2.1.5 Description Format of DRBG Functions

In the following subsections, the description of the DRBG functions are provided in sufficient detail with the following notation and restrictions:

*   The specification of DRBG functions includes a clause **parameters**, which specifies the fixed values or functions used to build the DRBG functions before calling them, while the clause **input** specifies the values used in each function call.
*   In the description of the DRBG functions, the test of cases of invalid calls (such as: the requested bit-length is greater than the fixed maximum value, the maximum number of requests is exceeded, etc.) are not included, assuming that the function calls are valid. Therefore, some specific details are omitted.

### 16.2.2 Hash-based DRBGs

Currently, two DRBGs based on hash functions are recommended: Hash-DRBG and HMAC-DRBG; their security strength is, at most, the same as the security strength of the hash function for pre-image resistance (see [Table 16.1](#c16.xhtml#c16-tbl-0001)).

The recommended values and functions for hash-DRBG usage are provided in [Table 16.1](#c16.xhtml#c16-tbl-0001) \[[4](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0004)\].

**Notes**

*   – SHA-1 is deprecated for its insecurity and not recommended in DRBGs.
*   – SHA3 is not recommended in \[[4](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0004)\]. However, it may be used to build (not NIST-approved) DRBGs.

A hash-based DRBG is characterized by its hash function. Its internal state consists of the common elements and two specific variables:

*   *V*: a variable of the same bit-length than that of the seed. It changes each time a new random bit-string is generated;
*   *C*: a variable of the same bit-length than that of the seed. It changes only when the DRBG is instantiated or reseeded.

The overall structure of hash-based DRBGs is depicted in [Figure 16.4](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0004); the pseudocodes of the DRBG functions are given below.

![Figure 16.4 Overall structure of Hash-DRBG.](images/c16f004.png)

[**Figure 16.4**](#c16.xhtml#rc16-fig-0004) Overall structure of Hash-DRBG.

### 16.2.3 HMAC-based DRBGs

HMAC-DRBG iterates on an approved keyed hash function (see the list in [Table 16.1](#c16.xhtml#c16-tbl-0001)).

In addition to the common elements, the internal state of an HMAC-DRBG instance includes two variables:

*   Variable *V*: bit-string of the same bit-length than that of the used hash function.
*   Variable  <math alttext="upper K e y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K e y](images/c16_233.png): key of the same bit-length than that of the used hash function. Such a key changes from time to time; but it must change when a new random bit-string is generated.

The overall structure of HMAC-DRBGs is depicted in [Figure 16.5](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0005); the pseudocodes of the DRBG functions are given below.

![Figure 16.5 Overall structure of HMAC-DRBG.](images/c16f005.png)

[**Figure 16.5**](#c16.xhtml#rc16-fig-0005) Overall structure of HMAC-DRBG.

### 16.2.4 Block Cipher-based DRBGs

CTR (CounTeR) mode of operation of block ciphers, which is introduced in Section 8.5, is used to build CTR-DRBGs. Recommended CTR-DRBGs make use of the encryption primitive of either 3-key TDEA or AES. Therefore, their security strength is, at maximum, the same as the security strength of the underlying block cipher (see [Table 16.2](#c16.xhtml#c16-tbl-0002)).

Two methods are proposed to build CTR-DRBGs:

1.  When the source of entry provides a full entropy, there is no need to use a block cipher derivation function.
2.  If the source of entropy cannot provide a full entropy, a derivation function is used to provide the needed randomness.

In addition to the common elements, internal state of CTR-DRBG includes two variables:

*   Variable *V*: bit-string of the same bit-length than that of the block length of the underlying block cipher (i.e. 64 bits for TDEA and 128 for AES).
*   Variable  <math alttext="upper K e y" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ![upper K e y](images/c16_282.png): key of the same bit-length than that of by the underlying block cipher (i.e. 56 bits for TDEA, and 128, 192 or 256 for AES) used to encrypt.

Limits on CTR-DRBG parameters are summarized in [Table 16.2](#c16.xhtml#c16-tbl-0002). The overall structure of CTR-DRBGs is depicted in [Figure 16.6](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0006); and pseudocodes of DRBG functions are given below.

![Figure 16.6 Overall structure of CTR-DRBG.](images/c16f006.png)

[**Figure 16.6**](#c16.xhtml#rc16-fig-0006) Overall structure of CTR-DRBG.

## 16.3 Prime Number Generation

Public-key cryptographic algorithms (such as RSA, Diffie-Hellman, and MQV algorithms) require prime numbers to select their domain parameters (i.e. public and private keys and other parameters). The first approach is to use true primes, also called provable primes. As discussed in this section, generating provable primes may be very time consuming. The second approach is to use numbers that are very likely to be primes; such numbers are referred to as probably-primes.

In the previous section, we discussed methods for generating large random numbers. Since there are no guarantees that a random number is prime, we need to test if a randomly generated number is prime before using it. The problem of determining whether a given number is prime has become a challenge for centuries. With the event of computer-based systems, the issue had become more challenging, because larger and larger prime numbers are required to strengthen the security of infrastructures and services. This section aims at introducing some basics of prime numbers and the NIST-recommended methods to generate primes for use in Diffie-Hellman, Menezes-Qu-Vanstone, and RSA algorithms.

### 16.3.1 Basics and Facts about Primes

#### 16.3.1.1 Definition of Some Prime Categories of Interest for Cryptography

***Definition 16.17 Provable prime*** *(or* ***true prime****)*: *it is a prime that is confirmed using a deterministic algorithm.*

***Definition 16.18 Probably prime*** *(or* ***pseudoprime****)*: *a large odd integer *p* is said to be probably prime if there is a high probability that it is prime. An integer *p* is probably prime if it has not been demonstrated to be either composite or prime.*

***Definition 16.19 Safe prime*** *and* ***Sophie Germain prime***: *a prime *p* is said to be safe prime, if there exists a prime *q*, called Sophie Germain prime, such that  <math alttext="p equals 2 q plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 2 q plus 1](images/c16_399.png).*

**Example 16.4**

11 is a safe prime, because  <math alttext="11 equals 2 asterisk 5 plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>11</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![11 equals 2 asterisk 5 plus 1](images/c16_400.png).

83 is a safe prime, because  <math alttext="83 equals 2 asterisk 41 plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>83</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>41</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![83 equals 2 asterisk 41 plus 1](images/c16_401.png).

381 is a safe prime, because  <math alttext="381 equals 2 asterisk 191 plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>381</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>191</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![381 equals 2 asterisk 191 plus 1](images/c16_402.png).

***Definition 16.20 Mersenne prime***: *a prime *p* is said to be a Mersenne prime, if there exists a positive integer *m*, such that  <math alttext="p equals 2 Superscript m Baseline minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 2 Superscript m Baseline minus 1](images/c16_403.png).*

***Definition 16.21 Strong prime***: *it is an integer *p* satisfying the following conditions:*

*   *p is chosen at random using a PRNG.*
*   *p is a large prime.*
*   * <math alttext="p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p minus 1](images/c16_404.png) has a large prime factor  <math alttext="p 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![p 1](images/c16_405.png).*
*   * <math alttext="p plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p plus 1](images/c16_406.png) has a large prime factor  <math alttext="p 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![p 2](images/c16_407.png).*
*   * <math alttext="p 1 minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p 1 minus 1](images/c16_408.png) has a prime factor  <math alttext="p 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![p 3](images/c16_409.png).*

**Example 16.5**

Below are two strong primes (not usable in cryptography)

*   – 127 is a (non-cryptographic) strong prime, because
    
    *    <math alttext="127 minus 1 equals 126" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>127</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>126</mn></mrow></math> ![127 minus 1 equals 126](images/c16_410.png) has a prime factor of 7.
        
    *    <math alttext="127 plus 1 equals 128" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>127</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow></math> ![127 plus 1 equals 128](images/c16_411.png) has a prime factor of 2.
        
    *    <math alttext="7 minus 1 equals 6" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> ![7 minus 1 equals 6](images/c16_412.png); and 6 has a prime factor of 3.
        
*   – 331 is a (non-cryptographic) strong prime, because
    
    *    <math alttext="331 minus 1 equals 330" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>331</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>330</mn></mrow></math> ![331 minus 1 equals 330](images/c16_413.png) has a prime factor of 11.
        
    *    <math alttext="331 plus 1 equals 332" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>331</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>332</mn></mrow></math> ![331 plus 1 equals 332](images/c16_414.png) has a prime factor of 83.
        
    *    <math alttext="11 minus 1 equals 10" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>11</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math> ![11 minus 1 equals 10](images/c16_415.png); and 10 has a prime factor of 5.
        

Currently, the method recommended to generate provable primes for FFC and IFC algorithms is based on Shawe-Taylor’s algorithm, which generates strong primes (see [Section 16.3.4](#c16.xhtml#c16-sec-02008)).

The prime number theorem is well-known in mathematics and tells us the following:

Thus, for a large integer *n*, the probability that a random integer, not greater than *n*, is prime is approximately  <math alttext="StartFraction 1 Over log left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mtext>log</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![StartFraction 1 Over log left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis EndFraction](images/c16_421.png); and the average gap between consecutive prime numbers out of the first *n* integers is approximately  <math alttext="l n left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![l n left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis](images/c16_422.png).

### 16.3.2 Methods for Primality Testing

Two methods are used for primality testing of numbers used in cryptographic algorithms: probabilistic and deterministic tests. Deterministic primality testing algorithms either confirm, with certainty, that an integer is a prime or output “Failure”, if the specified number of tries is exceeded. They are computationally intensive and require that tested integers have some properties, which makes them unusable in practice when the numbers to be tested are randomly generated and of bit-lengths of hundreds or thousands (e.g. RSA primes *p* and *q* are required to have bit-lengths greater than 1023). The second category of primality tests are probabilistic in nature; they either confirm, with certainty, that the tested integer is composite or they stop the algorithm, with a conclusion “the tested integer is probably prime.”

#### 16.3.2.1 Deterministic Methods for Primality Testing

First of all, it is worth noticing that deterministic primality testing methods are computationally intensive and/or applicable under specific assumptions. In this subsection, we introduce the three best known deterministic tests of primality.

##### *16.3.2.1.1 Generating Primes Using Sieve-of-Eratosthenes Method and Trial Division Test*

1.  *Generating primes using the sieve-of-Eratosthenes method*

The sieve of Eratosthenes is an ancient deterministic method for finding prime numbers up to a given *n* greater than 1. It is one of the methods recommended to generate a list of primes. The idea behind the method is that a number is prime, if none of the smaller prime numbers divides it. The list of primes are computed as follows:

1.  Build an initial set  <math alttext="s equals StartSet 2 comma 3 comma 4 comma Number ellipsis period comma n EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>&#8230;.</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![s equals StartSet 2 comma 3 comma 4 comma Number ellipsis period comma n EndSet](images/c16_425.png).
2.  For  <math alttext="p equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 1](images/c16_426.png) to  <math alttext="left floor StartRoot n EndRoot right floor" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8970;</mo><mrow><msqrt><mi>n</mi></msqrt></mrow><mo>&#8971;</mo></mrow></math> ![left floor StartRoot n EndRoot right floor](images/c16_427.png): discard any element  <math alttext="z element-of upper S" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> ![z element-of upper S](images/c16_428.png) such that  <math alttext="z equals k asterisk p comma" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>\*</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> ![z equals k asterisk p comma](images/c16_429.png) where *k* is an integer greater than 1.
3.  The final set *s* contains only primes.

The time complexity of sieve of Eratosthenes method is of  <math alttext="upper O left-parenthesis n log log n right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>log</mi><mi>log</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper O left-parenthesis n log log n right-parenthesis](images/c16_430.png).

*   b. *Trial division method for primality testing*

The basic method for testing if an integer is a prime is called *trial division primality testing*. It is applicable to any positive integer. It is of a naïve design:

1.  Let *z* be the integer to be tested.
2.  Using the sieve of Eratosthenes method (or another method), build a table of primes less than  <math alttext="StartRoot n EndRoot" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msqrt><mi>n</mi></msqrt></mrow></math> ![StartRoot n EndRoot](images/c16_431.png).
3.  Declare *z* prime, if no integer in the prime table divides it.

##### *16.3.2.1.2 Lucas-Lehmer Test*

When the integer *p* to be tested can be written as  <math alttext="p equals 2 Superscript m Baseline minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 2 Superscript m Baseline minus 1](images/c16_432.png), i.e. *p* is a Mersenne number, the following test, called Lucas-Lehmer test, is known to be efficient for testing, with certainty, if *p* is a prime. The test is based on a known fact that a Mersenne number  <math alttext="p equals 2 Superscript m Baseline minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 2 Superscript m Baseline minus 1](images/c16_433.png) can be prime only for prime  <math alttext="m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![m](images/c16_434.png). Hence,  <math alttext="2 Superscript 7 Baseline minus 1 equals 127" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>7</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>127</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 7 Baseline minus 1 equals 127](images/c16_448.png) is a prime.

##### *16.3.2.1.3 Lucas’s Primality Test*

In 1876, Edouard Lucas turned Fermat’s little theorem (Theorem 3.5) into a primality test. He proved the following theorem:

Lucas’s test is considered as the basis of modern primality tests; it outputs “Prime” only if the tested integer is prime. However, it requires too much time to find the integer *a* (if it exists), when *n* is a large integer.

#### 16.3.2.2 Probabilistic Methods for Primality Testing

The two well-known algorithms for probabilistic primality testing are addressed below. Miller-Rabin primality test is the one recommended by the NIST.

##### *16.3.2.2.1 Fermat’s Primality Test and Carmichael Numbers*

The following theorem, which is an alternate statement of Fermat’s little theorem, provides a fast method to check if an integer is not a prime.

Theorem 16.4 enables to answer the question: Isn’t an integer *x* prime? The inverse statement of Theorem 16.4 is not always true. That is, if  <math alttext="a Superscript p minus 1 Baseline identical-to 1 m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![a Superscript p minus 1 Baseline identical-to 1 m o d p](images/c16_469.png), for some *a* coprime to *p*, then *p* is not always prime, as shown by the following counterexamples. When  <math alttext="a Superscript p minus 1 Baseline identical-to 1 m o d p" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ![a Superscript p minus 1 Baseline identical-to 1 m o d p](images/c16_470.png), while composite, *a* is called a Fermat *liar* for *p*.

**Example 16.9**

 <math alttext="2 Superscript 10 Baseline identical-to 1 m o d Baseline 341" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>341</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 10 Baseline identical-to 1 m o d Baseline 341](images/c16_471.png); hence,  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 2 Superscript 10 Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript 34 Baseline identical-to left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Superscript 34 Baseline m o d Baseline 341 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>34</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>34</mn></mrow></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>341</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 2 Superscript 10 Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript 34 Baseline identical-to left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Superscript 34 Baseline m o d Baseline 341 equals 1](images/c16_472.png), but 341 is not prime, as it is equal to  <math alttext="31 asterisk 11" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>31</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow></math> ![31 asterisk 11](images/c16_473.png). Therefore,  <math alttext="2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![2](images/c16_474.png) is a Fermat liar for 341.

 <math alttext="5 Superscript 80 Baseline identical-to 1 m o d Baseline 561" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mn>80</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>561</mn></mrow></math> ![5 Superscript 80 Baseline identical-to 1 m o d Baseline 561](images/c16_475.png); thus,  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 5 Superscript 80 Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript 7 Baseline identical-to left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Superscript 7 Baseline m o d Baseline 561 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mn>80</mn></mrow></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>7</mn></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>7</mn></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>561</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 5 Superscript 80 Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript 7 Baseline identical-to left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Superscript 7 Baseline m o d Baseline 561 equals 1](images/c16_476.png), but 561 is not prime, as it is equal to  <math alttext="17 asterisk 11 asterisk 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>17</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> ![17 asterisk 11 asterisk 3](images/c16_477.png). Therefore,  <math alttext="5" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>5</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![5](images/c16_478.png) is a Fermat liar for 561.

One of the seminal works on primality testing was proposed by Fermat. The latter came up with the following algorithm, which is a direct application of Theorem 16.4:

Fermat’s primality test is not efficient to declare with a low probability that an integer *n* is prime. However, it was a starting idea for many primality tests in literature. Since, by design, a random integer *a* is picked for testing, the algorithms that improved Fermat’s test are probabilistic in nature. A number of iterations should be fixed in advance to stop the algorithm, if the input *p* is not declared composite. That is why the result of the test is “Probably prime”. In the sequel, the focus is on the most referenced and used primality test, the one proposed by Miller and Rabin \[[8](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0008), [9](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0009)\].

***Definition 16.22 Carmichael number***: *an integer *n* is said to be Carmichael number if there exists an integer *a* coprime to *n* such that  <math alttext="a Superscript n minus 1 Baseline identical-to 1 m o d n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![a Superscript n minus 1 Baseline identical-to 1 m o d n](images/c16_482.png).*

**Example 16.10**

561 is a Carmichael number, because  <math alttext="561 equals 3 asterisk 11 asterisk 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>561</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![561 equals 3 asterisk 11 asterisk 17](images/c16_483.png).

If we take any  <math alttext="a less-than 561" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>561</mn></mrow></math> ![a less-than 561](images/c16_484.png) and *a* coprime to 561,  <math alttext="a Superscript 560 Baseline identical-to 1 m o d Baseline 561" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>560</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>561</mn></mrow></math> ![a Superscript 560 Baseline identical-to 1 m o d Baseline 561](images/c16_485.png). For example,  <math alttext="2 Superscript 560 Baseline identical-to 1 m o d Baseline 561" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>560</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>561</mn></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 560 Baseline identical-to 1 m o d Baseline 561](images/c16_486.png). However,  <math alttext="3 Superscript 560 Baseline identical-to 375 m o d Baseline 561" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>560</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>375</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>561</mn></mrow></math> ![3 Superscript 560 Baseline identical-to 375 m o d Baseline 561](images/c16_487.png), because 3 is not coprime with 561.

***Property of Carmichael numbers***: any Carmichael number *n* is composite and will pass Fermat’s primality test, for any number *a* coprime to *n*.

As numbers become very large, Carmichael numbers become very rare. For example, it is shown in \[[10](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0010)\] that there exist approximately 20 million Carmichael numbers between 1 and  <math alttext="10 Superscript 21" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>21</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![10 Superscript 21](images/c16_488.png). Hence, the probability to pick a Carmichael number, from the interval  <math alttext="left-bracket 1 comma 10 Superscript 21 Baseline right-bracket comma" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>21</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>\]</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 1 comma 10 Superscript 21 Baseline right-bracket comma](images/c16_489.png) is very low (i.e. approximately  <math alttext="5 asterisk 10 Superscript negative 13" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>\*</mo><msup><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![5 asterisk 10 Superscript negative 13](images/c16_490.png)). Therefore, for randomly chosen odd integer *n* with hundreds of digits, the probability for *n* to be a Carmichael number is zero for practical purpose. Such a property limits the number of false positives yielded by Fermat’s primality test.

##### *16.3.2.2.2 Miller-Rabin Primality Test*

The basic idea of Miller-Rabin primality test is that given a positive integer *p*, if we randomly pick *k* integers less than *p* and if all of them are coprime with *p*, then it is very likely that *p* is a prime. Miller-Rabin primality test is probabilistic in nature; hence, it is prone to decision errors. The probability that a composite integer is declared probably prime depends on the number of iterations (i.e. the number of the tested random integers). Rabin \[[9](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0009)\] proved that the probability that a composite number *p* is erroneously asserted to be probably prime is smaller than  <math alttext="2 Superscript minus 2 k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript minus 2 k](images/c16_491.png), if *k* random integers less than *p* are tested. The interpretation of such a probability means that if the test is applied to  <math alttext="2 Superscript 2 k" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 2 k](images/c16_492.png) randomly chosen integers, the expected wrong answers is 1.

Miller-Rabin test for primality takes advantage of the following fact:

Below is the pseudocode of Miller-Rabin primality test.
