### 16.3.3 Generation of Probably-Prime Pair

The algorithms introduced below generate probably-prime pair that comply with the FFC and IFC domain parameter requirements (see Sections 14.2.2.1–14.2.2.2).

#### 16.3.3.1 Generation of Probably-Prime Pair for DH and MQV

The function below, recommended in \[[11](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0011)\], provides a solution to generate a pair of integers *p* and *p*, that are probably-prime, to be used in Diffie-Hellman and Menezes-Qu-Vanstone protocols. It makes use of a hash function, a DRBG, and Miller-Rabin primality test.  <math alttext="upper D upper R upper B upper G period g e n e r a t e left-parenthesis b l right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>G</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![upper D upper R upper B upper G period g e n e r a t e left-parenthesis b l right-parenthesis](images/c16_528.png) denotes the invocation of the underlying DRBG to generate an integer of a bit-length of  <math alttext="b l" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> ![b l](images/c16_529.png). In addition to the probably-prime pair, the function optionally may return a  <math alttext="upper S e e d" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper S e e d](images/c16_530.png) and a  <math alttext="upper C o u n t e r" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper C o u n t e r](images/c16_531.png) that can be used as an FFC domain parameters to check the compliance to standard of generated parameters.

Notice that the function above stops only when a probably-prime pair is found, while the other functions presented in the sequel have a limit in the number of tries and may fail in producing valid outputs \[[11](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0011)\] does not provide evidence that the algorithm terminates within a reasonable time.

#### 16.3.3.2 Generation of Probably-Prime Pair for RSA

The function below, recommended in \[[11](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0011)\], provides a solution to generate a pair of integers, *p* and *q*, that are very likely to be primes, to be used in RSA. It makes use of a hash function, a DRBG, and Miller-Rabin primality test. The inputs are the bit-length of the modulus (i.e. 2048, 3072, 4092, etc.) and the public exponent.

**Note**. The algorithm above may fail in finding a pair of probably primes.

***Minimum number of iterations***

When Miller-Rabin test is used, the accuracy (i.e. the probability that a number is erroneously declared probably-prime) depends on the number of iterations and the bit-length of the integer to be tested. The NIST recommends that the minimum number of iterations is of 40.

### 16.3.4 Generation of Provable Primes

#### 16.3.4.1 Shawe-Taylor Algorithm

Shaw-Taylor proposed an efficient algorithm to generate strong primes \[[12](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0012)\]. When the algorithm succeeds (it may fail to generate a prime), the generated number is guaranteed to be a true prime. Shawe-Taylor’s algorithm is recommended by the NIST for generating provable primes to be used in cryptographic algorithms (precisely, DH, MQV, and RSA) \[[11](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0011)\]. Shawe-Taylor’s algorithm is a recursive function, which takes a seed and a bit-length of the prime to be generated, and it provides the following outputs: a status, which indicates if a prime has been found or not, a provable prime (if any), and a counter (i.e. the number of tries before finding a prime). To make it easy to understand the principle of Shawe-Taylor’s function, assume that all the calls are successful. Shawe-Taylor’s function proceeds as follows:

*   Let  <math alttext="upper R e q upper L e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>q</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R e q upper L e n](images/c16_584.png) denote the bit-length of the prime to generate.
*   First case:  <math alttext="upper R e q upper L e n less-than 33" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>q</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>33</mn></mrow></math> ![upper R e q upper L e n less-than 33](images/c16_585.png):
    
    There is a single call to the function, which performs as follows: a random integer *c* is generated and its primality is tested using the trial division primality test (see [Section 16.3.2.1.1](#c16.xhtml#c16-sec-04008)). Then, an output, which depends on the primality test, is returned.
    
*   Second case:  <math alttext="33 upper R e q upper L e n Baseline 62" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>33</mn><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>q</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mn>62</mn></mrow></math> ![33 upper R e q upper L e n Baseline 62](images/c16_586.png):
    
    There are two calls to the function, which generate two primes. That is, the function is called with a requested bit-length of  <math alttext="upper R e q upper L e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>q</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper R e q upper L e n](images/c16_587.png), which is greater than 32. Then, the function is recursively called with a requested bit-length of  <math alttext="upper R e q upper L e n slash 2 plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>q</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper R e q upper L e n slash 2 plus 1](images/c16_588.png), which is less than 33, and it returns a prime (if any), denoted  <math alttext="c 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![c 0](images/c16_589.png).Then, an integer  <math alttext="2 asterisk t asterisk c 0 plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 asterisk t asterisk c 0 plus 1](images/c16_590.png) is generated. The value of *t* is chosen such that *c* is guaranteed to be less than  <math alttext="2 Superscript upper R e q upper L e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>q</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript upper R e q upper L e n](images/c16_591.png). Finally, the primality of *c* is tested using Pocklington-Lehmer primality test and an output is returned.

#### 16.3.4.2 Generation of Provable-Prime Pair for DH and MQV

The recommended method, for generating a pair of provable primes *p* and *q* to be used as FFC domain parameters is composed of three steps:

1.  Phase 1: generate a random number, denoted  <math alttext="upper F i r s t upper S e e d" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> ![upper F i r s t upper S e e d](images/c16_669.png), which is then used to generate a prime.
2.  Phase 2: use Shawe-Taylor’s algorithm to generate two primes *q* and  <math alttext="p 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![p 0](images/c16_670.png). The latter shall be of the half bit-length of prime *p*.
3.  Phase 3: use primes *q* and  <math alttext="p 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![p 0](images/c16_671.png) to compute  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 2 asterisk StartFraction x Over 2 asterisk q asterisk p 0 EndFraction asterisk p 0 right-parenthesis asterisk q plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><mfrac><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>\*</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 2 asterisk StartFraction x Over 2 asterisk q asterisk p 0 EndFraction asterisk p 0 right-parenthesis asterisk q plus 1](images/c16_672.png), where *x* is a random number in range  <math alttext="left-bracket 2 Superscript upper L e n Super Subscript p Superscript minus 1 Baseline comma 2 Superscript upper L e n Super Subscript p Superscript Baseline right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 2 Superscript upper L e n Super Subscript p Superscript minus 1 Baseline comma 2 Superscript upper L e n Super Subscript p Superscript Baseline right-bracket](images/c16_673.png). Recall that in FFC domain parameters, prime *q* divides  <math alttext="p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p minus 1](images/c16_674.png). The primality of the computed *p* is confirmed using Pocklington-Lehmer primality test.

#### 16.3.4.3 Generation of Provable-Prime Pair for RSA

To generate a prime pair that fulfills the RSA requirements, two calls to a function that generate a single prime are performed. The algorithm may fail in generating a pair of RSA primes. The public exponent *e* is assumed to be known before trying to generate primes *p* and *q*; and the modulus bit-length  <math alttext="n upper L e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![n upper L e n](images/c16_722.png) is assumed to be valid.

The function *Generate\_Provable\_RSA\_Prime* generates one prime of a bit-length of *L* in two steps:

1.  Phase 1: Generate a prime  <math alttext="p 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![p 0](images/c16_742.png) using Shawe-Taylor’s algorithm.  <math alttext="p 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![p 0](images/c16_743.png) is of the bit-length of  <math alttext="upper L slash 2 plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper L slash 2 plus 1](images/c16_744.png).
2.  Phase 2: compute a random integer  <math alttext="x" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> ![x](images/c16_745.png) in the interval  <math alttext="left-bracket StartRoot 2 EndRoot asterisk 2 Superscript p upper L e n minus 1 Baseline comma 2 Superscript p upper L e n Baseline minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt><mo>\*</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>p</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>p</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket StartRoot 2 EndRoot asterisk 2 Superscript p upper L e n minus 1 Baseline comma 2 Superscript p upper L e n Baseline minus 1 right-bracket](images/c16_746.png) and compute *t* using *x* and  <math alttext="p 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![p 0](images/c16_747.png); then, using the Pocklington-Lehmer test, check if  <math alttext="p equals 2 asterisk t asterisk p 0 plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>\*</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p equals 2 asterisk t asterisk p 0 plus 1](images/c16_748.png) is a prime.

**Note**. The algorithm above may fail to find a prime that fulfills the RSA domain parameter requirements.

## 16.4 Exercises and Problems

***Exercise 16.1***

Let *X* be a one-character random variable that takes its values in a set composed of 26 uppercase Latin letters, 10 decimal digits, and 8 special characters. Let  <math alttext="p r Subscript c Baseline comma p r Subscript v comma Baseline p r Subscript d comma Baseline" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow></msub><mi>p</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ![p r Subscript c Baseline comma p r Subscript v comma Baseline p r Subscript d comma Baseline](images/c16_788.png) and  <math alttext="p r Subscript s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![p r Subscript s](images/c16_789.png) denote the probability of selection of a consonant, a vowel, a digit, and a special character, respectively.

What is the entropy of random variable *X* assuming that  <math alttext="upper P r Subscript c Baseline equals 2 upper P r Subscript v Baseline equals 4 upper P r Subscript d Baseline equals 10 upper P r Subscript s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript c Baseline equals 2 upper P r Subscript v Baseline equals 4 upper P r Subscript d Baseline equals 10 upper P r Subscript s](images/c16_790.png)?

Consider a function *F* that generates an output of one decimal digit and the observed sequence is  <math alttext="StartSet 1 comma 2 comma 7 comma 0 comma 4 comma 6 comma 3 comma 5 comma 9 comma 8 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 1 comma 2 comma 7 comma 0 comma 4 comma 6 comma 3 comma 5 comma 9 comma 8 EndSet](images/c16_791.png), which repeats indefinitely. 2.  Consider an LCG with parameters  <math alttext="m equals 255" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>255</mn></mrow></math> ![m equals 255](images/c16_798.png),  <math alttext="a equals 25" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow></math> ![a equals 25](images/c16_799.png), and  <math alttext="b equals 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow></math> ![b equals 16](images/c16_800.png). What do you observe if  <math alttext="upper X 0 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 0 equals 0](images/c16_801.png) or if  <math alttext="upper X 0 equals 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 0 equals 4](images/c16_802.png)?

***Exercise 16.5***

How many prime numbers of a bit-length of 1024 are there?

***Problem 16.1***

How can an attacker, who knew five successive random numbers generated by a linear congruential generator, break such an LCG (i.e. he/she can find the LCG parameters)?

***Problem 16.2***

What is the category (i.e. safe prime and strong prime) of primes generated by the function Shawe\_Taylor\_Provable\_Prime? Use the pseudocode of the function in [Section 16.3.4.1](#c16.xhtml#c16-sec-03012).

***Problem 16.3***

By the prime number theorem, we know that the probability of an integer  <math alttext="z element-of left-bracket 2 comma upper N right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![z element-of left-bracket 2 comma upper N right-bracket](images/c16_807.png) to be prime is  <math alttext="StartFraction 1 Over l n left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![StartFraction 1 Over l n left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis EndFraction](images/c16_808.png). Consider *m* RSA public-keys, with moduli of at most  <math alttext="2 Superscript 2048" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>2048</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 2048](images/c16_809.png); and all used primes are no greater than  <math alttext="2 Superscript 1024" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>1024</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 1024](images/c16_810.png).

1.  Assume that all used primes are generated by a truly PRNG (pseudorandom number generator). Then, estimate the probability that there exist, at least, two RSA keys, out of the *m* known keys, that have a prime factor in common.
2.  Assume that you know 100 million public-keys generated using the same PRNG Π; and you find out that 1000 moduli share a common prime factor. What can you conclude?

### 16.4.2 Solutions to Exercises and Problems

***Exercise 16.1***

Let *X* be a one-character random variable that takes its values in a set composed of 26 uppercase Latin letters (20 consonants and 6 vowels), 10 decimal digits, and 8 special characters. All the 20 consonants have the same selection probability, and the same applies to vowels, digits, and special characters. Therefore,

 <math alttext="20 upper P r Subscript c Baseline plus 6 upper P r Subscript v Baseline plus 10 upper P r Subscript d Baseline plus 8 upper P r Subscript s Baseline equals 1 period" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>20</mn><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>.</mo></math> ![20 upper P r Subscript c Baseline plus 6 upper P r Subscript v Baseline plus 10 upper P r Subscript d Baseline plus 8 upper P r Subscript s Baseline equals 1 period](images/c16_811.png)

If we assume that  <math alttext="upper P r Subscript c Baseline equals 2 upper P r Subscript v Baseline equals 4 upper P r Subscript d Baseline equals 10 upper P r Subscript s" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript c Baseline equals 2 upper P r Subscript v Baseline equals 4 upper P r Subscript d Baseline equals 10 upper P r Subscript s](images/c16_812.png), then:

 <math alttext="upper P r Subscript c Baseline left-parenthesis 20 plus six-halves plus StartFraction 10 Over 4 EndFraction plus eight-tenths right-parenthesis equals upper P r Subscript c Baseline left-parenthesis 26.3 right-parenthesis equals 1 upper P r Subscript c Baseline equals 0.038" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>6</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>8</mn><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>26.3</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.038</mn></mrow></math> ![upper P r Subscript c Baseline left-parenthesis 20 plus six-halves plus StartFraction 10 Over 4 EndFraction plus eight-tenths right-parenthesis equals upper P r Subscript c Baseline left-parenthesis 26.3 right-parenthesis equals 1 upper P r Subscript c Baseline equals 0.038](images/c16_813.png)

The entropy of random variable *X* is:

 <math alttext="upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals minus sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript 46 Endscripts left-parenthesis p Subscript i Baseline asterisk l o g 2 left-parenthesis p Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>46</mn></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>\*</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mstyle></mrow></math> ![upper H left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals minus sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript 46 Endscripts left-parenthesis p Subscript i Baseline asterisk l o g 2 left-parenthesis p Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c16_814.png)

***Exercise 16.2***

The function *F*, which generates a cyclic sequence of  <math alttext="StartSet 1 comma 2 comma 7 comma 0 comma 4 comma 6 comma 3 comma 5 comma 9 comma 8 EndSet comma" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 1 comma 2 comma 7 comma 0 comma 4 comma 6 comma 3 comma 5 comma 9 comma 8 EndSet comma](images/c16_819.png) fulfills the first condition of PRNG, i.e. the outputs are independent and identically distributed. However, it does not fulfill the property of unpredictability, because the output can be easily predicted, when the first period is known. Therefore, *F* is not appropriate to be used in cryptographic applications.

***Exercise 16.3***

1.  Consider an LCG with parameters  <math alttext="m equals 256" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>256</mn></mrow></math> ![m equals 256](images/c16_820.png),  <math alttext="a equals 25" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow></math> ![a equals 25](images/c16_821.png), and  <math alttext="b equals 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow></math> ![b equals 16](images/c16_822.png). Below are the longest sequences generated, depending on the initial value of the seed  <math alttext="upper X 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper X 0](images/c16_823.png): 
    *   –  <math alttext="upper X 0 equals 255" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>255</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 0 equals 255](images/c16_824.png) results in a longest sequence of 32 numbers: {255, 247, 47, 167, 95, 87, 143, 7, 191, 183, 239, 103, 31, 23, 79, 199, 127, 119, 175, 39, 223, 215, 15, 135, 63, 55, 111, 231, 159, 151, 207, 71}
    *   –  <math alttext="upper X 0 equals 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 0 equals 2](images/c16_825.png) results in a longest sequence of four numbers: {2, 66, 130, 194}
    *   –  <math alttext="upper X 0 equals 6" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 0 equals 6](images/c16_826.png) results in a longest sequence of eight numbers: {6, 166, 70, 230, 134, 38, 198, 102}
    *   –  <math alttext="upper X 0 equals 10" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 0 equals 10](images/c16_827.png): results in a longest sequence of a single number:  <math alttext="StartSet 10 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math> ![StartSet 10 EndSet](images/c16_828.png), i.e. no new number can be generated.
    *   –  <math alttext="upper X 0 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 0 equals 0](images/c16_829.png): results in a longest sequence of 16 numbers: {0, 16, 160, 176, 64, 80, 224, 240, 128, 144, 32, 48, 192, 208, 96, 112}.
2.  Consider an LCG with parameters  <math alttext="m equals 255" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>255</mn></mrow></math> ![m equals 255](images/c16_830.png),  <math alttext="a equals 25" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow></math> ![a equals 25](images/c16_831.png), and  <math alttext="c equals 16" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow></math> ![c equals 16](images/c16_832.png). What do you observe if  <math alttext="upper X 0 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 0 equals 0](images/c16_833.png)? 
    *   – When  <math alttext="upper X 0 equals 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 0 equals 0](images/c16_834.png), the sequence that repeats is {16, 161, 216, 61, 11, 36, 151, 221, 186, 76, 131, 231, 181, 206, 66, 136, 101, 246, 46, 146, 96, 121, 236, 51}. We observe that the number 0 is not generated. In this case, 0 is called a tail, which does not repeat in the cycle of the PRNG.
    *   – When  <math alttext="upper X 0 equals 4" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ![upper X 0 equals 4](images/c16_835.png), the sequence which repeats is {116, 111, 241, 176, 81, 1, 41, 21, 31, 26, 156, 91, 251, 171, 211, 191, 201, 196, 71, 6, 166, 86, 126, 106}. We observe that the number 4 is not generated. In this case, 4 is a tail.

         <math alttext="19 equals 2 Superscript 1 Baseline asterisk 9 plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>19</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>\*</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![19 equals 2 Superscript 1 Baseline asterisk 9 plus 1](images/c16_838.png).     *   Step 4: (2^(nd) iteration)

          4.3  <math alttext="upper V equals 17 Superscript 9 Baseline m o d Baseline 19 equals 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow><mn>9</mn></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>19</mn><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V equals 17 Superscript 9 Baseline m o d Baseline 19 equals 1](images/c16_848.png)

    *   Step 4: (2^(nd) iteration)
        
          4.1 Let  <math alttext="a equals 76" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>76</mn></mrow></math> ![a equals 76](images/c16_859.png) be the selected random value
        
          4.3  <math alttext="upper V equals 76 Superscript 7 Baseline m o d Baseline 113 equals 71" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>76</mn></mrow><mn>7</mn></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>71</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V equals 76 Superscript 7 Baseline m o d Baseline 113 equals 71](images/c16_860.png)
        
          4.5.1 *j=1*:  <math alttext="upper V equals 71 squared m o d Baseline 113 equals 69" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>71</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>69</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V equals 71 squared m o d Baseline 113 equals 69](images/c16_861.png)
        
          4.5.1 *j=2*:  <math alttext="upper V equals 69 squared m o d Baseline 113 equals 15" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>69</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V equals 69 squared m o d Baseline 113 equals 15](images/c16_862.png)
        
          4.5.1 *j=3*:  <math alttext="upper V equals 15 squared m o d Baseline 113 equals 112 equals 113 minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>112</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>113</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V equals 15 squared m o d Baseline 113 equals 112 equals 113 minus 1](images/c16_863.png) ⇒ *go to* 4.1
        
    *   Step 4: (3^(rd) iteration)
        
          4.1 Let  <math alttext="a equals 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ![a equals 2](images/c16_864.png) be the selected random value
        
          4.3  <math alttext="upper V equals 2 Superscript 7 Baseline m o d Baseline 113 equals 15" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>7</mn></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V equals 2 Superscript 7 Baseline m o d Baseline 113 equals 15](images/c16_865.png)
        
          4.5.1 *j=1*:  <math alttext="upper V equals 15 squared m o d Baseline 113 equals 112 equals 113 minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>113</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>112</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>113</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![upper V equals 15 squared m o d Baseline 113 equals 112 equals 113 minus 1](images/c16_866.png) ⇒ *go to* 4.1
        
    *   Step 5: return “Probably prime.”
        
        Comment: the result is correct, because 113 is a true prime.
        

***Exercise 16.5***

By the Prime number theorem (Theorem 16.1), there roughly exist  <math alttext="n slash l n left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![n slash l n left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis](images/c16_867.png) prime numbers no greater than *n*. Therefore, there exist  <math alttext="2 Superscript 1024 Baseline slash ln left-parenthesis 2 Superscript 1024 Baseline right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>1024</mn></mrow></msup><mo>/</mo><mi>ln</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>1024</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 1024 Baseline slash ln left-parenthesis 2 Superscript 1024 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c16_868.png) prime numbers of bit-length of 1024 bits.  <math alttext="2 Superscript 1024 Baseline slash left-parenthesis 1024 asterisk l n left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals 2 Superscript 1014 Baseline slash l n left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis 10 Superscript 300" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>1024</mn></mrow></msup><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1024</mn><mo>\*</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>1014</mn></mrow></msup><mo>/</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>300</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![2 Superscript 1024 Baseline slash left-parenthesis 1024 asterisk l n left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals 2 Superscript 1014 Baseline slash l n left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis 10 Superscript 300](images/c16_869.png).

***Problem 16.1***

Recall that the *i* *^(th)* ,  <math alttext="i Baseline 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![i Baseline 1](images/c16_870.png), output of an LCG is defined by  <math alttext="upper X Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis a upper X Subscript i minus 1 Baseline plus b right-parenthesis m o d m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![upper X Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis a upper X Subscript i minus 1 Baseline plus b right-parenthesis m o d m](images/c16_871.png), where *a*, *b*, and *m* are the parameters of the LCG and  <math alttext="upper X 0" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![upper X 0](images/c16_872.png), the seed.

When an LCG is used for generating random numbers, the attacker only needs to know five successive outputs to disclose with certainty the LCG parameters and then predict the next outputs of the LCG. Let us take an example.

Assume that the attacker knows five successive outputs: 73, 42, 20, 50, and 55.

The attacker builds and solves the following 3-equation system:

 <math alttext="StartLayout Enlarged left-brace 1st Row 1st Column 42 left-parenthesis 73 a plus b right-parenthesis m o d m 2nd Column left-parenthesis a right-parenthesis 2nd Row 1st Column 20 left-parenthesis 42 a plus b right-parenthesis m o d m 2nd Column left-parenthesis b right-parenthesis 3rd Row 1st Column 50 left-parenthesis 20 a plus b right-parenthesis m o d m 2nd Column left-parenthesis c right-parenthesis EndLayout" display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mn>42</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>73</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi></mrow></mtd><mtd><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mn>20</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>42</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi></mrow></mtd><mtd><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mn>50</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>20</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>m</mi></mrow></mtd><mtd><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow></math> ![StartLayout Enlarged left-brace 1st Row 1st Column 42 left-parenthesis 73 a plus b right-parenthesis m o d m 2nd Column left-parenthesis a right-parenthesis 2nd Row 1st Column 20 left-parenthesis 42 a plus b right-parenthesis m o d m 2nd Column left-parenthesis b right-parenthesis 3rd Row 1st Column 50 left-parenthesis 20 a plus b right-parenthesis m o d m 2nd Column left-parenthesis c right-parenthesis EndLayout](images/c16_873.png)

First, eliminate parameter *b*:

Subtract equation (a) from (b) and obtain:  <math alttext="22 31 a m o d m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>22</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>31</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![22 31 a m o d m](images/c16_874.png) (d)

Subtract equation (c) from (b) and obtain:  <math alttext="negative 30 22 a m o d m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>30</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>22</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![negative 30 22 a m o d m](images/c16_875.png) (e)

Find the modulus *m*:

Multiply equation (d) by 22 and equation (e) by 31:

Equation (d) becomes:  <math alttext="22 asterisk 22 22 asterisk 31 a m o d m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>22</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>22</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>22</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>31</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![22 asterisk 22 22 asterisk 31 a m o d m](images/c16_876.png) (d’)

Equation (e) becomes:  <math alttext="31 asterisk left-parenthesis negative 30 right-parenthesis 31 asterisk 22 a m o d m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>31</mn><mo>\*</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>31</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>22</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![31 asterisk left-parenthesis negative 30 right-parenthesis 31 asterisk 22 a m o d m](images/c16_877.png) (e’)

Subtract (e’) from (d’), and obtain:  <math alttext="22 asterisk 22 plus 31 asterisk 30 equals 1414 0 m o d m" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>22</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>22</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>31</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1414</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![22 asterisk 22 plus 31 asterisk 30 equals 1414 0 m o d m](images/c16_878.png).

Hence, *m* divides  <math alttext="14 asterisk 101" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>14</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>101</mn></mrow></math> ![14 asterisk 101](images/c16_879.png). Therefore,  <math alttext="m equals StartSet 14 comma 101 comma 1414 EndSet" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>14</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>101</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1414</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ![m equals StartSet 14 comma 101 comma 1414 EndSet](images/c16_880.png). We discard  <math alttext="m equals 14" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn></mrow></math> ![m equals 14](images/c16_881.png), because the left part of the equations has values greater than 14. We need to check  <math alttext="m equals 101" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>101</mn></mrow></math> ![m equals 101](images/c16_882.png) and  <math alttext="m equals 1414" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1414</mn></mrow></math> ![m equals 1414](images/c16_883.png).

Find *a* using equation (a) when  <math alttext="m equals 101" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>101</mn></mrow></math> ![m equals 101](images/c16_884.png):

 <math alttext="a equals 22 asterisk 31 Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d Baseline 101 equals 22 asterisk 88 m o d Baseline 101 equals 17" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>22</mn><mtext>\*</mtext><msup><mrow><mn>31</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>101</mn><mo>=</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>22</mn><mtext>\*</mtext><mn>88</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>101</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn></mrow></math> ![a equals 22 asterisk 31 Superscript negative 1 Baseline m o d Baseline 101 equals 22 asterisk 88 m o d Baseline 101 equals 17](images/c16_885.png)

Finally, find *b* using equation (a):

 <math alttext="b left-parenthesis 42 minus left-parenthesis 73 asterisk 17 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis m o d Baseline 101 equals 13 period" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>42</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>73</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>17</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>101</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow><mo>.</mo></math> ![b left-parenthesis 42 minus left-parenthesis 73 asterisk 17 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis m o d Baseline 101 equals 13 period](images/c16_886.png)

Check using the fifth value:  <math alttext="17 asterisk 50 plus 13 m o d Baseline 101 equals 55" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>17</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>13</mn><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>101</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>55</mn></mrow></math> ![17 asterisk 50 plus 13 m o d Baseline 101 equals 55](images/c16_887.png).

If we take  <math alttext="m equals 1414" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1414</mn></mrow></math> ![m equals 1414](images/c16_888.png) and use the method above, the parameters *a* and *b* would be  <math alttext="a equals 360" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>360</mn></mrow></math> ![a equals 360](images/c16_889.png) and  <math alttext="b equals 720" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>720</mn></mrow></math> ![b equals 720](images/c16_890.png). These parameter values match the congruence system above. However, when we compute the next value, i.e.  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 50 asterisk 320 plus 760 right-parenthesis m o d Baseline 1414" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>\*</mo><mn>320</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>760</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>1414</mn></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 50 asterisk 320 plus 760 right-parenthesis m o d Baseline 1414](images/c16_891.png), the output would be 1116, which is different from the fifth known value, i.e. 55. Thus, the valid modulus is 101.

***Problem 16.2***

Recall that a prime *p* is a safe prime if it satisfies condition (a) below; and it is a strong prime, if it fulfills the following three conditions:

 <math alttext="p minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p minus 1](images/c16_892.png) has a large prime factor  <math alttext="p 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![p 1](images/c16_893.png) (a)

 <math alttext="p 1 minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p 1 minus 1](images/c16_894.png) has a large prime factor  <math alttext="p 3" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![p 3](images/c16_895.png) (b)

 <math alttext="p plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![p plus 1](images/c16_896.png) has a large prime factor  <math alttext="p 2" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> ![p 2](images/c16_897.png) (c)

Let *L* denote the requested bit-length. To generate primes for FFC- and IFC-based algorithms, the required bit-length *L* is too large that the prime generated by Shawe-Taylor’s algorithm is guaranteed to be large. Shawe-Taylor’s function is recursive. For example, to generate a prime of a bit length of  <math alttext="upper L equals 1024" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1024</mn></mrow></math> ![upper L equals 1024](images/c16_898.png), Shawe-Taylor’s function is called with the following bit-lengths:  <math alttext="upper L 1 equals 1024" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1024</mn></mrow></math> ![upper L 1 equals 1024](images/c16_899.png),  <math alttext="upper L 2 equals 1024 slash 2 plus 1 equals 513" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1024</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>513</mn></mrow></math> ![upper L 2 equals 1024 slash 2 plus 1 equals 513](images/c16_900.png),  <math alttext="upper L 3 equals 513 slash 2 plus 1 equals 258" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>513</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>258</mn></mrow></math> ![upper L 3 equals 513 slash 2 plus 1 equals 258](images/c16_901.png),  <math alttext="upper L 4 equals 258 slash 2 plus 1 equals 130" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>258</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>130</mn></mrow></math> ![upper L 4 equals 258 slash 2 plus 1 equals 130](images/c16_902.png),  <math alttext="upper L 5 equals 66" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>66</mn></mrow></math> ![upper L 5 equals 66](images/c16_903.png),  <math alttext="upper L 6 equals 34" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>34</mn></mrow></math> ![upper L 6 equals 34](images/c16_904.png), and  <math alttext="upper L 7 equals 18" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>7</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>18</mn></mrow></math> ![upper L 7 equals 18](images/c16_905.png).

Let  <math alttext="c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis](images/c16_906.png) denote the output of Shawe-Taylor’s function for a requested bit-length of *L*.  <math alttext="c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis](images/c16_907.png) is computed in step 15.2.4, as follows:  <math alttext="c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis Baseline equals 2 asterisk t Superscript left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis Baseline asterisk c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline plus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis Baseline equals 2 asterisk t Superscript left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis Baseline asterisk c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline plus 1](images/c16_908.png). Using Pocklington-Lehmer test, the output (i.e.  <math alttext="c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis](images/c16_909.png)) of each Shawe-Taylor’s function call is guaranteed to be a prime.

*   –  <math alttext="c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis Baseline minus 1 equals 2 asterisk t Superscript left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis Baseline asterisk c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis Baseline minus 1 equals 2 asterisk t Superscript left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis Baseline asterisk c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c16_910.png); thus,  <math alttext="c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis](images/c16_911.png) has a prime factor  <math alttext="c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c16_912.png). Thus, condition (a) is satisfied. Therefore,  <math alttext="c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis](images/c16_913.png) is a safe prime.
*   –  <math alttext="c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline negative 1 equals 2 asterisk t Superscript left-parenthesis upper L slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline asterisk c Superscript left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper L slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![c Superscript left-parenthesis upper L slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline negative 1 equals 2 asterisk t Superscript left-parenthesis upper L slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline asterisk c Superscript left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper L slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c16_914.png); thus,  <math alttext="c Superscript left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper L slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![c Superscript left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper L slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c16_915.png) has a prime factor  <math alttext="c Superscript left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper L slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![c Superscript left-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper L slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2 plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c16_916.png). Thus, condition (b) is satisfied.
*   – The third condition is much more complex to check; and it is not addressed here.

***Problem 16.3***

1.  By the prime number theorem, the number of primes, denoted *n*, in the interval  <math alttext="left-bracket 2 comma 2 Superscript 1024 Baseline minus 1 right-bracket" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>1024</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math> ![left-bracket 2 comma 2 Superscript 1024 Baseline minus 1 right-bracket](images/c16_917.png) is  <math alttext="n almost-equals StartFraction 2 Superscript 1024 Baseline Over l n left-parenthesis 2 Superscript 1024 Baseline right-parenthesis EndFraction equals StartFraction 2 Superscript 1024 Baseline Over 1024 asterisk l n left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis EndFraction StartFraction 2 Superscript 1024 Baseline Over 710 EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8776;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mfrac><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>1024</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>1024</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>1024</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>1024</mn><mo>\*</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mfrac><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>1024</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>710</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![n almost-equals StartFraction 2 Superscript 1024 Baseline Over l n left-parenthesis 2 Superscript 1024 Baseline right-parenthesis EndFraction equals StartFraction 2 Superscript 1024 Baseline Over 1024 asterisk l n left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis EndFraction StartFraction 2 Superscript 1024 Baseline Over 710 EndFraction](images/c16_918.png). To generate *m* RSA public-keys, a maximum of *2m* primes are required (because RSA modulus is a product of two primes). If among *2m* primes, two (or more) values are identical, then there exists at least two RSA keys that share a common prime factor. We randomly pick the first prime out of *n* primes. Then, when we randomly pick the second prime, there is a probability of  <math alttext="1 slash n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![1 slash n](images/c16_919.png) that the new prime is identical to the first one. Then, when we randomly pick the third prime, there is a probability of  <math alttext="2 slash n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![2 slash n](images/c16_920.png) that the new prime is identical to one of the two old primes, etc. Finally, when we randomly pick the last prime, there is a probability of  <math alttext="left-parenthesis 2 m minus 1 right-parenthesis slash n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>/</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis 2 m minus 1 right-parenthesis slash n](images/c16_921.png) that the new prime is identical to one of the  <math alttext="2 m minus 1" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![2 m minus 1](images/c16_922.png) old primes. Therefore, the probability to have at least two identical primes is  <math alttext="upper P equals StartFraction 1 Over n EndFraction plus StartFraction 2 Over n EndFraction plus ellipsis period plus StartFraction 2 m minus 1 Over n EndFraction equals StartFraction left-parenthesis 2 m minus 1 plus 1 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis 2 m minus 1 right-parenthesis Over n EndFraction StartFraction 2 asterisk m squared Over n EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>\*</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mrow></math> ![upper P equals StartFraction 1 Over n EndFraction plus StartFraction 2 Over n EndFraction plus ellipsis period plus StartFraction 2 m minus 1 Over n EndFraction equals StartFraction left-parenthesis 2 m minus 1 plus 1 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis 2 m minus 1 right-parenthesis Over n EndFraction StartFraction 2 asterisk m squared Over n EndFraction](images/c16_923.png). Notice that we can obtain the same result by applying the formula of birthday paradox, which states that the probability of a collision among *k* integers randomly picked out of a set of *L* integers is  <math alttext="upper P left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext></mrow></math> ![upper P left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis](images/c16_924.png)  <math alttext="almost-equals StartFraction k squared Over 2 upper L EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo>&#8776;</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![almost-equals StartFraction k squared Over 2 upper L EndFraction](images/c16_925.png).
2.  By the answer to the first question, if a truly PRNG is used to generate 100 million RSA public-keys, the probability to have two RSA keys that share a common prime factor is  <math alttext="StartStartFraction left-parenthesis 10 Superscript 8 Baseline right-parenthesis squared OverOver StartFraction 2 Superscript 1024 Baseline Over 710 EndFraction EndEndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mn>8</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>1024</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>710</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![StartStartFraction left-parenthesis 10 Superscript 8 Baseline right-parenthesis squared OverOver StartFraction 2 Superscript 1024 Baseline Over 710 EndFraction EndEndFraction](images/c16_926.png), which is by far smaller than that provided by PRNG Π, which is of  <math alttext="StartFraction 10 cubed Over 10 Superscript 8 Baseline EndFraction" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mn>8</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ![StartFraction 10 cubed Over 10 Superscript 8 Baseline EndFraction](images/c16_927.png). Therefore, we can conclude that PRNG Π is faulty; it lacks randomness.

## Notes

1.  **1** *Deterministic* means that given a seed value, the generator will always produce the same output sequence.
2.  [**2**](#c16.xhtml#rc16-note-0002) As far as we know, the NIST has not yet recommended CSPRNGs, which are mainly based on stream ciphers.
3.  [**3**](#c16.xhtml#rc16-note-0003) CMAC is an improvement of CBC-MAC. Some weaknesses of CBC-MAC have been addressed in literature; and CBC-MAC is not considered secure, under specific usage conditions (see some problems discussed in [Chapter 9](#c09.xhtml)).
4.  [**4**](#c16.xhtml#rc16-note-0004) In this chapter, user requesting DRBG outputs is referred to as “consuming application”.
5.  [**5**](#c16.xhtml#rc16-note-0005) The required minimum entropy bit-length is the same than that of the highest security strength that can be provided.
6.  [**6**](#c16.xhtml#rc16-note-0006)  <math alttext="upper B equals left-parenthesis 2 Superscript upper C t r upper L e n Baseline minus 4 right-parenthesis asterisk upper B l k upper L e n" display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>\*</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ![upper B equals left-parenthesis 2 Superscript upper C t r upper L e n Baseline minus 4 right-parenthesis asterisk upper B l k upper L e n](images/c16_928.png); *CtrLen* is a building parameter of CTR-DRBGs.
7.  [**7**](#c16.xhtml#rc16-note-0007) See Problem 3.19 for proof of Lemma 16.1.
